subtopic: MOTION BY MR. NICKLE FOR ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY TO REFRAIN FROM
speechtext:
I will deal with the resolution in a suitable manner before I have finished, if my good friend will give me the opportunity. In Canada titles have largely been distributed amongst partisan politicians, railway promoters and exploiters, big business financiers, and rich nabobs and plutocrats. Just look over the list of recipients throughout the Dominion. It embraces men of uncanny reputation, little capacity, no record of achievement

except it be in the line of the bedevilment of public affairs, and certainly no accomplishment of an altruistic or patriotic character. I should think that a considerable number of them possess a sufficient sense of humour and idea of the fitness of things to imitate the promised example of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in this House last session, and to hurl their decorations into a bonfire if they could only do it stealthily and by night. Especially in this critical and menacing time of social unrest and reconstruction, those responsible for the administration of public affairs, responsible for the impressions that are being . stamped upon the restless, uneasy, jealous, if you will, exacting, and in view of all the past, perhaps pardonably resentful minds of a portion of the populace with its varied factions, must exercise a determined and insistent care that the idea of social justice and equality and opportunities for all shall be the resounding and dominant key-note of every act of legislation. There must be no attempt to set up a cheap, tinsel aristocracy in this young western nation. The idea of conferring social distinctions must be effaced,-nay, the plant that has been inserted in our soil must be rooted out and destroyed. But if the mistake is to be persisted in, which God forbid, the authorities better have a care that the distribution shall embrace the dignity of toil, the genuine aristocracy of industrial and mechanical achievement, and the simple, modest dignity of living, exemplified in the life of Cincinnatus, the old Roman hero. The class of men who have received social distinction, compared with those worthy citizens who have been overlooked, has caused an offensive odour in the nostrils of decent-going reflecting Canadians.
I should not think that hereditary titles would have any defenders whatever, and especially not in this House. Surely we do not want to plant in this country an hereditary aristocracy. We see the evils of hereditary aristocracy in the Old Land, and 1 cannot conceive of anything that has done more for the enslavement or degradation of the people than an hereditary aristocracy -the " gentry " as they call them ovei there. When I visited the Old Land upon several occasions I used to sit with the drivers in the busses and used to take every opportunity to draw out the workingman, to get his viewpoint on the question of the aristocracy or the gentry, and I want to confess with most profound disappointment the experiences that I had. The men over there, the lower classes as they cal'.

thorn-and it is a term that I dislike very much to use-the- greater portion of them seemed to have an admiration and a love for the gentry, they seemed actually to wish to be patronized, to be spat upon as it were. The result of all these distinctions throughout, the old world has been the degradation of the human race, and we should not think for an instant of following the old European nations in maintaining such class or caste distinctions. Let us teach the race, the dignity of manhood, and the equality of opportunity. All men, says the American Declaration of Independence written by TLumas Jefferson, are born equal. I think if you took that pronouncement literally it is probably not true. All men are not born with equal endowments; but I suppose what Jefferson intended to say was that all men are born with equal opportunity and should before the law be regarded as possessing equal advantages. If we in this country were to allow the introduction of an hereditary aristocracy we would be striking a blow at citizenship, and a blow at the progress of our own country. We cannot afford to allow such a plant to flourish in Canada. It is doubtful if even the very limited number of possessors in the Dominion of these hereditary titles, after they have, like children, amused themselves with the tinselled toy, would not rejoice to be in a position to gracefully toss it into the Laurier bonfire. It must not be perpetuated in the life of the nation.
I was going to ask, what dignity would be added to Gladstone if he had accepted a knighthood or a peerage? What better would the human race have thought of him to-day, or of John Bright and Cobden, those great industrial and economic liberators? Why the very acceptance of a title, in my judgment, would degrade such names as theirs. Would Edmund Burke, perhaps the greatest orator the world has ever produced, be as dear in name to us all if he had been translated to a dukedom or a peerage? Coming to our own country, take Edward Blake, the great commoner, who sat in this House, I believe for twenty or twenty-five years, devoting that magnificent ability of his to the service of the nation, and Alexander Mackenzie, as honest a man as ever trod the soil. Would they be ennobled, would they be greater men had they been knighted in the old days? I think, Mr. Speaker, that every thoughtful Canadian respects and loves the names of the Hon. Edward Blake and the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie. Yes, and you might add to theirs the name of that other great
Canadian William Lyon Mackenzie, to whom this country owes far more than the average citizen dreams of to-day. Because the people have short memories and I find that we Canadians make a great mistake when we fail to study the lives of the men that served us. Think of William Lyon Mackenzie, who fought for representative and responsible government, who fought against the old Family Compact, a man with Scotch blood in his veins who refused to be domineered, who stood nobly -for right and principle, and was willing even to place his life and liberty in jeopardy by entering upon rebellion against what he considered the wrongs of the day. Perhaps he was mistaken-I would certainly in the light of history and of developments not like to venture the idea that he was mistaken-but he took the consequences of his act, and it is to William Lyon Mackenzie that this Dominion owes so much at the present day. Driven from his own country he became an exile in a foreign land for years, often going for days if not weeks without food. He was without friends, without a man to say a kind word to him. Then an amnesty was declared, and he returned to Canada and died a broken old man. Would it endear the name of William Lyon Mackenzie to the people of Canada if a knighthood or any other honour that a human potentate might control had been conferred upon him? Not at all. The memory and name of William Lyon Mackenzie to those who have studied and appreciated his life and work will live as long as Canadian history lives. These are the men who are entitled to honour, the men who spurned anything that kings could do for them, the men who fought for principle and placed their lives in jeopardy. This nation little dreams how much it owes to men like William Lyon Mackenzie and as a Canadian I would deeply deplore the conference of any title that a human potentate could confer.
' Let me add: How myriads of hearts the world over, whether descendants of Auld Scotia or not, would have burned with regret had their beloved bard who wrote:
The man o' independent mind;
He's king- o' men for a' that.
Been de-dignified-if I may be allowed to coin a' word for the occasion-by allowing any human potentate to transform him into "a belted knight"?
You cannot elevate men of the type of Burns or of Thomas Carlyle, the great Scottish philosopher and historian, by con-

ferring titular distinction on them. The other day I noticed in the newspaper an extract from one of Carlyle's essays, and I am going to take a minute or two to read this great literature that it may be embalmed in the pages of Hansard. It is entitled "Two men I honour":
Two men I honour, and no third. First, the toil-worn craftsman that with earth-made implement laboriously conquers the earth and makes her man's. Venerable to me is the hard hand-crooked, coarse ; wherein notwithstanding* lies a cunning virtue, indefeasibly royal, as of the sceptre of this planet. Venerable, too, is the rugged face, all weather-tanned, besoiied, with its rude intelligence; for it is the face of a man living manlike. Oh, but the more venerable for thy rudeness, and even because we must pity as well as love thee! Hardly-entreated brother! For us was thy back so bent, for us wore thy straight limbs and fingers so deformed; thou wert our conscript, on whom the lot fell, and fighting our battles wert so marred. For in there, too, lay a God-created form, but it was not to be unfolded ; encrusted must it stand with the thick adhesions and defacements of labour, and thy body was not to know freedom. Vet toil on, toil on: thou art in thy duty, be out of it w'ho may; thou toilest for the altogether, for daily bread.
A second man I honour, and still more highly him who is seen toiling for the spiritually indispensable ; not daily bread, but the bread of life. Is not he, too, in his duty; endeavouring towards inward harmony; revealing this, by act or by word, through all his outward endeavours, be they high or low? Highest of all when his outward and his inward endeavour are one, when we can name him artist, not earthly craftsman only, but inspired thinker, who with heaven-made implement conquers heaven for us. If the poor and humble toil that we have food, must not the high and glorious toil for him in return, that he have light, have guidance, freedom, immortality? These two, in all their degrees, I honour; all else is chaff and dust, which let the wind blow whither it listeth.
Unspeakably touching is it, however, when I find both dignities united; and he that must toil outwardly for the lowest of men's wants is also toiling inwardly for the highest. Sub-limer in this world know I nothing than a peasant saint, could such now anywhere be met with. Such a one will take thee back to Nazareth itself; thou wilt see the splendour of heaven spring forth from the humblest depths of earth, like a light shining in great darkness. .
I want to ask, Mr. Speaker, if you do not think it was really worth while to read to the hon. members such a classic?
I will continue my imperfect and perhaps somewhat rambling remarks with this amendment to my hon friend's motion. I move, seconded by Mr. Cruise:
That the following words he inserted after the word "message" at the beginning of the third line:
" May take measures to ensure the extinction of the hereditary titles at present in existence in the Dominion at the death of the present possessors thereof and "

Some people would probably be disposed to cut off these titles at once. I would not have any objections if it could be done easily and would not raise a constitutional issue in the old.land, but it might be considered a more graceful act to allow the four or five Canadians who possess hereditary titles to die in peace. The hand of time will remove them and with their removal let us earnestly trust that we shall see the last of this miserable institution in the Dominion.
You cannot make a man greater than he is, and no higher keynote should be sounded than that of service, because the Master Himself said that " Whosoever would be chiefest among you shall be servant of all." If men get the idea that the greatest honour is to serve their country and their fellow-men they will not think so much of having temporary titles conferred upon them. And at this time, after the sacrifices our noble sons and the country generally have made, this Parliament should hold up the highest ideals to the men who have served their country so faithfully and so well, and if we maintain those ideals, Mr. Speaker, I am quite sure that our nation shall measure up to the standard that God intended it should reach.

I am absolutely opposed to the amendment by the hon. member for Springfield, who first of all says that one of the objections to titular honours is that they have been incorrectly handed out.
That is an apology which logically and argumentatively means that if they had been correctly handed out, they might be excused. That of course, is absolutely a violation of the principle underlying the abolition of honours. We do not want titular honours in this country; that is the point. The people do not. want them and we, being representatives of the people, are here for the purpose of voting them out of existence.
The member for Kingston is labouring, I think, under a misapprehension. He has two exceptions in his resolution, one with respect to military and naval officers and

the other with respect to judges and administrative officers.
Mr. MtOKLE: No. Just read the resolution.
Mr. .BURNHAM: The resolution says:
It being always understood that this humble prayer has no reference to professional or vocational appellations.
"'Colonel" is not called by the King a title. A man may be John Smith, Colonel commanding the Buffs of Kingston; he is not called " Colonel " at all; that is simply a way of designating him. You do not call a judge "Judge So-and-So;" that is only our Canadian vulgarity. He is Mr. iSmith, Judge of the Supreme Court-or wherever he may be.

Mr. Justice Smith, of
the Supreme Cburt-there is no titular honour in that case. So that this resolution might convey a misunderstanding and might lead to very serious results, if what I say is true. It may be presumed that the member for Kingston knows all about it, and that the words of his resolution must refer to something else-that the exception could only be a title such as a knighthood, or something of that kind. But it mixes the resolution all up; there is nothing definite or clear about it. Away with the whole thing. These gentlemen may bring in their resolutions or their amendments, but the people will be satisfied with neither. They do not want any compromise. If this House has not learned what the feeling of the country is, they will probably learn it at the next election-and they will learn that titular honours must be abolished in this country. It will come; we need not hurry ourselves; we need not fret ourselves unduly. We need not have any serious apprehension about it. We need not deal in an hour-long historical review of it, for God knows the whole thing is founded on democracy, not on the aristocratic pretensions on which the historical review is given. Nor is there any necessity for arguing from analogy. 'The simple 'fundamental principle of social distinctions is abominable and must be done away with. The people are desirous of destroying it, and, that being the case, let us have no more of it.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. NICKLE FOR ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY TO REFRAIN FROM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thoroughly and heartily agree with all that the member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) said this afternoon, and likewise with what was said by the member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson). It is not
necessary, as the member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) said a moment ago, that this question should be laboured further. My own opinion is that titles are not good for the country, and I have very grave doubts whether they are good for the persons upon whom .they are bestowed.
I think we would be far better without them. Our country would be better; the people would be better. It is indisputable that the vast majority of the people are bitterly opposed to titles being handed out.
But I did not rise so much to discuss that question as to say a word or two with regard to the position I took last year when this matter came before the House. At that time much fault was found with me because I was the first to introduce this matter in the early part of a session a good number of years ago, and my position last year was regarded by my friends as very extraordinary. It was in May last-those days in May were dark and dreary days- that the question of titles came up in this House-and we had the very extraordinary spectacle of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), upon a private member's resolution, suddenly taking to himself the right to say that that resolution should be treated as a want of confidence motion, and that did the resolution carry he would feel it essential that his Government should resign and go to the country. To me that was most extraordinary. A general election in May of 1918 would have been an absolute calamity. I was returned on the question of conscription; I was given a mandate from my constituents to see that conscription was carried out. At the time that that resolution was brought up conscription had not been carried out, and had I, with others who felt just as strongly on the subject as I did, voted against the Government on this subject, and had the Government been defeated, it would have meant a general elec-tiitn; it would have meant the disruption of business; it would have meant that I was not carrying out the mandate of my constituents. Therefore, it was, Sir, that I absolutely sunk my own convictions, that I let them go where they might, and that I stood by tbe Government, with the result that you know of.
To-day I feel just as strongly on this question as I ever did. To-day I believe that the abolishing of titles is true Liberalism. May I say, if it is of any import to anybody, that I differed from my chief and from others of my party on one question, and on one question only? That question was conscription. I consider it to-day, how-

ever much others may differ from me, to have been good Liberalism on my part to support that policy. But my political faith and tenets are the same that I have always held. In these great days of reconstruction my Liberalism is, perhaps, better than it ever was, because I believe the country needs it. But as I say, when this matter was up last session, I sunk my convictions and voted as I did to support a Government in war .time. I do not consider that such is necessary to-day, but I do consider that so far as this country is concerned we must come to one form of government, and one only, and that is the party system.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. NICKLE FOR ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY TO REFRAIN FROM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to discuss upon its merits the subject of this resolution, because, having accepted the honour of knighthood, I should feel myself at a certain disadvantage in doing so. If I spoke in favour of titles, it might be considered that my view was biased or prejudiced. If on the other hand I spoke against titles, I might be regarded as ungenerous" to those having greater merits than myself. My intention to-night is to indicate the present position of this matter so far as concerns action by the Dominion Government and by the Imperial Government, and to suggest a certain disposition of the resolution and of the amendment to the resolution, which disposition will, I trust, be of advantage to the Government in giving the matter further consideration and will meet with the views of the House.
While this is a question upon which there is room for difference of opinion, a question upon which members may hot agree, it is not in any respect a party question. Both Liberal and Conservative Governments have in the past recommended to His Majesty the bestowal of knighthood and other titular distinctions, and adherents of both political parties have been the recipients of such distinctions. I think I am correct in stating that every Prime Minister of Canada, with the exception of one, has accepted knighthood. That exception was the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, who, I feel certain, must have been offered the distinction, although I do not know that that is so. I think, therefore, that in all probability he declined the honour; but

with that exception, as I have stated, all the Prime Ministers of Canada, Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir John Abbott, Sir John Thompson, Sir Mackenzie Bowell, Sir Charles Tupper and Sir Wilfrid Laurier, accepted the honour of knighthood at the hand of their Sovereign. In addition to these distinguished men in the public life of Canada, many other members of Government were similarly honoured. I recall amongst others Sir Richard Cartwright, Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, Sir George Ross, Sir James Whitney, in Ontario, and Sir Lomer Gouin in Quebec. I mention only outstanding men, for the purpose of showing that the acceptance of titular distinctions in this country has not been confined to any one party and that therefore the question is not in any respect a party one. The late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, while Prime Minister of Canada in 1902 had an Order in Council passed and forwarded to the Imperial Government, in which were these observations:
In Canada a Government similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom has been established, and the advisers of His Majesty in Canada are the proper advisers of His Majesty for every kind of reward bestowed upon His Majesty's subjects for services performed within the legal and constitutional sphere of Canadian jurisdiction. His Majesty's ministers in Canada are acquainted with the standing in the community of the persons upon whom it may be proposed to confer honours, and of the character of the services for which these honours are the reward, and to have those rewards bestowed by His Majesty on the advice of those who are but imperfectly informed as to the estimation in which the recipients are held, or of the character of the services for which the honours are bestowed, is practically an invasion of the right of local self-government.
This report was based upon the recommendation of the Prime Minister of that date, the late Eight Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. The Order in Council goes on as follows:
The Committee of the Privy Council concurring in the report of the Prime Minister, recommend that the same be presented to His Majesty's Principal Secretary of State for the Colonies, and respectfully ask that the Royal Instructions be modified to the effect that the same rules which apply for the exercise of the Royal Prerogative in granting honours and titular distinctions to subjects of the King in the United Kingdom be made likewise to apply to all recommendations by the Governor General for the exercise of the Prerogative to the King's subjects in the Colonies, and that all such recommendations by the Governor General to the Sovereign in such matters be made upon the advice of his responsible ministers.
I am quoting this in order to show the progressive steps which have been made in this matter of the bestowal of titles down

to the present time. In a despatch dated 23rd April, 1902, and signed by Right Hon. Joseph Chamberlain, then Colonial Secretary, the following observation was made with reference to the Order in Council which I read and which was submitted to the Imperial Government as I stated:
In dealing with this subject I have been desirous of meeting the views of your ministers so far as possible, but as the responsibility for making recommendations to the Sovereign in regard to appointments to an Imperial Order such as that of Saint Michael and Saint George rests with the Secretary of State and not with your ministers, it is his duty to obtain the best advice he can and he must be the sole judge of what is the best advice.
That was the position taken by the late Liberal Government and by the Colonial Secretary in 1902. The matter rested there until the present leader of the Government took it up shortly before the last session of Parliament. The present Prime "Minister took the most advanced ground that had been taken up to that time with respect to this matter of titles; and in order that his views may be upon Hansard for the consideration of the committee to which I propose asking this House to have this matter referred, and for the information of the members of the House, 1 hope I may be pardoned if I quote from the Order in Council which was passed at the instance of the Prime Minister on the 25th March, 1918. After submitting that the subject demands consideration and attention and that the bestowal or honours is a matter of concern to the whole community and has a direct relation to the orderly government of the State, and after referring to the Order in Council from which I have read, passed on the 19th February, 1902, the present Prime Minister proceeds:
The Prime Minister is firmly of opinion that the creation or continuance of hereditary titles in Canada is entirely incompatible with the ideals of democracy as they have developed in this country and that the time has arrived when their heritable quality or effect should be abolished in this Dominion.
The hereditary peerage as an institution can find neither historic justification nor scope for usefulness in a state structure and social tradition such as that which now exists in Canada. Consequently the effect of such an institution in this country is merely, on the one hand, to confer and to perpetuate arbitrarily for some members of the community a titular distinction or status of honour, and1 on the other hand to imply a position of special though ill-defined privilege to which there is not and) cannot be assigned any obligation or function in the activities of Canadian national life. Honours conferred directly upon deserving recipients under appropriate conditions and by proper authority will be respected by the community; but a
decoration or titular distinction which is attached to the holder not in recognition of his own services, but merely from incidence of birth, and which is invested with no special or public duties or responsibilities, will inevitably arouse in this country a sense of utter incongruity and a feeling of keen impatience.
That was the advanced ground with respect to hereditary titles taken by the Prime Minister of this country in March, 1918. The following recommendations were made in the Order in Council:
1.	No honour or titular distinction (saving those granted in recognition of military service during the present war or ordinarily bestowed by the Sovereign proprio motu) shall be conferred upon a subject of His Majesty ordinarily resident in Canada except with the approval or upon the advice of the Prime Minister of Canada.
2.	The Government of the United Kingdom shall exercise the same authority as heretofore in determining the character and number of titles or honours to be allocated to Canada from time to time.
3.	No hereditary title of honour shall hereafter be conferred upon a subject of His Majesty ordinarily resident in Canada.
4.	Appropriate action shall be taken, whether by legislation or otherwise, to provide that after a prescribed period no title of honour held by a subject of His Majesty now or hereafter ordinarily resident in Canada shall be recognized as having hereditary effect.
I am tracing the development of the principle of responsibility of government with respect to this matter of titles, and I think it will be clear from this Order in Council, which was passed before the last session of Parliament, that the present Prime Minister took at that time the most advanced ground which had been taken upon this subject.
The House will recall what I said a few minutes ago as to the reply which had been made by the Right Hon. Joseph Chamberlain, Colonial Secretary, in 1902. He stated in effect that the Colonial Secretary was responsible for the recommendation to His Majesty. Since the last session of the House, dispatches have been received from the Imperial Government with respect to this Order in Council, which was laid before the Imperial Government shortly after its adoption in March, 1918, and to which reply had not been received from the Imperial Government at the time of the debate in the House last session. The present position of the Imperial Government with respect to this Order in Council is as follows. They accept without question recommendations Nos. 1 and 2, reading as follows:
1.	No honour or titular distinction (saving those granted in recognition of military service d-uring the present war or ordinarily bestowed

by the Sovereign proprio motu) shall he conferred upon a subject of His Majesty ordinarily resident in Canada except with the approval or upon the advice of the Prime Minister of Canada.
2.	The Government of the United Kingdom shall exercise the same authority as heretofore in determining the character and number of titles or honours to be allocated to Canada from time to time.
That means that no honour or titular distinction, with the above exceptions, shall be conferred upon a subject of His Majesty ordinarily resident in Canada except with the approval and upon the advice of the Prime Minister of Canada, and that the Government of the United Kingdom will exercise the same authority as heretofore in determining the character and number of titles or honours to be allocated to Canada from time to time.
Now I come to the third recommendation of the Order in Council of March 25, 1918, which reads as follows:
3.	No hereditary title of honour shall hereafter be conferred upon a subject of His Majesty ordinarily resident in Canada.
The reply from the Imperial Government to that was as follows:
His Majesty will not hereafter be advised to confer any hereditary honour upon a subject of His Majesty ordinarily resident in Canada, save on the formal recommendation of the Prime Minister of 'Canada.
Now, the Prime Minister of Canada has recommended, and his recommendation is embodied in the report of the 25th March, 1918, that he is firmly of opinion that the creation or continuance of hereditary titles in Canada is entirely incompatible with the ideals of democracy as they have developed in this country, and that the time has arrived when their hereditary quality or effect should he abolished. That means that, as a result of the action taken by the Government of Canada upon the recommendation of the Prime Minister in March, 1918, hereditary titles, so * far as the future is concerned, are abolished.
The fourth recommendation of the Order in Council is as follows:
4.	Appropriate action shall he taken, whether by legislation or otherwise, to provide that after a prescribed period no title of honour held by a subject of His Majesty now or hereafter ordinarily resident in Canada shall be recognized as having hereditary effect.
The reply to that was:
This presents many difficulties that would require very careful consideration. Action for the present remains in abeyance.
There is one further step which has been taken since the last session of the House.

It will be recalled that the Order in Council expressly excepts honours or titular distinctions granted in recognition of military service during the present war. The word " military" there would include "naval." With regard to knighthoods to those who have rendered military or naval service during the present war, the Army Council, through the Et. Hon. Secretary of State, has advised that no grant of the distinction of knighthood to any Canadian military officer shall be recommended without previous reference to the Prime Minister of Canada.
I have shown the attitude taken by the late Liberal Government in 1902 with respect to titles, and the reply to their representations by the Imperial authorities. 1 have also shown the action taken by the present Government of Canada, and the reply to the Imperial authorities of to-day. 1 do not in any way contrast the two positions. I think the differing attitudes are entirely due to the advance in public opinion with respect to the subject under consideration; but I desire to emphasize the fact that the matter is not a party question. It was advanced considerably in 1902, when the Liberal Government took the view that the principles of responsible Government should apply to the bestowal of honours in Canada. It was further advanced in 1918 when the present Government, on the recommendation of the Prime Minister, took a position which has resulted in the abolition of hereditary titles so far as concerns the future and in the acquiescence of the Imperial authorities in the principle that titular honours and distinctions, with the exceptions which I have mentioned, should be granted only upon the recommendation of the Prime Minister or the Government of Canada. Eeference was made this afternoon to the debate of last session, and owing to the absence of the Prime Minister I feel that I must say a few words with regard to the position which then existed when he moved an amendment to the amendment of the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Eichardson). The Order in Council had been passed and forwarded to the Imperial authorities, and no answer had yet been received from them. Jin his speech on May 21, 1918, the Prime Minister used these words. I quote from page 2343 of Hansard:
There is another consideration which I submit to the House and it is this: His Majesty's Government have to take into consideration, of course, the relation of this proposal not only to Canada hut to all the dominions of the Empire and they have asked us, in a respectful and courteous way, that the whole subject be brought under discussion during the coming summer when certain of the Canadian minis-

ters are to visit the United Kingdom. It seems to me that as the Order in Council has been passed and has been communicated to His Majesty's Government, the delay that would ensue between this session and the next session, when the matter might be taken up again, if desired, ought not to stand in the way of our acceding to that respectful request. I do not imagine that the public interest will suffer by any action taken before Parliament shall assemble again. The Government of this country will then be in a position to announce to Parliament the result, of their conference with the Imperial authorities in respect to this subject. So, I would suggest to my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Richardson)-and I hope he will accept this suggestion-that the subamendment which I have proposed be accepted.
The Government, on the recommendation of the Prime (Minister, had taken certain advanced action with regard to this subject. The report embodying its recommendations was before the Imperial authorities, and request had been made that the matter should be allowed to stand in abeyance until they should have an opportunity of considering it in the summer. I am confident in my own mind that it was on account of the situation which existed with respect to the Order in Council and the Imperial authorities that the Prime Minister felt as he did with regard to the importance of the amendment to the amendment which he proposed.
There	is	just one other	matter to	which I	desire	to refer. It
has not been mentioned in this House but reference has been made to it outside. Owing to the fact that the Prime Minister and some of his colleagues were obliged to go overseas in May last at the urgent solicitation of the Imperial authorities, and at a time of great national danger-in fact, the most critical period of the entire war-the session of Parliament came to an end earlier than would have been the case in the ordinary course. Some three distinctions were granted after Parliament rose. I have taken the opportunity to inquire respecting these distinctions, and I find that they had all been recommended months before Parliament rose, and that in the case of one of them the person who was to receive the honour had requested that so far as he was concerned it should be deferred in order to allow some one else to obtain an honour of which it was thought he was' worthy. The point I desire to make with regard to that transaction is that the recommendations had all been made and were before the Imperial authorities before this House rose. I have explained the situation as it exists and the action taken by the Imperial Government since last session. The Order in Council of March, 93	-
1918, makes exception in cases of honours and decorations granted in recognition of military service during the war, and I have already explained that honours and titular distinctions can be conferred, under the existing regulations, upon subjects of His Majesty ordinarily resident in Canada only with the approval or upon the advice of the Prime Minister.
Now, Mr. Speaker, since the last session of the House and down to the present time, the Government has been confronted with a situation respecting honours which I should like to describe to the House. We have in the military forces overseas many who have distinguished themselves and who would be eligible for honours and recognition, subject to what I have said as to the honour of knighthood; and there are in Canada many officers of the Canadian Expeditionary Forces who have rendered distinguished service in Canada. These men were all desirous to go overseas and felt keenly disappointed at not being permitted to do so. Their duty lay in Canada, however, and many of'them have rendered service of a most meritorious character. With regard to those who have served overseas in the military or naval forces there is a well-established channel of recommendation for honours, namely, the Army Council, upon the report and recommendation of the Commander-in-Chief. No difficulty arises in connection with those. But with regard to officers in Canada who have served in Canada and have not been able to go overseas, the initiative had to be taken here, if taken at all. In addition to members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force and those who have remained in Canada, and in addition to those who have served in the navy overseas and those who have served in Canada, there is a very large number of civilian workers in the Red Cross, the Patriotic Fund, Munitions and many other services; and if Canada followed the same course as is adopted in Great Britain and, I think, the Overseas Dominions, there would be a considerable number of civilian workers in England and in Canada to be recommended for honours or decorations.
Now the Government last autumn, in connection with the New Year's list, decided that the granting of titular honours and decorations in respect of civilian services, viz.: the Red Cross, the Patriotic Fund, munitions, etc., should be suspended, with the object of having the whole question given the fullest consideration. I have explained to the House that a very large list



indeed was involved in Canada and in London. On January 3, 1919, we received a cablegram from the Prime Minister to which I especially desire to draw the attention of the House, because the suggestion is contained in it that I propose to make here this evening for the disposition of this motion. That cable stated that the opinion of the Prime Minister and his colleagues was that for the present there should be no deviation from the decision of the Canadian Government to suspend the granting of titular honours and decorations in respect of civilian services, viz.: Red Cross, Patriotic Fund, munitions, matrons, nursing sisters, and others.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. NICKLE FOR ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY TO REFRAIN FROM
speechtext:
What was the cablegram that brought forth this answer?
.Sir THOMAS WHITE: This cablegram came from the Prime Minister. The point that I am making is that the Prime Minister, having taken the ground that he had taken in March, 1918, in the House of Commons during the debate on this subject, had suggested the action which I propose to the House should be taken with regard to this motion. The same cablegram suggested for the consideration of council whether the question of civil honours for war ser

 vices, as well as the whole question of honours, might be referred to a committee of the House of Commons for consideration and report. It was not intended that the duty of personal selection should be referred to the committee, but merely the general question of the principle to be adopted. On January 18, the Government informed the Prime Minister by cable of the decision of council that no honours gr decorations should be recommended for the present for those engaged in military and naval service in Canada, and that action, in this respect should be deferred until after the whole question of honours is referred to a committee of the House of Commons for consideration and report. Just let me summarize the position. The Order in Council of March, 1918, excepted from its provisions honours or distinctions granted to those engaged in military and naval services in Canada. A well established channel of communications exists in the War Council, upon the recommendation of the Commander-in-Chief, as to those who have served Overseas, but with regard to those who have served in Canada in the naval or military service the initiative in recommendation is to be taken here. With respect to that latter class, and with respect to civilian workers both here [Sir Thomas White.!
and overseas, the Government view was that no recommendation should be made until the matter had been referred to a select committee of the House for consideration and report.
Now, with respect to civilian services I quote an extract from a letter of the Prime Minister:
If it proposed to recognize the work of this character as justifying a recommendation for honours by reason of service, the list will be a very large one, but not by any means so large as to do full justice to 'all those who have unselfishly and devotedly given their best effort to such service. The selection will be not only arbitrary but invidious, as it will not be possible to obtain that full knowledge of relative service which will be essential. On the other hand if such service is not to be recognized by Canada, then Canadians will feel a sense of injustice and discrimination. For example, scores of Canadian men and women have worked unselfishly and devotedly in London during the past four years. Persons giving no greater or perhaps less worthy service in the British Red Cross, or in the Red Cross of any Dominion, are recognized by the bestowal of suitable honours with the consent of their governments, while the Canadians receive no recognitions Whatever. There will undoubtedly be much bitterness among those who will feel themselves thus placed under an unjust discrimination. Possibly it may be considered desirable to include work in the Red Cross as work in the military service. If so we cannot very well shut out service in the Y.M.C.A. or similar organizations.
The Prime Minister there touches upon the essential difficulties of this situation, which, in my view, render it highly important that a committee of this House should consider the whole question deliberately and maturely with a view of making a report to this House before the end of the session in order that it may be fully discussed, and, if approved, adopted here.
During the war thousands of people have rendered services involving the utmost selfsacrifice and devotion. If, on the one hand recognition is to be given, the difficulty is to choose those-and there will necessarily have to be a limited number-who should be recognized. There would, of course, be grave room for dissatisfaction on the part of the others if they were not also recognized. That is one aspect of the matter. On the other hand, you have the undoubted fact, as pointed out by the Prime Minister, that there are in London, and it is within the knowledge of the House that there are in Canada, hundreds of men and women who have worked most devotedly in civilian services connected with the war, and it is put forward by many that if in other parts of the Empire and in Great

Britain there is recognition of such services, and no recognition of like services in Canada, there will be a feeling of injustice and discrimination. It seems to me therefore that the matter, as it relates to those who have served most devotedly the interests of the State, should receive the most deliberate consideration on the part of the House. I am going somewhat into detail, Mr. Speaker, because I desire to show the House how many questions are really involved in this matter. It is not only a question of abolishing hereditary titles, of abolishing titular distinctions such as knighthood, but it involves the question of what, if any, recognition shall be given to those who served in the Canadian Expeditionary Force Overseas and the Canadian Expeditionary Force in Canada only; in the Naval Service Overseas, and the Naval Service in Canada; and that multitude of civilan workers who gave so freely of their time, both here and in London, in connection with the various funds-Patriotic, Red Cross and others,-which I have mentioned.
Mr. DEVLIN; Will the Government accept the advice of the committee to he formed and be governed by it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. NICKLE FOR ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY TO REFRAIN FROM
speechtext: When I come to move my amendment I shall ask that the committee give careful consideration to this question and report back, and it will he for the House to adopt, modify, or reject the recommendations of the committee. The attitude of this House will, without question, be of the utmost value for the guidance of the Government. I do not wish to anticipate what the judgment of the committee and the House will be, but it is the sincere desire of the Prime Minister and of the Government to get the deliberate, reasoned opinion of this House upon all the questions I have mentioned this evening.

It may he, as my hon. friend says, that the House is willing to give that decision which will prevent any distinctions being conferred upon those who have served in the naval and military forces overseas and in Canada, but I did not understand that the resolution went so far last year. Possibly I am in error. As
93i
to the present resolution, it may have in contemplation the wiping out of all distinctions to members of the .Canadian Expeditionary Force.
A letter from Sir George Perley, dated 10th February, states that there is a strong feeling that civilians who have been doing war work for Canada overseas should be treated in the same way as those who have done it for Great Britain and other parts of the Empire. The following is quoted from his letter:-
A great many men and women have worked devotedly here, some of them throughout the whole length of the war, on various kinds of useful service. They did not do this for the purpose of obtaining recognition but when they see civilians from everywhere else in the King's Dominions getting honours it certainly seems strange that Canada should be the only part of the Empire which declines to make any recommendation for awards.
Now, I have pointed out the difficulty of making selections without injustice, and I propose, Mr. Speaker, to ask the House to adopt the suggestion of the Prime Minister, ijamely, that the whole question of honours be referred to a Special Committee of this House for consideration and report. It is not the desire of the Government to shelve this resolution, but to have a representative committee-whose names I shall give the House-take this matter up at once, consider it carefully and maturely, and report to this House with respect to the bestowal of various titular distinctions upon civilians, upon members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force who have served overseas and upon those who have remained in Canada, and also upon civilian war workers. I do not know what the view of the House is. It may he, as my hon. friend has said, that it is opposed to any decorations, let ' alone titular distinctions, for members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, but I should doubt if that is the opinion of all the hon. members.

I misunderstood. It seems to me that the Committee would have to consider the question of hereditary titles. The Prime Minister in the Order in Council of March 25, 1918, recommended the abolition of all such titles for the future, and that recommendation has been concurred in by the Imperial authorities. Then there is the further question whether the title of knighthood should be conferred either for public service or for naval or military service. If the Committee is oJ

the opinion that titular distinctions may be conferred upon members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, there is the question whether such distinctions should be limited to those who have served overseas, or whether they should also be awarded to those who have served with distinction in Canada. There is the further question whether there shall be lesser titular distinctions to civilians in future, and whether decorations or other distinctions shall be given to civilian war workers of the several classes which I have mentioned.
Since Confederation, titles have been bestowed in Canada for public service, and since the war many distinctions and decorations have been bestowed for distinguished naval and military service. Shall those be continued? It seems to me that the whole subject is so important, having regard especially to those who have served in the war, that the House of Commons might very well delegate it to a select and representative committee to consider and report as promptly as possible to this House for its conclusion upon the subject. I therefore beg to move the following amendment to the amendment; seconded by Mr. J. D. Reid:
That all the words after " that " in the first line of the amendment be struck out and the following substituted therefor: '* a Special Committee of this House be appointed for the purpose of considering- and reporting upon the question of the conferring of honours, titular distinctions and decorations upon subjects of His Majesty ordinarily resident in Canada, including those who have performed overseas, in Canada or elsewhere, Naval, Military and civilian service in connection with the war. The said Committee to consist of the following members: Messrs. Nickle, Green, Peck, Buchanan, Clark (Red Deer), Thomson (Qu'Appelle), Cowan, Richardson, Whidden, Nesbitt, Middle-bro, Pardee, Cockshutt, Murphy, McCoig, Ross, Ames, McMaster, Lemieux, Robb, Fielding, Elkin, Copp, McCurdy, Sinclair (Guysborough)."

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. NICKLE FOR ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY TO REFRAIN FROM
speechtext:
I am very glad that this is not a party question. I have had the honour to collaborate with the member from Kingston (Mr. W. F. Nickle) in this matter, and I am glad to know that we shall be able to express our views with regard to it irrespective of whether we sit upon your right, Mr. Speaker, or upon your left.
The present position has been gone into somewhat fully by the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White), but I do not altogether agree with some of the things that he has said. I am in thorough accord with him when he says that an advance has been made, but I am not satisfied with the present position. I am not satisfied, for in-

stance, that the Government of the United Kingdom shall exercise the same authority as heretofore in determining the character and number of titles or honours to be allocated to Canada from time to time. The number of knighthoods or the number of titles-I trust there will be none-to be granted to Canada should be a matter on which the Canadian people alone shall have the right to speak. I am not satisfied that the Government in London should say to us in Canada: "We shall decide how many knights or lesser luminaries you are to have in Canada."
Then, the Acting Prime Minister has said that no hereditary title or honour shall hereafter be conferred upon a subject of His Majesty ordinarily resident in Canada. That was the advanced ground taken by this House and by the Government-I wish to be absolutely fair-last session. But the authorities in London have made this addition to it: "Save on the recommendation of the Prime Minister of Canada." It is true that the Prime Minister of Canada has said that in his opinion it is unwise to have hereditary titles in Canada; all honour to him for taking that view. But always in the history of nations there is an 9 p.m. ebb and flow of advance, and it is possible that sometimes in the ebb of public opinion from what I consider right and just-in a temporary time of reaction-we might have a Prime Minister who would suggest that there should be hereditary titles in Canada. I see no reason why the Government at "London should not accept the general statement referred to-accept it holus bolus without any reservation whatsoever.
The fourth recommendation in the Order in Council of last session was that appropriate action shall be taken, whether by legislation or otherwise, to provide that after a prescribed period no title or honour held by a subject of His Majesty now or hereafter ordinarily resident in Canada shall be recognized as having hereditary effect. Well, what was the answer of the Government in London? The King's advisers in London gave what I might call a Scotch verdict; they merely suspended the matter- said that it might remain in abeyance. If this House, by an almost unanimous, if not an unanimous, vote accepts the resolution proposed by the member for Kingston, that will be a very good answer to these gentlemen and will impress them with the fact that the Canadian people not only do not want hereditary titles, but do not want titles of any kind. In saying this I hope

that no one will think I am dealing in personalities, for I am not. There are those in this country and in this House whose amiability of character and whose democratic bearing shine out, perhaps, with greater brilliance on a background of knighthood.
I am discussing this matter, therefore, merely as a question of principle.
Are we to have recognition of military service by way of title or distinction? I refer the House, as concerns this part of the discussion, to the following remarks of the member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) last year:
It occurs to me that if there ever was a time when a subject such as this should be brought before the House, it is a time when the nation is at war, because if war teaches us anything it teaches us this: that when the country is at 'war and when the war is over, you are likely to have the greatest crop, if I might use that term, of decorations and recognitions that are from time to time seen.
That reason is even stronger to-night than it was when the member for Kingston uttered these words, because we have the word of the Acting Prime Minister that a very avalanche of titles and distinctions is hanging over the Canadian people and may descend upon us at any time.

speechtext:
The Acting Prime Minister read a letter from Sir George Perley stating that civilian war workers in Great Britain, English folk, have received honours in large numbers from their Government, and that keen disappointment prevails among Canadians in London because similar showers-shall I say of blessing?- have not descended upon them. I wonder how far that is a correct statement of the fact. Some Canadian civilian war workers in London may be dissatisfied because knighthood has not been conferred upon them, but I doubt whether that is the sentiment of the majority of them. Although waves of titles have practically inundated the people of the British Isles, the matter of the conferring of titles is a subject there of keen criticism, aye, even of ridicule. I remember reading in a British paper not long since that people in England expressed the fear that under the administration of Mr. Lloyd George Great Britain was becoming one of the most decorated of nations. Certainly a great body of public opinion in England wants none of that sort of thing. Honours have been suspended since last session. Instead of putting them in a suspense account,'" may I implore this House to wipe them off the books altogether?
What is the position in regard to titles of all those who fought in the war, either on the field or at home? The vast majority of soldiers and sailors at the front or on the sea and the vast -majority of workers in Canada worked faithfully and well, and -if you are going to distribute titles or honours -among -them you must count them not in tens or hundreds, -but in tens of thousands. You cannot do that-. Well, then, let it be the proud record of this country that their people fought in the war not' for knighthoods, not for titular distinctions, but from sense of duty, love of -country, and regard for the principles for which the Allies contended.
Why are the Canadian people against -titles? First of all, I think it is because -titles are not in keeping with the very-air of British North America.
We in this country are a democratic folk, and the giving of titles is an attack on democracy. What is a title? A title means that a man, by the appellation which is used in regard to him from day to day, is set apart from the great body of the Canadian people, and that is a mistake. We must insist in this country upon the three great principles of democracy. A good many years ago when I was a student in Paris,
I was struck by the three great words which are found on the front of every public building, " Liberte," egalite, fraternite," and I believe the giving of knighthoods and titular distinctions in this country is an attack against the great principles oi equality and fraternity. In this connection let me just repeat what the Prime Minister said last year in regard to hereditary titles:
Consequently the effect of such an institution in this country is merely, on the one hand, to confer and to perpetuate arbitrarily for some members of the community a titular distinction or status of honour, and on the other -hand to imply a position of special though ill-defined privilege to which there is not and cannot be assigned any obligation or function in the activities of Canadian national life.
Exactly the same principle applies to knighthoods and titular distinctions of that sort. I had not the privilege of being present at the debate this afternoon, but I understand the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) raised the question that the resolution as introduced by the hon. member for Kingston did not do away with the right of the Government to confer knighthood on persons who happened to be judges or to enjoy rank in the army. That is not the intention of the resolution, nor do I think it is a proper interpretation to place upon it. The resolution says:

It being- always understood that this humble prayer has no reference to professional or vocational appellations conferred in respect to commissions issued by Your Majesty to persons in Military or Naval Services of Canada or to persons engaged in the administration of Justce of the Dominion.
All that that means is that a judge will continue to be called a judge; that a colonel will continue to be called a colonel; that g, captain will continue to be called captain; it does not in any way infer that a special privilege is to be given to judges or officers in the army to receive titles of knighthood. I ask this: In the present state of feeling in Canada and throughout the world, when those whom we have been prone to call the working classes, those who work with their hands as well as with their brains, feel that there is unfairness in society, when they feel that society as at present organized does not give them a fair deal, is it wise to perpetuate such things as knighthoods? I do not think so, I believe we shall in this country tend to carry on the nation's business more harmoniously, and therefore more efficiently, if we apply in fullest measure those principles of democracy-liberty, equality and fraternity, if we make it known to all the world that the Canadian people do not wish to have titular distinctions or knighthoods; that they are all prepared to adopt an almost Quaker like simplicity in the appellation by which one or another is called. As regards the form of this question, I think it would be well for this House to vote for the resolution. I do not say that there might not be room for a committee to consider the best way in which the expression of the House might be put into effect, but it would possibly be as well for this House to put itself clearly and emphatically on record as being opposed to titles of any sort in Canada.
Mr. MlIiOHAEL CLARK (Red Deer): Mr. Speaker, I shall with great pleasure vote for the amendment to the amendment which has been moved by the Acting Prime Minister ('Sir Thomas White), if for no other reason than this, that I think we should all want to be just a little careful in these times of world impulse before we do anything in haste to prevent this generation from doing honour to itself by possibly doing something to honour those who have borne themselves in the late war in Europe beyond their fellows in the matter of earning human praise.
I rise, however, not with the purpose of saying anything more than that upon the parliamentary position of this question, but to indicate that I am not quite at one with 
what I understood to be the attitude of my democratic, radical, iconoclastic and, I might almost say,Bolshevistic, friends from Springfield and Kingston. I am sure I shall have the whole-hearted approval of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) when, in attempting to secure a right ground of thought upon this question, I have recourse to any teaching that is to be found in Holy Writ. My hon. friend knows very well the writings of the Apostle Peter, and he will remember that Peter was very severe upon a certain class of individuals about whom he said: "Presumptuous are they, self-willed, they are not afraid to speak evil of dignities." St. Jude, as my hon. friend will also well remember, in speaking of a very bad class of people who were set forth as an example, suffering the vengfeance of hell-fire, said: "They despise dominion, and speak evil of dignities." I do not think that I need quote at greater length from that Book to show that my hon. friends to whom I have referred were, to say the least of it, treading on very dangerous ground this afternoon. That is* especially true of the hon. member for Springfield who, I think, actually went to the barnyard for comparisons of the peacock and turkey to those people who are referred to in Scripture as "dignities." Still, on the whole, seeking distinction from any one is not a Scriptural virtue.
I am bound to think honestly on this question, and there is a higher authority than even St. Jude or St. Peter, who said: "How can ye believe if ye receive honour one from another?"
' That is the acid test on this question, and it is a test to which I am sure my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Richardson) would not submit himself, because it would debar a man from seeking any honour from his fellows whatsoever; he would have to stand always in the naked dignity of his manhood,-I am not sure, after listening to my hon. friend this afternoon, whether he would even be allowed to dress himself as a modern man does. What the hon. gentleman objected to, indeed, was not that a man wore dress, but that he wore gold braid. Well, Sir, that is not a very democratic distinction after all. The acid test is whether we seek honours from one another at all. My hon. friend from Springfield does not mind a little honour occasionally. There was a band of journalists went to Europe last summer, and he was picked out with others from among his fellow journalists, and had the distinction conferred upon him of being sent over

to represent the journalism of Canada in the Old Country, where he conferred and confabulated with no less a person than Mr. Lloyd George. He had also the distinction of going over to the battlefields and parading with a few peacock feathers of his own.
The Quakers are the only people, I think, who have attempted to live literally up to the last Scripture which I have quoted; so they always refer to one another by their simple names. A Quaker is never anything more than William Simpson or John Richardson, but my hon. friend from Kingston and my hon. friend from Springfield pander with the rest of us to this inherent vice in human nature by which almost every human being seeks in some way or another-and I am not at all sure that he seeks it viciously-to raise himself above his fellows. I say that I am not at all sure that this is a vicious desire, because a fair amount of emulation in human life is a part of strong individualism, and I think there is a great deal of very frothy democracy going around in these days. But - the Quaker is consistent; he neither calls his friend Mister nor Esquire. As there are no Quakers that I know of in this House, every member of this House has failed to submit himself successfully to the acid test, because we all get our typists to address our letters with either "Mr." in front or "Esq." behind.
The churches themselves have failed in regard to the teaching of the Founder, because they, too, have their dignitaries their bishops, their moderators, and their presidents, showing that there is in human nature this tendency to be reaching out to higher positions. In society this same thing prevails. Mr. Speaker, it has not been without its uses in the case of hereditary aristocracies. I am the last man in the world to have any brief to speak for the British aristocracy, but I will say this: In the best hereditary families of Britain, there are traditions which have come down through generations-yes, through centur-20s-which have on the whole ennobled the public life of Britain. I say that as a Radical. Take the traditions of the house of Cavendish. The late distinguished head of that house, the late Duke of Devonshire,
. the uncle of his present Excellency, was a remarkable example of the best traditions of his family. Three times, without hesitation, in public life when the call of principle and of duty came to him, he left the party with which he had been associated, and on each occasion, such was his tremendous influence and such the clearness of his thinking, that he took the majority of his fellow-countrymen along with him. I hold that that ability to act independently, that ability to strike out for himself, was an adornment of British public life in his person, and an adornment which we should do well to reproduce some of, at least, in this Country; because if there is anything that has been a curse to Canada, it has been straightlaced party politics, and I say that without any hesitation. The traditions of the English nobility-and the very word teaches us that we should not too lightly speak even of dignities, because it is not wrong to be noble-their traditions in this war have been of the very highest. The sons of British peers, and the brothers of British peers, and British peers themselves, have stood in the trenches and fought in the trenches with the humblest Tommies from London and from the agricultural fields of Britain. They have done that of their own free will; they were volunteers. As officers at the very beginning of the war they left all the appurtenances of their rank and titles, all their wealth, their stately homes, their lordly fields and parks, to go and face the foe, and to taste of death	in	no	small	numbers for	thecause of freedom and democracy. I think	it	is	only	right, when	our
friends proclaim that this is a democratic country, that we should recognize these truly democratic qualities of character in those who were born in a very different sphere of society from that in which we had birth.
' Then, I do not know that it is altogether an evil thing in society to have something to aspire to. I am not looking up now much myself; I am coming to the time of life when I would rather control my spirit and teach it by looking down. But I am not sure that my friends from Kingston (Mr. Nickle) and Springfield (Mr. Richardson) are on safe ground when they say that the people of Canada are so very strongly with them on this question. We have titles in Canada that I have not heard any kick about in this House. There is the title of senator for example. Does anybody tell me that that is a title which is generally spurned in Canada? Sir, if one of the Senate's, functions is to be looked up to, it certainly fulfils that function to the letter because members of the House of Commons in large number are often looking up there with longing eyes. So that when we examine this thing, we see that there is an inherent quality in human nature which

recognizes, after all, that in human society, as in human nature itself, equality is sought in vain.
One of my two friends, the leading exponents of democracy in this House to-day
I think it was the hon. member for Kingston-described German autocracy, against which we have been fighting, as a state in which the few have the right to govern. Well, I do not quarrel with that; I think it would be a good definition of autocracy. But I should like to point out to my hon. friend that the few are not necessarily the titled few, and if Canada is to be a true democracy we must see to it that under democratic forms we do not allow ourselves to be governed by the few here-I was going to say, Mr. Speaker, even on such a subject as daylight saving. We must see to it, I repeat, that we do not allow ourselves to be governed by the few here. Government by the few is not necessarily government by the titled few, and if my friends will be radicals I will tell them what a radical is. A radical is a man who goes to the roots of things; he looks beneath the surface title to the real principles that prevail. If we accept .that title let us accept it in the fullest of its meaning. If this House of Commons is the representative of a democracy and does not believe in autocracy, then let us, in all our approaches to public questions, whatsoever their size, whatsoever their bearing, see to it that we " hew to the line, let the chips fall where they may." Let us see to it that on no occasion do we allow any influences of the few to control the many in this House, and through us to control the many in this country. Autocracy does not reside in titles, Mr. Speaker, but in power. Autocracy resided in power, and it is the power that men grasp for before they seek the title. The power is there in many cases before the title is conferred- the title is a mere external emblem of the power. Wealth is a form of power, and I say deliberately that the autocracy that is to be really feared in its operations upon the rank and file of the people, whether in this country or in the United States of America, is not an autocracy of titles but an autocracy of wealth. A man becomes a real lord, Sir, before he becomes a titular one, and for my part I cannot profess to get very excited about titles. We have heard a great deal about individual cases of titles in recent years and individual cases of lordship. What was the process by which the titles were attained? Some one makes a fortune overnight almost-a large fortune. He goes  '
to Britain and gets knighted, possibly finds his way into the British House of Lords and becomes, I suppose, an autocrat. But he was an autocrat by way of his millions before he was an autocrat through the peerage, and a real democrat would look into the state of the laws of his country to. find out how it is possible for a man to accumulate huge amounts of wealth in a very brief time, these huge amounts of wealth being the natural road to the mere surface decorations over which we have got so excited and spent the whole day talking about. My hon. friend from Kingston said that there was great unrest among the workmen of this country and he thought that that unrest was in some way traceable to the conferring of titles. Well, Sir, I scarcely think so. I do not think the workmen of this country are troubling themselves a very great deal about the inequalities of social distinction. I do not think the labouring men of this country, even where they have come from across the seas, have very much of that quality of the Englishman which is embodied in the well known proverb " The Englishman dearly loves a lord." As a democrat, I believe in the removal of inequalities, but as a radical I think we should go to the root causes of inequalities; and if you want to deal rationally and effectively with any unrest there may be amongst the workmen of Canada to-day you must deal with the real causes of the real inequalities of society. The inequality of society which goes home to the workman is that inequality by which our soldiers, to the number of 55,000 or 60,000,-most of them serving for $1.10 a day,-have laid down their lives for society, while most of us who have remained at home have benefited in the way of making filthy pelf by dint of their sacrifices, in many cases making that pelf to the amount of actual enrichment. That is the inequality of society that is troubling our workmen to-day, and I should recommend to my hon. friends that after we have finished with this question we should settle down to deal with the real, the serious, inequalities which are disturbing society and which will be a terrific trouble to us, as to all other countries, unless they are dealt with along the line of drastic reform. That is all the contribution I have to make, Mr. Speaker, to this enormous question of titles.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on this occasion merely to correct a wrong impression which may

have been created to-night by the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark). In the course of his address he made the statement that there was not in this House a member of the Society of Friends otherwise known as Quakers. I wish to inform the hon. member that the speaker who is addressing the House at this moment,. the member for South Renfrew, has the honour of being a member of that society. I might apologize somewhat for the extent to which I practise the tenets of the society, and possibly this fact may have influenced the hon. member for Red Deer in the conclusion at which he arrived. He must be aware that the Quakers of the present day are not the Quakers of the seventeenth, or the eighteenth or the nineteenth century. Like all other religious bodies they have changed considerably in recent years. So that, although they have adopted the plain language and the plain dress, and dispensed with titles entirely, even the common titles of " Mister," " Esquire," and so on, the Quakers of the present day are not as strict in the observance of these rules and regulations as they were in the days gone by. Consequently there is a possibility that the member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) has been misled in his judgment as to the personnel of the members of this assembly. I can assure him, though, that I am proud to be considered worthy of membership in that society, and I would be unworthy of that position if I sat silent on this occasion and failed to correct the impression that was left, although I know unintentionally, on this House.
I might say in passing that in regard tc the resolution now under discussion, I endorse to the limit some of the statements made by the last speaker, and I refer more particularly to his eulogy of the position taken by the scions of our aristocracy in the Old Land during the recent war. It has always been a delight and pleasure to me to look back on the history of the sons of the aristocracy of the Old Land who have been trained to live up to the privileges that they enjoy, which is so different from the condition that obtains in other lands in that respect. We find the sons of multi-millionaires, and of the so-called aristocracy, in this country, following a different course. They do not seem in many instances to rise equal to the occasion, or to their surroundings, whereas in the recent war there is no doubt that the aristocracy of the Old Land played qn equal part with the sons of the poorer people. Coming down to the question of titles or otherwise, in
this country I believe-and naturally it follows from my religious training-that titles do not improve the individual on whom they are conferred. Take some of the leading men of Canada; I do not grant for a moment that their position has been improved by the conferring of titles upon them. On the contrary, I know there have been individuals in this country and in the Old Land whose names were mentioned this afternoon-I refer to such men as Gladstone and John Bright in England, and Blake and Mackenzie in Canada-whose value would not be at all enhanced in the estimation of their fellow citizens by the conferring on them of titles. There are too, men in Canada who have had titles conferred on them and I know that these titles have not improved them in the estimation of their fellowmen-they wrere worthy men independent altogether of these honours. It is my intention, Mr. Speaker, to vote in favour of the resolution moved by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle), and I shall have very great pleasure in doing so.

subtopic: MOTION BY MR. NICKLE FOR ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY TO REFRAIN FROM
speechtext:
I do not intend to occupy the attention of the House more than a minute or two. but it appears to me that I might back up the very excellent remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer, whose opinion on these matters I value very highly, and also endorse the amendment to the amendment proposed by the Acting Prime Minister. This debate has been largely academic. I was considerably wearied with it this afternoon, and because I thought we had heard too much already about the subject of titles. I think the word "democracy" has been worked to death these days, and there are a great many panaceas put forward in connection with it, which are really doing it a great deal of damage. What we want is to get to work to make a democracy that is satisfactory to the people of Canada, and not talk so much about the matter and use the word so often, because simply shouting "Democracy!" is not going to make us any more democratic, and is not going to settle those questions that are agitating the people. I think this subject received quite sufficient airing last year, and I had hoped that the member for Kingston would have been of the same opinion and not have introduced his motion again this session.
In the first place, I have no objection to titles if they are properly earned and are lived up to after they are obtained. We have a few titled gentlemen sitting in this Chamber. Who would say for a mo-

ment, knowing the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) as we know him, that he has in any way lost his hold upon the people, or upon the members of this House, because he has accepted the title "Sir." I think that he is a great deal broader man than when he received the title. I think he is more in touch with the members of the House and more in touch with the people than ever he was before, and he is growing rapidly. And now, having paid a compliment to the leader upon our side, let me say of our good friend across the way, the newly elected leader of the Opposition, that "Sir D. D. McKenzie" would sound very well indeed.
