speechtext:
Well, Sir Donald be it; but I am saying this believing that the hon. gentleman is following in the steps of the great leader whom he has just succeeded, the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier. The *late lamented statesman bore the title with a great deal of distinction for a good many years, and although it is true that at times he spoke a little disparagingly of the title, he retained it, and lived up to it perhaps [DOT]as well, or better, than a great many other men that have borne titles.
Now my good friend from Kingston is generally very consistent, indeed, but in respect to titles I do not think he has quite lived up to that reputation. I understand-that he has a bosom friend, and if I were asked to mention that friend I would say he is a gentleman with a title. The hon. member will know to whom I refer. I do not believe the hon. member is any the [DOT]worse for spending a good deal of his time in the society of that titled gentleman. I congratulate him upon.having so brilliant a friend in a gentleman who is living up to the distinction that he has received, and, I think, has received deservedly.
The member for Red Deer has quoted a few passages from Scripture. He has quoted them remarkably well, and they are very apt and fitting to this question. It is true that some members of the House, if we were to believe them, would be quite prepared to call each other, Tom, Dick and

Harry across the floor instead of using the expression "honourable gentlemen." I cannot see, however, that the dignity, or the decorum, that we have in the Chamber would be enhanced if we were to so style one another. Every assembly must guide itself and try 'to live up to the dignity that belongs to it. If any gentleman who is elected a member of this House, or appointed to the Senate, fails to live up to the title appended to his name, in my opinion, he should abandon that title. It is hard to live up to these things, it is a difficult matter to realize -whalt the responsibility of titles means, but we use them everywhere, and there is no place where they are used more profusely than in the fraternal societies where " Worshipful Grand Master " is quite a common title. In some orders every one is a "Sir Knight." They have a lot of such appellations, there is no need to enumerate them all; and the very highest forms of titles are handed to these gentlemen as soon as they enter the cloisters of these secret societies. The world is full of titles, and the thing more necessary than anything else is to see that they aTe deserved and lived up to.
I am glad to see that the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) has just entered the Chamber, because I have a passage of Scripture to quote and I know that he is very fond of -hearing such quotations. The passage that I was going to give is from 'the ancient sage, Job, and I fancy my hon. friend has heard it before. Job said:
I know not to give flattering titles to men, for in so doing my Maker would soon take me away.
I want to draw the attention of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) to the word "flattering." Job did not say "titles;" he said "flattering titles." Sir John Macdonald gave an interpretation of flattery which I think has never been bettered since his day, and no dictionary contains as good a definition. He said that flattery was an agreeable untruth. Now, if I were to tell the hon. member for Brome that he was the greatest statesman in this House or on earth I would be using a flattering title.

If I were to tell him that he has a long way to go before he becomes a great statesman, I would be telling him what I believe to be the truth. The word "flattering" is where the prophet stumbles; and as long as titles are not flattering there is no fault to be found with them. The whole trouble is in a man getting a

title that he has not fairly won or does not live up to. It appears to me that the Acting Prime Minister has taken a very fair way of settling this thing, and I trust that the Committee, though a large one, will not take very long to settle the question. As I said at the outset, I think the subject has received far more attention than it deserves. The main thing is that our boys have won titles that are worth carrying, titles that they are entitled to for their heroism, their self-denial and their devotion to a great cause; arid I say it is a poor time to cut off such titles now when our boys are on the eve of receiving them. We should not belittle the D.S.O., the V.C., the M.C., 'or the other decorations conferred on those who have won them only after tremendous effort. If those men never do anything more to distinguish themselves in this world, they have achieved what many in former days never reached to. I have very much pleasure, Mr. Speaker, in heartily endorsing the Acting Prime Minister's amendment to the amendment.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North):

Last session when this question of titles was gone into very fully I was only able to be present and hear the concluding part of the discussion. For that reason I have been very much pleased to hear the present lengthy and interesting debate. 1 listened, as usual, with a great deal of pleasure and profit to the address of my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark). He is happy in mostly any realm, but he was particularly happy to-night when he launched into the realm of theology, although he went rather far afield for evidence in support of the amendment. The days of Peter are quite remote, and Jude lived about the same time, at all events their letters are in close juxtaposition. However, I am sure that there is nothing stronger in the mind of the hon. member for Red Deei than a sense of proportion and application -he always brings us severely to task if we are we not absolutely logical in everything that we say;-and I must tell him that the reasonings in the sphere of theology do not always fit in properly in the sphere of, legislation and statesmanship. When he quotes Peter and Jude as having said certain things, he must not forget that those men were evangelists, preaching the gospel of the Nazarene, which was entirely theological and moral and had nothing to do with the legislative or political sphere. Therefore, I think my hon. friend will see that those
quotations are not as apt as everything he quotes usually is. He must not forget that in those days the real dignitaries were the Scribes and Pharisees. But perhaps his recent acquaintance with such people constrained him to make those quotations. Another quotation from a higher source than even Peter or Jude might have come to his mind. He will remember that the Master himself said of those very dignitaries whom the hon. member for Red Deer defends to-day: "Woe unto you Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites."

speechtext:
He preferred to suffer privation with the people of God rather than enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season. That is authority to the point from one of the best men that ever lived, the man selected to take the people of God out of the darkness of Egypt. He refused a title, and that being the case, I have the very best reason for saying that no matter how excellent men may be, who have accepted titles, there are men equally as good who have refused them.
My good friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) was bordering on the realm of theology, but he did no go very far. There is something in the Scripture about people beating their swords into ploughshares and their spears into pruning-hooks; I would expect the member for Brantford to be

somewhat familiar with that quotation. The hon. gentleman said that the member for Brome (fl^Ir. MdMaster), would find the way weary and long to the Emmaus of the political heaven. Let me express the hope that the member for Brome will not be alone on that weary road; that others will be trudging along with him towards the sunset, saying, " It is toward evening and the day is far spent." So much for the delectable course into which the member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) assisted by the member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) has led us.
I listened with a great deal of attention to the remarks of the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle), whose .addresses are always logical and clear-cut and whose argument in support of any proposal that he makes is always satisfactory. We heard his argument last spring; we have heard him address the House several times on this question. About a year ago the House was quite ready to pass judgment on the question of titles, and but fox
10 p.m. the intervention of the Prime Minister on that occasion it would have done so. There was no dissenting voice at that time on the ground that there was not sufficient information. Now a year afterwards, the Acting Prime Minister says that we are not sufficiently enlightened on this question. For the last fifty years-all our lives, no matter how old or how young we are-we have heard about this thing. What information is to be gathered by this very excellent committee that is to be formed? What are they going to tell us? Where are they going to get their information? The member for Kingston, in dealing with this matter, did not go back quite as far as the member for Red Deer did, but he went quite a distance back. He was present at the battle of Hastings; he came into the country with William the 'Conqueror; divided up the lands with him, and did considerable surveying; so that he was able to come to us with a great deal of information, covering a period from the earliest times down to the present day. With the lucid and authoritative evidence that the member for Kingston presents to the House we ought to be satisfied. The House is as well prepared now to pass judgment on the question of titles as it will be a month hence or after we have heard the report of this committee.
Talking about committees, we have in the Government itself the very best committee that we could get from this House. Parliament is elected, and out of that Parliament the Governor General, on the advice of the

Prime Minister, selects a committee from the House of Commons known as the Government. There are eighteen or twenty of them; let me hope they are the select men of the party on that side of the House. They are responsible to the people; they should come down with a policy on this matter. Are they going to play daylight saving again? Have they not enough courage and strength of conviction to reach a decision upon this very simple matter of titles, come down to the House with it and ask the House to endorse it? Surely that is responsible government. Why throw the responsibility upon the whole House, and upon a very large committee who may find it difficult to reach a concrete conclusion? I submit, therefore that we are just as well prepared now to pass judgment on this motion as we shall be at any time in the future.
On the 25th of March, 1918, the Government reached a conclusion with regard to the question of titles. They put that conclusion into the form of an Order in Council and submitted it to the House. Hon. gentlemen on the other side voted for it by a very large majority. The Prime Minister said: We have put three weeks of our time on this matter; we have looked at it from all sides; and we submit this Order in Council as the wisdom that we could bring to bear on the question. That was not long ago. But the difficulty is that the Prime Minister and the Government cannot stay put; you cannot keep them anywhere. I am reminded of the time when I heard the member for Red Deer designate the Government that preceded this one-a Tory Government, nevertheless, and as close to this one as you could possibly get-as an "aggregation of funks." I think he was right when he said that. The words are on Hansard; of course, I would not use them myself, but, particularly when it comes from such an authority as the member for Red Deer, it is, perhaps, proper to use language which was not thought out of the way at that time. This Order in Council was submitted to the King, and by him considered in Council; upon it the King in Council made certain suggestions, and submitted them to the Government of this country. If the motion of the Acting Prime Minister to-night was to leave the matter as it was left by that Order in Council, and as it was left by the vote of this House, I should be disposed to agree. But, "How long, 0 Lord, how long," will the Government continue to hold to one thing? That was the order then; they want another thing to-day; to-morrow it will be something else. For

goodness sake, let us get clear of this title business and get down to something else that is of more importance to the people. Over a year ago the Government solemnly declared its position in this matter, and that position was affirmed by Parliament; now the whole thing, in the absence of the Prime Minister, is to he unravelled, and thrown back to a committee of twenty or twenty-five members from both sides of the House who, in all human probability will not agree. That is the condition in which we find ourselves now.
Here is an extract from a speech of the Prime Minister on May 21, 1918, reported on page 2364 of Hansard of last year. As the Prime Minister is not here, and as whatever else I may do, I want to be absolutely fair to him in his absence, I am going to read his speech which is short:
Sir Robert Borden: If by the leave of the House I may be permitted to say a few words, I shall make the matter perfectly clear so far as I am concerned. The subject was taken very fully into consideration by the Government at different times. We spent three or four weeks in reaching a conclusion as to our recommendations through the Governor General to His Majesty the King and to the Government of the United Kingdom. We dealt with it according to the light that we had. And when the motion of my hon. friend the member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) came before the House, I took the House absolutely into my confidence, told them of the discussion that we had had and of the conclusion that we had reached. I said that the Government of the United Kingdom, regarding some of the matters in the Order in Council as of very grave import, had asked us for an opportunity to discuss the whole subject, because undoubtedly it has relation to its ultimate effect not only to this Dominion but to all the Dominions of the Empire and to the United Kingdom as well. We reached a certain conclusion, and it has been stated frankly and clearly, as far as I was able to state it frankly and clearly, to the House. I can only say, so far as I am concerned, that if the House does not propose to accept the course which I have asked them frankly and with much respect to take, I should consider that I am relieved from my duty of carrying on any longer the Government of this country, and I should ask His Excellency the Governor General to seek other advisers. It seems to me that a somewhat peculiar course has been pursued by some hon. gentlemen on this side of the House in inquiring of the Leader of the Opposition as to whether or not this motion was to be treated as a motion of want of confidence. My understanding of the course to be pursued on such occasions is that the Leader of the Government should be asked with regard to that question, and I cannot quite understand the reason why there should have been resort to my right hon, friend on the other side of the House to learn how I should regard a motion of this kind. However, the course has been taken, and it is entirely in the judgment of the House to determine what course they propose to pursue in
the matter. So far as I am concerned my course is absolutely clear and open.
That is the whole of the speech, and it is perfectly clear what was before the House. It bears out exactly what I said. Now, if, when this motion was taken on the 21st May, 1918, the Prime Minister was going to resign if his friends on that side did not support his Order in Council, what guaran-'tea have we that we are not going .to bring the same catastrophe on the country to-day if hon. gentlemen opposite will do anything except just fall in line as the Prime Minister called upon them to do on that occasion? If, after three or four weeks of close consideration of the question, as the Prime Minister tells us, a conclusion was reached, surely as much learning was put into the matter then as can be brought to bear upon it by this committee. The war is not a new thing. Every phase and every condition of the war that exist to-day, except peace, for which we thank the Lord, was well to the fore on the 25th of March, 1918. Whether titles should be granted to men who fight, or to women who helped, or to anybody else who was engaged either here or in the Old Country in connection with the war-all that was certainly before the Government, and they decided with all that knowledge before them that the Order in 'Council which was read here to-night was the best and safest conclusion to reach. Surely there is no excuse now for reversing that decision and starting over again anew. For those reasons I think we should decide the question now, once and for all, and if this House will reach the conclusion that the Order in Council for which they voted last year was good enough, I do not understand how hon. gentlemen who voted for that Order in Council are going, in the absence of the Prime Minister, to tell him that he was wrong then, that they will not support that, but that they want another thing altogether. There is no finality to this matter at all. It is given a twist and a turn just to suit the exigencies of the occasion. That is about all I have to say on that particular phase of the subject; but in view of what I have read from .the Prime Minister's speech,
I think I should bring to the notice of wise, patriotic hon. gentlemen sitting on both sides of the House, particularly those supporting the Government and those who left their old friends, cut away from their old moorings on the high question of con-' scientious necessity and duty, as they thought, the weight which the Prime Minister attached to this situation. A few days before this motion he was returned from

the country by an overwhelming majority to fight the war to a finish; he was the selected champion of the Canadian people to fight this war. What weight does 'he attach to this question? There comes up in this House a trivial matter about titles-I say " trivial " advisedly, for it was trivial as compared with the great question of life and death of this war-and we find our friends who were honest and in earnest [DOT] about this thing told by their leader: Away with your war, away with your catastrophe, away with your loyalty, if you do not come up to the scratch on this question of titles, I will throw you to the dogs and will have nothing further to do with you. That shows to me the hollow mockery of the business and that it was politics, first, last and all the time. And I want to hear the argument to the contrary in face of the declaration of the Prime Minister himself that if they did not come to the mark on this little business of titles, there was nothing further to it and he was relieved from all the vast and great responsibilities of the salvation of this country thrust into his hands by the Canadian people. And I should like to know from hon. gentlemen who are sitting behind him for no other purpose than to see that the mandate of the Canadian people in respect to the war was carried out, why they were ready to permit that mandate to be torn to shreds and thrown to the dogs for the mere purpose of carrying the Prime Minister's views in regard to titles into effect.
The hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) spoke about unrest in this country, and the same matter was referred to by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark). There is unrest in this country, but that unrest is not created by reason of titles. I am a poor man and a poor man's son. I am in touch with the poor people of this country, working men and all classes. I know their pulsations and heart-beats and the circumstances in their houses and families, and I know they are not concerned very much about titles. They do not lose any sleep over who is a knight or a baronet or a lord, but it does concern them that the flour is getting down to the bottom of the barrel; that the meat barrel is almost empty. It does concern them that their children's shoes are getting thin and worn, and that they cannot [DOT]keep their children warm at night or in the day time; that they are not able to gather together enough of this world's goods to carry them along decentlv and comfortably.
There is another class of kmghts, an-

other class of autocrats, they are after in this country, and that is the combines and the trusts who are taking the money and the very heart's blood of our people. Let me hope, Sir, that the eloquence and learning of my good friends from Kingston and Springfield will be directed along this channel. I hope that an opportunity will be given them to strike a blow at these autocrats who are bringing pain, penury and trouble to the homes of the people by reason of the title which they have to control this Government. Why, we had the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) the other day saying right before hon. gentlemen who sit bn the Government benches that this Government is owned body and bones by the Baronet Sir Joseph Flavelle. Is that true or is it not? There are other chosen ones besides Sir Joseph Flavelle; he is not the only pebble on the beach. I repeat, it was said here openly by a supporter of the Government, that hon. gentlemen on the Government benches, with all their learning and all their ability, are nothing but a flock of sheep in a cart, with their legs tied, being driven to market by Sir Joseph Flavelle and other autocrats and plutocrats in this country. I invite my hon. friend from Kingston and my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) to let their voices be heard along these lines. My hon. friend from Red Deer will find in Holy Writ severe condemnation of those who are starving the poor, and robbing the people, and putting heavy burdens on the workers, which they will not touch even with a finger. My hon. friend will find the sternest condemnation in Holy Writ of these practices, and nobody can apply it better than he. If this discussion does nothing more than to compel us to think of these things and to help us make this a truly democratic country, it will have done some good. Let us show our democracy by going to the homes of the poor, and seeing to it that there shall be an even distribution of the great wealth of this country. Let us help to relieve the suffering so that every man, woman and child in this country will know that this is a Parliament to which they can look with confidence for redress, and that there is a Government in this country which has their interests at heart. These are the things which come home to my mind and conscience much more than the question of titles.

speechtext:
I
wish to add a very few words to the debate which has taken place to-night. First oi all, I wish to say that I shall vote for the

amendment to the amendment. I put this proposition to the House, and I do not believe it can be honestly contraverted by any man inside or outside of the House. We in Canada owe to all those who have served in our military and naval forces a debt of gratitude which we shall never be able wholly to repay, and having those men in mind, it should be an honour and a distinction to be able to serve on the committee which has been suggested by the amendment to the amendment by the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White)). I trust that the members of that committee will work most earnestly and faithfully in order to offer to this House their very best decision as to whether titles should be conferred on our naval and military forces. With regard to distinctions and decorations for those who have served in connection with the war in a civilian capacity, I will frankly say that I regard that service from an entirely different point of view. For the military and naval forces there is nothing too good that this country can accord in the way of distinctions or decorations, if this House believes they can be conferred with advantage. I believe, however, that no man who has not served in the military or naval forces in this war can feel for one moment that any act or accomplishment of his life is comparable for one solitary second to. the accomplishment of the youngest youngster who has served in either of those forces. That is my feeling, and I feel it deep down. I doubt very much whether the bestowal oi decorations in acknowledgement of civilian service will redound very much to tne advantage of this country. With all the complex problems facing us as an aftermath oi the war, and calling for solution, I think it would not tend to better the situation or to overcome our difficulties to confer distinctions or decorations on civilians. I believe there is a good deal in the widow's mite, and I think those who were well enough off to offer their services in a civilian capacity freely and without hope of reward [DOT] are entitled to no more recognition than the thousands of working girls in this country who have given of their small wages to send parcels to our soldiers, and who, in order to do that, had to exercise the direst economy and practise the greatest self-sacrifice from the commencement of this war until victory was achieved.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. J. MANION (Fort William and Rainy River):
subtopic: MOTION BY MR. NICKLE FOR ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY TO REFRAIN FROM
speechtext:
I regret very much that I find it necessary to say a few words in this debate. When the resolution on the Order
Paper came before the House, I had no intention of taking part in the discussion, which I had assumed would resolve itself into the clear-cut question whether this House favoured or did not favour the granting of such titles as knighthoods in this country. I had hoped that there would be a vote on that simple question, and I had intended to vote with the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) and the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson). I by no means agree with either of these hon. gentlemen that this country is at all agitated over the question of titles. I have never heard in my own constituency, or in different parts of the country in which I have been, anything of the great agitation over the question which they and other hon. members would lead us to believe exists. I believe there are a great many bigger questions which the people are much more agitated about to-day. I do not think the people of this country care very much about that question at all, although if it came to a vote I believe they would overwhelmingly support the hon. member for Kingston and the hon. member for Springfield. I do not believe there is any real open agitation in connection with the question, but I must take issue with some of the siatements contained in the letter from the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), in which it was implied that a good many decorations Should be bestowed in this country on civilians who have worked in Canada or in London in supporting the men at the front. I think that the most humble Tommy who has served in the line deserves far more in the way of decorations than nr.y of those who have worked on the Patriotic Society or the lied Cross Society either in London or in Canada. Another opinion I wish to emphasize is that the mothers of the boys who died at the front -even women who did nothing else than supply those boys-deserve ten thousand times more the gratitude of the country, whether in titles or anything else, than the people who worked in Red Cross or patriotic societies. I do not for a moment belittle those who have rendered service in these societies, because I have every respect for them; but in my opinion the giving of titles to such people is responsible for whatever agitation there may be in the country and whatever adverse opinion that may exist in regard to the conferring of titles. Speaking for myself as a returned soldier, and not for any group of returned soldiers, I wish to raise another point, and it is this: I do not believe any titles should be

conferred-and when I say "titles," I mean for example, knighthoods, with the title "Sir"-any more to the naval or military forces than to civilians, because I do not believe we have any right to establish in Canada a military autocracy or aristocracy.
I shall quote some of my words of last year on this question. Last year when the question came before the House I intended to vote as I intend to vote to-night, but the Prime Minister made a statement that if a vote were given against the conferring of titles he would resign. I then expressed the opinion that in the condition of world affairs that existed at the time the question was of too small importance to turn out any Government, and accordingly I voted with the Prime Minister. To-day I understand the Acting Prime Minister to say that the subject is not a party question. At any rate I shall vote against the appointment of a committee for the reason that I do not require any committee to instruct me on this question. I regret that I should have to take this position. I regret that the Government has found it necessary to make me take this position, and it is unfortunate that a question like this should be brought before the House, in my opinion, more or less unnecessarily at the present time. I think that a number of questions are unnecessarily introduced, and it is a matter for much regret that the House should be forced to divide on an issue which is not of paramount importance to the country. I feel it my duty, in view of the statement which I made last year and my sentiments in this matter, to vote against the Acting Prime Minister, but there are times when perforce we must take a stand, and, as my hon. friend from Red Deer said, " let the chips fall where they may." My position last year was stated in these words:-
I wish to say that, generally speaking-, I agree absolutely with the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) and the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) that not only hereditary titles but all knighthoods should be abolished in this country.

I repeat that 1 believe that this Government was elected for the purpose of carrying out the Military Service Act and sending soldiers to the front. I do not believe that it is the duty of this Parliament, of men who are elected as I was with that specific purpose in view, to turn out this Government on such a question as this without due consideration. If after due consideration this question comes up again, if it comes uip in the next Parliament, I am willing to say here to-night, that if the hon. member for Springfield moves this motion I shall be willing to support it at that time.

There is one point I wish to make before I sit down, a point in regard to naval and military titles.
I do not agree that there should be titles given only to naval and military men in this country.
I agree absolutely with the Prime Minister in' that. We should not make a military caste to stand over and above the other people of this country. While we are fighting to put down autocracy in Germany, we do not want to create a military aristocracy or autocracy in our own country. I do not believe that the military should be given titles any more than any other class. But I do believe that for deeds of valour the military should ibe given decorations.
That is where the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) was somewhat confused in thought when he spoke of the Military- Cross and the Victoria Cross. There is no resemblance between these distinctions and titles. I believe that Military Crosses and Victoria Crosses should be granted for deeds of bravery, and I may point out that while the Republic of France does not confer titles it gives such decorations as the Legion of Honour, which the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Le-mieux) wears.
Now, Mr. Speaker, after quoting what I said last year, I do not see how I could consistently or honestly take any other position than to vote against .the appointment of a committee. If the hon. member for Springfield and the hon. member for Kingston can take any other course, after introducing this motion on two different occasions and forcing men like myself to take the stand I am taking on the question, then I say they have more elasticity of mentality than I have.

Mr. Speaker, when .this question was before the House last year I took the liberty to discuss it and I shall endeavour to avoid repeating the arguments which I then advanced. I rise merely to support the position taken by my hon. friend from Rainy River and Fort William (Mr. Manion). The resolution involves a declaration of principle, and certainly does not necessitate the consideration or report of a committee. As far as I can learn, a question is usually referred to a committee after the principle which is involved has been decided upon by the House, hut when the whole question resolves itself into a declaration of principle I do not see why it should be referred to a committee at all. Are we or are we not in favour of the continuance of bestowing titles upon citizens of Canada? That is the whole question. I do not wish to employ harsh terms, but I think that this Parliament would stultify itself if it accepted the

amendment to the amendment proposed by the Acting Prime Minister to-night. Such an action would simply mean the postponing again of the settlement of a question which was before the House last year and upon which the opinion of the House was perfectly clear. Every one remembers, as has been stated to-night, that all the hon. members who spoke upon the question last year were emphatically opposed to titles, apart from the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), and, I believe, the hon. the Secretary of .State (Mr. Burrell), so much so that the right hon. the Prime Minister was compelled to resort to what I think was a most arbitrary position to save an unpopular institution. The Prime Minister virtually said to Parliament: We are passing through the most critical period of the war; this Government has been elected to conduct the war; it has been elected on a policy which has as its object the winning of the war; but if this Parliament decides that the Government shall no longer have the right to bestow titles on its friends and on such citizens as it may deem fit, the war can take care of itself and I shall quit and go home.
That was the position taken by the Prime Minister last year, and it was on account of that position, an hon. gentleman stated, that his amendment was voted on and accepted by the House. Sir, since that [DOT]took place public opinion has asserted itself in this country and in no mistakable manner. The people are utterly tired and sick of this title question. The Prime Minister last session, when moving his amendment to the amendment, as reported at page 2343 of Hansard, said:
* There is another consideration which I submit to the House and it is this : His Majesty's Government have to take into consideration, of course, the relation of this proposal not only to Canada but to all the Dominions of the Empire, and they have asked us, in a respectful and courteous way, that the whole subject be brought under discussion during the coming summer when certain of the Canadian ministers are to visit the United Kingdom. It seems to me that as the Order in Council has been passed and has been communicated to His Majesty's Government, the delay that would ensue between this session and the next session, when the matter might be taken up again, if desired, ought not to stand in the way of our acceding to that respectful request. I do not imagine that the public interest will suffer by any action taken before Parliament shall assemble again. The Government of this country will then be in a position to announce to Parliament the result of their conference with the Imperial authorities in respect to this subject. So, I would suggest to my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Richardson)-and I hope he will accept this suggestion-that the subamendment which I have proposed be accepted.
So the Prime Minister moved his amendment last year for the purpose of having another year to confer with the Imperial authorities at the then coming conference, and stated to this House that at this .session the Government would come down with a definite policy upon the question. Instead of that being done, when the hon. member for Kingston again introduces his resolution on the very same subject, the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) moves another dilatory motion, and asks again to postpone the settlement and the decision of this question. As far as I am concerned,
I am prepared to vote now on the question.
I have the greatest confidence in the hon. gentlemen whose names have been proposed as members of the committee, bu't I do not wish any of those gentlemen to make a finding or to form an opinion for me on a question of principle such as that which forms the subject of the present resolution.
Nobody has tried to defend the institution, although perhaps my hon. friends from Brantford and Red Deer went close to it. My hon. friend from Red Deer pointed to the fact that there are men in this country who got rich overnight, wqnt to Britain, and then found their way to knighthood. Well, Sir, I think that no stronger indictment can be preferred against the whole institution than those very words. Honours which are bought are no honours at all, and we do not want them in this country of ours. The hon. gentleman also said that the nobility of England conducted itself splendidly during the great war. That is true, but so did the plain citizens of England, so did the workingmen of England, so did the democracy of England. I know something else: I read only recently in an important British review that it was a misfortune that when war broke out commissions in the army had been confined exclusively to the sons of the aristocracy, and that it took some time for the brains of the country to be called and trained to serve as officers in the army. My hon. friend from Brantford said that the word " democracy " was worked to death in this country. There are words which my hon. friend does not like. I remember that a few years ago-I think it was during the naval debate-my hon. friend said he was tired of the word " autonomy." Let me tell him that the words " autonomy " and " democracy " will be used quite a few times in this country again, and if he does not like them he had better change his mind and tolerate them at all events. Mr. Speaker I am going to vote against the amendment of the Acting Prime Minister.

I think it was the hon. member for Red Deer who said that if you were going to be radical you should start at the root of things. I do not know whether the people that I have the honour to represent in this House would come within that category or not, but one thing I do know, that they have been very consistent upon this matter. They have not let an'opportunity slip, for the last few years, of passing resolutions upon this subject, and voting against not only hereditary titles, but titles in all forms. And as their representative, I feel that I would be very derelict in my duty if I did not express that opinion in this House. I am heartily in favour of the resolution as introduced by the hon. member for Kingston, and whilst I do not feel like going a,s far as the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Maniom) I feel that the Government has not treated me properly ;by putting me in the position that it has done in this matter. I believe that the members of this House should be left to decide this matter for themselves. As has been very well pointed out, it is really a matter of principle upon which every man should be able to'make up his own mind.
The hon. member for Brantford made some comparisons which I think were altogether unfair in his application to members of this House of the term "honourable gentlemen." We all know, at any rate I think I know, that is a term which is merely used for convenience in the transaction of the business of the House, and as soon as we go outside the portals of this Chamber the term is used no longer. Reference has been made also to the titles conferred upon the officers of fraternal organizations, but I think the comparison was ill-advised. The people of my constituency are absolutely opposed to titles in any shape or form, and, as a member of this House, I intend to back them up as' far as I can.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queens):
speechtext:
I regret that I was prevented from being present at the earlier stages of this debate, and have only had the pleasure of hearing the last two or three speakers. It is quite conceivable that if I had had the pleasure of hearing the whole of the debate I should have reached a different conclusion. However, I am disposed to fall back upon the view which I ventured to express when this matter was before the House a year ago. The motion of the hon. member for Kingston has been repeatedly referred to to-night as 
if it were the same motion he made a year ago. That is not the ease. When my hon. friend brought forward his motion last session, I had great pleasure in giving it my very cordial support. It dealt with hereditary titles, and upon that question I had no hesitation whatever in expressing an opinion. On the wider question of titles generally I frankly confessed that I had some hesitation in agreeing with the amendment moved at that time by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson). I did feel that these titles had been rather freely distributed, and in that way there was an abuse of the system which had tended to make it very unpopular. But when you look back to the days when Macdonald, Cartier, Galt, and a few others, received titles, there was no condemnation of them in the community, as these titles were then granted but rarely and to men of undoubted distinction. If that had been the case in later years, I presume the conferring of titles would not have been as unpopular as it is to-day. I am hesitating a little in this matter. It will not break my heart if the ultimate decision is that all titles of the kind are to be abolished, and probably that will be the outcome ; but if in the meantime the Government thinks that it can get any help from Parliament, that this is a matter for a committee, I have no objection to letting it make the trial, although I have not much faith in it. I would have some hesitation in voting for the resolution of my hon. friend from Kingston, but I am quite content to let the Government make a trial of its committee, although I do not expect it to make much out of that course.

The question of titles is one that appears to engage the attention of this House to the exclusion of a great many other matters of very urgent importance. I thought a year ago when the question was under discussion that we were possibly devoting too much attention to what was a question of very minor importance compared with the urgent questions then before the House; and although the war has ended I believe that the reconstruction period with which we are confronted demands not only our closest, but almost our exclusive attention, and that we could well afford to leave matters such as this to some time in the future without any great injustice to the country. I do not mean that I approve of the conferring of titles upon people in this country. There have been times when titles were consider-

ed a great honour and the recipients were deserving of them, but I agree with the hon. member for Queens and Shelburne (Mr. Fielding) that titles have been conferred in a manner which has taken away from them any prestige which they might at one time have had, and that we do not regard them to-day in the light in which they were intended to be regarded, or would be regarded if they were properly conferred. I think that the amendment of the Acting Prime Minister to refer this to a committee to report upon will be much more satisfactory than attempting to dispose of it here. I must again repeat that I believe we are devoting altogether too much attention to matters of minor importance when other matters of urgent public importance are demanding our attention.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
With the consent of the House I should like to substitute for my amendment, in order to improve the phraseology, the following:
That the subject matters ot the said motion and amendment together with the questions ot conferring honours, titular distinctions and decorations upon the subjects of His Majesty ordinarily resident in Canada, including those who have performed overseas, in Canada or elsewhere, naval, military or civilian services in connection with the war be referred for consideration and report to a Special Committee consisting of the following members: Messrs. Nickle, Green, Peck, Buchanan, Clark (Red Deer), Thomson (Qu'Appelle), Cowan, Richardson, Whidden, Nesbitt, Middlebro, Pardee, Cockshutt, Murphy, McCoig, Ross, Ames, Mc-Master, Lemieux, Robb, Fielding, Elkin, Copp, McCurdy, Sinclair (Guysborough).

speechtext: This can only be put with the unanimous consent of the House. I would direct attention also to the fact that under Rule 11 a committee consisting of more than fifteen members can only be appointed with the unanimous consent of the House. The question is on the amendment to
Before the debate is closed I would like to exercise my privilege

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has risen at a very peculiar stage of the proceedings.
I endeavoured to rise but I did not catch your eye, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I did not see the hon. member. I will accept his statement that he purposed to rise.

What I want to say before this debate is closed will be very brief. As has been said by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding), the
resolution I introduced this afternoon differs from the resolution I introduced last year in this respect, that last year's resolution was aimed at hereditary titles, while the resolution of this afternoon is aimed at titular distinctions. I do not intend at this late hour to go fully into the various arguments that have been advanced both for and against the resolution and the amendments, but I do not think I should allow the remarks of the hon. member for Red 'Deer (Mr. Clark) to pass entirely unnoticed. One is always charmed to hear him, he has a wealth of comparisons, a vigour of diction, and a charm of style peculiarly his own. But sometimes in the swing of his argument, it seems to me, that he is not entirely consistent. To-night, if I judged his argument correctly-and I endeavoured to give due weight to everything he said-it seemed to me he failed to make the distinction that exists between officiary appellations-if I may use two very large words-and titular distinctions of an honorary character. He elaborated and laboured the point that one was inconsistent in contending for the abolition of titular distinctions provided one were prepared to admit that such terms as "senator," "minister" and "president" should be used.
I am utterly at a loss, Sir, to understand how we can express ourselves in the ordinary parlance of every day life unless we use some words to describe the objects about which we intend to talk. I do not see how you can describe the presiding officer of an assembly unless you call him "president". I cannot see very well how you can make a distinction between male and female, man and woman, unless at times you use the words " Mr." or " Mrs.". I am also at a loss to understand how you are to make the distinction between the commoner and the senator unless you use the ordinary parlance of every day life to describe those who happen to sit in this assembly or those who sit in the assembly across the way.
The member for Red Deer waxed eloquent-and probably rightly so-when he described the magnificent service which those who occupied positions of importance in England had rendered in this great war. He described in glowing terms the service-rendered by the sons of those who belonged to a long hereditary line, and for a moment I wondered whether he was forgetting the men in the trenches, because I know with what favour he views the services these men have rendered. But in a moment his natural impulses overcame his argument,

and he paid just as glowing a tribute to the simple men in the trenches as he paid to those who came from the aristocratic homes of Britain. All of which only demonstrates that valour is not confined to any particular group of men. When the call of country is heard, brave men, no matter what their birth, come from cottage or from castle and render efficient service to the State in a great time of need.
The member for Bed Deer said that I said labour unrest and labour trouble were traceable to titles. I do not think I used any such expression this afternoon. I said-and I quoted from the speech of Lord Shaughnessy-that there was labour unrest in this country, but I did not say that the question of titles was that
11 p.m. which was disturbing labour. I said that labour was dissatisfied in respect of the status that it occupied in this country and that it was a pity that at a time like this we should accentuate that unrest by the establishment or the recognition, or the granting, of fresh titular distinction.
I am not going to follow the member for Brantford (Mr. W. F. Cockshutt). He spoke of the men at the front winning titles in the trenches. The men at the front do not win titles in the trenches; they win distinction in the trenches for which sometimes titles are given. The member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham), in referring to my motion as it appears on the Order Paper, stated that he was against it because I had made two exceptions; that is, that a title might be granted to persons in the military or naval services of Canada or to persons engaged in the administration of justice of the Dominion. With all due respect for the ability and academic knowledge of the member for West Peterborough, may I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the House that the hon. gentleman has not correctly read my resolution. What my resolution said, in effect, was that no more titular distinction should be granted, it being always understood "that this humble prayer has no reference to professional or vocational appellations conferred in respect to commissions issued by Your Majesty to persons in military or naval service of Canada or to persons engaged in the administration of justice in the Dominion." That is, when a commission was issued by His Majesty that carried with it a professional or vocational appellation, that professional or vocational appellation should be enjoyed by the person to whom
[Mr. Nickle.l
the commission was issued, but not that a titular honorary distinction should be so enjoyed.
I now come to a question that has caused me some consideration^ to-night. The question with which I am confronted is this: Am I to vote for the amendment to the amendment as moved by the Acting Prime Minister, or am I to stand firm, if I may use the expression, and vote for my resolution? Now, I want to be perfectly frank with this House. Last year, when this question came to a crisis, late in the evening, after a bitter yet brilliant debate in which many members took part, I voted against the amendment of the Prime Minister because I did not think that this question should be made at that time a want of confidence motion. I thought it was a question on which the House should reach its own conclusion, each man thinking for himself; I therefore stood to my guns and voted for the amendment proposed by the member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson). What I want is results, not notoriety. I am absolutely sincere in what I am urging this House to do and in advocating the reform which I want this country to adopt. I am not playing politics; I am not looking for recognition by way of notoriety in this quarter or in that. I realize that difficulties have to be met, obstacles have to be overcome. I realize, as I said this afternoon, that this is an involved and confusing subject. The Acting Prime Minister made to me this afternoon what I consider an eminently fair, a just and a judicial offer; and I am going to accept his proposal in exactly the same spirit aS he offered it to me, to this House and to the country. He said that the Government had no desire to shelve this question. He said: We have held up honours that might have been granted; honours have been granted in all parts of the British Empire except Canada; we realize the difficulty of the situation and we want the deliberate judgment of the House on the question. Had the Acting Prime Minister submitted to this House a blanket resolution without naming a committee, I doubt very much whether I would have voted for it. But he has been honest with me, and I am going to be quite as frank with him. On the committee named by the Acting Prime Minister are representatives of all shades of thought, all shades of opinion, from the radical to the Conservative in this House. He says that the Committee is to meet promptly and is to prepare a report, and that that report is to be considered in this House this session.

If I and those who see eye to eye with me ,on this subject cannot convince as fair a committee as the Acting Prime Minister has suggested of the merits of the subject that we have been debating to-day and that we debated last session, then I say that we are not entitled to win, because if any contention in a matter of public interest cannot win on its merits, cannot win on the arguments that are advanced in favour oi it, it should not win at all. I believe that there is a preponderance of opinion from one end of this country to the other in favour of the resolution that I have propounded this afternoon. Such confidence have I in .public opinion; such confidence have I in the merits of the matter which I have introduced to this House for consideration, that I am going to vote for the committee proposed by the Acting Prime Minister. I believe that that committee will give honest and thorough consideration to the broad questions that have been relegated to it for consideration-broader questions by far than have been embraced in my resolution-and that we shall get out of the way, once and, I hope, for all time, questions that have caused, are causing, and will cause unless finally settled, unrest and disquietude in Canada.

I rise to a point of order. Sixty-four members have just voted against the appointment of a special committee of 15. I raise a point of order whether this Committee can sit or not, because Rule 11 of the House says:
No special committee may, without leave ot the House, consist of more than fifteen members-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am in a position to rule now, if the hon. member will only permit me. I drew the attention of the House to that rule and pointed out that the motion of the Acting Prime Minister could only be put by unanimous consent, and that consent was given when the motion was first put.
It was certainly not given by unanimous consent, when 64 members voted against it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must direct the attention of the hon. member to the fact that I especially drew the attention .of the House to Rule 11 and stated that a special committee of more than 15 members could not be appointed except by unanimous consent. That was done before the motion was put in the first instance. The hon. member, to be in order, should have raised the point of order prior to the time the motion was put in the House. He is not in order now.

I wish to raise another point of order. Rule 11 says further:
No member who declares or decides against the principle or substance of a Bill, resolution, or matter to be committed, can be nominated of such committee.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson), and two or three others who have already decided, are nominated of this committee.

With respect to the
second point of order raised by the hon. member, I am in the judgment of the House; but in my opinion the rule does not apply here, because the subject of the resolution and also that of the amendment have not been determined upon. subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.

speechtext: On the motion of Sir Thomas White (Acting Prime Minister), that the House go into Committee of Supply.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
Before the House resolves itself
into Committee of Supply I wish to refer to some matters which have engrossed the attention of the public of late. In rising I must say I am not casting any reflections on the administration of the Militia Department.	[DOT]	,
I cannot forget that my hon. friend took office when the conditions to which I intend to allude briefly this afternoon were in existence. I w'ould certainly impugn his administration if, after the disclosures that have been made of late and which I intend to re-echo this afternoon on the floor of this House, he did not think it proper to take the necessary action in order to probe the whole matter to the bottom. My object this afternoon i3 to elicit information, first, and then having shown the conditions that exist, and have existed of late in connection with the administration of the Department of Militia and Defence overseas, to ask for an investigation to be held at the earliest moment. The country is entitled

to know whether or not the charges which have been made of late are true. It is not a good answer to say that the war is over and that bygones should be bygones. It is true that the war is over, but if conditions continue to exist until complete demobilization has taken place, we have a right to ask the Government to put an end to the state of things which has been denounced. It is not a good answer to say: The war is over; therefore we must not investigate. At the time the war was being carried on the only answer the Government had to our criticism was that it was not fair to bring charges whilst the war was being carried on. From whichever angle you look at this question, certainly, the Government must see to it that these charges are probed to the bottom.
The effort of Canada during the war has been simply marvellous. The total enlistments have been, according to the official report which I hold in my hand, 595,441 men, and the total casualties, died of wounds, died of disease, wounded, prisoners of war, 218,433. The loans made by the Canadian people to the Government amount to the fabulous sum of $1,436,000,000; or in other words, $192 per capita of the population of the Dominion. The net debt of Canada, chiefly as a result of the war, amounted, on the 30th November, 1918, to $1,307,449,661. The proceeds of taxation during the last fiscal year amounted, in round figures, to $76,000,000. So, from this cursory reference, you have an idea of the magnitude of the effort on the part oi Canada in connection with the war. This has been accomplished with a population of less than 8,000,000.
By all means, our country is entitled to the fullest information as regards the conduct of the war. Although the war has been happily ended, there have been fatal errors in connection with the demobilization plan adopted by the Government, which errors, I submit, must be avoided in the future. Our returned soldiers constitute a national asset of the first importance, and therefore theii grievances cannot be disregarded with a wave of the hand. Besides, the honour of Canada is at stake. The other day my hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Murphy) drew the attention of my hon. friend the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) to the charges which have been made by a returned officer of very high rank-I refer to Brigadier General Smart-and when he drew the attention of the Acting Prime Minister to the very serious charges made by that gallant officer, my hon. friend, I

regret to say, did not give the matter the attention that he should have given to it. He simply gave a denial in toto of all the charges which had been made by a responsible and gallant officer who had served the Empire and the King since the beginning of the war overseas. Now, Sir, the matter cannot be hushed up; the bald, naked truth must be told. There is, I am sorry to say, dissatisfaction in every province of this Dominion, not excepting the good province of Ontario, against the administration of the Department of Militia and Defence, bar always what I said a moment ago that my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence came late into the present Administration and found conditions existing for the creation of which he was not responsible. But there is general dissatisfaction. We can hardly meet a soldier, or an officer back from the trenches, or fiom the camps in England, who has not his tale of woe to repeat.
The gentlemen who have become very prominent of late in their denunciation of the administration of the Department of Militia and Defence overseas are very well known. I am glad to be able to refer to the evidence of General Smart, of Colonel Pratt and of Colonel Price not as constituting biased, ex parte evidence but as the evidence of men holding high and responsible positions in the Canadian army besides being prominent members of the Conservative party and supporters of the Union Government. Of course, you cannot expect that petty officers will dare speak on this question. They are afraid to think even, but General Smart and Colonel Pratt and Colonel Price are not afraid to speak and speak boldly.
Since this cloudburst, the press which supports the present Administration has been very vociferous in asking for a thorough investigation. I shall not quote extensively from that press, but I may be pardoned, Mr. Speaker, if I take what I consider the most influential newspaper in the great province of Ontario-I refer to the Toronto Globe, which has given the present Government very faithful support-and quote from an editorial which appeared in its issue oi April 3rd. This editorial, which is entitled " Investigate General Smart's Charges," was published a few days after the denial made by the Acting Prime Minister, when his attention was called to the Smart charges by my hon. friend the member for Russell (Mr. Murphy). I will quote a couple of paragraphs:-
Thousands of people in Canada-

Not a few members of His Majesty's loyal Opposition.
__Thousands of people in Canada are dissatisfied
with Sir Thomas White's rather offhand manner of dealing with the chargee made by Brigadier-General Smart, a member of the Quebec Legislature, In which he alleged inefficiency and neglect on the part of the administration of Canadian Medical Services in England, and inefficiency and favoritism on the part of the overseas administration generally. There has long been a good deal of anxiety and uneasiness among Canadians over these questions, particularly in view of the unsatisfactory method of dealing with the report of Colonel Bruce. It is not surprising to find General Smart returning to the attack and using emphatic language in the repetition of some of his allegations, nor is there much room for doubting that the public generally feels that an inquiry is in order; but the partial excuse that his charges deal with the condition existing in England in 1916-
Now, mark this: General Smart mentions reports and occurrences of a later date, and I shall draw the attention of the Acting Prime Minister to them. Among those is the report of Lieut.-Colonel J. S. Jenkins, submitted to the Overseas Minister of Militia in November, 1918. The Globe concludes its article in the following words
The country is entitled to the truth, good or bad, and the Government ought not to be afraid to probe for it, no matter who may be hurt in the operation. If the charges are shown to be without foundation, all Canadians will be happy; meanwhile they are suspicious and uneasy.
The Globe is an influential organ friendly to the present Union Government, and it states positively that thousands of people are suspicious, uneasy and dissatisfied with the offhand answer given by my hon. friend the Acting Premier. I remember that during the early part of the present session the member for Russell called the attention oi the Minister of Militia to the existence oi the report of Lieut.-Colonel Jenkins, and the hon. minister disclaimed any knowledge of that report. I have not seen that report, but I will convey to him the information which I have in regard to it, so that he may take the necessary steps to make sure thai that report will be tabled during the present session, in order that the Canadian Parliament,-which constitutes after all, as in England, the voice of the nation,-may know how the Department of Militia overseas has been administered. I am informed that Colonel Jenkins was asked by the Minister of Militia overseas-just as Colonel Bruce was asked-to investigate the financial administration of the Canadian Medical Service in England, and that he reported, after a very close investigation, a leakage of Government funds to the amount oi $10,000,000. I have that information, Mr. Speaker, on thoroughly reliable authority. My hon. friend says that he has no knowledge of the existence of that report. Thai report does exist, if I am well informed, and is in the hands of the present Minister of Militia overseas, Sir Edward Kemp. I do not know when he intends to sail for Canada, but now that all the German submarines have been surrendered to England I hope it will not be stated as a reason for withholding that report that it cannot be sent to Canada lest it should become lost through submarine activity. It is the duty of the overseas Minister of Militia, to table that report during the present session so that we may have full knowledge of the conditions of things overseas.
Now, Mr. Speaker, coming to the charges made by General Smart. General Smart.
I need not say, is a well known citizen oi Westmount, and represents that constituency in the Legislature of Quebec. He enlisted during the early days of the great war; he rallied to the colours the yeomanry of Westmount and Montreal, and crossed the ocean in the early fall of 1914, remaining overseas until quite recently. He served his King and country faithfully and gallantly.
Brigadier-General Smart said the other day that, now that the war was over, he felt it his duty to tell the people of Canada that the moving factors in the whole administration of the medical service branch of the Canadian army in England were patronage, influence and pull. He gave facts and data concerning the evil treatment and abuse of our sick and wounded soldiers, and he traced all these troubles, all this scandalous state of affairs, to the evil influence of what is called Argyll House, and especially to the interference of Sir George Perley, the High Commissioner.
Let me quote briefly what General Smart says about the medical service in England.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
I will read what General Smart said, and my hon. friend may draw his own conclusions. He said:
I feel It is up to me to tell the people of Canada how the Canadian Medical Service blundered overseas; how patronage, influence, pull, went to paralyse the good work of the medical services.

I perfectly know who is responsible for this state of things; official Ottawa knows it too; Sir Robert Borden does not ignore it, but no one dares tell. And that is why I feel it is up to me to show all the evil that has been done, to show the abuse, the ill-treatment our wounded and sick received overseas at the hands of the improperly managed1 medical service. The whole trouble is to be traced to Argyll House.
And I may add that personally, after seeing all that I have seen, X have not the slightest confidence in those who administer the affairs in England.
I pass over the uncomplimentary references he makes to Sir George Perley; also -because this should come up later-what he says about the death of General Steele. He goes on to say:
Gentlemen, X tell you, without fear of impartial contradiction, that the medical service overseas was directed in an insensible and neglected way. Our Canadian wounded were afforded a medical service that was absolutely inadequate, and I have seen instances where medical officers, ridiculously inapt to care for the sick and wounded, were put in charge of important hospital units. I have pitied the poor soldiers that were made to travel through the British Isles to far-off hospitals when they passed close to the unit that should have received them for their particular treatment.
So it would appear that this happened in England. I quote further:
He stated instances where men medically found unfit in Canada, were, however, sent to England. These men cause hard work and worry to the officers overseas,, went through hardships, and are now coming back a charge to the country, for they will be getting pay pension all at the expense of the country.
Then General Smart told of what he saw in his own military district of Shorncliffe, which again justifies my saying that his words have special reference to what happened in England. (Reading):
He said he could not criticise the medical officers and nurses. They were up to what he had expected from them, but, he says, I feel I must and do criticize the headquarters of management of this service.
General Smart said that each Canadian hospital had its full staff of competent doctors and nurses, but outside of these hospitals, there had been organized Voluntary Aid Detachments, made up of people of good-will, but who knew little or nothing of medical care, and he stated instances where soldiers were left for definite treatment in these Voluntary Aid Detachments while cots were empty in the regular hospitals. He stated that, in eases he knew of, men-
This is a very serious accusation. ' (Reading) :
He stated that in cases he knew of, men had lost the use of their eyes because of this practice. When such cases reached the proper hospitals, said Generol Smart, it was too late for treatment to have any effect.
General Smart then mentioned cases where patronage placed in responsible posts men who 
had not even diplomas of medical studies, while competent men without the "pull" were kept in England or in posts where their science and experience could not be used to succour our wounded and sick.
Talking of the riot, General Smart said that the Rhyl outbreak was not the first of this kind; there had been outbreaks previously at Shorncliffe, Witley, Bramshott, and even at Rhyl before.
This is the gist of the charges made by Brigadier-General Smart. They are not new, Mr. Speaker, in this House. During the sessions of 1916 rumours came to us that the medical service overseas had been impaired through the intrusion of outside influence. The member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) denounced that intrusion and the fussiness of certain people in the Old Country. The Government appointed Colonel Bruce to investigate. I have no't the honour of knowing Colonel Bruce personally, but I know from some medical friends that he enjoys the highest reputation in the part of the country in which he lives; indeed, he is known as one of the best surgeons in Canada. The Government, then, appointed Colonel Bruce to investigate the conditions said to exist in connection with the medical service in England. His report created quite a sensation.
I have here the conclusions of that report, divided into twenty-three parts, each of which is a charge against the administration of the medical service in England. Bet me refer briefly to those conclusions. It was in September, 1916, that Dr. Bruce was deputed by the then Minister of Militia ' and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes) to conduct this investigation. His report says:
1.	Many soldiers are arriving in England from Canada medically unfit, who should never have been enlisted.
2.	The system of disposing of casualties from the front to Imperial hospitals in England, Wales, Scotland and Ireland, is extremely unsatisfactory.
3.	The present method of having Canadian hospitals scattered over a large area is very objectionable.
4.	There is unnecessary detention in hospitals. There has been no medical inspection by the Canadian Medical Service of Canadian soldiers in Imperial hospitals, and there has been no efficient medical inspection of Canadian hospitals, in consequence of which Canadian soldiers are retained in hospitals in Great Britain, many of whom would have been returned to duty and others should have been returned to Canada, where they could have been more economically and efficiently treated. The lack of system permits of the aimless moving of patients from hospital to hospital.
5.	The use by the Canadian service of Voluntary Aid Hospitals is very undesirable as they are inefficient, expensive and unsatisfactory.
6.	The administration of the group of 57 Voluntary Aid Hospitals under Shorncliffe Military Hospital by the Canadian Medical Service is unsatisfactory and expensive.

7.	The present method of operating, jointly with the Red Cross, certain hospitals built and equipped by them is unsatisfactory. Such dual control is undesirable.
8.	Impropriety of detailing Canadian Army Medical Corps personnel to Imperial hospitals and still retaining them on Canadian pay-roll.
9.	Unsatisfactory situation at Shomcliffe owing to our Canadian A.D.M.S. acting in a similar capacity over a large area for the Imperial authorities.
10.	No attempt has been made to restrict surgical operations which produce no increased military efficiency.
11.	The installation of an expensive plant at Ramsgate was inadvisable, as a large number of cases treated there should be 6ent to Canada for treatment.
12.	The establishment at Buxton of a special hospital for the treatment of rheumatics which is ill-advised as the majority of rheumatics will not be fit again for active service and could be better and more cheaply treated in Canada.
13.	The present system of handling Canadian venereal patients is very strongly condemned.
14.	The method of handling infectious diseases is most unsatisfactory.
15.	Medical Boards which regulate the classification of casualties when convalescent have not been adequately provided for.
16.	Satisfactory records regarding individual casualties are not available.
17.	The exceedingly important question oi pensions, which will involve the expenditure of large sums of money by Canada annually has been neglected by the Canadian Medical Service.
18.	Lack of co-ordination in the Canadian Medical Service between Canada, England and the front.
19.	The medical personnel is not being used to the best advantage.
20.	The policy of the department has been opposed to the use of experienced medical and surgical consulting specialists.
21.	Discontent concerning promotions, especially in regard to regimental medical officers serving at the front.
22.	The Canadian Army Medical Corps training school in England has never been properly organized, although of the greatest importance to the Canadian Medical Service.
23.	In the operation of the Medical Service sufficient regard has not been paid to economy in management.
Such are very briefly the conclusions of the report made by Colonel Bruce at the request of the Government. That information was handed to the Government, and Sir George Perley, who was then Acting Minister of Militia overseas, found the report so severe against the Government of which he was a member that he thought, by appointing another commission, the Government might, perhaps evade the responsibility which they bore. As if Dr. Bruce had not been an authority on such matters-and besides he was surrounded by some of the ablest men-another commissioner, Sir William Babtie, an Imperial officer who had seen service in Mesopotamia, was appointed with other commissioners, the object of the new commission being to investigate Dr. Bruce's commission-a most ridiculous state of affairs. Sir William Babtie, however, reported on the whole matter, and, strange to say, he, biased as he was, had to admit that 18 out of the 23 charges made by Dr. Bruce were found to be true; but practically nothing was done. What do'we find? We find that the Government, or, rather, Sir George Perley, instead of standing by a Canadian officer appointed by the Government who had fearlessly done his duty by the Canadian army, practically dismisses Dr. Bruce and gets him another appointment in France through the Imperial Government.
