I have received many letters from far distant places, approving my stand in exposing this matter and offering to furnish me with ample evidence, if required, to substantiate my statements.
We have won the war against the Huns but we still have a heavy task on our hands to clean up the rottenness that exists in high places and which those in power seem disposed to cover up.
I have acted as I have done solely from a sense of duty and have refrained from going into many details that would only wound afresh the hearts of those who have already suffered much, but if the government persist in their present unwise policy of attempting to protect
those who should be dismissed from office, no matter how high a position they hold, then it may be necessary to publish further details. I am a firm believer in a continuance of the Union Government for some years to come

I must say his faith is greater than mine.
-but the present administration will have to show greater capacity and more backbone if it is to hold the confidence of the public.
Further on he says:
But whether that administration was a bit ' of statesmanship or a crafty and discreditable political plot will be more apparent when the people of Canada realize the magnitude of the pension burden which has been thrown upon the country by the conditions of which I have complained, the injustices which will re-act upon the veterans of the war and the needless suffering and waste which this administration produced.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that after such an arraignment, coming from a responsible officer of the rank of Brigadier-General Smart, the Government cannot do otherwise than appoint investigators to probe this whole matter. These are very specific charges. It is no answer to say that he refers to conditions existing in 1916, for he declares positively that the same condition of things has continued since that year. Can these specific and serious charges be ignored? These things are not very complimentary to the administration of Sir George Perley, but he is not the only one who has complained of the activities of Sir George Perley in connection with the Overseas administration. Although Sir George Perley is a knight and/ is High Commissioner of Canada in England, he must not forget neither must any one else forget, that he is a paid servant of Canada. We vote his salary at every session of Parliament, and therefore he is amenable to this Parliament. I must repeat again, that it is no answer to say that the war is over. I can well understand that when the war was on there might have been state reasons why certain matters-for instance, the reply of Dr. Bruce to Sir William Babtie-should not be tabled. But now that the war is over the Government should have sufficient confidence in Parliament, which was, to say the least, very liberal and generous to them, and in the taxpayers of Canada to tell the whole truth, not only as regards the contents of Dr. Bruce's report, but also as regards that mysterious Jenkins report, which, as I	am informed, contains

While discussing the returned soldier, Col. Price spoke of the high cost of living which had prevailed in Canada for some time. "I had to pay 68 cents a pound for bacon when I came back," he said, "and I don't know whether to blame the United Farmers of Ontario or Sir Joseph Flavelle. but I know that it was between them. subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
To the administration service. As regards the doctors, General Smart seems to say that they were good men, but their services were not utilized. Sir George Perley scattered the wounded and sick all over England, Scotland and Wales,-even Ireland,-in order to promote, as he said, " the cause of Imperialism. The blending of Australians, New Zealanders, Canadians, Englishmen and Welshmen would make for a greater and better Empire.'' That was the definition of Sir George Perley. I remember at the time when this question was discussed in the Press, a lady, well known in Montreal, who has taken a very active part in the V. A. D. organization in England, stated that the reason given for the scattering oi our boys all over the country instead oi centralizing them at our Canadian hospitals, organized by Canada and placed under the care and control of our own doctors, was for " the sacred cause of Imperialism." General Smart, who is a good Imperialist himself, says in his speech, "If that is Im-

perialism you talk of, then I aim not an Imperialist."
Coming back to the Rhyl riots, an inquiry took place and a verdict was rendered on the 27th of March last. Here is the verdict:
That the soldiers came to their deaths by the wounds described by the doctors, but that there is no evidence to show how the wounds were inflicted. Evidence was taken which showed that both the rioters and the defenders of the camp fired ball ammunition, but no one was identified as having actually killed one of the soldiers.
Not a word as, to the cause of the riots or the responsibility for them. This is an extraordinary verdict. The surprise of the public in Canada with regard to it is expressed in the following article from such a responsible paper as the Montreal Gazette, of March 31:	,
A meaningless verdict was returned by the coroner's jury which inquired into the cause of the deaths of the victims of the Kinmel Camp riots. If any one is to be punished, it will be as the result of military inquiry and court martial. A military inquiry has been held, the results of which will be learned in time.
And further on the Gazette says:
This, as well as the fact that men were killed in the course of the demonstrations, is to be remembered in forming judgment on the unhappy incident and its causes, the whole truth in regard to which has yet to be made public.
So that the verdict is most unsatisfactory, and this inquiry held by the coroner should be implemented at the earliest moment by the Government in order that Canada may know what caused the riots and how it was that Canadian boys were killed and were buried so unceremoniously as they were on that occasion. This is one of the worst tragedies of the war. Our boys were sent overseas to fight, to die, if need be, for liberty. Their sacrifice was great, but because of the sacredness of the cause, they bore the burden with equanimity all through this long war. Now we hear of riots on the occasion of their return to England prior to their coming home. Some of them are murdered in a cold-blooded manner. Some of them are languishing in dungeons in the Tower of London. Others are left penniless on the streets of London. Others are exploited by Shylocks and grafters. Yet, when such facts as these are brought to light, the Acting Prime Minister, with a wave of the hand, simply denies the charges in toto and says that this one or that one may come back from England in the near future with similar charges, and that his denial in the case of Brigadier-General Smart will be his denial of all other similar charges. This is a very poor answer indeed.

The charges are made by responsible officers holding high rank, friends of the Government. It may be that during the war the Government had some excuse for not covering the charges that were made. But now, speaking on behalf of the boys, speaking on behalf of Canadians generally, I say that an investigation is urgent. The Government owe it to Canada, owe it to the returned soldiers, owe it to themselves as a Government. The widest powers were given to the Government by a benevolent Parliament and a benevolent public during the four years of the war. Is it against the public interest that the truth be known? I always go back to England, the mother of Parliaments, for my precedents. In England, whether during the bright days of victory or during the black and bleak days of defeat, public men are not afraid of the truth; they are not afraid to speak boldly. During the South African war, when there was a surrender of British troops in the veldt,- much against the grain of Britishers generally-the Government granted an investigation, and court-martials and inquiries were held. If you go back to the eighteenth century, at the time of the famous Marlborough charges, you will find that the British Government granted an investigation while a war was in progress. During the Seven Years' war, Admiral Byng, with all his glorious career behind him, was the subject of an inquiry, and' at the time of the Napoleonic Wars, Lord Melville was impeached as the result of a naval inquiry. And at the time of the Crimean war, when it was discovered that the commissariat of the British troops had failed, the Duke of Newcastle was removed during the war and replaced by Lord Panmure. As to the matter under discussion, the war is over, and here are specific and serious charges, made not by civilians, but by returned officers who served faithfully their King and country during four successive years, who hold the highest rank in Canadian armies, and who are friends of the Government in office-yet the Government would disregard these accusations. I say that the sooner an investigation is granted the better for the Government and the better for the country. I repeat that the Gov-vernment should hold such an investigation. They owe it to the country; they owe it to the soldiers, both the living and the dead.
Major-General MEWBUR'N (Minister of Militia and Defence):	Mr. Speaker, in
opening his somewhat lengthy statement, during which he has covered almost the entire period from the beginning of the war in 1914 down to the present date, the hon. gentleman (Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux) was good enough to say that I as Minister of Militia was not responsible for what took place before my regime.
I feel in a somewhat delicate position, because, when I accepted office, I was aware that there was an Overseas Minister of Militia authorized by Parliament, and that the Minister of Militia in Canada was not in any way responsible for anything that took place in the administration, organization, or direction of the Canadian forces after they left Canada, that matter being in charge of the Overseas Minister of Militia, who was charged with the responsibility therefor. Nevertheless, in so far as in my power lies, I am prepared to take the responsibility of defending to the best of my ability any officers absent on duty overseas, whom I consider to be slandered, or as having mud thrown at them without cause. I do not know whether any hon. gentleman has ever experienced the sensation of being a legatee, but when I was burdened with the responsibility of the administration of the Militia Department I felt it was a pretty large legacy that was given to me. I looked upon it as the young man did whose father left him a very large estate, who thought it was a wonderful thing to have this big estate to manage, and who took upon himself the burden and responsibility of managing it. About a year afterwards, when a friend asked him how he was getting along, he said: "Well, I know the responsibilities are somewhat heavy, and I almost wish my father were alive again." Well, Sir, I sometimes wish that one of my predecessors were back again in harness.

I say, without fear of contradiction from any impartial source, that the medical administration overseas has been bad.
Further on he says:
In the area that I commanded at Shorncliffe, in addition to other units, I had seven hospitals under my command

four of them special hospitals, two dealing with shell-shock cases, one hospital for eyes, ears, nose, and throat, and one for venereal diseases, all of which were under me for administration and discipline.
Therefore, General Smart in his own statement almost contradicts his own charges, as he admits that he was responsible for the administration and discipline of all those hospitals in his area, and, consequently, if the administration was faulty, General Smart himself would be responsible. He goes on in a general way to blame High Commissioner Sir George Per-ley for certain things and then he proceeds to blame Sir William Babtie. I have no brief for General Babtie; I know Colonel Bruce intimately and he is one of the finest medical officers the Dominion of Canada has ever produced. I have never had an opportunity of seeing or reading either the Babtie report or the Bruce report; but General Smart according to his statement, regards Sir William Babtie as though he had been discharged from the British army and was not a responsible man at all, although General Smart complains about his being responsible for the break-down. I notice from what I saw a few days,ago that this same Sir William Babtie, as reported in the British Hansard of the 7th of June, 1918, was "not only under no personal as-
[Major-General Mewburn.]
persion from Mesopotamia investigation, but has since been advanced to Inspector of Medical Services. Babtie has also been promoted to Lieut-General." I imagine, therefore, that Sir William Babtie is pretty highly thought of in the British army today. General Smart goes on to say in his statement to complain that the recommendations regarding the hospitals made in the Bruce report were not adopted; he says that practically all of Col. Bruce's recommendations were turned down. But in another paragraph he says:
Practically every recommendation made by Col. Bruce has since been adopted and put into effect by General Poster, showing that they were sound.
That shows that, no matter what the Bruce report was and the Babtie report was General Smart, in his statement in the Quebec Legislature, said that all the recommendations made by Col. Bruce were put into effect. The statement he makes is that he wants an investigation into certain things that happened in 1915 and 1916, particularly in 1916. That is some three years ago, and General Smart himself admits that those recommendations of Colonel Bruce have been put into effect. .General Smart, as I said before, was an officer who was in charge of the Shorncliffe area. I have know him for many years, and I have always known him to be an officer who took an interest in the active Militia in Canada. Far be it from me to criticise General Smart who is, I believe, highly recognized as an officer and held in high esteem by his brother officers; but why is he making these statements at this late date on his return to Canada, I am not prepared to say. General Smart went overseas in 1915; he proceeded to France, I understand, in October, 1915, and he was returned to England on December 13, 1915. I understand that altogether General Smart's services in France covered 78 days. He was returned to England for service in England and I understand that subsequently he took over the Shorncliffe command.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
I know my hon. friend desires to be absolutely fair. He mentioned that General Smart was only in France 78 days. Did General Smart refuse to accept service in France, or did he only obey the orders that were given to him.
Major-General MEWBURN: I am not saying anything to belittle General Smart's good-will, but General Smart, I am informed, had actually 78 days' service in France, during part of which time he was in a convalescent hospital.

On the reorganization of the Mounted Rifles he was offered the command, but declined it, contending that he should have been made brigadier-general, which he had been continuously urging since 1915. Then when the policy was adopted that no officer should hold a position in England who had not had six months' service in France, the overseas forces in France were asked if they could use him, and they replied -that -there was no employment for him with the rank of colonel in France. I am not suggesting for one moment that Colonel Smart was not prepared to serve in France from -the start;
I am only giving the actual facts. I was going on to say that General Smart did command the Shorncliffe area. When I was in England in July of last year, he did me the kindness to call on me. I saw him on more than one occasion, and he knew that I was Minister of Militia in Canada, but never at any time did he intimate to me that there was anything wrong in any part of the services, medical or otherwise. If he had knowledge at that time that the administration of the Medical Services was faulty or wrong, or that -there had been -maladministration, why was he not frank enough to tell me, as Minister of Militia in Canada? Several of General Smart's friends came to see me while I was in England, and asked if I could get him a permanent military -position in Canada. My reply was that I should he very glad to do what I could for him, but that I was not ma-king-and I have not made, and I am not making-any permanent military appointments, because those positions are being reserved for men who have seen service in France.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext: Was not the proper course for General Smart, if he had complaints to make, to make them to the Minister of Militia overseas, and not to the Minister of Militia in Canada?

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
Perfectly true. I am just pointing out that if he had all these worries over there, one would have thought he would have mentioned them to me. Subsequently, the Shorncliffe command was practically done away with as the troops were moved from there, and I went out of my way to see if any further employment could be found for General Smart in England. After that command, I do not know what employment he did have until he was returned to Canada and transferred to the C.E.F. Reserve. If General Smart, while he was in command at Shorncliffe
95i
or since then, had any knowledge of maladministration or had any reason to believe there had been wrong-doing, then it was his duty to bring the matter to the attention of the Overseas Minister of Militia. But I am not aware of his having done so, though he had ample opportunity.
The hon. member (Mr. Lemieux) has re-fered to a report of Lt.-Colonel Jenkins. I was asked a question in the House early in the session regarding the Jenkins' report, and I replied that I had no knowledge of it;
I never heard of it. I referred the matter to Sir Edward Kemp. I may not he correct, but I surmise that if Lt.-Colonel Jenkins did make a report-and this is only a surmise-it was for the information of the overseas minister, and not for the Government. It may have been for some personal use; I do not know. The fact remains that that report has never come to the Militia Department here, or to the Government so far as I am aware.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
There is no such thing as a report made for a minister personally.
A report of that nature is made for the department, for the Government, and for Parliament.
Major-General MEWBURN: That is perfectly true. I say that the report may have been made at Sir Edward Kemp's personal request or for him, but that so far as I know it has never reached the Militia Department or the Government here.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
Shall we get the report later on?
Major-General MEWBURN: I was going to refer later on, but I may as well do it now, to General Smart's reference in his letter to three water-tight compartments in France, England, and Canada, and his statement that there is no co-operation, and that intrigue is going on. I wish to say in the most emphatic manner possible that since I have been Minister of Militia in Canada the relationship between the Overseas Minister, Sir Edward Kemp, and myself, has been most harmonious. There has been the closest co-operation between us in our respective spheres of activity. I know that Sir Edward Kemp fully intended to return to Canada so that he could make a statement to the House this session regarding his administration overseas, but hon. members must be well aware how impossible it has been for him to leave his post during the terrible trial of demobilization that he has had on his hands since the armistice was signed, and up to the present time. I know

that it is his full intention to return to Canada at the earliest possible moment, and before this House prorogues, for the purpose of making a full statement of his administration. I wish to repeat most emphatically, that ever since he has been Minister of Militia overseas, and since I have held the position of 'Minister of Militia of Canada, there has been the very closest co-operation and harmony between us, although Sir Edward Kemp is in no way under my control, being a minister of the Crown and responsible to the Government, not to me.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
Does not General Smart's
complaint refer, not to the lack of co-operation between the Minister of Militia overseas and the Minister of Militia in Canada, but to the lack of co-opefation between the commands of the Canadian Expeditionary Force and between the various departments?
Major-General MEWBURN:	No. He
says distinctly that there is no co-operation between the Department of Militia and Defence in Canada and the Minister of Militia overseas.
Mr. LEM1EUX:	Referring to the Jenkins report, whioh I understood the minister to say had been made to Sir Edward Kemp personally, if it is true, as is rumoured and as far as my information goes, that a leakage of 510,000,000 has been discovered, does not the minister think that that report ought to be tabled?
Major-General MEWBURN: As a matter of fact, I do not know if there is such a thing as the Jenkins report, except for what has been said by my hon. friend this afternoon and by the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) about three weeks ago. The hon. member read a statement this afternoon that a report had been submitted to the Overseas Minister of Militia. If there is such a report, the Overseas Minister of Militia when he returns to Canada will be prepared to answer fully any questions with regard to it.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
Can you not cable him in the meantime?
Major-General MEWBURN:	I have already cabled to ascertain if he has such a report.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
What was his answer?
Major-General MEWBURN: I have had no definite answer. Regarding the treatment of Canadian soldiers overseas, I had the privilege of being in England and France last July and August, when I vis-
(Major-Generai Mewburn.]
ited very many hospitals in both countries and saw a majority of the medical officers, and I never heard of one single complaint regarding the treatment of Canadian soldiers either in France or in England. I may say further, that an officer from Canada proceeded overseas in July of 1918, a doctor of very high standing in his profession, Dr. Charles Martin, of Montreal. He has been over there since, and he has visited every single hospital in France and in England where Canadians are being treated. He has informed me that he has heard no complaints but, on the other hand, that there are no patients in any of the Allied Armies who receive such admirable treatment as do the Canadians in the Canadian hospitals. I think, Sir, that the statement that our Canadian invalid soldiers have not been properly treated oi have been neglected is nothing short of a slander on the medical profession. If there is one service in the whole war more outstanding than any other it is the medical service, and I think that the citizens of Canada have reason to be deeply indebted to our magnificent doctors who, neglecting all that was profitable to them in civil life, went to the front to help our soldiers. The surgeons and doctors who went overseas in the early days of the war, and who continued to go steadily until the armistice was signed, abandoned lucrative practices, many of them giving up thousands oi dollars a year in order that they might serve their country. I do not think that anything is too good for these splendid men.
A few days ago I received a couple of letters which indicate the opinion which some people have on the question of the treatment of Canadian soldiers, and one of these letters I shall read:
I thought perhaps that you would like to see the enclosed extract from the last letter which has just come to hand from my son Austin, officially Major C. A. Bell, M.C. and Bar, 3rd Bn. Engineers, who you may remember was dreadfully wounded August Sth last at the opening day of the battle of Amiens, losing both legs below the knees and the right eye.
In sending this I do so not so much for the item of news but as an evidence of his wonderful early recovery. As an original first campaigner, badly wounded twice before, one would have thought, so the politicians tell us, that these hardships would have undermined his constitution, but not so. Thanks to the skill of such surgeons as Col. Armour and eye specialists at the I.O.D.E. hospital as well as the constant personal attention of the nursing sisters, among them Miss Robertson, matron of the Christie St. Hospital, he has made a wonderful quick recovery.
Unfortunately our soldier boys do not tell us of the names of their attending surgeons and it is left to chance for the folks at home to find

out to whom they are indebted for the wonderful work that has been done in this respect.
I am persuaded that one great reason of Austin's quick recovery has been his spirit of optimism and good cheer as well as his belief that he was not yet done for. One of his college chums just returned told me that Austin had counted upon returning to France, figuring the war would last a long time, and believing that he could still make good behind the lines.
1 trust. Sir, that in due time the people of Canada will find out the names of the surgeons and nursing sisters who have been satisfied to work out of the " limelight," only looking for results.
I have received one or two other letters written in the same strain, and it fairly makes my blood boil lo bear people criticising the work of the medical profession in this war, in view of the splendid, indeed the wonderful service our doctors have rendered.
General Smart has referred to the case of General Sir Sam Steele, and I feel it my duty to make a statement regarding that matter, because General Smart blames the Militia Department in Canada for certain alleged treatment as a result of which General Steele, it is said, died of a broken heart. I am at a loss to know why a man of General Smart's standing should make such statements. General Steele was an officer who was held in the very highest esteem and admiration by every Canadian who had the pleasure of his acquaintance. He had served continuously in the Royal Northwest Mounted Police for some twenty-nine years, and he went to South Africa where he served with great distinction. Returning to Canada he was granted leave of absence from the Northwest Mounted Police, without pay, from the first of June, 1902, to enable him to accept a commission in the South African Constabulary. His leave was extended to 1903 when he was finally retired from the Northwest Mounted Police on pension. When the war broke out the then Minister of Militia, in the winter of 1914, appointed him Acting Inspector General of Western Canada. He subsequently proceeded overseas, the intention being, I think, that he should take command of the Second Canadian Division.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
He went over in command of the Second Division.
Major-General MEWBURN:	Before he
left here he met with an accident in Toronto, and unfortunately he suffered another accident in England. He was in France for a very short time, returned to England and was given a command under the Imperial Government, known as the South Eastern Command in England, being in the pay of the Canadian Government. IHe continued in that command until sometime last year when it was practically abolished. Prior to that, the first I knew of General Steele's retiring, or of there being no employment for him, was the intimation from England that the Imperials did not require his services any longer because they had sufficient British officers available.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
I think the real reason was that Dover, which is in the South Eastern District, was established as a separate command of its own, and therefore General Steele would be only a Canadian officer after that.
Major-General MEWBURN: Well, there was no further employment for him, and! although General Steele's ability and experience were highly regarded by the Imperials, they said that his services would have to be dispensed with, not because of any inefficiency, but simply as a matter of administration. I had several letters from General Steele who made every effort to be retained on the strength on pay until the war was over.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
Was it on account ol his age?
Major-General MEWBURN:	No, but
simply because there was no further employment for him. As there was no employment for him in England or in Canada the only alternative was to pension him.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
If the minister requested the overseas military authorities to keep General Steele on the strength and they did not do so, is that one of the examples of the cordial co-operation that exists between the Overseas people and this ministry?
Major-General MEWBURN: I did not ask the Overseas ministry to keep him on .the strength. There was no further employment for him, and naturally in such a case he would go on pension because his time had expired and he was' three years over age. General Steele asked me, as a personal request, if he might be permitted to take his discharge in England instead of coming to Canada for discharge, and I gladly coh-sented, and he was retired on a pension of $2,485. As to his having died of a broken heart, I may say that I have a certificate from Colonel J. A. Roberts, F.R.C.S., who was his medical adviser, in which he replied to a telephone conversation that I had with him when that statement appeared. I very much regret having

to refer to this matter, but under the circumstances I think it is my duty to read Colonel Roberts' reply:
Replying to your telephone conversation regarding my professional associations with the late Major General Sir Sam Steele, I would state that I performed the necessary operation subsequent to his accidental injury at Exhibition Camp, Toronto, in April, 19J.5.
Again in August of 1915 I attended him at Shorncliffe, England, when he was thrown from his automobile and sustained a slight concussion of the brain.
Approximately fourteen months ago General Steel consulted me at his home in Putney, London, and it was learned that he was suffering from diabetes. This condition persisted for over a year, to my knowledge, and in my opinion was directly responsible for his death.
(Signed) J. A. Roberts, F.R.C.S., Eng.
My hon. friend referred to Argyli House, which seems to be the most unpopular place there is in England according to some of the press. Give a dog a bad name and it never leaves him. Argyll House, as 1 have no doubt that many hon. members of this House know, is the headquarters of the administrative service in England and of the overseas forces. In the early stages of the war I understand there was considerable complaint about the administration and the handling of the officers coming from Canada. I heard it. Lots of us heard it. My gracious, if it were a case of investigating everything, I could myself make hundreds of complaints, but I do not know what good it is going to do. I think one of the troubles that existed at Argyll House was largely due to the number of battalions that went overseas in the earlier days oi the war and which of necessity had to be broken up. There were many officers and there was no employment for them. I think that the mannerisms of some of the young officers at Argyll House caused some of the trouble. But I will say that when I was in England in 1918 I heard no complaints about Argyll House. I was in all the camps in England and France. In July 1918 the Overseas Minister laid down the policy that all officers fit for general service who had not served in France would not be given employment in England except in very special cases. I know that as far back as June, 1918, there was a total of 67, all ranks, employed in Argyll House of whom 49 had actually seen service in the front line with the troops in France, 11 were either over age or unfit, and only 7 had not actually seen service in France. The policy which was then adopted by the Overseas Minister has been adhered to from that time on in all the camps in England -any officer, if employed in any of these
[ Major-General Mewburn.]
camps, who had not seen service, had to get out.
There is no special charge against Argyll House. I have no brief for Argyll House. General Smart and Colonel Pratt speak of the intrigue that is going on. When I was in France, during July, 1918, I found, from my observation and from talking with officers of all ranks, and non-commissioned officers and men in very many of the units, that there was the happiest co-operation. I found that the most wonderful team play existed in France from General Currie down to the latest recruit. I found in Eng. land that everybody had the utmost respect and esteem for General Currie. I never found any evidence of intrigue going on. On the other hand, I found that there was the most cordial co-operation. There may have been many complaints made; officers may have had personal grievances, but I have no knowledge of any complaints about Argyll House as to its administrative character.
As to the statements of Colonel Pratt, I may say that he went overseas in 1916. He had never had any military experience, as had General Smart, prior to 1916, when he was appointed Lieut.-Colonel and authorized to raise the 133rd Battalion of Norfolk county. Colonel Pratt, in conjunction with an old political enemy, although a great friend, Mr. Hal B.' Donly, of Simcoe, worked night and day-

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
Of the Simcoe Reformer?
Major-General MEWBURN: Yes; the Reformer and the old Tory pretty nearly slept together during that campaign, but they did some splendid work and set a fine example to other places in Canada. * They worked hard and they recruited some 800 men within that county when it was not so easy to get men. Colonel Pratt took his battalion to camp that summer. He went overseas with 665 men. His battalion was broken up within ten days after he got there. Colonel Pratt was employed with the British at Dunkirk, in France, and how long he was there I cannot say.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
A good man?
Major-General MEWBURN: Do you mean as a military man?

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
As a military man.
Major-General MEWBURN: His experience as a soldier began when he took command of the battalion. I cannot make any statement about his ability as a military man, but I know that he worked hard to raise that battalion. He had in camp when

I happened to be there same 800 men and he took 665 men overseas.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
Had he had any previous military experience?
Major-General MEWBURN: I understand none whatever.
Colonel PECK -. Have you any confidential report on Colonel Pratt?
Major-General MEWBURN: There is on file a confidential report on every officer.
I do not know that it is for me to present any confidential report here on Colonel Pratt or General Smart. There have been confidential reports in connection with several officers. Colonel Pratt was in France, at Dunkirk, and was employed by the British. I saw Colonel Pratt in England last summer. He was then employed by the British, but he was not doing any military duty at that time. He told me that he was coming to Canada to look into the flax industry. I understand he did proceed to Canada in connection with the flax industry. I think in its relation to aeroplanes. As I say, I saw Colonel Pratt over there and 1 had a long chat with him. He and I have always been good friends and I have a great admiration for the way in which he took up the work of raising his battalion. I met him in Toronto not long ago before he had proceeded to England again. I have heard of him since he came back from England.
I do not propose to enter at any length into these statements which have appeared in the press particularly in regard to Rhyl. Colonel Pratt was not there and he could not have spoken authoritatively. I would like to point out to my hon. friend from iMaisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) that what he read was simply the report of the coroner's inquest. I may state that there is a court of inquiry now being held whose duty is not yet completed. [DOT] It is making a most thorough investigation of the whole trouble at the Rhyl camp and the report of that inquiry no doubt will be made public in due course.
Mr. MoGIBBON (Muskoka):	In order
to be perfectly fair to Colonel Pratt is it not a fact that Colonel Pratt has on record an application, repeated no less than three times, to be allowed to revert in order to get into the trenches and serve there?
Major-General MEWBURN: I would not deny that but I have no knowledge of it; that application would be overseas. I can say quite frankly that I think Colonel Pratt is a man who would be just as willing to go
to the front as a private as he would be to go to the front as an officer, but as to any letter from him asking to be allowed to revert, I am not in a position to know.
I do not know what age he is but I presume that he would be considerably over 35 years and it therefore would not be permissible under regulations to allow him to go to the front.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
Would not my hon
friend say that also of General Smart?
Major-General MEWBURN:	I dare say
that General Smart would be equally willing; I have not the slightest doubt but that he would. I was informed that he was offered the command of a mounted rifle battalion which he declined, but I do not know the details as to that. An application was made to us that General Smart should proceed to France but the trouble was that we could not have him proceed there with the rank of Colonel. I have the highest respect for General Smart and for Colonel Pratt.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
I think I can explain that point. The cavalry went over at a certain strength. We broke up the regiment and formed it into a battalion in order that there might be no trouble in holding a certain part of the front. Colonel Smart was supplanted, but not through any fault of his own. Before the debate closes I will give my version of Colonel Smart s case in regard to this battalion at the front. Everything was honourable and straightforward, with regard to Col. Smart. He was a most efficient officer, but his health failed him.
Major-General MEWBURN: I have never suggested for one moment that Colonel Smart was not a most efficient officer and an officer held in very high esteem, but I do object to these charges being scattered around broadcast. The hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) made a statement regarding the trouble at Rhyl camp -speaking of Colonel Pratt's charges-with regard to holding back the Olympic and other large transports. As early as January 10, I had considerable cable communications with the Overseas Minister, and I then dealt with the question of speeding up the demobilization of the Canadian troops, advising him what we had been able to do regarding the use of various ships, and that we had arranged for five ships to repatriate civilians, when it was decided not to bring civilians back on the troopships. I also advised that we had

arranged for some 24 or 25 ships to accommodate troops. I need not read the cable, because it only goes into the question of disembarkation and the number of troops we could handle, information that I have already given to the House, but I may say that at that time these ships had broken away from the Ministry of Shipping and I sent the following cable overseas:
Agents here have not yet been able to obtain rates on Olympic, Aquitania, and Mauretania. Please negotiate direct with companies and cable rates quoted by them for confirmation by War Purchasing Commission.
We were attempting at that early date to secure those ships, and we only succeeded a short time ago in getting the Olympic back; the other boats have not yet been given back to us. But we have been doing everything in our power since December and January to secure those ships to bring back our men.
With regard to the trouble at Rhyl camp, I would not attempt to say what occasioned it until I see the full report of the court of inquiry
With respect to Col. Pratt's charges about the Flying Corps men being left stranded in England, the article my hon. friend read from the press appeared in the London papers, and it was repeated here. I may also read a cable from London which says:
Lt.-Col. Pratt's bribery accusations in the Ontario Legislature, evoked expressions of the deepest resentment at the military headquarters here. The feeling is these particularly mean attacks on defenceless officers, are the outcome of personal spite, or, the disgruntled failure of those whose own military career can in no way be considered successful.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext: Who signs it?

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
What paper did it appear in?	,
Major-General MEWBURN: This was in the Montreal Star.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
What paper was it published in in England?
Major-General MEWBURN: It is a special Star cable.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext: It may be signed by Sir George Perley.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
It may be signed by Windermere.
Major-General MEWBURN: It is not signed by anybody. This cable continues:
Regarding the charges of bribery from airmen, this statement is absolutely denied. It i* pointed out that the charges must be untrue, because the Canadian Headquarters exercise no control over the repatriation of Canadians in [Major-General Mewburn.]
the Royal Air Force, the sole responsibility resting with the Air Ministry.
I may say that when I heard there was any suggestion of any Canadians in the Royal Air Force not getting proper attention in regard to repatriation, I cabled twice to Sir Edward Kemp, and I took the responsibility of stating that if there were any Canadians from the Imperial service who were having difficulty in getting back to Canada he was to look after them and see that free transportation was furnished.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
What answer did you receive from Sir Edward Kemp? T
Major-General MEWBURN:	I received
no definite information. I did not think any answer was necessary. I simply requested him to take action. Some of those men came by New York; in fact they came any way they liked. There may be a few isolated cases of distress, but I am not aware of any. Mr. CYRUS W. PECK (Skeena): I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that we are all very gratified to see the Opposition showing a lively interest in the soldier. It is a little late, but at the same timeiMr. McMASTER:	I rise to a point of

In a Pickwickian

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
And I have no hesitation in withdrawing what my hon. friend takes exception to. I would be the last man in this House to impugn the loyalty and honour of the hon. members of the Opposition. If all hon. members will observe the same rules as I do, there will be less of these wanton, cruel, and foolish charges flung out against my gallant comrades of the war. Now, I do not rise to justify the whole administration of the Militia Department or the Government overseas.
It is one of our customs to think that the Government is responsible for all its officers and employees. Our Government is in a very bad situation in that regard, because a great deal that takes place in connection with administration in England is noi known here for a long time afterwards. I do not mean to justify all that has taken place in Argyll House or in connection with the administration overseas; I may have occasion later to bring some of these things
to the attention of the House. But I shall not do anything of that kind for the sake of cheap notoriety or of attaining some cheap political purpose. I saw a great deal of the administration over there, and I would not be doing my duty as a soldier or as a Canadian citizen if I did not stand up here and say that whatever mistakes have been made by Sir Edward Kemp, he is a very conscientious, hard-working patriotic minister.
Certain charges have been flung against General Turner. I repeat that I am not going to justify the administration of Argyjl House, not for a moment. But no man who ever served his country did it with the same absolute patriotism and the same fine sense of loyalty as did Major-General Sir Richard Turner, V.C.
With regard to the administration in Canada, I do not say that I will not criticise it sometime, but I believe that the present Minister of Militia and Defence (Major-General Mewburn) in his policy and in his conduct is as straight as he is in his personal carriage and appearance.
I have risen simply to say a word or two with regard to some statements made by General Smart in the Quebec Legislature. Whatever any one jnay say as to his statement, it read as though it was directed against the whole Canadian Army Medical Corps. I saw General Smart a few days ago. He seemed to think that I had a sort of Bolshevist notion, and I said to him at once: " There is one respect in which I do not agree with you; if you have anything against the administration of the army medical corps in England, that is all right, but you should not also make a charge against the whole Canadian Army Medical Corps." He said: "I do not do that." But the reports in the press, including those 'referred to by the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), indicated that the statement was made against the entire medical forces overseas. Members may bring up anything they please by way of conducting a cheap political campaign or something of that nature, but nobody is going to play football with the reputation of my comrades in this war while I sit in this House. And, Sir, if there ever was an efficient service in any army in any country, it was the service of the Canadian Army Medical Corps in France. To make a cruel, inconsiderate statement against that service should be beneath the dignity of any member of this House unless he has most ample proof. I have had considerable experience with these officers. I have seen them in times of peril

and in times when we were at rest. There was never too much danger for the officers, and the personnel of the Canadian Army Medical Corps to face. When it came to going into the trenches or when we were in action, your medical corps was there, " Johnny on the spot " every time, doing their duty. No class of men made more sacrifices than the members of the medical corps. The great bulk of them were captains or majors, and up to last June the captains were drawing the magnificent sum of $4.75 a day and the majors corresponding pay. I know lots of men there who had a practice at home that brought them anywhere from $5,000 to $20,000 a year; yet they sacrificed it all, went overseas and served faithfully and uncomplainingly. And now we are forced to stand up in this House and defend that noble profession. I say, Sir, it is humiliating that such a duty should become necessary.	.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
I read a story some time ago
about Peck's Bad Boy, and, like others on this side of the House, who have probably read that story, I remember a few things in it. Peck's Bad Boy was an awful boy; he would say and do terrible things-but, of course, I do not say that the member for Skeena (Mr. Peck) is the same as he was.
I wish to point out that the medical profession has not been attacked by this side of the House; the discussion has been with regard to the management of affairs. A few days ago I was informed that some one wanted to speak to me in the corridor outside. When I went out I found that it was a returned soldier, an old friend of mine, and I took him to my room. I noticed that he was a little lame and I asked him what was the cause. He said he had been in the army and had got his leg broke in France. Before he was sent to England for medical treatment he was sent to a place where, he said, there were a few old maids and an orderly or two, but no doctors. He suffered nine days in that place with a broken limb; just think of it, Mr. Speaker. Of course, they were kind to him in other ways, and he got his board. He was going to break away and get out on the streets, but they got word to Sir George Perley, and he looked after him and took him to a Canadian hospital where there was plenty of room and lots of doctors and nurses. He made inquiry and found that at that hospital they had been without work for some time. Here was one of our good Canadian soldiers suffering day and night in a hospital where there were no instruments to treat his

broken limb and where there was nobody to help him. I said: " Why do they treat the 'Canadian soldiers that way?" " Well," he said, " the Minister of Militia "-he was referring to the member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes)-" had made good arrangements for hospitals, but after he was discharged-"

speechtext: Oh, oh.

" -they would not keep a man in a hospital that the ex-Minister of Militia had arranged for, notwithstanding the fact that in those hospitals there were paid Canadian doctors and nurses." He told me that they distributed the men all over England and Ireland. I asked him what was the reason for that, and he said that so far as he knew anything that had been done by the ex-Minister of Militia was claimed by others as being not right and was not acknowledged at all.
That is one thing. Then he said there was another thing, if they did go to the Canadian hospitals, there was no chance of graft or of rake-offs, and that was, he thought, the principal part of it. He was side-tracked and lay nine days in this place without medical aid. I do not think any hon. member on this side of the House criticises the doctors.

speechtext: The doctors have done wonders. My sympathy goes out to members of this House and others who have lost sons in France in this great war and, it is not surprising that we endeavour to have an investigation in order to find out who is to blame. No doubt many other soldiers were treated like my friend with the broken limb, being sent to places where they did not receive proper attention. I think, with all respect to the Union Government, it would be in their interest to have an investigation, without politics being brought into it, in order to find out where the blame lies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) has taken a good deal of responsibility upon himself in placing before the House and the country the exaggerated statements which he has read to us to-day respecting the Canadian Army Medical Service. It is my purpose to deal more particularly (with certain charges |which have been made respecting the Canadian Army Medical Service and the policy adopted with respect to the treatment of wounded in 1916, at the time when the

Babtie commission was appointed. I purpose dealing with that period because it chanced that I was overseas in the fall of 1916 and was closely associated with Sir George Perley who has come under severe and, in my view, wholly unjustifiable criticism respecting the appointment of the Babtie commission.
Before, however, dealing with that period and the conditions which then prevailed,
I desire to make reference to some of the sweeping charges which have been made by General Smart with regard to that gallant soldier General Sir Richard Turner and his gallant associates at Argyll House. It is a very simple matter to make general statements regarding a body of officers, but no general statement of a condemnatory nature regarding any body of officers in Great Britain can be true. Gentlemen returning to Canada may feel, with respect to certain officers with whom they have been brought into contact, that they might have been, let us say, more courteous or more considerate in any particular matter in which they were concerned, but to make a general condemnation of the officers of Canada at their Argyll House headquarters appears to me to be a proceeding absolutely without justification. I do not believe any such charges will find support in London where the situation is known, amongst the members of this House who have returned from overseas, amongst officers generally who have served overseas, or amongst the people at large.
General Smart is reported in the Montreal Gazette as stating with respect to General Sir Richard Turner that he is a weakling, surrounded by weaklings, and a man who listened too much to tattle and intrigue. I leave it to any hon. gentleman in this House who has served overseas if that is a proper description of General Sir Richard Turner. I saw him at the front before he was appointed to command in England, and I know of no man who had in higher degree the respect of the Canadian Expeditionary Force than had General Turner. He won the Victoria Cross, and it seems to me a most extraordinary thing that any returned officer should criticise as a weakling a man of his proven courage and high standing.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.

General Smart in telling of medical conditions brought condemnation to bear against certain high officials, and' as regards general army administration described General Sir Richard Turner as a weakling, surrounded by weaklings, and a man who listened too much to tattle and intrigue.
In a cable report which I have before me General Turner is stated to have made, at a luncheon held in London on April 5, the following remarks with respect to these charges:	.
General Turner followed, and said: " 1 have never spoken or written to anybody in Canada asking them to take up the cudgels on my behalf. I do not consider there is any need to do so. Criticisms have been made upon men associated with me at headquarters. I have been responsible for recommending to the minister the following officers: Generals Thacker, Hogarth and Foster; Colonel Hastings, and my personal aide, Major Nickle. Argyll House, which has been so much abused, consists of only 63 officers. I know what a load they carry. There have been remarks lately concerning lack of co-ordination and co-operation between Canada, England, and France. I cannot help feeling that these lying and malicious statements have been bred and fostered in many instances by disgruntled and discredited officers, some of whom have been returned to Canada for inefficiency or for other causes."

I ask this House if, within a period of four months, 117,500 men have been returned to Canada, if Argyll House can be so inefficient as is evidently the opinion of some of these returned officers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
I cabled Sir George Perley to ascertain what he had to do with the members of the Royal Air Force, and he replied as follows:
There must be some misapprehension as I have no authority regarding Royal Air Force. Have, however, on all occasions assiduously promoted their interests and done everything possible to give support to reasonable claims all Canadians serving in Imperial Forces. For example, I have intervened and secured that Canadian cadets in Air Force should be entitled to honorary commissions on discharge and outfit allowances. Have also taken up many personal cases and have arranged with Air Ministry for special investigation. Have also pressed in direction of expediting demobilization and must say my representations have been received sympathetically by Imperial authorities. Chief difficulty is inadequate shipping accommodation regarding which we are seeking in every direction for relief.
Sir George Perley responsible? He has no authority respecting the Royal Air Force. He has done everything a man could do. What does Sir Edward Kemp say about the matter? Replying on April 2, 1919, he says:
Assume you refer to Canadians not on our strength hut those who enlisted in Canada in R.A.F. or were transferred outright by us here to R.A.F. Imperial Government admits its obligation to repatriate these men free of charge. Difficulty is entirely one of shipping accommodation. On behalf these airmen for some time past we have been pressing Imperial authorities constantly with necessity making 
arrangements for their return to Canada. We have arranged for two hundred to sail on Me-gantic leaving to-day. There are eleven hundred still to go and Imperial authorities expect will be able to repatriate all of these during April. Will do all possible to assist.
I ask this House,.is it fair to assail these two men-Sir Edward Kemp, one of the ablest administrators I have ever met, and one of the most honourable men that I know, and Sir George Perley, of whom I may say the same thing-with regard to their conduct respecting Canadian members of the Royal Air Force? Is it fair play? I ask my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr Lemieux) if it is fair play that these oflficers who have come back should assail these defenceless men in England who cannot make their defence here? Is it fair for my hon. friend to bring forward and sponsor these charges that they make against defenceless officers of the highest standing at Argyll House, against the Overseas Minister of Militia, and against the High Com missioner?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
General Sir William Babtie is. He was the medical officer who was responsible for the break-down of the medical services in Mesopotamia, and the Royal Commission who investigated that gave a finding that was strong in the terrible responsibility and crime that was perpetrated on the men in that particular campaign. It is almost unfit to print, the terrible things that those men had to endure, and this man, Sir William Babtie, was responsible for it.
There are two features of the indictment to which I wish to draw the attention of the House. First, he says that there existed a system of scattering our wounded throughout the British Isles. It is very difficult to refute, except by the evidence of those who have had experience, any statement in respect to the quality or character of the service in Great Britain or on the continent. My hon. friend from Maison-neuve said this afternoon that General Smart was a gallant officer and a good Conservative. These are high qualifications, and I am quite willing to accept my hon. friend's statement. I have known General Smart for many years, and certainly I have no intention of in any way reflecting upon his character or standing. My hon. friend knows however that General Smart is not a physician, nor has he had to do immediately with the problems with which the Canadian Army Medical Service' has had to grapple. These problems have had to be dealt with by the officers of the Canadian Army Medical Service. As against this statement of General Smart, which generally condemns the Canadian Army Medical Service by reason of the policy which it states ought to be adopted, I desire to cite an opinion which will, I venture to say, command the attention and respect of this House. Only within the past few days, I have received a letter in respect to General Smart's charge. It is from a man of the highest standing in the medical world of Canada. I refer to Sir Andrew Miaophail, D.A.D.M.S.
