speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend
will; I was paying him a compliment. Sir Andrew Macphail is a professor in the medical faculty of McGill University. He served in Canada for five months and overseas for four years two of which were spent in France with the second Canadian division, and two in England at various camps, and at medical headquarters, London. I have received from him within the last week this letter:
To those who, like myself, are returning from overseas after four years' service in the British Expeditionary Force it was an extremely painful experience reading an account of the attack which was made upon the Canadian Army in the Quebec Legislature by Brigadier-General C. A. Smart, himself at one time holding a command in that force.
That part of this vague and wandering attack which concerns the medical service I feel competent to meet. I have been in this service continuously since November, 1914. During those years I served five months in Canada, two years with the Second Division in France and two years in England. At the front my service extended from Ypres to the Somme, and from the western front to the extreme limit of the bridge-head beyond the Rhine. In England it was my business to visit every hospital, and every camp in Scotland, and I was of that headquarters which is so wantonly attacked. With the experience so acquired it may fairly be considered that I am qualified to deal with one charge at least of which I have specific knowledge.
Brigadier-General Smart's most specific charge against the Medical Services, is that " there is a scheme for scattering Canadian wounded throughout the British Isles."
The exact contrary is the truth. The whole policy of the administration is, and has been-for years, to collect Canadian patients, as far as possible, into Canadian hospitals in well defined' areas. Not for years have any Canadian patients been' so scattered-none to Scotland, to Ireland, or even to the north of England. The Canadian hospitals in England are all placed in three areas; in the South-eastern area, to accommodate casualties from France; in the Liverpool area, for the reception and dispatch of troops; and in the London area for the local sick, and as a general reserve.
A complete organization exists for doing the very thing General Smart suggests, namely, to assemble Canadian patients in Canadian hospitals, and Col. Roberts was charged wirth this duty. There never was a policy of " scattering Canadian patients over the British Isles." The policy has been to evacuate casualties from the field with the utmost speed by convoys, and shelter these convoys for the time being, in any *hospital available. Soldiers from all over the Empire fall side by side. There is no time on the field of battle to sort these men according to their place of birth. The battle of Messines Ridge opened at daybreak, and by luncheon the

wounded were coming by train-loads into Charing Cross.
Canadians who happened to be in an ambulance convoy cannot be left on the station platform, and a special ambulance train cannot be provided for a small number of men.
At all times during the war provision had to be kept in reserve for 10,000 Canadian casualties, and part of this reserve was in English hospitals. Otherwise it would have been necessary to keep 10 Canadian hospitals empty, though fully staffed, against such an emergency. Apart from the wastefulness of such a policy there are not ten buildings in England available for standing empty against the hour of need.
The Canadian Army was not an allied army. It was of the very essence of the force. Canadian casualties could not be immediately separated from their stricken comrades who were not Canadians. In the early days when hospital accommodation was yet incompletely organized any refuge-even V.A.D. hospitals- was welcome.
The movement of patients is one of the most delicate and technical in the operations of war, and all movement would cease if a rigid rule were made that every wounded Canadian should in the first instance be sent to a Canadian hospital.
The speed with which cases could be passed through Canadian hospitals depended in turn upon the speed of evacuation to Canada, and that was governed to some extent by the activity of German submarines. Now that hostilities are suspended there are comparatively few Canadians in English hospitals so that the policy of the service is being fulfilled and General Smart's objections met.
Andrew McPhail.
I stated that a couple of weeks after his speech in the Quebec Legislature General Smart addressed a communication to the Montreal Star, and on reading that carefully I find that he practically withdrew the charges he had made against the Canadian Army Medical Service and its staff, with the single exception, so far as I understand his statement, of those against one or two men. Therefore, so far as these charges against the Canadian Army Medical Service are concerned, General Smart has practically refuted himself. And yet my hon. friend brings his statement before the House with the intention of having the country believe that these charges of negligence in the care and treatment of the Canadian sick and wounded soldiers are well founded. I do not know anything more calculated to distress those people of Canada who have wounded or sick sons or other connections overseas.
Before taking up the question of the Babtie Commission, which alone remains of the charges put forward by General Smart, I desire to refer to one of the specific charges. I have stated thaA it is difficult here in Ottawa to refute general charges made with respect to the administration
of a service in Great Britain or on the continent. It is impossible, apart from inquiry, to meet specific charges, which may or may not be founded in fact. One of General Smart's specific cases by which he would substantiate his charges against the Canadian Army Medical Service is as follows:
Then there is another case. A friend of mine living in London told me-
Second-hand evidence.
-that on his visits around the various hospitals looking for Canadians to do something for them, he came across the case of a Canadian who was suffering from a severe wound in the spine-so severe that he would never be right again and would not live long. Instead of being taken care of in one of the Canadian hospitals, where he would get the best treatment from trained nurses, he was in a lean-to attached to a V.A.D. hospital. (Cries of "shame".)
On the statement of a friend of his General Smart makes a charge that a Canadian, severely wounded, had been placed in a lean-to attached to a V. A. D. hospital, and such was the impression made upon the minds of those who heard him that there were cries of "Shame." The attention of the Overseas Minister was drawn to this matter, and he cables me as follows:
First, the case of man with wounded spine.
Is doubtless case of tuberculosis of spine. Man was sent to be treated at hospital within three miles of home of his people, the recognized treatment being open air. Lean-to is a chalet, an open-air structure specially built for such cases. Man is being treated among his own personal friends and relatives by medical officer who fought with him and shared his dangers in firing line. Man himself has earnestly expressed wish That he be allowed to remain and continue treatment in neighbourhood his family. Also may add he is improving.
Now, I ask this House, is it fair to make a charge against an overseas minister based upon a statement made in conversation by a friend without inquiry by General Smart?
Is it in the national interest at this time that a man burdened as Sir Edward Kemp is, with the duties of administration of the Canadian forces, first in Great Britain and then in Canada, should have to make inquiries with regard to a charge of this kind, which rests absolutely upon no foundation? And I refer again to what I stated before six o'clock, that it does seem to me that it is objectionable in the extreme that charges should be made against defenceless ministers and defenceless officers overseas. Many of these men at Argyll House, it has been ' drawn to my attention, are working literally day and night. They are making great personal sacrifices. Their private affairs urge

their return at the earliest possible date; yet, impelled by the sense of duty and devotion which has carried them so far, they are going on. But charges of this kind made in Canada by returned officers is tending to demoralize those men, because they feel absolutely helpless and defenceless. They do not know what charges are being made behind their backs, they are not here to answer for themselves, and it seems to me that the least that could be done by returned officers, if for no other reason than a sense of chivalry, would be to communicate their charges to the officers overseas against whom they are making them, so the latter may have an opportunity of reply and defence.
Before I leave the matter of the Rhyl riots, let me repeat what was stated by the Minister of Militia this afternoon, that a full inquiry is being held into that matter. It does not appear to me, therefore, that it is open for discussion, pending the findings of the court of inquiry which was at once constituted by the Minister of Militia. I do not, of course, desire to limit the freedom of the House in debate-I have neither the power nor the will to do so-but it seems to me to be a recognized rule that where a matter is under judicial inquiry it is well that comment should be refrained from until the inquiry is completed and decision rendered.
But the member for Maisonneuve referred to the fact that shipping had been available since the riot. I- wonder whether the hon. member realizes what the shipping situation of the world has been since the armistice. Consider the supplies that have to be taken down the Mediterranean to areas where there are still forces of the Allies, to Mesopotamia, and to other ports of Asia Minor; consider the shipping required for the transportation of the troops back to India; the shipping required to move the Australian and New Zealand contingents home; the shipping required to bring home the troops of the United States and to bring home our own troops. And in addition to all that, shipping is required for commercial purposes on an ever-increasing scale. The demands upon the shipping of the world since the armistice have been tremendous and it is with the greatest possible difficulty that shipping is arranged for in advance. Even after arrangements had , been made in perfect good faith between the Admiralty and the Overseas Ministry, sailings sometimes have to be cancelled; arrangements cannot be carried out because of the exigencies of after-war conditions.
TSir Thomas White.l
That is not to be wondered at. It is normal for a period of this kind; it is what you must expect. In the face of these shipping difficulties, the Canadian Overseas Ministry and our Militia Department here have demobilized to Canada nearly 120,000 troops in four months. It is a wonderful achievement, Mr. Speaker; I do not believe there has been a like achievement on the part of any of the Overseas dominions. We are closer to Great Britain than Australia or New Zealand and more shipping is available as between Great Britain and the American continent than between Great Britain and Australia and New Zealand. But after stating that, it must be recognized that the feat of bringing practically thirty thousand men a month-dependent as we are upon two railways to the Atlantic coast and the accommodations of our ports there-reflects the highest credit upon all concerned.
My hon. friend suggested that if the riots had not occurred possibly as many men would not have been brought back; in other words, that the riots brought about a greater amount of shipping for the transportation of Canadian troops. Well, I do not say that that is true, but assuming that it is, is there any reflection upon the Overseas Minister of Militia or the Militia Department here? How is Canada to obtain shipping from the British authorities except by influence and persuasion? Ever since he went overseas Sir Robert Borden has used his best endeavours-and I do not know of any man who is more influential with the British authorities than he-to obtain as much shipping as possible, not only for the transportation of our troops but for the movement of commerce to and from Canada. Sir Edward Kemp has given the matter assiduous and continuous attention, and so, to my knowledge, has Sir George Perley. That being the case, suppose shipping was not available before the Rhyl riots and that as a result of the riots certain shipping which had been allotted to other purposes was allotted to the purpose of bringing home Canadians; is the Overseas Minister of Militia to be blamed? Not if he had used his best endeavours to secure shipping- and I have stated that he has used his best endeavours, and that the Prime Minister has supplemented those efforts in every way possible. I recall that before the armistice, as high an authority as Lord Shaugh-nessy- and there is no higher authority upon transportation - estimated that it would take at least ten months, if not longer, to bring home the Canadian forces at the front. Yet, such has been the ad-

ministrative ability of the Overseas Ministry of Militia and the services there that they have demobilized in England some
300,000	men, of whom 120,000 have been returned to Canada-all in the period of a little more than four months.
Now I come to the Babtie Commission. General Smart visits severe condemnation upon Sir George Perley, holding him responsible for the appointment of the Babtie Commission, and suggesting that his purposes were not creditable. He says that Sir George Perley desired to get rid of Colonel Bruce and that he appointed the Babtie Commission for the purpose. My hon. friend said this afternoon that Sir George Perley found Colonel Bruce's report so severely against the Government that he appointed the Babtie Commission. He says that Colonel Bruce made a report and that it was ridiculous to have other commissions investigate that report; now he asks us to investigate the report of the Babtie Commission. Let us hear what General Smart has to say about Sir William Babtie:
He was the medical officer who was responsible for the breakdown of the Medical Service in Mesopotamia, and the Royal Commission which investigated that gave a finding that was strong in the terrible responsibility and crime that was perpetrated against the men in that particular campaign. It is almost unfit to print, the terrible things that those men had to endure, and this man, Sir William Babtie, .was responsible for it.
Now let us find out what this man Sir William Babtie is. He graduated from Glasgow University, entered the Army Medical Service in 1881, served in the South African war and received a medal and five clasps, also the Victoria Cross. General Turner, who is also a winner of the Victoria Cross, is spoken of by General Smart as a weakling. Sir William Babtie, winner of the Victoria Cross, is spoken of as a man who committed a crime in the Mesopotamia campaign. He says that it is "unfit to print the terrible things that these men had to endure," and that "this man Sir William Babtie was responsible for it." It seems to be a bad day for the winners of the Victoria Cross-one of them a weakling and the other guilty of a crime. Let us see what else Sir William Babtie is. In 1901 he was the Assistant Director General of the Army Medical Service; in 1907, Inspector of Medical Services; in 1910, Deputy Director of Medical Services; in 1916, Director General of the Medical Sendee of India, and, at the time he was chairman of the board, Director of the Medical Services at the War Office.
Sir William Babtie did come under certain animadversion in connection with the Mesopotamian campaign, but I find that in the British Hansard of the 17th June, 1918, Sir William Babtie is referred to in the following manner:
-is not only under no personal aspersion from the Mesopotamia investigation, but has since been advanced to Inspector of Medical Services. Babtie has also just been promoted from Major-General to Lieutenant-General.
Winner of the Victoria Cross, with the experience in the army which I have mentioned and having been recently promoted to be Lieutenant-General, General Sir William Babtie ought not, after all, to be so bad a man to associate with.
/In the fall of 1916 I happened to be in England, and I want the House to realize the condition at the front and the condition behind the lines at that time. It was in November and the battles of the Somme had been going on for months. This was one-' of the most critical periods of the war and a time of the greatest British and Canadian casualties. This war was not won in the last two weeks before the armistice; it was won in every one of the fifty months of its duration, and the hammer blows of the British army at the Somme, following the heroic resistance of the French at Verdun, wasted the German armies to such an extent as to make the campaign of the next year and the victory of last year possible. Sir Douglas Haig was applying the strategy of attrition, the same kind of strategy which General Grant used against General Lee at the battle of the Wilderness. It was a strategy of attrition, of wastage, of victory by killing. iSir Douglas Haig told me that at the Somme in 1916 there were 550,000 casualties in his army, and that he calculated the Germans had sustained a loss in casualties of over 700,000, a balance of 150,000 of wastage, of human casualties, in favour of the British and against the Germans. That is a terrible way of looking at the matter, but it was a condition of that static war. Think of 550,000 casualties, with the wounded to be brought back from the front to dressing stations, to base hospitals, to be brought in convoys across the Channel, to be taken to British or Canadian hospitals and, in fact, to be taken any place where there was a hospital or hospital accommodation. The British expected that their wounded would be counted by the thousands; they were counted by the tens of thousands and by the hundreds oi thousands. I am told that the V.A.D. hospitals throughout the United Kingdom had in their care, in the fall of 1916, 53,000



patients. This meant providing accommodation equal to that of 53 hospitals of 1,000 beds each. I discussed the matter with the British as well as with the Canadian authorities, and they required all the hospital accommodation there was in the British Isles to take care of the wounded being brought back from the front.
I come now to speak of the report of Colonel Bruce and of the appointment oi the Babtie commission. Colonel Bruce is one of the ablest surgeons in Canada. He is a man of international reputation as an operator. He has long held a distinguished position as Associate Professor of Surgery in the University of Toronto and as head of one of the surgical services in the Toronto General Hospital, and he had also other high professional positions. The then Minister of Militia, the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes), believing that the Canadian Army Medical Service in England required re-organization, appointed Colonel Bruce for the purpose of making an inquiry and reporting upon conditions. Colonel Bruce made his report.

I think not; 1 think he went to France himself. When I went to London in November, 1916, I found this condition. A fierce controversy was raging in the Press and throughout the entire Canadian community with regard to what was called, and I think erroneously called, the question of segregation. It was almost as if the Canadian community was divided into two camps. I found the great majority of those men in the Canadian Army Medical Service, men whose distinction and ability were unquestioned, with whom I discussed the matter, were of the opinion that Colonel Bruce's report, while excellent, as I have said, up to a certain point, was not such that it could be put immediately into effect.
There was a very strong feeling prevailing in the Canadian Army Medical Service because in his report-I am speaking from memory, but I think I am right-Colonel Bruce had stated that the Canadian Army . Medical Service needed reorganization from top to bottom. It was also put forward- because the men of the Canadian Army Medical Service were men who had given up their profession and had gone overseas at a great sacrifice-that Colonel Bruce had not sufficiently regarded the very heavy tasks and responsibilities which had devolved on General Jones and the Canadian Army Medical Service in the first two years of the war. Colonel Bruce, in his report, no doubt because he had immediately before him the question of making recommendations, had entirely overlooked the good work that had been done and was being done by the Canadian Army Medical Service in Great Britain and France. The spirit of the Canadian Army Medical Corps for the most part was offended by the report, because it failed to give them what

they regarded as their just meed of praise and appreciation for the work which they had done.
It is only fair to say that many members of the Canadian Army Medical Service, and distinguished men, too, whom I know personally, and in whom I have high confidence, were strong votaries of Colonel Bruce. They believed in his report. But I recall distinctly talking the matter over with two of these men, outstanding men in the medical world, who believed that the Bruce report was sound for the most part, but that it was not practicable to put it into effect at once. Now Colonel Bruce wanted to put it into effect at once, and there was a great deal of feeling about the whole situation.
More than that-and I come now to the most important point in Colonel Bruce's report-his theory was that the Canadian sick and wounded should be assembled, so [DOT] far as possible, in purely Canadian hospitals in England.

I say "Hear, hear," too, if it would have been practicable and fair to do as he proposed, having regard to the arrivals of British sick and wounded from the front. Colonel Bruce, while an eminent surgeon, had had no military experience so far as I know. Just let me put it this way to the House: Supposing we had set out to build Canadian hospitals to accommodate all Canadian sick and wounded in London. That would mean that we must have a maximum of hospital accommodation. Supposing that after a great engagement there were thirty thousand Canadian casualties. To accommodate that number we would require thirty Canadian hospitals of a thousand beds each. Now the Canadians might not again be "in action for months, and your hospitals would be gradually emptying. Let us say that through the gradual discharge of these patients you have 15,000 beds vacant, what are you going to do with them? Are you going to await the next great action in which the Canadians are engaged, or will you allow the Australians and the New Zealanders and the English and the Scotch and the Irish to go into those hospitals? If you say, " Yes, we will let them in to the extent that the hospitals are empy of Canadians," you have the hospitals filled. Then may come another great engagement of Canadians, and where are you going to put the casualties? The fact of the matter is that it was absolutely necessary that the. hos-96i
pital resources of the United Kingdom should be pooled for the purpose of taking care of the hundreds of thousands of sick and wounded from the front, no matter whether they were English, Scotch, Irish, Australian, New Zealand or Canadian wounded. Not only that. In all the hospitals that I visited I talked with hundreds of Canadians lying side by side with English, Scotch, Irish, Australian and New Zealand comrades, and enjoying the conversation of them all, and I asked them whether they believed that Canadian hospitals should be used solely for Canadian wounded. They said: " No, we do not want that; that would not be fair. These men have fought with us at the front, and why should they not have the advantage of these hospitals as well as ourselves?" They did say this, however: " We like a substantial number of Canadians in our hospitals, two or three hundred Canadians perhaps, because then we feel at home; but so far as the additional beds are concerned, by all means let them be filled up with the English, Irish and Scotch casualties and the wounded from the other overseas dominions." They liked to talk and exchange ideas with one another.
Now the controversy was raging in London, and it was put forward that Colonel Bruce's plan contemplated the segregation of Canadian wounded, or what is called in the Babtie's Commission's report "a watertight compartment for the Canadians." Now I do not believe that Colonel Bruce intended that; I want to be scrupulously fair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
I am not aware personally that Colonel Bruce was dismissed. It is news to me if he was dismissed; besides, I have not seen his report at all. I have read to the House the words of the Prime Minister dealing with it. Now, the board was constituted of the members I have mentioned, and was instructed to report as quickly as possible on the following points:
(a)	The criticisms made by Colonel Bruce: as to whether they are justified, in whole or in part.
(b)	The recommendations made by Colonel Bruce; as to whether the Board endorses and concurs in them ; if not. in what respect does the Board differ from Colonel Bruce, and its reasons therefore.
The report goes on to state:
It will be convenient to summarize here the principal points emerging from Colonel Bruce's report. These are:-
(a)	The concentration of Canadian sick and wounded in Canadian hospitals.
(b)	The suitability of V.A.D. hospitals for the care and treatment of Canadian soldiers.
(c)	The system of Medical Boards.
Before offering any general remarks on these topics, the Board thinks it right to explain that up to February, 1916, the accepted policy was to provide special hospital establishments for Canadian patients; that about that date, owing to various considerations, practical and sentimental, it was determined, with the consent of the War Office, to deal with Canadian patients in the same fashion as British patients are dealt with, that is, by distributing them through-the United Kingdom to the great series of central hospitals, each with its group of affiliated auxiliaries.
In the report of the special Inspector General-
That is Colonel Bruce:
-the latter system is condemned, and a return to the policy of Canadian hospitals for Canadian sick and wounded advocated. The issue is a fair one, for there is much to be said on both sides, but the board after very careful consideration, has come to the conclusion that the policy therein recommended is not only unwise, but impracticable, having regard to the amount of accommodation that would be required owing to the increase of Canadian troops in Europe.
All through the report of the Inspector General the dominating idea is a conception that the Canadian Expeditionary Force is something separate and apart from the Imperial Army, a conception that may be summarized as the " water-tight compartment " policy in matters medical. The board is of opinion that as long as the Canadian Expeditionary Force forms an integral part of the Imperial Army, such a view is no more possible in the United Kingdom than it is in France, and so long as Canadian troops continue to operate under the command of the Commander-in-Chief, British Expeditionary Force, it must continue to be impossible to discriminate in the medical arrangements of Canadian and British troops. The personal experience of the majority of the members of the board amply confirms this view, so far as the arrangements at the French front and at the overseas bases are concerned, and

the board has satisfied itself that it would be inadvisable to attempt separation on the return of the sick and wounded to the United Kingdom.
It d^xpears to the board that to separate, on their return to England, men who have fought side by side, must tend to undo the bond of brotherhood sealed in the face of the enemy. The board is aware that these considerations of high policy do not strictly come within its purview, but cannot refrain from adverting to this aspect of the matter, because it would almost appear as if the report under consideration was based upon the conception that the Canadian Forces had a similar relation to the British Armies as that held by the Allied nations.
The policy that the board ventures to attribute to Colonel Bruce would have prevented the use of Canadian Medical Units in the Mediterranean, because Canadian troops did not happen to be employed in that theatre of war, and the sending of Canadian hospitals to Paris for the use of the French sick and wounded.
The board, too, is at variance with the contention that the services of the Canadian Army Medical Corps should in the main be confined to Canadian troops; Field Ambulances serve primarily the Canadian formations, but in the case of the Line of Communication units, their work must, of necessity, be largely with other than Canadian troops. This aspect of the case, it is fair to say, was repudiated by the Inspector General when placed before him.
The board feels bound to place on record that in some of the opinions-
In some of the opinions.
-expressed by Colonel Bruce he is misled by a lack of intimate knowledge of army organization and of the inter-relation of the various branches of the service, as, in some of his criticisms he has failed to make allowance for the sudden expansion of the army and for the unavoidable want of specialized training in its ancillary services. Such imperfections as have existed are rapidly being remedied, and it is plain truth to say that in no war in history has sickness been so well controlled or the sick and wounded so well cared for. The board, relying on its own observations and the evidence laid before it, is abundantly satisfied that the Canadian sick and wounded have been thoroughly well cared for, not only in the Central hospitals, whether British or Canadian, but in the Voluntary Aid Hospitals, which Colonel Bruce criticises. These latter hospitals are the outcome of a mobilization of the medical resources of the United Kingdom, and in them Canadian soldiers are not only well cared for professionally but are comfortable, happy, and at home. The board desires to emphasize its dissent from the criticisms of these institutions, which it believes to be unjust and undeserved.
Then the report goes on:
The other principal issue raised in the report of the Inspector General, the system of Medical Boards, is dealt with in detail hereafter, and the board agrees that there is much justice in the criticisms levelled at the complicated arrangements that have been permitted to grow up. With the reorganization proposed, the board is unable to concur, and has ventured, as the result of the combined experience of its members, to suggest a system that it believes to be simple and likely to be practical in operation.
I Sir Thomas White.]
There is no violent attack upon Colonel Bruce in this report. The report recognizes the good features of Colonel Bruce's report and agrees with certain of his criticisms. They do not agree with him as to the practicability of confining Canadian troops to Canadian hospitals having regard to the conditions prevailing at the front and the limited hospital accommodation at the time in Great Britain. The report goes on:
The Board does not concur in Colonel Bruce's view that a complete reorganization from " top to bottom " of the Canadian Army Medical Service Is necessary. In its opinion the reforms he suggests would not remedy the defects he deplores, which are not due to .the system but to inexperience on the part of officers, military and1 medical, and to defaults in .administration which are oommented upon in the detailed criticisms that the board has felt it its duty to record.
Then the board goes on to pay a tribute to the good work done by Surgeon-General Jones and his staff under circumstances of novelty and great difficulty.
The Board has not hesitated to criticise those matters, wherein, iin its opinion, the Director of Medical Services has failed, but does so with great reluctance, for it is satisfied that much of what has been accomplished has been the result of his zeal and industry, while the good relations of the Imperial and Canadian services are largely due to the tactful performance of the many delicate duties that fell to his lot.
After dealing in detail with the question of the distribution of casualties and the concentration of hospitals, and pointing out that it is impracticable to earmark and collect Canadian casualties at the base in France, and that it would be difficult and inconvenient to direct them solely to Canadian hospitals in England, they go on to point out:
The special advantages that Colonel Bruce claims for a policy of concentration can be attained with existing arrangements, which are sufficiently extensive to permit of the utilization of the special skill1 of Canadian physicians and surgeons in all branches of medioine and surgery.
There are twenty thousand Canadian soldiers in hospital in the United1 Kingdom to-day, and: the provision of special Canadian hospitals for them all would necessitate additional accommodation for nine thousand, and even this would not allow a margin for battle casualties. Of this number, the board is Informed that between two and three thousand are being provided for by special arrangements with the Ontario Government and the Red Cross, and -there are a large number of patients now in the United Kingdom who the board agrees should be returned to Canada, as they are unlikely to be fit for general service within a reasonable period.
The board cannot agree that there is a lack of efficient medical inspection in hospitals, but, while not reflecting on the efficiency of these inspections, the board agrees with Colonel Bruce and Surgeon-General Jones that additional In-

spection of Canadian hospitals, and of Canadian patients in British hospitals throughout the United Kingdom, is desirable, from a Canadian standpoint.
The report also makes the observation:
The comments made in Colonel Bruce's report on the V.A.D. Hospitals have been widely resented, and this Board is of opinion that these strictures are unjustified and regrettable.
While the Board agrees with Colonel Bruce that patients could sometimes be more advantageously treated in, and more sipeedily evacuated from, large military hospitals, the advantages of the V.A.D. system should not be overlooked In this regard. In these hospitals the board found the Canadian patient well fed, comfortable and happy, and receiving an amount of care that is only possible in Institutions organized on the line of " the home." This has been an enormous asset in the case of soldiers widely separated from their kith and kin.
Then there is this extract:
The Board disagrees with Colonel Bruce and is strongly of the opinion that the forces and resources of the Empire must be pooled to the utmost in this struggle, and that, therefore, interchange of personnel is desirable and necessary, in the interests of both services.

The situation, as I understood it when I was over there in 1916 was that the V.A.D. hospitals were absolutely needed. I am speaking from memory, but I am positive the number was 53,000 in V.A.D. hospitals, the equivalent of 53 hospitals with an accommodation of 1,000 each.
The Report goes on to state:-
With reference to the remarks of Colonel Bruce that "the present Medical Board situation is a disgrace to the Canadian Army Medical Corps," and that "Medical Board work has often degenerated into a farce," the Board thinks it right to begin their comments on this section by remarking that on examination Colonel Bruce agreed that the use of the words first quoted were unjustifiable and had little or no application to the part taken by the Canadian Army Medical Corps in carrying out the procedure prescribed for them.
The Board agrees that there is a necessity for reformation in the Medical Board situation and in the classification of casualties, and is of opinion that an easy solution of the problem would be to adopt the British system so far as applicable.
Then with regard to the matter of records:
The criticisms made by Colonel Bruce are generally agreed to by the Board, which, however, would point out that they are of universal application and apply to all Medical Services in all wars.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to read further from the report. I have dealt with the essential features of its criticisms, unfavourable and favourable, of Colonel Bruce's report. But I desire to make this point again. There has been a misunderstanding of Colonel Bruce's report and of the inquiry held by the Babtie Commission. My personal view is that it is a case where medical authorities differ, as frequently happens. They differed upon the important point whether it was practicable to carry into effect the recommendations of Colonel Bruce with regard to the assembling of the Canadian sick and wounded exclusively, or so far as possible, in Canadian hospitals.

speechtext:
The Babtie Commission's report is dated 22nd December, 1916. Whatever was done was done in absolute good faith and to" meet an exceedingly difficult practical situation which confronted Sir George Perley. He agreed with many of the proposals put forward by Coloner Bruce, but in the face of the adverse opinion of many of the Canadian Army Medical Service and of the doubt as to the practicability of carrying the proposals into effect, Sir George Perley felt justified in asking to be advised by a commission of experts who had had practical experience. That is all there is in the matter. In order that I may not by any possibility be misunderstood, I desire to say that I know Dr. Bruce to be a man of the highest professional ability, that he entered upon his work in all good faith, and that he made valuable findings, with most of which, so far as I was able to judge, I was in agreement. The question was: Could they be carried into effect? And in tire situation

which 1 have described-and I think fairly described, because it developed quite naturally-the course taken by Sir George Perley was one for which I think he should not be criticized, to say the least. Whether the findings of the Babtie report are sound in all particulars, I am unable to say. I think to-day in England and on the Continent among authorities in the Canadian Army Medical Service and the Imperial Army Medical Service a difference of opinion would be found. Doctors differ; they differ in hospital practice, and they differ in military practice.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have dealt with all the charges brought forward by General Smart, and I submit that, on his own admissions and on what I have placed before the House to-night, they are without foundation. It does not appear to me that any purpose- connected with national interests could be served by an investigation of the findings of the Babtie Commission or of the situation that existed in England from 1916 down to the present with regard to the concentration or the disposal of our Canadian sick and wounded soldiers. There are no charges brought against the integrity of any person. At most there was a difference of opinion, which Sir George Perley tried to resolve by the appointment of a commission of experts.
With reference to the laying upon the Table of Colonel Bruce's report and the report of the Babtie Commission, I find that on the 7th of February, 1917, the Prime Minister laid both upon the table of the House.
