speechtext:
Sir George Perley, my former colleague, who is now Canadian High Commissioner in London, during this war has rendered service to this country upon which it would be difficult to place too high a value. I have been in almost daily cable communication with him during the war upon all manner of subjects, and I can confidently say that he is without exception the most capable business man that I have ever had communication with

respecting important subjects. His efficiency is of the highest possible character. Any matter that has been entrusted to him has been handled promptly, efficiently, and in a way to reflect the highest credit upon himself and his office.
1 do not believe that the burdens which are cast upon these men in war time are generally realized. I think it is not too much to say that Sir Edward Kemp and Sir George Parley literally worked day and night during this war. They have had exceedingly heavy responsibilities. They would be the last to ask for any sympathy on that account; I certainly do not ask it for them. But when charges are made against men discharging the important duties that they have been and are now discharging in our national affairs, they should be capable of complete substantiation, and, it seems to me, should first be brought to the attention of those against whom they are made in order that opportunity of answering them may be afforded. We have come through the war, but we are in the midst of the most critical conditions ever known in Canada or in the world. These men are burdened with day-to-day duties, and it seems to me that it is unfair to overburden them with obtaining information on all manner of subjects in order to answer charges made against them in their positions overseas.
Lt,-General Sir SAM HUGHES (Victoria): Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to enter into a discussion of the matter which has been brought to the attention of the House, namely the charges of General Smart, Colonel Pratt, and Colonel Price, for the simple reason that I have not yet had the privilege of reading their letters or their speeches. I missed the papers containing the reports and have not since obtained them. In any event, I shall not enter into a discussion of these things tonight.
I congratulate the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) on the very plausible statement he has made in regard to the Bab-tie and Bruce reports. I watched for these reports in this House, and tried to find out whether they had been laid on the Table. I went to the committee room and endeavoured to ascertain if the reports had been laid on the Table in order that I might see the Babtie report; but whether they were laid on the Table or not I have never yet been able to obtain-and I tried twice-a sight of either. I have the Bruce report but I have not the Babtie report; and the Bruce reply to the Babtie report has not
yet been published. If the Acting Prime Minister were actuated by a spirit of fair play, as he professes to be, he would have seen that the Bruce reply to the Babtie report was presented to the House to-night. He knows that it is in existence; he knows that it is within his reach. Why the Babtie report is presented here to-night and the Bruce reply thereto is not presented passes my comprehension.
The Acting Prime Minister has stated that he is sorry those who make these charges do not run to Messrs. Perley and Kemp and to the officers at the front with their complaints with regard to maladministration and so on. But has the Acting Prime Minister himself been in the habit of doing this? Has he gone direct to men against whom complaints were made-men who were within his reach? I am afraid that the policy has been that the matter has gone in whispers when the gentleman to whom such a report might be communicated was within easy reach. Side-stepping and choosing the backdoor way has been the policy of these gentlemen.
I do not agree in the slightest that Sir George Perley is a great business man. I had experience with him from the start in the war. One of the first things that met me in 1914 when I reached England was that concurrently with the arrival of the Canadian Corps, Sir George Perley, in conjunction with Harrod's and Sir Edward Ward, had made an arrangement to tax Canadian officers large sums daily for their rationing at Salisbury Plains. I had rationed the boys for twenty-five cents a day at Valcartier, and they were well rationed; but they were being charged, if I remember aright, seven and six pence, or something of that kind, on Salisbury Plains. I declined to accede to the business arrangements made by Sir George Perley, and two shillings a day, I 'think, was all I allowed officers to pay for rations in addition to the rations supplied. I could point to scores of other business transactions of a similar nature on the part of that hon. gentleman in connection with the force. So far as I could form a conclusion they all gravitated around the society influences of London, not around that which would benefit the Canadian service.
So far as Sir Edward Kemp is concerned, I have nothing to say with regard to his administration, as I was not therp. But I was somewhat surprised to see that the policy now theoretically advanced by the Acting Prime Minister in regard to the criticism of other officers has not been car-

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
know for what purpose Jenkins was ap- * pointed?

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
I really do not know. The first I heard of his report was when the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) asked a question about the " Jenkins report." I made inquiries and I found

out about it from the boys, because any fellow coming home can tell all about it. There is no secret about the Rhyl riots. I have talked with two of the ringleaders in the Kinmel riots who have returned home hale and hearty, and they have no hesitation in giving the facts. The statement is openly made by officers that the cause of the riots in the Rhyl camp was a cablegram sent by the Government of Canada to the overseas military authorities not to send any more troops out, to cancel the steamers because they could not get the men away by rail and could not demobilize them quickly enough in Canada. And this is confirmed by a statement made by Sir Edward Kemp the other day at the same public dinner to which the minister referred when he spoke of this love feast between Turner and Currie and Perley and Kemp and the whole gang of them-I. do not know at what period of the dinner it occurred - that the Canadian authorities were wrong in seeking to keep back the demobilization of the men; that his, Kemp's policy from the beginning has been to shove them over, but that he had been held up by the authorities in Canada.
Major-General MEWBURN:	Does the
hon. gentleman make the statement that a cablegram was sent overseas to stop demobilization?

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext: came to the subordinate military officers no one could be found who was not anxious to grasp and control everything. When I went overseas first as Minister of Militia of the Dominion of Canada I was not even recognized by General Alderson as 'having any say in connection with the force. Lord Kitchener himself, as I pointed out before in the House, said to me: "You do not claim any control over these troops, do you?" I said: "None excepting what the law allows." Sir George Perley said to me: "You do not pretend to have anything to do with these soldiers, do you?" I told him I was not aware that he was thoroughly posted on military questions and I did not want to discuss the matter with him. When Lord Kitchener asked me what control the law allowed, I referred him to Section 177 which is the one that deals particularly with troops such as we were sending over, that is, where a colony raises and pays for her own troops in the field.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext: Is that the Army Act?

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
Yes. I have brought that up half a dozen times in this House. The British law says that a colony raising and maintaining her own troops in the field is supreme with those troops as regards making every appointment from the highest to the lowest, and in the management of those troops in the field except as regards the direction of the Commander in Chief of the British Army. Under the law the British authorities have no control direct or indirect of the training at Salisbury. Under the law they have no control of the rationing of provisions or supplies. Under the law they have no control over discarding wagons and harness and saddlery and things of that kind, all of the very best and unused. At Salisbury we had no say. I took the matter into my own hands the next year, and over-rode them completely. When the Canadian troops left Salisbury Plain, they left millions of dollars' worth of Canadian material piled up there in the mud that had been discarded by the British and supplanted by other equipment. They discarded our trucks costing from $1,800 to $2,400 apiece. They said we had three different kinds of trucks, and they could not get supplies for them in France. They supplied us with 51 trucks of seven different kinds: the details are all on Hansard, I have given them time and again. These fifty-one trucks cost us fifty-five thousand pounds sterling, or a little over twice the price we had paid for just as good a truck. 
I challenge any one to name one solitary item of equipment of any description that these subordinates of the British War Ofliee did not attempt to throw out at the beginning of that campaign, and supplant with their own equipment.
It was the same with the Pay Corps. While I was over there in 1914 I received a cable from Canada: "Are the Canadians in action?" I wired back "No " and a cable came back from my home county saying that so-and-so, a British reservist who went over with the Canadians, was reported killed. I looked the matter up and found that he had been drawing his pay up to a day or two before I looked at the record. And yet the British record showed that he had been killed in Flanders. We had muster parades then, and at the first parade a thousand men who were reported to be present were absent. We wiped out the British system of pay, and I put General Carson in charge. All I could get from the Canadian Minister of Finance and the Canadian Cabinet for General Carson was that he should "look after supplies," but I managed to slip in the words "and for other purposes." That is all I could get after a bitter fight. The whole thing was kow-towing to these subordinate officers of the British War Office who wanted to run the whole Canadian show. I said: We will run our own pay service, and put a stop to these fellows carrying money around in valises which very often got lost. We put a stop to that, and had every man paid by cheque. From that time on, although the Minister of Finance was worrying his great brain about the condition of affairs in England, on the financial side, when he came back from that famous trip to England with the Auditor General, he was forced to admit that he found the pay system perfect in every way from start to finish.
We were being charged two prices for our supplies. I wiped that out ruthlessly.
I did not ask permission of the Canadian Government, because I knew it would take six months to get their consent. It took three months to get Max Aitken, the greatest man in the Empire, one who has done more to win this war than any other man living, appointed an officer. The objections came from here, not yonder. I will say this much:	Lloyd George, Kitchener, Bonar
Law, all recognized the rights of Canada at once. Section 177 was taken as the standard, and we were treated by them as an independent entity, subject only to the commander-in-chief.
When it came to the question of supplies I put Colonel Murphy and Colonel McRae

in charge, and everything went smoothly and well; but it was an up-hill fight. The medical service was run on British lines in the same way as the pay service and the transport service had been, all being run by subordinate officers in the British service. That was done awrfy with. Our Canadian men who knew more about transport in five minutes than these men had known in a lifetime had to take the advice of young sprigs from the War Office.
I also objected'to the canteen system over there, and wanted to follow our practice in Canada, where each battalion runs its own canteen. I,was politely told by a British otficer-you never saw anything to equal the politeness of these grafters-that this was a matter wholly within British control, that contracts had been let, and that these people could charge our fellows what they wanted. We soon regulated that, but it was an up-hill fight.
The next step taken was in connection with the medical service. I was not satisfied with it when I went over there in 1914. i was satisfied with the men, mark you, because no finer body of men, no equal body of men ever donned the uniform of a medical officer in this or any other country. When the Minister of Finance says that one of our universities was talking of withdrawing their unit, why .was he not fair enough to say that the plan proposed was to divide these university men up amongst the different hospitals, so' that instead of one hospital having four or five or six men from the best university in Canada wasting their time in one hospital their services could be utilized in other hospitals helping the more inexperienced men? I challenge comparison between the Bruce and Babtie reports. I will back the Bruce report every day in the week, and every week in the year. I challenge any one outside of the V.A.D. and the society organizations that wanted to keep these hand-holders and brow-rubbers going, to find a solitary word against the Bruce report that is worthy of consideration.
T want to speak of the Medical Service. In 1915 when I was over there I went to review a battalion, and only 300 out of
1,000	men turned up. I inquired the cause, and was told that they were convalescing here and there around the camp. I asked what the mischief convalescing men were doing around there. These men were doing no good to themselves nor to the men in training when they were allowed to convalesce around the camp in that way; so we had the convalescents gathered in central camps, and arranged in fifteen different grades, so that when a man stepped out of the fifteenth grade he was fit to take his place in the line against the Germans the next morning. The result was that instead of returning only about thirty per cent of our wounded, within a certain period we returned sixty-five per cent, which is nearly double the percentage ever shown by any other force in the world. That saved the country millions of dollars.
What else did we find? I asked General Jones, for the Prime Minister, then in England, for a list of hospitals where Canadian wounded were the first morning I arrived in England. Nearly three weeks later I got it. One week-end I was taking a run out into the country to call on some of these hospital people, and in Oxford I found sixty Canadians wounded, and not a solitary report from General Jones on these men. I went on to Cheltenham, Aberystwith, and to Cardiff, where 200 were reported to be present, and I found only three. General Jones' report was not worth the paper it was written on. The next year, in 1916, I found that a great many of qur men were teetotally lost. However, I will not go into that aspect of the case further than to say this: I asked, with the authority of the Canadian Government, that Colonel Bruce should be appointed with a good strong committee of the most capable men to report upon the whole situation, and his report stands there.
The society influence around London has had a detrimental effect in this respect, but they have been forced to accept almost every recommendation he made in that report, and have adopted it to-day, I see, with the exception of these society influences around London. I shall not enter into that aspect of the matter to-night, as perhaps it may come again. At that time I went out of office. - Colonel Bruce was not continued in office by the Canadian Government, but through the influence of friends, of whom I have the honour to be one, he was given service in the British army and his work was well recognized and has redounded to the credit of himself besides being of great advantage to the British army. But if his report had been carried out the men would have had the service of these splendid medical men who were wasted to a certain extent, being duplicated instead of being more generally distributed among the hospitals. As regards the segregation of these men, there is a society aspect that I shall not touch on at the present time, but which was a strong influence in

preventing the segregation of Canadians in Canadian hospitals. So far as the V.A.D.'s are concerned, Dr. Bruce objected to them because of their total inexperience, lack of proper supervision and isolation. We were paying seventy-five cents a day for the untrained nursing of our soldiers, and the British soldiers were getting our highly trained nurses, and were only paying seventy-five cents a day, which was unfair. I remember one morning the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy), who occupied your place for a time to-night, sent me a telegram stating that the mother of a soldier had spoken to him in regard to her son, who was in Welsh hospital and had written her a letter saying that he was dying, and would like to be taken to a Canadian hospital. The hon. member wired me to know if I could do anything in the matter. Within twenty-six hours we were notified by Gen. Carson that the boy had been taken from the Welsh hospital, where he did not understand the language, to a Canadian hospital; and three weeks later we received a second telegram saying that he was absolutely restored. I could give thousands of instances where boys cabled to be removed, and when I was in England they begged me, scores of times, to send them to Canadian hospitals where they would be among friends and not total strangers. There was a question of administration. Colonel Bruce undertook to hunt up lost cases, and it was found that there were seven hundred that were absolutely lost sight of. The medical department had totally lost them, but they turned up in less than a week, and hundreds more every week thereafter. Hundreds were lying around England that should have been sent home. There was no suppression of facts then, and wherever an officer was found to be negligent, or where it was discovered that there was anything wrong, we wanted matters remedied as quickly as possible, whether or not any one was hurt. Of course, we did as little as we possibly could to hurt any one, and if any excuses were offered we were willing to listen to them; but we took pains to see that the work was properly done. If not, those who were at fault had to make place for others. I shall not enter upon anything of a controversial nature.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext: My hon. friend has spoken of Brigadier-General Smart. Can he give us his opinion as regards Colonel Pratt and Colonel Price?

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
I am sorry I forgot Colonel Pratt. A seemingly confidential

report has appeared in the Ottawa papers against Colonel Pratt. I do not for a moment think that the Minister of Militia and Defence in Canada would permit a report of that kind to get out, but it has got out. What are the facts of the case? Colonel Pratt offered to go over in any capacity in order that he might fight. He was too old and so they put him in a command at Dunkirk.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext: He raised his regiment?

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
Yes. He had no military experience. But ninety-nine per cent of our boys had had no military experience, and some who had military experience were not too ready to go to the front, and so we took men like Colonel Pratt who was anxious to go. The point I want to make is that Colonel Pratt was at Dunkirk. The senior officer did not like Colonel Pratt's energetic, free and easy Canadian way, and so spoke of it. But when this old gentleman got into trouble with the Chinese coolies, Colonel Pratt undertook to handle these fellows, and in less than three hours he had restored peace among these five thousand Chinese and saved the butchery of a lot of Chinamen because they got scared at the shelling of the German guns. The senior officer was practically helpless. I do not think anything can be said that is too complimentary of Colonel Pratt's work in this war. When I was a member of this House twenty-five or thirty years ago, I found that sneaking reports could be made by divisional officers, some of whom held their positions because they could not earn their own living at anything else. These reports could be put in against a man, and the officer would not see therm I fought session after session until I forced the Minister of Militia and Defence to see that no adverse reports should be made against any officer by a senior unless a copy of the report was signed by the officer. I have never heard, directly or indirectly, one word derogatory of Colonel Pratt, and if this officer at Dunkirk has passed any such report, he has violated all the rules of honour. Colonel Pratt is impulsive, but it is the impulsive and daredevil men who do great deeds and not the easy-going men. I have never heard anv criticism of Colonel Price. He is a gentleman of the city of Toronto and raised a splendid battalion. Military men are somewhat like preachers and doctors. I remember once having heard an old lady say that if you want to get into the good graces of a preacher you must disparage

his rival. The same truth applies to military men. Tell a military man that he is a much' greater soldier than Colonel So-and-so, and he is highly pleased, and there is a great deal of that sort of thing going on in the military service.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext: It is human philosophy.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext: It may be, but it is cowardice. I have studied the characters of Canadian soldiers, and while some have faults and weaknesses, I do not think you can find better officers and men, taking them altogether than the Canadians at the front.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
After hearing the remarks of the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes), I have come to the conclusion that Canada owes him a great debt of gratitude. He has saved us from the ravages of Imperialism, and has been able to go to the highest authorities in Great Britain and tell them that the Canadian soldiers were entitled to certain things, and to get them. I have always had a high opinion of my friend, the ex-Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes), and I take this opportunity of expressing it to him in the House. He has said, very properly I think, that the answer of Colonel Bruce to the Babtie report should have been taken cognizance of by the Government, and tabled. Colonel Bruce, who was a good soldier and a good medical man, made a certain report, eighty per cent of which is approved by the Acting Prime Minister; yet, the Government profess to have heard nothing from ever about certain aspersions cast upon him. Almost every one else has heard about them. It should have been the duty of the Minister of (Militia, or of the Acting Prime Minister, to have inquired into this matter.
I listened very carefully during the whole course of the speech of the hon. Minister of Militia (Major-General Mewburn) I have always found him to be very frank on all questions in regard to which I have had dealings with him, and he was almost equally frank this afternoon. In making his answer to the Smart Pratt charges, he stated, in almost every case that he did not know. Every time some hon. member asked him for some information, the minister would say:	Overseas knows; I do not. I
have come to the conclusion, therefore, that the co-operation of which the minister was so proud this afternoon can hardly have existed to the extent which he boasted. If it does exist the minister should at any
rate have more information from the other side. I think that, in this Parliament of Canada, we should have some one able to answer any questions we may ask in regard to our boys at the front, their treatment, and the general conduct of the war. I am not intending this as any great criticism of my hon. friend the Minister of Militia; as I said before, il have the greatest respect for him. But, constitutionally, some one should be in this Canadian House of Parliament to answer questions. I think that to a great extent the Minister of Militia is suffering from some of the faults of his immediate predecessor, and perhaps a little also for the faults-for he had some-of his former predecessor. Therefore, while giving him all the credit I can, I am simply making the statement that perhaps if he had been more ready to stand up like his predecessor and say to the people in England, and to the overseas ministers:	"I want
this done; I want it quick and I want you to ruthlessly cut off any expenditure"- and- if he had carried on, in a word, as his predecessor did, we would have had greater satisfaction in this House.
To sum up the answers to the charges made by General Smart and Colonel Pratt, I have found them, as given both by the Minister of Militia and the Acting Prime Minister, to be to a large extent these: General Smart does not know anything about it; Colonel Pratt does not know anything about it; these men should not have carried on this way; they should have come to us and told us about it; we are the people they should have come to instead of going and telling the people of Canada that the boys were badly treated at the front. Is that the answer that is wanted? Is that the answer	that the	House	ofCommons is	entitled to	from	the
Prime Minister or the Minister of Militia? It is no answer to say that General Smart remained in England and that he was on,ly 72 days in France. From the fact that these charges concern England, and England alone, General Smart would be in a better position to know something of the hospital administration there than if he had been in France for four years.- The same thing would apply to Colonel Pratt. It is no answer whatever to say that these officers, both of whom had excellent records, did not go to France. One of them, we are told, offered to revert in order to go to the front. The other one was prevented, on account of the organization of the unit to which he belonged, and he later offered to revert to the rank of Colonel in order to proceed to France. It was found that there

was no place for him as a colonel in the Expeditionary Force in France. If he was not fit to be a colonel in the Expeditionary Forces, why is it that they kept him as a general training our Canadian troops?
To come to the main question, I have no * doubt that had any complaints reached the Minister of Militia When he was in England he would have done his very best to remedy them. But it is not the custom in the army -it has never been the custom, and it is something which has been greatly discouraged-for army officers to go over the heads of their military superiors and make complaints. If they did make complaints, as happened in this case, if they did divulge some of the knowledge which they are presumed to have, we would find, as in this case, that they would be attacked by every sheet that is Government owned and Government controlled. In this case they are told that even their private lives will be exposed and that their conduct is discreditable. These men who have served in France must not, at the risk of their own reputations, or advancement, make any charges or statements.
In so far as the medical services are concerned, I was an orderly in that service myself, and I have nothing but praise for my gallant comrades, those men who, under fire of the worst possible description- stretcher bearers, doctors, and orderlies- were always able, courageous, and willing to perform their duties as Canadians should and to the credit of the Canadian service.
I have nothing to say of the conduct of the men of the Canadian Medical Corps. I have nothing to say of the majors, captains, and sergeants. But in my opinion-and I have a certain amount of knowledge on the subject-the administrative end of the Canadian medical service, in so far as the higher command was concerned, was not, in 1915 or 1916, what it should be. I can very well understand that such should be the case without attaching any particular blame to any one. The Government of Canada were anxious to obtain for the service the very best doctors. They went to Montreal, Toronto and all the large cities and"' obtained them. They could not reasonably hope that a man who had a practice of $20,000 or $40,000 a year would work on the pay of an ordinary captain. Therefore, they made these medical men colonels, and these colonels, as a rule, were placed in administrative capacities at the head of hospitals. It is not reasonable to expect that an eye, ear, nose and throat specialist, or even a family physician, the moment he be-

comes a soldier, will be able to administer a hospital containing a thousand beds.
So it is only natural and a logical consequence of the state we were in that there should have been mismanagement and inefficiency in the higher command of the Canadian army. If there was no inefficiency after the Bruce report and the Bab-tie report were made, why was Sir Guy Carle ton Jones later returned to Canada? I understand that shortly after these reports were made the then Director of Canadian Medical Services, Sir Guy Carleton Jones, was literallydeprivedof his,command. If there were no administrative mistakes why did the Babtie report say there had been mistakes made by the administration? And that, Sir, is about the foundation of the Smart and of the Pratt charges. Why, therefore, should the hon. Acting Prime Minister say that these men are not doing their duty by their country and are not good officers when they make such charges?
Now the question of so-called segregation. In 1916 I was in hospital just a little outside London about the time the Acting Prime Minister stated he was there, and I remember the controversy which raged about this question. I think it was an extremely difficult question, a question which required the very best men to handle and a question about which, as the hon. minister says, literally one-half of the Canadian forces was against the other half. However, if the question was handled and decided only from the standpoint of the efficiency of the Canadian service, I agree with the Acting Prime Minister that it was properly handled, because at that time with the number of casualties coming in, I maintain, it would have been impossible to have segregation of the Canadians. But if the dispersal plan was adopted merely to please the Imperialistic friends of Sir George Perley who were parading the streets of London, or the medical men who were on the Babtie commission and stated as their principal reason for adopting such a system that they wanted to improve the Imperial ties, then, Sir, -I am against it. I do not believe in carrying on Imperial propaganda at the expense of the casualties inflicted in the war.
Now, Sir, I come to the question of Argyll House. I have had very little experience with Argyll House. On most of the occasions that I had anything to do with it I was too junior an officer to be admitted to anybody I wanted to see-I did not even have a chance to get near him. But although the Minister of Miilitia may not have heard

of any complaints in regard to Argyll House, I can assure him that I have, and I know scarcely an officer or a private who has ever had anything very much to do about Argyll House but will say that it is one of the worst and most mismanaged institutions in the world. As to General Turner, I know him personally. He is a Quebecker *-and I would Like to say for the benefit of some hon. gentlemen opposite that there were eleven other generals from the city of Quebec in this war. So if these hon. gentlemen complain that we did not send the brawn to the war, at least we furnished the brains. General Turner is a hero. He won his V.C. by the greatest gallantry in the field in South Africa; he carried on in France; and 'there he attained as great success as any general in the British or Canadian army. He was taken away from the front and brought to Argyll House. I have heard it said that the appointments made in Argyll House were mainly political and mostly from Canada. The appointments were of such a nature that there is hardly a man in the Canadian force who did not have a word of complaint or something derogatory to say about Argyll House. Complaints were general. Nobody wanted to make any specific complaints, because he was afraid, as I have said already, of losing his place or chance of promotion in the Army; but nobody who could possibly avoid having anything to do with Argyll House went near it.	'
The question of demobilization has been raised. I wonder if the hon. minister is aware that either late in 1916 or early in 1917 a committee was formed in England, with Sir George Perley as chairman and Sir Montague Allan or Sir Andrew Allan as one of the members, and Major Sullivan of Winnipeg as secretary. That commission set to work and planned for the demobilization of the Canadian Expeditionary Force. I congratulate the Government of the time upon having taken those steps; but the complaint I have to make is that a lot of time was lost in useless work. For instance, some practical jokers got busy, and sent out questionnaires asking for information of your wife's ancestors, and, in the style of the Ordnance Department, in describing your wife you would have to add " female," and so on and so forth,-this department got to work and those questionnaires were sent out all over the country. A plan was arrived at I understand-the hon. minister will correct me if I am wrong-by which the Canadian troops were to be demoblized by trades or occupations; that is to say, trades 97
most needed in any particular district were to be sent home in their order of urgency, probably transport workers first, carpenters second, and so on. I do not know whether this plan was adhered to very long, but I think it probably could have been carried out. At any rate, when the armistice was signed we found the Government without any very pronounced plans. We found that there were complaints with regard to the boats when the first troops returned; we had an inquiry into the Northland, then we had the Metagama trouble and other troubles about the accommodation on the transports. The plans for demoblization were changed again, and very recently it was decided that the men wanted to come home by units. It seems to me that when these questionnaires were being sent out in 1917, and later it might have been ascertained by these same process as now whether the men wanted to come home by units or not, and the matters might have been arranged in far better fashion than they were. 1 was informed the other day by an officer in France who had just recently left the Rhine district, that at least three days a week the men were paraded to answer another lot of fool questions, and they were getting just a bit fed up on it. The rumour was about-I do not know whether it was true or not, but I think it was-that the Canadian Government had given up the Olympic and the Aquitania to the transportation of the American troops back to the United States, leaving the Canadians who had been over there for four years to freeze in English camps. I think that was one of the proximate causes of the Rhyl riots. It is more than likely that the extreme expedition with which our troops are coming home-expedition with which I agree-is due in large measure to the Rhyl riots. Inquiry was made in the House this afternoon as to how many men have been returned since these riots. I glo not know, but I think that a very large percentage have been returned since that time. It is a fact, however, that the Olympic and the Aquitania have been taken away -from the work of transporting American troops and have been bringing our boys home. That would seem to be somewhat of a justification of the riots and somewhat of a condemnation either of the Minister of Militia here or of his colleague overseas.
I understand also-and this I say to the credit of the Minister of Militia-that within the past month the authority which Argyll House had with regard to the em-



barkation or the disembarkation of Canadian troops has been taken away and has been vested more particularly in the Canadian Minister of Militia. If such is the case, the charges made against Argyll House would seem to be proved by the very action of the Canadian Government.
We should have a full, fair and frank investigation of these charges. If they are not true-and I do not know whether they are true or not-the Government has no reason to fear them. If they are true, then the Canadian Government and the people of Canada have a right to know how the Canadian soldiers were treated overseas. I maintain that if any Canadian soldier, whether he be an officer or the meanest private, has been ill-treated in a British or in a Canadian hospital to such an extent that he suffered physically in any way or to such an extent that he died; if Canadian soldiers are being kept in England or were kept in England beyond the time for demobilization by the inefficiency of Argyll House or of any other body, those who were guilty of such inefficiency and neglect should be brought to book. I believe that the people of Canada share that view.
Some charges were made this afternoon against British hospitals. Constitutionally, tempermentally and racially, I have had no great liking for England. But during the years that I was there, on the two occasions on which I was wounded I went to British hospitals, anld for the brave nurses, the doctors and the orderlies of those hospitals I have nothing but the highest praise. I was in Miss Pollock's hospital on Weymouth street, London, for something like a month and a half, and later went to an English convalescent home. The treatment there was the very best you could get in any civilian hospital. On the second occasion I spent almost a year at the Royal Herbert hospital in Woolwich, one of the largest and oldest hospitals in the British Empire. There also everybody was kindness itself; all those engaged in work there went out of their way to do what they could, particularly . for the colonials, more particularly for Canadians and Australians. They said: "These poor boys are from across the sea; there is nobody to look after them; we will look after them." We were looked after in the British hospitals so well that I cannot but refute any statement made against the people of England or the medical authorities in England with respect to the treatment of Canadian soldiers in English hospitals.

speechtext:
The member for Muskoka (Mr. Peter McGibbon) intended to say a few words this evening, but had to leave to take a train. I had not intended saying anything on this subject, but as there are in the House three members of the medical profession who have served at the front, it might seem strange if they did nc*t say a word. or two to show that they are not absolutely ignoring this discussion. Of course, the three members of the medical profession who are in this House and who served at the front were not among those distinguished medical men men-mentioned by the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White); they were just ordinary captains serving over there. Consequently, the trickeries that Argyll House is accused of are not, perhaps, within their purview.
The member for Skeena (Mr. Peck) through the generosity of his heart, made a defence of the medical men this afternoon. The reason that the medical men themselves have not risen to make any defence is that we are of the opinion that the medical men at the front require no^defence. I look upon these charges as being directed not against the medical men, but against the administration of the medical department; so that those of us like the member for South Essex (Mr. Brien), the member for Muskoka, and myself, who served in various branches from the base hospitals to battalions in the lines (and who are probably familiar enough with many phases of this question to contradict some of the statements made to-day on both sides of the House, consider that it is not necessary for us to defend the medical men.	-
The member for Skeena said that the medical men were brave. Certainly they were brave, but they were no braver or no less brave than the other Canadians and Britishers who went to the front, from the Tommies to the Brigadier-Generals. Practically everybody who went out there was brave; there was no cowardice at the front so far as I was able to see. I may mention in passing that one of the first Victoria Crosses won at the front was won by a Canadian physician of Montreal, Dr. Scrim-ger; so that the medical men do not feel that they are required to speak very much for themselves.
The member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) was also very kind; indeed all the speakers during the course of this discussion have been kind in their references to the medical profession. But the member for Victoria

made some remarks with regard to the women of the Voluntary Aid Detachment at the front, referring to hand-holding and brow-rubbing and so on. So long as human nature is human nature, a certain amount of that will go on, but outside of the ordinary amount of that which goes on in all spheres of life, I believe that there was no more of it among the women of the Voluntary Aid Detachment than there was among any other class of women. I saw their work out there in the base hospitals, and I believe that the vast majority of the V.A.D.'s deserve the gratitude of the whole civilized world for the work they did at the front. I do not think, therefore, I should be doing my duty if I did not say a word on their behalf, even if at the same time I have to take exception to some of the statements of the member for Victoria, for whom I have a very deep personal affection. But, like all good guns, he sometimes goes off at half-cock.
I repeat, in closing, that to my mind it is the administrative end of the medical profession at the front that has been attacked here to-day. For that reason, and because the Government have defended it, I do not feel that it is necessary for any medical man in the House to take up the cudgels on its behalf.

speechtext: I was not speaking of the system; I was speaking entirely of the V.A.D. work at the front, and according to my experience the Voluntary Aid Detachments, both Canadian and British, did wonderfully good work at the front and deserve the gratitude of all Anglo-Saxon people at least.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the charges that have been levelled here this afternoon by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) with regard to the whole medical administration in connection with the war through which we have passed must cause some of us to ask ourselves how long our feelings are going to be harrowed in this House and out of it by charges of this nature. It is only a short time ago in this House that we were told frankly and fairly by one who, at least we presumed should know, that our boys had been forced into positions that meant practically nothing more nor less than deliberate and wilful murder in order that some officers in the Canadian corps might cover themselves with personal glory. This afternoon we heard it stated that a similar condition prevailed in connection with the Canadian and British hospitals in which our boys were put when they were wounded at the front. We heard it stated by the hon. member for Maisonneuve that this country is going to be saddled with a burden of tens of millions of dollars in pensions due to the maltreatment criminally administered to our Canadian boys in the hospitals in England.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
Was it chivalrous
for them to make the charges they did against the comrades who served with them? What about that aspect of the case? I have on file in my home five hundred letters from boys who served in England

and France, more than two hundred of those letters being written in hospitals in France and in England, and every one of those two hundred boys speaking in the highest terms of the treatment they received in those hospitals. My own boy spent five months in a hospital in England, and writing to his mother he said: " For heroism, and devotion to duty, no man who ever went over the top in France has done more in this war than the doctors, and nurses who are looking after the wounded men when they come back from the front." And the whole trend of the charges that have been made this afternoon, say what you will or clothe it in as nice language as you may, comes back to nothing else but this, that the doctors and nurses did not do their duty. speechtext:
Just one or two words with regard to the riots at Rhyl Camp. In some of the charges referred to by my hon. friend this afternoon, and made by Colonel Pratt, and Colonel Price, it was stated that the riots at Ryhl Camp were due to maladministration on the part of " armchair officers." I happen accidentally to know the officer that was in charge of Ryhl Camp previously to and during those riots. The information came to me in an indirect manner. Major M. C. McLean, who won the Distinguished Service Order for taking his company across the canal, and practically taking the city of Valenciennes, who went over with the McLean Highlanders, and came back with that decoration and stayed with the fight until the Canadians went into Mons-he is the man who is held up as the " armchair officer," the " safety-first " man who led the Canadians at Rhyl to riot.
There is one other point in connection with demobilization. It has been stated to this House and to the country that the Government are criminally responsible for these riots, because they did not bring the men home fast enough. I have not heard the Government make the statement, but I am ready to say here and now that the men were brought back to Canada as rapidly as it was reasonably possible to handle them at the Atlantic ports as they came in. We are handling 30,000 men a month, and in March 42,000 were handled. For every thousand men that come, into Halifax, forty passenger cars are required

to take them to their destination, and it takes on an average ten days at the very least to get those passenger cars hack to Halifax for the next contingent. How many men could be handled with the total equipment of the Canadian railways? Personally, I think it is a marvel what has been accomplished, when we consider all the difficulties surrounding the transport of Canadian troops after landing in this country. It is quite true that two million men have been brought back to England, but they had only the Channel to cross, which takes only two or three hours or at the most half a day. But transporting the Canadian troops is a different proposition. They have to be transported 2,500 or 3,000 miles across the Atlantic, and then by rail, one-half of them at least, to Winnipeg and points West, making a furthei distance of from two to four thousand miles, and the equipment has to be back at Halifax in time for the next contingent. Yet hon. members will say, because our troops have not been brought back in larger numbers, the Government is criminally responsible for the Rhyl riots. If we are going to fight this whole war over again, and if the fathers and mothers who have suffered as a result of this war are to be forced to continue to listen to these charges made by disgruntled officers-because that is what they are pure and simple, when it comes down to the ground-then Heaven help the Canadian people! If we have not passed through enough without listening to this kind of stuff, then I do not know what is going to become of us. A great deal has been said about the dissatisfaction among Canadian soldiers. Where are they getting their leadership in this dissatisfaction? Right here in this House, and from men who ought to know better.

subtopic: MILITARY MANAGEMENT OVERSEAS-THE ALLEGATIONS BY BRIGADIER-GENERAL SMART, COLONEL PRATT, COLONEL PRICE.
speechtext:
It has been repeated several times by bon. members on the other

side of the House that the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) has made charges against the overseas administration in connection with this war. The hon. member has made no such charges. He has discharged his duty, as I understand it, in bringing to the notice of this House a very important matter bearing upon the life of our soldiers beyond the seas. That duty he owed to those men who have risked their lives in the defence oi this country. It does not require a great deal of courage on the part of any member of this House to sit tight and say nothing about anything that may be put in circulation as to the administration of public affairs. It is the man who is anxious for a clean administration, that the affairs of this country shall be properly conducted, who takes upon himself to bring questions of this kind to the notice of the House. If questions of this sort are not to be brought to the attention of this Parliament, this high tribunal, where shall we go with them? What are we here for, if it is not to safeguard the interests of the country?-for this is the only federal Parliament we have. I submit, therefore, that no apology is required for the action of the hon. member for Maisonneuve. I am not going to say whether the charges are right or wrong. All I would say to the Acting Prime Minister, if he were in his seat, is that he has taken the course he usually takes in matters of this kind, of putting up a straw man and then knocking him down. He spoke of things that had nothing whatever to do with the question before the House. There was no mention in those charges, as I understood them, of the Bruce or the Babtie report.
The Bruce report dated in August or September of 1916, and the Babtie report is dated September 22, 1916. When we inquire about things that took place after 1916-1917, 1918 down the years to the present day-is it any answer for the Government to say:	" Oh, why, there was a report on September 22, 1916. What are you talking about? 'That report settled the whole thing then, and of course settled everything down to the present day." Nobody would say that, and I am sure that it is only fair, if there is anything to investigate, at all events from September 22, 1916, to the present day, that it should be investigated. I was brought up to believe-and I would impress this view on every hon. member -that an officer wearing His Majesty's uniform was in every sense of the term a gentleman, beyond reproach, that his word was his bond, and that what he said was absolutely the truth, should the heavens

fall. I have always believed that we should accept without question the word of a general, a colonel, a captain, or any other officer of His Majesty. And, Mr. Speaker, it is highly necessary that this should be so. The fathers and mothers of this country who allow their sons to be placed under the control of these men should have implicit confidence in their integrity; and I hope that there is not a member in the House who would countenance any man bearing the title of general, or brigadier general, or colonel, or any of these high-sounding names, which mean so much, if, in the ordinary vulgar Anglo-Saxon term he were a liar. Those men who made the speeches in the legislatures of Ontario and Quebec are officers, and we have a right to believe that they have made statements that are absolutely true as far as they know. If the statements are not true, and they do not believe them to be true and consistent with the facts, they have no right to the titles they bear, nor to wear His Majesty's uniform. They should not be in the army of either 'Canada or the Mother Country and should be stripped of their honours and driven out of positions of responsibility. If there is no other investigation than to find out whether or not those men are telling the truth, it is well to ascertain that fact. If they are not telling the truth an example should be made of them, so that officers now, hereafter, and for all time, will understand that the Canadian people expect of them truth, integrity and honour, and a dignity that will be above reproach. I make no accusations against anybody. I appreciate the responsibilities of the men in office, and until I know to the contrary I believe they are doing the best they can. But I insist that men who hold important offices of this kind, in whose care the lives of the young men and women of the country are placed, should be gentlemen above all else, true to the traditions which we have always cherished in the British army and in our militia as well. I trust that those who are in authority over these men-I care not whether they are in office or out of office; so long as they bear the titles and wear the uniform they are under the control of the Government-will see that they tell the truth, and that if they do not, they shall suffer the consequence and be stripped of any honour they now possess. If, on the other hand, these men are telling the truth, we should know it. The people have the right to expect that this or any Government that may be in power will not tolerate irregularities or abuse of our men and

women who serve the country faithfully and well, as has been done in this war.
