speakeroldname: Mr. SAMUEL FRANCIS GLASS (Middlesex, East) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the impetus given to the extension and development of fibre flax production in Canada has achieved results which justify further serious consideration, co-operation and encouragement by the Government, and to this end it is desirable:-
First: That a modern experimental and demonstrative station should be established at the most convenient and central point within the area where flax for fibre is being produced so that growers may be advised and educated in the most modern and improved methods of retting, scutching and generally preparing their fibre for the market.
Sec'm.l: That improved mechanical appliances and equipment being necessary for the economic harvesting of the crop, as well as for the preparation of fibre, constant watchfulness should be exercised by the Government to insure that Canadian growers may be supplied with most modern machinery for harvesting and scutching and instructed in the newest and best method of retting.
Third: That in order to secure full economic value to the grower, it is desirable that the Government should establish a system of grading and standards consistent and consonant (in so far as possible) with continental standards so that the world's best markets may be available for our exportable surplus.
Fourth: That Canadian farmers, urged by the stress of war and the Empire's insistent needs

for increased production, have increased their fibre flax acreage more than eighteen fold, at a time when the world's markets were at their highest figures, and have thus developed a source of natural resource which has materially added to the value of our agricultural wealth, not only so, but have demonstrated in the world's markets that Canadian flax fibre is equal in quality to best continental standards and superior to any produced in Russia, which hitherto produced 75 per cent of the world's supply; therefore, in view of these results attained, the Government should jealously guard the interests of growers and lend such co-operation as may be necessary to increase production and to encourage by every means possible the full development of its manufacture from the field to the loom, so as to obtain the full economic a;ue of the production to the country.
He said: Mr. Speaker, having regard to the important part that the flax industry has played and must play in the economic wealth and development of this country, I feel that I do not owe any apology to the House for again directing the attention of hon. gentlemen to this matter. I desire to express my appreciation of the very valuable assistance lent to this industry through the encouragement given by the Department of Agriculture-encouragement which has resulted to some extent from the discussion which we had in the House in 1916 and 1918.
In 1915 the flax industry in Canada was but a small and struggling one of very little significance; the total acreage of flax fibre under production-I am speaking of the fibre end particularly-was only about 1,400 acres. Due to the necessities of the war and the very urgent demand of the Empire for an increased supply of flax fibre -a demand resulting from the need for linen cloth to be used in the manufacture of aeroplane wings-earnest efforts were made in this country to increase the production of fibre flax to meet the national need. In 1916 Lloyd George, urging the agriculturists of the Empire to increase their production of cereal and foodstuffs, said that 'this matter was of so much importance that the man who was doing his honest duty in endeavouring to increase the production of foodstuffs and cereals was serving in the second line of defence and doing as important work for the Allies as those who were serving in the front line. Lloyd George said at that time:
The line which the British Empire holds against the Germans is held by those who work on the land as well as by those who fight on land and sea. If it breaks at any point it breaks eveiywhere. In the face of the enemy the seamen of our Royal naval mercantile marine and the soldiers gathered from every part of our Empire hold our line firstly. You workers on land must hold your part of our

line as strongly. Every full day's labour you do helps to shorten the struggle and brings us nearer victory. Every idle day, all loitering, lengthens the struggle and makes defeat more possible. Therefore, in the nation's honour, heed ! Acquit yourselves like men, and as workers on land do your duty with all your strength.
In the early part of last year the Board of Agriculture and Fisheries in Great Britain, who were in charge of the matter of flax production, sent out a circular letter urging an increased production of flax for fibre. The circular letter said:
The Board of Agriculture and Fisheries have decided that any flax grown for the Government in your district shall rank of as equal importance to cereals and your War Agriculture Committee has been informed accordingly.
A message came over the seas to Canada in this matter because it was found that we could produce fibre of a sufficiently high quality for use in the manufacture of aeroplane wings. The necessity of speeding up production in Canada, therefore, was evident, and the Experimental Farm Branch of the Dominion Department of Agriculture early in that year issued a circular to the flax growers of Canada, from which I quote the following:
The Canadian Farmers' opportunity to save the lives of many of our men and aid directly in our victory. Aeroplane wings must be covered' with linen. The supply of flax for this purpose is alarmingly short and most sources of supply are out off. Canada is expected to do her utmost to make up the deficiency.
The mastery of the air is proving a great, perhaps the determining factor, in the struggle now going on. Aeroplanes are being built in vast numbers as rapidly as possible. As a covering for the wings of these, linen is the only material found satisfactory. Large quantities are also needed for machine-gun webbing, ambulance and truck covers, thread for sewing uniforms, and a number of other uses. Were the supply of fibre flax for these purposes to fall short, as is threatened it would directly and profoundly affect the success of the Allied forces.
So serious is the situation that the British Government has commandeered all flax products entering the United Kingdom, and Ireland has taken extraordinary steps to increase the 1918 flax acreage in the British Isles. It has to this end imported large quantities of flax seed' from Western Canada, although but little is known of the possibilities of the prairie-grown seed for fibre production.
'The Resources Committee of Ontario,, also active in stimulating production by facilitating matters affecting the gathering of the harvest and the securing of the necessary labour, issued a circular and did splendid work in developing the flax resources last year. They asked the people of Ontario to grow flax this year, pointing out that each additional acre of flax provided wings for another aviator; that one-

third of all the aviators in the British Air Service had been supplied by Canada, and that these brave boys must have further help from Canada-in order that they may fly; we must give them wings. In concluding their circular they said:
If you cannot fly yourself, help others to fly by growing flax.
During the early part of the year this matter was taken up among the farmers, and, stimulated by a sense of patriotic duty and by a desire to increase the economic wealth and production of the country as urged by the Government, Ontario put to fibre seed some eighteen thousand acres. In Quebec, in the district which the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) represents, fibre of a quality superior to anything grown elsewhere in Canada has been produced under experimental tests. In Ontario, fibre is being grown superior to any quality of fibre produced in Russia and quite equal to the highest continental standard. It would seem, therefore, as if there were great possibilities for the production of fibre in Quebec and Ontario. In Ontario' last year, under the stimulus of greater production and patriotic duty, we seeded. 18,000 acres and produced over
3.000	tons of flax. What might this country do, not only in meeting our national needs, but in increasing our economic wealth, if the same earnestness in flax production were developed in all parts of Canada in which it is possible to grow this fibre? This is not an industry peculiar to Ontario, or to any particular part of that province, because at the present time, the number of flax mills is increasing and they are springing up all through eastern Ontario and throughout Quebec. In such parts of the country as cereals can be cultivated, a very high quality of flax can be grown. Years ago it was demonstrated that in Nova Scotia a very high quality of flax could be produced, and in British Columbia, and in certain districts of the provinces of the Northwest flax for fibre can be successfully grown. It would, therefore, seem as ii there were plenty of opportunity for the development of flax growing in this country at the present time.
Before the war, Russia produced about 80 per cent of the total world production of flax, namely, about 400,000 tons, about
200.000	tons of which were exported from that country and used in other countries in which flax fibre spinning was developed to its highest degree. We are led to believe at times that France and Belgium are the countries which have hitherto produced the
high qualities of fibre, and that if we are to develop this industry in Canada in the future, our fibre must measure up in quality to that produced in those countries. Notwithstanding the fact that Belgium and France have in the past produced a high quality of fibre, the quantity they produce is really an insignificant portion of the total world production. Before the war, the fibre production of Belgium was about
10.000	tons, and that of France about 30,000 tons, or a total of 40,000 tons, which is small as against a total world production of
500.000	tons.
We have, in the face of difficulties, increased and improved the production of flax in Canada. I am not going to go over the ground that I covered last year as regards the prejudice that exists amongst farmers as to the effect of flax on the soil, but I desire to refer to a matter I overlooked last year, namely, that while this prejudice may be founded, it is founded on causes which are now controlled. Mr. Clark, Seed Commissioner of the Department of Agriculture, in a report for the year 1916, referring to the examination of seeds, says:
Most of the so-called cleaned grain contained large numbers of very small weed seeds as well as small, light kernels and inert matter, clearly indicating poor results from the attempt at cleaning. With flax, this is shown by the presence of such small seeds as tumbling mustard, cinquefoil, wormwood, lamb's quarters, worm seed mustard, and also grain, black bindweed and other large seeds in samples that had been through fanning-mills. One sample reported as cleaned with a common fanning-mill contained seventeen species of weed seeds, including over 2,500 tumbling mustard-
This was a seed cleaned and ready lor the market.

over 1,000 lamb's quarters, 803 black bindweed, and 140 wild oats per pound, besides wheat, oats and barley. Some of the grain samples furnish equally striking examples of failure to remove even small weed seeds by the fanning-mill.
It would not be surprising that seed of that kind sent out to the farmers and seeded would produce disastrous results and disappointment to the farmers. Mr. Clark says further:
Nearly all the samples of flax would have been much improved by the use of a woven wire riddle .3 x 16-inch size (three spaces to the inch one way and sixteen the other), to carry the large foreign seeds over the back of the mill, and a zinc sieve below, with 1-12-inch perforations, to let through the small seeds with practically no loss of flax.
I desire to bring to the attention of the minister and of the Department of Agri-



At this moment we have at our disposition the crops of 1914 and 1915.
The crop of 1914 is very superior and we have obtained two qualities of fibre-average and superior-(about 50% of each). From the crop of 1915 Which was very mediocre, we have inferior and average quality.
France planted in 1913 30,000 hectares. Belgium "	"	" 23,000Holland "	'*	" 14,000
In the same year Canada planted 6'2>8,000 hectares in flax.
These figures indicate clearly that the Dominion of Canada is capable of organizing a very powerful linen industry.
With 30,000 hectares, France obtained 25,000,000 francs of seed, that is 1,000 francs worth per hectare.
In Canada 628 000 hectares produced 450,00-0 tons of seed valued at 90,000,000 francs, that is about 150 francs per hectare.
Russia planted 1,448,000 hectares and her exportation in fibre in 1913 reached 250,04)0,000 francs as against 50,00'0,00fl francs of seed.
The conclusion is that flax culture is very interesting from the point of view of the fibre, but very little remunerative for the seed, and it seems certain that cultivators will be quickly and easily persuaded to sell their flax straw, and to regulate their flax culture according to the conditions necessary to obtain good straw for fibre.
I should also like to refer to a report that reached me only a day or two ago from New York. I cannot say anything as to its reliability, but it appeared in the March number of Cotton, a textile trade journal published in the United States. It draws attention to the possibility of the production of linen from flax fibre at a price to compete favourably with cotton. Referring to the flax and linen industry dn the United States, the March number of Cotton says:
Whether the stimulus afforded by the necessity of war will prove of lasting benefit is still to be demonstrated, but from the report from William J. Robinson, Chairman of the Division of Flax, Fibre and Linen Manufacturers, U.S. War Industries Board, hope of this result is given.
If it comes true, the United States will in one more direction be free from that dependence upon .foreign nations which was such a handicap in 1915 and 1916, though happily it has turned out to be a blessing in stirring American initiative.
According to Mr. Robinson, the cotton belt will have to look to its laurels. At any rate, he says that " recent discoveries in the treatment of flax make it possible for America not only to grow flax successfully and profitably, in every state of the union, but to produce flax fibre with an average yield of two-third of a bale to the acre more cheaply than cotton can be produced, and with more profit to the farmer. Synthetically prepared American flax has been converted info linen _ commercially for the first time in America, in a mill in Wisconsin.
Following are some parts of the report made by Mr. Robinson:
" After long and painstaking research a new synthetic process has been discovered, which is one of the most important discoveries to +he

entire field of commercial industry. The process dissolves the gum from the flax straw in less than an hour, without any injury to the fibre, and produces a strong, clean, beautiful fibre, ready for the spinner when dried and prepared. The process can be operated in either summer or winter, and has no disagreeable features, costs 70 per cent less in labour, time and expense than either of the other processes, and makes bleaching, except to secure extremely white linen, absolutely unnecessary.
In a test of the comparative strength of water-retted fibre-
This is a very important part of the report, because the objections to the process of chemical retting and any other process except the old one of dew retting, has been that it weakens the tensile strength of the fibre. Mr. Robinson says:
In a test of the comparative strength of water-retted fibre and the retted fibre by the United States Bureau of Standards, October 15, 191S-water retted flax broke at a strain of 115-while retted fibre by this new process stood a strain of 183. Flax by this new method can he produced more cheaply than cotton.
I do not affirm or accept the statement as accurate, but coming from such an authority as the chairman of the Division of Flax, Fibre and Linen Manufacturers, United States War Industries Board, and in view of the tests made by the United States Bureau of Standards, we should at least give some attention and weight to the report presented.
Is the flax produced in Canada manufactured into linen anywhere in Canada?

Yes, I am coming to that feature of it; it is being done now. I said, Mr. Speaker, that in the year 1914 we were producing a small acreage of 1,400 acres only of fibre flax in Canada. We had nine mills in operation and they were scattered over a very small area of southwestern Ontario, not because the weather conditions there were more favourable than elsewhere, but simply because these few mills were the only remaining ones of a large number that had gradually, from time to time, gone out of operation owing to the competition of the Russian fibre and the cheap labour in European production. Now, however, the industry is extending well over the province of Ontario and at the present time 47 mills are reported ito the Department of Agriculture with a total flax area last year of 18,000 acres, and an area rented for the purposes of next year's production of 25,000 acres. I have here a list of mills distributed as follows:
Nicholson & Hodgins, Crediton; McMurchy & Anderson, Bipley; Amerlin Flax Co., Petrolia;

Wra. Forrester. Mitchell; O. Geiger, Hensall; Doon Twines Ltd., Floradale; Tipling & Mills, Wingham; T. A. G. Gordon, Sarnia; Jas. McColl & Co., Alvinston; H. "W. Ehel, Conestogo; McDonald Burns Ltd., Dresden; H. A. Griffin, Arthur ; Barbour Flax Co., Moorefield, Alma; Ontario Flax Co., Parkhill, Ailsa Craig, Shipka, Exeter and Tilbury; Wm. Ward, Lucan; A. Heiderman & Son, Zurioh; V. Stock, Tavistock; H. Fraleigh, Forest; Dashwood Flax Co., Dash-wood ; F. Kalbfleisch, Zurich; Sebringville Flax Co., Sebringville; R. J. Nicholson & Son, Mer-ner and Seaforth; Blyth Flax Co., Blyth; Netherlands Flax Co., Winnipeg.
The Netherlands Flax Co. of Winnipeg, a new company, have 700 acres under contract for next year, and this is evidence of the confidence they have that flax fibre can be grown in the province of Manitoba.
Canadian Flax Mills, Drayton, Arthur, Seaforth, Wallaceburg, Essex and St. Catharines;
A.	L. McCredie, St. Marys; Stratford Flax Co., Stratford; Flax Spinners Ltd., Guelph and Lis-towel; Wm. Weir, St. Marys ; Edward Weiler, Bowmanville; Canadian Flax & Seed, Oshawa ; J. Flock, Windsor; James Rose, Pickering; J.
B.	Hudson. Millbank.
I point out this distribution to show that the cultivation of flax is spreading out into new areas which for some years have not made any progress. The fact that we have to such a large extent devel-3 p.m. oped this industry under the stimulus that has been pressing us, and the fact that we have increased our production considerably is not, to my mind, the most important thing that we have discovered. We knew that we could produce a good fibre. Our fibre previous to 1915 found its market entirely in the United States, in the mills of Massachusetts and New Jersey,- where it was spun into yarns for shoemakers' and har-nessmakers' purposes, and for twines for fishing nets, as well as for coarser purposes; but that we	were able
behind it all to produce a quality of fibre fine enough to make the fine linens that were being made, seemed absolutely unknown to us. I have pointed out that the Ontario Flax Mills Company have five different mills in that province, and it is interesting to tell the House who the Ontario Flax Mills Company are. They are an organization directly representing in Canada the Belfast Spinning Mills of Belfast, Ireland, the largest linen mills in the world. Knowing that a good fibre must be produced and that they could not count on the fibre of Russia as regards its quality, and realizing that the supply from Belgium must be shut off, and as there were limitations to the amount that could be grown in Ireland, the Belfast mills four years ago sent Mr. F. J. Lockhart, a most
98i	.	. i
capable man who understands the flax business from A to Z, to Parkhill in the county of Middlesex to try out our Canadian flax. They obtained a small acreage of four or five hundred acres altogether and seeded flax in that district with the Dutch child seed. The crop was so satisfactory that every pound of it was scutched and sent over to their mills in Ireland, and the next year they put in 1,000 acres, increasing the acreage in 1917. Last year they had over 1,800 acres, and according to the statement I have, they have under contract 2,500 acres for fibre for the Belfast linen mills for next year. Why should men of their experience go to -the expense of establishing industries here, if it be not because they know that they can obtain in Canada the raw material necessary to keep their mills in operation and cannot get it so satisfactorily elsewhere? That is their reason for being here; and may we not hope that, as this large industry in Ireland, the largest in the world, sees the possibilities of producing raw material here, the time will soon come when under the stimulus and encouragement of the bounty now being given for the spinning of yarns in Canada -they will transfer from Ireland some of their large spinning plants? May we not hope that the time will quickly come when this industry, which was of such insignificant importance here a year ago but which is gradually blossoming out, will be an important factor in the economic and industrial develoment of this country? Last year in discussing this subject I urged on my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture and the Government to connect up the fibre industry with the weaving industry by giving encouragement to the spinning of yarns. This was the position we-occupied and have occupied: We have had a linen mill in the city of Guelph representing an investment of $750,000, a mill that can weave as fine cloths as those produced in any part of the world. This mill had to bring its yarns from Ireland to weave cloths. We were producing the raw material; were the "hewers of wood and drawers of water" for the other fellows, doing the hard, laborious and difficult work which gave the least value in money We sent this material over to Ireland and Ireland spun it into yarn. Our mills bought back the yarn as their raw material, and this is what they are weaving in the city of Guelph. I am told this is the only linen weaving mill on the continent of America. Whether that is right or wrong I cannot say, but I do know it is the only on* in the Dominion of Canada.

The (Government did not take action in the early part of last year in the direction I suggested, that of giving a bonus or a bounty on the spinning of yarns in (Canada from Canadian fibre. But in September last the demand for aeroplane cloths and linen products was so insistent that the British War Board represented to the War Trade Board of (Canada the urgency of the situation. The War Trade Board of Canada made their representations to the Government and as a result a bounty was given for the spinning of yarn varying according to the fineness of the yarn. These yarns are known by the word " lea " which defines their fineness. On 20 lea, which is a comparatively coarse yarn, the Government allowed a bounty of three cents a pound; on yarn over 20 and under 40 lea, they allowed six cents a pound and on all yarn over 40 lea of fineness nine cents per pound was allowed. What happened? The ink had scarcely dried upon the paper putting that Order in 'Council into force when contracts were negotiated for the establishment of a big spinning mill. That only happened last September and notwithstanding the difficulties of procuring machinery and establishing such industries, in the city oi Guelph, a spinning mill has been established representing an investment of some $300,000 and instead of sending our fibre out of the country to Ireland, the Canadian Spinneries Limited in Guelph are spinning our fibre into yarn which is a step in the right direction. But the Canadian (Spinneries Limited at Guelph, operating to their full capacity, could not spin one-eighth oi ;the fibre that was produced in Canada last year and it will be largely increased for the coming year. That is not all. I desire to tell the House that a very large corporation interested in the linen trade and which has been doing much to develop the linen Industry in this country, have their buyers to-day in England buying the necessary machinery to establish a mill in Canada for the production of linen in all its departments. Their slogan is:	"Flax from the
field to the mill." They are going to grow, ret, scutch, heckle, spin and weave the flax. They are going to carry on the whole operation. This concern is going to establish a very large industry. It is expected that $2,000,000 will be invested and its plant will be up to date in every respect. It seems to me that there has been sufficient justification for the Government in carrying out the recommendations that were made to it at that time.
In the Canadian Textile Journal, published at Ste. Anne de Bellevue, a series of

articles has appeared under the name of Alfred S. Moore, a very prominent trained flax man in Ireland. He is giving considerable attention to the development of flax in this country. I noticed that in the number of February 4, speaking of Canada and the possibilities of the flax industry, he points out tlhe achievements of Canada in the development of flax fibre. But there is one feature which I desire particularly to call the attention of the House to and that is the high standing we have achieved in the British market for our product. He says:-
Despite the high price and scarcity of Canadian labour it is at present the most promising country for flax and seed supplies. There is an active Canadian Flax Growers' Association in existence and the Dominion Government in its Experimental Farm at Ottawa, has also shown itself most energetic. Nor should one forget the stimulus given to the industry by the " Canadian Textile Journal " and the " Monetary Times "... The great Belfast York Street Flax Spinning Company-the world's largest linen mills-and also several other Belfast firms have proved the excellent quality of Canadian flax, and, as a result, large tracts of flax lands are now being cultivated in the Dominion.
It is a matter for congratulation, however, that a step has been taken in the right direction, and it is hoped that Canadian flax will soon take the place of that grown in Russia in providing the flax for the world's linen trade, and it is to the benefit of the Dominion and ourselves to develop the promising field.
It is due to Canadian seed that the extended flax acreage in Ireland this season has been possible. Most of the Canadian flax is exported to the United States, and what is most needed in Canada is the development of a good flax pulling machine. In the Canadian Northwest also two million acres are annually planted with flax-not grown for the fibre, as the climate of the West is not considered the best for fibre production. To the linen trade of Ireland it is tantalizing that thousands of tons of flax fibre should be annually burnt up in Canada.
What I desire to especially draw to the attention of the House is that tests have been made under Government direction in England and Ireland in their experimental farms in regard to the production of flax, and they have demonstrated that Canadian seed, side by side with the world's established standards, Dutch (White Flowering), Yorkshire, French, Irish, Russian (Perneau Crown), and American (Minnesota), ranks amongst the very first. At present Great Britain is controlling all the seed that will be sown for fibre in Great Britain next year. Great Britain controls the price at which the seed shall be sold and the profit that wholesalers shall receive for the sale of it. In the list of prices issued to the trade only in March last, which appeared in the Linen Circular, a linen journal in

Ireland, Canadian standard fibre is the very highest priced seed offered to the growers of Great Britain of all the world's standard varieties. It seems to me that it is very important that we have been able to attain so high a reputation in the production of our seed. Great Britain this year will be dependent largely on the seed grown in this country for- her crop of 1939
To this end, in September or October last, the British Government asked the Canadian Government to commandeer all the available export flax fibre seed in this country for use next year. The Canadian Government did so, and the price obtained by the growers amounting to something like $8.30 a bushel, or thereabouts. Some one hundred and ten thousand bushels of this seed were commandeered, and after doing that sufficient supply was left to seed the crop ol 1919. The British Government, I am sorry to say, instead of using this seed for the purposes for which it was commandeered has directed a certain amount of it to the West to produce seed for their supplies next year. However, the reputation we have made in the world's best market must be jealously guarded, and carefully maintained. I know personally that the Minister of Agriculture has given very serious consideration to this feature, and that he will throw about it such safeguards as are necessary to maintain that reputation.
It is said that in the West a large amount of flax is grown for seed only, and the question has been asked by members from the West: Why cannot we grow fibre out there? I say to our friends from the West: If we attempt to grow flax in this country as you grow it out there we would not produce fibre either. There are two methods of growing flax, one for seed, and one for fibre. Where flax is grown for seed, about half a bushel of seed to the acre is used. It produces a short stubby stalk which throws out very large seed bolls, which are grown for seed for manufacturing oil and certain by-products. Where seed is sown for fibre, a bushel and a half to two bushels to the acre is used and produces a thicker and longer straw with only a few seed bolls in the top. The lands of the West, I understand, have produced as high as twenty-eight bushels to the acre of flax seed. That, no doubt, is a very large production, a great deal larger than the average. From lands where flax is seeded for fibre the maximum average production of seed is about eight bushels to the acre. In the United States and in Canada considerable effort has been devoted to research in the hope of ultimately
using the waste straw of the Western provinces. I have a report here in which a Mr. George Harrison claims to have made considerable progress in discovering a method for using the western straw for gas purposes. This gentleman says:
Plain loose threshed straw is placed in an air-tight retort, and when roasted, not burned, for half an hour in three hundred degrees of heat, the gas leaves by the only means of escape, through a pipe into a scrubber or refiner. At this point a by-product in the form of jet black tar is taken from the gas, and the purified product passes into the gasometer, or large storage tank. From there it is piped to the various cooking or heating appliances and operated in the same manner as by city users of gas. The bluish flame is similar to coal gas, though claimed to be of a much higher grade and having greater heating propensities.
Without going into this report very fully,
I may say this man claims to have discovered a means of manufacturing gas from this straw whereby a ton of straw, which is of small value compared to a ton of coal, will develop more gas than a ton and a quarter of coal. I have no doubt this matter is being looked into by the Government, and by the Research Department, and, if it has any merit, that full advantage will be taken of this process. The United States Government are making extensive investigations along the same line, and they also hope to find some use for this straw.
A few years ago the Canadian Pacific Railway Company obtained the services of Arthur D. Little & Co., the most prominent research chemists, I presume, in the United States. They established a branch in Canada and were directed by the Canadian Pacific authorities to devote their energies primarily to the solution of the problem of the utilization of western straw in industry. Dr. Howe, wrho had charge of their research bureau in Montreal, spent some considerable time in the work, and I was disappointed that it had not been prosecuted to a point where some definite proposal for the utilization of this straw could have been presented. It appears, however, that they had been making their investigations in Canada up to 1918, and about this time the Canadian Government established its research bureau. The Canadian Pacific thereupon feared they would be treading on ground that properly belonged to the Federal Government, and withdrew before completing their experiments. I hold in my hand a sample of linen paper produced from our western prairie straw-and Dr. Howe says that this paper is of a quality suitable to the highest requirements that

the Government would demand for bank notes. He also says that it is commercially possible to manufacture pulp from the straw in small mills in the western provinces, and then ship it to the paper-mills where it can be converted into an industrial product. This paper, Sir, looks to be a most extraordinary sample in point of quality, and I am sure would prove very interesting to any member of the House who cared to examine it. It was sent to me by Dr. Howe, of the Canadian Pacific Railway Research Department, as a product of paper manufactured from western flax straw.
In connection with this matter, Mr. Speaker, my attention has been drawn quite recently to the possibility of the utilization of this straw in the spinning of yarns. I have-had some very interesting correspondence with a gentleman in New York, in which he expresses absolute confidence in the merit of his process for treating this western straw and manufacturing it into fibre. In a letter, written to me on March 15, this gentleman says:
I thank you for your favour of 13th, and appreciate your courtesy in keeping me informed as to the progress of your work on flax in Canada. Shall he very glad to receive a copy of the discussion in the House when you can send it.
I wonder if I made it quite clear that the process of handling flax straw to which I referred can be successfully used on oil seed flax straw so largely burned and wasted in the great Northwest? The inventor has produced some splendid goods, comparing favourably with the best Irish linen, both as towelling and table cloth fabrics. He uses standardized textile machinery, and claims to be able to produce the spinning fibre and yarn at a small fraction of the cost for the same kind of product by the ordinary process.
There are a number of American inventors who seem to be producing a yarn from this oil seed flax straw suitable for crash towelling, etc., but this man is the first one I have discovered who shows anything in fabrics even approximating the best Irish linen goods. For your information, I am sending a small sample of a table cloth which this man says was produced by this method. I did not see the goods made, but have confidence that the inventor's statement is true as I have known the man for over thirty years and know that he has a large experience in textile work. At present he is without resources and is looking for financial backing to start a factory to turn out linen goods. He has suffered greatly at the hands of apparently unscrupulous promoters who tried to tie him up, hand and foot, but failed to supply the requisite capital. He is now free from this entangling alliance and no doubt can be arranged with on a reasonable basis to take charge of a factory which should use his process.
Consultations were held with ihe Minister of Agriculture and Dr. Macallum of the Research Bureau, and it was considered that

enough material had been presented in his letters to suggest that there might be some merit in the process that he claimed to have discovered. As a simple means of getting information concerning it, I suggested that it would be desirable to have this man come here and present his process and his plans to experts. Dr. Van Bruyssell of 'Montreal, who is on the Flax Research. Committee, Dr. Grisdale of the Experimental Farm, Dr. Shutt, and the head of the Fibre Department, Mr. Hutchinson, and others. If there be merit in his process, it is a matter of vital importance to the whole of Western Canada that this material which represents such a large waste year by year should be used in economic industries. With reference to my suggestion, he said:
My friend would be glad to accept the Government's invitation for a visit and conference. He is a man of attainments, a gentleman and a scholar, a trained engineer, graduate of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and a textile expert in every sense of the word, with an actual mill experience of some twenty years. I am confident that if given the opportunity, be can convince Dr. Macallum and his associates, theoretically, at first, that he has solved the problem, and that the Government would be warranted in equipping a plant under his direction, which can produce from seed flax fibre all kinds of linen goods, equal to those now produced by the so-called long line method.
As I have previously written you, I think, I do not know of my own personal knowledge that my friend has already done this. He tells me he has and I believe him. To my mind there is only one practical question to be settled: Can he do it on a commercial basis, that is, at a cost to compete with normal cost of long line linen production? On this point I am so far affirmatively convinced that if I had the means, I certainly should equip a mill and give him a chance to prove out his claims. I have spent months investigating the matter, have met many experts who said it cannot be done, have seen the wreckage following several failures to do this thing, and believe thoroughly that my friend has solved the entire problem. I think he has taken advantage of all the good points of other processes, so far as he can legitimately use them and not infringe existing patents ; has eliminated a lot of useless steps, has avoided some pitfalls present in other processes, and by skilfully combining and utilizing standardized textile and other machinery, has a process that is simple, economical and practical.
I submit that the representations this man makes justify at least an investigation of his claims.
If Canadian flax fibre is to maintain the reputation it has gained through the stress of necessity and through the exigencies of war, we should take advantage of this opportunity to guard jealously the position that we have attained. While Russia and Dther European countries where cheap labour prevailed were able to manufacture a fibre at a price that prevented our competing

with them successfully, the advantages they have had have been largely overcome by the invention and utilization of mechanical appliances for harvesting the crop and scutching it, and by scientific research in the matter of a simpler and cheaper process of retting. If the Government establishes a Department of Research as is suggested by the resolution of the member for London (Mr. Cronyn) on the Order Paper, there would be a wide field of usefulness in connection with zymo-technology, the study of fermentation, which has played an important part in industry. It is admitted that the process of retting in flax production is a bacteriological, micro-biological process. Professor Rossi seems to have separated and segregated the bacilli necessary for this process, and they are successfully carrying on the work by the use of these bacteria. If we solve the problem, of cheaper retting, and the cost be reduced by seventy per cent, as is stated here, if we solve the problem of mechanical appliances for harvesting machinery

and we believe we have done that-having demonstrated that we can produce a better quality of fibre than Russia can, there is nothing under heaven to keep us behind the producers of Europe. If it be true, as stated by Mr. Robinson, of the American War Board, that the process of separating the gum and retting the flax can be completed in an hour; that the tensile strength of the fibre produced stands in a ratio of 183 to 115, and that we can produce in various parts of Canada a flax fibre that will compete with cotton, who can estimate the possibilities of accomplishment in this line? Here is opened a field for thought and investigation that should commend itself to the very best consideration of the Government.
It so happens that fibre is being produced at the present time in a comparatively small area consisting of seven or eight counties, the production being largely in Western Ontario. These producers are groping in the dark and working by the methods of years ago. If we are to help these men to solve the problem of retting, improved scutching, and reduction of the cost of labour in handling, Government experimental mills along the line of the Experimental Farm station in Ottawa, although possibly on a larger scale, should be established in central parts of the flax growing areas. If we are to make a success of the production of flax fibre, we have to put it within the power of the farmer to get the full economic value of all the straw that he produces, not to sell his straw to
the flax mill, and thus get the small end of the deal, but to do as he would with his wool, to produce his own fibre from the straw and then to sell his fibre in the market.
We ask also that the Government take i ito consideration the matter of establishing standards. We know that in the past few years a marked advance has been made in tiie value of his wool to the farmer on account of the higher price obtained by grading. There is just as great possibility of increasing the value of his flax to the farmer by proper grading and standardizing as there was in the wool, and the Flax Growers Association, at a meeting held in March last, passed a resolution endorsing the resolution I have moved as embodying those principles which most essentially would benefit the flax men of this country. Therefore in this way the Government may be able to lend further encouragement to this industry, and to develop it, not only in Western Ontario, but in other parts of Canada by similar processes by which it may be originated and developed.
The matter of standards for flax fibre is very important, and no less important is the desirability of having a Government cleaning station where the seed, after it is cleaned, and set to a standard, may have its pedigree, character, and reputation standardized and maintained in the markets of the world. I need only to refer to the deplorable report from the Seed Commissioner as to the results of his investigation of samples of flax seed which were handed to him as being properly cleaned. He found them so foul and full of weeds that they would befoul the land of any farmer who attempted to use them. Suitable machinery has been invented for properly cleaning flax seed, and we have it on the authority of the Linen Circular published in Great Britain and Ireland that Canadian fibre is recognized in the world's biggest and best markets in Great Britain as being the highest standard that is sown and as commanding the highest price. We have built up that reputation during the past few years, and it is most important that that reputation should be maintained.
While I am on that question, I purpose reading a report made by Mr. Moore, a cultured gentleman in Ireland, who has written several articles on this subject to the Canadian Textile Journal: He says-
The most important deductions to be drawn from this table of seed productivity, is that of the several varieties teeted, Dutch (White Flowering), Yorkshire and Canadian gave better, amid French and Irish slightly poorer results than Russian (Pernau Crown), and

I shall say only a few words on this subject, as the hon. member for East Middlesex (Mr. Glass) has covered the ground very fully, and I am sure we have all appreciated what he has said. I want to congratulate the Government on the assistance they have given to this great industry. I am sure the Government is willing to make every effort to make flax growing one of the successful industries of the country.
I rose merely for the purpose of urging upon the minister the need of standardizing and classifying the seeds and the fibre. It is absolutely necessary that the growers of flax in Canada should take advantage of the market that is offering in Ireland and elsewhere, but unless our seed and fibre is properly classified we cannot expect to receive the returns we otherwise would. The day is not far distant when we shall have a Government-owned elevator in the province of Ontario, and I hope when that day comes the elevator will be used, to some extent at least, for the purpose of cleaning not only the seed grains and other seeds that are largely used in the province, but also the flax that is sent out of the country

stamped by the Government as Canadian-grown flax, x know that the minister fully appreciates the fact that 'this flax and flax seed that we export to Ireland compares favourably with the very best flax seed and fibre imported into Ireland from any other country. I would respectfully urge the minister to give consideration to these few points, and particularly to seeing if it is not possible to classify the seed and the fibre.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. IGRERAR (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
The subject mat is covered by the resolution which has been discussed so ably by the hon. member who has introduced it this afternoon (Mr. Glass) is one of growing importance in the agricultural field of our endeavours in Canada. My study-my limited study, I should say-of the development of the fibre flax industry in Canada has taught me that some forty or fifty years ago the flax fibre industry in the older provinces of Canada was one of considerable dimensions. The flax produced at that time was spun and handled mainly by the growers themselves. Owing, however, to the difficulty of getting cheap labour and the consequent inability to compete with the flax fibre products of countries like Russia, Belgium, and Holland, where labour has been very cheap, the industry declined in Canada, and very little attention was paid to it until a few years ago. The revival of the industry in Ontario has been quite marked within the last few years. That revival has been due primarily to the impetus given to the industry by war conditions. In 1912 there were approximately
2,000	acres of flax planted for fibre purposes in the province of Ontario. Next year, I am informed, there will be 25,000 acres, which, taking all the circumstances into consideration, is a very remarkable development indeed.
When we were producing flax in Canada quite a number of years 'ago, I am in-"' formed, the growers were able to get for the flax fibre between ten and twelve cents a pound. During the last year or two, owing to war conditions, the price has ranged from seventy-five cents to one dollar a pound.
As the hon. member has stated, the quality of the fibre produced in Canada is fully equal if not superior to the best produced in any of the European countries, and this fact itself affords a very substantial foundation for the building of a permanent and secure industry. It seems to me-and I referred to this aspect of the subject in the few remarks I made when 
it was under discussion at the last session that the future of the industry in Canada depends almost altogether on the development of labour-saving devices for harvest-* ing the crop and for manufacturing it into the finished fibre after it is harvested.
I would like to give a brief outline of the work that is being carried on in the Experimental Farms branch in this connection. In the carrying on of this industry I find that there are several stages, the first, of course, being the planting of the seed, followed by the pulling of the plant when it is ready for harvesting. In Western Canada where we have been accustomed to produce flax for seed purposes, or rather for the production of oil, the crops are harvested in the ordinary way, but when the plant is used for fibre purposes it requires to be pulled from the ground in order that the slender threads running through the stem will not be broken or cut. Consequently the first part of the operation is the pulling. After the flax is pulled it has to be deseeded, and then the retting or rotting process takes place. After that process is over the plant has to be passed through what is known as a breaking machine where the woody part that is already rotten from the process of retting is broken up. After that comes the scutching, when the woody part is all stripped from the plant and ithe rough fibres are left. The next process is heckling, whereby the fibres are passed through another machine and stripped of any remnants of woody matter. The completion of this process leaves the fibre in the fine silky condition necessary for spinning. It was quite clear to the officials of the department, when this matter was first undertaken by them, that there were several of these processes that would have to be closely examined into. In Russia, Holland, and Belgium, where this plant is produced for fibre purposes and where labour is cheap, it was a comparatively easy matter to get the necessary labourers to pull the plants from the ground and attend to the processes of retting and scutching. In Canada, however, where our labour is much more expensive we would obviously be at a very serious advantage as compared with our competitors in Europe, and consequently the attention of the department was directed at first to discovering a machine if possible that would supersede hand labour in the pulling process. The officials of the department were fortunate after, some enquiries in meeting a gentleman, who had been carrying on considerable

experimental work in this respect. The name of this gentleman was Yessat. I believe he had the distinction at one time of being a preacher of the gospel, and had in his spare time turned his attention to the invention of a machine that would do this work. This machine was tested out and found to be defective in some respects, but with some financial assistance given by the department, and with the aid of experienced officials in the department, he continued his work until it was finally in a completed form. Last fall the machine was given its first test and the results were very satisfactory indeed. It was demonstrated beyond any question of doubt that the machine would pull from 4 p.m. four to six acres of flax a day, and would thus do the work that under ordinary conditions twenty men would be required to do. It therefore appears that as a result of the assistance we have given in this matter we have in Canada a machine that can attend to this part of the work, which is really the most laborious and expensive of all the processes.
There was also the question of retting. A few years ago there was established at the Experimental Farm a building for the purpose of carrying on experiments in this direction, and experiments were conducted with a view to determining the best process of water-retting. The ordinary method of retting that prevailed in the olden days was to take the plant after it had been pulled and spread it out on the ground so that it might get the rains from heaven and the dews of night until it had been sufficiently retted. That process, of course, was subject to the vicissitudes of the weather. The energies of the officials of the department were directed to discover if possible a water-retting process that would apply to our conditions in Canada. These experiments have achieved quite satisfactory' results but they are not by any means completed. These things [usually have to run for a series of years in order to fairly test every method to ascertain which is actually the best. The next process is the scutching, and until very recently no machine has been discovered to take the place of hand scutching. I have seen the process in operation and it is a rather difficult one to explain, but I might state that every particle of flax straw that is scutched has to be handled by the hands of the operator. About two months ago the head of our flax development work in Canada was sent to Ireland to investigate the development of modem machines for this purpose, and we received from him a
few days ago a cable to the effect that he had discovered a mechanical scutcher which, in his judgment, produced excellent results. He cabled for authority to purchase this machine and that authority was given him a short time ago. The machine will cost, I believe, some $4,000, and it is the intention of the department to place it, along with other equipment we have, on the Experimental Farm and test out the various classes of fibre that come before us to see to what degree of perfection the machine will do its work. I do not need to go over the ground that the hon. member has so ably covered in respect to the market of our product in Canada. Up to the present, I might say, our market has been chiefly in the United States; but if we can provide-and I emphasize this point again, because in my judgment it is the important matter in our successful development of the industry-if we can provide labour-saving machinery that will handle these various processes, I am reasonably sure that we in Canada can occupy a position in this industry that will not be surpassed by any other country in the world. Until we can do that, we must continue our experiments in that direction.

Comparing the yield
from an acre of ground, sown to flax, with a similar area sown to oats, for instance, how many crops of flax, without manuring, would an acre of ground in Western Ontario yield? Would it yield the same amount . without manuring, or would it yield less?

I am sorry, I cannot give the hon. gentleman definite information as far as fibre production is concerned. I know that when it is produced for seed only one crop can be taken off without a rotation of crop. There is a question whether or not successive crops of fibre flax can be produced from the same land without rotation. I am not sure that it can be.

The idea is that it
exhausts the soil very much?

Undoubtedly it exhausts
the soil. I am of the opinion that it has to be rotated with other crops and probably a great deal of manure supplied. I would like to deal now briefly with a few of the points in the resolution. The resolution calls for the establishment of an experimental and demonstrative station:
_^at the most convenient and central point within the area where flax for fibre is being produced so that growers may be advised and educated in the most modern and improved' methods of retting, scutching and generally preparing their fibre for the market.

For the present I think we had better confine our efforts to the plant we have already established at the Experimental Farm. The establishment of another plant would largely mean the duplication of the one we already have. I would not say, however, that later, when we have carried our experiments and investigations farther, the establishment of an experimental station in Western Ontario, or in some other part of Canada where this industry is being developed, would not be justified. At the present time I am inclined rather to the view that we should proceed for another year with the experimental work we are conducting before we consider incurring the expenditure which will be necessary to establish a new experimental station.
There is this advantage in connection with the plant we have at Ottawa, that we are able to conduct these experiments with flax gathered from all parts of Canada. As the hon. gentleman has stated, the best results in actual fibre content have been produced from flax taken from the Gaspe peninsula in Quebec. Excellent results have also been obtained from flax produced in British Columbia. The second point is this:
That improved mechanical appliances and equipment toeing necessary for the economic harvesting of the crop, as well as for the preparation of fitore, constant watchfulness should be exercised toy the Government to insure that Canadian growers may toe supplied with most modern machinery for harvesting and scutching and instructed in the newest and best method of retting.
I have already referred .to what has been accomplished with the flax pulling machine. I have also mentioned that we are now securing additional machinery from Europe to assist in the scutching process.
I can assure the House that it is the intention of the department to follow up every avenue of (information that is available with respect to the development of modern machinery that may be useful in this work. The retting process does not require machinery. This is really a matter of fermentation, and of experiment as to the length of time the. fibre shall be under treatment. The third point is:
That in order to secure full economic value to the grower, it is desirable that the Government should establish .a system of grading and standards consistent and constant (in so far as possible) with continental standards so that the world's best markets may toe available for our exportable surplus.
I heartily agree with the observations of the hon. member who introduced this resolution with regard to the importance of this part of the industry. I think it quite pos-
sib]e that a great improvement could be made in standardizing our seed, in cleaning it, and in putting it in proper shape for the market. The proper cleaning of the seed and raising it to a proper standard, gives it a reputation that will, if we live up to it, ensure it a prominent place in those countries in Europe that have to import their seed every year. With reference to the other point that the hon. member for Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) alluded to, the standardizing of the fibre itself, a greater difficulty is presented. The quality of the fibre depends, as I am informed, on the conditions of retting, conditions of weather, the condition of the plant when it is grown, and many other things, ftnd you will find variations in quality of the fibre as between plants grown in the same field or in the same district. As far as my information goes, it has always been a difficult matter in the countries of Europe where this industry has been long established _ to secure absolute standards of quality in the fibre. Even to this day the fibre product is purchased almost, entirely on the eyetest. The representative of a mill who is purchasing the commodity wants to see and examine it before he fixes the price for it. Every encouragement and assistance possible should be given to instructing and educating our growers and mills in the proper methods of preparing and treating the flax in order to get the best possible fibre product. That matter is receiving the attention of the department and will continue to do so.
These are the. main points that have been referred to by the hon. member. We have, in the experimental work we are conducting, the assistance of an Irish and a Belgian expert, and their knowledge is of very great value because, this industry being a comparatively new one in Canada, we have a great deal to learn in respect to it.
There is another point I would like to mention, and that is the possible use that may be made of the flax straw that is threshed in Western Canada. There we have not produced the flax for fibre purposes, but a good deal of consideration has been given to the fact that annually in those localities hundreds of thousands of tons of straw, containing a certain amount of valuable fibre, are burned and destroyed dn cleaning up of the fields. A few years ago some experiments were conducted by private parties with a view to ascertaining whether or not there could be produced from this threshed flax straw fibre that could be converted into twine suitable for

binding our Canadian crops. As hon. gentlemen know, the raw material that enters into the production of our binder twine comes from foreign countries.
A large proportion of this raw material is very closely controlled and we are altogether dependent on outside sources of supply. The experiments that were carried on by the gentlemen to whom I have referred indicate conclusively that a twine could be prepared from this straw'. The factor that had to be determined was the cost at which it could be produced; and I might state for the information of the House that last fall the Department of Agriculture took this question up with the view of getting reliable information upon it. We arranged to secure several carloads of the straw in Western Canada and have it treated. We intend to take that straw to Ontario this summer, have it spun into twine, and keep correct data as to the cost of production, in order, if possible, to arrive approximately at an idea of what the cost of producing this twine would be. I see no reason why, with the development of modern science and its application to an industry of this kind, we cannot produce from the vast quantities of this material that is now destroyed every year, the twines that are necessary for all our crops in Canada. It may take a few years to work out the experiments, but I am confident that will eventually be done, and to that extent we will make ourselves independent of the sources of supply for these necessary twines that are now, as I have already*said, very closely controlled in other parts of the world.
The information given to the House this afternoon in respect to the possibility of utilizing the fibre produced from this Western flax straw for the manufacture of linens and cloths was indeed very interesting, and served to show that we are only on the threshold of the development of what is possible in utilizing this material. I had not been aware that experimental work had been carried on in this respect.
I do not know that there is anything further that I can contribute to this discussion beyond saying that the suggestions made by the hon. gentleman in his address this afternoon will be taken into serious consideration. I think the flax industry of Canada owes a considerable debt of gratitude to the hon. member for Middlesex East (Mr. Glass) because of the able and continuous manner in which he has studied this problem and brought it to the attention of the House and the Canadian people. The flax growers of Canada have been well represented in this House in that respect. Let me
say that the industry is a growing one in Canada, and I believe it contains great possibilities. It should receive, and will receive, the most careful consideration and assistance that can be given in the way of conducting experimental work and ascertaining the best processes of treating the product and the most economical methods ol handling it. It is rather a difficult matter for a private person to expend large sums of money in testing out different classes of machines, and I think that is work which can be properly undertaken by the Government. I can assure the hon. gentleman and the House that the department is thoroughly alive to the importance of this subject, and is gathering all the latest and best information with respect to it that is available. Under the circumstances I would suggest to the hon. gentleman that he either allow his resolution to stand or withdraw it, the object which he had in mind in introducing it having doubtless been served by the discussion which has taken place.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is my duty, before the hon. gentleman exercises his undoubted right of closing the debate, to remind hon. gentlemen that the debate is about to terminate, in case there are any other members who would like to speak upon this subject.

I shall detain the House but a moment or two in answering what has been said with respect to the possibility of soil exhaustion by growing flax. I did not refer to that point to-day to any extent because it was fully covered in my address to the House last year. This subject has not only been dealt with in Dominion Experimental Farm reports, but has been treated by Professor Zavitz, of the Ontario Agricultural College, Professor Doidge, of the Bureau of Agriculture, Washington, and Dr. A. W. Thornton, of Bellingham, Washington, a recognized authority who has done much research work and study for the Washington Government. These authorities have all expressed views entirely opposed to the theory that the growing of flax exhausts the soil; in fact, expert agriculturists are commonly agreed that the growing of flax, when used in rotation with other crops, does not cause any more exhaustion than other cereals, and not quite as much as oats. One cereal may take certain chemical properties out of the soil- for instance, flax takes considerably more nitrogen than wheat or oats-but that is easily replaced by rotation where clover is grown. The adoption of scientific agricultural methods can easily overcome the

temporary loss of such chemical constituents, and therefore I say that the growing of flax does not result in any greater injury-in the way of exhaustion of the soil than any other crop when it is used in proper rotation. I appreciate very much what the Minister of Agriculture has said on this subject. I brought this matter to the attention of the House in order to further the development of this industry throughout Canada, and having achieved my purpose, I now beg leave to withdraw the motion.
Motion agreed to and resolution withdrawn.
Motion by Mr. Steele for inquiry by a committee of the House.

-
That, in the opinion of this House, a special committee should be appointed during the present session to inquire into and report wherein the Inside Civil Service staffs in the various departments can ibe reduced and re-arranged with a view to securing the greatest efficiency in the service with the minimum number of employees, with power to send for persons, papers and records, to examine witnesses under oath and to report from time to time.
He said: At the outset I wish to state that owing to the very brief time now remaining for private members, this being the last day at their disposal, I propose to abbreviate the remarks I should otherwise have made, so as to allow other members to have an opportunity of bringing forward the resolutions standing in their names.
I am sure that I need not apologize to the House or to the country for moving this resolution. The Civil Service is the great working force of the country, and the country gets just such administration as the character of the Civil Service permits. A vast interest is being taken in the Civil Service throughout the country to-day, which is due to several reasons. One is that, largely owing to the war, there is a demand for efficiency in every line of industry and every occupation. Efficiency is being advocated in everything, and the country is demanding efficiency in the Civil Service. The abolition of patronage brought clearly before the minds of the people the fact that a great change had come in the method of appointments to the Civil Service. The new Act takes the matter of appointments out of the hands of members of Parliament, which in itself is a great revolution; and on that account the interest of the people has been awak-

ened to the importance of the Civil Service. Another thing that has interested the country in the Civil Service is the fact that last fall the Civil Service made certain demands upon the Government which they followed up by threatening to go on strike and paralyse the work of the country. People began to wonder whether it was possible that in a time of war, when every one was putting forward his very best efforts to serve the country in one sphere or another, the five thousand civil servants in Ottawa would go on strike. That, perhaps, more than anything else led the people to realize that it was time that they took an interest in the Civil Service. It may be said, then, that a deep and widespread interest is being taken in the Civil Service by the electors, the taxpayers, the business men of this country, from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
It has long been believed that the conditions in the Civil Service are not satisfactory. I need not argue that in this House; that is a question on which members on both sides agree. In 1911 the Conservative party in the House of Commons apparently strongly believed-and I have no doubt did believ.e-that the Civil Service was in a bad condition; and since 1911 members of the Opposition have apparently believed even more strongly that the conditions are bad. Indeed, many of us who came into the House in 1911 were convinced by the arguments put forward by the Opposition in the last Parliament in regard to conditions in the Civil Service.	[DOT]
In 1907 the Courtney Commission was appointed to investigate conditions, and their report led us to believe that conditions existed at that time which should be remedied. The evils prevailing then were chiefly over-manning, incapacity and inefficiency; and to correct those evils the Civil Service Commission was appointed in 1909. But the Civil Service Commission could control only the flow of new members to the service, they could see that only efficient appointments were made; but at that time the commission could not correct the abuses inherent in 'the service. So that some evils which existed then still remain in the service, and many of us believe that they have not been lessened since 1909. If we want evidence of that, we have only to look at the report on the Printing Bureau made a few weeks ago. The committee appointed to investigate conditions in the Printing Bureau found that the inefficiency in that department of the Government service was shocking. They found certain the labour inefficient. They found certain

staffs over-manned. They found the conditions in one department pitiable. In another department three men -were employed where two could do the work. They found conditions in another department preposterous, and they found still another department a dumping ground for those who could not otherwise be placed. That is the condition that was found to exist in the Printing Bureau, and many of us believe that similar conditions, though perhaps not in the same degree, exist in many other departments. If an investigation were made by qualified men they would probably get information that would substantiate that assertion.
As long as political patronage existed the members of this House-at least those supporting the Government-'were held responsible for these conditions. It is time that members should be relieved of that odium. We have no longer any responsibility for any of the appointments; that responsibility should be placed where it belongs. In future the responsibility for conditions in the Inside Service will rest upon the deputy heads of the departments. Section 47 of the Civil Service Act passed last year says:
The deputy head of a department shall, subject to the directions of the head of the department, oversee and direct the officers, clerks, and employees of the department, and shall have general control of the business thereof, and shall perform such other duties as are assigned to him by the Governor in Council.
The deputy minister is the business head of his department. It is only reasonable that members of the House who long have been accused of making improper appointments and being responsible for conditions in the Civil Service should be relieved of any responsibility in that regard, and that we should now turn around and see that the men at present responsible shall clean up the Service and put it on a business basis.
I rather regret that the Government proposes to increase the salaries of deputy ministers to $6,000. The deputy who can manage his department efficiently and as any good business department should be managed is worth more than $6,000 a year to this country. But during this year I think we should have put the deputies on trial with a view to seeing whether they are qualified to clean up the Civil Service, and those deputies who proved themselves equal to the occasion might well have had their salaries increased next year to a figure commensurate with the work they are doing.
There is a good deal of over-manning in the Civil Service. May I point to one or two facts which I think will satisfy the House, that there is over-manning? We have in the Civil Service to-day 220 people who are of the age of 65 years or over, and 403 people over sixty years of age. While I would be the last to say one word of disparagement of the old man or woman in the Civil Service who has given good service in the past-and there are many of them-we are not so much concerned with that as with the efficiency of the service as a whole, and I think any person will admit that, where there is such a large percentage -about 8 per cent-of the civil servants over sixty years of age, that is a condition which does not tend to the greatest efficiency. The question is: What should be done with these men? That is for the House to deal with at a later date. A few days ago the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) stated in this House that there were in his department 24 men who were of an age that made them of very little use in the service; that he believed a similar condition existed in the Outside Service, and that the services of a very considerable number of men employed in his department might be dispensed with. We find that condition running throughout the whole Civil Service. We know efforts are being made at the present time to reform the service; but even if the plans proposed are carried out, that is not going to give us the reform which Parliament and the country desire in connection with the matter. We want to know what the condition is; we want to know whether there are too many men in the service or not, and if there are too many, this House is going to demand that the staffs be reduced and that the service be put on a business basis.
We have not only the old men who- especially those who have been efficient in their younger days-have the sympathy of every hon. member, but the inefficient class, the incapable class, and the idlers. Those men or women, because there are some women who come under one or another of those heads, deserve little or no sympathy. The man who is incapable today should not be in the service of the country. The man who is idling ought to be dismissed at once. The man who is inefficient ought to be either put in a position to become efficient or asked to retire from the service. Then we have another class which I think deserves the attention of the House as it is receiving the attention of the Government to-day. I refer to agi-

tators in the Civil Service, men who are drawing salaries from the country for work which they are not doing, but whose time is being spent in agitating, agitating, agitating, stirring up strife in the service amongst other employees who are willing to give this country efficient service, disorganizing to a large extent the whole Civil Service, so that we are not getting the service and the work to which the country is entitled. We want to know the relations of those men to the Civil Service and tc the country, and when we know that, this Parliament will be in a proper mood to deal with them. This is not a matter any longer for the Government or entirely for Parliament. It is a matter for the country, and let me emphasise that the country is demanding of its representatives in this Parliament that something shall be done, that the Civil Service shall be cleaned up and put on a business basis. I believe, if I correctly understand the spirit of this Parliament, that Parliament is going to demand from the Government that this be done, and we hope and believe that the Government, with this demand behind them, will have the courage to do this.
I am not one of those who feel disposed to offer lengthy criticism of the Civil Service Commission. I do not think they have yet had an opportunity of showing what they can do. I am not introducing this resolution to-day to excite any controversy - or anything of that kind, and as far as I know, we have, as chairman of the Civil Service Commission, a man who is eminently qualified for the position and for performing the duties which he has undertaken to perform. I believe, in the course of a year or two, when the preliminary reorganization work of the Commission is completed, the country will be very well satisfied with the work the Commission has done.
I am not going to say anything further than simply to suggest to the Government that such a committee as I ask for in my resolution can be of vast service to the country and to Parliament at this time.
I believe we can get information which cannot be got in any other way; and when we have that information, we shall be in a position to discuss intelligently the whole question of what shall be done with the Civil Service.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend taking up much of the time of the House in respect of the motion moved by the hon. member for iSouth Perth (Mr
