Steele). He proposes that a committee be appointed to investigate whether the Inside Civil Service might not profitably	be	reduced and rearranged
with a view to -securing greater efficiency. The purpose of the resolution is quite a laudable one, and the Government have no desire whatever to object to the motion; in fact it will accept the same and consent to the appointment of a committee, which will be named after the Easter recess.
I am not, however, disposed to agree with the general statement that the -Inside Service is to-day very greatly overmanned; but that is a question of fact and is well worthy of investigation by this committee and when the evidence is presented we shall know definitely whether the assertion that the Civil Service is overmanned is correct or not. Under our political system it would not be surprising if I were compelled to admit that there might be found an overmanning of the service in some departments, and more in some departments than in others. This is unavoidable, but nevertheless we -should make every possible effort to keep the number in the service to the lowest possible minimum.
The hon. member, in speaking to the resolution, referred to the fact that there was in 'the service to-day a large number of people who were 65 years of age and over, and that there was further a large number who were over 60 years of age. The hon. gentlemen suggested' that such members of the service had seen their best days and should, in some way or another, be retired. This question presents a very great difficulty, and I think the hon. gentleman himself admitted that difficulty, as, I am sure, will every hon. member. Prior to 1907, we had a Civil 'Service Superannuation Act, and it is very regrettable that that Act was ever repealed. I 'think T may say so, because the repeal was made by a Liberal Government which I was then supporting and of which the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding), who is now in the House, was a very prominent member. T have reason to believe that, since the repeal of the Superannuation Act, most of the members of the ministry of that day regret the step then- taken. I hope that at a very early date the Government will take into consideration the question of the restoration of a superannuation system for the Civil Service. I do not know how popular that view is in the House or in the country, and I do not care very much, because I say, as a matter of principle, we should have such a superannuation system.

That statement is true not only of the Civil Service, but of all the great employing industries of this country. All these industries must adopt some form of superannuation. It is a fact that many of oui leading industries to-day are adopting some scheme of insurance or superannuation 'for their employees; for instance, the banks and insurance companies. There is' no reason in the world why any industry in Canada employing men in large numbers should not provide out of its income some system of superannuation and I hope the day will soon come when some form of insurance or superannuation will be open to every man who has followed the same employment for a certain number of years. Therefore, I should like, when the opportunity presents itself, to have an expression of the views oi this House on a superannuation scheme for the Civil Service. As I have already intimated, within two or three weeks the Civil Service Commission's new system of classification will be presented to Parliament for consideration-I hope early in May. I think when presented it will be found to contain many improvements which will be readily accepted by the House, and I trust that the proposals will ultimately prove of great advantage to the public service and to the country.
When the Civil Service Act amendments and the classification resolutions are presented, ample opportunity will be afforded to hon. members to discuss the very matter which my hon. friend brings up in his resolution. The Government accepts the motion, and immediately after the Easter recess a committee will be named by the Government.

I do not propose to discuss other features of that report now, but I certainly should like to bring to the attention of the-House and of the Government that means of securing retrenchment and economy in the whole -public service, not merely in that part of the service called the Civil Service-the wage list-but in all expenditures.
Mr. ROBERT H. BUTTS (Cape Breton South and Richmond): I am not always as keen an economist, Mr. Speaker, as some hon. gentlemen who sit around me, but while this resolution is, before the House I would like to bring to the attention of the hon. minister an important fact. There is a large number of men who are servants of this Government performing various duties, for instance, at that door and at the other door, and in other occupations around the gallery and the House, and who are looked upon as merely sessional servants. I have talked, or rather half a dozen of them have talked with me lately, and have informed me that during the last decade or so the wages of the different other civil servants have gone up year after year and year after year, while there is one class-so I am told-that for twelve or fifteen years have been working for the same wages. I think that is absolutely unfair, and I would ask the minister, feeling that he will take cognizance of my appeal, to see that ample justice is done these men. They tell me that fifteen years ago they were receiving the very same wages they are working for to-day. There is an old and respected gentleman at that door who told me the other day that when the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier died there passed away the last man who was in this House when he came here. Yet his wages are still the same, with the difference that in former years he came up to this House from Pictou county on a half railway fare, whereas to-day he has to pay the full fare. I can mention other cases, but I am only speaking for my own province. I have other cases; one from Inverness county, and I am speaking because my hon. friend (Mr. Chisholm) is absent; and I am speaking because I think my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. McGregor) is absent. I am speaking for the absentees, and I am going to ask the hon. minister if it is not advisable, or if at least it would not be praiseworthy that these men should be accorded an equal consideration with all other working men. or all other servants of the country.

Mr. HERBERT M. MOWAT (Parkdale): I will support this resolution for the one chief reason that it asserts the principle that this House has not given up control of the Civil Service. I am heartily in favour of the efforts that are being made to improve the Civil Service; but I am inclined to believe from what I have heard that there are quite a number of senior officers in the Civil Service who since the passing of the Civil Service Act have not been playing the game as they should in supporting it. They have asserted themselves in many little ways to show that the whole matter of appointments on recommendation is with them. That should be so, but their actions should also be on the principles on which the Bill is founded. Here is a resolution for the appointment of a committee -I am glad to find that the minister says it is assented to by the 'Government, and that, indeed, might be made a permanent committee-which indicates that the'Civil Service is yet to be under the control of Parliament. While it is a very important desideratum that the appointments should be made as they are, yet if in the administration of the Act the deputies and principal officers, superintendents and inspectors should exceed the powers which have been given them and appoint or recommend friends and on personal grounds, as has occurred in a few instances, this resolution serves notice upon them that Parliament has not given up control of the

speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. SINCILAIR (Antigonish and Guysborough):
speechtext:
We have already
elaborate machinery for controlling the Civil Service. We have a minister whose, duty it is to deal with that, and a Civil Service Commission with jurisdiction over all appointments throughout the Dominion of Canada, and I am not sure that it would he advisable for a Committee to interfere at the present time until the minister has had an opportunity to look into the matter. I was somewhat surprised when he seemed to express a doubt as to the question of the Inside Service being overmanned. I do not think there is much doubt on that question. It was constantly contended, when hon. gentlemen opposite were in Opposition, that this service was over-manned. The present Prime Minister was constantly telling us that the service was over-manned, but after a change of

Government took place we discovered that in about twelve months some 12,000 men had been dismissed or retired from service chiefly because they exercised the right of free citizens, and that some 25,000 had been put into their places. There has been a constant stream of appointments since that time, and there is no doubt that the service has been over-manned.
We had a report from SiT George Murray on this very question some years ago, and he said that the service was overmanned and that the conditions were confusing. He proposed some very important reforms that have not yet been fully carried out. I trust the present Minister of theCivil Service will undertake to carry them out and not confine himself too much to the question of superannuation. The question that is before the House is that of improving the Civil Service and making it an efficient instrument to do the work of the country. That is what we expect the minister to do.
I know it is a big contract but he has a splendid opportunity to make a record. One of his first duties will be to get efficient men to take the places of those who are inefficient. Every man who has dealings with the departments knows how inefficient some of them are. I could show you files of letters in my desk which have accumulated when I was dealing with a little question like a sailor's -wages that have been due since last January. A little balance is due him and I have been unable, after a lot of correspondence to secure a settlement. I get a polite answer from one officer, who sends me to another; I go to him and he sends me to another. One man told me that I had got into the wrong place and that I should know that the Minister of Naval Affairs was the man to go to. Notwithstanding all this correspondence I have not been able to get the few dollars that are owing to the sailor. I do not say all the departments are like that. There are some departments of the Government that I have had dealings with where a different condition obtains. If I write them a letter with regard to any matter of business I can get to the end of the transaction at some time, but there are other departments in regard to which I seem never to reach the end of the case with which I am dealing. This is a very important question. What I want to impress upon the minister is that the country is looking to him to give us an efficient Civil Service.

I do not want to have the country looking to me with regard

to matters for which I am really not responsible. There is really no such person as a Minister of the Civil Service.

I think the thanks of the House are due to my hon. friend for South Perth (Mr. Steele) for having introduced this resolution. I have not heard anybody speak in a concrete way o'f the constitution of the committee that may be appointed. I think this is a most important matter from the standpoint of the efficiency of the committee and the relation that the soldier bears to the Civil Service and the other life of the country. There has been a good deal of pressure brought to bear upon the Government to have a soldier or two appointed to the Civil Service Commission. I think whether this is done or not-I do not speak of that at present-the minister will be well advised to consider the personnel of the committee that is under contemplation by virtue of this resolution. If the Government want efficiency in the public service I believe that owing to the training of the returned soldier, he having been amenable to discipline himself, efficiency will be brought to bear by giving an opportunity to returned soldiers from this House to be appointed on such a committee as is here proposed. The reason I say that is probably, in a general way, obvious to the members of the House. But, I have a personal reason for saying it. In conversation with a civil servant

temporarily connected with a rather important branch of the Service in Ottawa-he suggested 'that he had noticed a great many abuses within the department administered by himself and that he could not have corrected these abuses in 'the same way as he had, if he had not been a returned soldier. There are no doubt men in any public or private service who at times do not live up to their duties, are inclined in the performance of them to a laissez faire, don't-care sort of fashion, and if a returned soldier happens to have some authority, being accustomed to discipline himself, he naturally tries to discipline his staff. I think one of the weaknesses of the Civil Service to-day largely arises from overmanning. Whether due to political pressure or pressure of friends having the ear of a minister in the old days, or maybe having the ear of the Civil Service Commission to-day, the Civil Service has become overmanned, and girls and young men are employed in too great numbers. The returned soldier will not stand for very much of that sort of thing because he is not only trained disciplin-fMr. A. K. Maclean.]
arily but he is trained to efficiency. If 1 mistake not, I can see signs that the returned soldier, with the capacity for any walk in life, if employed by this Government, will bring to his service in aid of the Staite a great deal of strength and efficiency because he has been accustomed to discipline. I therefore think that the country will profit by looking to the returned soldier who has had the experience of war. The man who has gone througn the war has gone through the stress and strain in the greatest crisis in the life of any man, and what I have observed in the returned soldier is that if he is anything he is not arrogant, he is absolutely fair. He has a big heart and that brings to his mind the necessity for fair judgment in regard to the services that he is rendering to the State and in the treatment of those who may be under his control. Therefore, I would ask the minister to -take note and see that the returned soldier is well represented upon any such committee, so that in that regard, there being a common feeling throughout the country that the returned soldier should get the best the country can give him, the returned soldier who is seeking employment at the hands of his country in this period of reconstruction and development shall have some little . consideration paid to him-rather would I say, shall have some great consideration paid to him. I think the minister would be well advised if he considered that carefully when he was appointing this committee because in that way he will get efficiency where probably if it were overlooked we will fall back mu the humdrum wavs of the past and into the old conditions, and will lose what, to my mind, is the most salient feature in the new public life that is coming in this Canada of ours. I leave that suggestion with the minister in the hope that he may act upon it.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I fully realize that there is a good deal of merit in the suggestions contained in the resolution and that there are a good many things about the Civil Service that might be put in a better position than they are now in.
I have no hope whatever that those remedies or good results will come from the appointment of this Committee. I know this House pretty well, and have known it for a good many years-, and if I were asked today to select three or five of its members to bring in satisfactory recommendations as a result of conducting inquiries as to the proper operation of various offices in the

Civil Service, I would be at a loss where to begin. I do not think any member oi this House, even a returned soldier, or anybody else, is possessed of the necessary training or experience to bring about. the needed reforms. I would! suggest to the minister, although we have at present a great many administrators, a great many departments, and a great many officials, as a result of my experience in the district from which I come where there are in operation big industries employing a great many men, that if a superintendent of the Civil Service in Canada were appointed-an officer of equal rank, influence and independence with the Auditor General-to act as general supervisor of the Civil Service and the several departments in this country, a big man and possessed of the necessary training for the position, then we might expect to derive some beneficial and permanent results. I do not expect such results will follow from the appointment of a Committee of the House, and I say that without desiring in the slightest to cast any reflection upon such Committee. If we are going to effect reform in the 'Civil Service, we must have somebody who is thoroughly familiar with the work of that service, who follows every move that takes place, and who is in a position to systematize the whole of its operations. I think the great fault in the Civil Service to-day, just as much as overmanning, is the lack of system. No system prevails in the departments whereby one man if given the opportunity and a proper allotment of work might perform perhaps just as much service as two or three men now render. The present defects are not so much the fault of the men themselves as of the existing system. I therefore venture to make [DOT] this suggestion to the minister who has spoken on behalf of the Civil Service, and who has so many departments to look after that we scarcely know how to correctly address him.
The mover of the resolution (Mr. Steele) said that the country had its eyes on the Civil Service and was interested not only in the proceedings of this House but in the work which all branches of the Service have to do. There is no doubt about that fact, and that is just as it ought to be. We should strive to cultivate a live public opinion in respect to every matter with which we deal, because such an opinion will have a most wholesome effect upon the members of this House and upon the Civil Service, as well as upon public officers generally. This is the last day that private members will have for the ventilation of
matters before the Easter recess, and I had hoped to have an opportunity of saying a word to the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White.) about some things that touch the membership of this House, and the service of the country as a whole. In view of the prevailing conditions the present is a time when above all other times, public matters should receive proper attention. The meeting of wartime conditions, the carrying out of a reconstruction policy, and the development of the country generally, call for the exercice of our very best judgment. Had the acting Prime Minister been here I would have urged upon him although perhaps I should not be quite in order, that the whole of the people should be represented in this Chamber. However, I will tell the other members of the Government who are present and impress upon them the necessity of giving representation in Parliament to large bodies of people all over the country who are now without that representation, and I hope that during the recess they will take the matter under serious consideration.

In my opinion it is the most opportune time, although possibly a little late in the session, for the principle of such a resolution as this to be approved by the House and to go into effect. I was a little surprised at the remarks of the leader of the Opposition, who might well say that his remarks were out of order, in advocating class representation in Canada. I will not imitate the hon. gentleman's example, except to say that we have representative government in Canada, although at times I have doubted whether the Government rules, and whether the people are the ultimate tribunal, or whether the Civil Service are going to conduct public affairs. When we came here at the beginning of this session we experienced a condition of affairs that, in my opinion, warrants some action being taken. We have seen these people, as a result of the legislation passed by the House a year ago, form an organization which I consider a menace to the country if those concerned endeavour to carry out what they are now attempting to do. We have seen the business of this country held up for days at a time, and the proceedings of the Parliament not being printed, as the result of the attitude of a certain department of the public service. The hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) referred to the reforms that might take place in the Civil Service through the admission to its ranks of the returned sol-

dier; but unfortunately, out of some thirty thousand appointments made, permanent and temporary, since the enactment of the amended Civil Service Act of last session, only about twelve per cent of the number have been made from the ranks of the returned soldiers. I do not know whether that is the danger they foresee or not. Meetings are being held in this city from time to time that are having a tremendous influence on the legislation of this country as regards the whole of the people. Under the circumstances 1 am surprised to find the leader of the Opposition getting up in this House and advocating class representation in this Parliament.
I think the hon. member misunderstood me. Upon what remarks of mine does he found the statement he has made?
The hon. gentleman regretted that various bodies were not represented in Parliament, and hoped that in the future they would be.

I have reference to
counties such as Glengarry and North Ontario, that are at present without representation in this House.
The hon. gentleman was by inference leaving the impression that the agitation which is now abroad in this country should be recognized.
Certainly not: I had no such intention. What I said was that the counties that are now without members should be given representation in the House as speedily as possible.

I am very glad to hear the hon. member make that statement. I rose to take part in this debate only because I was under the impression that the hon. gentleman was advocating something entirely different.
Certainly not.

You can scarcely go into a passenger coach on any railway in this country without hearing something of that kind advocated, and I may have been a little too ready to associate the hon. gentleman's remarks with what we hear so much of these days. However, if there is a lack of system in a body which exerts such a tremendous influence as the Civil Service does, in a body where the most thorough system should be employed, then we should have such a committee as is suggested by this resolution to inquire into this matter. Such a thing as happened DM)r. Sutherland,]
during the early part of this session should not be permissible. It should not be possible for these people to hold up the business of the country as it was held up; some regulation or some means should be provided to ensure that such a thing shall , not again occur. maintopic: PUBLICATION OF OWNERSHIP, ETC., OF NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS.
PUBLICATION OF OWNERSHIP, ETC., OF NEWSPAPERS AND PERIODICALS.
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, all newspapers, magazines, trade journals and other periodicals publishing articles designed to influence public opinion shall be compelled from time to time to publish sworn statements setting forth the names of the owners, managers, editors, stockholders, bondholders and of any other person having an interest in such newspaper, magazine, trade journal or other periodical.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the object of this motion is self-evident and the principle which it embodies will, I am sure, be adopted by the House. I had intended to bring this motion up earlier in the session, but unfortunately it has not been reached on the Order Paper until to-day.
I look upon the press as a 'torch, but as a torch which must at times be held in the hands of the people; thus the torch -may be shaken so that it may burn brighter. It is said that a stream will not rise higher than its fountain; the St. Lawrence will not run backwards over the Great Lakes. In other words, the press of Canada will be what the representatives of the people choose to make it. The honest and independent press of Canada will I am sure, support this motion, because the honest press stands for light, not for darkness; stands as a beacon, not as a false light. This motion does not mean an abridgment of the liberty of the press. The liberty of the press in the English-speaking world is merely a matter of history. We know that at the beginning the press was under the control of the King, that nothing was published in book or pamphlet form or otherwise that did not bear the stamp of His Majesty. Then, later came the censorship, and finally by a gradual process the liberty of the press was proclaimed. We have in the words of ILord Wynford a statement of the exact status of the press to-day in the English-speaking countries. He said in a very famous case:-
My opinion of the liberty of the press is that every man ought to be permitted to instruct his

fellow subjects; that every man may fearlessly advance any new doctrines, provided he does so with proper respect to the religion and government of the country ; that he may point out errors in the measures of the public men, but he must not impute criminal oonduct to them. The liberty of the press cannot be carried to Oils extent without violating another equally sacred right, the right of character. This right can only be attacked in a court of justice, where the party attacked has a fair opportunity of defending himself. Where vituperation begins, the liberty of the press ends.
That is the dictum of Lord Wynford in the famous historical case of Rex vs. Bur-dett. The press in all liberty-loving countries is an instrument which serves the public; i,t carries the news and pretends to educate the public. The newspapers to-day circulate in hundreds of thousands, advocating causes, presenting issues, and swaying public opinion. That being the case, the press should not sail under false colours; the greater the freedom of the press the greater should be the protection to the public. I say that the mission of the press is not only to disseminate news, but to educate the public. In the education of our young people there is a very close inspection not only of the pupils, but also of the educators themselves, the professors, the masters. There is a board of supervision, and you cannot clothe that board with too much power in order to protect the rising generation. In the United States they have realized the necessity of protecting the public against the evil influence which the press may exercise through its freedom, and they have passed a law which does exactly what my resolution suggests. In Canada the immense privilege which the press has obtained to-circulate almost freely from one end of the country to the other has been accompanied by very little effort on the part of the press to repay the public for that privilege. In 1882 an Act was passed to provide for the free transmission of Canadian newspapers by mail within the Dominion. The proviso establishing the conditions of that power of free transmission was as follows :-
It must be known and recognized as a newspaper or periodical in the generally received sense of the word, and published regularly at intervals of not more than one month.
The full title, place and date of publication, and the distinguishing number of the issue must he printed at the top of the first page, and also on any paper purporting to be a supplement to it, and sent with it.
It must be addressed to a bona fide subscriber, or to a known newsdealer in Canada.
That was the only condition exacted from the proprietors of newspapers in 1882, when this law was enacted by Parliament. It has
not been changed since. In the United States much more progressive legislation has been enacted. I find in the United States:
That it shall be the duty of the editor, publisher, business manager, or owner of every newspaper, magazine, periodical, or other publication to supply to the Postmaster General and the postmaster at the office at which said publication is entered, not later than the first day of April and the first day of October of each year, on blanks furnished by the Post Office Department, a sworn statement setting forth the names and post office addresses of the editor and managing editor, publisher, business managers, and owners, and, in addition, the stockholders, if the publication be owned by a corporation; and also the names of known bondholders, mortgagees, or other security holders ; and also, in the case of daily newspapers, there shall be included in such statement the average of the number of copies of each issue of such publication sold or distributed to paid subscribers during the preceding six months.
Then there is a proviso that this does not apply to religious, fraternal, temperance and scientific, or other similar publications. It was further provided:
That all editorial or other reading matter published in any such newspaper, magazine or periodical for the publication of which money or other valuable consideration is paid, accepted, or promised, shall be plainly marked " advertisement."
This is a very wise legislation, and all that I ask by this resolution is that Canada should adopt similar legislation in order to give to our press the stamp of honesty and respectability. Let me give a case in point. The Montreal Herald, for over a century, was an old and faithful adherent of the Liberal party. It was the old, recognized organ of the Liberal party amongst the English-speaking minority of my province. It had a large clientele. Suddenly, after the election of 1911, Mr. Brierly who had become the proprietor of that paper, mysteriously sold it first to Mr. McGibbon, then to Sir Hugh Graham, who afterwards became Lord Atholstan, both being Tories. But Mr. Brierly was the mask; he was still generally supposed to be the owner. One day Mr. Brierly disappeared. As I said, he first sold the paper to Mr. McGibbon and Mr. MoGibbon finally sold it to Lord Atholstan, and during all that time the paper retained the appearance of being a Liberal paper, whilst it was kept in existence by Lord Atholstan, only to prevent a rival from coming into the field against the (Montreal Star. This was disclosed in a celebrated case in Montreal, and the respectable English-speaking Liberal people of Montreal were shocked to find that such a game had been played at their expense. From that moment, I decided that I would introduce this resolution in order that the owners,

stockholders and mortgagees of papers should be known, so that a paper preaching morality, respectability, should be ' known under its true colours. The people are entitled to know who are behind the newspapers, who are their backers, if I may use that sporting expression, and the respectable papers of Canada will favour the United States legislation. There is need for such publicity. We live in an era in which publicity is necessary. I cannot forget that during the past two or three years, the country has been flooded with newspapers and magazines, publishing huge-advertisements. By whom were those costly advertisements paid; and how is it that at a given moment the whole of the Liberal press of Canada suddenly passed from the Liberal party to the Tory party? When I read those advertisements, il could not help saying in the House, and I repeat it again to-day, that the press, with few honourable exceptions, had been chloroformed, if not bought. The respectable papers of Canada object to being branded as having been bought, and they will, therefore, support my motion. The other day I was reading one chapter of the American Commonwealth by Viscount Bryce, and I cannot better close my remarks than by quoting what that great English writer says about publicity :
The genius of universal publicity may have some disagreements, hut the wholesome ones are greater and more numerous. Selfishness, injustice, cruelty, tricks, jobs of all sorts shun the light. To expose them is to defeat them. No serious evil, no rankling sore in the body politic, can remain long concealed, and when disclosed, it is half destroyed.
Once more, I say that this is a progressive reform, and I hope the Government will accept it and that a Bill will be introduced along the lines of the American legislation.
Mr. JOHN H. SINCLAIR (Antigonish and Guysborough): Mr. Speaker, I desire to support the resolution of my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux). I am in favour of publicity with regard to ownership of newspapers. The purport of the resolution is, of course, that the Government will afterwards, if they see fit, introduce legislation somewhat similar to that which exists in the United States. It will, I think, be conceded by everybody that anything that will tend to increase the responsibility of newspaper editors and proprietors is a good thing. I have no quarrel with the newspapers, which are doing very good work, and of course, we all recognize the splendid work that many of them did in connection with the war. I am also well aware DMr. Lemieux.]
that they are privately-owned, and that the owners have a right to control their paper and to dictate its policy. I have no objection to that. At the same time, the newspaper moulds public opinion, and it has a good deal to do with the Government of the country, so much so that it has been given the name of "the fourth estate." We are in this country governed by the Governor General representing the Crown, the Senate and the House of Commons. We know who the Governor General is; the .senators are well known; the members of this House are public men and well known, at all events, in their own constituencies; but the fourth estate, we do not know anything about; we do not know who they are, and we all recognize that they have a very important place in the government of the country, and they always will be so in the government of a democratic country like ours.
In addition to this the newspapers receive large concessions from the public in this country in connection, for example, with carriage in the mails. If you or I, Sir, wish to mail one issue of a newspaper of
50,000	copies to our constituents, it would cost us a cent apiece, or |500, but under the postal laws of this country a newspaper proprietor is required to pay only a quarter of a cent per pound, and I have been told that on an average, or at all events in a great many cases, it takes five newspapers to weigh a pound. If that is true, the newspaper proprietor would have to pay only about $25 for the service of the mails, while the private individual would have to pay $500, or twenty times as much.
I took occasion a few days ago to ask some questions about the cost of carrying newspapers in the mails, and the Government answered, as follows:
1.	What was the gross postal revenue derived from (newspapers for the year 1918? Answer-$291,539.21.
2.	What is the estimated expenditure for the same year in so far as newspapers are concerned? Answer: The department has no data on which a close estimate of the expenditure involved in handling newspapers can be made, except that newspapers make up about 66 per cent of the bulk of the mails. The total expenditure for the carriage of mails and the cost of mail bags during the fiscal year 191S was $8,293,515.24.
3.	Wlhat is the average daily weight of newspapers oa/rried in the mails? Answer: 239,731 pounds.
Now, 65 per cent of the total cost amounts to $5,390,784, so that we only received from the newspapers $291,539. After crediting what we received, there is a difference of

over $5,000,000 which the people of this country contributed to the cost of delivering newspapers to subscribers. That is a very large sum of money. But that does not exhaust all that we do. As members of this House we vote $50,000 a year to the Press Association, on the principle that it furnishes the people with information. The farmers of the country recognize the great importance of the press. I saw a few days ago that the farmers of the province of Ontario are purchasing a weekly newspaper, with the intention of running it as a daily, as an organ to boost their views before the country. They understand that it is of vast importance to them as a class to have their views put before the public. The Union Government have also resorted to this method of establishing themselves in the country, as witness the publication of that organ of public opinion known as the Canadian Official Record. The people are not deceived as to the object of the Official Record. Sometimes it publishes Orders in Council and official documents, but when it resorted to printing the political speeches of my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder) and other ministers, it became plain to the public that its real mission was to strengthen the party machine by circulating Union propaganda at the public expense. The Germans understood the importance of controlling the press. In the investigation that took place recently in the United States, it was disclosed that they had purchased newspapers. These men had even invaded the capital and had purchased the Washington Times for something like $375,000. Referring to this, the Montreal Witness said:
The serious feature of all these German plottings is the faith that the emissaries of evil place in the purchase or manipulation of the press. They at least do not doubt that in buying newspapers they are buying the souls of men. It will soon be necessary for free peoples to make the facts as to the ownership of newspapers, and every money interest that affects them public property.
That is the object of this resolution-to give publicity as to the ownership of newspapers. The question arises, will this not be objected to by the newspapers themselves. I see no reason why the owner of any responsible high-class newspaper should object. There is no better work in which a man can be engaged! than in the newspaper business when it is conducted as it should be conducted, and the man who is conducting a respectable high-class journal certainly will not object to having the ownership of the paper disclosed to the public.
They did not object in the United States, and I see no reason why they should object in Canada.
Of course, this is a matter for the Government. No private member could hope to succeed in passing a Bill of this kind, especially at this late state of the session, unless it was adopted as a Government measure. It is up to the Government to say whether this shall become law or not.
I want to say to the Government that they could not do anything more democratic or anything that would please the public better than to enact legislation along the lines of this resolution. I express no opinion as to what their attitude will be but simply invite the Government to take this matter into consideration, and if possible, to embody the principles of the resolution in a statute before the end of the present session.
