Sir THOMAS WHITE moved the second reading of Bill No. 54 (from the Senate), to amend the'Insurance Act, 1917. He said:
I desire to have this Bill referred for consideration to the Banking and Commerce Committee. As it is of a technical character,
I think I can best explain its purpose and object to the House by reading a memorandum prepared by the Superintendent of Insurance:
The object of this Bill is to provide additional safeguards for the members of fraternal benefit societies operating in Canada, and to make it necessary for foreign fraternal societies to obtain licenses under the Insurance Act, before transacting business in Canada.
The Insurance Act as passed in 1917, and as it has existed since 1885, exempts from its provisions fraternal benefit societies, and at the present time the only fraternal benefit societies licensed under the Act are those societies which have been incorporated by the Dominion Parliament and whose Charters require them to obtain such licenses. Of these there are at present seven. There is in addition one provincially incorporated society which has voluntarily submitted itself to the provisions of the Act.
In addition to these societies there are operating in Canada sixteen foreign fraternal societies and large number of fraternal societies incorporated by the legislatures of the various provinces.
The Dominion Parliament has jurisdiction to require the foreign societies to obtain licenses before transacting business in Canada and this requirement is imposed by the Bill.
For foreign societies not now transacting business in Canada the Bill provides that they must be actuarially solvent before obtaining licenses.
For the sixteen foreign societies now transacting business in Canada, many of which are actuarially insolvent the Bill provides that they may receive licenses up to 1925, provided they properly secure their new members by deposits in Canada, held for their protection exclusively. After 19215, however, the societies must be entirely solvent if their licenses are to be continued.
Foreign societies now transacting business in Canada which are unable to get a license, may continue business in respect of existing policies without incurring penalty.
Parliament has not the same jurisdiction in respect of the provincial societies, and the provisions of the Bill are that these societies may obtain licenses under the Act if they are actuarially solvent, but they are not compelled to do so.
If such a society applies for a license and is not actuarially solvent, it may obtain a license until 1925 if it either deposits with the minister securities to fully protect new members, or

creates a separate class, whose fund is actuarially solvent, into which new members will be admitted. After 1925 the license will be continued only if the society as a>
whole is actuarially solvent.
One of the most important provisions of the Bill is that requiring annual valuations by an actuary, and an annual certificate by an actuary that the society is actuarially solvent.
The standing of the actuary is assured by requiring that he shall be a Fellow of the British Institute of Actuaries, or the Faculty of Actuaries of Scotland, or the Actuarial Society of Am'erica. It is believed to be essential that the many serious problems facing these societies should be dealt with by actuaries of the highest standing.
The Bill repeals certain sections of the Act respecting Assessment Companies under which the licensed societies have been operating and which have been for some years more or less inapplicable to these societies, and substitutes a new Part IIA applicable solely to fraternal societies.
The Bill also repeals the exemption granted to fraternal societies.
In. a word, the object of this Bill is more effectually to protect members of foreign fraternal societies. Before it was introduced in the Senate it had been carefully considered by the Superintendent of Insurance, who took it up with the societies concerned.
I believe that the Bill as now drafted meets the desire of all parties interested and effectually protects the public. As the Bill is of a rather complicated and technical character, I suggest that it be referred to the Committee on Banking and Commerce. It has already passed the Senate.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.
On motion of Sir Thomas White, the Bill was referred to the Select Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce.

On motion of Hon. A. K. Maclean (Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce) the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to amend The Fertilizers Act, 1909, chapter 16, and to provide that on and after the 1st day of February, 1920, the phosphoric acid contents in the guaranteed analysis of a fertilizer shall be stated in certain terms; that the registration number and guaranteed value shall be plainly printed upon a tag of prescribed size, shape, and colour, and attached to every package sold, or to the invoice if sold in bulk, and such invoice and tag shall be delivered to the purchaser; that the vendor who sells to the consumer shall affix to every package of fertilizer sold in Canada special stamps, to be provided and sold by the Minister for the purpose, to the value of one cent for every hundred pounds or fractional part of one hundred pounds of fertilizer contained in the package, which the vendor shall 
cancel upon sale, and which shall not be removed until the package is emptied, and if sold in bulk such stamps shall be affixed to the invoice and cancelled by the vendor; and also that an analysis of a registered fertilizer may be obtained upon application in prescribed form, that certain authorized inspectors may enforce the provisions of the Act; that the results of analysis shall be published, regulations may be made and penalties enforced for violation of the Act.

The amendments proposed by the resolution are not very numerous. The Bill will provide for a definition of the word "analyst"; it had been assumed that the word " analyst " had the same meaning in this Act as it had in the Adulteration Act. Owing to the fact that lime has in recent years very extensively come into use as a fertilizer, the Bill will provide that lime shall be included as a fertilizer. The Bill will also recognize the administration of the Fertilizers Act under the Department of Trade and Commerce instead of under the Department of Inland Revenue. It was intended that the Bill should provide a method of stating the phosphoric acid content in the guaranteed analysis of a fertilizer; I propose, however, when we reach the Bill, to have this section deleted and to cover the matter by regulation. The other amendments proposed are amplifications, of the existing sections of the Fertilizers Act, with one exception: it is proposed to make provision-this has not hitherto been the law-for securing a revenue from the inspection of fertilizer. The Bill will provide that the vendor who sells to the consumer shall affix to every package of fertilizer sold in Canada special stamps to be provided and sold by the minister for the purpose, to the value of one cent for every hundred pounds or fractional part of one hundred pounds of fertilizer contained in the package. When the fertilizer is sold in bulk, it is provided that the stamp shall be affixed to the invoice. This is the principal amending feature of the Bill.

What is the purpose of
the stamp?
To secure a revenue to pay for the administration of the Act. This is done in the case of almost everything else which, before sale, is inspected under federal statute.

In some countries
a great impetus is given to agriculture by encouraging the production and use of fertilizers. Is this proposed legislafion intended to that end, or is the department taking any steps to encourage it?
The legislation is not of the nature suggested by my hon. friend. I cannot say that at the present moment any special or practical steps are being taken to encourage the production of fertilizers.

Or ,the use thereof.
, Mr. A. K. MACLEAN: I imagine that the Agricultural Department . is \ doing everything it can to encourage the general use of fertilizers. During the past summer Investigations .were made by a department of the Government into the matter of securing potash as a by-product from cement works. The report of the officer making the investigation has not yet been submitted ,to the Government, but it will very soon. The other amendments are very trivial and might better be considered after the Bill is introduced.

About what amount does the minister expect to realize from this stamping provision? It seems to me that this business of tagging one cent on every hundred pounds of fertilizer is very foolish legislation. A man is almost afraid to sell anything now on account of a multiplicity of regulations, and if you are going to regulate this thing to death, it might as well be left out of account.

At present all fertilizer produced in Canada is subject to inspection by federal officers; it is proposed that this charge shall cover the cost of that inspection. The policy may be wise or unwise; I suggest that my hon. friend allow that point to stand till the Bill is printed.
Mr. CAHILL; Is lime to be included as a fertilizer?
Yes.
Is all lime to be subject to this stamping provision?
All lime that is manufactured and sold for the purpose of fertilization.
Has it been found that improper substitutes for fertilizers have been sold?
Just at the moment I could not speak with a knowledge of the facts, but I think it frequently has occurred that fertilizers below the standard required by the statute have been manufactured and sold.

I do not think any hon. members will question the great importance
of fertilizers being used for the encouragement of greater production, but it seems almost ridiculous to have a one-cent stamp placed on every hundred pounds of fertilizer and lime that is sold for fertilizing purposes. This would probably necessitate the appointment of some additional officers to carry out these regulations.
No.

At the present time, manufacturers of fertilizer have to state on the package the different ingredients of the contents. Is the Minister of Agriculture or is his department recommending this change which might have a greater importance than we may at present be aware of?

People interested in the fertilizing industry in Quebec have asked me to oppose this resolution on the ground that for some years past they have made very strenuous efforts to induce the farmers of that province to make a greater use of fertilizer and that, in their opinion, the imposition of such a tax will set their strenuous efforts at naught. They consider that this is not the time to impose such a tax when farmers are just beginning to realize the importance of fertilizers and the benefit that can be derived from them.

When we come to consider the Bill I should be glad to hear the representations of my hon. friend. If he can then satisfy me that those provisions of the Bill are against the public interest, I shall be glad to meet what are the interests of the public.

I would not raise any particular objection to the imposition of a tax on this commodity, but has the minister seriously considered whether this is the best method of collecting such a tax? In this case, as in the case of 'the tax on patent medicines, stamps have to be affixed to the packages, and this is a most awkward and inconvenient method of collecting these taxes. The druggists are raising a great deal of objection to this method of imposing taxes on drugs, and this is simply an extension of the same idea. Will the minister consider very seriously whether, if it is necessary to obtain this revenue, it could not be obtained much more readily and with much less inconvenience to the public by having the stamp affixed to the package by the manufacturer?

That is the principle in this Bill. This Bill will hardly be comparable with the tax on drugs to which

my hon. friend refers, because in that instance it was found impossible to impose a tax on the wholesaler or manufacturer, and, therefore, it is in some measure a very objectionable tax to the public because the stamp has to be affixed to the article when it is sold in the retail drug store.

Why should it be impossible to have the stamp affixed in the wholesale drug store? Four or five good, decent druggists in my constituency were fined fifty dollars each because they sold a patent medicine box without a stamp on it.

I should not say it was impossible to impose the patent medicine tax upon the manufacturer or the wholesaler, but it was very difficult to administer the Act otherwise than it is now being administered. I remember that the tax when first introduced provided that it be paid by the manufacturer and wholesaler, but during the same session the Act had to be amended to its present form. There are, of course, very few manufacturers of fertilizers in Canada, and it is the intention that the tax be paid by the manufacturer, so that the retailer will not be troubled. At least that is my understanding of the matter at present.

What is the idea of the
provision to attach the stamp to each package containing 100 or a fractional part of 100 pounds? Does not that indicate that the stamp must be affixed by the retailer?

That will be done as the package leaves the factory.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Hon. Mr. Maclean thereupon moved for * leave to introduce Bill No. 74, to amend the Fertilizers Act, 1909.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext:
The House in Committee on the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, That it is expedient to amend the Live Stock and Live Stock Products Act, chapter thirty-two of the statutes of 1917, and to provide for the preservation of rights of farmers, drovers, and other persons to sell and buy at stockyards, for regulations regarding inspection, for the size of packages of wool, for compliance with the requirements regarding inspection, branding and marketing before shipment, for the issue of inspectors' certificates, and for the increase of the penalty for violating the Act.-Hon. Mr. Crerar-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Will the minister please explain the necessity for this legislation?

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The purport of these amendments is to strengthen in some particulars the Live Stock and Live Stock Products Act which was passed by this Parliament two years ago. The resolution provides for establishing more clearly the rights of farmers and drovers in dealing on live stock exchanges. It provides also for the inspection of certain live stock products, for the grading, handling and marketing of which'provision had been made under the Act as it stood. It goes further and gives the Governor in Council power to establish regulations governing the marking and branding of certain of these products when imported into Canada, that are subject to regulation when produced in Canada. It also provides for the passing of regulations for the closer control and inspection of shipments in Canada, and for the enforcement of any regulations that may be passed under the Act.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I presume the word
"wool" refers to Canadian wool. It has been brought to my notice that there are some difficulties in the use of Canadian wool by our woollen manufacturers. I am told that our woollen manufacturers for the most part import their wool;-that may or may not be the case, I have no knowledge of the matter myself. I have also been told that large quantities of our Canadian wool are bought and taken across to the United States and there treated by American woollen manufacturers. It has also been intimated that this slight difficulty in connection with our wool is overcome by a certain process used by American manufacturer. If this be true, I think it is advisable that the Government should encourage our own manufacturers to make use of that process, so that Canadian wool may be used by our own manufacturers of woollen goods. This will, of course, have a tendency to cheapen the price of woollen goods.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I believe that the chief wool markets in North America are in the United States. As to the treatment and preparation of wool for manufacturing purposes, I cannot speak with any definite knowledge of the facilities in Canada. One of the objects of these amendments is to establish more clearly the grades and packages, so that both the purchaser and the seller will know more definitely on what basis they are working.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The resolution provides: "for the preservation of rights of farmers, drovers, and other persons to sell and buy at stockyards." Does that mean that to-day a farmer or drover cannot dispose of his live stock at the stockyard except through a broker? I understand the business has changed considerably in the last five or six years. Then, a drover could ship a carload of stock to the yards and dispose of the stock as he saw fit; but to-day, I understand that the selling has to be done through a broker, and that entails a commission.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Clause 2 of section 3 of The Live Stock and Live Stock Products Act, 1917, provides as follows:
Nothing in this Act, or in any regulation made hereunder, shall take away, or in any manner limit, the right of any farmer or drover to sell his live stock at any stockyard.
We are proposing an amendment to make more clear the right of a farmer or drover to buy live stock in any stock yard, which right is not clearly defined in the present Act. For the information of the House, I may say that the existing Act empowers the Governor in 'Council to formulate regulations governing in a general way the conduct of stock yards, the manner in which live stock shall be handled, guarantees oi good faith on the part of commission agents, and other matters of that character. These regulations have been under the consideration of the department for some time.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Why not have them approved by Parliament, which comprises a great many farmers who have just as much knowledge of these matters as the officers of the department?

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The Act as it at present stands empowers the Governor in Council to make regulations prescribing tbe manner in which the stockyards are to be constructed and operated.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: More Orders in Council.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: That may be. The present Act was passed two years ago, and these regulations have been under consideration for a considerable time. The producers, the farmers, and the Live Stock Associations have been consulted and the regulations, which are now practically completed, are the result of our joint collaboration.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Where are these stockyards located? I do not think there are any such institutions in my part of the country.
Are they all under the control of the department?

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The chief stockyards in Eastern Canada are in Montreal and Toronto, and in Western Canada at Winnipeg. 'Calgary and Edmonton. There is also a stockyard at Moosejaw, and another at Prince Albert. Some of them are private enterprises, and others are under the control of the railways. In Winnipeg, for instance, the railway companies have formed a stockyards company. The purpose of the Act of 1917, and I think the purpose was entirely commendable, was to provide for a closer supervision of these yards, so that those who were handling live stock would have proper facilities for the carrying on of their work.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Are these stockyards anything in the nature of an exhibition?

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: No, they are purely for market purposes.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I understand
that the amendments will more clearly define the right of a farmer or drover to purchase and sell stock at a stockyard.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The farmer has now a right to sell. We are going to make it clear that he has la right to buy.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: What supervision has the department over by-products imported from the United States. Chicago, for instance, ships in many tons of canned meats, which are used very extensively in the hot weather. Does the department provide for a standard weight and quality of these meats?

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The control of canned
meats comes under the Meat and Canned Foods Act. They have to come up to certain standards. '

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The minister speaks about giving to the farmer the right to buy as well as to sell. What does that mean? Who has had the authority hitherto to deny the farmer the right to buy in the market, and who controls these stockyards? Is it under Dominion, or provincial, or private charter?

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The stockyards are I understand all incorporated under provincial Acts, and I presume the purpose of the amendment when it was introduced into this Act two years ago was to make it absolutely clear that no company privately chartered and conducting the business of a stock-

yard could deny the individual farmer or drover the right 'to go in and sell his stock.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: We could not override a provincial statute.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
We have the power to pass regulations governing these stockyards, the same as we have to regulate the handling of grain through elevators.
Mr. MeCOIG: From what source does the request come for this change in legislation? I understand that in Toronto the farmers can buy all the stock they wish without interference. The resolution has some reference to the matter of marketing wool, and I do not see why the two things should he connected,-'the purchasing of livestock, and the branding and the marketing of wool. Would it not be better to have them in separate resolutions? What I would particularly like to knpw, however, is where the request comes from to have this change in legislation.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I do not know that any request has been made respecting the right of farmers to buy in these stockyards. That right, as. I understand it, has not been interfered with, and the purpose of this resolution is to make it clear beyond any doubt. As regards the grading of wool and the size of packages in which wool has been marketed, the request for the regulation of these matters has come practically from all the wool producers in Canada, who have asked that some definite standard be fixed as a medium of sale in this commodity.
Mr. MeCOIG: The greatest compliment I have heard from the farmers in reference to the markets in Toronto is as regard the quotations for the different products that are being sold there, and the way in which they are sent out. A great number of producers have expressed a desire that the Government should control the prices that are paid each day for stocks at different markets and that one quotation should be sent to the press throughout the country. Very often contradictory reports are seen in the press and in some cases you will find a discouraging report in one paper and in the same paper of another date possibly an encouraging report as to different stocks being sold. If the minister is anxious to do something in regard to the markets of the country I think he should see that if there are going to be inspectors at these different places they should have full charge in the matter of quotations that are submitted to the press, and see that these quotations are uniform.
[Air. Crerar.J

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The suggestion which the hon. member makes is a very radical one, and one which I do not think it would be wise to adopt. Quotations governing the sale of live stock are available in the same way as are quotations on grain or any other article of commerce. If I understand the hon. gentleman's suggestion aright, it is that the Government should establish soime means of definitely controlling the prices that would be paid daily to the public. That certainly is not contemplated in the legislation, and I thing it is rather a radical idea.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The farmer can purchase in the market, but must he purchase through the agent? In the privately owned stockyard, as I understand, you are not permitted to dispose of your stock except through an agent, and you have to pay a percentage to him which reduces your profit. Under this amended legislation will one farmer be able to purchase from another independently of the agent?

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I cannot explain that matter more clearly than by referring the hon. member to the provision of the Act:
(2) Nothing in this Act, or in any regulation made hereunder, shall take away, or in any manner limit, the right of any farmer or drover to sell ....
We propose to amend that to read, "sell or buy," so that the farmer can have absolute freedom to sell or buy.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I think it is well that such a law should be provided. We have experienced some difficulty along that line in the West with regard to the handling of live stock. During the last year or two we have been taking out of the stockyards large quantities of cattle for feeding purposes, and the right has been questioned of the individual farmer to go and make his own purchase. The commission men have asserted themselves on that point and have claimed the right to do the purchasing . for the farmer, exacting a commission from him. If the Bill intends to cover those two points of selling and buying/ I think it is splendid legislation and should go into effect. We should make it clear that the producer has the right to go himself and sell and to go personally and buy and take out his stock. If that is the intention of the Act it should be supported.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
If I understand the minister to say that these associations are organized under provincial statutes, then it is not good practice that they should be regulated by legislation of this House. While

we have no power to repeal an Act of a local legislature, we can render it inoperative by-depriving it of all its effectiveness. But it will stand on the Statute Books of the province which enacts it, and I submit to the minister that if there is any local legislation creating a corporation such as a stockyard, and if there is any ground of complaint from the farmers, the legislature of the province creating that institution should be asked to provide the necessary remedy. That should be done under extreme necessity, and if the legislature of the province should refuse to remedy the matter, then we could regulate any provincial institution by legislation in this House. It is a very clumsy and inconvenient way of doing it, and if the institutions which the minister intends to regulate are creations of provincial statutes, I do not think that this House should pass legislation which would have the effect of annulling those statutes. I think that under a local statute a man should know exactly what his rights are without having to consult any Dominion enactment as well.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Do the words "for regulations regarding inspection " refer to the inspection of live stock?

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: They refer to live stock products such as wool or hides.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Do they not refer to live stock itself?

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
It is intended to cover live stock products such as wool, hides and eggs-such live stock products as are not already under the Meat and Canned Foods Act.
Resolution reported, and concurred in
Hon. Mr. Crerar thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 75, to amend the Live Stock and Live Stock Products Act, 1917.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Acting Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 69 (from the Senate), to amend the Criminal Code respecting prevention of fire.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This is a Bill that 1 asked to be introduced into the Senate for expedition. Its purpose is to prevent fires, and the methods employed are these: (1) It
makes it a criminal offence on the part of the owner, occupant or tenant of a building to refuse to obey any law of the country looking to the prevention of fire provided that upon his being prosecuted for the offence the jury find that but for his negligence in so omitting to obey the law the fire would not have occurred.
His criminal negligence?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It makes it criminal negligence now. The second clause makes it obligatory upon the owner, or occupier or tenant of a property to carry out any instructions of a provincial officer looking to the prevention of fire, which instructions would be in the nature of the removal of material, the construction of fire-escapes, or making some alterations, providing these instructions are reasonable and are passed upon as reasonable by federal officers.
Will that entail the creation of a number of agents, officers, etc.?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, I do not think so.
I really have not given much consideration to that.
That is a bad thing.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think that the existing officers in the various provinces can take care of this work. There will be officers of the Government who will be locally situated and who will be competent to perform these duties. At all events, even if that were considered necessary it would be amply justified. The losses from fires in this country in the year 1918 aggregated some $33,000,000 of which 75 per cent are believed to have been absolutely preventable. That is an average of about $4 per head for every man and woman
4 p.m. in Canada; a per capita average that is simply appalling. In European countries, where legislation similar to this is in effect and where greater governmental care is taken, as well as care by associations and societies, the rate of loss is trifling compared with what it is in Canada.

There they have
tile roofs and mud floors.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Very true, but tile roofs and mud floors would be a rather cheap inconvenience if purchased by the saving that might be effected in this country.
Is it not a fact that most municipalities have laws regulating this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, but this is to give effect to these laws. If the hon. gentleman will read the Act he will see that the law of the municipality is made effective. Wherever there is an enactment which is not obeyed and a fire occurs as a result, which would not have occurred but. for the disobedience, then the persons guilty of such disobedience will be guilty of an indictable offence.

Most of the municipal enactments are to the effect that such and such structures may not be put up unless with the permission of the municipal authorities. I do not see therefore how this enactment would apply.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Some of the enactments are of that nature. Other provincial and municipal laws would deal with the distance between buildings, the nature of the material employed and various features like that looking to the safety of the structure when erected and to the safety of the people in it. This Bill says that those laws must be obeyed under penalty of being guilty of an indictable offence provided that the disobedience is found by a jury to be the cause of the fire. As this is a motion for the second reading, I think it would be proper that we should move the House into Committee and let the discussion take place then.

Motion agreed to, and the House went into Committee on the Bill, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-negligently causing fire which results in loss of life or property:
Mr. 'SHEARD:	I would like to ask the
minister if the proposed statute provides that the owners of the building must receive notice of these defects and that a reasonable time be allowed for complying with requirements after the notification has been given?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That question would be applicable to the next section. This section merely refers in disobedience of an enactment by the owner, and everybody else presumably acquainted with the law.
What effect will this provision have upon the insurance rates, if any, and where would the insurance company come in?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The passing of this enactment will not affect any contractual relations at all between the insurer and the insured. It will be just the same as if the Bill had not passed. pMr. Power.]
Will it not affect the insurance rates?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I hope it will. It will not perform the work unless it does. The impression that fire losses are insurance losses only if the buildings are insured is a wholly unsound impression. Losses by fire are national losses whether the buildings are insured or whether they are not, because the increase in the fire loss is reflected year by year in the increase in the insurance rates. Conversely anything that diminishes fire loss must be reflected in the decrease of insurance rates. Consequently, if this enactment has the effect intended of diminishing fire losses it will result in a diminution of insurance rates. Of course this Bill has no power to diminish rates, but it will enable companies to diminish them, and if companies refused to put such reductions into effect then it would give the Provincial Legislatures ground upon which they might act.

I think this Committee
should consider this measure with extreme care, because the provisions of the Bill are very far-reaching, and the underlying conditions very onerous. For instance, the penalty is made applicable to the person owning, the person occupying, and the person controlling the property. All three classes of persons will be liable to the penalty imposed by this Bill, and yet any one of the three may not have been officially notified of its requirements. The minister's comparison of the fire losses of Canada with those in European countries, I submit, is hardly fair for several reasons. The insured property in the Old Country is not as valuable as the property in this country carrying insurance, neither is the population of Canada as dense as the population there. Therefore, the per capita comparison of the fire loss given by the minister is not fair and is not justified, and does not warrant the stringent provisions proposed here. The fire insurance companies and the Conservation Commission of Canada have been trying to establish, more particularly during the last year or so, that the fire loss per capita in this country is enormous as compared with the fire loss in other countries. I submit that their method of comparison is not at all justified for the reasons which I have already given. Moreover the fact should be borne in mind that during the last few years we have had enormous losses in Canada through fires in munition plants. One great fire occurred in Trenton which

resulted in a loss of $5,000,000. Another great fire resulting in a similar loss occurred elsewhere, and so on. These losses have been included and have swollen the total fire losses of Canada. The comparison therefore is not a fair one because the fires in question vrere extraordinary in character, and should not be included so as to increase the per capita fire loss of the country. Had I known that this Bill was coming up for consideration I would have studied the matter more carefully, and been in a position to deal with it more satisfactorily, because I have given considerable thought and attention to it. In my opinion the business interests of the country should insist upon delay before enacting a Bill embodying such stringent provisions at the present time.

The danger which I see in a clause of this character it this: As we all know, after almost every big fire which occurs in a city or municipality, a large number of new by-laws are introduced; a panic occurs and it is said, "This kind of thing must not happen again." The result is the adoption of various new by-laws, more or less well studied, and after a certain length of time, when the scare has subsided, they are no longer enforced. We have in most of our cities, I should say, a number of antiquated'laws and regulations with regard to the character of buildings to be erected, and the provision of fire protection, fire escapes, etc., and these are made applicable more particularly in places where the labouring people congregate. In the city of Quebec we have had a large number of such by-laws, and at one time it was decided to insist upon the use in buildings of cement products, asbestos tiles, and so forth. It was found, however, that these articles were too expensive for the ordinary labouring man's dwelling, and the by-law was thereupon allowed to drop, or the inspector did not perform his duty by enforcing it. Now, should a fire occur in the poorer quarters of the city, and should someone discover that such a law exists, under the present provision the owner, the occupier, and the person controlling the property-possibly the janitor, or even the nightwatchman,-would be responsible, and would be liable to a fine of $1,000. As at present worded the clause is rather too stringent. If there was a possibility of amending it in the direction indicated by the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Sheard) so as to provide for the giving of notice to the proprietor or occupier that he is not carrying out the law, 1004
I think the provision would be a reasonable one. Otherwise I am afraid it will result in a great deal of hardship to the labouring classes and to others against whom such an enactment should not be enforced.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I did not catch the point made by the hon. member for Renfrew, but apparently he is of the view that we should not compare our fire losses with those of European countries, because their population is more dense than ours. It would occur to me that the more dense the population the larger the number of cities having fire losses, and the higher the per capita fire loss, is likely to be. It is a well-known fact that our insurance rates are higher in our cities than in our rural districts, because when the population becomes congested the danger is greater. Therefore, if the hon. gentleman's argument has any force it leads to exactly the opposite conclusion from what he intended. However, I do not know that it has very much force one way or the other. The fire loss in Norway in 1918 was 55 cents per capita and in Belgium, where the regulations would, presumably, be equally strong and enforced with equal care, the loss was $1.02 per capita.

How could the
figures for Belgium be got in 1918?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In the case of Canada the year given is 1914, and from the statement which I have it would he inferred that 1918 was the year in the other cases. It must have been the year before the war. At all events, Norway has a population of about 2,000,000, spread over a large territory, and Belgium is very thickly populated. The thicker the population the higher the fire loss per capita; consequently, the comparison of the figures for these countries with those for Canada is all the more striking and all the more unfavourable to ourselves, for our loss is $4 per capita. In the Netherlands the fire loss is 11 cents per capita.
The figure given by the Conservation Commission of the fire loss in Canada is $2.92 per capita.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Our fire loss was $33,000,000, and, taking the population as something over 8,000,000, the figure would be $4 per head. The loss for January, 1919, is the.' highest on record.	,

The losses would be
specially heavy during the last few years, on account of munition plants and so on.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There are munition
plants in other countries, too. They made munitions in England; the fire loss there was 64 cents per capita.
The munition plants were not destroyed by fire there, but they were here.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We had better have some laws, then, to prevent their burning here. My hon. friend says that business interests should be consulted with regard to this legislation. I know he must have great respect for the Retail Merchants' Association -I 'hope he is a member of it, That association has written a letter strongly commending the Bill. Representatives of the following associations have been consulted with regard to these amendments-I do not think it can, be said that they are not ail business institutions: Canadian Manufacturers' Association, Canadian Fire Underwriters' Association, Non-tariff Insurance Companies, the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada, the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, the United Farmers of Ontario, the United Farmers of Alberta, the Wholesale Grocers' Association, the Canadian Bankers' Association, the Dominion Mortgage and Investment Association, the Fire Chiefs' Association, the Commission of Conservation. So that I do not think we have failed to take into account the views of the community, and while we do not need to act precipitately, there is no very great reason for delay.
Could the minister find it possible to get the United Farmers and the Manufacturers' Association to agree on any other subject?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We hope they will.

All business men, property holders and those interested in protection against fire will agree with the principle of this Bill. But it occurs to me that confusion may arise from the fact that the fire laws in the different municipalities conflict to some extent. I understand that in the next section of the Bill you take care of anything that might be unjust in municipal fire laws by placing further responsibility upon an officer approved by the Governor in Council; is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, but a man to be guilty under the first section must be guilty of a breach of a law, not merely of a breech of instructions of a local fire officer. If he is guilty of a breach of the law and his guilt is found by the jury to have been the

only cause of the fire, then he is liable. Neither the occupant nor the owner or controller is guilty unless the law of the province fixes the responsibility on him. If the law of the province fixes the responsibility on more than one, then it is for the province to amend its law if necessary.
Most provincial and municipal fire laws provide penalties for infractions.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is true, but very
often the people responsible for fires have less to fear from any punishment that the province can impose than from the punishment that follows the breach of the Crim-. inal Code.

The minister did not quite answer my question. In section 2 . the responsibility for recommending to an owner or property holder that certain changes be made within thirty days does not rest alone with the municipal or provincial officer; the recommendation must be approved by an officer authorized by the Governor in Council.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That applies to the
second clause. The other sanction is only the opinion of a provincial officer. We think there should be a second sanction.

When the minister says
that there is to be no punishment except for breach of the law, does he include bylaws passed by municipal, town and city councils? Many of these by-laws vary in the different cities and towns. In fact some of them consist of many pages of printed matter and the people in the municipalities may not be acquainted with their contents.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: A law passed legally by a municipality on the authority of provincial legislation is just as much a law as any other law. It is true that these laws vary among the municipalities; still we may assume that the residents of a municipality know the law of that municipality. If the law is too complicated and too long, it is for the municipality to amend it. Our law is neither complicated nor long.

The second paragraph oi section (1A) says that a person shall be deemed to have caused a fire through negligence if such a person has failed to obey the requirements of any law intended to prevent fires. But suppose a building is considered to have defective electric wiring and the owner has been notified of the defect; if a fire originates in that building from some other cause and is destroyed, the

owner would be liable to a penalty of two years' imprisonment.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, the jury must find that his disobedience was the cause.

While I agree with the principle of the Bill, it seems to me that its drafting requires consideration. The first clause says:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to two years' Imprisonment who, by negligence, causes any fire which occasions loss of life or loss of property.
Negligence might consist in a man going out to his stable with a lantern and setting it down on the floor, and then, perhaps, while doing something else, backing up against his lantern and knocking it over and setting fire to his own barn. In such a case he would, under this clause, be liable to two years' imprisonment, while under the Ontario law the insurance company would be bound to pay his loss. A lady in a house might accidentally leave her electric iron with the current turned on; it might burn its way through the board and drop to the floor and set the house on fire. That would certainly be negligence, but under the law of Ontario, the insurance company would have to pay her loss, and yet under this clause she would be liable to two years imprisonment. Unless the word negligence" is defined in some better way, there are many cases of negligence which are perfectly innocent and in which the^e is no wrong intent, and there is no reason in making a criminal of a person who unwittingly acts in a negligent manner. The gist of every crime is the guilty intent, but as far as I can see, under the first clause standing by itself-and the second clause, which says certain things shall be deemed .to be negligent, does not limit it-a person guilty of these innocent, though negligent acts, would come within the purview of the Bill and be liable to imprisonment.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think my hon. friend's interpretation is right. That is the intent of the law and, I think, a proper intent. There is no definition of negligence here, but negligence in law has been interpreted ten thousand times and one hundred times that again, and will have to stand as so interpreted.
Mr. MeKENZIE: How about criminal negligence?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This makes what before was negligence that was not criminal, negligence that is criminal. Unless you
do that, you do not get to the root of the trouble; you leave things absolutely as they are. Undoubtedly, a man who intentionally does something to cause a fire is liable now, because there is criminal intent, and there is no use in legislating to meet his case, because it was met long years ago. But by this legislation, we are trying to reach the careless person who does not think of fire at all, and it is this kind of negligence that causes over 75 per cent of fires. If we leave this out, we had better not go on with the Bill. The law of the land to-day places criminal responsibility upon persons who have no criminal intent. For example, if the guardian of a ward, by negligence, by insufficient attention, by failure to procure medical attention, and without any guilty intent at all, causes the death of that child, that guardian is guilty of murder. The same thing runs through the law in many respects, and many other instances could be cited. This extends the operation of that law into the field of fire prevention and says to those, who by mere carelessness, taking no thought of what may happen to them or the loss that may happen to others, allow an electric iron with the current turned on to sit upon a table, when any one with common sense would know that if it were not properly insulated it would burn the table and perhaps the house and perhaps even the neighbour's house. You, through your negligence, caused that loss; it is probable you suffered no loss at all, but other innocent people did; your negligence was the primary cause; you are impervious to punishment by fine, but we say to you in advance: You must be more careful afterwards, and if you fail to be more careful, then you must suffer the only punishment that has any effect upon you.
Would not the owner be liable also under the wording of the clause?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the provincial law said that -the owner shall be responsible for no person in his house doing anything carelessly, then he would be liable, but no provincial law says that.
Supposing there is a case of defective wiring, which the owner should fix and which the tenant is forbidden to use, but the tenant continues to use it, are they not both liable in case of fire?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly.
Whom will you prosecute in such a case: will you prosecute both?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If both are liable, both should be prosecuted.
The owner may have intended to repair the defective wiring, but in the meantime the tenant continues using it. Is there not some unfairness in making both liable?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If there is any unfairness in the matter, the unfairness has its root in the provincial law. If the provincial law makes it the duty of both, and both neglect their duty, we cannot help that; both are liable.

The case I was discussing was not one of owner and tenant. If I own a house and pay insurance on it, and I am paying a sufficiently large insurance premium to justify a company paying me for a loss if I should make a mistake in my own house, for instance, if I should leave an electric iron with the current on, ot if my wife should do so in her own house, or in my house, under this clause, she is a criminal and liable to two years' imprisonment. It is not an accident; it is due to her negligence in not turning off the electric current, because forgetfulness is negligence. Under those circumstances, while according to the Ontario law. the insurance company would be bound to pay the loss, my wife would be liable to go to prison for two years. If that is the purport of the Bill, I should like the House to know it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend is not quite as careful in his statement as he was before. If the provincial law makes it an offence on the part of a wife of an owner, this would not apply at all, because I do not think the hon. member could be the owner and his wife the owner, too, nor could the hon. member and his wife both be said to be occupiers.

My hon. friend does not get my meaning. I am not speaking about the second paragraph at all. If the word " only '' were put in the second paragraph, I would understand that the meaning of the word " negligence " in the first clause was being defined. The second clause says:
The person owning, occupying, or controlling the premises in which such a fire occurs or on which such fire originates, shall be deemed to have caused the fire through negligence if such person, etc,-
But that does not define the only persons who are liable, under the preceding clause, because of negligence. The minister should 
insert the word "only" in the second clause if negligence is confined to the commission of the breaches set out in the second clause.
. ^r-1 MEIGHEN: The hon. member is right in that respect. I was thinking about the second paragraph.- Where he understated the intent was this: The punishment will, we must presume, be proportionate to the guilt. If the negligence is not gross, if it is of the nature of an accident-and the two merge together very often-then we must presume the magistrate or the judge will take that into account, and it may be a judge if the person so elects under this legislation. The punishment is within the power of the judge to inflict: he cannot go higher than two years, but he can inflict punishment of a day's imprisonment if he wishes. He can inflict suspended sentence, if he wishes. He can invoke section 1035 of the Code, and, instead of imposing punishment by imprisonment, he can impose a fine. All that we create is the statutory offence, placing it within the power of the judge to impose such fine or such imprisonment as may be appropriate. Surely that is not too much when the result of the negligence alone is fire. If we are not prepared to go that far, I do not know \Vhat we can do to assist in preventing or reducing this annual waste.
Does this apply to forest fires?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes; it does not matter what the property is.

I thought at one time that this legislation might be amended so as to make it more humane and Christian, but I have come to the conclusion that that is an absolute impossibility. The minister is proposing to go to a length to which we never went before in this country, or any other country, as far as I know. I think the illustrations that have been given are sufficient to bring home to the mind of the minister that this is really dangerous legislation. If a very slight accident is caused in a house, even by a child-I suppose the parent will be responsible for the child-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

Well, then the child
is responsible. I think the minister should withdraw this Bill, and wait for another year or so until he hears that anybody wants this legislation. I do not think anybody does want it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I quoted quite a few
institutions which did.

There may be some institutions looking for extraordinary protection, so as to make bigger money out of their insurance; but I am not in sympathy with legislation of that kind, at the expense of making criminals out of people who are absolutely innocent. It has been said a thousand times in this House that it is impossible to have a criminal without a criminal intent, and it is ridiculous to say that some person with the innocent heart and mind of a child and incapable of conceiving a crime, should be sent for two years to the penitentiary on any of these grounds. 1 cannot see any force in the suggestion that the province may intervene and render this law harmless, because the Act explicitly sets forth that any person guilty of the offence shall suffer such and such a penalty. I do trust that the minister will not find it necessary to put any such legislation as this on the Criminal Statutes of this country.

The point that strikes me is this:	Suppose I am an insurance
agent and an applicant for insurance comes to my office and says: "I want to insure my house." I say: "Yes." He says: "Does this policy cover a fire loss due to leaving on the electric iron, for instance, or to the pipes becoming overheated?" I say: "Yes, you would get your insurance in full. The insurance law so provides." Then when the fire occurs the man is told he is liable to go to jail for these very offences. That is where the inconsistency comes in, to my mind.

I quite agree with the minister that the losses from fire in this country are very great, and I think they should be curtailed in some way or other Not only are they a loss to the country, but all policy holders in mutual companies have to make up for these losses and their rates are consequently much higher. I think anybody who has studied the fire records as given by the insurance companies will agree that Canada's fire losses are very large. Section 1 of this Bill provides:
The person owning, occupying or controlling the premises in which such ia fire occurs, or on which such fire originates, shall he deemed to have caused' the fire through negligence, if such person has failed to obey the requirements of any law intended to prevent fires.
His want of knowledge of the law is construed to be negligence. I do not think that is right. If he knew the law and failed to obey it, that would be negligence; but this legislation is convicting him of negligence even though he has not had an opportunity of knowing what the law is. I
think this provision should be modified in some way. Let me read it again.
The person owning, occupying or controlling the premises in which such a fire occurs, or on which such fire originates, shall he deemed to have caused the fire through negligence, it such person has failed to obey the requirements of any law intended to prevent fires or which requires apparatus for the extinguishment of fires.
A man might well be said to be guilty of negligence if, after an insurance or government inspector had visited his premises and advised him that certain conditions must be remedied, he did not remedy them. Many people will come under this law who do not know what the law is in regard to fires. I think that is unfair. Steps should be taken to advise the public of the law, and want of knowledge of the law should not be construed as negligence.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I really think hon. members are of the view that some principle is being adopted here that is new and of a perilous nature, but such is not the case at all. No law in the world can proceed on any other assumption than that the people know it. We never legislate in this House on any other assumption. If, however, the punishment is made greater, it may be the duty of the federal or provincial authorities to disseminate more widely a knowledge of the law, and when the punishment becomes of a nature differing in certain respects from what it was before, it may well be that the province in enacting a law shall see that the provisions are better known. What I want to impress is this: You cannot legislate on any other hypothesis than that the law is known. If you legislate on any other hypothesis, nobody will make it his business to find out what the law is, because he will not need to care. To-day, the law has the very same defect, if it may be called such, that the hon. member for Grey points out and at which the hon. leader of the Opposition was so horrified this afternoon. The law provides now on this very subject:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to two years' imprisonment who by such negligence as shows him to be reckless or wantonly regardless of consequences-
I would not be a bit surprised if the woman who left a heated iron on the table was considered reckless or wantonly regardless of consequences. In my judgment, she would be liable now under the law.
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to two years' imprisonment, who by suidh negligence as shows him to be reckless or wantonly regardless of consequences, or in viola-

tion of a provincial or municipal law of the locality, sets fire to any forest, tree, manufactured lumber, square timber, logs or floats boom, dam or slide, on the Crown domain or on land leased or lawfully held for the purpose ot cutting timber, or on private property on any creek or river, or rollway, beach or wharf, so that the same is injured or destroyed.
Is not that bad enough without making it worse?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext:
I have no objection to the second part of the clause, that is, as to where a person has been guilty of a direct breach of the present law, provincial, municipal or otherwise. But apparently the law which is now on the Statute Books ;s not drastic enough in the opinion of the minister. The law says that a person must be wantonly reckless before he can come within the code. The word "reckless is a much stronger word than "negligent, and wantonly reckless" is stronger still, and a man has to be guilty not only of recklessness but of wanton recklessness before he comes within the provisions of the code to-day.

Under the present amendment the first subsection standing by itself says that every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to two years' imprisonment, who is negligent. That is what it says in effect. Now, I venture to say that in seven cases out of ten the fires that occur in this country would, according to this subsection, be due to negligence. A fire may be caused by electric irons, or by a man not sufficiently looking after his electric installation, and under such circumstances he .would be held to be guilty of negligence. Or perhaps a man going into a stable might .accidentally back on to his lantern and start a fire, and he might also be guilty of negligence. Do we intend, or are we willing, to go so far as to say that a man shall be liable to two years' imprisonment in such a case, and be held to be negligent although the insurance company admits that his negligence is unavoidable inasmuch as they pay him his insurance?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He pays for his insurance.

He signs a contract which says in effect that although his electric iron may start a fire, or he may knock over his lantern or do all these things which amount to negligence on his part, they will pay him his insurance, notwithstanding the fact that he may be liable, under this law to two years' imprisonment.
I do not think it is the intention to go as far as that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The law says "if by negligence that is reckless or wantonly regardless of consequences." I think those are perhaps a little stronger than just the ,word "negligence." But who is to say that ,we should not make it an offence against the State for one negligently to cause loss to the State? It is an offence to-day. We use the word "negligence" throughout the Code over and over again. For example, if a man to-day by any manner of negligence causes the death of another, is he not answerable before the courts of the land in criminal law? Undoubtedly he is. If his negligence causes the death of or injury to another he is liable now, because he has offended against the law of the State, and you must impose punishment. Of course, it would not be reasonable to make him liable to the same extent as if his negligence merely resulted in financial loss to the community But it is just as logical to make one an offence against the code as to make the other. The character of the injury is the same although in the one case it is greater
in degree than in the other. The community suffers in one case financially through his negligence while the community suffers the loss or maiming of a citizen in the other case. I have given one illustration where negligence resulting in the loss or injury to the State is punishable now under the code. I could give many others. We are simply adding another and we say that for loss to the community by reason of a fire you must answer before the courts. We place it in the power of the judges -of the land to say just what measure of punishment should be inflicted upon you. There is nothing new in it at all; it is merely the sound principle that is everywhere found in the code extended to another class of cases.

This clause has evidently been built up entirely upon the foundation of negligence. The difficulty that will arise under this enactment will be to prove negligence. There are two sets of electrical wiring inspectors to-day operating in Ontario. There is the inspector of the HydroElectric Commission and there is the inspector of the Canadian Underwriters' Association. I know of one instance where one of these inspectors visited a building, condemned the wiring and ordered it reconstructed. That order was carried out to the letter. Subsequently the other inspector came along and condemned the wiring done under the order of the previous inspector and consequently the work had to be done all over again. Supposing that a fire had occurred in the meantime with the wiring carried out under the instruction of the first inspector, who would have been negligent in the case? The owner of the property under this law. The difficulty is to establish negligence. It will be almost impossible, as the hon.. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) says, in seven cases out of ten.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Then nobody will suffer.

I would like to have this Bill withdrawn or delayed so that it may receive further consideration. I think that the whole subject of fire insurance should be considered at the same time. A large proportion of the fires that occur in this country are attributable not to negligence on the part of the occupant, owner, or person controlling the property, but largely because insurance agents are trying to effect 'insurance regardless of the result. All they care for is the commission. With a Bill of this kind you should also couple the responsibility of the insurance agent. He is largely responsible for a large proportion

of the fires that occur. I believe that a large proportion of the insurance . agents will take a risk on any property they can get through with their companies because all they are interested in is the commission. I think the minister will be well advised to delay the enactment of this Bill until the whole subject of fire insurance is considered from every standpoint. I do not think that negligence on the part of the
5 p.m. property owner is at all responsible for a large proportion of the fires that occur. You talk about negligence. To whom do you attribute negligence in the case of the Great Fire in Chicago? Those of us who remember that fire know that it occurred because a cow kicked over a coal oil lantern. What are you going to do with the cow? That fire destroyed millions and millions of dollars worth ot property in Chicago. I think the House will be well advised to delay the passage of this Bill until it has had an opportunity to look into the question from other angles than that which has evidently impressed itself upon whoever drafted the Bill.

There is another
feature of the Bill that perhaps has not been fully considered. A man may have a fire by any one of the innocent means of which I have spoken and yet it is negligence. He is insured, he goes over the matter with the insurance company and the insurance company say: We will offer you so much and if you do not take that, you have two years' imprisonment ahead of you; your wife may have neglected to turn off the electric iron. The insurance company would be practically the only people who would know the circumstances under which the fire occurred, because they would have investigated them. This Bill puts them in the position of being able to force a settlement to their own advantage.

I do not see how the draughtsman of this measure could have chosen language better fitted to carry out the intention. Negligence is something to be proved in each case. Hon. members of this House seem to have it in their minds that carelessness or negligence on their own part, or perhaps on the part of their wives, may bring them within the clutches of the criminal law. That is what is intended. It is to make the people of Canada more careful, in order that Canada may take [DOT] a fresh step forward and occupy a position on all fours with other nations that do not have these enormous fire losses. I am quite sure that if hon. members had followed

the proceedings of the Fire Underwriters' Association, the Conservation Commission, the Retail Merchants and other bodies which have been enumerated here by the minister, they could not but realize that something must be done in Canada if we are not going to fall behind the people of other . nations. Our losses are enormously out of proportion to what they should be. It is true that our houses are, generally speaking, more inflammable than houses in some other_ countries, but that should not excuse our people from the consequences of such negligence as has produced this enormous percentage of losses. I quite understand the feeling of hon. members, such as the hon. member for South East Grey (Mr. Ball), who is afraid that hardship will be brought upon people because of their mot knowing the law. But this House is not concerned about that, because the enforcement is left to the provincial authorities. All we have to do is to state what the law is and then if the provincial authorities, the magistrates and judges who try these cases, are convinced that the negligence is excusable, they will find some way of instructing the jury, or themselves deciding, that there is no negligence under the law. Thus hardship is avoided. It would be a great pity if in this House we failed to make a declaration upon this matter simply from the apprehension that the law might be carried out harshly by the provincial authorities. Our duty is to do what is right and define and declare the law as we are asked to do by these important bodies who have considered these matters from time to time. I would be very much disappointed if the reasons which have been advanced and the doubts which have been expressed as to the supposed harshness of the law and the hardships that it might create should prevent us from doing what seems to me our manifest duty.

I suppose that all of us, whether we are lawyers or not, could form some idea of the character of a law, particularly criminal law frpm the class in which it is placed. The Criminal Code makes a great many classifications of different kinds of law; it is divided into certain parts, and each part deals with a certain class of criminal law. The law which the Acting Minister of Justice proposes to put on the statute-book now, goes into the category, or under the sub-division, of Part 8 of the Criminal Code. The legislation which the minister proposes is put into the class which deals with wilful and forbidden acts

in respect of certain property, and the first section under that reads as follows:
Every one who causes any event by an Act which he knew would probably cause it being reckless whether such event happens or not, is deemed for the purposes of this Part to have caused it wilfully.
Now the very first section of that part of the Code starts out by saying that a person cannot be liable under Part 8 unless he does the thing recklessly, whether such an event happens or not, and knowing that probably the mischief would happen. That is, any ordinary man must know that what he was doing would result in mischief. Then the very next section is under the heading of " Mischief." What does any person think of putting such a case as my hon. friend from Grey North (Mr. Middleboro) has described in the part classed "Mischief"? Let us suppose that a woman is ironing in her house and her iron is connected in the proper way with an electric current. She is called out for some purpose, and by the time she returns the house is afire. Is it to be said that because that woman went out when she was called, either to look after a sick child or to do something else that urgently required her presence, was mischievous in her conduct, because she forgot to turn off the current? Yet that is the class of case in which such conduct is put, and it is classed as mischievous. Then again in the same section and under the same category in which my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Justice puts this offence, is the crime of arson.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not the same section.

It is in the same part of the Code, under the same heading, and in the same class of legislation. Now is this woman, whom I have just described, to be pronounced guilty of arson and put in the same class of criminals as a man who commits arson because she neglected to turn off the electric current in her house when she was called out by some urgent summons?
Now there is another heading dealing with setting other fires. The main section, to which my hon. friend expects to add 515A has the same criminal idea running through it, and any lawyer, or any person, who at times acts as a juror although he is not a lawyer, must know that all these sections must be read together, and he must understand the current or thread that runs through them all. Very well, here is what section 515 says:
Every one is guilty ot an indictable offence, and liable to two years' imprisonment, who,
by such negligence as shows him to be reckless or wantonly regardless of consequences, or in violation of a provincial or municipal law of the locality, sets fire to any forest, tree, manufactured lumber, square timber, logs or floats, boom, dam or slide, on the Crown domain, or on land leased or lawfully held for the purpose of cutting timber, or on private property or any creek or river, or roltway, beach or wharf, so that the same is injured or destroyed.
That is the section to which my hon. friend wishes to add subsection 515A, making it ten times worse, and bringing criminal law into domestic relations in a way in which it was never done before. What are the kind of cases that may come within this law? It applies whether there is any insurance or not, and the minister tells us that it does not make any difference. Suppose a private individual has a little house with a stove pipe running up through the middle o'f it. If a fire occurs by reason of that stovepipe being defective, that man is just as liable as if the fire occurred in a large house that was insured, and he is liable to go for two years to penitentiary if he happens to neglect something that he was told to do by an officer. We will suppose that an officer is passing and he enters and tells the man, " You should have a flue in this place. You should build a flue from the cellar to the top of your house and connect your stovepipe to that flue. If you do not do that I am afraid you may have a fire some day." The man says, " I am poor, and I cannot afford a flue. I have no bricks, I have no money, and I cannot afford to hire a mason. I will get along just as I am and be as careful as possible." An accident happens and the little house is burned down, the proprietor loses his house and is sent to the penitentiary for two years because he did not build a flue as he was directed to do. Is it well for us to enact legislation of that kind? I am sure my hon. friend will have to admit that the cases which I have described would come within the meaning, force and effect of this Bill. It is a measure of such drastic character, and is so absolutely unnecessary that I have much pleasure, seconded by the hon. member for Kent (Mr. McCoig) in moving that the Committee rise.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is moved that the
Chairman leave the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Before the Committee
rises may I be permitted to say a few words in reply to my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. minister
would he out of order in so doing. A motion that the Committee rise is non-debatable.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That may be the case.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is it the pleasure of the Committee to adopt the motion?
Some hon. GENTLEMEN: Aye.
Some hon. GENTLEMEN: No.
