In my opinion the
nays have it. I declare the motion lost.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Refeiring to the last
complaint of the leader of the Opposition he apparently now suspects the Bill not so much for its contents but for the company it is in, and he quotes other offences, very serious in character, in the same part of the Code that this proposed legislation would be under, to sustain him in his contention.
Part 8.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
IThe hon. gentleman
thinks that in view of that it is a pretty serious matter to adopt this legislation. Well, if my hon. friend will go back just a few pages in the Code to Part 6 he will find common assault made an offence, and defined as follows:
An assault is the act ot intentionally applying force to the person of another, directly or indirectly, or attempting or threatening, hy any act or gesture, to apply force.
So that according to that law, if I walked across the floor of the House and held my hand in a threatening attitude over the head of the hon. member, I would be guilty of the offence set out in this section. In the same part of the Code- indeed, on the very same page-I find the offence of so doing defined and, just two pages back, the offences of' murder, manslaughter, and rape. All these are in the same portion of the Code as the reference to the offence that I would be guilty of if I walked across the floor and held my fist over the magnificent shining dome of the leader of the Opposition. So that it cannot be argued very powerfully that you can judge of the nature of a newly-made offence by the part of the Code into which you place it.
The hon. gentleman mentioned one or two very trifling offences which, he said, would be made offences under this law and would subject the persons who committed them to two years' imprisonment. That may be true, but no one will suffer two years' imprisonment if his offence is trivial. You cannot legislate on that assumption; otherwise I would be liable to seven years if I went across the floor and did what I have described. No judge in the land, not even
(The Chairman.]
the hon. member himself were he on the bench, would impose that punishment on me. The maximum punishment is for the maximum offence; the minimum punishment, or none at all, for the minimum offence. Surely two years' imprisonment is not too great a punishment to impose on a person who by his own gross negligence causes very serious loss to the community. The effect of a punishment not only has its application to the individual; it is a matter of example to the community, and a punishment of two years for a gross offence of this kind would have such an effect on the community in general that its adoption by this Committee is absolutely justified.

The word "negligence"
as used here is entirely too wide. A house might be burned down by what we might call an act of God; it might be burned by the act of some person other than the owner. If a man burns his own house with his mind accompanying the act, he does it wilfully and he is guilty of arson; but I cannot conceive of the house being burned in any other way except through his negligence. If the mind accompanies the act, surely it must be a wilful act; if the mind does not accompany the act, it is simply carelessness or negligence. Negligence as set forth here simply means that any act other than one which is wilful which you commit or which you fail to commit and which results in your house being burned, will make you a criminal. I do not think that is the proper principle to apply. The principle of wanton recklessness, set forth in that part of the present Criminal Code which was read by the minister, is the principle that we ought to apply. That principle is well known among lawyers; it is well known in the civil law. It is one of the ingredients of fraud; it sets forth the difference between misrepresentation and fraud. It is a sort of quasi-criminality, and I think it is the only sort of act other than an act accompanied by criminal intent that we should make criminal. The issue is quite clear between the two sides in this controversy. One side desire to make every act other than a wilful act which results in the burning of a building a crime; the other side think that only such carelessness as is in itself a sort of quasi-criminal act should be made criminal. As I say, the present use of the word "negligence" in the section is going entirely too far and is putting into the list of crimes something that has not a tinge of criminalty about it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member, as a lawyer, must know that negligence is today a crime in many places in the Code of the very same character exactly. Does he mean to intimate that if a man by his negligence-not intentionally in any way, but simply through carelessness-causes the death of another man, he is not criminally responsible? The only difference is in the result; the word used is the same in one case as in the other. In one case the act causes a person's death; Parliament has legislated that that is crime. In the other case it causes, say, the loss of a million dollars to the community; we make that a crime, but with a far less punishment. I fail to comprehend the apprehension of hon. members in this regard. A man whose mind accompanies his act in such a way that he knows what is going to result from his act, and intends it, commits a crime which is punishable now by a far greater punishment than two years' imprisonment-I think fourteen years, at least. The class of people we want to bring home are those who, by mere carelessness, by not realizing their duty to the community, causes this loss. If the same carelessness now causes loss of life or the maiming of another, the offender is criminally liable. Now we propose to make that same carelessness a crime, but with a fair less punishment, if it causes destruction of property. A man of substance who by his mere carelessness causes a building worth $100,000 to be burned is liable to-day for that $100,000 in the courts of the country. All we say now is that he is also answerable before the criminal courts. Very often these things are done by men who have no financial responsibility; why should they escape? Why should the community be always at the hazard of careless, reckless acts on the part of people who have no financial responsibility? Unless we are prepared to bring home to them some punishment, we are saying: Let things take their course; let the community suffer year in and year out to the extent of $30,000,000 or $40,000,000 because we are afraid to make a man responsible and to make him suffer appropriate punishment for his own negligence.
The minister cited the cases of Norway, Belgium and England. Have they such a law as is now proposed here, and if so, has that been the reason for their smaller fire losses?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think they have, but I cannot answer for certain. The United
States has now before its Congress a much more drastic law.

To what does the minister attribute the smaller losses in the other countries? Have they better building restrictions or more effective fire restrictions, or is it because they have some law of this kind?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I quote a memorandum furnished to me by the Insurance Department, the language of which very clearly indicates and, I think, necessarily implies, that these laws are in effect in the European countries mentioned:
The effect of this drastic legislation is seen in the per capita loss in European countries, which averages less than 50 cents, while the average in Canada is approximately $3. In 1908 it was $4.
So this memorandum says in effect that this drastic legislation is in operation in those countries.

Would it not be well to get the exact laws of the different countries so that we might have some idea as to how they work out? If this legislation, as proposed, is as good as the minister maintains it to be, that is, to reduce the loss from three or four dollars per capita to fifty cents per capita, and if it is not working any great hardship in Norway or Belgium, it may not be so bad. But if such legislation as this is not the cause of the lesser losses in those countries, then why inflict this legislation on the people if it is not going to produce satisfactory results? For instance, the minister stated that 75 per cent of the losses in Canada were preventable, that is, that they were caused by negligence. What is the nature of that negligence because 75 per cent of a loss of $33,000,000 would not occur simply from leaving stove pipes in houses without proper safeguards? The losses are, I presume, in our larger cities and larger buildings, and most of the cities have fire regulations. Are they living up to them and are they living up to their building restrictions, that is, that certain classes of buildings are not allowed to be built in certain areas? Have the people of Norway and Belgium and other countries better buildipg restrictions, thus causing a lesser loss, or is it that they can, by legislation, scare people out of allowing their houses to burn? This question could, perhaps, be handled better by another of the innumerable commissions appointed by the Government to investigate the whole matter and treat it from a business standpoint. If the loss can be

reduced, that would be a direct benefit to the whole of Canada, because it does not matter where the fire is, we pay the loss through the insurance premium. The people of this country desire to reduce our fire losses. If this legislation brings that about, it may be beneficial legislation, but if it does not, we are only incumbering the people with more legislation.

I would like to refer to
a question that I asked of the minister some

time ago. I am heartily in sympathy with the object of the Bill, the prevention of fire, but I believe, with many hon. members who have spoken, that it is just a little too broad in its application. The point to [DOT]which I wish to draw the attention of the committee particularly is this, that it makes every council of every little municipality a criminal law-making body, or at least, a law-making body that can make a law which will constitute men who commit a breach of that law criminals. It seems to me that it is taking away the authority from this Parliament and handing over to any small body of men in any municipality throughout the country, power which, perhaps after all, it was never intended should be given to them. For example, we have heard in this debate a great deal about negligence and what negligence means. It may be rather presumptuous for one who is not a lawyer to attempt to interpret that which is to be a law, but as I read the Bill, it states thiat a breach of any regulation which may be made by any council, by any municipal body, will in itself constitute negligence, because the clause reads:-
The person owning, occupying or controlling the premises in which such a Are occurs, .... shall be deemed to have caused the fire through negligence if such person has failed to obey the requirements of any law..
It is quite .possible that some of those smaller law-making bodies in some of the smaller municipalities might make regulations, the breach of which would not be negligence in the ordinary accepted sense of the term at all, but by this enactment it will be considered negligence, and if it be negligence it makes the person who commits it liable to criminal prosecution and two years' imprisonment. While the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) said that this law states exactly what it is intended to mean,-1 say it does not. We are simply handing over the power of this Parliament to any small body of legislators there may be throughout the country, and the breach of whatever regulations they may make, whether right or wrong, shall be considered negligence and the person committing such negligence shall be liable to two years' imprisonment.
Bill reported.

On motion of Hon. J. D. Reid (Acting Minister of Customs) the House went into Committee on the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:

That it is expedient to amend the Inland Revenue Act, chapter fifty-one of the Revised Statutes of Canada, to provide for the definition measured content, and use by a chemist or druggist, of chemical stills, ; for abatements to be allowed in the computation of duty upon spirits when stored in warehouse in wooden or in ventilated metal tanks, and when stored in warehouse in wooden barrels; and further to provide that the license fee for a bonded manufacturer shall be such sum not exceeding three hundred dollars as may be prescribed by the Governor in Council; that there may be a remission of duty on malt used in the manufacture of vinegar under prescribed conditions; that the department may authorize the preparation of tobacco and cigars in packages of such size, and the issue of stamps to cover the same, as may appear advisable; that the words "Methyl Hydrate-Poison'" in letters of certain size be affixed to certain medical preparations; that no less quantity than five thousand cigars shall be entered for warehouse by one entry, and except for export, no less quantity than two thousand cigars shall be ex-warehoused by one entry; that an excise duty be imposed upon acetic acid produced in Canada by the destructive distillation of wood, or any other process or from any other source, of four cents on every gallon of six rp-er centum acid, and so in proportion for any greater or less strength; that section 251 and Part X of the said Act be repealed, and in lieu thereof that provision be made respecting the manufacture in Canada of alcohol without the admixture of any denaturants, and denatured alcohol and specially denatured alcohol, which is intended for use in the arts and industries or for fuel, light or power, or for any mechanical purpose; with restrictions as to place of manufacture, sale, delivery and transport of such alcohol and its use in incorporated hospitals, universities, and research laboratories for scientific purposes only ; and providing that no alcohol shall be manufactured or sold under these provisions for beverage purposes; with such other enactments as to the use of recovered alcohol and its redistillation and purification, and for labels on containers of wood alcohol or denatured alcohol, and for penalties for violation of the law, as may be prescribed.
He said:	Several amendments are proposed, the first being a change in the computation of the duty. Sub-paragraph (2) of section one hundred and fifty-five of the present Act is repealed. Where spirits are stored for over two years a certain percentage is allowed for shrinkage. The distillers claim that this percentage should be higher, as the loss is. very serious now that prohibition is in force.
How is the shrinkage determined?

The contents are measured going in and coming out of the tank. The shrinkage in no case exceeds the deficiency found in the tank. Another amendment to section 250 reads as follows:
The person in whose favour a license is granted to manufacture in 'bond for exportation, shall, upon receiving such license pay to the collector such sum not exceeding three hundred
dollars as may be prescribed by the Governor in Council.
That is, instead of a flat rate of $300, the Governor in Council may make regulations prescribing a lesser amount. There is also an amendment to section 255 remitting the duty when the alcohol is used in the manufacture of vinegar. Section 282 is amended by adding thereto the following words:
The Department may authorize the preparation of tobacco and cigars in packages of such size, and the issue of stamps in such denominations to cover same, as may appear advisable, but as to the necessity of advisability of issuing such stamps, the department shall he the sole judge.
Section 316 is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
1.	No less quantity than one hundred pounds of raw leaf tobacco or the contents of one package, five hundred pounds of cavendish or other tobacco, five thousand cigars, or eight thousand cigarettes, shall be entered for warehouse by one entry.
2.	Except for export, no less quantity than fifty pounds of raw leaf tobacco, five hundred pounds of cavendish or manufactured tobacco, two thousand cigars, or five thousand cigarettes, shall be ex-warehoused by one entry.
Section 366 is repealed, and the following substituted therefor:
There shall be imposed, levied and collected upon acetic acid produced in Canada by the destructive distillation of wood, or any other process, or from any other source, except as by this Act otherwise provided, the following duty of excise, which shall be paid to the collector, etc., etc.
The only change there is that we are adding the words: "or any other process."
Section 368 is amended, and defines denatured alcohol as follows:
Denatured alcohol means alcohol in suitable admixture with such denaturants as to render it in the judgment of the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue non-potable and to prevent recovery of the ethyl alcohol.
Section 369 is amended to read as follows :
Alcohol without the admixture of any denaturants and denatured alcohol and specially denatured alcohol as defined in section one of this part, which is intended for use in the arts and industries or for fuel, light or power, or for any mechanical purpose may be manufactured in Canada free from any excise duty.
It has been represented to the Government that alcohol can he manufactured to a very large extent by the distilleries for fuel, light and power, and this amendment simply empowers the distilleries to use denatured alcohol for that purpose.
Section 370 will read:
Excepting as provided by this Act, no alcohol shall be manufactured, denatured or recovered

in Canada except in distilleries thereto licensed.
I think hon. members wilt approve of * these amendments when the Bill is before them and they have had an opportunity to study it.

Why does the minister want to differentiate in the various amounts that he would charge for the licenses? Importunists might tell him they were only going to manufacture a very small amount and should therefore be given the license for a smaller sum, and I think it would be well to fix the license fee in the Act, so that the person getting the license would know how much he had to pay. It would be inadvisable to leave it open to people to come and ask for favours, and it might place patronage to some extent in the hands of the department.

I have not discussed that point very closely with the officials of the department, but- when, we come to the Bill I shall have the information and be glad to discuss the matter on its merits.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Railways and, Canals):
speechtext: There is a decrease in this yote of $13,812.50. The staff in the department coming under the vote for Civil Government for the fiscal year 1918-19 numbered 110. We have reduced it to 96. The increases in salary are all in accordance vyith the Civil Service Act with the exception of the following: The deputy ministe, has been increased from $5,000 to $6,000 in line with all the deputy ministers who have been increased by $1,000. We had last year the position of assistant to the minister. That was Mr. Graham Bell's position and the salary was $5,000. We have dropped that position. The salary of the chief engineer, Mr. Bowden, last year was $5,000; we have increased that by $500. The solicitor, Mr. Fahweather, remains at $5,000. The assistant chief engineer, who was at $4,000 last year, is now increased to $4,500; the electrical engineer from $4,000 to $4,500 and the Inspecting Engineer fro-m $4,000 to $4,500 The names of these gentlemen are:	Mr. Bell, deputy minister; Mr. Bowden, chieE engineer; Mr. Fairweather, solicitor; Mr. Sherwood, assistant chief engineer; Mr. Murphy, electrical engineer; and Mr. Alexander Ferguson, inspecting engineer.
