I am sure the Committee will be very much disappointed if the minister departs from his usual custom of giving at this stage a full statement as to the financial condition of all the railways that the Government is operating. If the hon. gentleman will refer to page 2161 of last year's Hansard he will find that he is' reported as stating:
It has been customary for the Minister of Railways and Canals to make a statement in connection with the operation of the Government Railway System from year to year.
The minister is now at the stage to which he referred when he made that statement, and the Government has many more miles of railway under its control now than it had then. I see no reason why some explanation in regard to the financial operations of the Government railways for the year should not be submitted to the Committee now.

It must be remembered that there has been a change in the entire organization of the Government Railway system since a year ago, owing to the transfer of those railways to new management.
I intend to make a statement later when the Intercolonial Estimates are being considered. I think perhaps that in a week or two I will be in a much better position to present a statement as to the whole railway situation than I am at the present moment. The hon. gentleman knows that a reorganization is proceeding, and that changes are taking place from time to time, and the present is hardly the proper time to give a statement such as he has asked for.

I do not understand
that there is any difference between the estimates of the Intercolonial Railway and the estimates of any other railway that may come up for the committee's consideration.
I gather that the whole system of Government-owned railways is now under the one management and responsible to the Minister of Railways', and when that minister comes here with railway estimates we ha\e a right to suppose that he is dealing with the whole Government system. The statement submitted to the House last year dealt with the Intercolonial, the Transcontinental, and the Prince Edward Island Railways, and some small lines in New Brunswick, and the receipts and expenditures were given as for the whole system. Are we now to understand that the minister has been keeping separate accounts for the Intercolonial apart from the other lines, and that there is a different system of management in certain sections of the Government lines, or is the Government system to be dealt with under one head? If the latter is the case I do not very well see how we are to get one statement about the Intercolonial, and a different statement about other portions of the Government Railway system. I find that last year the minister made an estimate as to what the operations of the Government system of railways were to cost for the fiscal year which ended in March' last, stated what purchases of rolling stock he was to make, and gave a general outline of the financial operations of the Government system. I think the minister, as in a sense the President of the Government railway system, should, when he asks for more money, give us, as representing the owners of the railway, an exact statement as to how these railways have worked out during the year. The minister told us last, year that he anticipated a deficit, and the only question in that regard is 101
whether it is any larger than he thought it would be

My intention this evening was first to take up the Canal Estimates, and some smaller items about which there probably would not be much discussion, deferring the railway statement until a later period, because I am not in a position to furnish the necessary information this evening. With reference to the operation of the Government Railways the situation is this: Last year we took a vote for the operation of the Canadian Government railway system. That was for the Intercolonial Railway and its branch lines, and the Transcontinental Railway between Winnipeg and Moncton, which then comprehended the Government railway system. We took a vote until the end of the then fiscal year, the receipts were deposited to the credit of the Receiver General, and the disbursements for operations were made in the same way as for many years past. Three or four months ago the control of the Government Railway operations was transferred from the Railway Department to the Board of Management of the Canadian National Railway System, of which Mr. Hanna is the president, and that board will report to the Government and to Parliament through the Minister of Railways and Can-
When the Intercolonial Estimates or some of the larger amounts that are in the Estimates in connection with the Government railway systems are before the Committee I shall be pleased to make a statement such as I made last year and to give all the information I can as to the results of the operation of the Intercolonial, the Transcontinental and the several companies of which the Government has purchased the controlling stock. I had intended simply to have the Civil Government Estimates passed and then to go on to the Canal Estimates.

I wish to draw the attention of the minister to something that happened last night in Toronto. Before the departure from Toronto for Ottawa of the 10.55 Canadian Northern train, I had wired from Chatham for a berth in the sleeping car, and naturally expected to be able to get one. When I arrived in Toronto, however, I was informed by the conductor of the train that on account of the number of special cars that were on the train containing Government officials, it was impossible to put on any more sleeping cars. I asked the conductor how many private cars were on, and he said that there were three, one carrying the Minister of Finance,



another carrying the Minister of Militia, and a third carrying the Chairman of the Railway Board. He said: "The car of the Chairman of the Railway Commission cannot be pulled because we refuse to take on a fourth one." The conductor said that if we wanted to do so we could go into the day coach and sleep on the seats. I refused to do that, and ran to catch the second section of the Canadian Pacific railway train, on which I got a berth; but many others who wanted to go to Ottawa to transact business had the choice of sleeping in the day coach or smoker or of being unable to travel on that train. Because three special cars occupied by three public men were attached to the train, fifty people were unable to travel from Toronto to Ottawa on that line. The Canadian Northern could not put on any more sleeping cars because these three special cars carrying three or four of the public men of Canada were attached to the train. If the minister thinks he is going to economize in that way he is making a very, sad mistake. If ministers want to run * private cars for their own special comfort during the holiday season, surely two of them ought to be friendly enough to get into one car and let us poor individuals have the privilege of occupying berths. Providence was against the Government in this particular matter; the train ran off the track before it got to Smith's Ralls, evidencing its disgust with the action of the Government in carrying three special cars while other folk slept in the day coaches. Moreover, after the train ran off the track, those who had managed to get berths were deprived of the privilege of having their breakfast until a special dining car was sent from Ottawa; but the gentlemen who occupied the private cars had their breakfasts, while the other people on the train watched them through the windows, with empty stomachs. There is not another railway system in the country which, on the occasion of delay caused by a wreck, does not furnish meals free of charge to the passengers. On this occasion, however, I am credibly informed that every man had to pay for his breakfast in the dining car which came from Ottawa. This matter may seem somewhat of a joke, because the whole thing is so ridiculous.' But this treatment of those who were anxious to patronize Government roads was so unkind and so unfair that the minister should take some action in the matter and should see that ministers of the Crown may not in future occupy half a train so that 
the plain people are unable to get berths in the sleeping cars.

I agree that a train should not be loaded down with private ca.rs- If happened last night that several ministers were returning from their Easter holiday and were coming down on that train. The president and directors and Sir Henry Drayton were in one car. Sir Thomas White was in another; he had intended to come to Ottawa the night before, but unfortunately there was a death in his family and he could not come until last evening. General Mewburn could not come either; so they all happened to come together on that train. But a thing of that kind probably would not occur once in a year
probably will not occur again. As to the accident, of course that could not be helped; we believe that a switch was tampered with and that that w*as the cause of the accident. Fortunately, no lives were lost. As to the people paying for their meals on the dining car, I did not hear anything about that; probably in the excitement that matter was overlooked. I am sure that the management of the Canadian National Railways would do everything they could to make things satisfactory for the passengers, as they have done in the past. I understand that in the case of a wreck, the railways have some such understanding with regard to meals as that mentioned by the hon. member. However, I am glad the hon. gentleman has drawn attention to the matter of the private oars and of the furnishing of meals to the passengers after the accident. It does good to bring these matters before the House; at the same time, it was really accidental that two or three private ears were on last night's train. I do not think the members of the House or the people of the country can complain much about the use of private cars by ministers; they are not used very much. After all, it is almost an absolute necessity that they be used occasionally. Ministers have hardly sufficient time to do their work in Ottawa and when they travel they have to take work with them and do it on the train. I think I can safely say that the use of private cars is less to-day than it ever has been at any time during the last ten or fifteen years.

How many piivate cars- The CHAIRMAN: I have to call the Committee to order. The item under discussion is that of salaries for Civil Service, Department of Railways and Canals, The matter of private cars certainly comes under the Outside Service.

I did not happen to be present when an Estimate -was passed raising the salary of any other deputy minister. I do not want to make any invidious reference to the deputy minister of this department, but I should like to know the grounds upon which the additional $1,000 is being paid to the various deputy ministers of the departments at this particular time and whether there is a comparable advance to the other members of the Civil Service.

The members of the Civil Service, as a whole, have received advances during the past year. They have received bonuses and then there are the usual statutory increases each year. The salaries of deputy ministers, however, have not been increased for many years. The cost of living has gone up with them as well as with others, and it was felt, when the matter was brought to the attention of the "Government, that they, along with the other civil servants, were entitled to >an increase, and all the deputy ministers were given the same increase.

I should like, so as to be thoroughly understood, to say on that point that I suppose the deputy ministers are feeling tire increased cost of living with every other inhabitant of Canada. Personally, I think a deputy minister is, in ordinary times, worth quite the salary which he is getting, including the increase; but as the cost of living is the cause of this, I venture, while not opposing the appropriation, to express the hope that the Government are directing their attention to the question of the cost of living. We had in this House a statement of the most funereal description as :to the condition of the finances of the country, and we were also told, in so many words, I think, on two different occasions, that we are $100,000,000 in the hole. Under those circumstances, something has to be done, and I hope the Government are not going to be misled by the state of customs returns, which is, I believe, very good for the moment, into thinking that we can go on spending money and increasing salaries without attempting to do something at the other end, that is, to reduce the cost of living. If it goes on mounting in This way the ministers may have to come before the House next year with another proposal to increase salaries, and with this sum of $100,000,000 not yet provided for, one is naturally waiting with anxiety, and, indeed, with some degree of apprehension, for the Budget statement in
101 i
this connection, and I can see nothing but very great financial disorder. I hope the Government, as a whole, will, in the next few weeks, pay very serious attention to this question of the cost of living and the general financial condition of the country. Unless history is absolutely misleading, we shall, within the next two or three years, have times very different from the present. We are still running the country under war conditions, and our soldiers are not, by any means, all back. We are selling a great deal of material, as other nations who have it to sell are doing, to our Allies to feed the Central European nations. A summer's harvest in these nations will alter that condition, and if we have good crops ourselves,
I want to assure ministers that the financial embarrassment and economic disturbance will be such as they do not seem at present to be quite as apprehensive of as they should be. I venture to say these things at this point without any special reference to the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid), who, I think, gets his work through this House wonderfully well-and I am the last man to want to obstruct him-and without opposing this particular vote. The general position, however, is one which should commend itself to the consideration of any Government which desires to be credited in the next two years with average foresight, discretion and economy.

There is no doubt at all what the hon. member says is true. The cost of living in this, as in every other country, is a very serious question. The Government are certainly considering the matter, and when the Budget speech is brought down, we shall have to discuss the whole situation and consider what can be done. When I see the prices that people have to pay for the necessaries of life, such as clothes and so on, I feel that the cost of living has become so high that people must have higher salaries or they cannot live. I believe every member of the House is anxious to consider the situation and to do what he can to improve matters. This is a big question and one that it will tax the ingenuity of the best people in this country to solve. 1 hope, when the matter comes up on the Budget, some means will be found by which the cost of living may be reduced.
With reference to the item regarding the solicitor, does the Department of Justice not look after the legal affairs of the department?

The Justice Department looks after the outside legal work of every department, but it has always been necessary, in connection with railway matters, to have a solicitor in the department to prepare the briefs and give opinions as to cases coming before the department. If those cases are not, or cannot be, settled, then, of course, they are sent to the Justice Department which selects lawyers outside of the department altogether who take the cases up and go. to the courts with them; that is, if the Deputy Minister of Justice or the Solicitor General does not deal with them. In many cases, the Deputy Minister of Justice, if he has time, or the Solicitor General, appears before the courts.
How many solicitors are there altogether?

We have one solicitor in the Department of Railways and Canals. Of course, on the railways, there are several solicitors. When the Intercolonial Railway and the Transcontinental Railway were being administered by the Department of Railways, we had at Ottawa one solicitor, Mr. Fairweather, and then we had Mr. Al-ward at Moncton, who had one assistant. That was the total staff of solicitors on the whole railway system.-

If I understand the matter aright, each branch of the Canadian National railways, that is to say, the Intercolonial, the Transcontinental and the Canadian Northern, has one or two solicitors. I am at a loss to understand, if each railway refers its legal business to its own solicitor, what the particular solicitor mentioned in this item does. What are his duties?

When the Department of Railways administered the Intercolonial and the Transcontinental, we had at Ottawa a solicitor to advise the minister on matters1 coming before him, and there was also work in connection with the canals, such as leases, agreements an<J things of that sort that were prepared at Ottawa. There is work for solicitors in matters of that kind.
Of course, with a system of 13,000 miles of railway there is a great deal of legal work to ao. We have a solicitor at Moncton, for instance. There are legal matters continually cropping up in connection with the Canadian National Railways which have to be referred to the Government, and the minister must have a solicitor at his call. Mr. Fairweather is very busy with the work DMr. Power.]
he has to do in connection with the department. I do not think it possible for a minister to carry on without a solicitor at his call. -
Could the work not be done as well by one of the solicitors in the Department of Justice Is there nobody sufficiently competent in that department to do the work?

It would simply be transferring the work to that department. They would require another solicitor to do the work. Besides, the Justice Department does not do the departmental work that Mr. Fairweather does. Most of the departments have a solicitor, I believe. It would - be very inconvenient to have to send our files over to the Justice Department or to have the solicitor continually coming over here to explain matters. Hardly a day passes but a lease or a contract lias to be prepared, and a solicitor is absolutely required.

Is the legislation which is submitted to Parliament on behalf of the Railway Department drafted by the solicitor of the department or by the parliamentary counsel-for instance, the Bill incorporating the Canadian National Railways?

I asked Mr. Fairweather
to' consult with the solicitor of the Canadian National Railways and with the Railway Commission, if necessary, in drafting the Bill.
Is it not also part of his duty to assist the Minister of Railways and Canals in the Railway Committee?
Oh, yes, he appears before the Railway Committee.
Who was the assistant to the minister? How did that position come to be done away with?

Mr. Graham Bell was assistant to the minister. When Mr. Campbell, who was deputy minister, became Commissioner of Highways, Mr. Graham Bell took the position of deputy minister, and the position of assistant to the minister was abolished.
Welland ship canal-construction, $8,500,000.

Hon. gentlemen will remember that the new Welland ship canal . was under construction at the time war was declared. Work was carried on for a time afterwards, then was closed down. There were four sections under construe-

tion: No. 1, for dredging the harbour, completing the concrete work, and regulating the weir; that contract was with the Dominion Dredging Company at the time work closed down. Then there were sections 2, 3 and 5 also under construction. These were the four largest sections of this canal. When the war ended and demobilization took place we felt it was necessary to go on with some of the work to provide employment. A great many of the men who had been working on the canal had enlisted, and there were also in that district a great many men who were thrown out of work owing to the closing of munitions plants. Hon. gentlemen will remember well the feeling of unrest there was in .the country at that time. We therefore decided to go on with the work that we had under construction. We had, of course, settled with the contractors; the contracts had been cancelled. When we decided to start work again, we thought that the cost of materials and labour was so high that it would be almost impossible for the contractors to tender at a fair and reasonable price. We therefore put the old contractors at work on these four sections which would employ a large number of men, and we decided to let them proceed with the work on a cost-plus basis. We agreeed to pay .them 8 per cent. These contractors understood the work, had their organizations, .and we thought they would be able to do .the work in the most economical way. The work goes on only from month to month, because we stipylated in the contract that we can stop the work on the costrplus basis at any time and call for tenders, so that we oould take advantage of conditions when they become normal again.
We also stipulated in the Order in Council that, the contract would not extend longer than the present year, that is December 31, 1919, so that there could be no misunderstanding with the contractors or with the public. In section No. 1 we estimate that the total amount that could be expended on that work would be $500,000; No. 2, $600,000; No. 3, $700,000; and No. 5, $500,000. Then for the purchase of plant, cement, bridges, steel rails, engineering, etc., $1,200,000. They do not get any percentage on the $1,200,000, but only on the other. So that, although we have $3,500,000 in the Estimates we will pay a percentage only on $2,300,000 at the very most, if they do that amount of work.

The work ceased about two years ago. Before construction is xe-started it would be well to know what
the condition of the work is at the present moment. Has an inspection been made to know the condition the work is in?
The engineering staff looked over the work.
What is the condition of it?
I am informed by the Chief Engineer that the work is in the same condition as when we closed down, with the exception of a couple of earth slides where there had been excavation.

Has an inspection been made recently? If so, the engineer will find that it is not as the minister says. There are large abutments that cost many thousands of dollars that are not in their proper condition.

One of the slides occurred at Queenston Road Bridge. It was absolutely necessary to close the works down at the time, and of course we could not expect the work to be in as good condition as it would be if we had proceeded.
I am informed that the large abutment that did slide in was at Queenston Road.

The hon. member for East York (Mr. Foster) raised the very question I was going to ask the minister. Near the city of St. Catharines, since the work on the canal was discontinued, the cement walls collapsed and damage to 9 p.m. the extent of thousands of dollars has occurred. Upon whom will the loss fall-the contractors or the Government?

If there is any loss of that kind it falls upon the Government because we settled with the contractors a couple of years ago. However, I can only give the hon. member the information which the 'Chief Engineer gives me, and he tells me that the hon. member has been misinformed regarding the damage.

I am not ;an engineer, but any person who drives past the work must see that there is a great deal of damage; the work must be reconstructed. If, of course, the damage is due to the discontinuance of the work at an improper time I suppose the loss must be borne by the Government, but if it is due to inferior work it seems to me the people who put up the work should shoulder the responsibility.
What do these contractors furnish for the eight per cent plus which they get, and who are they?

The contractors are,
for No. 1:	The Dominion Dredging Company, whose head office is at Ottawa; No. 2, Baldry, Yerburgh & Hutchison, an English firm; No. 3, Doheny, Quinlan & Robertson; No. 4, the Canadian Dredging Company. We furnish the plant. They do not get any percentage on the plant, but only on the materials and labour.
They get a percentage on $2,300,000?
That is, if they do that amount of work.

What do they do for that 

just walk around the job?

These contractors furnish for the 8 per cent what is usually furnished by contractors on a percentage basis. They furnish their organization and do the financing, and their percentage is on the same basis as that paid to any firm. The percentage I consider reasonable. They asked at the time the same percentage as is allowed by other corporations, and the hon. member will know that the Exchequer Court decided that 10 per cent was a fair and reasonable basis.
What case was that?

Take the Dominion Dredging Company: $40,000 would be the total amount they could possibly get during the year, and there is the head of the firm, the superintendent's office, the financing, and so on. So that I think the percentage is very reasonable.
What financing do they do?

They purchase materials and pay wages twice a month, and we pay them once a month. They pay their men in the middle of March and again at the end of March, and we do not pay them until the 15th of April, and there is, therefore, a good deal of financing in connection with the work.
Do they get 8 per cent plus on that financing, too?
They get 8 per cent on the amount of money paid out for materials and labour, but not for the financing as well.

I do not know if I understand this matter correctly, but it seems rather strange. We have a contract, I understand, to build the Parliament buildings on a percentage basis the same as this. Whoever is doing the work-I think it is Lyall-supplies all the equipment. In this 
case the minister says the work was under contract and he tells us: We have settled with the contractors and it is all off. These contractors must have had the equipment and all the material that was necessary to carry on the work. If I understand rightly, the contractors are employed because they know the work best, and that is as it should be; but the mode of payment is what I cannot understand. The minister says the Canadian Dredging Company are going to do part of that work. You are going to buy the dredges and they are going to put their men on them. They are experienced men and will handle that machinery, You are going to pay these men and you are going to pay the Canadian Dredging Company a percentage on the salaries they are paying their own men. Supposing I am in the position of these contractors; you are going to pay eight per cent on every cent that is expended on these sections, and all I have to do is to sit in my office. The minister seems to lay great stress on the question of financing. In ordinary times I would be willing to finance any one, or anything, with the credit of Canada behind me. All you have to do is to make estimates of the progress of the work and when these estimates are made you have only to go to the bank and the bank will be quite willing to advance the money to the contractors. The contractor is getting eight per cent to supply the staff which is being paid by the Government. The bookkeepers and office staff are paid by the Government, in addition to which the contractor is not using his own plant which is lying idle or is used on some other work, and the Government are buying the plant. It would pay the Government better if they would go a little farther, as they have done in connection with the Parliament buildings, have the contractor supply the plant, and give him a little higher percentage. The Government are not going to dig canals all their life and the plant may be worth nothing to them when they get through with the Welland canal, and there will be
81,200,000	gone to waste. It would pay the Government to pay ten per cent on the equipment and not be loaded up with this material and equipment when the work is done. I cannot understand what service will be rendered by the contractor for the eight per cent which will be paid on $2,800,000.

We could not make a contract of this kind on the cost-plus basi3 and ask them to furnish the plant because

this contract might only last for two or three months. I do not think that any member of the Government expects to do this work on this basis very long or to continue it any longer than is absolutely necessary. We will call for tenders-
What about the plant?

Whoever tenders for this work will want the plant and we will ask those who tender to take it over. They will have to take the plant over in order to carry on the work. While we have the plant we are not paying any percentage on it.

Is that not the contract
with Peter Lyall & Sons for the Parliament buildings?

I do not know what
their contract is; I am talking about this one. Take the Dominion Dredging Company's plant; their dredges are worth $350.000, and it probably costs $10,000 a month to operate them. We are only paying a percentage on $10,000 being the cost of operation, or $800. If they had $350,000 in that plant they would want more than eight per cent on $350,000.
Certainly; I know that.

'So we have the plant, and whoever takes this contract off our hands will have to take the plant when we call for tenders. In addition to that, the contractors are not getting eight, per cent on all that is really going into the work. They are not getting it on the cement and the cement is a large item in connection with the work. We do not pay them a percentage on any of the materials we are able to supply. They do not get it on the cement, or the reinforcing steel; we have that on hand. There is a very large amount of stuff that we have on hand from the original contract and they do not get any percentage on that. When we take everything into consideration, the percentage is really, in my opinion, very reasonable. These are very large contractors and very reliable men. They always have an organization on hand that'they must pay even though they are not employed in order to keep their organization together. They are out of employment for some time and they must figure on reimbursing their men to a certain extent for the time that they have not been employed. The Chief Engineer, his staff, and I went into this matter, with Council, and threshed it out, and I believe that the percentage is a fair and reasonable amount considering everything.

I cannot agree with the minister. Supposing the material that the contractors supplied cost sixteen per cent; that would amount to $36,000 over the $2,300,000 that the minister is going to expend. Now he is going to put $1,200,000 'into plant and this plant has to be maintained. There will be wear and tear and depreciation. You will have that $1,200,000 which will be sunk anyway; whereas, if you pay double the commission and have the contractor supply his own plant a great deal of benefit to the country will result.
It is human nature to take care of that which belongs to yourself better than you take care of that which belongs to your neighbour and therefore you would be better off in the end. I do not criticise the cost-plus basis only I think that it is a big mistake for the Government to supply this dredge -and equipment and spend $1,200,000 and in addition pay this commission. The minister says that the percentage will not be paid on the cement which they have on hand. If I understand rightly -that is cement which the contractors bought and on which they got a profit.

Out of this $1,200,000 we are going to purchase plant, cement, bridges, steel rails, and pay for engineering, and so on. When the hon. gentleman states that we are going to spend $1,200,000 out of $3,500,000 on plant that will be of no value when the contract is ended he speaks without a full understanding of the situation. This is to purchase plant, the cement that is going into the work and on which they do not get a commission.
Why do they not get a commission?

Because that is the contract; on anything furnished by the department- they do not get any percentage. It is estimated that $1,200,000 will be required for this purpose, and they do not get any percentage on that. It is not -all lost, because the bridges and steel rails will, perhaps, be sold later on at ia small loss. They are second-hand rails that we are purchasing now. Of course, if steel rails were to depreciate in value in the next three or four years there might be a loss, but there will not be a loss altogether, for the reason that they can be sold as scrap.
Are the steel rails and the cement included in the $1,200,000?
Yes, and the bridges and the engineering work. That is, in the $3,500,000.
That will pay the wages and material that will go into the contract?
Yes.

The cement is regarded here as equipment, which I do not think it is. I would count as equipment all the tools-for instance, the dredges, the derricks, and the machines which were used for boring. That is what I say will be of no use to the Government after this job is completed. What portion of this $1,200,000 is going into cement and steel rails? Then we can get down to closer figures.

The Chief Engineer tells me we are purchasing about $300,000 of plant other than what we had on hand. That will leave $900,000 of this estimate that will go into the purchase of cement, bridges, steel rails, and so forth, and pay for engineering.

I understood the minister to say that one of the reasons for carrying on the work on this basis was that the contractors had to be reimbursed for maintaining their staff during the time they weTe idle.

The hon. gentleman has unduly expanded my statement. What I said was that the contractors have a staff that they must always maintain in order to keep the organization intact, and an putting these men on this work they probably made an estimate for the time during which their staff was waiting for work. Everybody tells me that the percentage these men are working on is a fair and reasonable one. Then, again, when you consider that we can close down the work at any time and call for tenders-
By giving thirty days' notice.

W7e can give thirty daj?s' notice and we will do that when times are normal. I do not think it is a good time now to call for tenders, because some contractors tell me they would hardly know what prices to charge on account of the abnormal cost of material and labour. We could see no other way if we were to start up this work than to carry it out on a percentage basis.

I do not object to the system followed, but what seems to call for criticism is what has been done in regard to equipment. This equipment is going to cost the Government $300,000, being paid for at abnormal prices. I think it is a mistake not to have the contractor 
supply his own equipment. In those sections of the canal that are under contract the contractors supplied their own equipment. They had, and have still, all that is necessary to carry on the work. If the Government had paid the contractors as much as sixteen per cent on the job, it would have resulted in a very considerable saving. Let the man who is going to do the work supply his own equipment. Buy the material if you will, but let the contractor supply his own dredges and other plant Naturally there is an inducement in this, because a person will take better care of property that belongs to him than he will of what belongs to his neighbour.

There is a possibility that we will lose on the plant when we ask the contractor to take it over in the future, that is if prices go down so that we can call for tenders. That is one of the penalties that must be paid in going on with this public work at this particular time. There is no doubt that we paid more for the plant than we would expect to pay in a year from now, if times become normal again, plant and everything else will be cheaper.
Have the contractors not got the plant? They are the same contractors that were doing the work before, are they not?
Yes.
Have you settled with them for the plant they sold to the Government?
When we settled with these contractors, we purchased the plant from them, and then re-sold a great part of it.	.
To whom?

We sold all of the movable plant to the public, and at prices quite a percentage higher than we paid to the contractors. We took the plant on a valuation basis made by a firm in Montreal, and then sold it at higher prices than we paid.
I he plant that we have left was also purchased from the contractors when we settled up.
That settles the question then.
Two years ago, when we closed up with these men, we had to take the plant from them.
If the Government owns the plant it is all right.
Four-fifths of the plant we have on hand belongs to us, and the other one-fifth is what we are purchasing.

Has the minister decided on finishing this work at any certain time? If so, how much does he think it is going to cost, and what is the policy of the Government with regard to it? Is the minister going right on, just making work for the time being for these contractors, and for other fellows that he wants to have on the job?
We have decided to carry this work on until the end of December next, that is all that we have provided for in the Estimates. Next session the Government will have to decide what will be done.

Were thfre no other contractors that would have been willing to take this work at a percentage plus? It seems an extraordinary thing that these men should go to these works with a lead pencil on their ear and get eight per cent on the expenditures made.

It seems to me we ought to have some further justification for entering upon this extraordinary expenditure. There must be great necessity for starting this work at this particular time, and motives of economy must have influenced the minister to close it down when the war broke out.
I assume that he took a proper inventory of what had been done and ascertained how matters stood when the works were closed down. The present works were started in midwinter, at a time when contractors, under ordinary conditions, would have stopped working. I assume that there is a good deal of clay work and masonry work on this canal, all of which is done at great expense in the winter season. The minister has not told us that anybody who had been overseas came to him looking for work on this canal. If a large body of men who had been overseas or who had been working in munition plants came to him and said: We are out of work; we have been working for the country in connection with the war, and we think that the Government should look after us; then the minister could figure out whether it would be cheaper for the country to give these men so much a day for doing nothing or to pay their board or to take some other step than to start this enormous work at such great expense and under such unfavourable circumstances- not for the purpose of doing the work itself, but for the purpose of giving employment.
So far, however, we have not been informed that any such men have been looking for work or were actually put on the job. After all, the purpose of this work is more or less charitable; as I say, it is the giving of work to men who are out of employment, not the carrying on of an enterprise for the sake ol the results for the country. If he can say that he has accomplished that purpose, he would be affording some satisfaction to the committee, although we should be paying very dearly for it. But I rather fear that there was no such justification for starting the work at this time. I should like the minister to tell us how the officials, after given periods, arrive at the amount that has been expended on this work. It is extremely difficult to make a proper estimate of the amount of clay that is removed in winter, having regard to the slides that frequently take place; and it is difficult also, in cases where tons of water have to be pumped out of the cuttings every morning, to tell how much should be allowed for work of that character. This is the first time that canal construction has been proceeded with on force account. I have never heard of a railway, a wharf or a canal being built on force account, and only because of absolute necessity should the minister carry on such a work as this under the circumstances. Formerly, these works were proceeded with under tender and contract. The minister can tell us therefore., what was the cost per unit of the various kinds of work that were being done and how the cost in pre-war days compares with the cost of the work being carried on under force account. If the minister finds that the work per unit is now costing very much more, he would be well advised to put an end to it as speedily as possible and to wait until he can carry the work on in the ordinary way.

In the Niagara peninsula, thousands of men have been thrown out of work since the war ceased and since the munition plants and otner w'ar industries discontinued operations. These men were not looking for charity. They did not come to me and say: Pay me so much a day to keep myself and my family living. What they asked for was work in order that they might earn a living for them&elves and their families. We did not wish to proceed with the work in the middle of winter, but we were faced with this condition of affairs. Men had been thrown out of work, families were in want, the cost of living was high. Accordingly, the Government were forced to try to provide

work in every part of Canada where there was unemployment. I remember, about the time that the war ended, there was consternation down at Sydney; the Dominion Iron and Steel works were going to close down and thousands of men were to be thrown out of employment. The Government was asked to do something to keep these men employed and to keep the Dominion Iron and Steel works going. They were asking $70 and $80 a ton for rails. I believed then that if we waited until normal times came or until we wanted to use the rails, we could buy them at a great deal less. I say frankly that if we had carried out with the Dominion Iron and Steel works the policy now suggested with regard to the Welland canal, thousands of men in the Domin ion Iron and Steel works would have had nothing to do during the last several winter months. We did make a contract with them and paid them $65 a ton for rails which, if we had waited until to-day, we could buy for $47 a ton. I do not regret that we gave the contract in order to keep these men employed. The men of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company worked hard to furnish materials to win the war; so did the men in the Niagara peninsula. So it was the duty of the Government, even though they were facing a loss, even though they might get the materials cheaper a few months later, to try to keep all the plants going and all men employed. I go further and say that wherever plants are thinking of closing down because of the changed conditions, I believe it is the duty of the Government and of every member of the House to do all they possibly can to keep the wheels turning in every industry. The Niagara peninsula is a manufacturing centre; it was necessary to do something to keep the men employed, and in my judgment we acted rightly in starting a work about one-third of which had been constructed, which must be continued and which will be completed.
Had it not been for the changed war conditions the Government would have waited until things became normal. I could give the hon. member instances where private corporations should, in my opinion, have gone ahead and done more than they did in order to give employment, but when they did not do so, it was up to the Government to keep the men employed, and I have no regrets in connection with this work, with the Dominion Iron and Steel works, with the Algoma Works, and with any shipbuilding and other plants in Canada to which the Government have been able to give work until times become normal.

The minister has, as he knows and admits, made a departure from the custom in this country of giving contracts by tender, and to justify his position he has appealed to patriotism and endeavoured to prove that the country was undertaking this work in order to give employment to a large number of men who otherwise would not have had employment. The minister would have made his case stronger had he told the committee just how many men were engaged in that work. I suppose the minister will willingly admit that the system of doing work by force contract is, to say the least, a vicious one. The man who has the work in charge finds it in his interest to do it, not as cheaply as possible, but as expensively as possible. It men are employed at $4 a day, his commission out of that is 32 cents, but if he jacks them up to $5 a day, he gets 40 cents out of them, so that it is in the interest of the contractor to do the work just as expensively as possible. I am not going to follow this feature of the matter further. What I rose more particularly for was to say that it seems to me that, in view of the large vote asked for canal purposes, this would be the time for the minister to make a statement as to the transportation problem from the Great Lakes to the seaboard. If the Welland canal is to be deepened, what is to be done with the other canals? We hear rumours; in fact, we are told, that before the close of this session the Government may submit a policy of new canals to replace the present Cornwall canal and the Soulanges canal. The transportation interests and the grain producing interests of the Great West have a right to know now the general policy cf the Government as regards the canal system.

With reference to the first criticism the hon. member made as to the cost-plus basis, if I were giving a contract of my own, I believe in the cost-plus basis. I believe, moreover, that almost ' every corporation had, while the war was on, to go on the cost-plus basis. Wages and material are in an abnormal condition, and I do not believe any private individual or corporation would at the present time accept a contract on a tender basis.
If the minister had given a contract for the Welland canal, would wages have gone up?

Wages vary from fiine to time. If, say, just after the war was over, one were to call for tenders for work

on the Welland canal and to 'let the work on a contract, as wages were very high at that time, the contractor would probably base his tender on those wages. Every person believed they might fall, and yet the contractor could not take any chances. Wages on the Welland canal are arranged in this way: there is a fair-wage clause in the contract, and the wages paid are the same as those received by other employees in the locality. The men nearly all belong to unions, and a regular wage is arranged by the unions of each locality. As to the policy of the Government with reference to transportation from the Great Lakes to the seaboard, there cannot be any change in the water transportation situation until the Welland canal is completed, and that, even if the work is pressed, will take at least three or four years. What we are doing at the present time is just keeping the work going on the four contracts that were partially, and some of them very nearly, completed. We are not calling for tenders nor proceeding with the other work, nor have we any intention of doing so during the present year, for the reason 1 have mentioned. The hon. member can, therefore, see that we are not pressing navigation construction work between Welland and Montreal at present. I have in mind what the hon. member wishes to learn, namely, as to the system between, say, the head of the canal system, that is, just east of Prescott, and Montreal. That is a big question, and I do not believe it will come up during the present session. The hon. member knows this question has been before the people for a number of years. Some years ago an American corporation made a proposition to place a dam across the St. Lawrence at Cornwall for power purposes only. I opposed that at the time, not so much on account of damming the St. Lawrence, but because I believed that when that work was proceeded with it should be done by the Governments of the two countries, and not by private corporations, in order that the power developed would be supplied to the people of each country at the lowest possible cost, instead of on the basis of dividends on stock issues. The power question has been taken up very seriously by the Government of the United States, and it has, diiring the last few years, developed in this country much faster than we expected a few years ago.
Between the head of the canal system and Montreal I have been informed-and I understand it is a minimum estimate-that about 2,000,000 horse-power can be developed
on the St. Lawrence river. My own impression is that all that power will be required; at least, Canada will require her portion of it. I believe that the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National railways running from west Montreal can use all that power. My opinion is that if the United States will assume their portion of the cost of this work-for it is an international work-Canada should assume her portion, and then we would have a complete waterway system for ocean-going vessels right up to Port Arthur. If this 2,000,000 horse power were developed, and our portion sold to the people at a minimum cost, I think it would be a great thing for the future of Canada. I can only express my own opinion. The American Government had the matter before Congress, and many people on the other side of the boundary, who are privately interested are anxious that this water-power should be developed. The chief engineer of our Railway Department and his staff have been surveying and going into the whole situation for a number of years; they have the whole matter right up to date, and are prepared to take it up at any time it is thought advisable by both governments. Of course we can do nothing more than discuss the matter with the American Government if they feel inclined to take up the proposal, and the whole matter would then be submitted to Parliament for consideration. Personally, I do not think the matter will be taken up during the present session, unless the American Government should approach us.
Arei they not developing power now?

A large appropriation Bill has passed Congress for assisting in the development of water-powers in the United States; but the American Government is not developing power on the St. Lawrence as a government. Of course a great power is being developed at Messina, and is being used by the aluminum company there; I think it is from
60,000	to 100,000 horse-power. The same company is taking 60,000 horse-power from Valleyfield.
Ninety thousand.	[DOT]

Sixty thousand is all
they have an export license for. Then there is another power company at Waddington; they want to develop on the American side Under the treaty between the United States and Canada no dam can be placed on the St. Lawrence without the consent of the

Dominion Government. The position I have taken in this House, both as a private member and as a minister, is this: If the power is to be developed, the two governments should build the dam and place the lock in the dam. They could build it as cheaply as any private concern. I believe that after the dam was completed, and after deducting what was necessary on account of navigation, they could sell the power at a nominal price which would pay both interest and something on the principal. In that way the people of Ontario and Quebec would be given cheap power, and the cost of operation of the railways, which will be operating under eleotric power in a few years, would be decreased very materially. Apart from navigation purposes, I believe this work would prove one of Canada's greatest assets in the way of supplying power to farmers and the railways, and, of course, the public would benefit by the decreased cost of operation.

The minister has skillfully
evaded saying whether the Government have a real navigation policy or not from the Great Lakes to Montreal, and has simply taken up time trying to draw a red herring across the trail by talking of power. The minister, when a private member, opposed the construction of a dam west of Cornwall because, as Hansard will show, he objected to the power going into the United States. If I remember well, the power was going to Messina, and the minister objected very strenuously. But he had not been a member of the Government for many weeks before he himself was party to a contract that was given to the Cedar Rapids Power Company to develop power on the Soulanges canal, off the St. Lawrence river. The idea was that this power should be developed for use in and around the city of Montreal. The minister states to-night that he knows that an export license was given for 60,000 horse-power. The newspapers say that 60,000 was granted in the first place, and subsequently another 30,000. The minister granted that- license . himself for the carrying of power, developed forty or fifty miles away from the United States boundary, over to Messina.
I think the country will want to know what' is going to be the policy of the Government with respect to this power which it is proposed to develop. Is it to be developed for canal purposes? The people of this country are not so much interested in power. The Government has placed a great load on the western grain growers; the rates have been enormously increased since this Government

came into power, and that is a tax on the earnings of the man who grows grain for export. Something must be done to lighten that load, and the only way in which it can be lightened, as the minister knows, is by water transportation. What the country wants to know is whether this Government has a real policy in regard to waterways between Fort William and Montreal.

I did not want to evade the hon. member's question. With reference to the export of power1 the hon. member says that I was a party to an agreement to export this power. Previous to my becoming a minister, or at least previous to the change of Government in 1911, permission was given for the export of power, and since I have been a minister 1 have been trying to reduce the export. In fact, we have had a very difficult time during the last three or four years trying to decrease the export of power that was arranged prior to 1911.

There was no power prior
to 1911 at this point I speak of, it was not developed until after 1911.

I think some of it was developed by that Montreal firm. With reference to the policy of the Government in regard to transportation from Port Arthur to Montreal, the Government, in 1912, I think, announced its policy; that is, they were going to enlarge the Welland canal in order that these 300,0C0 or 400,000 bushel freighters should go to Kingston and bring it that much nearer to Montreal. That policy was decided on then, and as to future transportation between Kingston and Montreal, that of course had not been considered up to that time. They started on work in the Welland canal. The war came and everything was changed and they have not considered any other policy up to the present time, except carrying out what they commenced on, the Welland canal. The hon. member knows that the Government could not possibly consider anything while the war was on. The treaty has not yet been signed, and until it is signed' we will not consider what will be done east of Kingston to Montreal.

The minister has so far
failed to. give the Committee the answer asked for by the hon. member for Chateau-guay-Huntingdon, that is, the number of people who are going to be benefited directly by the work on the Welland canal. It' is well that we should know that. We are asked to vote $3,500,000 in a lump sum. The minister has told us that although the

work is not absolutely essential, yet in order to keep people employed it is necessary it should be proceeded with. I think the Committee and the country would like to know how many men in the Niagara Peninsula are to be benefited by the work.

We have about 1,200 men at present but we expect to have probably 3,000 or 4,000 during the summer months. In addition to that, there are men employed outside, not directly
10 p.m. on the canal, in connection with materials and so forth.
Was this work, which is now being done by force contract, let by tender previous to the war?
Yes.
That work was abandoned when the war broke out, and it is now being undertaken under a different form of contract?
Yes.
Well, is that the policy of the Government with respect to all work of that kind done throughout the country?

Yes, it is. On a long contract, where you are going to spend a lot of money and when the work takes considerable time, I would not think of calling for tenders, owing, as I said a few moments ago, to the abnormal conditions that have to be contended with.

Then how is it that only to-day tenders were opened in the regular way in connection with some excavation at the Customs House at Montreal? It is an important piece of work running into about a quarter of a million dollars, and the minister of that department w'ould not think of doing the work under a force contract.

That work will take a very short time. In connection with this work, as I stated before, a lot of plant must be purchased which the contractors would not want to purchase, as the contract may terminate at any time. This contract is not for a definite period. We can cancel it at the end of any month.

How does the minister propose to give skilled munition workers work on the canai? He has told the Committee that the work is to take the place of that which was closed down owing to the termination of the war. I understand that the men who were engaged in munition work were skilled men who had special
training. Does the minister expect that they will be satisfied with ordinary day labour on the canal?

In connection with munitions they no doubt require skilled labour, but skilled labour is also required on the canal. You must have skilled men to operate dredges, drills, steam engines and various machines'. A great lot of this labour I believe went from the Welland canal to munitions.

What were most of these men doing before the war broke out? How is it that we have to provide work for these men now if they could go back to their ordinary occupations? If these men were employed in legitimate work in which they were earning proper wages, why should we now have to provide for them a sort of glorified soup kitchen?

I think it is hardly fair to say that we are providing a "soup kitchen'' for the employees of the Niagara district. On behalf of the employees there I certainly resent that statement. We do not undertake to provide any "soup kitchens" but simply to give legitimate work to these men in that district. That is what we started to do, and what I believe we are doing now. A great many of these men went overseas, and coming back they want their positions again on the Welland canal. The hon. member asks me, where do these men come from, and what they were doing before? Surely he does not expect me to answer a question of that kind. How should I know? All I know is that in that district, as in others, as in Montreal, there were thousands of men who were out of employment. Will the hon. gentlemen tell me where all the munitions workers came from that were working in Alontreal?
They left their positions to get higher salaries working on munitions.
They may have done that in Alontreal but not in other places; not at the Welland canal.
The munition contractors in Ontario kept employment agencies in Montreal throughout the war hiring men from the farms in Quebec to work on munitions.
Has the minister given any instructions to ensure that the men employed on this work are Canadians?

Orders have gone out to the contractors to employ as many re-

turned soldiers as possible. The other men are Canadian citizens. As far as I know they were Canadians only that they were employing.

The minister says that as
far as he knows only Canadians were being employed, but sometimes he does not know. Has he inquired, and is he in a position to inform the committee that only Canadians are being provided with work under this system of contracts on a cost plus basis?
Yes, those are the instructions that went to the contractors.
Written?
I had the contractors in my office and told them to do that. I am satisfied that is what they are doing.
As part of their contract?

The contract is to proceed with the work and the instructions are to employ Canadians. Unless there may be some special man that the hon. member may refer to, these contractors, who are all Canadian citizens, are employing Canadians and men who have been at the front. None of these contractors will take on any others than Canadian citizens unless it may be for some particular reason. I do not know whether the hon. member refers to foreigners, Italians, or some other people of that kind living in that particular locality. There (may be some other people of that kind who have been living in that locality, but they are citizens of Canada and they have been living there for a number of years.
Is it not a fact that twenty five or fifty per cent of the men who are seeking employment, and who "will be employed on this work, are Italian labourers?
That is absolutely untrue.
Will the minister give us the proportion of the Italians employed?
I cannot do that.
If my statement is untrue how is it the minister cannot give me the exact figures?
Who had the contracts at the commencement of the work?

I gave them a few
minuteis !ago. They are the contractors who are doing the work now-the Dominion Dredging Company, of Ottawa, Baldry, Yer-burgh & Hutchinson, Doheny, Quinland & Robertson, Montreal; and the Canadian Dredging Company of Midland.
fMr. J, D. Eeid.]

When were the contracts
cancelled?
Two years ago.
What were the arrangements between the Government and the contractors, and what are the conditions of cancellation?
We simply paid them for the work they did up to the day when the contracts were cancelled and took their plant over.
How much did you pay for the plants of these various corporations?
I could not give the hon. member the exact figures this evening. We took them at the invoice price less a percentage for depreciation. Then we sold a lot of the plant at a profit.
To whom?

Any person. There were engines and cars, a great many people wanted that kind of plant at the time, and we were able to dispose of a lot of it at a profit. Part of it we kept. The Dominion Dredging Company had three dredges and steam tugs and scows. That plant we kept, and the contractors are now using it and we are not paying any percentage on it. It is the intention, as soon as we feel that times are normal, to ask for tenders for this work and to ask the contractors who tender to take over the plant we have purchased. We are purchasing about $300,000 worth of new plant for this work. I explained that a few moments ago. Of course that plant would cost a great deal more than it would if times were normal, but it was. necessary to purchase the plant in order to proceed with the work. When the contractors take it over there may be a loss on that because we have asked the contractors to proceed with the work in abnormal times.

As far as I can judge from the statement of the minister, the Government has no very fixed policy. The other day the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) told us that unless for some very imperative reason, or for carrying on works necessary for the prosecution of the war, the policy of the Government was never to give a contract on force account. The Minister of Public Works told us that he gave a contract on force account only on one occasion and that was for the construction of buildings for aeroplanes and seaplanes. He said it was the policy of the Government to give no contracts on force account. We see now that

the policy of the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) is at variance with that of the Minister of Public Works. It is very curious to see there is no fixed policy of the Government. I would like to know if there is not a law which prohibits the letting of contracts without calling for tenders?

No,' there is not any
law.

The minister says there is
no law. I say to the minister that there is a law which prohibits the letting of contracts exceeding in amount $5,000 without calling for tenders. Will the minister explain on what authority he has taken upon himself to violate the law by letting contracts of such magnitude?
There is the law with reference to contracts not exceeding $5,000, but in an emergency you can also let a contract other than by tender.

Will the minister tell us
what the emergency was?
I have explained that several times.
Not satisfactorily.

I am sorry I cannot satisfy the hon. member, but I say again that these contracts were let in order to provide work for the people in that locality. In other parts of Canada we had to do the same thing. It would be unfair and unjust, the war coming to an end so quickly, to say to these people:	We will
do nothing to provide you with work; the war is now over and you can do without work and your families can starve during the winter. That is what I call an emergency.

The emergency was not because the Government had not time to call for tenders. Surely the minister is not going to try to make the committee believe that he had not time to call for tenders? Now I want to know from him what statutory authority he had for adopting such a course?
I have not the statutes before me, but as I understand it, we were quite within the law in acting as we did.
I contend that you were not.
I can only put the Department of Justice's opinion against that of my hon. friend, and
