Very well, Mr. Chairman, 1 bow to your ruling.

We certainly let the contract in accordance with the law, as it was interpreted to me by the Justice Department. I go further and say this: I do not believe that Parliament, or indeed any one, would justify the calling for tenders and letting a contract under such abnormal conditions as prevailed at that time. We made a contract from month to mopth, which is not to extend later than December 31 of this year; that is all we have done. The contractors could not possibly figure on giving us prices for any length of time that we would be justified in accepting while the war was still on. They would have wanted quite a period oi time to complete the contract, and to stipulate for provisions with respect to the purchase of equipment, machinery, and so on. Any contractors I talked to did not think that we would at all be justified in calling for tenders.

The minister stated previously that when the former contract was cancelled the Government took over from the various contractors the plant that they had on hand for carrying on the work. The policy of the Government then, was at a certain future date to give to certain contractors the order to go on with the work. Now the Government had the necessary plant in hand, and all that was needed was to call for tenders, and award the contracts in the ordinary way according to law. The minister has failed to convince the Committee that such an emergency existed as to justify him in ignoring the law. It seems to me that the law should be adhered to at all times, and that the minister will fail to find any statutory provision to justify his action. I now ask him to lay upon the Table the contracts entered into between the Government and these men for the carrying on of the work, also the opinion of the Department of Justice stating that he was justified in ignoring the law and not calling for tenders.

I will very gladly lay
the contracts on the Table to-morrow. With reference to the opinion of the Justice Department the department has its own solicitor with whom I took the matter up. That solicitor consulted the Department of Justice and advised us as to whether the

work was being carried out legally. There was no doubt at all in his mind tha't it was being legally done, nor was there any doubt in the minds of officials of other departments where the same kind of contract was entered into. The Department of Public Works is an instance of that.
Mr. ViIEN:	In what respect?

If the Department of
Public Works could adopt that policy in one instance, would we not also be justified in this case?

No, because the Minister of Public Works explained that the buildings for the aeroplane plant-I suppose that is the case to which the hon. gentleman alludes-could not be completed if there had been a delay of four Weeks. The expenditure was for war purposes, it was late in the fall, and the buildings had to be completed before the snow came. The Minister of Public Works furthermore clearly explained at the time that it was the settled policy of the Government to always call for tenders, and never to enter into contracts on force account unless there was such an emergency as the one he cited, and which instance has been the only one in his department. I ask the minister when he lays on the Table to-morrow the contract for the renewal of this work, to also advise us of the statutory authority which permits him to dispense with the calling for tenders.
The hon. member is a lawyer and can more readily consult the statutes than I can.
I am afraid that the complicated Orders in Council which apply to the matter will not allow me to discover the information as easily as the minister can.

There is no Order in Council except as to the contract that was let, and the statutes are easily available. I could not give any legal information on the matter other than what is to be found in the statutes with which the hon. member is familiar.

Surely the minister will not
refuse to tell the Committee on what statutory provision he bases his authority for acting as he has done? Was there any provision in the Estimates voted last year which authorized this expenditure?

The hon. member will notice in the present Estimates that the sum of $1,860,000 was voted last year. In the Estimates for 1919-20 the sum of $3,500,000 is asked for the Welland ship canal.

Mr. JAOOiBIS:	Might I ask the minister
if this paternal solicitude on the part of the Government to supply work to the unemployed in the Niagara district will be extended to other parts of the country where unemployed may also be found, and where public works are in abeyance?

I can give the instance
mentioned by the leader of the Opposition at Sydney.
It is a far cry from Niagara to Sydney. If the minister would investigate, he would find a good deal of unemployment in other districts.
Who are back of the Dominion Dredging Company?
Colonel Gordon Stewart, Mr. Larmonth, and Colonel McNeill, the Chief Engineer tells me. I do not know the others.
Is Senator O'Brien a member of the firm?
No. He was a member, I think, of the firm that originally had the contract, but he dropped out of the firm.
Is it not a fact that he dropped out only in respect of this contract?
He is not in this contract now.
He is still with the firm?
No, he is not in the firm, I understand.
He is a senator; he could not be.

The minister takes shelter behind the statement that some money was furnished for the supplying of rails at Sydney and he looks hard at me as if that was of immense concern to me-thinking, I suppose, that Sydney is in my constituency.
I know that Sydney is not in the hon. member's constituency.

There was no such depression in Sydney as the minister suggested. The Dominion Steel Works were going at full swing; there was not the slightest let-up in any department. There is no comparison between that situation and the conditions with respect to the Welland canal construction. The Department of Railways and Canals have been getting steel and steel rails from that company for

the last ten or fifteen years, and if they continued getting that material a little in advance, that was only ordinary business precaution. If the minister could get steel rails from the Dominion Steel Company cheaper than he could get them anywhere else, no great virtue is to be credited to him or to his department if a little contract was made in advance. In the county from which I come the Nova Scotia steel people were almost exclusively engaged in the manufacture of munitions during the war. That work stopped suddenly -and two or three thousand men were thrown out of employment in the town of Sydney Mines. As the member for the -county, I -made application to the Government for assistance to the Nova Scotia Steel people by way of an advance order or something to help them out, but not twenty-five cents worth of assistance did the Nova Scotia Steel people get from the Government. That is the kind of sympathy and support that the thousands of men of the Nova Scotia Steel works who are out of employment in Sydney Mines received from the Government. Hundreds of these men were returned soldiers and had families to support, but they were obliged to get along as best they could until the company started work again. The difficulty with the minister was that- these contractors who were round his office looking for jobs and reminding him of past favours that they had extended to him and to -his party, were bothering him, and at least, like the woman who bothered the unjust judge who neither feared God nor regarded man-and the minister was somewhat in that frame of mind- he made up his mind that he would rather let them plunge in -the mud of the canal than bother him in his office. These contractors had staffs who were unemployed, and these are the men who are engaged on this work to-day. I venture to say that not a dozen returned soldiers are engaged on the whole work-not as many as would save Sodom and Gomorrah-five just men. The emergency on the strength of which the minister attempts to justify evading or passing by the law is not the kind of emergency that the law recognizes-that is, the necessity for getting the work done in a hurry. He is proceeding as he is simply because some people are looking for work; that is not the emergency contemplated by the statute.
I asked the minister quite a while ago to give us some information -as to the cost of this work compared with the cost of the work done under the old contract. He did not tell us that; perhaps he can.
If we are not losing very much money on it, perhaps we should not be very critical of the minister, but I do not think we should throw away a large sum of money; we have none to waste. This work is being carried on in a very unbusinesslike way. What is the s-ense of sipending millions upon -a section of a work which can be o-f no service until the whole project is completed? It would be -ridiculous for a man to finish one-half of a house and do nothing to the other half if he knew that he could not use the house until the whole was completed. The minister is spending millions on certain sections, and when he finishes those sections he is going to stop. Large portions are not finished and will not be finished for four years. What is the use of spending money on works that will, cave in, as has happened to work that has already been done? Would it not be good business to put this whole work under construction at once and see that it is all finished -as quickly as possible in a uniform and proper manner so that the country will get some benefit from the expenditure? I throw out those suggestions to the minister, which, I think, are along business lines and which he would do well to follow.
Mr. J. D. REID; With reference to the first statement made by the hon. member, as to the wotk given to the Dominion Iron and Steel Company and other corporations, representations were made to us that a large number of men in the Dominion Iron and Steel Works as well as in many other works throughout the Dominion would be thrown out of employment. Rails were the only things that the Government could take, and the order was given in order to keep the rail plant going during the winter. With reference to the Nova Scotia steel plant at Sydney, there was nothing that they manufactured that the Government, could use, and not a fifty cent piece was given to that company. A very large order was, I understand, given to the Nova Scotia Steel Company at New Glasgow, I think, for cars.

I am not speaking
about New Glasgow.
I know that, but that company got an order.
The car company and the Nova Scotia Steel Company are two different companies.
I thought they belonged to the Nova Scotia Steel Company.
No.

At all events, contracts for steel ships, cars, rails and other equipment were given to companies in different parts of the country, wherever the Government could use the material. With reference to the construction of the Welland canal, the policy was settled five or six years ago that the Welland canal would be enlarged, and many millions of dollars were spent on those contracts. The hon. member stated that, by proceeding with and completing those contracts, the work would not be of much use unless we went on with all the work. The hon. member hardly understands the situation, or he would not make that statement. The situation is this, that if we completed those four contracts* we could use that part of the canal with seven locks instead of the tw'enty-four that are used at present; that is, with the present canal size, the work would be of great assistance. That, of course, would be the only portion that would be deep, but those are the heavy contracts for the locks, and it would probably take four years to do the work. The other work, which is mostly dredging, could be done in about two years, so that we could start it in about a couple of years from now and have the whole work completed. The hon. member will, therefore, see that we are not losing any time by proceeding with the four contracts now. When we were taking up this matter, the chief engineer and the engineering staff went into it thoroughly, and the chief engineer makes this statement at the end of his report:
After giving the matter careful consideration,
I Strongly urge and recommend that arrangements be made with the former contractors to resume work upon their respective sections bo that we may have the benefit of their experienced organizations. The value of such organizations is evidenced by the practice of contractors carrying many men on pay-rolls during periods of idleness.
When first requested to submit an offer for the resumption of work on a cost plus percentage basis, they proposed a ten per cent basis.
I refused to recommend this, and after further negotiations they agreed to accept an eight per cent basis, *' cost " not to include the materials and supplies furnished by the department. For this, they agree to supply their own office staff, general superintendence, bookkeep-mfs, purchasing and the capital necessary to carry on under the proposed conditions.
I strongly recommend the acceptance of their offer, reserving our right to call for tenders for the completion of the work as soon as it may be deemed expedient to do so.
The chief engineer and his staff negotiated for some time; the whole matter was carried on by them; and after they had nego-[ Mr. McKenzie.]
tiated with those contractors and figured the matter out, as they believed, in the very best interest of the public, the matter was submitted to me; we went into it very thoroughly, and I really believed it was the only thing to do at that particular time. As I stated a few minutes ago, just as soon as the time is opportune to call for tenders, we intend doing so and not to proceed any longer on a percentage basis.

It is now nearly eleven o clock, and I do not think we should allow this item to carry to-night, because there seems to be good reason to believe that this contract was illegal. I am quite familiar with the statute as to proceeding with work costing over $5,000 without calling for tenders. The minister may be well advised, and he may have a perfect right to go on with the work; but he should have time to consult his legal advisers, and tomorrow or w'henever he goes on again with his Estimates, he can inform us as to the opinion he receives from the Department of Justice upon work of this kind, namely, whether it is legal for any department of the Government under such circumstances to proceed with work under force account without1 calling for tenders. The point is well worth considering, and as so much money is involved, I am sure every member of the Committee would feel better if we were satisfied that this was a legal transaction and that we were voting money for absolutely legal purposes. So far as I understand the matter, the minister has not asked for tenders, and there is no good reason why the time should not be utilized in getting tenders from different contractors on this work, the work to commence at such a time as may be deemed advisable. There is, on this side of the House, no factious opposition to the item passing; but there is really a legal point involved, and it would be as well to settle it so that we might know once and for all that we are justified in voting the money, and that the minister was legally right in giving the contract. It would be well for the minister to let this item stand, and when the legal point is settled, I do not think he will have any trouble in having this item pass.

Even if it were deemed advisable to call for tenders, on account of prevailing abnormal conditions, I cannot agree with the hon. member that it would be advisable to call for tenders now and to proceed with this work on contract. As the contractors state that material is so high in price and labour is so high, if we were to say

to them that they must take a contract,
1 do not think it would be possible to make a satisfactory one. I think it is in the public interest to go on with the work on a cost-plus basis for the present; it is the only way that I can see for this or any other similar work at the present time. As to the awarding of the contract, I took this matter up with the solicitor of the department and was informed, and believe, that we were within our legal rights. The hon. member knows that around the Council board there are a number of legal men who certainly understand the law, and would not approve of a contract that was improper from a legal standpoint. I do not know where I can get any better opinion.

We want to see the
opinion.

I did not ask for a
written opinion of the Justice Department. My solicitor gave his opinion, and he would consult the Justice Department if it were necessary. Furthermore, the Auditor General would not pass an account that was improper. If there was any other information I could give, I should be only too glad to give it. I have no desire whatever to withhold information, and so far as the . contracts are concerned I will lay them on the Table. I cannot see what advantage there would be in letting the item stand, because there is no further information I can give. Some hon. member has asked me to state the difference in the cost now and before the war. We have not got into very heavy work as yet, and I do not know that I could get the details my hon. friend wants; it would be pretty hard to do so at the present time. I think the hon. member objects to our proceeding with the work at all. The Government, of course, must assume that responsibility. We believed that the possibility of unemployment in that district, and the advantage we should derive from the work, made it necessary for us to go on with it. The hon. member states that he does not believe there were five returned soldiers on that work. My information is that there are at least a dozen returned soldiers on the engineering staff-

The hon. member did
not let me finish my sentence. I stated that there wore at least a dozen men on the engineering staff, and a hundred or more with the contractors. Why does not the hon. member cheer that? We expect to have between 1,000 and 2,000 returned soldiers within a short time.

I can assure the minister that he will not get returned soldiers to dig ditches in the Welland canal. They have dug ditches in France, and they will not do it again.

The hon. member is trying to put into my mouth the statement he himself makes to the public. I rise to ia point of order.
I never said that I wanted the returned soldiers .to dig ditches, and I want the minister to apologize for having said so. I think I am perfectly within my rights in asking him to withdraw that statement.

The minister, of course, is obliged to accept the statement of the hon. member that he never made such a statement in the House, but I do not know that there is any point of order raised, or that any statement has been made which should be withdrawn.

The point of order is this: The minister said that I was the only member of the House who would make the statement that I wished the soldiers to work in the ditches. I most certainly object to a statement of that kind from the minister or anybody else, and I think the Chair ought to support me in .asking the minister to withdraw his statement.
The hon. member stated that I was asking returned soldiers to dig ditches. I made no such statement, and I said the hon. unembpr was the only one who would charge me with making such a statement.

I heard the minister state that within a few days he would have 2,000 men employed on the canal. Now you could hardly have 2,000 engineers on the job, so if 2,000 returned soldiers work on the job some of them will have to dig ditches, and I objected very strongly to the minister giving positions of that kind to returned, soldiers, saying that they had had enough of digging ditches in the four years they-were at the front.

The minister told us a few
moments ago that there are quite a number of lawyers around the Council board, and

that he sought their advice as to whether this contract was legal or not. Now that he has lifted the veil from what transpires at the Council board I should like to know whether the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) was satisfied that this $3,500,000 work should be done by force account, when the policy of the Department of Public Works is tender and contract.
When an Order in Council is passed, the hon. member knows Council all agree.

The minister is trying to convince the committee that it is sound policy to give such a contract without calling for tenders, because of some emergency. Sir, there are a number of contracts let, not only by the Government, but by private concerns, for construction work. What are the abnormal conditions of which the minister speaks? Is it the cost of labour, or of materials? Surely the same conditions exist for private companies. To give the minister but one example of the different views held by his colleagues, what did the Minister of Naval Affairs (Mr. Ballantyne) do when he wanted ships built?
He gave contracts not on a cost-plus basis, but on so much a ton to all shipbuilders in Canada who were willing to undertake the building of ships at the price agreed upon. In the building of ships there are the same abnormal conditions that exist in connection with the digging of canals: the men must be employed; steel must be bought and all the other material required in the building of ships must be secured, and yet the policy of the Marine Department has not been the cost-plus basis. In regard to public works, the hon. Minister of Public Works said the other day that unless there was an imperious demand that the work should be let out it was the policy of the Government never to give contracts unless tenders were called for. The Minister of Railways and Canals is now trying to induce the Committee to believe that there was such an emergenoy by reason of the unemployment-caused by the return of our soldiers, and he is compelled to admit that there are twelve returned soldiers employed in the digging of the canal.
The hon. member should add that I said there were over a hundred men on the contractors' staff.

If the minister had waited a moment I would have completed his statement. He said that there were about a dozen returned soldiers employed in the digging of the canal and that on the staff 
of the contractors there were perhaps a hundred-he would not swear to it or make a positive statement. He does not know, and it is the general policy of the Government never to know or to be aware of anything. When a minister is embarrassed he simply says, "We do not know; we are not aware of it; we have no information as to that." It is a Cabinet of non-information or lack of information. The other day the Minister of Public Works made a statement on this very subject. On the 26th of February he said:
Somewhere on lake Ontario, I believe. I am also going to take the responsibility of starting these works before the money has been voted by Parliament, because I believe Parliament will concur in our views and vote the money in order that we may relieve a certain amount of the unemployment that already exists in the large centres. It is the duty of tile Government to relieve that unemployment as far as possible. . . . By tender and contract, most certainly. Perhaps I should qualify that statement to this extent: there may be some buildings which will have to be torn down to clear the site for the new ones. That work * possibly might be done by the Government, but it would only be-
I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman is reading from a debate during this session. That is against the rule.
I am merely quoting the words of the Minister of Public Works on this very question of policy.
My point is that the hon. gentleman cannot read from a previous debate of this session.

The point of order is certainly well taken. It is very clear that an hon. member cannot read from a previous debate in the Official Report of the debates of the current session. That rule applies to the Committee as well as to the House.
Mr. \ IEN: Will the Chairman read me the rule.

Bourinot at page 357 says:
Neither can a member, in speaking, refer to anything said or done in a previous debate during the same session-a rule necessary to economize the time of the House, and a restraint upon members to prevent them from reviving a debate already concluded.

There is no doubt
about the accuracy of that rule which is the one rule-
Order.
It is the one rule-
Order.

I must remind the
hon. member for Brorne (Mr. McMaster) that the ruling of the Chair cannot be discussed.

I will abide by your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but I must say that there is a divergence of opinion in the present Cabinet as to the policy that should be followed when contracts are made. One minister tells us that contracts should never be let unless tenders are called for, and I must admit that this view
11 p.m. is in accordance with the law, and it is high time that we should do things properly and according to regular procedure. During the war various emergencies might have excused a different system, but we are now on a peace basis, and the last body to realize this fact seems to he the present Administration. They are trying to reorganize the country on a basis of peace, but they are reluctant to adopt the principle which prevails in times oi peace, that contracts should not be given by favoritism to any particular contractor to the detriment of others. They do not seem to realize the important principle that in the expenditure of public moneys great care should be taken not to spend more than is absolutely necessary. There is a law in this country which provides that a contract which exceeds $5,000 must not be let unless tenders are called for. This is a wise law and one which has received the approbation of the majority oi the members of this House. The only emergency the minister could mention was that employment had to be provided for the unemployed workmen, but he has not been able to convince the Committee that it would have taken very much more time or caused any serious hardship if he had waited three or four weeks to call for tenders. The minister argued also that the conditions were abnormal as regards the wages of workmen and as regards material that it was not expedient to call for tenders and give the contracts according to a fixed hasis, but that it was preferable to give the contracts on a cost-plus basis.
In so far as the wages of the workmen are concerned, we do not anticipate any immediate reduction or any immediate downfall in the price of labour. Not only do not the Government expect such a thing but in the contracts that the Government entered into with the various contractors they have specially provided the scale oi wages that is going to be paid to the labourers. Surely a scale of wages is provided in the contract. There was absolutely no necessity to give to these men the advantage of carrying on such a tremendous contract, amounting to $3,500,000, without taking upon themselves any risk whatever. They had the plant the Government bought from them and which the Government now place back in their hands without charging anything for it. They know the market quotations of the various materials that are required. They have the wages fixed in the schedule included in their contract.
I fail to see any reason which can justify the Government or the minister in letting contracts without calling for tenders. There is a certain degree of honesty and candour which the minister owes to this House but I do not believe that he has succeeded in proving that there was any such emergency as he has urged in justification ol the course which he pursued. I believe it would have been mbre in the public interest to have delayed the work for two or three weeks which would have been sufficient time to have allowed for the calling of tenders.
I think I should emphasize the point raised by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) that we can hardly be called upon to vote this large amount without seeing the contracts which have been let by the Government or of having the advantage of studying these contracts and seeing what we are voting this $3,500,000 for. With reference to these contracts, we have only the reference that the minister made to them to-night. I think we should let this item stand until the contracts are laid on the Table and until we have an opportunity of going into them more fully.

The point raised by
the hon. member now that the item should stand until he sees the contracts, is well taken. I had no idea that that was the particular point that was being emphasized. If hon. gentlemen want any information or if they want to see the contracts, I have no objection to allowing the item to stand. I certainly will agree to the suggestion at once and let the item stand. I will lay the contracts on the Table and be glad to get any further information any hon. members wish. They are entitled to any information they want. I have been trying to give all the information it was possible for me to give on this item to-night. The hour is getting late and I do not wish to ask the Committee to proceed with any other items; these can come up some other time.

I tried to make it clear that we wanted to see these contracts and the legal opinion upon which the minister acted. I am not at all an authority on cabinet practice, or the practice that is followed when an Order in Council comes before the Government, but I understand that when a minister is putting through a contract in connection with which he does not comply with the statute he must furnish council with his reasons for not complying with the law. Perhaps the minister will be able to give us a legal opinion and the reason that he gave to council for non-compliance with the statute. I must remind the minister that there is nobody on this side of the House who desires to stop the work if it can go along and within a reasonable time produce such a result as to give the country the benefit of the operation of the rest of the canal. If the minister would call for tenders we would have the satisfaction of knowing whether or not he could get along better after he receives these tenders than by continuing as things are now. He will find that he can get tenders to carry out this work now at very much less cost than before. He is doing it in the most expensive way. If there is a proper call for tenders from one end of the country to the other I have every reason to believe that under present conditions there being many contractors looking for work, he will likely receive very reasonable tenders.
Progress reported.

On the Orders of the Day:

In the Financial Post of April 19 there is an .article in connection with the credits -established by the Government in favour of Roumania, Serbia, and Greece. The Acting Prime Minister explained the nature of those credits to the House the other day. One paragraph in that article announces that in connection with those credits an intermediary agency has been established through Sir Clifford Sifton, which acts as fiscal agent for manufacturers securing orders by marketing Roumanian bonds to cover the amount. May I learn from the Acting Prime Minister whether Sir Clifford Sifton has any authority from the Government to act -as intermediary agent in marketing Roumanian bonds?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend must refer to the private marketing of Roumanian bonds. My attention has not been drawn to the article ir question, but there is no marketing of bonds in connection with the extension of Government credits to the countries mentioned. The Dominion Government makes advances to those countries to enable them to purchase goods in Canada and it takes their bonds, not for sale, but to be held in the Treasury until repaid. No intermediary agency is connected with
the transactions between the Dominion Government and the governments in question except the Canadian Trade Commission established here, and the Canadian Trade Commission established in London. The members of those commissions are appointed, my hon. friend knows, by the Dominion Government. What must be in the mind of the writer is some transaction whereby bonds of the Roumanian Government or other governments would be sold to private investors in the ordinary course. There is no connection whatever between the transaction referred to and the extension by the Dominion Government of credits to the countries in question.

speechtext: I once again direct the attention of the Leader of the Government to the fact that there are five vacancies in the membership of this House. What steps are being taken to fill these vacancies in order that the people of the country may be fully represented?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: VACANT SEATS IN THE HOUSE UNTIL DEMOBILIZATION.
speechtext:
While it is common ground that vacancies in the membership of this House should be filled as rapidly as practicable, it will, I think also be common ground that these vacancies should not be filled until demobilization is completed. There are very many soldiers who have not yet returned from overseas, some of whom might possibly be candidates in the constituencies in question, but undoubtedly all the soldiers now overseas

should have the right to vote in the constituencies in which they are domiciled. It would, therefore, appear to me, as it does to the Government, that there should be no by-elections until demobilization is complete or practically complete. When it is complete, it will be for the Government to consider when the by-elections shall be held. I can assure my hon. friend that I appreciate the desirability of filling vacancies in the House as soon as practicable and so soon as it will be fair to those citizens of Canada who by reason of being overseas, would be debarred from exercising the right of franchise in this country should any elections be now held.
THE 22nd BATTALION-PLACE OF DEMOBILIZATION.
On the Orders of the Day:

subtopic: VACANT SEATS IN THE HOUSE UNTIL DEMOBILIZATION.
speechtext:
May I ask whether the Minister of Militia and Defence has come to a definite decision as to the demobilization centre of the 22nd Battalion?
Major-General MEWBURN (Minister oi Militia):	The Department of Militia and
Defence has not determined the locality in which any overseas unit shall be demobilized; the selection of the demobilization centre always being left entirely to the unit concerned. The first intimation I had from overseas with regard to the demobilization centre of the 22nd Battalion was that it had selected the city of Quebec. On hearing that, the city of Montreal was very much perturbed, and I have no objection to reading a cable which I sent overseas:
You have advised the 22nd Battalion will proceed to Quebec for demobilization. Strong representations being made by Montreal that unit raised and organized there, and has been reinforced largely by men from that district Quebec also submits strong claims. Owing to controversy, please ascertain and cable feelings of officers and of all ranks of this unit as to whether they desire to be dispersed at Montreal or Quebec. Advise number of men of this unit for Quebec and number for Montreal.
On the opening of navigation on the St. Lawrence, at the end of this month, it is hoped troops will thenceforth come to Quebec. Personally, I am anxious to meet the views of both Quebec and Montreal, because I know both cities are desirous of paying proper tribute to this wonderful battalion. It has therefore been suggested, and I am sure the Government will be glad to oo-operate, that if this battalion demobilizes at the city of Quebec it shall, before demobilization, be taken.to the city of Mont-
real, so that the people there may have an opportunity of seeing it; but if any men of the 22nd desire to be dispersed at Quebec I do not think it would be right for us to dictate that they shall go to Montreal, or any other place.

subtopic: VACANT SEATS IN THE HOUSE UNTIL DEMOBILIZATION.

Major-General MEWBURN: I think that would be a happy compromise.
On the Orders of the Day:

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO WHEN THEY WILL BE BROUGHT DOWN.
speechtext: I desire to draw the attention of the Government to a matter of importance to the public and to Parliament. In the speech from the Throne on the 20th of February certain legislation was promised. We have now been in session for over two months, and there has not yet been brought down legislation respecting the Franchise Act, the establishment of soldiers on the land, vocational education, pensions for soldiers and their dependents, nor regarding the housing loan provided by Estimate No. 299. I should like to know when this legislation will be brought down.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO WHEN THEY WILL BE BROUGHT DOWN.
speechtext:
Replying to my hon. friend (Mr. Robb), who was courteous enough to give me notice of his question: the matter of pensions for soldiers and their dependents was at an early date in the session referred to a committee of this House, under the chairmanship of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell). That Committee has been prosecuting its work, and as my hon. friend is aware, it has power to recommend the form the legislation should take.
The Bill which it is hoped the Committee will agree upon will be presented to Parliament in the usual way when the report of the Committee is received.
With regard to the matter of housing, there seems to be a misapprehension concerning this legislation. The provision for housing is given effect to already, and is contained in the Estimates, Item No. 299.
Loan of 12:5,000,000 to Provincial Governments to encourage erection of dwelling houses in congested districts throughout Canada, on the terms and conditions set forth in' the Order in Council of the 3rd of December, 1918

'the amount of loan to any one province not to exceed the proportion of the said $25,000,000 which the population of the said province bears to the total population of Canada, as shown by the last federal census, $25,000,000.
The Government, under the War Measures Act, enacted legislation which the provinces have already acted upon. No further legislation than the item in the Estimates is therefore required in connection with this loan.
With regard to the matter of technical or vocational training, the legislation is under the consideration of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Robertson) who will be represented in respect of it, in this House by the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder).
With regard to the important measure of soldiers' land settlement, the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) has practically completed the Bill, which I am advised will be presented probably next week.
As regards the Franchise Act, its provisions are now under consideration by the Government.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO WHEN THEY WILL BE BROUGHT DOWN.
speechtext: How long will they be under consideration?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO WHEN THEY WILL BE BROUGHT DOWN.
speechtext: I think my hon. friend-

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO WHEN THEY WILL BE BROUGHT DOWN.
speechtext: What we want to know is, how soon may we expeot to get this legislation before the House?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO WHEN THEY WILL BE BROUGHT DOWN.
speechtext: When consideration of this legislation by the Government is complete, it will be brought down like all other legislation. It is impossible for me to say whether it will be brought down next week or the week after, but it will be brought down in due course. I should like to make this observation with regard to what the hon. member (Mr. Robb) suggested as to the session having already extended over two months-during the war the business of the administration was necessarily emphasized to the disadvantage of private members bringing forward and discussing matters of public interest to the various sections of Canada which they represent. The war having come to an end, it seemed proper to the Government .and, I am sure, to the House, that hon. members who had not been able during the war, owing to the pressure of administrative business, to discuss such matters should have opportunity to do so, and the policy of the Government this session has been to allow private members ample time, as we have done, to discuss matters of moment to themselves and their constituents which they might desire to bring forward either by resolution or otherwise.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO WHEN THEY WILL BE BROUGHT DOWN.
speechtext: Speaking only for myself, may I suggest to the leader that as the session has already lasted t.wo months and, if all this legislation is to be brought down, will probably last three months more at least, it might be advisable, as there will be no elections until demobilization is complete, that the Government should postpone its legislation on the Franchise Bill until next session. This, it seems to me, would put a speedy end to the session after proper business had been disposed of.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO WHEN THEY WILL BE BROUGHT DOWN.
speechtext: I do not agree with my hon. friend that three months should be required to pass the Government's legislative programme. I may suggest to him that with the facilitation which I am sure we may expect from His Majesty's loyal Opposition, we should be speedily able to clear up the Order Paper and take on additional legislation which the Government has prepared.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO WHEN THEY WILL BE BROUGHT DOWN.
speechtext: If I may be permitted to speak once more with regard to the question of the franchise legislation. As the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) does not agree with the hon. member for Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux), is it not fair to the country that, the Franchise Act should be brought down at once and referred to a Committee representing both sides of the House in ordeT that it might be threshed out, and so expedite matters?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO WHEN THEY WILL BE BROUGHT DOWN.
speechtext: As I stated, the Franchise Bill when prepared will be brought down and the Government will take such course with regard to it as may be proper, having in view the fair consideration of its terms.

speechtext: May I bring to the attention of the Minister of Railways (Hon. J. D. Reid) a letter I received to-day from the secretary of the Prince Albert Trade and Labour Council, in connection with some difficulties that appear to be outstanding between the National railways and the Government employees, and to ask if the minister has any explanation as .to a possible settlement of the trouble?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext:
I do not know' what the hon.

member refers to. Any difficulties in connection with the employees of the Canadian National railways, as well as other railways, are settled now by a board in Montreal that has been organized by the several railway companies. The hon. member will remember that last year the railway companies and the employees got together and organized what is called the Labour Board, comprising six representatives of the employees and six of the companies, and all difficulties are referred to this board. Since the board was organized they have dealt with very many of these troubles, and in every case the result has been satisfactory. I have no doubt whatever that if there are any troubles now at Prince Albert or any other place they will come up in the usual way before the board and be satisfactorily settled.

I hope the minister received a copy of this letter which I sent him to-day, in which it is stated that the board which the hon. minister mentions decided in favour of the employees but that the Government or management refused to carry out the findings of that board.
I have not yet received the letter.
