Bill No. 38, to amend the Canada Evidence Act.-Hon. Mr. Meighen.
Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Acting Minister of Justice) moved the third reading of Bill No. 69 (from the Senate), to amend the Criminal Code respecting the prevention of fire.

We did all we could yesterday to prevent this Bill from passing through the Committee. We have a very full House to-day and I think there should be an expression of opinion in regard to this Bill. This is a criminal enactment which subjects any man, woman or child, in this country, to two years in the penitentiary if by some possible accident they may be the cause of a fire in their own house or anywhere else. I think this is going entirely too far and that it is infringing upon the necessary liberty of the people. It should not for one moment be stated that we in this House are creating a criminal offence where by no possibility a criminal mind or criminal intent exists. By some slight accident a person might have a defective stovepipe and if, by means of that stovepipe, a fire occurs in his house, it is, I think, a most extraordinary proposition that that person should be subjected to two years in the penitentiary. I therefore move:
That this Bill he not now read the thiid time hut that it he read the third time this day six months.
Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved the second reading of Bill No. 70, to incorporate Canadian National Railway Company and respecting Canadian National Railways.

Before the Bill is read a second time, I think we ought to have some further explanations from the minister. I agree with the object Qf the measure as set forth in the preamble, and if the provisions of the Bill harmonized with the preamble they would be satisfactory. The preamble states that it is expedient to provide for the incorporation of a company under which the railways, works and undertakings of the companies comprised in the Canadian Northern System may be consolidated, and, together with the Canadian Government Railways, operated as a national railway system. I understand from that that the Government wishes the Canadian National Railway System to be operated as much as possible on the same lines as privately owned railways are. That impression I gather from the preamble, as well as from the remarks made by the minister when we were discussing the resolution upon which the Bill is founded. On that occasion the minister said that one of the reasons for introducing this Bill was to bring the Intercolonial under the General Railway Act of Canada, and he further said, as reported at page 1451 of Unrevised Hansard, that that railway will have to be placed under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners. Now, if the idea

is to place the Canadian National Railway System on the same footing as privately owned railways, except where the conditions are such that that cannot be done, L do not think we require two railway laws in this country. The General Railway Act is sufficient to meet all requirements, and the only matters in regard to which its provisions might not apply would be with respect to stock, stockholders, shares, capital, and anything relating to shareholders. Otherwise I do not see any necessity for the various provisions which it is proposed to enact in this Bill, or for removing the National Railway System from the operations of the Railway Act, and for changing other things that are most essential and important to the public. I admit that the Government ought to appoint the directors, and should also have certain other powers of control, but I object to the Government exercising the whole right when that right can be profitably exercised for party or political purposes, and freeing itself from responsibility so far as the burden of finances is concerned, or when risks are to be taken by the company operating the system, and criticism might ensue as a result of any action it might take. The whole tenor of the Bill is such that when anything in the way of exercising patronage or taking over the lines is concerned the power is reserved to the Governor in Council, but in financial matters the burden is left entirely with the company-there is no control by the Governor in Council or by the Canadian Parliament. In certain essential matters Parliament will have no voice whatever; it is to be ignored just as it has been in many other things since the war started, and just as is proposed to be done in that very innocent Bill No. 71 which proposes to extend the life of various Orders in Council passed by the Government. I repeat that the principle enunciated in the preamble is all right, but the various clauses of the Bill are all wrong. In my opinion the Bill should not now be submitted to Committee of the Whole, but should be l-aid over for farther consideration, because I see no reason for the differences and the exceptions that are contemplated under it.
For instance, the Canadian National Railways are empowered to build lines whenever they please with the sanction- of the Governor in Council. I think that is a wrong principle and that the Bill ought to be amended. If the Canadian Northern Railway has a charter to build a line, then the Canadian National Railways might be allowed to construct; but I do not believe

in giving a blanket lease of life to any railway company and its subsidiaries. Why not submit the Canadian National Railway System to the same ordeal as other railway companies? Then another thing, this measure would exempt the Canadian National Railways from the operation of the general Railway Act in expropriation proceedings, and give them the advantages of the Expropriation Act. The Canadian National Railway System ought not to be put under the Expropriation Act; I think that the courts of the various provinces where the other railway companies go in expropriation matters are quite capable of administering justice to the Canadian National Railway System or the Canadian Government. I think, too, that it is an autocratic and highhanded procedure for the minister or his deputy to sign the expropriation plan, file it in the registry office, and thereby have the ownership in the land vested in the Government. As I have said, Mr. Speaker,
I take no exception to Government ownership in this case-it is the best that can be done under the circumstances-but I do not believe in Government ownership any more than I believe in Government operation. If we are- to take the experience of the United States, I think the enthusiasm that has been displayed in this House and in the country for Government ownership and Government operation is likely to be somewhat dampened. The United States have the poulation and the resources to make the experiment; Canada has not the population nor the resources to indulge in the experiment to such an extent as the United States have. From the figures given by the hon. minister to-day we see that for equipment he will require this year $35,000,000, if I understand him rightly, and that the deficit last year on fixed charges was $7,000,000. May I ask the hon. minister if that deficit covers the interest on all the bonds which ' the Canadian Northern Railway System has issued?

The answers that I gave
to-day I thought were very plain. Those answers stated that there were surplus net earnings of some three million dollars odd, but that after payment of all interest and other charges there remained a deficit of $7,000,000.	-

Interest on all bonds
which are outstanding?
Yes, everything.

You have not assumed
the debt of the Canadian Northern, and
still you are paying the interest on that debt, It looks like acquiescence on the part of the Government to pay that debt; but be that as it may it has nothing to do with this. For my part, Mr. Speaker, I do not believe that we can get the right legislation by having this measure put before the committee now and discussed. As I said, we do not want two railway laws in this country. If you are going to incorporate this railway company, let it compete with the other railways with the same advantages and disadvantages that those railways have. I do not see why we should accept the expropriation clauses neither do I see why we should accept the other clauses. Except the matters relating to stockholders, there is nothing w'hatever to prevent the general Railway Act applying, to the Canadian National Railway System, and I would suggest to the hon. minister that this measure [DOT] be referred to some committee where we could hear not only the views of hon. members, but also the views of the men who are to-day operating this system. We will then be in a better position to judge of the necessity of some of the clauses in this Bill.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must point out to hon. members that when the hon. minister exercises his right to reply he closes the debate on the second reading.
Mr. D. D. iMcKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):	I wish to endorse
what has been said by the member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau), particularly on the point that we should have this measure sent to a committee. This is named as a railway company, and in most cases, according to the terms of the Bill, the Railway Act and the railway laws of this country governing railway companies will apply to it. For that reason, Mr. Speaker,I think the hon. minister would be taking the proper course if he would send this Bill in the ordinary way to the Committee of Railways and Canals. Such action would not at all take away the power of the Government over the Bill, and, as the hon. member for Three Rivers has pointed out, it would give us an opportunity of hearing what the management has got to say about it. I do not think I am giving away any secret when I say that to-day I happened to meet the gentleman who is in charge of the Government railways, Mr. Hanna, and I mentioned this Bill to him and what my view was, that is, that it should go to a committee. Mr. Hanna and his lawyer both expressed satisfaction at the idea. Mr. Hanna 'stated it would give him and his staff an oppor-



tunity of coming before the committee and explaining their views as to the necessity of this legislation and the operation of the road generally. As Mr. Hanna and the legal side of the management hold that view, I think the hon. minister should comply with the request and have this Bill go where it can he fully dealt with and then be reported back to the Committee oi the Whole.
Mr. FRANK S. CAHILL (Pontiac): 1 think the minister would do well to accede to the wishes of the leader of the Opposition and have this Bill go before the Railway Committee of the House, where it can be more freely discussed than here, (for the' reason that the supporters of the Government would naturally hesitate to criticise the Bill and then have to vote for it if an amendment is moved in the House or in Committee here; whereas if the Bill were before the Railway Committee they would feel free to discuss it and vote as they saw fit. It is probably the most important legislation that this House will have to deal with for many years, and from my reading of the Bill I think many changes could be	made in it that
would be beneficial to this country. There is, no doubt, considerable opinion in this country in favour of public ownership, but the large majority of those who favour public ownership are not the investing public; that is, they are not people who have invested money in public corporations or public utility undertakings. They seem to be in favour of public ownership merely because, as a general rule, the railway companies were making in the earlier days what they consider to be large profits, and they want to be in on the profits. But few men are at all interested in public ownership from the standpoint of management, from the standpoint which we must take into consideration if we are to make a success of this undertaking. I differ from those who say that this railway undertaking is going to be a loss to us for all time. There is no reason why, in a country of this kind, a railway system of this size cannot be made to pay its own way-unless the people have so little interest in it that they allow it to become a political rather than a business undertaking. If branch lines are built where they should not be built; if terminals are developed at points where they cannot be made profitable; if unnecessary employees are taken on and others dismissed who, though good men, may not be of the right political faith; in 
short, if the system is treated generally as a political machine, as the political adjunct of a party, we are. sure to come to grief. The history of the public ownership of railways the world over shows that railways handled by the Government direct have been a failure in every case. Australia made a failure of direct government management of railways until they put it into the hands of a commission, and even then they did not make of it what railroad men would look upon as a success, because they charge exorbitant rates. In no country has public ownership of railways been made a success until it has been taken as far as possible out of the hands 'of the Government. There is no reason why this undertaking should not be taken out of the hands of the Government and made responsible to Parliament. It is quite feasible, and the results would be very much better than they will be if the railway system is treated as a political machine. Our business here is to try and get this undertaking in the best possible shape for the people. The minister would be well advised to take this Bill before the Railway Committee and let us thrash the matter out and have these clauses adjusted so that they will be more workable and more satisfactory.
One very important point that the minister apparently has not taken into account is profit sharing with employees. A commission is now investigating the possibilities of closer co-operation between capital and labour in Canada. Why should we not consider this matter in connection with the largest Government undertaking that we have? The Government cannot lose anything by it. If the minister and the Government expect the railroads to go on losing money, why not offer an inducement to employees in the way of profit sharing that might be the means of producing a profit instead of a deficit? If the railroads make a profit, of course the Government should be generous enough to give the employees a share of it. It would not cause a loss to the country; it would not cause a loss to the shipper; it would produce greater efficiency and better work from the employees. Thousands of people will be employed on this railroad undertaking; why not establish some basis of co-operation between capital and labour in connection with it? It is in the interests of the minister, of the Government and of the country generally that this Bill be sent to the Railway Committee. The minister promised us certain information the other day; that information came down about thirty-five minutes ago, and now we

are asked to consider this Bill. I think it should be delayed.

It is not usual for a Bill of this kind to be referred to the Railway Committee. When the Canadian Northern Bill was before the House in 1914- it was a very important Bill-it was taken up in Committee of the Whole. In fact, Government Bills are, as a rule, taken up in Committee of the Whole.
This is an unusual Bill.

Since this Bill was
discussed in the House a few days ago I took it up with some of the officials of the railway and of the department, and it is my intention to ask that some of the things against which objection was raised be removed from the Bill. Serious objection was taken to section 20; when we come to that section I intend to ask that it he eliminated. Since the discussion of the Bill took place, representatives of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the only company that would have any serious objection to the Bill, discussed the matter with me and informed me that they could see very little objection to the Bill as a whole, though there might be some objection to three clauses, one of which, I think, was section 20. When we come to these sections in committee I will explain the objections which have been raised, and it will be for the committee to decide whether we amend the clauses or not. This is a very important Bill and every member of the House should have an opportunity to say something with regard to it or to make any suggestions which he may wish to offer. It is hardly fair, therefore, to refer it to a sub-committee of a few members, or to the Railway Committee, and then have it come back here and probably be discussed all over again. When we go into Committee on the Bill hon. members will see that, on the whole, very little objection can be raised to it. The two clauses that the member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) mentioned are those against which the strongest objection has been raised; I intend to ask that one be taken out, and the other we can discuss. Let us proceed with the Bill. If it goes to the Railway Committee we shall either have to discuss the Bill again when it comes back to the House, or have it passed without giving members an opportunity of understanding exactly what the Bill means. I do not think it would be fair to the members of the House to refer the Bill to a subcommittee, and I therefore ask hon. gentlemen to agree to the motion.
May I be allowed one word?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It would be out of order at this stage.

With your permission, Sir, I would say just this: I quite appreciate that the members of the House desire to discuss this Bill, and I have no doubt there is considerable railway talent in the House, but tny object in proposing a committee w'as that we might have the benefit of the advice of the experienced railway men who are practically the operators of the railway. It is only in a committee we can hear these men, and for that reason I insist upon referring the Bill to a committee. I am not suggesting for a moment that I have not confidence in the House.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On the preamble being read:
I wish to say, on the preamble-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman would not be in order in discussing the preamble at this stage. By the rules of the House, the consideration of the preamble must be postponed until after the clauses have been considered.
I thought we were considering the clauses. The preamble should not be read if it is not to be considered now. My mistake followed your error.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Rule 55 says:-
In proceedings in Committee of the Whole House upon Bills, the preamble is first postponed, and then every clause considered by the Committee in its proper course; the preamble and title to be last considered.
On section 1-nomination of directors:
What will be the salary of the directors?

Section 5 provides:-
The directors may be paid by the company such sums for their services as directors as the Governor in Council may from time to time approve;

But we have not reached
section 5 yet. Cannot the minister on this section inform us about how much the directors will get? We know that the Governor in Council may pay any salary at all.
The present directors are getting $2,000 per annum, and as far as I know, that will continue to be the salary.
What duties will the directors be supposed to perform for this remuneration?

At the present time the directors hold a meeting every week or every couple of weeks. The operation of the railway entails a lot of work, and the directors have to attend the meetings and perform the usual duties of directors of a railway company.

I was going to say something about your ruling on the preamble, Sir. but will not just now. Section 1 says that the Governor in Council may nominate such persons as may be deemed expedient. Why not qualify the word "persons" to ensure that persons with railway experience will be appointed? Otherwise, the Governor in Council may appoint ordinary men like us. We have to suppose, of course, that the Governor General will always be advised wisely by Council; but we have seen such strange things lately that our minds are open to all sorts of suspicions, and the members here, representing the people, have had their privileges restricted to such an extent that we ought to take advantage of what remains to protect the people, who will pay for this railroad. A man cannot be assistant commissioner on the Railway Commission, for instance, without so many years' experience at the bar. Why not state the qualifications required, and then the Governor in Council could choose from those possessing those qualifications.
I cannot- agree that we should limit the directors to those having railway experience.

Not all of them, but a
certain number.

It is always understood that there will be a certain number of officials on-the board, but other companies, the Canadian Pacific, for example, have business men on their board. I think it is well to have business men on the board to assist and advise the officials of the road. Of course, a certain proportion of the board of directors should have railway experience. The Governor in Council would never appoint a board of directors composed entirely of men without railway experience. I hardly think it would be well to accept my hon. friend's suggestion.

I would urge upon the Committee the advisability of eliminat-
ing political patron-age from the administration of the- Government Railway System. The credit of the country is' involved in this undertaking to a tremendous extent, and this Government has been elected upon a pledge to abolish completely political patronage. I do not know whether that has been done. As far as the present board is concerned, I know that one of the gentlemen appointed, Mr. Laporte, is a successful wholesale grocer of the city of Montreal. As he is one of the very few friends of the Government in the province of Quebec, he is appointed to all the commissions set up by this Administration. I do not know that he has any special qualifications as a railway expert. Indeed, I believe that hi3 qualification to be a member of all the commissions appointed by the Government lies in the fact that he is a friend and supporter of the Government.
He is a Commissioner-General.

Yes, Commissioner-General for the province of Quebec.
I am -sure that policy will -be continued if, when this Bill is passed, the authority of appointing directors still lies with the Governor in Council, notwithstanding the protestations of the Government that patronage has been abolished. I would suggest that instead of having the five or fteen directors, as the case may be, appointed by the Governor in Council, they be appointed by this Parliament, which, after all, is the supreme authority. Let the majority of them be appointed by the Government and the minority by the Opposition. My hon. friend the Acting Minister of Justice is laughing at the suggestion Well, I knew he would laugh at it because, if it were adopted, it would deprive him and his friends of a fine source of patronage.
It is a Union Government.

Yes, it; is a Union Government, but a queer union.
If the suggestion I put forward were adopted it would be a guarantee to the people that there would be less political influence in the administration of the railways.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I really did not know that my hon. friend intended his suggestion to be taken seriously, or I assure him 1 would not have smiled; but I was appreciating what I thought he himself understood to be a good joke. The suggestion that the Government should appoint the majority

of the directors and the Opposition appoint the others, as a means of abolishing patronage, did appear to me to show a source of humour in the hon. member. His logical mind will, of course, immediately perceive, that so far from abolishing patronage it-would ensure its creation, and that in double measure. It would be simply patronage squared. If the suggestion is seriously made that the Opposition should nominate the minority of the members of this Board, and the Government nominate the majority, and that this should be done in the name of the abolition of patronage, the matter admits of no discussion. I understood the hon. member for Three Rivers to state- clearly and frankly that the proper method of appointment was by the Governor in Council, and that is the method now employed in the appointment of commissions certainly of equal responsibility. It is	indeed the	only	method thathas been found practicable at all in	this or in	any	other country.
Can the hon. member suggest any commission that is appointed in any country by vote of Parliament? The Government, of course, is responsible to Parliament, but no one can point to a case where Parliament was divided into two parts, each part in its turn selecting its due proportion of the members of a commission. The bench of the country is appointed by the Governor in Council and for each appointment the Governor in Council is responsible to Parliament. This is the basic central and integral principle of our Constitution, and there is no reason for departing from it here, and for the life of me I cannot picture the consequences that might ensue from such a departure.
.Mr. DEVLIN:	The position taken by
my hon. friend from Kamouraska appeals to me as a very sensible one. He asks that the majority of the directors be appointed by the Government and the minority by the Opposition. We in this House occupy, I suppose, a position different from that in any other Parliament in the civilized world. We have one side of the House divided into two camps-the Liberal camp and the Tory camp. .
Camp followers.

Camp followers. My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior must not forget that the shareholders of this new company will be the people of Canada, not one section of the people, but all sections. We on this side of the House, as the hon. minister must observe, perhaps with regret, are a goodly number and withal a
healthy number representing practically half of the shareholders of this company.
It is true that hon. gentlemen opposite have a majority of seven. With all their forces gathered they went up to eighteen to-day, and that is about the smallest normal majority that a Government has ever had in this country. They do not, therefore, represent very many more of the people of Canada than we do on this side of the House, and the hon. member for Kamouraska asks that the people represented by the Opposition should have some say in the nominataion of the directors who are to represent them. I heartily approve of the suggestion of my hon. friend and trust that the Minister of Railways will take it into earnest consideration and act upon it.

I think that if the Minister of the Interior really regards this suggestion as a joke, he easts a slur upon the Prime Minister. He will remember that in this House when conscription came up and it was the desire to eliminate patronage and favouritism, the Prime Minister asked the then leader of the Opposition to suggest a number of names of gentlemen who might act as judges. Was it not Parliament that did that? The Government chose their men and then the leader of the Opposition suggested names.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They were nominated in Committee.

The same thing should be done here if it is the intention to eliminate politics. My hon. friend refers to the appointment of judges. You cannot remove a judge unless he is impeached. Under this Act it is provided: "The directors shall hold office from year to year unless removed by the Governor in Council for cause." The chairman of the Railways Commission, if he were a judge of the Superior Court could not be removed by the Governor in Council even for cause; the matter must be brought before Parliament. The chairman of the Railway Commission cannot be as politically useful to this or any Government as the Board of Railway Directors who will manage these railways. We know very well what it means, for we have seen it in operation on the Intercolonial, and I think there is nothing to be laughed at in the suggestion. If the Government desire the people to believe that the Canadian National Railways are operated for the advantage of the country, honestly and free from political influence, I think the suggestion of the hon. member

for Kamouraska should be taken up by the Minister of Railways, and if fifteen directors are to be appointed the Opposition should have the right to nominate five, and the Government ten, and if you are going do appoint five the Opposition could appoint the minority. The proposition is a [DOT]fair and democratic one, although it may be hard for my hon. friend to appreciate it, as he has been accustomed to run the show his own way, coming to Parliament and saying, "Swallow this," as he did to-day and yesterday. He had a little innocent Bill of five lines. We were asked to swallow a whole sheaf of Orders in Council. I do not intend to swallow them in that way. There may be some of them that I might have to spit out before I got them down. I submit that this suggestion of my hon. friend from Kamouraska ought to be adopted and that this proposed provision should be inserted in clause one. All the appointments I have seen have been made through the Governor in Council so far, but these appointments have been safeguarded. The case of judges was cited by the Acting Minister of Justice, but the judges are safeguarded by the fact that the Governor in Council, once they are appointed, cannot put them out. The chairman of the Railway Commission is in the same position; the Governor in Council cannot touch him. You have to come before the House and practically impeach him the same as you would have to do in the case of a judge. But in this case it is entirely different. Patronage is going to be exercised and these appointees are going to control the business of a railway line extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific and involving the expenditure of millions of dollars. As has been said by my hon. friend from Kamouraska, we in Quebec have reason to ask for this amendment, because Sir Hormidas Laporte has been a universal commissioner both under the Tory and the Union Governments. It is the same thing so far. I would suggest that the clause be amended so as to read:
The Governor in Council may nominate such persons as may be deemed expedient, not less than five, nor more than fifteen, to be directors of the company hereby incorporated, upon the suggestion of the House of Commons, the minority being nominated by the minority in the House.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I want to assure the hon. member (Mr. Bureau) that I have no intention of asking the House to swallow anything. Certainly I never need ask the hon. member for Three Rivers, because he 
has shown a wonderful capacity for swallowing himself. It is only about fifteen minutes since he told this Committee that these people should be appointed by the Governor in Council.
I have seen better since.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He has seen better since. So that I never could ask the hon. gentleman to swallow anything; he is capable of doing that himself.
Anything that is reasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext:
The
railway commissioners are not operating railways. They have no occasion to exercise patronage.
They may favour one company or another but they cannot exercise patronage.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They favour one company and they favour individuals; they are one of the most powerful commissions that the country ever had. They have an authority that is vast and could be exer

cised, if one could conceive of it being so exercised, from the patronage standpoint, which is altogether inconceivable. I think the apprehensions of hon. gentlemen opposite are not justified and really I do not think they are serious in suggesting that the officials, who must be responsible to the country for the actual operation of a great business enterprise, should be appointed not by the authority that itself is responsible to the people's representatives, but by a division of the forces in Parliament.

Was there not a recommendation in the Drayton-Aeworth report that the directors should be appointed in same other way than by the Government? The minister speaks of the Governor in Council. The Governor in Council would nominate ultimately the directors suggested by the Opposition party, but they would be more apt to have a more uniform set. of directors if they were nominated in that way than if they were nominated by the Government alone. Before we vote on this question I would like to ask the minister what were the oauses that led to the conclusion that those who are now members of this board should be appointed as directors. On what ground did he arrive at the decision that these were the proper men?

Mr. Hanna and Mr. Mitchell were officials of the company. Mr. Hanna was president and Mr. Mitchell was vice-president and financial controller. They are two of the leading officials of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. On account of their positions in the company they were appointed to the board. Then Mr. Woods, another director, had been on the board for ten or twelve years. He is a prominent citizen of Toronto and by reason of his experience in connection with the work of the road we considered that he would be a very valuable man to have on that board.	.
Mr. Hobson is a very prominent man in Hamilton and a man in whom, I think, the people pf Canada have confidence. ^ His father was chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Railway for very many years, and I understand that the son worked for seventeen or eighteen years as assistant engineer under his father on the same railway. I considered that Mr. Hobson would be a valuable member of the Board. Taking the province of Quebec, Mr. Jones is a man of prominence, who has had a good business experience, and he also is one in whom everybody has great confidence. Mr. Jones, I think, was for a time general manager of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, Nova Scotia, and knows the country well. The company, I understand, owns and operates a railway, and doubtless Mr. Jones has acquired some experience in that regard. At all events he is a leading business man, and one in whom I felt the people would have confidence il he were made a member of the Board. Mr. Laporte has been in business in the city oi Montreal as a wholesale grocer, but is likewise connected with numerous public institutions. I think he is president of one of the banks there, is more or less identified with various industries, and is held in high esteem. I think his appointment was well received in the province of Quebec. As to Mr. Barnhill, I believe he was a barrister in St. John. He is a very prominent citizen in New Brunswick, and is connected with large business interests in that province. From the reports that I received when we were making these appointments, I think that no better selection could be made from that province. Mr. Cantlie is from Nova Scotia, and is identified with various large industries there. He was selected on account of his standing in Nova Scotia and his connection with the industrial life of the province. Turning to the West, we have Mr. Riley, of Winnipeg. He is a citizen of undoubted standing and connected with large institutions in Manitoba. Mr. Hamilton is a foremost citizen of Saskatchewan and has been associated with Farmers Institutes in Western Canada. I felt that we should have on the Board a representa-

tive of farmers in Western Canada, and that was the reason for appointing Mr. Hamilton. In choosing these directors our main object was to secure prominent and reliable men in whom the public would place every confidence. Any person who is not familiar with these gentlemen will, by making inquiry, satisfy himself that better appointments could not have been made, bearing in mind business ability and reputation for honesty. Political patronage did not enter into these appointments for the reason that the gentlemen selected have not been prominent in politics in the past as far as I am aware. They have not had any political affiliations at all, to my knowledge, and were appointed solely on their merits.
Mr- CAHILL: The minister has said that politics was not taken into consideration in making these appointments. Would he be good enough to say how many of the men whom he has mentioned as directors cf the Canadian Northern railway voted for the Liberal party at the last election?
Mr. .1. I). RFID: I did not inquire personally of these gentlemen but I believe that a great many of them have been Liberal in their political views in the past. They may not have voted' for the Liberal party at the last, election-I cannot say whether they did or not-but there is no doubt that they have been known and recognized as prominent Liberals in the past.
Ex-Liberals.

I am somewhat surprised to hear the minister, particularly after his declaration last evening in favour of the returned soldiers, name a whole board of directors, not one of whom comes within that category. The minister should know, as every person in the House knows, that our Canadian railway troops accomplished miracles in France, and showed the Old Country how to build and operate railroads.
It seems to me that this is peculiarly a sphere wherein the work of the returned soldier, who surpassed himself in building and operating railroads in France, should be utilized for the good of the country. We have been told that efforts are being made to give returned soldiers positions everywhere, but the very moment an important position is available, a position which the returned soldier could fill with undoubted success owing to his special qualifications, be is passed over, and we get instead the hacks of the Canadian Northern railway.
1 am opposed to this clause for another rea-
son. The Government nominates a certain number of directors and naturally and inevitably the men so nominated will favour it. They are removable for cause but I never knew a Government, be it Liberal or Conservative, who could not get rid of a public servant when it wished to do so; and I imagine that whoever is appointed a director on this Board will feel it incumbent upon him, if he wishes to keep his position, to satisfy the demands of the ministers and the members who support the Government. We will therefore have, as we have had in the past, on both sides of politics, a carnival of political patronage and corruption such as has been witnessed on the Intercolonial railway for the past fifty years, and to such an extent that we will be unable ever to see our way clear out of the railway mess into which the country has got. I cannot in conscience give my support to a measure which will place eight or nine thousand, and perhaps more, miles of railroad under the control of men who are responsible to nobody but the Government.

I suppose the appointments under discussion are only of a temporary character, and are not necessarily confirmed by this Bill. Should the measure be adopted by Parliament it will be necessary, I presume, to make new appointments under its provisions. Whether the board be composed of the same members or not is another question. With all that the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) and the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) have said as to the desirability of having this board so organized as to put it beyond the question of political patronage, and of having it so organized as to represent all the interests of the country, and that the Government must be held responsible for making appointments of that character, I very heartily agree.
I must say, however, that I cannot agree with my hon. friend from Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) in the suggestion that Parliament should make the appointments. WTe have no precedent for that. In our system of Government it has always been deemed necessary to mark the distinction between the executive and the legislative powers. I think I am right in saying that, with the exception of the hon. Speaker and the Deputy Speaker, it is not a part of our system that the House of Commons shall directly appoint anybody; all appointments must properly be made, and should t>e made (with the single exceptions I have mentioned) by the Governor in Coun-

cil. To that extent I think the hon. member for Kamouraska if he presses his amendment-I hope he will not-will be laying down a principle which will be most embarrassing not only in this case but in all cases hereafter. I entirely agree with him that in the making of appointments to this board due regard should be had to see that it represents all classes and all interests in the country.
This is a tremendous experiment upon which Canada is entering. It is a big thing even as it stands to-day, but it is going to be much bigger apparently before this session ends. I would strongly urge my hon. friend from Kamouraska not to press his amendment. I think that all that has been said by him with regard to the appointment of the board, and the views of my hon. friend from Quebec (Mr. Power) with respect to the appointment of returned soldiers from the Railway Engineering Corps, should engage the serious attention of the Government. But I do not think we should be asked to declare that this House shall exercise executive powers.

The hon. member is quite right, the present directors were only appointed pending the passing of this Bill, when the whole matter will have to he again considered. The suggestion as to returned soldiers and the other suggestions that have been made will have to be dealt with. There is no doubt that the Government will have to give its most serious consideration to the matter with the view to having the very best men appointed to the board of directors. We want to make this railway system a success, and it cannot be a success unless it is operated free from political or any other interference. If we take in the Grand Trunk we will have nearly a billion dollars railway investment, and the Government will be responsible for its proper management. It must be remembered that the Government really will have put in these railways only $10,000,000, the amount which we have so far in the capital of the Canadian Northern Railway. It is true that the Government will have to look after the bonds outstanding, and see that every care is taken in the protection of the investments, although it did not itself borrow the money.
So far as I am personally concerned, while in the past I was not in favour of public ownership, let me say that I have the greatest confidence in the railway system that the Government now owns. I do not think after all that the results of last yeaT were so very bad in regard to the Canadian
Northern Railway. The net earnings were . about $3,500,000, and the loss, after paying fixed charges, was some $7,000,000 odd. It is true that a large amount of money had to be expended in rolling stock, that-money being borrowed on equipment bonds, as was done in the past; but we all know that the Canadian Northern had very little rolling stock when it was taken over. I am satisfied that if we all join in excluding patronage or any other interference with the board of directors our railways will be a success. So far as I am concerned as minister, I think that the board of directors would not hesitate to say that I have done everything possible to prevent any interference with them since the Government took these railways over.

Might I ask the hon. minister if it is proposed to appoint a director from British Columbia? I have not heard him mention British Columbia, but, as he knows, the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific have large interests in that province and considerable mileage, and there is a very strong feeling that there should be a director from that province. Of course, I know that perhaps here in the East it is not considered necessary to regard the views of British Columbia on all occasions; but really in connection with these railroad matters we feel it is very necessary that a man from British Columbia should be on the directorate. There should be no trouble in getting a returned soldier there, one who is fully qualified in all respects to act as a director.
I hope the minister is considering such an appointment.

That question will have to be taken up when we are settling the new Board of Directors. Every province is asking for a man to be appointed from within its boundaries. Other suggestions have been made to me in connection with the operation of these railways which might also be taken into consideration. One gentleman suggested that we appoint a board of about seven or eight men, such board to comprise at least four of the most prominent officials of the road. And remember, the officials that we put in these positions must be the very best men that we can appoint. Then he suggested that we also appoint a prominent labour man and about two prominent outside men who would give their whole time and attention to the operation of this road, reporting, of course, to the Government from time to time. Other suggestions have been made, such as the appointment of a returned sol-

dier, or the appointment of a man from British Columbia or some other province. If this were my own property I would turn it over to seven or eight of the very best men I could get in Canada at good salaries, and I would not care whether they all came from British Columbia, Quebec or any other province, so long as they were the very best men, men with extensive railway experience and enjoying the confidence of the people of Canada. Unless we start out with the very best men in charge of this system, with a free hand to operate it as the Canadian Pacific railway is operated, I do not believe we can make it a success.
Hear, hear.

And I have the fullest confidence that the members of this House and the people of this country will give the directors to be appointed an opportunity to show what they can do with this railway system. If they are given that opportunity and that policy is carried out, I am confident that good results will follow the operation of the railway. Canada will have one of the best assets it has ever had; the people, in the East as well as in the West, will get a better service than they have ever had, and more people will be induced to come into the country. When this Bill passes and the Government comes to appoint a Board of Directors, we will consider the suggestions made by British Columbia and the other provinces. The Government, of course, must assume the responsibility of deciding what is the best way of managing this railway. If the Grand Trunk is taken in we shall have twenty or twenty-five thousand miles of railway to operate, and I repeat that we cannot take chances on any man or any board of directors by restricting ourselves to taking them from any particular provinces. Let us get the very best men we can find in Canada. The employees whom I have learned to know on the Canadian Government railways, including the Canadian Northern, are as good a lot of men as can be found on any railway in the world. Give them a chance, and you will see what the result will be.
When does the minister expect to get the Grand Trunk?
I cannot answer that.
Has the minister any idea when he is going to get the Grand Trunk?
No.
Does the minister know anything about the acquisition of the Grand Trunk?

The hon. member knows exactly what the position is. The Acting Prime Minister said a few days ago that negotiations were going on in connection with the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Those negotiations cannot be completed in a day or in a few days. They are proceeding, and as soon as any information is available that should be given to the House, it will be given.
Has any progress been made in the-negotiations?
Progress is always being made.

I am sure that the country will be gratified to hear the minister say that although at the outset he was prejudiced against public ownership, the limited experience that he has had has satisfied him that public ownership of this great system or galaxy of systems that the country has acquired can be made a success. That statement is particularly gratifying, coining from the source that it does. It is also gratifying to hear the minister's reply to our friend from British Columbia (Mr. McQuarrie). It would be a mistake to restrict the selection of members of the, board to particular sections of the country. While there is no objection to various sections of the Dominion being represented on the board, no course that I can think of would be so disastrous as that of subordinating the selection of the best men that can be obtained in the country to selection from particular sections of the Dominion. If Kamouraska had the men who were required to run this system of publicly-owned railways then the men should be taken exclusively from Kamouraska. It is gratifying to know that the minister's view is so clear in that regard. I was struck with an interview given by Lord Shaughnessy in which he sneers at public ownership and tries to discredit it in advance. I hope that the views of the more or less noble lord will have no influence on the action of this House or on the opinion of the people with regard to public ownership. I should like to tell the noble lord that this country contributed to the Canadian Pacific Railway enough in cash, in exemption from taxation, and in other things more than double the cost of the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway and of its equipment. It does not reflect very highly on ' the more or less noble lord that he should sneer at public ownership and use his influence to destroy the idea in advance. Through no fault of its own, through no action of its own, this country must adopt

public ownership of railways. What is the alternative? After this country has paid such enormous sums, such colossal sums, such appalling sums, for the construction of these various railroads, are we to continue pouring hundreds of millions into the maw of the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk Pacific, or even the old Grand Trunk? Surely the time has come when-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. When the hon. gentleman referred to the interview in question I thought it was merely by way' of illustration. He is now discussing the merits and demerits of public ownership, which certainly is not in accordance with the rule that speeches in Committee of the Whole must be strictly relevant to clause under consideration.
What is the clause, Mr. Chairman?

The nomination of
directors for the new Canadian National Railway Company.

I am one of those
members who always bows to the ruling of the Chair, but in a manner my discussion was relevant, because if we were to follow Lord Shaughnessy's suggestions we would not have any

speechtext: Order. The hon. gentleman's discussion would have been in order when the principle of the Bill was being considered on the second reading, biit certainly is not in order when the discussion is confined absolutely to the clause now under consideration.
I bow to your ruling, Mr. Chairman. I had practically finished the remarks I proposed to address to the Committee, anyway. I have nothing further to say.
Call him " Air. Shaugh-nessy," not " the noble lord."
