speechtext: Order.	.

I suppose my hon. friend wishes me to adopt the language that he would adopt if he were speaking. I am quite willing to follow his suggestion; if he thinks it ought to be " Air. Shaughnessy," I have no objection.

The member for Shelburne and Queen's (Air. Fielding) says that this amendment is a departure from the old rule. I think that what we are doing to-day is a departure from the rule that has been followed up to now. Formerly we had one Government-owned railway, the Intercom
lonial, which was run by the Minister of Railways; to-day we have a number of railways, which are going to be run by a company on the same principle as that on which a privately-owned railway is run. The hon. member' (Mr. Fielding) says that Parliament is assuming executive powers.
I do not agree. We are delegating the executive power to the company, and control over that executive may be retained by the Governor in Council. I say that we are the proxies of the shareholders, and the directors should be appointed by the shareholders.
Then they would have to be appointed by the people direct.

We are the proxies of
the people. We have their mandate to represent their interests here, whether it is to appoint a board of directors or do anything else. This is not a question of legislation. It was not a question of legislation when the Prime Alinister asked my leader in 1917 to help choose a joint committee to appoint the judges in connection with the exemption tribunals. The object then was to remove from the mind of the people the idea that any political patronage would be exercised by the people nominated. I say that we are the natural and the actual proxies of the people, and we should have our say in the appointment of the directors. I quite agree that there are details of administration which should be under the control of the Governor in Council, and for which he should be responsible. Aly hon. friend the Acting Minister of Justice has said that I have swallowed1 miyself. I am ready to swallow myself a thousand times when I see a member of this House make a better suggestion than my own. I am willing to judge myself when I have rendered a Bad judgment. I am not proposing this amendment for effect; I do not want my hon. friend to measure me by his own yard-stick. I am proposing it because I believe it is for the good of the country, and my hon. friend's sneers and irony will not prevent me from stating in this House what I think is right and taking the position which I think is right. I think in this case the hon. member for Kamouraska was right in principle. I beg leave to withdraw my amendment, to give my hon. friend from Brome an opportunity to present another which is better worded.
Mr. AIcMASTER: I beg to suggest an amendment along the lines proposed by the hon. member for Three Rivers. The situation that confronts this country is this:

whether we like it or not, we are entering upon public ownership on a large scale, and many of us are entering upon it with a certain amount of fear. But we wish to see the experiment succeed, because if it does not succeed the situation which will confront the country will be very serious indeed. One of the conditions which will operate for the success of public ownership will be to remove the administration of the railways from any possibility of political or party control. How can we do that? The Government in this Bill proposes to name a Board of Directors, not less than five, nor more than fifteen. The suggestion is made that the board should be named, not by the Government, which after all represents only one party in this House,-the Unionist party,-but by Parliament, the representatives of the people. I have worked out a scheme which I commend to the sympathetic consideration of the House. I would amend section 1 to read as follows:
The Governor in Council may nominate such persons as may be deemed expedient, not less than five, nor more than fifteen, to be directors of t)he company hereby incorporated, from a list of not more than fifteen to be furnished by the House of Commons, said list to be composed as follows: Sixty per cent thereof by nomination of those members supporting the Government, and forty per cent by nomination of those members composing His Majesty's loyal Opposition, and upon such nomination being made the persons so nominated, and their successors, and such other persons as may from time to time be nominated in accordance with the above mentioned plan muitatis mutandis by the Governor in Council as directors shall be and are hereby incorporated as a company, under the name of 'Canadian National Railway Company,' hereinafter called the Company.
This is an attempt to have the Government furnished with a list of the full complement of directors for this company, sixty per cent being named by the supporters of the Government, and forty per cent by those who oppose the Government; and from that list the directors shall be chosen. If it is decided that only ten directors are required, the Government would name six and the Opposition four. It may be said that there is no precedent for this. I quite admit that, but we are launching on an absolutely new plan, and I think I am right when I state that the plan adopted by the Government of forming a quasiindependent company to operate the Government railways is a plan which has not been tried in any country in the world. The Government, however, has thought that it is the best plan. Let us endeavour to

start right by eliminating all possibility of , party patronage. We have no precedent to guide us; we are breaking new ground; let us break that new ground right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This amendment is no
different in principle from that moved by the hon. member for Three Rivers. It is more vicious in introducing the principle of patronage, because it introduces forty per cent of it whereas the other motion introduced only thirty-three per cent, or five out of fifteen. We have had an illustration here this afternoon of the practical inability to get along when you have factions in a House; and the same thing applies to a board of directors. The Government of the day Is responsible to this House; this House meets annually, and it is within the jurisdiction of this House to haul over the coals annually the Government of the day and the directors of this road. So I do not see why we need trouble so much about the question of patronage.
An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I agree, and it is for that very reason I say we should not adopt this principle, because it would open the door to patronage much more widely than if the appointments were left to the Government of the day, which would be responsible for the acts of all these directors. The Government of the day could not be responsible for the appointees of the Opposition on the board of directors. The Government is not responsible to-day for the acts of the Opposition in this House-I am speaking in a friendly and logical way. There is a vital principle here at stake-the principle of responsibility to the people. Now if this Government is going to make ducks and drakes of this road, they may do it for a year, hut I take it that the people of this country and this Parliament are sufficiently independent to see that no Government shall hold office for more than twelve months that makes ducks and drakes of the millions of dollars worth of capital invested in this system. Section 2 specifically provides that the directors shall hold office ' from year to year '. I do not like that expression. I prefer ' from one annual meeting to the next '. Therefore, any complaints against the board of directors can be threshed out annually in Parliament.

There is one respect in which the amendment of the hon. member for Brome is important. We are living in times when, I suppose, we must establish

new precedents, but my hon. friend is introducing in the form of statute law something that is not to be found in the law of Canada, and I doubt if it can be found in the statute law of any British country in the world. The hon. member seeks to introduce into our statute law the recognition of political parties. It is a curious fact that while our British system of Government is derived from parties, and party is its very essence, there is no formal recognition of parties.
Is it not true that the leader of the Opposition receives a salary?

It is, that is the exception, and I think the precedent has been followed recently in the Legislature of Ontario. In the United States parties are often recognized. There Acts of Congress provide that certain commissions shall be composed of so many Democrats and so many Republicans. Under our system of government, however, we have never so recognized that principle. It is, as I say, an interesting and curious fact that while we have party government and party is the essence of the system, nevertheless our statute law has never recognized party at all, except in the one case referred to.
What about the War-Time Elections Act?

I am not as familial with all that Act as I should be. To what does the hon. member particularly refer?
Mr. PO^ER: I refer to the fact that the leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister named the candidates that received their approval, and also the fact that the ballot was printed, " Vote for Government," or " Vote for Opposition." If that is not recognizing parties I d,o not know what is.

The War-Time Elections Act is about the last Act that I would be willing to accept as my guide. But I think it is a grave and serious thing for us to introduce into our general legislation this principle of recognizing parties.
What my hon. friend says as to the desirability of having both sides represented and abolishing patronage is all right. Of course the idea of taking these railways entirely out of politics is a dream and a delusion. You will never take any service completely out of politics so long as a dollar of the people's money goes into it. We may as well make up our minds to that. But an effort is being made, we are told, to conduct this enterprise without reference to politics and I should like to be helpful in that direction. I sympathize with the object of my hon. friend from Brome, but I think he is introducing a very inconvenient principle which would embarrass us hereafter.

The hon. member for Port Arthur and Kenora referred to the fact of the Government being responsible to Parliament. He will probably remember that a few days ago there was a question on the Order Paper inquiring of the Minister of Railways whether the Canadian Northern were buying their ties from the Northern Construction Company, at what price, and so on, and the Minister of Railways answered that it was not in the public interest to give the information. Will the hon. member support a government that makes an answer of that kind, or is he sincere when he says that hon. members are independent? I can see no independence on that side of the House. I think this Bill should be taken before the Railway Committee in order that we might have a clear non-partisan discussion of this question. The minister insisted that it should be kept here, and the moment an amendment was moved, hon. members began to come into the House. I think I am quite safe in the prediction that when this amendment is voted on you will find most members on this side of the House-possibly not all because we sometimes vote independently- will support it but all members on "the other side will vote against it. That is practically assured. Now, if at this session, when the people are vitally interested in public ownership of railways, questions put on the Order Paper are to be answered by the statement that it is not in the public' interest to give the information asked for, what can we expect from the supporters of the Government in this matter? The Acting Prime Minister in 1917 stated, as will be seen in Hansard, that this road should be taken out of politics entirely, and its management made responsible only to Parliament. The Prime Minister himself made absolutely the same statement last year when he said that the administration should be taken out of politics and be answerable only to Parliament. The Drayton-Acworth Commission in their report recommended that it should be taken out of politics and now we have a iBill before us with absolutely no explanation of where the Government have received the information that has led them to change their minds from the view clearly expressed by the leader of the Gov-

eminent and by the Acting Prime Minister. If on this important subject of the Directorate, their appointment, and their recall, and the management, there is no greater interest among the members to your right than has been shown here to-day, the outlook will be serious. Will the Acting Prime Minister explain on what authority he now bases his change of view in regard to the appointment of directors, and on what authority does the Government change the view expressed by the Prime (Minister when he said that this matter should be taken out of the hands of the Government and be made accountable only to Parliament. I think the answer to that question would be of value to the committee and to the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are two
ways in which the Government Railways of Canada could be administered. In the first place, they could be administered, as the Intercolonial was administered, by direct action of the Department of Railways under the immediate authority and control of the Minister of Railways. That would mean that in the case of the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the Intercolonial, which for administration purposes is now connected with it, the Government of the day would immediately control the administration and operations of the entire sys-*tem of railways. Now we are getting away from that. The Government of the day will appoint the directors of the Canadian National Railway system. Those men will have as their duty the administration of that system and will not be subject to immediate interference on the part of the Government. 'We appointed .some time ago a Board of Directors of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and so far as 1 know, these men have had an absolutely free hand, subject only to this, that with regard to expenditures the Government must be consulted.
I am exceedingly desirous, as I am sure the Government is, that this system should be administered absolutely in the public interest without interference on the part of governments having regard to political considerations. I do not know of any way in which it can be done consistently with the principle of responsible government other than that suggested here, namely, that the Government should appoint those who are to administer the system, these men to have a free hand in the administration.
If they are the right kind of men-and I submit that the appointments which have been made have been creditable to the

Government-they7 will not brook any interference on the part of the Government. The greatest safeguard that could be had against political interference should be in the character and standing of the men appointed to the board. My own view is that public ownership will be a success in Canada in almost direct proportion to the character, integrity, responsibility and ability of those who control and direct the operations of the Government system. The greatest service that the Government can render in reference to transportation in so far as it is under Government administration, is in the appointment of first-class men of the highest standing in the community, men of such self respect that they will feel that they will be judged so much by the success of their administration ol the system that they will not brook any interference on the part of the Government.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding), we are working under the British constitutional practice in this country. I cannot conceive of a division of responsibility between Government and Opposition. Even if we agreed to a division of responsibility between Government and Opposition, it is the Government who would be responsible both in Parliament and before the country. The Government cannot under any system free itself of its responsibility for the administration of the Canadian National Railway System by permitting the Opposition to name forty per cent of the board. If we did that and $here was friction, let us say on the board, who would be held responsible? Who are the Opposition in this House? You might have three parties in the House. As pointed out by the hon. member for Shelburne arid Queens there is no such thing as a recognized Opposition under our constitutional system.
There is under the statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, it is for a particular purpose only; it must be general. The War-time Elections Act was mentioned. But look at the situation; there were hundreds of thousands of soldiers overseas whose votes had to be taken.
That is not the case I refer to. I refer to the statute that provides for a payment of $7,000 to the recognized leader of the Opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is particular legislation from which general conclusions should not be drawn. I think it is incontrovertible that under our constitutional system every Government must assume re-

sponsibility and it cannot devolve it upon the Opposition. It must be responsible for the administration of the National Railway system. The Government will be held responsible by this Parliament. It is absolutely unsound, in my judgment, to get' away from that principle.
I think 1 have met all the arguments put forward by my hon. friend who preceded me. As I said, the Government desires, as far as possible, that this system shall be administered absolutely without regard to politics. An earnest of the 'Government's intention in that regard may be found in the character of the men who, from time to time, have been appointed to the board. Public ownership will be a success only as a result of the human agencies which are employed in its administration. You may have the best machinery in the world, but it is from the men who administer that machinery that the results are to be got. It seems to me that my hon. friend, who is thoroughly familiar with constitutional practice, might very well consider whether he is wise in pressing a resolution which is in violation, as I understand them, of the constitutional principles upon which the Government is conducted under the British system.
At six o'clock the Committee took recess.
After Recess.
The Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

I was rather surprised to find gentlemen with such good sense as the member for Brome (Mr. Me-Master) and the member for Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) take the position which is represented in the amendment before the Committee. They, and those who think with them, must see, because they are gentlemen of experience, how impossible the proposition is that the Oposition should be allowed to nominate forty per cent of the membership of the Board of Directors. Let me point out the practice that is followed in the case of the election of directors of joint stock companies. When there is an election of directors of a joint stock company, there may be different factions, but a slate is selected, and those composing the slate that wins are the directors who administer the affairs of the company for the ensuing year. Now if the plan suggested in the amendment proposed here were adopted it would defeat, I fancy, the very object that its supporters have in view. You would introduce factionalism into the board, you would immediately have a
division, you would doubtless have in addition to the gentlemen representing the majority of the board a leader of an opposition as well, and there would be in my judgment no possibility of arriving at amicable decisions-you would have two factions on the board and you would have complications in the administration of its affairs. The members of the board nominated by the Opposition would feel themselves under a special obligation to those who nominated them and would be sure to run with their whisperings and promptings to the leaders in the House. Under circumstances of that kind you could not have governmental responsibility at all. It seems to me that the position which the Acting Prime Minister took in the House this afternoon is the only tenable one. After all, the Government must be responsible for the administration of the affairs of this railway system. We all recall the position of the leader of the Opposition taken a few days ago on the subject of Daylight Saving, when he twitted the Government with abandoning its responsibility. The position then taken by him was that the Government should have accepted the responsibility in regard to Daylight Saving and should have come before the House with a proposition. Because the matter was thrown open for the judgment of the House the Government was criticised, and you would find identically the same thing occur in the case under consideration only in a much more aggravated form. I was particularly struck with the logical position taken by the member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) a man of large political and business experience who enjoys the respect of the great majority of the people of this country. That hon. gentleman pointed out with great force how absurd and unworkable is the proposal of the hon. member for Kamouraska and the hon. member for Brome. It is perfects ly true that the Opposition in a British Parliament is not recognized constitutionally, although a precedent has been established by paying the leader of the Opposition a salary. Far be it from me to minimize the valuable services that an Opposition leader renders to a country. I am prepared to admit that the present leader of the Opposition in this House is a man of very great ability and performs services that are very valuable to Canada, but I do not believe that the precedent laid down of recognizing an Opposition in the way it has been recognized is after all a good one.

The hon. member for Pontiac Mr. Caiiill) spoke of the creation of a new precedent, and claimed that the Government was evading responsibility. The Drayton-Acworth Report, as I remember it, suggested this very thing-the creation of a company to carry on the affairs of a national system of railways.

Would the hon. member
be kind enough to read just what the Dray-ton-Acworth Report says on that subject?
I have not a copy of the report before me.
I will give the hon. gentleman a copy.

The hon. gentleman can read what he wishes after I have concluded my remarks. I am speaking subject to correction, and I do not wish to put the hon. gentleman in a position which he does not wish to occupy, but my recollection of the report is that the commissioners suggest the creation of a company to carry on the affairs of the nationally-owned railways. It seems to me that that is the only proper and feasible plan under which this great enterprise can be conducted. As the Acting Prime Minister said, you have either to adopt that plan of continue the old system of managing these roads under the Department of Railways which has not proven an entire success in the past. I take it that it is in order to get away from the old system that the present proposal of the 'Government has been submitted to the House. As the Acting Prime Minister stated, the matter is one that public opinion will regulate. We have some little idea of the class of men that the Governor in Council in its present mood would appoint as directors of the company. If you take the calibre of the men who were appointed as directors of the Canadian Northern Railway after that road passed into the hands of the country, you will find that it would be very difficult to improve upon the personnel of the Board, because some men of the highest character and integrity have been appointed. I like the argument advanced by the . Acting Prime Minister:-that there is so much at stake in this great issue, so vast and far-reaching will be the interests of the nationally owned railways, that the whole country would be in jeopardy if this railroad system were not well managed. The Acting Prime Minister pointed out further, and I think pointed out with great force, that public opinion would regulate the appointments. After these appointments were made, under the system

proposed in the Bill, year after year, when this House meets, it will be possible to criticise, and criticise severely, if occasion necessitates, the conduct of the Board or of any member of it. I am satisfied that a keen public opinion, in view of the vast importance of the question, will regulate the matter of the membership of the Board. I suggest to my hon. friends opposite the desirability of considering the effect of the amendment which they have proposed before pressing it upon the committee. I fee! sure it must have been brought forward without due consideration, and I am also satisfied from my knowledge of the gentlemen responsible for it that if they carefully consider its effect they will not press the amendment.

I listened with a great deal of attention to what the Acting Prime Minister said this afternoon concerning the unconstitutionality of the amendment which I proposed, and I believe that a great deal of weight should be given to his opinion. I have the gravest doubts as to the constitutionality of the whole scheme as outlined; it seems to me that the Government is swallowing a camel and straining at a gnat. However the responsibility has to be upon the Government and I shall withdraw the amendment, at the same time stating that if anything would have led me to insist upon the proposition, it would have been the remarks made by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson).
Amendment Withdrawn.

My hon. friend, the Acting Minister of Justice, this afternoon argued, if I understood him correctly, that such a long term would not he advisable in a case like this.
Three trustees, one of whom should he chairman, should, if possible, be men of railway experience. They should be required to give their whole time to their duties, and salaries should be fixed adequate to command the services of the best men. Of the two remaining trustees, we think it would be desirable that one should be selected on the ground of business and financial experience, and the other as specially possessing the confidence of railway employees.
The Acting Prime Minister said this afternoon that the only way to make the Canadian Government railways succeed was to appoint the best men in the land to manage them. We all believe that; in fact, we all know it. If you get the best men, and they give all their time and attention to the Government railway system, it will be a success. But we do not think the Government will appoint the best men. That is why we want the responsibility to be taken by Parliament. My hon. friend from Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) said this afternoon: Let the Government take the responsibility, and get after them when you come to the House if they do not do right. What is the use? Take the Star last night, which contained a comparison between the way in which the troops were handled by the Canadian Pacific Railway and by the Canadian Government Railway. An instance is given of the Canadian Government Railway train being three hours late at a point a few miles out of Quebec, but the Canadian Pacific took the troops over and brought them into Montreal on time. Yesterday they were waiting for a Canadian Government train which was first announced at two o'clock, then at three o'clock, and at seven o'clock it had not come in. Who raises a kick in the House, who calls attention to the fact? When our troop trains were jumping off the track every now and then nobody said anything in this House. What is the use? Suppose we say: Those trustees are no good; they have done this or that. Well, they have done it, and it is no use locking the stable door after the horse is
gone. You need to have such a board as will command the confidence not only of the railway employees, as the commissioners say, but of the public in general, of all the stockholders, and I think that that or a similar suggestion ought to be adopted.. I do not see that we are getting away from any constitutional point. As the Acting Prime Minister said this afternoon, there are only two ways of running Government railways-you have either to run them by the Government through the Minister of Railways; or to run them by a commission or board of trustees or a company. We arp now proposing to organize a company, and if we are to organize it, I think there ought to be no difference between it and any private railway company. The stockholders ought to elect the directors, and then the administrative duties of the directors ought to be looked after by the Governor in Council.

Since speaking on this clause this afternoon and making a suggestion to the Minister of Railways, I have come to the conclusion that it would be well to put my suggestion in the form of an amendment to the clause in question; that is to say, to give the minister an opportunity to show the country that he and the House are serious when they say that they intend to do the best they can for the returned soldier. As I pointed out this afternoon, the Canadian soldier in France has shown to the world that he can construct railways and run them under the most difficult circumstances possible, and I see no reason why he cannot do it in this country when he is backed by a Government so powerful as this is. I know an objection will be urged from both sides of this House, that by consecrating in our statutes the principle that returned soldiers should be appointed to such and such positions we are liable to create a militaristic class. I think the objection is a good one, but the present circumstances are isuch, and the wording of the Bill is such, that I do not think we need fear any such calamity-for it would be a .calamity to create such a class in this country. We are going through a period of reconstruction. The returned soldier has been promised practically everything; he has been told time and again that the people of *Canada will do everything for him-will [DOT]find him a position. In the past few months since the troops have been coming back in large numbers I have had great difficulty in finding positions on the Government railways and on other railways for



returned men with some railway experience. For one reason or another perhaps they are not fitted mentally-that is to say, their *mentality has not come back to the absolute normal, pre-war standard, or perhaps they are somewhat incapacitated by their wounds t-for the first month to perform their duties in the fashion in which the ordinary concern expects them to be performed. But 6'hould there be a returned soldier placed on the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways, he will be able to enter into the feelings of the returned man, and ithe returned man will be able to appeal to him and say, " Well, give us a little better ichance than the man who is tied down by the hard and fast rules and regulations of ihis board." Under those circumstances I ithink the best thing I can do is to embody the suggestion I made this afternoon in the form of an amendment, as follows:
That clause 1 be amended as follows: By inserting after the word " fifteen," in the sixteenth line, the following words: " At least one of whom shall be a man who has seen service as a soldier at the front."
I may say that the two amendments made this afternoon have come to a rather isad conclusion, but in this particular instance I can assure the House that I will not withdraw this amendment under any icircumsances whatsoever. Should I withdraw it I would feel very much like a five-cent piece,

I support with pleasure the amendment of the member for Quebec West (Mr. Power). The member for Spring' field (Mr. Richardson) took exception this afternoon to the strong language used by Lord Shaughnessy in an address which he made the other day in Montreal. But what Lord Shaughnessy said was that this board would turn out to be a political organization. He was Tight, because the whole system of appointments smacks of strong partyiem. I quote the following from a Government organ, the Winnipeg Telegram-one of the rivals in Winnipeg of the Tribune and the Free Press-of 19th April:
Making Railway Experts.
To the Editor Winnipeg Telegram:
Sir:-The west has furnished our Government with two men to fill national railway positions. A short biography of them should provide a tip to President Beatty of the C.P.R., and should1 also point the way to thousands of ambitious Canadian youths. It should also quiet the disbeliever in Government ownership of railways, as it clearly shows that our prairies turn out captains of industry by the simplest of training.
Charles McGill Hamilton, in the early '90s, was attending school in Indian Head and later

in Regina. About 1902 he settled on a section of land near McTaggart, Sask., a village about ten miles north of Weyburn. He followed this worthy but uneventful career until two years ago, when he was nominated in opposition to the Unionist candidate for Weyburn. Mr. Cal-der was managing Unionist affairs in Saskatchewan, and Hamilton was prevailed upon to withdraw. A few months later he was appointed a director of Canadian National railways. Farming a section of land in Saskatchewan is a mighty good training for directing the affairs of a national transcontinental. The Canadian Pacific railway have been slow to see this.
Sydney P. Porter in Moose Jaw's early days, was a C.P.R. baggageman. Many years of this work was followed by years as homestead inspector. This latter position developed into confidential political agent of the Saskatchewan dominant party. When the by-elections were on, Syd. was there oiling the machine. This week he becomes assistant to the general manager of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, with headquarters at Ottawa.
Handling baggage, homesteaders and political campaigns are, some say, an excellent training for managing a national transcontinental. President Beatty, please take notice. Calder can show him things in selecting men for big jobs.
Government Ownership.
This shows that we are giving too much power to the Minister of Railways and Canals. After all, biased as Lord Shaughnessy may be in regard to the whole question of Government ownership, he is right in intimating that after a while the whole thing will be a huge political system in the hands of the government of the day. Here you have two concrete cases.
What would my hon. friend propose as to the management of this great system of railways that has been literally dumped on the people of Canada?
My hon. friend would not take my advice, anyway.

A man who criticises is in duty bound to offer aa alternative.
Mr. FIELDING! I see no objection to the appointment of a returned soldier on the board. I do hope that in the selection of the members of the board a competent returned soldier may be found especially one of the engineering corps to which reference was made by the member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). But I do not approve, if I may use my hon. friend's own words, of "consecrating" in an Act of Parliament the appointment of a returned soldier in the form he proposes. I do not think that is a wise procedure.
Amendment (Mr. Power) negatived-Yeas, 23; nays, 38.

There is no provision
in this clause for a quorum. I suggest,

therefore, that the following words be added after the word " incorporated " in the seventeenth line:
A majority of those appointed shall constitute a quorum for the transaction of business.

Section 13 makes applicable all the provisions of the Railway Act except certain provisions. The Railway Act, by a provision that is not within the exceptions, provides that a majority shall be a quorum, consequently, there is no need of an amendment.
Amendment withdrawn.
' Mr. CAHILL: In order that we may get the best expression of opinion on this allimportant section of the Bill, I move an amendment to the effect that this clause be referred to the Railway Committee or to a committee to be selected by the Railway Committee, consisting of fifteen members from the Government side and ten members from the Opposition side. Any vote that is taken here is practically a party vote. Some members t>n this side may express their opinion by their vote, but members on the Government side always vote with the party. The question of directors is one of the most important that we have to deal with in connection with this 'Bill, although there are about thirty sections in the Bill, all more or less bad, but some not so bad as others.
I think if a committee were appointed to consider the best means of appointing these directors we should get very much better results than we can hope to get in this Committee of Parliament, for the reasou that when we sit down in a committee outside of this Chamber the suggestion of a member of the Opposition is taken for what it is worth, whereas in Committee of the Whole any suggestion made by a member of the Opposition will undoubtedly be voted down by the supporters of the Government. As this is an all-important Bill, I do think the Government should be willing to meet the Opposition in their suggestions for arriving at the best possible means of dealing with this matter, and I therefore beg to move that a committee of twenty-five be appointed, fifteen of whom shall be supporters of the Government, and ten members of the Opposition, to consider the best method of selecting the directors.
May a committee not appoint a sub-committee? I would suggest that the Government appoint a committee.

Section 1 provides:
The Governor in Council may nominate such persons as may be deemed expedient, not less than five, nor more than fifteen, to be directors of the company hereby incorporated, and upon such nomination being made the persons so nominated, and their successors, and such other persons as may from time to time be nominated by the Governor in Council as directors shall be and are hereby incorporated as a company.
Section 2 provides that the directors shall hold office from year to year. It would, therefore, seem that the directors have the privilege of filling vacancies, with the approval of the Governor in Council. Would these new appointees have to be nominated by the Governor in Council in order to form part of the company?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, that is what the Bill says. The Governor in Council fills the vacancy by the appointment of a successor.

Section 2 provides that
the directors " may " fill the-vacancy by the appointment of a successor. Is there any .conflict between the two sections. But perhaps that can be considered when we come to section 2.

The Minister of Railways
told us this afternoon, and we are very glad fb accept his statement, that so far as he was concerned, as Minister of Railways, he would see that no politics or patronage entered into the appointment of the directors or the operation of the railway. Now, section 1 of the Bill bears very distinct earmarks of a huge political machine tha,t is being built up in this country the like of which we have never had in the operation of our railways since Confederation. A great deal has been said of the operation of the Intercolonial. I have always been a very strong supporter of Government ownership and operation of that road, because it was a part and parcel of Confederation. Yet when I consider the mileage that is being added to the Government system and that will be controlled by this board of directors-while, of course, I realize, as does this country, that politics and patronage will not creep in so long as the system is

under the efficient management of the present Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) -I shudder to think what may happen when the present minister retires from his position, to be succeeded perhaps by somebody imbued with more partisanship than he. For instance, suppose my hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) whom I am glad to see near the minister to-night were Minister of Railways, what a great power would be in his hands to be used in support of his party. When the minister asks us to believe that politics will not be considered as a qualification of a director of this company, it is like asking us not to believe what we have seen going on for years in the operation of the different branches of this (Government. In the operation of this huge system, which my hon. friend from Springfield is eo prone to say has been wished, or forced, on the Government-I do not say so; these roads have not been forced on the Government, but have been taken over by the Government at a very great price to protect some *of their political friends-all possible safeguards should be provided against political influence. Because, as surely as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, when this great mileage is added to the Government system of railways (and I understand still more mileage is to be added) it will be as impossible for any board of directors or any minister of railways or any government-and it is really the Government who will operate the road-to operate this gigantic system without political patronage as it would be 'to win an election in any constituency in the Dominion without bringing in politics.
Section 1 provides that the Governor in Council may nominate such persons, not less than five nor more than fifteen, to be approved by the Governor in Council. I want to ask my hon. friend if in all fairness he could not lay the cards on the table, at least to the extent of informing the Committee how many directors will be appointed. Does the Government intend to appoint five of their prominent supporters at large salaries, or will they find places for fifteen?'I think we should have that information. The Minister of Railways says that politics are to be eliminated, but the Acting Prime Minister was not by any means so emphatic in this respect. He said that the railway would be operated, as far as possible, without regard to politics. I took his words down at the time and have them before me,-politics would be eliminated "as far as possible." Now that is a very elastic qualification. My hon. friend

knows, as well as I and every man and woman in the country know, that it cannot be operated independent of politics. He has studied the matter and I think he should be able to tell us whether there will be five, seven, nine or fifteen directors. Many valuable suggestions have been made in regard to the selection of these directors. It has been suggested that different organizations might be considered, and I have no doubt that every hon. member will concede that if a returned soldier had experience or knowledge regarding railway matters he should at least be given a first place on the board. But if you are to accept the qualifications for membership on the board as suggested by the Winnipeg Telegram, from which my hon. friend quoted a few moments ago, of course the returned soldier would not be considered unless he had been a candidate endorsed by the Unionist party. If there is a board of fifteen directors selected, I suggest that at least two of its members should be representative of the labour interest. There is no class or body of men who are more interested in the operation of the railway than the railway employees, and if there are fifteen directors they should have two representatives; if the number of directors is seven or eight, then only one. At all events labour organizations should be represented on the board of directors.

With reference to the question of my hon. friend as to why 1 have fixed the number from five to fifteen, I may inform him that when we get all the railways consoldidated it will then be decided how many directors should be appointed for the operation of the whole railway system. Probably we have made the number larger than will be really necessary, but it is impossible just at present to decide on any definite number of directors. As to the appointment of labour men and a returned soldier, I believe I stated this afternoon that I thought a labour man and a returned soldier should be on the board. These classes of men will receive the consideration of the Government. As to the question of patronage, I think it is hardly fair to compare the present operation oi the Government railways with the conditions that existed a number of years ago. It is now almost impossible to have patronage on the railway system because every employee of the railway belongs to one union or another. You can not dismiss a single employee without an investigation by the union to which he belongs, whereas formerly an employee could be dismissed

and some one else appointed in his place on the recommendation of a member. In connection with promotions, if there is a vacancy in the railway the senior man receives the appointment, and there is no way by which political influence can interfere with his promotion. During the short time I have been administering the department vacancies have occurred, sometimes an agent retiring or resigning from the service, when some other man in the particular village or town sought the position. He had no possible chance of getting it, because the senior man on the road under the union was entitled to it. I think this is a fair and equitable way of filling these positions. It is obvious, therefore, that political patronage in appointments to the railway system as a whole has been abolished by the employees themselves. There is one direction in which, perhaps, political patronage might obtain; but if the directors carry out the policy they should carry out, and which I believe they are carrying out at the present time, and call for tenders for all the supplies that are required in the operation of the road there will be no possibility of patronage in that respect. The whole success of the operation of the road depends entirely on the men who are appointed as directors, and when this Bill goes through, I am certain that the men who will be appointed as directors will command the respect and confidence of the people.
If they do not they can be removed at the end of the year, or by the Governor in Council for cause at any time. If there is any dissatisfaction it can be discussed in the House. There has been, in my opinion, the possibility of interference with the operation of this great system as a result of parties outside trying to get information that it will not be in the public interest to give. That question was raised by the hon. member for Pontiac (iMr. Cahill) this afternoon. I will illustrate what I mean. A return was asked for giving a statement of all the business done at each and every station on the Transcontinental railway, the amount of money received, and the number of cars that left each station during the year 1918. If that information is given, there is no reason why there should not be an order for a statement of all the business done between Toronto and Montreal, or between Winnipeg and some other place, with the result that the railways that are being operated in opposition to the Government system will get all the information as to the business that is being done at the stations adjoining their own railway, information which, if given, would surely injure the Government Railway system. Other questions are being asked as to what is being paid for coal and whom it is purchased from. I will tell you what happened on the Intercolonial railway during the past few years-I think that hon. members from the Eastern Provinces will bear out the statem&nt I make; perhaps they will not say so here but I think they will not hesitate to confirm what I am going to say. We have in Nova Scotia 9 p.m. one or two mines where the coal is much more valuable than that produced from other mines-coal that is worth probably a dollar a ton more than that of some other mines. Years ago a difference was allowed for this coal, because of its quality. A question was asked each year and the information given to the public as to the prices that the Government were paying for coal. Political influence came in each year-it is probably just the same on one side as the other- with the result that influence was brought to bear in consequence of which in the lower provinces we are paying just as much for coal that is not of this high quality as we are for the high-quality article. Ii the same system is followed throughout the country the directorate will not be able to get the advantages that they should get in matters of this kind. You could not get information from the Canadian Pacific, which will be the great opposition company to the Government-owned system; they do not disclose information of that kind to their own shareholders or the public. We should have men operating this system of such a character that it would not be easy for us to criticise any of their management of the road. Of course, it is possible that the men appointed may not live up to the expectations formed of them. I do not think that any Government would have any hesitation in removing a director who was not able to perform the duties satisfactorily bot only to the railway but to the public. We must start out with men in whom we have confidence and we must trust these men for at least a year, or until Parliament meets again, when, if they have not carried out their duties satisfactorily, they can be removed.
Why wait until Parliament meets if they are not satisfactory?

We will not wait until Parliament meets if any information has been given to the Government that would justify their removal. The Bill gives us

power to remove them for cause. If there has been any information given to the public, or if the matter is brought before the House, Parliament can take action if the Government has not acted.

My hon. friend must be
very innocent; or he mus't think I am - I do not know which. He tells us that it is impossible to exercise political patronage on a Government railway. 1 happen to live in a community where we have some connection with the working of a Government railway. He says you cannot dismiss men from a Government railway because you will have a strike on your hands at once. My hon. friend apparently has not been Minister of Railways and Canals long enough to get on to the game, or he does not want us to think that he has. If he will come to the city of Moncton, or if he will visit any other place in Westmorland county traversed by the Intercolonial railway, he will find that the statement that there is no political patronage in regard to employees on the Intercolonial is not altogether correct. I do not need to go back a year to prove that; I can cite him an instance occurring in the month of January last. A stationrnaster wanted an employee temporarily. He wanted some one in a hurry, and he employed a young man. This young man remained, there a few days, or weeks, till the patronage committee in that locality -went to the stationrnaster and demanded that he be dismissed because he did not belong to the Conservative party. I did not know who he was or what party he belonged to or did not belong to. The station-master referred the matter to Moncton and a man was sent from Moncton to investigate. He investigated the case and found that this young man did excellent work, and he did not want to displace him. Finally he made a dicker. IT ere was another nym required and he said to the stationrnaster:	"You had better select a
Tory for this other position and maybe this young man will be kept on as well, and there will be nothing more heard about it," but the man in question wae soon dismissed. That is taking place in a three-dollar-a-day job. Yet the Minister of Railways tells me, and expects me to accept his statement, that there is no political patronage in connection with Government railways. If there is going to be a cutting out and hewing away with political patronage, why has it been allowed to go on until today? Why not cut it out? I do not believe that the officials of the Intercolonial railway want to play party politics, but

there must be somebody who is interested in it. I am only speaking of my own locality, and I know whereof I speak. This does not come to me second-hand or as a matter of hearsay; I know it
If that is the case with respect to a little job on the Intercolonial, which is not worth more than three or four dollars a day, what must be expected under this Bill and under the arrangements to go into effect when the Bill is passed? The minister may think that we are suspicious and too sceptical because we bring these matters to his attention, but nobody knows better than he does What may happen at any time on the Intercolonial Railway. A foreman in any shop, or the head of any branch, on that railway says to half a dozen of his employees " We do not want you any longer because we have no work for you to do." Accordingly these men are laid aside. However, when men are again wanted for these positions the former employees are not recalled, but other men are sent for, some political friends of that foreman, or some particular friends of the party in- power. This is not held to be a dismissal-you cannot ask the railway to keep men in their employ if their services are not required.

I rise to support the demand made 'by my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Copp) that employees of the Government railways should be appointed to the directorate of this board. At the present time a commission appointed by the Government is engaged in an investigation of industrial conditions, interviewing employers of labour and employees in various centres in Canada for the purpose of- ascertaining whether it would be possible to give the workingmen a share in the management of private industries in this country. That is a recognition that the principle involved is sound, and such being the case that principle should be embodied in this legislation and the declaration made that employees of the Government railway system ought to he represented on the Board of Directors of that great public enterprise, the Canadian National Railways. The idea of giving labour a share in the management of industries is now pretty well accepted by all the students of industrial conditions in other countries. In England the great labour unions are asking that this progressive step should be made. The Federation of Miners there are asking that the control of the mines should be vested in a council of ten, five of whom would be appointed by the miners and the other five by the Government, and as they

are supported by public opinion in England I think they stand a fair chance of obtaining what they demand. In the United States the same idea prevails, and very recently it was supported and recommended by such a conservative body as the American National Catholic War Council, the administrative committee of which is composed of four bishops. Such an advanced paper as The Nation, of New York, speaking on this policy in its issue of March *29th said:
The bishops have taken a courageous step, possibly one that some day will be designated as the most serviceable that Catholicism has recently ventured in America. The paucity of constructive thinking in .these last months has been in keeping with our inveterate opportunism in dealing with the subject of economics. That a quartette of Catholic clergymen should give the country stronger labour doctrine, more intelligibly presented and more persuasive, than the reconstruction committee of the American Federation of Labour, is a clue to the times.
I merely mention this to show that this *idea is entertained not only by radicals [DOT]and socialists but by all students of labour conditions in every country, and I say that ,in Canada we should keep abreast of the [DOT]times. I move, in amendment, that the following word3 be added to the clause:
At least two of the directors shall be appointed upon the recommendation of the employees of the Canadian National Railways.
What method would my hon. friend suggest by which the, employees [DOT]would make the nominations?
Through the brotherhoods.

At the present time I happen to live in a railway centre *where all the railway employees are voting [DOT]for two representatives on the Pensions Hoard and the Insurance Relief Fund. The employees of the Canadian Government *Railways have two representatives on those boards.
Does that refer to all [DOT]classes of employees?

All classes.
The same means can be easily taken to choose representatives of the employees on the Board of Directors of the National Railways.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The suggestion
put forward by my hon. friend in his amendment is, I submit, unsound in principle. The same considerations apply to it as were advanced by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) with regard to the appointment of returned soldiers to the
Board. The Government is responsible to Parliament and to the country for appointments to the Board of Directors of the Canadian National Railway System. In making these appointments it has all classes of Canadian citizens before it from which to make selections, and it is its duty to make such selection as will give the best results in the administration of the railway system. This question has come up frequently in this House, and the position which I have always taken when the suggestion has been made in connection with Bills which I have had in charge is this: That I would not discriminate against any citizen in making appointments to a commission which is to act for the Government. On the other hand I think it inadvisable in the extreme to embody in legislation a specific provision that the Government shall make an appointment from a certain class of our citizens, or upon the recommendation of a body outside, because, as I have pointed out, the Government is immediately responsible; the responsibility cannot be with those whom my hon. friend would have elect these two representatives on the Board. If we adopted my hon. friend's recommendation, the Government would have to select the parties put forward. At present it is open for the Government to appoint representatives of labour on the board of directors if it regards it as expedient and in the national interest to do so, but that is a different matter from accepting names put forward by an organization outside of the Government, and in no way responsible-not responsible to the public of Canada in the sense that the Government is responsible.
In my view, the amendment of my hon. friend should be negatived. I would point out further, Mr. Chairman, that at present there is a Railway War Board on which all classes of railway employees are represented, and very capably represented.
It is a temporary board.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is .a temporary board, but it is probable that it will be continued.
It is a good board.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a good board, and I have heard no complaints whatever from labour organizations with respect to the administration of the Government Railways.

And it is a very satisfactory board to all the railways.
Amendment negatived.
Shall clause 1 carry?	-

The Acting Prime Minister, Mr. Chairman, says that in the selection of directors the Government have in their mind's eye all of the people of Canada, but he forgets that the Government in this case have but one eye and the only people they can see are the supporters of Union Government, as is exemplified in the appointments which have been made. Some hon. members opposite in commending the Government for their excellent selection of directors said that they expected everything would be fine for the Government-owned railways, and that the Government had taken a very wise course. If my recollection is correct, the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals stated that oi the directors with railway. experience they had appointed Mr. Hanna, Mr. Mitchell, and Mr. Wood-three ex-directors of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. This House and the country were told by the Government that the company had made a failure of the management and operation of the Canadian Northern Railway System, for which reason we should take over their road-and incidentally we paid them some $10,800,000 more than the commissioners said should be paid. These gentlemen are to be the directors, the men who made a failure of the Canadian Northern Railway System-and the Drayton-Acworth report states that the estimate of the probable earnings and requirements of the road were out millions of dollars. These men, by getting into a position to draw their money directly from the public treasury rather than by the indirect route of getting it through Mackenzie & Mann and their friends in the Government have now been transformed into expert railway operators. The hon. minister says that it will not be in the public interest to give any information concerning the operation of this railway; he practically tells us that this is to be an air-tight political machine whereby millions of dollars can be expended through the friends of Mackenzie & Mann interests and this Government-which seem to me to be practically one and the same thing. Hon. members opposite who are blinded by their public ownership enthusiasm are quite willing to let the Government expend millions of dollars in extravagances for the benefit of the Government and themselves, thus incidentally through government management allowing themselves to again get into office at some future time. How can the Government expect to convince any

man who is looking for honest information that it is not in the interest of the representatives of the people, who are the real shareholders, that we should know from whom iwe are buying railroad ties and what price we are paying, and who is doing our contracting on these extensions, and whether it is being done by tender and contract or by a force contract, as the Welland Canal is being done at the present time? If he insists, as he did this evening, that it is not in the public interest that the people who own this railroad and supply the funds should get any information regarding the expenditures, then it must be apparent to hon. gentlemen opposite, even though they will vote with the Government regardless of their own opinions, that this is nothing more nor less than a political machine for the sole purpose of making places for the friends of hon. members opposite, of bolstering up their bad record, and of again getting them into power. I would like to ask the hon. minister if he will tell us in what way it is opposed to the public interest to let the public, who own this road, know who supplies ties and equipment and who does the construction work. My information is that it is being done by the same old gang that has robbed this country for years, and I do not think there is any doubt about that.

There certainly is not any intention to keep from this House or from the public any information that should be published, and of course the information has been given to a very large extent in the past and will be given in the future.
Why not answer that question?
But there are certain matters in connection with the operation that you have to keep private.
Not ties.

I will tell the hon. member why it should be kept private. Supposing information is asked as to how much business is done at every station between Ottawa and Toronto by the Canadian Government Railway, and that information is published, any travelling freight agent of the Canadian Public railway at once knows what business we are doing at Co-bourg, Port Hope and the other stations.
Mr. BOSSn That is not what is asked.

You are placing in the hands of your competitors information that will enable them to interfere with the

legitimate business you are doing. That is one case.
That question is not asked The hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) asked a specific question. Why is not that answered?

I am giving the reason why I say that some kinds of information should not be disclosed. The member for Pontiac says that the Canadian National Railway Board are giving contracts to "the same old gang," Mackenzie & Mann. He is trying to lead the House, and the country to believe that the board are giving contracts to Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann, and that these are the owners of the Northern Construction Company. He knows that the Mackenzie & Mann of the Northern Construction Company are not Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann. He knows that the man named Mackenzie in the Northern Construction Company is Alexander Mackenzie, who is not a relative of Sir William Mackenzie. He knows also that the Mr. Mann in that firm is not Sir Donald Mann, but a nephew of Sir Donald Mann. Why, then, is he not honest about it; why does he seek to give the impression that contracts are let by the board of directors to the same old gang, do Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann?
And their friends.

Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann are not interested, directly or indirectly, and never were interested, in the Northern Construction Company; and it is unfair to make the statement that Mackenzie & Mann are the owners of the Northern Construction Company, and thus mislead the public. Surely if these men have a company they have a right to tender as well as any other private individual or corporation. I repeat that the hon. member's statement that the board of directors are letting contracts to the " same old gang," Mackenzie & Mann, is not correct.

The only applause that
the minister gets is from the member for Centre Toronto and some other Ontario members who are not familiar with the Northern Construction Company.
Where is the member for Centre Toronto? Will the hon. gentleman point him out?

They wander around so
much when the whip cracks that it is impossible for me to tell just where they are.
I meant the member for Toronto South (Mr. Sheard) and other members from Ontario.
It is well known to all members from Western Canada that the Northern Construction Company practically built all the Canadian Northern railroad, and that the Northern Construction Company is the Mackenzie & Mann crowd. When the minister was asked what price was paid to the Northern Construction Company for ties, he felt the necessity for getting under cover and refused to answer the question. Why should he not give the Committee the information? If there is nothing to hide, why hide anything? The minister admitted that if Mackenzie & Mann had a company they were entitled to contracts. He tells us that the men who are conducting these National Railways are the men who have been with Mackenzie & Mann for twenty odd years. I remember when Mr. Hanna was with the Canadian Northern Railway Company over twenty years ago, when they had less than two hundred miles of railway in Western Canada. You cannot tell me that men who have been connected with these concerns practically ever since their inception are not still friends of Mackenzie & Mann. D.B. Hanna fought public ownership to. the last ditch. He fought it while the Board of Arbitration was sitting in Toronto to determine how much was to be paid for this [DOT] worthless stock. He was fighting public ownership less than two months ago in Hamilton, and he is still fighting it. Mr. Hanna, Mr. Mitchell and Mr. Wood, who are the absolute controllers of the road to-day- with the advice, of course, of Mackenzie & Mann and the Minister of Railways-are practically the same people who have always controlled the Canadian Northern Railway Company.
The minister told us this afternoon that all his appointees-he used the words "my appointees" were men of integrity and honesty. I am not doubting that; but what have they to do with this railway enterprise? Hanna and the executive, the railway men, tell these gentlemen what they are to do, and they sanction it. We are still leaving this whole enterprise in the hands of the Canadian Northern crowd, the same -people who have been filching money from this country for years. No hon. gentleman can deny that and substantiate his denial. If these men had been good railway operators before they came into the hands of the Minister of Railways, they should have been able to make the road a profitable enterprise. But they were not able to do so, and we were opposing them and saying that they

were net building and operating in a businesslike way. Now we not only take them into our lap, as the member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) says, but we are taking also the fellows who promoted the enterprise and who have been tapping the treasury of the country for years; and we are letting contracts to these same people. There is no getting away from that. If it is not a fact, why does the minister not give us the information? When the minister says that Mackenzie's nephew and Mann's uncle, or grandmother or somebody else, owns the stock in this enterprise, that is getting us nowhere. We know that it is the same family arrangement, and we want to know how long this state of affairs is to continue and how much money these people will be satisfied with. It would be better to give them a lump sum, get rid of the whole outfit, lock, stock and barrel, and put somebody in charge of this railway enterprise who will make it a success. If the minister is not willing to tell us who are getting the contracts for the railway construction, from whom the ties and supplies are being bought and what prices are being paid, he must expect opposition from at least some members of the committee, if not from the docile supporters of the Government.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-term of office of directors:

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think the first line is not
very well phrased and I beg to move:
That the words * from year to year ' in line 25 of the Bill be struck out and the following substituted therefor: " from one annual meeting to another or until their successors are appointed."
One of the first things done at an annual meeting is to appoint the directors, but for tsome reason or another it frequently happens in the case of companies that the matter may go over for two or three days, <and in that case you would be without a hoard of directors.
What is the intention? Is it proposed that they shall be appointed [DOT]annually?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I agree that the language is not very well chosen. There is another [DOT]point. The section provides that the annual meeting shall be held upon the second [DOT]Thursday in April of each year. Who are the .persons who are to attend this annual [DOT]meeting? We know what an annual meeting of shareholders is, but who are to be

summoned to this annual meeting? We [DOT]already have provision for the meeting of directors; we are told they meet every week. There is another thought. A little further ion in the Bill it is provided that wherever *there is anything to be done by the shareholders, the Governor in Council shall do it. Therefore, the shareholders and the Governor in Council are one, and this annual meeting would seem to be an annual [DOT]meeting of the Governor in Council. That is merely a question of drafting to which I would draw the minister's attention. But there is a more serious objection to that clause, I think. Provision is made that in the event of a vacancy occurring the directors are to fill the vacancy. In the discussion this afternoon the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) very nroperlv, as I thought, took the ground that the power of the Governor .in Council must be upheld, and Parliament must hold the Governor in Council responsible. But in this clause you are deliberately getting away from the power of the Governor in Council, and proposing that the Board of Directors shall be a self-perpetuating body, because whenever a vacancy occurs the board must nominate the man to fill that vacancy, and the Government will have a veto power. I do not think that is a wise provision. Surely, if the power of the Governor in Council is to be upheld, as we were told this afternoon, whenever a vacancy -occurs on the board it should be filled by the Governor in Council, and the Governor in Council should not have to apply to the Board of Directors to ask their permission to fill it either.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend will observe that by section 3 that the Governor in Council may declare that the company shall have a capital stock with or without shares as may from time to time be deemed expedient. At the commencement there will be no shareholders of the company, and the annual meeting provided for under section 2, until there is a share capital, would be a meeting only of the directors; but I do not see any objection to that. When a share capital is created the sole shareholder will be the Minister of Finance holding on behalf of His Majesty, and it would be for the Government or the minister, who would naturally have the approval of the Government, to appoint a representative to attend the meeting. The directors will also be shareholders, so that the meeting of shareholders, after the capital stock had been created, if it is created, would consist of the directors and the representative or proxy of the Minister of Finance.

With regard to the filling of any vacancy occurring during the year, the drafting follows the legislation which is usual in Companies' Acts; that is to say, if between annual meetings any vacancy should occur, the vacancy may be filled by the directors, because it is only of a temporary character. The safeguard from the standpoint of the shareholders is the fact that at the next annual meeting they have power over the appointment of the board. My hon. friend points out that the Government is entirely responsible for the appointment, and I quite agree with him in that. He will observe that section 2 provides that upon any vacancy occurring the directors may, subject to the approval of the Governor in Council, fill the vacancy by the appointment of a successor. That really gives the Government power to make the appointment. Personally, I see no objection to adopting the suggestion of my hon. friend and having the appointments made to the vacancy directly by the Governor in Council, and therefore I would suggest that the section be amended by striking out, after the word " occurring," the words " the directors may, subject to the approval of the Governor in Council" and substituting therefor the words " the Governor in Council shall."	.

I would suggest that unless the Bill is to be disposed of to-night it would be well to reserve this clause so that it may be drafted more carefully in the line of my hon. friend's suggestion. In the case of an ordinary company, a vacancy that occurs during the year can be filled by the board because it is not convenient to call the shareholders together; but as the Governor in Council is the shareholder here, and as the Governor in Council is very much in evidence, the practice of a private company would not seem to be necessary.
Mr. MeMASTER: I understood from what the hon. member for Port Arthur and Kenora (Mr. Keefer) said, that his idea was that the directors should be appointed anew every year. If I am right in that idea, and I believe I am, I would point out that the amendment which he has drafted does not to my mind express very clearly the view he entertains. It looks as if the directors continued in office from annual meeting to annual meeting until their successors were appointed or until they were removed for cause. I would suggest that if they are to be appointed anew every year, that should be set forth clearly in the Act.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Section 2 provides for the annual meeting being held upon the second Thursday in April of each year. One of the first things done at an annual meeting is to appoint directors, but sometimes that is left over for a day or two, and in that case there would be a period during which there would be no' board of directors.
Mr. MeMASTER: There is no difference of opinion between the hon. member and myself, but I submit that neither the clause nor his amendment makes it clear that every year the Governor in Council must appoint new directors.
I suggest that after discussion the minister reserve the clause and have it re-drafted in the light of the discussion that has taken place.

I think the word
" may " in the second sentence is preferable to the word " shall " and is more in keeping with the sentence immediately following.
