I move that the whoD
clause be struck out.
What would be the ob ject of having this capital stock?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This clause providing for the company having placed capital stock if the Governor in Council should so declare has been placed in the Bill for the purpose of meeting a situation which might arise. I confess I do not see at the present time any reason for it but at any time a situation might arise which might make it desirable to have capital stock.
As all stock is to be owned by the Government and as the company can operate without stock under section 2, I am of the opinion, speaking offhand, that a share capital will not be necessary, and I would suggest to the Minister and to the committee that the section be allowed to stand until to-morrow. I have not been able to give it very much consideration to satisfy myself as to whether it is necessary or not.
Section stands.
On section 4-Head Office:
I move that the clause he amended to read that the head office of the company shall be in the city of Montreal, in the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understood that the position of hon. members opposite was that there should be no politics in this matter.

I support the amendment of my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs). The hon. minister says there- ought not to be any politics in the matter, but the mere fact that Toronto has been selected for the head office of the Canadian National Railways proves that there is politics in it. You have only to look at the map of the Canadian National Railways to see that Toronto is only on a branch line of the system. Who ever saw a town or a city on the branch line of a railway selected as the headquarters of the railway? Montreal, geographically, nationally, financially and otherwise, ought to be the railway centre of Canada, and the head office ought to be there. As soon as there was a rumour that the head office of the Government Railways might ' be in Montreal there was a delegation from Toronto. The Toronto Globe and the Toronto Star and all friends of public ownership clamoured that Toronto should be selected as the place of the head office. They are in favour of public ownership -and are opposed to politics in the administration of the railway, but they want the head office to be in Toronto. I think the people know that Montreal is naturally the centre of the railway and is best suited for headquarters.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think that the propei place for the head office should be about the centre of the road where all three roads concentrate. Therefore I move an amendment to the amendment that Port Arthur be selected as the place of head office.

My reason for suggesting Montreal as the place of head office is that the head office of Canadian Pacific Railway is there, as is also the head office of the Grand Trunk Railway, which I understand we propose to take over shortly. The Canadian Pacific Railway has achieved some success operating its line from Montreal, and the Grand Trunk, had it not been saddled- with the Grand Trunk Pacific incubus, would probably also have been successful. Montreal is headquarters of ocean navigation, and is a live up-to-date city. You cannot expect to run fast trains from a slow town like Toronto, and that is one of my reasons for asking that Montreal be selected as the place of head office. I think the Committee will agree that our directors, no matter how clever and astute they may be, could learn something from the heads of the Canadian Pacific.

If the Government acquires the Grand Trunk, as it probably will, that system will be so vast that it may be necessary to divide the official authority. While Montreal might very well be the financial head office I suggest that, inasmuch as the West has such a large portion of this system, Winnipeg should be the operating headquarters.
Oh, Oh.
Hon. gentlemen opposite may laugh, but if they will study the map they will agree that, inasmuch as the West embraces such a large portion of the system,-
It is on the main line now.

It is on the main line; it is not like Toronto. It is very important that the West should be represented in the operation of this road and it should be represented from some point in the West.
I suppose that Winnipeg is the natural point. I do not suggest it because I live in Winnipeg.
Oh, no.
Hon. gentlemen may smile, but let them look at the map and study it for themselves. It will be more difficult to operate the road from Montreal than it will be from the centre of the continent.
Gaspe would be the ideal spot.
If my hon. friend thinks so, he may move a motion to that effect.

I just wish to say, as representing Toronto, that when the war was on and there was pressing need of every man, Toronto did not come second to any other place in its energy in meeting the situation. Our friends opposite are very deeply interested in securing places for returned soldiers 'and in other matters concerning them. If they will come to Toronto they will find more returned soldiers now than in the whole province of Quebec. They will find more wounded men,
I venture ito say, two to one, in the city of Toronto than in any other place. When it came to patriotic contributions, I think Toronto held its head up pretty well with Montreal. In reference to Red Cross contributions and to all the energies in connection with this great war, which has sustained and maintained the reputation of Canada amongst the nations of the * world, Toronto has done its part as well as any other city in the Dominion. If there is to be any advantage in connection with the administration of this great national railway system, I think Toronto will speak for itself in reference to its ability, energy and capacity for great undertakings. I need do no more in defence of the constituency which I represent, than point to the great record which it has made in this titanic struggle.

Although living far
away from Montreal, I rise to support the amendment of my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) and I do so for many reasons. In the first place, Montreal is the business centre of the Dominion. I do not quite share the opinion of the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Sheard). You are not going to run railways on-the Red Cross system; you are not going to run railways on patriotism; you have to run them on business principles and you have to come to the place where business is done. The head office of the Canadian National Railways is in Toronto at the present time, but the passenger agent, Mr. H. H. Melanson, who was on the Intercolonial, had to have an office in Montreal because Montreal is the centre. It is proposed to choose the location of the head office by Order in Council. We have had enough Orders in Council. Montieal is the business centre; Montreal is the head of navigation, and
Montreal is the place for the railway. I want to register my protest against the head office being located in any other city. Toronto is a magnificent city, I have had the honour and pleasure of visiting it, but it never will be a great Canadian national railway centre. You have to come to Montreal.
I desire to second the amendment of my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier.
Too late; it is seconded.

It is not because I am representing one of the constituencies in Montreal that I favour the selection of that city. I am not the same as those gentlemen who, when a business question comes up for discussion in this House, raise the question of soldiers, of nationality, of Quebec, or something like that. Economically it is desirable that the headquarters should be located in Montreal. The directors will have to come to Montreal very often in order to deal with the matters of business which are centred there. If the head office is located in Montreal their travelling expenses will be saved. Everything comes to Montreal in the way of business, and the directors will of necessity have to come. We see big magnates travelling to Montreal in private cars. Gentlemen, save that expense as far as possible and adopt Montreal.

Is Montreal not satisfied with conditions as they are? She has got the Canadian Pacific head office, the Grand Trunk head office, and now she wants to play the hog and get the Canadian National. Surely she ought to be satisfied when she has the big end of it, or two out of three. But she is still grumbling. Industrially, commercially, from the standpoint of shipping, the amount of wealth, energy, ability and also from the standpoint of being near the centre, Toronto is the proper situation for the head offices oi this railway system. Toronto is some hundreds of miles nearer the centre of the Dominion than Montreal and it is the natural location for a great enterprise. Toronto is the city of the Dominion, and will be in the near future the largest city in the country. We are preparing there for overseas shipping of which Toronto will be the headquarters. We are spending $25,000,000 to give accommodation to those liners that wall run from Toronto through the Welland

canal to the head of the lakes and to my hon. friend's destination where he would like to have the Canadian National centred. We have a larger amount of stock carried in the wholesale houses of Toronto than in any other place in the Dominion and from the standpoint of shipping, finance, business and everything necessary to build up a great institution, Toronto is the natural place. You must concede that. I have heard no argument in support of the claim that the head office should go to Montreal. There is no better place for it than Toronto. We will have the Grand Trunk before you know where you are, and then you will have something to murmur about.

Without wishing to detain the House for any great length of time on this subject, it seems to me that the city through which all these roads pass should have the head office. Toronto, I am credibly informed, is only on a branch line. Montreal has the Intercolonial, and the Canadian Northern. Winnipeg, I understand, has the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Intercolonial; hut Quebec has all the systems.
It has branch lines.

So there is a strong reason in favour of locating the head office in Quebec, and I submit it veTy humbly to the consideration of the Committee.
_ The CHAIRMAN: Is the Committee ready for the question?

I should like to say a word at this juncture. I do not for a moment understand that the member for Port Arthur and- Kenora (Mr. Keefer) was serious in moving a sub-amendment. I do not think it is fair that the House should be asked to designate any one place in Canada in which to locate the head office of the National System of Railways. I think both amendments should be withdrawn. I believe that the proposer of the first_ amendment submitted it with the intention of enlivening the proceedings of the House for a few moments-
No.

-and I anticipated that he would eventually withdraw his proposition. This company should have the same right that every other company has of selecting the place for its head office. The head office of the company can be fixed by it at any time.
By the Board of Directors?
By the Board of Directors. I submit, Parliament has no right to be called upon to fix the place for the head office of this company.
Why not?

There is no special advantage in having the head office in Toronto or Montreal. Very good reasons might be advanced why it should not be at either place. It might very likely happen, and perhaps will happen some time, that the head office will not be in either city, but that would not diminish in any degree whatever the' amount of business that might possibly go to either by reason of the operations of this railway system.
I would think that both Montreal and Toronto are very well represented on the board, and they should be satisfied with the advantage that comes to these two great metropolitan centres by reason of that representation. I submit that both amendments should be withdrawn and that the committee should not be asked to designate in this Bill where the head office of the company is to he.	v
Withdraw the * amendments and select Toronto.
The selection may well be left to the directors of the company.
Will the hon. gentleman give some reasons why the head office should not be fixed in the Bill?
It provokes debate, it is purposeless, and serves no good end.
It is always done.

If the head office of the company were located in Montreal it does not necessarily mean that more traffic will flow through that city by reason of the fact. The head office of a company is very frequently in a place far removed from the company's operations and activities.
Who decides about the head office?
It might as well be Three Rivers as Montreal.
We don't want it.
I think both amendments should be withdrawn. If not, they should be defeated by the committee.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I wish to withdraw my [DOT] amendment. I did submit it jocularly,.

thinking I would say a word for my own city, of which I am very proud.
Amendment to the amendment withdrawn.

Section 4 of the Bill provides that the head office of the company shall be in such place in Canada as the Governor in Council imay from time to time determine. So it is the Governor in -Council and not the Board of Directors which is to determine where the head office is to be.
If the Government is to determine the location of the head office that is better still.
But the minister stated that the Board of Directors were to make the Selection. If it is left to the Board of Directors it will be quite satisfactory.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no objection to a vote being taken on the amendment, but I would submit that as the designation of any place is likely to be regarded unfavourably by the Committee, those hon. gentlemen who are urging that a selection should be made here are not doing their favourite town a service by pressing for a vote. It seems to me that the head office from time to time might, as stipulated in the Bill, be determined by the Governor in Council-that is to say, by the Government which is responsible to Parlia-nrent. If the Government at any time takes action that is contrary to the wall of Parliament, Parliament has its own means of dealing with the situation. However, I have no objection to the vote being taken.

According to the model
Bill which has to be followed whenever application is made to Parliament for the incorporation of a railway, the location of the head office of the company must be mentioned, and therefore I do not see why we cannot fix the head office of this company in the present Bill. Make it Toronto, Moncton, or Winnipeg, or any other city. These proceedings must take place in accordance with the General Railway Act, and the directors may change the location by notifying the Railway Commissioners. I do not see why an exception should be made in this case and the location be left to the Governor in Council. If the directors see fit to change the location afterwards let them do so, but by all means follow the procedure that is authoritatively laid down. It looks as if the Acting Prime Minister feared that if a vote now took place it might displease some of the constituents of members who
represent an important centre. It would seem as though the Government was afraid that if the location of the head office was fixed in this Bill it would arouse some criticism. If we are going to try and bring the Canadian Railway System as much as possible into harmony with the privately-owned railways, why not follow the procedure laid down in the model Railway Bill? Let the Government take a stand and we will share the responsibility with them. Let them ' select Toronto, Winnipeg, or any other place they choose.
Is it customary for Acts of Parliament incorporating railways to contain the location of the head office?
Certainly.
T doubt it very much.
It certainly is the custom.
It may be done some times, but not always.
The procedure is set forth in the model Railway Bill, and you will be asked to mention where the head office is to be if you apply for a charter of incorporation for a railway company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is it not the incorporators who have to insert in the Bill the name of the city in which they desire to have the head office of the railway company?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Then this case
is precisely analogous; the only shareholder of the company is the Dominion Government.
Oh no, it is the people of Canada as represented by Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Dominion
Government is the shareholder in this case.
In trust for His Majesty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
:My hon. friend, if 1 may say so, is confusing the Government and Parliament. They are two distinct entities. The Government has its responsibility and its duties, and Parliament has its responsibility and its duties. But in this case the analogy is absolutely complete-the Government of Canada is the sole shareholder. The Government comes down to the House with a Bill and asks Parliament to support it. Either the head office is designated and the Government will carry its point on a majority vote in the House, or, as in this case, it leaves

the matter open. I submit that it should be left open for the reason that the Government railway situation is a changeable one.	.
Prior to 1917 we had the Intercolonial, and also the Transcontinental from Moncton to Winnipeg; then we acquired the Canadian Northern Railway System with its head office in Toronto; now we have the Grand Trunk Pacific in receivership, and negotiations are proceeding with the Grand Trunk Railway Company. The situation is a changeable one, and that to my mind is a strong reason why this section should be left precisely as it is. The situation may change further in the future, although no one can foresee what will occur. The principle of responsibility is here. If the Government desire to name the city where the head office should be located it would come down to the House and ask Parliament to support it. If Parliament declined to support it, the constitutional position would be as my hon. friend knows. On the othei hand, the Government comes down with a Bill in which it provides that the Governor in Council may from time to time name the place of the head office of the company. If the Government names a place that Parliament disapproves of, Parliament of course has its remedy; but I submit that the responsibility must be with the Government and the place should be such as the Governor in Council designates from time to time.

I cannot share that view If the place named in the Bill were determined forever as the head office of the company, the Acting Prime Minister's argument would be valid, and I could not object to it; but you have under the Railway Act the right, not in the Governor in Council [DOT]but in the directors,-and I think rightly [DOT]so-to change the head office at any time, provided they notify the Railway Board and advertise in the Canada Gazette. But in every Bill that has come before the House so far, and in the standard Bill, the place is designated. I do not see why the Governor in Council should take away from the directors the power which is given to them by the Railway Act.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman is wrong in his recollection. The Railway Act does not provide that the directors may change the head office as fixed by Parliament. What the hon. member is thinking of is the Companies Act, which I understand does so provide.
I may be mistaken, but 1 think not. I will verify it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It seems very cleat that if in this Act Parliament were to fix the place the directors could not thereaftei change it. In this Act Parliament empowers the Governor in Council from time to time to fix the place, and that place being fixed the directors could not change it. That is the way I think it should be.

If the Bill proposed that the head office should be in Toronto, and the amendment said Montreal, we would have rather an embarrassing situation. 1 think in that case I might have a "slight inclination towards Biddy "-Biddy being Montreal-but I think the principle that the Governor in Council shall- have power to determine the head office is fair and reasonable. I may say to my hon. friend that this Government is not going to be in power for ever, and if it does not determine that question wisely, another Government may want to make a change. Geographically the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) has the best argument, because a glance at the map will show that in regard to the extent of the territory that this system covers Winnipeg is the more central place. I think the determination ought not to be made definitely now, and while I have a preference, I think, for Montreal, I am of opinion that the argument for leaving the matter to the determination of the Governor in Council is a fair and reasonable one.

In order to settle the
matter between Montreal and Toronto, I would suggest to the committee that the place for the head office be Moncton in the province of New Brunswick. As a matter of fact the head office was settled down there half a century ago when the Intercolonial was built, and I think the office should not be moved so far away as Toronto or Montreal. It seems to me that it is interfering with the selection made at the time of Confederation, and in order to settle the great trouble between Montreal and Toronto it seems to me that the very central railway city of Moncton should not be neglected. The most important officers should certainly not have been taken away to Toronto. It is true that the railway situation is different entirely from what it was at the time the Intercolonial was built, but I think it could be arranged to leave the great bulk of the old Intercolonial staff in the city of Moncton where the railway offices were originated half a century ago.

Mr. Chairman, I have not been able to lay my hand on the Railway Act, but I take the new Consolidated Railway Bill, section 73:
The head office of the company shall be in the place designated in the Special Act, but the company may, by by-law, from time to time, change the location of its head office to any place in Canada: Provided that notice of any such change shall be given to the secretary of the board.
You are reading from the new Bill.
I am. It is the same thing in the old Act; that has not been changed.
The section which my hon. friend has just read is analogous to the section we are considering. If a railway company is incorporated by statute, the statute might very properly designate-
It always does.

the head office;
but it also gives the directors or shareholders power to change that head office from time, to time, which is practically what this Bill asks.

It is quite the contrary. You say in the first clause that you incorporate this company; and those directors whom you appoint are the company, are they not? The object is to form a company to operate the railway. They are the people who have the right to change the head office, even taking my hon. friend's argument. The company is not the Governor in Council, the company is the body that is going to be formed by this Bill we now have under consideration. Therefore, they have power to change the head office any time they please.
Amendment (Mr. Jacobs) negatived.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does clause 4 carry?

Before that is passed 1 would ask permission to read the Railway Act as it is now. I do not want to be taken as incorrect.
The head office of the company shall be in the place designated in the Special Act, but the company may, by by-law, from time to time, change the location of its head office to any place in Canada: Provided that notice of any such change shall be given to the secretary of the board.
Absolutely the same.
Who is the company in this case? Is it the Governor in Council, or the directors?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Section 1 says:
The Governor in Council may nominate such persons as may be deemed expedient, not less than five, nor more than fifteen, to be directors of the company hereby incorporated, and upon such nomination being made the persons so nominated, and their successors, and such other persons as may from time to time be nominated by the Governor in Council as directors, shall be and are hereby incorporated as a company.

Section agreed to.
On section 5-payment of directors:
The directors may be paid by the company, but the directors are the company. It is like saying that the directors may be paid by themselves. I do not think it is good drafting.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think that is the only way it could be drafted. The company pays the money, but the directors, in deciding what they as a company pay themselves, are subject to the supervisory power of the Governor in Council.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I suggest that the clause read:. "May be paid from the funds of the company such sums," and so on.

If the company has the financial career which attended the Canadian Northern and Intercolonial, there may be no funds to apply to the salaries of the directors; therefore the suggestion of the member for Port Arthur and Kenora (Mr. Keefer) may be a dangerous one.

Is (here any particular objection to stating in the Bill the amount to be paid to the directors or to the president? We do it in the case of the Railway Commission, the Civil Service Commission and the Superior Court and other judges who are paid by the Dominion Government. Why should tne amount to be paid to the president be determined by the Governor in Council instead of by Parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The number of the directors runs between five and fifteen, for the reasons clearly stated by the Minister of Railways and the Acting Prime Minister. The number will depend not only upon the composition of the system, but also upon what is found most convenient in the management of the road. The amount to be paid will necessarily depend, in some degree, at least, upon who constitute the directorate. Furthermore, the number of officers appointed will also be governed by that as a very important factor. The vicepresidents are themselves officers of the company and will be paid as such. It



would seem to me that we cannot possibly fix the salaries to be paid to the directors until we know what, in p'oint of numbers, shall be the constitution of the directorate.

Can we not fix the salary of the president of the Board of Directors?
I do not see why he should be paid more if there are eight or nine directors than he would if there are six or seven. If these men are to make a success of the operation of the railways they will have to devote their whole time to the work; therefore their salaries ought to be determined by Parliament.

It would be an unusual procedure to state in a statute what should be the salary of a president. It might be possible to fix the salary to be paid to the present president, but if he resigned to-morrow it might be impossible to get another man to fill the position at that salary, in which case the statute would bar the appointment of a president. There should be some flexibility both as to the number of directors and as to the remuneration. In a year's time, after some experience in operating the National Railways by a board, it may be found wise to reduce the number of the directors to three; and this suppositious board of three might be required to be technical men, in which event they would be paid very substantial salaries. I think, therefore, that the suggestion to leave the section in its present form is fair and that the committee should approve of it. It is not desirable that the statute fix definitely the number of directors, although perhaps that is not so objectionable; but it would be unfortunate if the statute fixed the remuneration of the directors. I do not think that the remuneration of directors is ever fixed by the constitution of a company-and this is the constitution of a company. The remuneration of officers is always a matter of by-law or resolution.

1 do not agree with the member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau); I think that no amount ought to be fixed as the remuneration of the directors, especially of the president. We have seen an example of this during the course of the present year in connection with public ownership. Mr. McAdoo, the former Director of Railways in the United States, left the service of the country to enter the service of Mary Pickford and Charlie Chaplin because these movie stars were offering to him higher salaries than were being paid by the United States of America. We ought not to
tMr. Meighen.]
place ourselves in such a position as to be unable to compete with any private concern if we have a good man and wish to retain him at the head of our railways.
Mr, L. A. LAPOINTE: I do not agree with my hon. friend (Mr. E. Lapointe). The gentleman he mentions was receiving $10,000, and I suppose he was replaced by a good man at the same price. It is currently known that railway companies pay their presidents and directors fabulous sums. Everybody knows that the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company gets $70,000 a year, and that the directors get proportionately large amounts. If the salaries of the president and directors of the Canadian National Railway Board are not fixed in this Act, is there not the danger that the Cabinet may pay them extraordinarily large amounts? I suggest that minimum and maximum amounts be stated so that excessive sums may not be paid to any one, no matter how good he is. This is particularly necessary because in the first section we do not say that these men shall give all their time to the work. They may continue to practice law, to carry on the work of a contractor, or to do anything they like, and still get the salary allotted to them by the Government.

I do not want to be understood as criticising, I simply want to know what special reasons there are for not mentioning the salaries of the president and directors of this railway company. The salaries of all the other officials of the Government-of the Railway Commission and the Civil Service Commission, for instance-are known, but no reason has been given for withholding the information as to the salaries of the officials of this road.
What are we paying the directors who are now operating?
I think it is $2,000 per annum. The information was given the other day.
What is the president of the road getting?
I could not say what his salary is as president and general manager. As a director he receives $2,000 per annum.
How much as manager?
I do not know.

Surely the Minister of Railways and the Government must know

what they are paying the manager. It is inconceivable that our money is being paid out through the Minister of Railways without him knowing the amount. He must suirely be in a position to answer that question if he wants to.
I said that as director he got a salary of $2,000 per annum. Before being promoted to the position of president, he was vice-president. I will inquire what his salary is as general manager.
Who provides the salaries foT the present board of directors?
The Canadian Northern Railway Company.
Do these directors fix their own salaries?
The salaries of the directors of the Canadian Northern Railway have been fixed at $2,000, by by-law, for several years I believe.
The present board has not been there for several years.

I said that the salaries of the directors of the Canadian Northern Railway have been $2,000 per annum for several years, and the present board of directors, -when they took office, simply continued at the same salary.

I understand that a certain Mr. Hanna is the gentleman in charge of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, whose stock the Government of this country, representing the people, acquired about a year ago at an expense of something over $10,000,000. We have present in the House the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid)-, the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen), the Acting Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), the minister from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean), who is minister of so many departments I cannot remember them all, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Car-vell), the Minister of Militia and Defence (Major-General Mewburn), the Secretary of State (Mr. Burrell), and under-secretaries too numerous to mention. Do I understand that not one of these gentlemen is able to tell the representatives of the people how much public money is given to Mr. Hanna per annum for administering the affairs of this road, which belongs to us, the people of Canada? What is the aggregate amount of money paid to Mr. Hanna? Surely that is within the knowledge of the various heads of departments that we, with so much pleasure. see before us this evening.
105i	*:rH

While it may seem strange that the Minister of Railways might not know the salary received by the general manager, I submit that that remark cannot apply to other ministers, and it is quite understandable to me that the Minister of Railways himself might not know the salary with such exactness that he would care to answer the question at the moment. I assume that the general manager is paid a very substantial salary; I hope he is. We are, however, dealing now with the allowances made to the directors, and the Minister of Railways has said that they receive $2,000 a year. I assume that they are paid this amount simply in pursuance of the precedent established some few years ago when the Government nominated directors at the time we obtained control of forty per cent of the Canadian Northern Railway stock. My own recollection is that the allowance made to the directors appointed by the Government was $2,000, and that salary has no doubt been continued. I understand it was intended to cover merely the out-of-pocket expenses of the directors in attending the meetings, or, perhaps, a little more than that. I km sure my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McM-aster) will be able to get precise information on the point tomorrow.
I may be quite wrong, but I believe that if the Minister of Railways applied to the gentleman sitting upon his left hand he could get the information immediately and give it to the House.
I was going on to remark that the fact of ministers not knowing the salary of the general manager is pretty good evidence that there is no politics in the administration of the road.

Interference is one
thing, and an entire lack of information is another. I really think that the Minister of Railways knows what the general manager of this great system belonging to the people gets a year. If he does not know, it would not become me to characterize such want of information on the part of a gentleman administering one of the most important departments of the Government.

I do not want to make a statement until I am sure of the facts. I have already promised to get the information. The gentleman sitting on my left has not the information. If he had, I should be verj glad to give it.

Parliament is entitled
to certain consideration on the part of the Government and the ministers. The Acting

Prime Minister said this afternoon that the object in forming this company was to make a success of the operation of these Canadian railways, and that to make a success of them, it was necessary to get the best men. Would any man of ordinary intelligence believe that these directors would give their best ability to the road for $2,000 a year, when the draymen of Montreal are striking to-day for $1,560 a year? To tell the House that shows no respect for Parliament or for the men who inquired what the salary was. We want to get at the bottom of this thing. Either the directors occupy other positions in the company and are paid for those positions, or they do not. If they are receiving only $2,000 a year as directors, you cannot, expect them to give the best of their ability or much of their time to the railway company for the good of the country.
If they occupy any other positions, such as general manager, or vice president, or secretary, or under-secretary, and get additional salaries, we should be so informed. We want to know what these men who are going to act as directors* are being paid for their services to the country. If we are going to go begging for men to work gratuitously, you will not get the best results. My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) has just said that $2,000 is practically pin-money to pay their expenses travelling back and forth. That means that they are giving their services gratis. No man will leave his business and work for the Government for $2,000 as a director, and if that is the class of men that it is intended to appoint it is high time Parliament took the matter into its hands. 1 do not care how much you pay a man provided his services are profitable. When 1 hire an employee I pay him a salary based on the degree of his usefulness to me in my office, and the same principle ought to apply in connection with the railway. To give us the bare answer that the directors are getting $2,000 is not fair, and is tantamount to saying, "You have been our laughing-stock; we have been just jollying you around and are still going to make you believe that we are going to get the best genius and ability in the country to manage the railroad."
The directors are getting $2,000, and some in executive capacities may be getting additional salaries.
That is what we want to know. Are they simply directors or do they occupy other positions to which salaries are attached?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The suggestion that we are flouting Parliament by telling the truth is indeed a new one.
Telling the truth partly.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What the directors are actually getting is $2,000 a year. There are two directors who also occupy other positions for which they receive salaries- Mr. Hanna, president of the road, and Mr. Mitchell, financial controller. As such they receive salaries voted by the directors, just the same as the management of any other company votes its money. There is no question that Parliament is entitled to know what the general manager gets, and Parliament will know. But Parliament is just as much interested financially in what the engineers on the road get as in the salaries of the general manager or the financial controller. In fact, five cents an hour in the payment of the engineers would amount to more in all probability, many times more in actual outlay, than the cost of the general manager. We do not happen to know the exact figure, although I can assure the Committee that it is a fraction of the figure that is given as being paid the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. But I do not think that Parliament need necessarily know that in order to vote Clause 5, because that simply puts it in our power to pay to the directors such sums as may be deemed expedient. The principle we have gone on in the past is this: We have not asked the directors as such to give their full time to the road. They give a proportion of their time anala-gous to that which the directors of the Canadian Pacific Railway give to that company. I do not know what the directors of the Canadian Pacific Railway get, but usually directors of a large company receive something in the neighbourhood of $20 a meeting. If that is what the Canadian Pacific Company allow it would practically amount to $2,000 a year, as we are allowing in this case. In the future it will not be deemed wise to ask from the directors only a portion of their time, and if the number is smaller and we ask them to give more of their time, they will have to be paid more than $2,000.

Listening to the discussion during the last ten minutes, it has struck me that we are an easily deluded crowd both in this House and in the country generally. We are foolish enough to think that the business of the country is conducted in a sane, considerate, careful manner by the Government. I was think-

ing when the railways were taken over- and I am sure hon. gentlemen sitting on the other side thought the same-that the Minister of Railways would call into his office the heads of the different departments of these railways, particularly the management, and that he would say to them: "You have been in the service of the Canadian Northern for the last twenty years-or whatever it may be-and you must understand that you are no longer in the service of that company, but are in the employment of the Government. We want your full time and want to know what your salary is; and we want you to know what is expected of you by the Government. Further, we want to know the members of your staff, what they are getting and what salaries they are willing to work for." That would be something .like business. But we have here to-night a sad spectacle displayed by this learned and able Government, who, in the management of this great enterprise on which they pride themselves as handling in so magnificent a manner, are unable to give an answer to a simple question that is asked incidentally. They are asked what is the salary of the chief man in the management of the road, and there is absolute silence from Dan to Beersheba. I am sorry for the hon. gentlemen who sit around the Government-I am not sorry for the Government because they could have put themselves right-for these hon. gentlemen must feel sadly humiliated by the ignorance displayed by the iGovern-ment in so important a matter. Perhaps the Minister of Railways will put the question in the same category as the railway ties, and suggest that it is not in 'the public interest that we should know the facts. But it will never kill the public to be aware of all that this aggregation knows. What would be thought of the secretary in the most backward rural school section in any province who, if he were asked at the annual meeting how much the teachers were being paid, should say he did not know? Why, he would be told, " You are a very stupid owl, and have no right to be in the position you hold." Now, we have a great Government appointed by a big majority and consisting of a combination of the talents of two parties, and yet to-night they are absolutely unable to tell us anything at all about the working of this system as regards the most important feature of the whole thing, the services of their chief men and the salaries that are paid them. I think it is time that the people should know really what is going on, or at least, that there is nothing going on, so far as
the proper management of this government-owned railway is concerned. We should hesitate before passing any further clauses of this Bill in view of what we have learned of the knowledge, the calibre and the degree of information possessed by the hon. gentlemen who propose to operate under this Bill.
On section 6-no personal responsibility of directors:
I would ask that section 6 stand.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Section 6 stands.
On section 7-first meeting:
, Mr. FIELDING: I venture to suggest that the members of this House and the people have a right to know the salary of every official who is paid out of the public treasury of Canada, and if the minister is not able to give us the salary that Mr. Hanna is getting, I say that we ought not to proceed further with this Bill until we get that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) that in connection with the Government railway system information as to the salary of any officer or director should be brought down to the House, by reason of the fact that the Government is the corporation and the sole shareholder of the Canadian National Railway system. There is no doubt in my mind as to the correctness of that position. But when information is asked for it is desirable that it should be given accurately. I have no doubt whatever that the Minister of Railways has in his mind approximately what the president of the Canadian National Railway system has been receiving.
I have that information myself; but if the question is asked me positively, what is the precise sum-then I desire to obtain the information. in order that I may give it accurately to the House. It does not occur to me, in view of the fact that the Minister of Railways has stated that he will obtain the information and give it, that the position which is taken is in any way improper or lacking in respect for the House... As he has undertaken to get the informa

tion, it would occur to me that the Committee might very well proceed with the/ other sections in order that we may make; progress with this legislation.
It is eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, that is another reason.

I might say to my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) that a question was asked the other day about a number of officials. I brought down the information and the question was answered. It is as the Minister of Finance has stated; I would not like, offhand, to state the salaries of officials with-
11 p.m. out looking them up and being quite sure I was accurate. That is the only reason why I have asked the committee to let matters stand until to-morrow. When the Bill is again before the House I will have the information.

I heartily endorse the
statement made by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr.Fielding). It is really a most intolerable situation when the minister who is responsible to this House and the country cannot give approximate information on an important subject of this kind. Surely he can give us the basis on which the salaries are paid if they are paid on a sliding scale or percentage. If he cannot give us the exact figure, and if the salary is on a percentage or commission basis, surely we should at least receive that information to-night. It is a most astonishing situation that the minister is not able to give the House even approximate information on this subject.
I understand that the minister is willing to allow the matter to stand to-night and adjourn.
No; I said I could not see any reason why we could not proceed with the Bill as I had promised to get this information and have it for to-morrow.
I think the minister will be well 'advised and that he will get along just as rapidly if he does not insist on further progress to-night. It is eleven o'clock now.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have sent out, and if hon. gentlemen will be patient we will have this very valuable information in a moment or two.
Mr. McKENZIE; We never broke the agreement we made early in the session that eleven o'clock is a reasonable hour to adjourn.
Sir THOMAS WHITENlf my hon. friend puts it on the ground that this is a reasonable hour to adjourn that is one thing, but if he puts it on the ground that the information asked for is not immediately forthcoming, it is another thing. I am entirely agreeable to adjournment on the

ground that the hour is late, but not on the ground that information which is to be brought down is not immediately forthcoming.	i
Whichever ground is the more agreeable to my hon. friend's sensibilities will be acceptable to us.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I asked that telephonic communication be had with a member of the directorate who is in town, and the information that he gives is that the present salary is $25,000.

Shall clause 7 carry?
Mr. LU'ClEN CANNON (Dorchester) (translation):	Mr. Chairman, before proceeding any further with this Bill, I should like to get some information form the Minister of Eailways (Mr. Eeid) about clause 7. Prior to my being returned to the House of Commons, Mr. Chairman, I had enjoyed the privilege of sitting in the Quebec legislature, where for four years I represented the very same constituency the views of which I have the honour of voicing and upholding on the floor of this House. In the Quebec Legislature I evidently had a favorable opportunity for making myself familiar with the procedure which is in force in the committees of that legislature and with the way in which the members of the provincial Government dealt with the people's representatives, whenever a public bill came up before the House. And although I sat there for several years, I must admit in all candour-and I do so without fear of contradiction from the hon. Minister of Eailways-that never did I attend and I do not believe any member of this House either on this side or on the other side; ever witnessed such a sorry spectacle, such a painful sight, such a baffling spectacle as the one offered by this Government to-night. Here we have this Government drawn from the most brillant talents of both political parties throughout the country, the gifted men whom Mackenzie and Mann, after touring the provinces, could pick up and whom they-intrusted with the several portfolios and Departments of the Canadian Administration. These are the men who are called upon to grapple with one of the most important problems, a reconstruction problem which has to be solved and cannont be shelved, I mean the railway problem. A Bill is brought down. We debated it this afternoon, we have discussed it to-night, and when we demand information, when we ask the Minister of Eailways to bring

down and communicate to the House such data as we are entitled to, he evades answering our questions, or replies that he knows nothing about the matter.
Mr. Chairman, I want to declare this, I want to tell the members of the Government, I want particularly to tell the Acting Minister of Justice that we are sitting here as the representatives of the people, that we have been sent here to protect the most sacred interests of the Canadian people, and so long as I am able to lift my voice here, so long as I have any strength and vigour left in me, never shall I allow such a Bill to pass, without the representatives of the people being given the most elementary information with regard to this legislation. We have had enough legislation in this country which was carried by snap votes, we have had enough legislation which the representatives of the people were forced to pass under the pressure of a so-called war emergency. Those days are over. We have come back to the days when the Constitution and Parliamentary traditions in this country have to be respected, and if the Government wants to govern, the Minister of Railways ought to remember that he must govern according to Parliamentary procedure and not otherwise. Let him come before the House, supported by the acting Minister of Justice or by the Under Secretary of State for Lx-ternal Affairs, let him come down here, supported by the Acting Minister of Justice or Maclean), let him come down here even with the support of the whole Cabinet, and I tell him, that never shall he succeed in having a Bill like this enacted and crystallised into law, unless he does us at least the elementary favour of acquainting us with the subject of his words.

There is no provision in the Bill as to where the directors are to meet, o.r who shall call the meeting. Section 7 is certainly a most unusual one; it provides:-
The first directors may after appointment hold a meeting at such time and place as they think proper, for the purpose of passing by-laws and organizing the company.
It is most extraordinary that the so-called first directors are to hold a meeting, but there is no place mentioned for that meeting and no person designated to call it. I cannot understand how the company can hope to do business properly if they are going to act in this half-hearted way.

The company is not organized yet, and it has no secretary. The
directors will meet and organize and appoint a secretary.

May I draw the minister's attention to the fact that some one will have to take the lead in the matter, some one will have to call the directors together. They will not all the together in one place and all be moved by the spirit to get together to pass by-laws and do other things. It seems to me that the point of the ihon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) is well taken. There should be sotme one designated to perform this very necessary duty. The Government might give the first director named the power of calling a meeting, or, perhaps, the not unusual method of passing an Order in Council might be adopted. By Order in (Council it might be provided that the first meeting might be held at a certain time and at a certain place.
Mr. J. D. iREID: The directors are to be appointed by Order in Council. When such appointment is made they would be notified and the notice sent them could state that they might meet at a certain place at a certain time and organize.

That would be a propel method, but that is not the method that is contemplated by Clause 7. That clause merely says that the first directors may, after appointment, hold the meeting at such time and place as they think proper. If the minister would insert that the directors should meet " as they may be directed by Order in Council to do," or something of that sort, it would make the clause workable. As drafted it is not workable.
Why?

I will do my best to answer the hon. gentleman. The clause reads as follows:-
The first directors may after appointment hold a meeting at such time and place as they think proper, for the purpose of passing bylaws, and organizing the company.
Now, when and where are they to get together? It is quite clear that some procedure must be outlined. The Government must summon the meeting by Order in Council, or the directors may meet on the call of the Minister of Railways.
There is a secretary of the company.

How will the secretary know when to call a meeting? The secretary does not call a meeting of his own motion, he does it on instructions from the

president or the board. The point is, there is no procedure in this clause indicating how the first meeting is to be called.
What secretary does the minister refer to who would call this meeting together?
It might be the secretary of the company.
The secretary of what company?

My recollection of most, companies incorporated under Acts which correspond to the English Companies Act is, that the first meeting is called by the provisional directors, and they can meet anywhere they like.
Who are the provisional directors?
The directors who are subscribers to the memorandum of association in the first place.
There is nothing of that kind mentioned in this Bill.

Still it is an analogous case. The subscribers to the memorandum of association are the first directors, absolutely so if they state that in the articles of association. Very well, the provisional directors call the first meeting in any way they see fit.
Which provisional directors?

The hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) suggested that the name of the place of meeting should be designated in the Bill. That is hardly a fair objection because the provisional directors-or the first directors, which means practically the same thing-should not- be required to have their meeting at one particular place because it may not be convenient to have the meeting in one place more than another. The directors may not themselves at the time have received their charter. There is no purpose therefore, as iar as I can see, in designating the place of the first meeting. In any event, the objection is very technical.

How should the first meeting of the directors of this company have been organized if this omission in the clause had not been pointed out.
. Sir THOMAS WHITE: They would proceed under this Bill precisely in the same way as they do under the Railway Act. Even without the direction which is eon-

tained here the provisional directors mentioned in the Railway Act get together.
There are none in this case.
I draw the minister's attention to the fact that there are no provisional directors mentioned in the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The directors mentioned by the Government are analogous to the provisional directors. The Governor in Council nominates directors and these directors, get together at such time and place as they deem proper, and the business of the company commences. I am quite satisfied that the hon. gentlemen are not [DOT] over-earnest in putting forward this objection.
We are.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am glad to have the assurance of my hon. friend, but I had a higher regard for his knowledge of company law. Provisional directors, without any such provision at all, have been able under the Companies Act and the Railway Act to organize a company and commence its business. Here we have directors appointed by the Governor in Council. Even without this section they would get together for the very purpose mentioned. But to make it quite explicit there is this provision, that they shall get together at such time as they deem proper and commence the operations of the company. According to the view put forward by the hon. gentleman there would be an absolute dead centre, so to speak, no action could be taken; although the Government had appointed the directors and this provision is in the Act, still the company would remain without organization and business could not commence. I submit that that is an untenable position.
Mr. 1L. A. LAPOINTE: I would like to know that the word "may" in this section means. Does not the hon. minister think the word "should" is more appropriate. 1 would suggest also that you put "after fifteen days of their appointment" or " after thirty days of their appointment." It seems to me you should provide that a certain number of days after their appointment they "shall" do this, instead of "may."

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It seems to me that the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) is thinking of shareholders and so confusing himself.
No.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The shareholders appoint their directors, then the directors meet at any time they see fit and pass by-laws, and thereafter they are governed by their by-laws. This is the same position exactly. The Government appoint a board of directors just as shareholders would do, and then it is the duty of those directors to meet, which they do whenever convenient, usually immediately after appointment. I do not see what difficulty the hon. member is labouring under.
I want to know, Mr. Chairman, what would happen in that ease with the word "may" there instead of "shall."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
"May" is the
same as " shall."	.

They may not
take any action. What would you do then?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I assume that my hon. friend is earnest in his desire for information, and as far as I can I am very glad to impart it to him. The duty is upon the directors of getting together and organizing. The word " may " is properly used in legislation of this kind, and really has the mandatory force of " shall." That is a well known principle of construction.

Before poceeding
any further, may I suggest that my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) should answer the question asked by my hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Cannon). He is certainly entitled to the information, and it ought to be given to him.
Mr. A. K. MA0LEAN: I intended answering my hon. friend from Dorchester, Mr. Chairman, but I was prevented by somebody on the other side of the House getting the floor ahead of me. I wish to say that I dissent entirely from the remarks of the hon. member for Dorchester and I do not recollect one single particular in which I agree with him. I can very strongly commend to the Committee the adoption of this section, and after that I think we might very well rise feeling we have done a very good day's work. I cannot see any purpose in phrasing this section in" any other way. As the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer) has well stated, in a company where there are shareholders it is perhaps necessary for their protection that the first meeting of the directors be made public, that is, that the shareholders should know the time and place, and therefore that machinery should be set up in order to protect the rights of the shareholders; but here the
first directors are nominated by the Government, they ar.e the shareholders as well as the directors, and I do think that hon. gentlemen opposite are rather too critical of this section. I submit, with all due deference to them, that no purpose could be served by enacting the clause in any other form.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 7 carry?

The hon. member for
Halifax, the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce, must expect difficulties in connection with this Bill. It is a thing he can fall down and worship, because there is nothing like it in the heavens above or in the earth below, or in the waters under .the earth. My hon. friend never saw any body consisting solely of directors, with no shareholders, no head office, no beginning or ending-
No capital stock.

When we are talking of directors we always have in mind a body separate and apart from shareholders; but when we consider this Bill the directors are the whole thing, because they are pushed forward and backward, like railway time and other time, by the Governor in Council. My hon. friend will find his education and training in company law-I must give him credit for knowing a good deal about it -do not fit in here at all, and he must go to school again, because this is a company that expects to live in an atmosphere of company law, but has nothing in common with the ordinary company at all. I hope the Acting Prime Minister is in a better humour now-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am always in
good humour.
-and is willing to let us go home, especially if I say it is well on in the night. I will forget everything concerning the lack of information and say it is time we adjourned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I know my hon. friend is a good Presbyterian like myself, and, consequently, does not like late hours; and as he is in a very obliging and genial frame of mind at the present time we will have very much pleasure in agreeing to his suggestion. I therefore move that the Committee do now rise. I think we will make just as much progress to-morrow.
Progress reported.

Thursday, April 24, 1919.
The House met at Three o'clock.
Mr. W. F. NICKLE (Kingston) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 77, respecting divorce.
Explain.

The object of the Bill is to constitute divorce courts in Canada. In each province the Supreme Court will be constituted a divorce court, and the Exchequer Court will be a court of divorce for the Dominion. The Bill sets out the reasons for which divorce may be granted and for which annulment of marriage may be declared. It deals with the question of domicile of husband and wife and touches also the question of alimony. There are further provisions concerning the decrees of the court. The general purport of the Bill is not only to facilitate divorce, but to harmonize the divorce laws of the country and to make the position of man and woman equal.

subtopic: DISCHARGE OR LEAVE FOR SOLDIERS AT HALIFAX.
speechtext:
I wish to bring to the attention of the House a matter of importance, referred to in a Charlottetown paper of April 21, and to ask the Minister of Militia a question regarding it. This is the item on which I base my question:
Important to Farmers. Premier Arsenault will meet a delegation of farmers having sons in the military at Halifax and who desire to have them granted home leave, or discharge, on Friday 25th inst. at 1.30 p.m., in the Y.M.C.A.
Has Premier Arsenault any authority from the Government to grant home leave or discharge to any of the soldiers who are at Halifax? May I also ask why soldiers who were called to the colours after the armistice was signed are still being held at Halifax?
Major-General MEWBURN (Minister of Militia): I may say, offhand, that the Premier of Prince Edward Island has no authority, whatever, from the Militia Department regarding the soldiers at Halifax. I am not aware of any men having been sent there since the armistice. A certain number of troops are, of course, held there during disembarkation, and for carrying on garrison duty. If the hon. gentleman will put his question on the Order Paper, I shall be very glad to give him the answer.
The House again in Committee on Bill No. 70, to incorporate Canadian National

Railway Company and respecting Canadian National Railways.-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 7-first meeting:

When the Committee rose last night, this Bill was under discussion. Sections 1, 4 and 5 had been adopted. Sections 2, 3 and 6 had been allowed to stand. The Committee was discussing section 7 concerning the first meeting of directors. Shall section 7 carry?

Have the Government, over night, framed an amendment to this section to make it more understandable and workable? It says that the directors may hold a meeting, but there is no provision as to when or where the meeting shall be held.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Section 7 is, in my judgment, all right, as it stands, and there is nothing practical in the objection of the hon. member. When the board of directors are appointed, undoubtedly, one of them will be asked, or all may be asked in the appointment to meet at a certain time and place. That is one way of arranging a meeting. If that is not done, then they can, by correspondence, without meeting, arrange where they will meet the first time. That may be done by wire.

Supposing a director in Saskatchewan should decide to call a meeting at McTaggart and a director who is appointed down in St. John should decide to call a meeting at St. John, just as last night members of the Committee wanted the head office at every way station along the line. Why not make the thing practical? Surely the Government have had time to make this clause understandable to people reading it. Why not insert at the beginning of the clause, or after the words "organizing the company," a provision that the first meeting shall be called at the instance of the Governor in Council by whom the directors will be notified when and where to meet; or, it might be provided that the first named director shall name the place of meeting? In the Bill, no head office is provided; no capital stock is provided; there are no directors and no shareholders. Surely it ought to be within the ability of some members of the Government to draft a section to take care of this.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is no difficulty in drafting a section to take care of this, but I am afraid we are not able to draft a section to satisfy the hon. member. It is possible that one man appointed might [Major General Mewburn.]
make one excuse, and another, another, and that they would never agree to meet at any place or time. The imagination might reach to that possibility, but, if that ever takes place, then I shall have the very greatest deference for the hon. member. Such a thing is utterly unthinkable. These men, if they are not by their appointment asked to meet, will, by wire, arrange to meet at once, and there is no practical or even remote possibility of their not doing so. That is the way it is always done. As a matter of wording, of course, you might tell them where to meet the first time, or tell one of them to tell the others, but that is wholly unnecessary. A message would do the whole thing, so why go to the trouble of putting unnecessary words into this section? It is in the first place drafted by a man who has, undoubtedly, the most experience in corporation law in Canada. As to its working, there is no doubt iii the mind of any sensible or reasonable man, and I do not think there is any doubt in the mind of the hon. member.
Who is the gentleman who drafted this section?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Zebulon A. Lash.

Here you have the result of the first error that was made. In any ordinary railway Bill it is provided that the first meeting of the directors shall be held at the head office of the company, on the call of the secretary, but here the Government do not want to determine where the head office of the company shall be for fear of hurting some friends behind them, for fear they will kick. This, they think, had better be done in the silence of the council room, after the members have gone away. Then let the word slide out that the head office will bo in Toronto, or Montreal, or wherever it is. If the head office weTe determined, the rest would be easy. The Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) need not stand behind the fact that the ablest man in Canada drafted this section. I think in the 'heads of the 232 members of this House there is more than in the head of one man, whoever he may be, even if his, name be Zebulon. The objection of the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) is rightly taken. This is our railway and we want to know when the directors are going to have a meeting to organize. We are giving them extraordinary powers, and the Government is taking extraordinary powers and setting its own powers aside whenever it is threatened with anything that is important, when-

ever it will have to guard the public treasury and see that expenditures are not made recklessly or uselessly. Section 6 of the Bill, which protects the directors from any liability to anybody, stands, and I want to have some discussion about it. It makes those men safe from the operation of the law if they do anything crooked. Further on the Bill authorizes them to do certain things, which, under the General Railway Act, no railway company is permitted to do.
I think we are entitled to know what these men are going to do and when they are going to organize, and to be in a position to see every step they take hereafter. I would ask my hon. friend to let the clause stand, and if Mr. Zebulon Lash is the only man who is sufficiently informed on the subject he should be consulted again in order that we might have a clause that would be satisfactory to the House.

I think the meeting should be called at some specified place, it does not matter where, and at any -time and by any person you wish to designate. I do not think there would be any objection as to where the meeting should be called, or as to who should call it; but it should be 'stated in this clause. It ought to be at the call of the Governor in Council, the Minister of Railways, the Minister of the Interior, or the Acting Minister of Justice.

I approve of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Pontiac, that it would be well to have the meeting called by some particular minister, preferably the Minister of Railways, who is the proper person to convene the first meeting. I suggest that the first meeting should be held at the seat of government here in Ottawa, where the directors might be in immediate touch with all the representatives of the Railway Department. I have no particular preference for Ottawa, but if Ottawa were selected as the place of meeting it would remove any jealousy on the part of cities like Toronto, Montreal, Quebec, Vancouver, Three Rivers; Regina, and Calgary.

I disagree with hon. members who are opposing this clause. It seems to me that on the face of it it is workable and reasonable and provides all that any business man would want. If this House were to name a place it might happen to be the worst place that could be selected. I think that this is .a matter for the directors themselves and that it is only reasonable that they should hold the meeting at such
time and place as they think proper. Business men will have complete charge of the matter, and it is unreasonable to presume that they are going to act like school boys or that they will quarrel and disagree as soon as they meet. "As they think proper" means as they consider most convenient for the purposes of the meeting. They are the operative and executive officers, and surely it is fatuous to contend that they are going to behave like school boys. They are business men and we must assume that they will take the wisest course open to them.

The general Railway Act provides " all general meetings, whether annual or special, shall be held at the head office of the company." If the Government, for fear of displeasing somebody, are afraid to select the head office, the rest of the Bill will suffer. We are all interested to see the organization under way and the Canadian railways put on such a footing that the company will not be ashamed of them and we will not read of wrecks, and trains running behind time and passengers being disappointed. I would like to see them organize and pass their by-laws be

fore we prorogue, so that we may be afforded an opportunity to criticise their work if it is not as it should be. There is no reason why, as my hon. friend from Pontiac says, it should not be provided that the first directors shall, after appointment, call a meeting within a month in the city of Toronto, if you will, or at the place where the head office now is. I suggest, therefore, that the directors shall within thirty days after, appointment hold a meeting at the head office of the Canadian Northern Railway in the city of Toronto for the purpose of passing by-laws and organizing the company.

The hon. member for Three Rivers fails apparently to distinguish between general and special meetings of the company after it is once formed, and this clause in question, which really provides for the meeting is preliminary to the formation of the board. This clause is intended to provide for purposes of organization so that the board may get together and, after consideration, determine where the head office of the company shall be.

Why not say who shall call the meeting? You have a number of directors, five, ten or fifteen, and any one of them would have power to call the meeting. I think some one man should be designated to call the meeting, as is done in ordinary companies. This is an extra-

ordinary condition of things, for here is a company without a head office. There is no place where the meeting might be held. In all probability it will be held in Mackenzie and Mann's office, where no doubt they will have the counsel of Mr. Lash. I do not care where you hold the meeting, but I think it is only reasonable that some person should be named to call the meeting.

I do not think the matter is of very great importance, but I am not sure that the clause is workable. This is to arrange for the first meeting of the directors who, it says may, after appointment, hold a meeting at such time and place as they think proper. How are they going to do the "thinking" if they have had no meeting? What is to be the evidence that they did that thinking unless they meet for that purpose? If it is proposed that they shall hold a first meeting and before that decide the time and place of meeting; they have to do some thinking hut how are we to know that it is the wish of the directors? I am not captious in the matter but it does not look to me to be very practical. I do not attach as much importance to that as some other hon. gentlemen appear to do, hut I think the section might be made clearer.

I think the point made by the hon. member (Mr. Fielding) is a very strong one. I mentioned it in private last night after we rose. The clause says that they may meet at the time and place they think proper. They must therefore have met together if they are doing that thinking in common. The clause provides for a meeting before the meeting. I't would be a simple matter to accept the suggestions of the other side and fix a definite place and time when the business of the company shall commence in connection with this very serious and large undertaking.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
First of all, on the general question of thinking and meeting it is not necessary that men shall meet together in order to think. They can think as to whether they wiH meet without being physically together. The thinking is usually, as a matter of practice, expressed by telegraph. There is nothing new in this. This Bill combines certain things that are not combined in the usual run of legislation. Usually provisional directors are appointed; the provisional directors meet and they call a meeting of the shareholders. They pass certain by-laws and then the place where they shall meet afterwards is fixed. The 	.
general Railway Act, which contemplates provisional directors, does not say where they shall meet the first time. These people are not strictly speaking provisional directors but in so far as meeting for the first time is concerned they do the same as provisional directors. Section 74 of the Railway Act reads:
O The persons mentioned by name as such in the Special Act shall be the provisional directors of the company.
(2)	A majority of such provisional directors shall form a quorum.
(3)	The provisional directors may,-
(a)	forthwith open stock books and procure subscriptions of stock for the undertaking;
(b)	receive payments on account of stock subscribed;
(c)	cause plans and surveys to be made; and
(d)	deposit in any chartered bank* of Canada moneys received by them on account of stock subscribed.
(4)	The moneys so received and deposited shall not be withdrawn, except for the purposes of the undertaking, or upon the dissolution of the company.
(5)	The provisional directors shall hold office as such until "the first election of directors.
The provisional directors have to meet to do that, but the Act does not provide where or when they shall meet. It is merely done as a matter of course. I quite agree with the hon. member (Mr. Fielding) that the matter is of no possible consequence at all.
