This is just the same as the provision with regard to provisional directors which has been in operation during all these years without any trouble or inconvenience whatsoever occurring.

The conditions are different. When you ask for a charter you have no organization whatever. You have subscribed money and deposited it in a bank whereas in this case you have a going concern. If it is possible to delay this meeting they might wait for two or three months before calling it. The Acting Minister of Justice may say that that is unthinkable but we have seen such things here that no member of this House can conceive of a thing that would _ not be done by hon. gentlemen opposite. Here the conditions are known; they are at present existing. We have a going concern; it is now practically what it is going to be except that there have been certain manipulations of the Railway Act in connection with this Bill to give the Governor in Council certain powers that may be advantageously used for political purposes, and putting upon the company certain obligations in ordeT that the Government cannot be criticised if certain things are done. The Bill gives

powers to the company that the general Railway Act denies to ordinary companies and the general directors are made immune from any responsibility to any shareholder, director, officer, or employee of the company. Why not determine that within thirty days after the appointment of the directors, the president shall call a meeting in the city of Ottawa for the purpose of organizing. They have to be near the Governor in Council or the Minister of Railways, who is supposed to be the Governor in Council in this connection because they have to be checked up and he has to give his approval to everything they do.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is no actual
president.
The manager, if you like.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
You might create one,
I suppose, but that is absolutely unnecessary. We can only pass legislation like this and hope for good results on the assumption that the men who are going to be appointed will be reasonable business men. You might say that they must meet within a week, but that does not ensure that we will get good results. They might meet within a week or they might not. If they met within a week they might never meet again. Then you would not have any clause compelling them to meet. Assuming that they will act as business men, the Bill is all right because a similar clause has proved all right during all these years.

There can be no objection to saying that the directors shall meet at such time and place as the Governor in Council may direct for that purpose. I do not expect that there shall be a time set, but that would meet the objection of some hon. gentlemen. I cannot see any objection to that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is no objection
to it. It makes the Bill neither better nor worse, but if it will expedite the Bill it might as w'ell go in.

Just as the hon. member (Mr. Fielding) rose I wras about to propose an amendment. The Bill now reads:
The first directors may after appointment hold a meeting at such time and place as they think proper, for the purpose of passing bylaws, and organizing the company.
I would move that the words " they think proper " be struck out and that the following words be substituted: "may be designated by the Minister of Railways and Canals." Then it will read:
The first directors may after appointment hold a meeting at such time and place as may
be designated by the Minister of Railways and Canals for the purpose of passing by-laws, and organizing the company.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is all right as it is, but that is all right too.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 8-executive committee:

The board of directors are going to have an executive committee and they are going to give the executive committee powers for the administration of the road. The executive committee will not be the creature of the Governor in Council because I do not see anything in the Bill whereby the actions of the executive committee will be subject to ratification by the Governor in Council.
I theiefore presume that the executive committee, or some of them, will be appointed by by-law by the board of directors, and the executive committee is practically and actually the managing body of the railway. In this case the Government declines to assume any responsibility and says: "You may create an executive committee, but if the executive committee makes any recommendations we do not have to ratify them, because we were not consulted. Go to the board of directors- we cannot go into the management of this railway; it is up to the directors to see that everything is all right." Now I want this executive committee and the powers to be entrusted to it to be controlled by Parliament.

In all large .corporations such as this, where the board of directors do not live at the place where the head office is located, they appoint an executive committee for the purpose of carrying on the business between the regular meetings. In the present instance the directors live a long distance apart. One of them resides in Saskatchewan, another in Manitoba, and the rest live in Eastern Canada. The object of this clause is to enable the executive committee to carry on business in the interval between the meetings of directors. The directors, of course, are appointed by the Government and are responsible for the action of the executive committee, and any action taken by the executive committee in the interval would be ratified and confirmed by the directors at the regular meeting. Otherwise, of course, the directors would be supposed to live where they could be called together at any moment, frequently on only an hour or a day's notice. At the present time, in connection with the operation of the Canadian National Rail-

ways, I think six is the quorum for an executive committee meeting.
To whom does the present executive committee report?
To the board of directors.
As actually constituted.
Yes. The executive committee reports to the directors at the regular meeting.
That is only as regards the by-laws that were passed for the operation of the old Canadian Northern Railway.
Of course the directors of the old Canadian Northern Railway passed the by-laws under which the executive cornmmittee is now acting. Presumably the new directors w^U pass new bylaws.

There is where the
trouble arises again. The by-laws may be passed by the company, which consists of directors appointed by the Government, and my hon. friends opposite take it for granted that faultless, sinless and impeccable men are going to be appointed. We on this side do not believe in that because we do not believe in the appointors, if I may coin a term, and that is the reason why we want to be careful, and desire to have some check put upon all these powers that are being conferred. As the minister says, the executive committee will be responsible to the board of directors, and the latter very often will be desirous to have some excuse with respect to the actions of the executive committee if it will only help the Government. That is what we fear, and that is what we want to guard against. There is nothing in the Bill which provides that the by-laws shall be controlled by anybody. In the case of an ordinary company the bylaws would have to be submitted to the shareholders, that is to the people whose money was invested in the enterprise, but here there is no such safeguard. II want these by-laws, .and the powers which are to be entrusted to the executive, to be controlled by Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Under the Railway Act certain of the by-laws of a railway company, if not all, must be approved by the shareholders. In this case the by-laws that ordin-. arily would be approved by the shareholders have to be approved by the Governor in Council. iSection 9 of the Bill says:

Whenever under the provisions of the Railway Act, or any other statute or law, the approval, sanction or confirmation by shareholders is required, such approval, sanction or confirmation may be given by the Governor in Council.
Consequently, the by-laws would have to be approved by the Governor in Council wherever the Railway Act required them to be approved by shareholders.
That is a vicious principle.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is a pretty old one.
Mr. 'BUREAU:	Not in other countries.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is a pretty old one
in Canada.
Only since the war.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I thought the hon. gentleman was arguing that the by-laws should be approved by the Governor in Council.
No, I say they should be approved by Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Well, I am afraid I will have to take issue with my hon. friend there. If the functions of Parliament are to be extended in that way I do not know when it is going to get its work done. However, the point I rose to speak to was that the by-laws are now required to be approved by the Governor in Council. Those by-laws, according to section 8 of the Bill, may provide for the appointment of an executive committee, but that committee must all be members of the Board of Directors. Consequently, those members of the executive committee already have received the sanction of the Governor in Council. It appears very manifest that the board, particularly if the membership is Canadian-wide, will require an executive committee.

What is the necessity for section 9 at all? Is it not understood that the Board of Directors has the right to appoint managers, and is as a body responsible for the whole management of the affairs put in their hands? Is it not also a custom, as well as a thing understood, that the board can exercise its powers in such a manner within itself as it may deem advisable? If it is the judgment of the board that a committee, the working part of that body, shall exercise the powers of a few of their own number, why should we tell them what to do? Have they not the general powers to carry on the business of the company as they deem proper?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Undoubtedly they have the powers within the very same sphere of authority as the powers of directors of any railway company, except as modified by this Bill. That is to say, where any railway company does not require to come to its shareholders for sanction, then this board of directors would not require to come; but if it requires to come to the shareholders, the method of doing so is to make application for an Order in Council ratifying any Act of the board which requires ratification by the shareholders.

The minister did not
touch exactly 'the point I asked about. Why should we tell them' whether they have the right to appoint an executive committee within themselves, when as a matter of common law and. practice they have that right?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think they
have that right unless it is statutorily given. No executive committee could exercise any but statutory powers.
They can exercise general powers vested in such bodies.
From among themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not unless they are authorized to elect an executive committee with those powers, and they could, not under common law or under any practice-
They could appoint a manager.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Of course; but they can. not delegate their powers to an executive committee unless they have statutory authority for that purpose.
The directors are themselves in fact an executive committee.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are.

Because they could not delegate to themselves powers that they do not possess. They have power to act as an executive committee. Each individual is a member of the executive committee. Why do you require statutory authority to 'tell them that five or six shall act as such. You say the members of the executive committee shall be taken from among the Board of Directors; to be a member of the executive committee you have to be a-director, and you have executive power in your hands; that means something or nothing. I should judge the object of that section would be to allow the Board of Directors to appoint to that executive committee men who are not on the directorate.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The effect of this section is simply to enable something smaller than a quorum to do the work of the entire directorate. A quorum can do it under the Railway Act now. We are empowering the Board of Directors to constitute a smaller body and, if they desire, call it an executive committee, and give to that executive committee the powers which the directors themselves have.
How many members have you now?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Eleven.

Under this section 8 you give the directors power to appoint an executive committee and by by-laws you empower them to clothe that executive committee with any powers they see fit. You appoint eleven directors from all over the country for the protection of certain interests and to secure the advantage of certain knowledge which is supposed to be possessed by them. Are you not going to arrive at this point: That these
4 p.m. eleven men will appoint five or six of their number, so that we will have the old gang in charge, as the member for-Pontiac (Mr. Cahill), pointed out last night. They may be in a majority, and then by by-laws, which they have power to enact without the approval of the Governor in Council, they may appoint two or three of their number as an executive committee.
Nine.
It does not specify any number.
Six is the number we have now.

I know; but you have given the committee power to appoint any number, and they may appoint two, three, or four of their number. The minister says that under the Railway Act there has to be a quorum of the Board of Directors; but this section will allow the directorate to form an executive committee, and the result would be that those directors might get together and pass a by-law appointing two or three of their number members of the executive committee, with the possibility of the old gang getting in control of the Canadian Government railways,-Mackenzie & Mann and D. B. Hanna -the same old crowd. There should be some protection in the form of providing power to the Governor in Council to approve or disapprove of the executive committee appointed by your board.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is another feature that I did not bring out. Any member of the board may, if he desires, attend a meeting of the executive committee.
It does not say so.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
You cannot say everything. You must assume that men are going to act as reasonable business men. If you are going to state every little thing in a Bill it will be endless. The executive committee may be small, that is very true, but under the by-laws as now provided any member may attend that executive committee if he desires; and it is further provided that any action taken by the executive committee as such may he reversed at the first subsequent meeting of directors. We do not want to tie down these men, who are to be entrusted with great powers, more than directors usually are tied down, and I do not think we would gain very much by doing so. I think the proper principle is to entrust them with the necessary powers, hold them responsible for the exercise of those powers, and not hold over them statutory clubs. Upon the assumption that they are not going to act as reasonable men.
%

My hon. friend says that the by-laws now provide for certain things. But this Bill does not incorporate those by-laws, and we do not know if those bylaws will prevail when the new directors are appointed.

Why are not the bylaws submitted at the same time as this Bill?
* Mr. MEIGHEN: The by-laws will have to be submitted to the Governor in Council for approval.

I did not hear the hon. minister say whether the policy of the Government was to have each-province represented on this board of directors. Seeing that this is a national undertaking, are all the provinces through which this railway runs to be represented on the directorate?

That question has not 'been decided yet. The whole matter will have to be considered when we are considering the number of directors to be appointed. We may not appoint nine, there may be fewer than that number. The object would be to select the very best men possible, and it might be that we would not be able to have every province represented.
Then they might all come from one province?
That is not likely. Possibly two or three might come from one province, in which case you could not have all the provinces represented.
Did I understand the hon. minister to isay that the by-laws will have to be approved by the Governor in Council?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, because under the Railway Act they have to be approved by the shareholders, and under section 9 such approval has to be given by the Governor in Council, in lieu thereof.

The previous clause gives the right to the directors to make by-laws and organize the company, and according to this clause we are giving the right to the directors to appoint an executive committee. I would like to know from the Minister of Railways or the Acting Minister of Justice what the Minister of Railways will have to do with the management of the railroad after this Bill is passed; and if the Minister of Railways will have nothing more to do with it, what control will Parliament have over the management of the road. I think this is a very important question. Our railways are going to be run by a board of directors, and these directors we know nothing about. The Government tells us the present directors might be changed later, but they might be maintained in that position, and so the action of the Government in regard to the directorate is very uncertain and indefinite. The only way the representatives of the people can control expenditure in connection with our railways or exercise jurisdiction over their management is to have in this House someone who has authority to speak for the management. If the powers contemplated in the Bill are given to the directors, the management of the railways will be taken from the minister; his department will become useless, and we shall no longer have in Parliament a minister responsible to Parliament in connection with railway matters.

The Minister of Railways does not really operate railways; he did not operate the Intercolonial. He depends on his officials for the actual operation of railways. But the Government must keep in touch with the system; every day matters arise that must be brought before the Government. Moreover, there are matters in connection with the other railways throughout Canada that must come to the attention of the minister. The minister must be the medium between Parliament or the Government and this system.

The hon. member need not worry about the Minister oi Railways not having very much to do.
He has the Welland canal on his hands.

Yes, that will assist in giving him something to do. The Canadian National Railway Company must come before the Government from time to time so far as construction is concerned and in connection with many other matters affecting the system. The minister and the department will have plenty of work to do without looking after the operation.

I should be the first to regret the abolition of the minister's department; I 'enjoy very much his presence in this House and I should be sorry if he disappeared. But after the Acting Minister of Justice has this Bill passed the Minister of Railways may discover that it goes much further than he thinks it does and that he will be deprived of powers which he thinks he still has. The example of the Intercolonial does not fit in with this case at all. The Intercolonial is a Government-owned railway operated by a commission; the Canadian National Railway Company is a company separate and distinct from the Government itself, with the powers of an ordinary railway company. The Minister of Railways has nothing to say with regard to the management of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and similarly he will have no control over the Canadian National Railway Company. Five, ten or fifteen men selected by the Government will have in their hands the management of all our Government railways and Parliament will have absolutely nothing to say with regard to that management. The minister pointed out that he would have something to say with regard to construction and with regard to the relations existing between this company and the other railway companies of Canada. Well, my experience indicates that quite the opposite will be the case. A few months ago I wrote the minister asking him what he intended to do in connection with certain conditions existing in a parish in my country, and he replied that he had absolutely nothing to do with the matter; that, a commission having been appointed to look after the Government railways, I would have to apply to Mr. Hanna. Three months ago, therefore, the minister acknowledged that he no longer had authority over the railways; after this Bill passes, his position will be worse.
106i
What railway was that?

The Transcontinental.
The minister said that he had no authority to apply to the chairman of the new commission. Parliament should see that in this Bill the privileges of the people are preserved. Nobody knows who the new directors will be. The minister said last night that the directors might be changed. After this Bill is passed the Government will be free to appoint whom they choose. I hope they will be good men, but sometimes the Government makes bad appointments. Will the Government appoint competent railway experts to the board of directors, or will they appoint political friends to reward them for past services? I do not know; members of the committee do not know. We should insert in this Bill as many safeguards as possible. The people are getting sick and tired of the railway situation and of railway legislation brought down by this Government. The Canadian Northern Railway Bill, which was passed a few years ago, brought forth a good deal of opposition; this Bill will certainly agitate the minds of the people. We must examine this Bill very carefully and see that we do not simply hand over to the old gang of Mackenzie and Mann the railways that we bought and paid for with our millions. We want to have no more squandering of public moneys such as we had in connection with the Canadian Northern in past years.

The Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) stated a minute ago that by-laws passed by the Board of Directors will be subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. I understand the. minister bases that on section 9, which provides that whenever, under the provisions of the Railway Act, the sanction of shareholders is required, the sanction of the Governor in Council will be required under this Bill. Section 122 of the new law, which is going through the House at the present time, provides for the enactment of by-laws by the Board of Directors, but it does not provide that those by-laws shall be submitted to the shareholders.
The hon. member is now discussing section. 9. Shall section 8 carry?
Both sections work together.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member's law is right. I do not know that in my last sentence I repeated what I said previously

in answer, I think, to the hon. member for West Middlesex, namely, that such by-laws as by the Railway Act require confirmation by the shareholders will now require confirmation by the Governor in Council. There are certain by-laws, such as those that have to do with appointment of officials and the general running of the road, which do not require confirmation by the shareholders, but all by-laws of major importance have, as will be seen by reference to, I think, section 132 to be approved by the shareholders, and consequently will now have to be approved by the Governor in Council. Then section 120 says:-
The directors shall be subject to the examination and control of the shareholders at their annual meetings, and shall be subject to all by-laws of the company, and to the orders and directions from time to time made or given at the annual or special meetings if such orders and directions are not contrary to or inconsistent with any expressed direction or provision of this Act or of the Special Act.
I	apprehend the Governor in Council will have power under that section as well.

Under the sections of the
Railway Act referred to, will the sanction of the Governor in Council be necessary to a by-law of the directors appointing certain of their number as an executive committee?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Where does the minister get that?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Because the directors
are expressly given power to pass by-laws of a certain character without reference to the shareholders, and unless, in a word, that power is included within section 122, the directors must get the assent, and on inquiry, I find that assent is always obtained to the by-law which constitutes the executive committee and gives its powers.
Will the minister point out the clause in the new Act which makes by-laws of the directors subject to the approval of shareholders?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The law is, as I understand it, that unless powers are expressly given to the board of directors, such powers cannot be exercised except with the approval of the shareholders of the company.
Where is the clause?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
You do, not need any. What I mean is this, the directors have only such powers as are statutorily given to them. The company are the shareholders, consequently, the directors cannot derive, from the company, any powers except such

as may be given to them. The law gives them certain powers. Anything the law does not give them, they do not have, and therefore, they must secure confirmation of any such acts from the shareholders.
How do the shareholders have the right?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Because the shareholders are the company, and the directors are acting for the company, and unless the directors have something to prove their authority for any act, they cannot do it.

They can by section 120.
Mr. MEIGHEN* But they cannot go beyond that.

The shareholders cannot do anything inconsistent with law, but the directors may make by-laws or pass resolutions from time to time not inconsistent with law. The argument of the minister falls to the ground. The directors can do anything not inconsistent with this Bill by passing by-laws.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The directors may make by-laws or pass resolutions as provided in clauses (a), (b), and (e) of section 122.
That does not restrict the power of the former clause.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Any power specified in section 120 they can exercise so long as it is not inconsistent with law, but anything that is not specified there, they cannot do.

They can, because the directors have power under another clause to manage the railway, and that implies the power to do anything which is necessary for the management. Section 122 siim ply says that the directors shall have power to make by-laws or pass resolutions, not inconsistent with law, for the purposes of the management. The word "manage-, ment" covers everything.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
The minister's argument absolutely destroys itself. He says that if the directors are given power by the Act to do a certain thing, then they do not need to get the approval of the shareholders.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If they have statutory powers, they do not require power from the shareholders.

By this Bill, we are giving them statutory powers. Section 8 says:
The by-laws of the company may provide for an executive committee of the board of direc-

tors, to exercise such powers as the by-laws may specify.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is the by-laws ot the company, not the by-laws of the directors.
Who is the company,
Who are making these bylaws?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The company.

If I ask who is the company, the minister says "the directors." If I ask, who are the directors, the minister says " the company." That is the minister's style of arguing. In this case the company is a body of directors appointed by the Governor in Council?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Then what is the difference between the company and the directors? The directors are the company and the company is the directors.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend is going round in a circle.

The minister made the
circle, I cannot get out of it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Section 8 says:
The by-laiws of the company may .provide for an executive committee of the board of directors, to exercise such powers as the bylaws may specify.
That is to say, whatever powers the directors may have as a directorate, they may revest in the executive committee. Under section 120 of the Railway Act, the directors are given certain powers, and any powers there vested in them, they may revest in the executive committee. Any powers not given to them, they cannot revest in the executive committee. If any powers are given to them by the shareholders, they, in turn, could revest them in the executive committee, provided those powers were not inconsistent with the by-laws.

What are the by-laws
that require to be ratified by the shareholders, and in what section does the minister find that?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Section 132, if I remember correctly, contains certain of them. It is a very long section and I do not suppose the hon. member wants me to read it.
It provides that if you want to issue securities you must have a two-thirds vote of the shareholders.

I see it is provided that the directors can make by-laws
relating to the business affairs of the company, the appointment and dismissal of officers, and the conduct of the general business of the company. Now, the Governor in Council are the shareholders of the company?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Well, as there are no shareholders in the proper sense, should not all by-laws be submitted to the Governor in Council?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Committee might
very well discuss that point. I do not think there could be any objection, unless perhaps it would be that it would virtually give to the Governor in Council a dictating power as to salaries and management. Whether that is wise or not is a matter that is open to discussion, but it certainly would tend to place the management of this road more on a footing of political patronage than it is at present. There is, however, much to be said the other way.

I for one am not alarmed at the power given to the directors, and I hope the Government will be in a position to appoint independent directors who know something about the management of railways and who will not be interfered with.
I am strongly opposed to the suggestion that the by-laws as drafted by the directors should be submitted entirely to the Governor in Council. Of course there are certain by-laws which have to be submitted to the Governor in Council, such as those relating to the issuance of securities. But to require the directors to submit by-laws relating to the real operation of the road, as for instance the appointment and dismissal of officers, would be to bring it immediately under the influence of political patronage, and that is what I hope we shall avoid. Clause 8 is simply the ordinary clause passed by all large corporations. You have to have an executive management. Frequently very large powers are given to executive bodies who, of course, have to report to the directors before taking any particularly important step. It is a simple every-day proposition to allow the board of directors to appoint an executive committee to have the immediate management of the road.
Not in railway companies.

Yes, look at the Canadian Pacific Railway and you will see who the executive committee are. It is they, and

not the board of directors, whom we have to thank for the very great success of the Canadian Pacific Railway. As to submitting all by-laws, I think we ought to take it for granted that we are going to appoint, or at least endeavour to appoint, as directors and especially the executive, men who know something about railways. As to the Minister of Railways being relieved of his responsibility, that is impossible, for so long as we are owners of the railway, the Government will be responsible for the actions not only of the executive committee but of the board of directors.

My hon. friend seems to be surprised at the suggestion that the bylaws should be submitted to the Governor in Council. The Railway Act provides: "All such by-laws, rules, and regulations, except such as relate to tolls and such as are of a private or domestic nature and do not affect the public' generally, shall be submitted to the Governor in Council for approval."
What are you reading from?
The Railway Act, Chapter 37, Revised Statutes, 1906.
Get the new Act.
Well, last night I was called down for using the new Act and that is my reason for quoting from the old Act to-day.

I can see no objection to having all by-laws subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. It would be a safeguard and I think it should be added to Section 8. It can do no harm, and 1 am not disposed to allow the people of the country to be governed by laws made by independent bodies over whom we have no'control. The provision is in the general Act as read by the hon. member for Three Rivers, and I think we should very well add it to Clause 8 that all by-laws shall be submitted to the Governor in Council for approval. These by-laws, 'if they are submitted to the Governor in Council, will come under the eye of the Department of Justice and I presume it will be seen that they are proper by-laws.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The section which the hon. member for Three Rivers read concerns by-laws that have to do with the public safety.
I think I so stated.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Similarly, by-laws passed by this company will go to the Governor in 
Council for approval when they are of the same character as those mentioned in the ' section read by the hon. member. As to having all by-laws submitted to the Governor in Council for approval, I am personally" disposed to agree with the hon. member for North Oxford, but at the same time I cannot help expressing my joy at finding the leader of the Opposition so much in love now with Orders in Council. If we are to approve of all by-laws passed by the Canadian National Railways we will have to approve of them by Orders in Council, and 1 sincerely hope we shall not again be taunted by the leader of the Opposition with government by Order in Council. We are endeavouring to avoid that, and at all events we feel disposed to leave the railway management a freer hand in the actual management of the road.

The Acting Minister oi Justice is wrong if he thinks that I am a convert to government by Order in Council.
I have always advocated in this House the principle that the law should be found in the statute, and every one who has paid any attention to what I have ever said knows that. But these by-laws should be submitted for approval to a body that is responsible to this House. I am not in favour of by-laws; I want the enactment to be specific and clear in the statute, but if we must have them let us have some check on them. I do not think we should give a free hand to these directors to make such laws as they may see fit without having them approved of by some body responsible to Parliament. You are creating them a miniature parliament capable of making laws binding on the people.
I am not in favour of giving such a free hand to anybody. No matter who is making the laws touching the property and liberties of the people, they must ultimately come to this Parliament and submit to the jurisdiction of the body that represents the people. That is the only purpose I have in wanting to have the by-laws subject to the approval of the Governor in Council.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I would like to say a
word or two on behalf of the railway men.
I know what their desires are in regard to this matter because I was called before them a year ago. They distinctly state that it is their desire that the management of this road shall be, as far as possible, divorced from all political action. They would like to see the road, if possible, operated by a commission. The proposal contained in this Bill is the nearest approach

to a commission that we can make. A company only acts by its board of directors, and through its by-laws, and if we are going to have every Act expressed by a by-law supervised by the Governor in Council, we are going to drag into the management of the road that political interference which is directly opposed by the railway men. Take the question of promotion, for instance. If a man serves faithfully, his superiors know whether he should be made a locomotive foreman, a yard-master, a trainmaster, a divisional superintendent or something of that kind. These men go up to more important positions. Surely it is better to leave all such questions as that to the management whether it be the executive committee or whether it be the general manager of the company. As the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) said, any promotion to a treasurer-ship or anything else, should come from that independent tribunal, instead of having to come before the Governor in Council. The Government of the day, no matter what it was, might have some person that they would like to have appointed to a position. I earnestly hope that this House will never dream of having every act of this independent tribunal or board of directors confirmed by Order in Council. It is against the wishes of the men in every respect.
Mr. McKENZlIE: il do not want the hon. gentleman to have any misunderstanding as to what I propose. I do not at all think that every movement in connection with this concern, or every act, must be authorized by a by-law. That before a man can be appointed or promoted, or a locomotive purchased or repaired, a by-law must be passed is something that I have not suggested and I have no such idea. These men that the hon. gentlemen speaks of must be sane and sensible men, We trust them to do their work properly. I would be very sorry to think that what we call politics should be divorced from this enterprise. To divorce politics from it would be to divorce from it every influence that should be brought to bear on the question of public ownership. The people that are selected for the management of this road are not any better than the rest of us. They are human beings, influenced by human proclivities and human ambition. We do not propose any petty interference with them in the management of the road, but we maintain that the general supervision of the Government property and of the people's property must be in the hands of the representatives of the people of this
House. To suggest that for the buying of such stock as may be required, the engagements for freight and such measures as are necessary for the general advancement of the road it is necessary to pass by-laws is absurd. We must give these men a free hand but there are certain things on which they will want by-laws as well as they want statutes and if there is anything in the operation of the road that requires a by-law, it ought to be submitted to the Governor in Council and indirectly in that way submitted to the influence and control of this House and of the people as represented by the Governor in Council.
On section 9-approval by Governor in Council instead of shareholders:

I would ask the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) for his reasons why that which, under the provisions of the Railway Act or any other statute, requires the approval of shareholders has to be confirmed by the Governor in Council? It seems strange that we should supersede all statutes applicable to an ordinary company when we are creating a company to manage the railways that the Government are acquiring. This is another example of a resort to Order in Council under which the Government is allowed to do anything. We do not know where the end is going to be. The war is over now and I think that this company which we are incorporating by Act of Parliament should be subject to the very same rules and regulations as any other company.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Committee will appreciate how difficult it is to meet the wishes of the hon. gentlemen opposite. We have just been suffering a volley of criticism because we do not require that all bylaws of the company shall be submitted to the Governor in Council, and now we are attacked because we admit that any should be submitted to the Governor in Council. All we ask to be submitted are such as under the Railway Act are compellable in the case of the ordinary company to be submitted to the shareholders before they are effective. We say that such by-laws of major importance as are required to be submitted to the shareholders must in this case be submitted to the Governor in Council. We think that a fair line of division.

I do not think that this clause should carry immediately. Under this clause the Government are taking the power by Order in Council to issue securities against this new undertaking which

would include the Intercolonial and the Transcontinental. They might therefore, with the sanction of the Governor in Council, be permitted to go into the markets of the world and sell some $150,000,000 to $250,000,000 worth of bonds and we in this Parliament would have absolutely no control over the expenditures of that money. We are handling an asset free of incumbrance to the company. The company by this Act, are taking power to do all things necessary to carry on the undertaking, to extend the lines and operate the railway.
They also have power to issue securities. If they did so they would have the privilege of floating all these securities against this undertaking and spending the money, and there is absolutely no provision in this ' Bill requiring them to come to Parliament for sanction of such action, or to account for the expenditures.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What the hon. gentleman fears is expressly forbidden by section 26 of this Bill.
Are there any ishareholders of the Canadian Northern Railway who have not sold their shares to the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There are no shareholders, that is, owners of shares, whose shares are not sold. There are, however, certain shares which the owners have pledged with the Government of British Columbia for some contract, which shares they have not been able to deliver to the Minister of Finance, and consequently they have not been paid for.
What is the number and value of such shares?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Speaking from memory, and not attempting to say that I am certainly right, I think it is about a million and a half of shares, the value of which would be only $200,000.
Has the Government entered into negotiations with the British Columbia Government for the acquisition of those shares?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Government has not; it is simply waiting for delivery.

If I remember rightly, the only class of by-laws that require to be submitted to shareholders for approval under the Railway Act, are those dealing with the issuance of bonds and the placing of mortgages on the road. Is it intended that this board of directors shall have power to issue bonds, or execute

mortgages, in connection with the railway system under its control? I would like the minister to state what by-law's he refers to, if if is not intended that the board oi directors in this case shall have the power to issue bonds or execute mortgages?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot say that I can enumerate all the classes of by-laws that require submission to shareholders, but the class that my hon. friend refers to does, namely, the class, providing for the issue oi bonds or stocks. Also under section 151 oi the Railway Act of the present session all by-laws that have to do with agreements for sale, lease and amalgamation of lines require submission to the shareholders as well, and there may be others also as to which this is necessary. Those two classes of by-laws passed by the directorate of this company will require submission to the Governor in Council. The general question which the hon. gentleman raises also, as to the issue of bonds, is covered by section 26 of this Bill, and a reference to that section will show that the directorate will not have power, with the sanction of the Governor in Council, or otherwise, to bond any lines except the Canadian Northern Railway. They cannot bond the Canadian Government Railways, which include the Prince Edward Island, the Intercolonial, and the Transcontinental.
They cannot bond those.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They cannot bond them. That will be made apparent when we come to the discussion of clause 26.
I think the minister confirms my argument. The Canadian Government Railways are being incorporated in the Canadian National Railway System are they not, they are being taken over?
Only for operation purposes.
There is no limitation oi that character in the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is section 26. The hon. gentleman's argument was that this directorate would be able to bond the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railways, and he says he finds confirmation of that in my speech. All I said in my speech was that they could not bond them at all, because section 26 forbids it. If that is confirmation of his argument, it is easily confirmed.

There are contradictory
statements in this section. By this Bill you

are incorporating the Canadian National Railway Company.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What has that got to d<^ with it?
You are incorporating a company through whom you take over the Canadian National Railways.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, we do not.
Where is the provision for operating merely?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In the Act we provide for operating the Canadian National Railways.

Section agreed to.
On section 10-Definitions, "Canadian Government Railways:"
Will the taking over of the branch lines connected with the Government system rest in future with this company, or will it rest with the Minister of Railways?
The branch lines will all come under the operation of this Bill.

I mean branch lines now owned by private companies. An Act has been passed which authorizes the Governor in Council to take over any railroad not exceeding two hundred miles in length, which connects with the Intercolonial or any other Government railway. Will that power in future rest with this new corporation, or will it continue to be vested in the Governor in Council?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The power continues as it is at present under the statute, it is not affected by this Bill.
Is it the intention that the Intercolonial, and its branch lines, shall come under the management of this company?
Yes.
We are proud of the old Intercolonial Railway, and we do not want its identity to be lost in the Canadian Northern System.
This section defines what " Canadian Government Railways " and what " Canadian Northern " means.
I would gather from the Bill that the Canadian Northern System will dominate everything else.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Section 11 makes quite clear what is contemplated.
I think the Order in Council which was laid on the Table of the House defines what has been placed under the operation of the Canadian National railways.
The hon. minister misunderstands me. I want to know what other railway companies are operated under the Canadian Government railways referred to in this Bill?
The Intercolonial railway and the branch lines that were being operated by the Intercolonial railway-
From Montreal to Sydney?
From Montreal to Sydney; the Prince Edward Island railway, the International railway
All the branch lines.
The Transcontinental between Winnipeg and Moncton.

The Quebec and
Saguenay?
It is being operated by the contractors at the present time. Then the Hudson's Bay railway is also being operated
The Quebec and Lake St. John?
That was part of the Canadian Northern system before.
I would like a plain statement of the railways operated by the Canadian Government railways without interruption from hon. members.
Perhaps I might repeat and say, all the railways that were being operated by the Minister of Railways until they were transferred.
When was that?

I think some time in January the Order in Council was passed. So far as my memory goes, it includes the line between Winnipeg and Moncton, the International railway between Montreal and Sydney, all the branch lines connected with the Intercolonial, and the Prince Edward Island railway. The Quebec and Saguenay is being operated by the contractors at the present time, but when it is completed it will also come into this Canadian National system. The Hudson's Bay railway has been placed under the management of the Canadian National Railway system.
Was it with the Canadian Government system before the Order in Council?

Yes, it was under construction and the contract was taken out of the hands of Mr. McArthur, a settlement was made with him, and then the operation of the road was handed over to the Canadian National Railway system. In other words, putting it concisely, all the railways that were being operated by the Minister of Railways have been handed over to the management and operation of this Canadian National Railway system.

Will the hon. minister be good enough to say what he refers to in this clause:
" Canadian Government railways " means and includes all such railways or parts thereof, and all such properties, works, powers, rights and privileges or interests or any of them

What does he propose to include there?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The definition in (a) oi section 10 says that it includes all these railways or parts thereof and all properties, works, powers, rights, and so on.
" Powers," for instance, might be running powers, which would be appurtenant to a railway. I do not need to define the word " rights."
I understand that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Rights, privileges, and so forth-anything we have a right to entrust,, under section 11, to the 5 p.m. company having been so entrusted and then becomes part of the Canadian National railways. That is the definition.

The information I am seeking is this; what, for instance, in connection with the old Intercolonial Railway system from Montreal to Sydney, Halifax and St. John would be included in regard to works, powers, rights and privileges? What would there be besides the railway itself?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: All it has. Has it not works in the city of Moncton? The hon. gentleman knows all about that. It will have certain rights ahd powers. I do not know whether it has running powers over some other road; it may not; if so, none can pass. The same applies to the Transcontinental or any other road which comes within the meaning of what is embraced in Section 11, so that the Governor in Council has power to entrust such powers, rights, works and properties to the Canadian National Railways. If they have no special powers, rights, works or properties, none can pass; but if they have they will be included in what passes under the Order in Council; that is all. They might have agreements, for example, as to exchange of traffic; if so those would be part of what would pass. All would be included in the subject matter embraced in the Order in Council, and having been so embraced it would become part of the Canadian Government Railways.

If it is thought proper by the board of directors to absorb a branch line, will the board be entitled to act upon its own initiative, or will it have to come before Parliament or the Governor in Council? Mr. Hanna and his colleagues might think it advantageous for the Canadian National Railways to get control of a branch line. What would happen in such an instance? It would be managed on business principles, I suppose, like any other railway company, but would the board of management be empowered to act in such a case?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Section II answers that.
_Mr. J. D. REID: Sections 11 and 12.
Do rights, powers, privileges, etc., include the owning and operation of hotels?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If they have any they would be included.
Mr. MARCH.: Will this company have the power to open hotels?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman mean to build them?
Yes, to operate them?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not considered the subject, but I would say yes, in this way-the Canadian Northern Railway Company will be operated by the Canadian Government Railways, but the Canadian Northern Railway Company will ' still possess the powers it formerly possessed, and it has power to build hotels. I presume that under the charter of the Canadian Northern, hotels could he even built, but I do not like to speak too definitely on that. This Bill merely provides for a unified operation of these various systems.
Has the hon. minister any idea of the number of hotels formerly under the management of the Canadian Northern Railway Company? They have a number of large hotels in Winnipeg.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No; just two-Brandon and Port Arthur.
The hotel in Winnipeg is operated by the Grand Trunk Pacific.

Should the company desire to manage hotels in Quebec, I would highly recommend to the consideration of the President of the Privy Council that he should have them licensed.
Mr. BUREAU; Does section 10 empower the Government to turn over the Intercol-* onial to the Canadian National Railway Company?
That section is merely a definition. The power to entrust the company with the management and operation of a Government-owned railway is in section 11.

But section 10 really
leaves the definition to the Governor in Council.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Governor in Council may entrust to the Canadian National Railway Company only such Government-owned railways as section 11 permits.

Then the two sections
ought to be considered together?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

The thirty companies
mentioned in the schedule of the Bill operate certain railways which are parts of this Government-owned system. I suppose some of these companies are created by local Act; their powers are independent of this House. When and by what method is the physical transfer of these companies from the old to the new management to take place, if it has not taken place already? We had some
evidence last night that the Minister of Railways does not know much about the officers of these Government-owned roads or what salaries they are receiving. It is about time we knew who our officers are and how much we are paying them. Are they subject to our control, or to the control of the thirty oi forty companies mentioned in the schedule to this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's
first point is a legal one. He says: When and how are we going to transfer the Intercolonial and other roads to the Canadian National Railway Company?

I am not concerned
about the Intercolonial. I refer to roads that are operated by companies.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In the Canadian Northern system?
Yes.	.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are owned by the Canadian Northern Railway Company and are operated as part of the Canadian Northern system; nothing that I am aware of requires to be done in that regard. Two companies that have independent charters will be taken care of under section 21 of this Bill, which provides for an agreement between His Majesty and the company for any of the purposes specified in sections 361 and 364 of the Railway Act. The intention is to bring about a unified management of all these roads immediately after the passing of this Act; there is no reason for delay, so far as we are aware. As to the salaries of the officers, information was given to the committee some time ago in response to a'question. It is true that these salaries are not fixed by the Governor in Council, hut that is because, with a view of divorcing the road from political control, the Governor in Council is not directly managing it. All this will now be under the care of the directorate of the Canadian National Railway Company; that is the system we submit to Parliament for approval.
Are these companies named in the schedule still to exist under their respective names?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They can be amalgamated under section 21.
Do I understand that we are to have general control of the management, but that the names of these companies are to be continued?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Not necessarily. The intention is to amalgamate the companies

that have independent charters, as well as a great many more. That amalgamation, as I say, is already provided for under section 21.

We have taken over these vast properties and are maintaining them, but they are operating under private names, and to the outside world they are owned by private corporations. The names of all these constituent companies of the old Canadian Northern System are still in use; when are we to discard them? When are these trammels to be thrown off? When will these properties be owned by us just as the Intercolonial and Transcontinental are owned? The taxation on these properties in the different provinces, amounting to a considerable sum of money, is paid by the Government, as are the salaries of the manager and of the employees.
If. these properties actually belonged to the Government, we would pay no taxes at all, because the property of the Crown is not subject to private taxation in school sections or municipalities. No taxes are paid on the Intercolonial, nor on the Transcontinental from Winnipeg to Moncton. Why, then, should we be paying taxes on these thousands of miles of railway as private concerns when, in fact and in law, we are not liable to taxation at all? I am giving this as a reason why we should wipe out these conventionalities which stand in the way of actual, real ownership of those properties which we are supposed to own and for the management of which we are now providing. If this is a Government railway, why should it be called the Canadian Northern and why should it have around it all the machinery that it had when it was the Canadian Northern? The country thinks it owns these properties altogether, when in fact there are in the way what seem to be unnecessary machinery and complications which should be wiped out.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Under section 21, an amalgamation is provided. The hon. member's question is: To what extent shall we take advantage of that, and when? One of the purposes of this Bill is to pave the way for amalgamation and for getting rid of the various entities that have comprised the system as separate entities. It is the intention to amalgamate just as rapidly as we can, but all cannot be amalgamated, because in respect of some there is still outstanding stock. Where there is outstanding stock, amalgamation would be very inconvenient because stock would have to

be given. Where there is not outstanding stock, it is the purpose to amalgamate without any unnecessary delay. Of course, immediately amalgamation fakes place, the name goes out of existence.

If I understand rightly, there are only two sets of railways owned by the Government, the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Government railways, the latter comprising the Intercolonial and the Transcontinental. The object of the Bill is to consolidate those two systems. The preamble says:
Whereas His Majesty on behalf of the Dominion of Canada has acquired control of the Canadian Northern Railway company and of the various constituent and subsidiary companies comprising the Canadian Northern system, as specified in the schedule to this Act.
The schedule mentions a number of constituent and subsidiary companies- of the Canadian Northern. Does the list contained in the schedule show the names of all the constituent and subsidiary companies, because I see in the list of subsidiary companies the Canadian Northern Steamships, Limited? Would that come under the control of the company which is now being incorporated?
Yes; we now own the stock in that company.

I find in the Canada
Gazette, of January 11, 1919, a notice signed' by Mr. Colson, Acting Under Secretary of State, headed " Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Ltd.," and stating:
Public notice is hereby given that under the first part of chapter 79 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, known as "The Companies'. Act," and amending Acts, letters patent have been issued, etc.-
I want to read the names of the petitioners for this charter, and also a few of the powers granted by the Government to this company. My object in bringing this before the House is to find out whether or not this is a separate concern incorporated for a separate purpose, or whether the Government will allow people at large or foreign to the Government to use the name "Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Ltd.?" This seems, on reading the names, to be a first cousin to the Canadian Northern system. Some of the petitioners, whom I happen to know personally, may not be directors, but they are closely connected with the Canadian Northern. The notice continues:
Letters patent have been issued under the seal of the Secretary of State of Canada, bearing date the 30th day of December, 1918, incorporating Gerard Ruel, barrister-at-law.

If I am not mistaken, this gentleman is general counsel of the Canadian Northern.
Lome William Mitchell, treasurer.
I think this gentleman is also closely connected with the present administration.
Wilfred Bankart Langmore, solicitor; Charles Durno Cowie, secretary, and Frederick Joseph Buller, paymaster, all of the city of Toronto, in the province of Ontario, for the following purposes, viz:-
To construct, purchase, lease, or otherwise acquire, charter, own, maintain, operate and manage:

(a)	steamships vessels, tugs, car ferries, dredges, lighters, barges, boats, and water craft of every, description.
That would include the steamers, the King George, and the other "Kings" that plough the ocean.
(b)	structures, erections, buildings, hotels, shops, stores, works, appliances, mills, machinery, plant and equipment of every nature and kind whatsoever, on land or on water deemed by the company to be necessary or required for or in connection with the construction, manufacture, maintenance, operation, navigation, management, renewal or repairs of the company's vessels, works, undertakings, appliances or equipment, etc.
I am not going to weary the House with an enumeration of all the powers that are asked for, because they are very numerous. Will there not be a conflict of authority in this case, if those people are really Canadian Northern railway people who are incorporated under the Companies Act to manage that part of the "properties, works, powers, rights and privileges or interests," which the Canadian Northern railway have, which are enumerated in the schedule and which contain inter alia a subsidiary company, the Canadian Northern Steamships, Ltd. There must have been some reason for this incorporation, and if the company incorporated by letters patent is to exercise all the powers it asks for in these letters patent, it covers the construction of docks, the erection, equipment and management of hotels and all those things, part of which form an asset of the Canadian Northern Railway. I want to know what authority or control it exercises over any part of the system.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The last company which the hon. gentleman named, Canadian Northern Steamships, Limited, is a [subsidiary company. While the Canadian Northern Steamships Company did own certain vessels-the Royal George and the Royal Edward-I believe it owns now only the Perry at Vancouver and a new steamer built at Quebec. The Canadian Northern Steamships Limited is a subsidiary company of the Canadian Northern Railway Company whose stock we own. The Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited, is a new company not yet organized. The charter has just been taken out at the instance of the Government and the stock when issued will be owned by the Government. The stock of that company so owned by the Crown may, under Section 29 of this Bill, be transferred to the Canadian National Railways for the purposes-of amalgamation if the Government so desire. The intention is to have all operated together. The company is formed merely for the purpose of taking over the Government steamships being built.
Mr. BUREAU; For the purpose of taking over Government steamships?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Government ships that are being built and such as we will operate ourselves. The stock will be owned by the Government and under Section 29 may be transferred to this company, so that the whole may be operated together.
Does the Government intend establishing a line of steamships as well as railways?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are building steamships now and it is contemplated they will be operated by this body.

It has been found advisable by railway and steamship companies to have a separate charter for each steamship. A steamship worth $20,000 or $30,000 might run into an ocean liner worth a couple of millions and under marine law all you would lose if your captain were held responsible would be your steamship provided she was regularly incorporated. But if you took her in as part of the Canadian Government Railway and there were a collision, I presume you would have to pay a considerable sum for damages.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have a charter for each steamship.
Has any consideration been given to the Gaspe line?
We have not considered taking over any other than those mentioned in the Estimates of last year. Two of those refused to accept the offer-the Caraquet and another.
What about giving Quebec a show in the matter? The Gaspe line is 200 odd miles long and was built ten years ago.
I have not had any request from them to be taken over. I think they are paying well and do not want to be taken over. *

Both the hon.
member for Gaspe and myself have been advocating this matter for twenty years in this House. Unfortunately the road fell into the hands of a local company who became insolvent and the country has been held back for want of a proper service. The service is nothing compared to what it would be under Government control. Gaspe is a seaport open ten months of the year, and there is a great opportunity there for the Canadian National Railway Company to get a splendid feeder. The roads taken over in New Brunswick are important, but they are not more important than the Gasp6 railway.
The shareholders have never, so far as I know, approached the Government to sell their railway and we are not anxious to purchase.
Is it the intention of the Government to take over the Lotbiniere and Megan tic?
We have not considered that matter since it was taken up in the House a couple of years ago.

Is the Minister of Railways now considering the question of taking over the Caraquet and Restigouche railway? In further efforts to have this road absorbed or taken over, I would like to be informed whether I shall have to apply to Mr. Hanna, say, or the company, or shall I have to deal again with the Minister of Railways?

If the railway is taken over it will only be a matter of negotiation between the Government and the owners. If the Government took it over, under this next section we could hand it over, if we so desired, to the management of the Canadian National railways for operation.

The minister said that the Canadian Northern Steamships Limited formerly owned the Royal George and the Royal Edward, but that now they own only the Perry at Vancouver. What has become of the Royal George and the Royal Edward?
They were sold some years ago during the war.

What is the object in getting letters patent to constitute the Government a company to operate steamships? Why not come before Parliament and let the people know that you have an organization within an organization and tell us what you are going to do. The Department of Marine looks after the interests of our waterways generally, and if you are going to operate a system of steamships in connection with the railway it will be well to have a Parliamentary charter. I do not see that there is anything to gain, and it seems strange to me, and I am sure to those who are not acquainted with the devious ways of the Government, suspicious, that you should get letters patent to have these men run a railway line and a hotel system which would be better run as a branch under the executive of the railway company.
I asked what was the reason for this incorporation and the Acting Minister of Justice did not answer, but said that they formed a company and that the stock is owned by the Government. That million is the property of the Government. We know that the Government must be behind this company because with a million dollars they could never begin to have plans of the road and surveys made and to accomplish all the great things that they have taken power to do. There is nothing serious about this Bill except that the Governor in Council wants to take hold of this railways system and avoid criticism by this House by getting behind the company that #e are creating. If you are going to take a subsidiary company like the Canadian Northern Steamships Limited, is there any necessity for this charter which was granted, in September last to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine Limited? Whenever the Government wants to exercise power of this kind or to become a competitor in any kind of business, whether merchant marine or railway, Parliament is the proper authority to appeal to. The members of this House, having a mandate from the people, are the persons to discuss these matters and to say whether or not the Government ought to go into this business. In this case, if the object is to form a company to operate a line of steamships for and on behalf of the Government, why not come before Parliament and ask for a charter to that effect and let us have an opportunity of discussing with you the wisdom or otherwise of forming such a

company. I do not see why you should issue this charter when you already have the Canadian Northern system charter authorizing you to do the things that you say you desire to do. I have not read the law but still that company have been operating the Royal George and the Royal Edward. They must have power in connection with their railway to operate any kind of steamers connecting their railway terminals with Europe or with any other country beyond the seas. The Acting Minister of Justice said that while these gentlemen were incorporated by charter the stock was owned by the Government. I want to know why this charter was issued instead oi using the charter of the Canadian Northern Steamships Limited which was granted by Parliament. I do not think it is right for the Government to launch into an enterprise like that, issue from itself to itself, or to certain men the right to use the Government's name and to operate any kind of an enterprise without the authority of Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
could not have been listening to the very clear explanation of that very point made by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair): Charters are taken out first of all for each of the boats constructed in order that the liabilities for each boat may be limited to the boat itself. That is the practice of those operating steamships. That is the practice we are following precisely for the reason stated by the hon. member for Guysborough. Then all the stock of the various companies representing the various single boats, is connected with the Canadian Government Merchant Marine Limited more for convenience than for any other purpose. It costs practically nothing to get the letters patent-only $100 which comes to ourselves-and then all the stock is collected and held by this company. Either the Minister of Finance or the Government holds that stock and it is that stock which may be transferred under section 29 to the Canadian National railways. That is the reason this company has been incorporated.
I understand the minister to say that he wants incorporation for each steamer so as to limit the liability.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

For what particular
steamers was the charter for the Canadian Government Merchant Marine Limited issued?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have just explained. This is a holding company and it holds the stock of the separate companies. That is more convenient than to have the stock of all the separate companies held separately and each one separately transferred to this road. They are all collected together in that way and we have the whole thing in one.
Why did you not come to Parliament? This company could have been as well incorporated by Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no need to come to Parliament for everything. It is very pleasant to come to Parliament but if we came to Parliament for every single thing it would be a slow process.

If you are going to incorporate a body of men to handle public money and to operate the property of the people, Parliament is the proper place to come for the incorporation of that company. If the hon. gentleman takes the ground that it is no use coming here, I say that we are not going to sit here like dummies or like an Indian figure in front of a cigar store. We have come to the point where the ministers think they are gods, think they know everything, and that they can do anything without regard to Parliament. I object to that principle. Whether this is a holding company, an operating company or any other kind of a company that is going to handle the moneys or do the business of the people of Canada, the Government have no right to confer upon a certain number of their creatures rights which are conferred generally on outsiders who apply for incorporation. Parliament should be consulted and we should know what we are doing with these operating companies, what they are going to hold and why we are incorporating them. Parliament is entitled to be consulted as to whether or not it is advisable to have such a company.
