The principle is absolutely wrong and my hon. friend need not say that it is a slow process to come to Parliament with everything. You are going to take a million'dollars of the people's money and put it into the hands of this operating or holding .company without consulting Parliament. It is not fair to the people that the Government should enter upon any such policy. If that is their policy let them say it and then we will go to the people and tell them that our usefulness is gone and that the Government is prepared to act without reference to the views of the people.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend is getting unnecessarily excited. All this is done under the authority of Parliament. This is done under the Companies' Act.
The War Measures' Act.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, not the War
Measures' Act, but the Companies' Act, and it is just what the hon. member would have power to do in regard to any company.

The hon. gentleman is shifting. I do not say you have not power to do it, but the principle is wrong, because you should come to Parliament in such a case even if it does happen to come under the Companies' Act.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: One would ordinarily understand that Parliament meant to give the powers it did give anid did not mean to be bothered with the exercise of those powers in each individual case.
This gives authority to spend $1,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Every dollar has been spent with the direct authority of Parliament.
Would the Minister of Railways tell the committee how many steamers he has at present?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There are five altogether.
May I be allowed to draw the attention of the Minister ^ of Railways to the desirability of developing Canadian trade rather than United States trade?.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must draw the attention of the committee to the fact that we have been discussing clause 11 for the last half hour, although clause 10 has not yet been passed.

It was understood that
clauses 10 and 11 should be considered together.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Clause 11 has not yet been reached.

I asked the Acting Minister of Justice if it would not be better to consider both clauses together and he replied in the affirmative, and il understood the committee unanimously consented to that being done.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The question just
asked by the hon. member (Mr. 'Sinclair) would be quite in order if clause 11 was under consideration.

I move that clauses 10
and 11 be considered together.

And shall both be
passed together?

That is another question. The first man who made a break in referring to clause 11 was the Acting Minister of Justice.
'Motion agreed to.
Mr. J. H. 'SINCLAIR: Now, Mr. Chairman, am I in order in referring to this matter?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes, under clause 11.

I took occasion
to ask the minister what use he was making of these vessels, because the people wish to know if they are to be employed in developing Canadian trade. Much surprise was caused by the Canadian Voyageur being chartered last November to carry sugar to New York from the West Indian Islands, which is not promoting Canadian trade. Not even the insurance was taken out in Canada, it being placed with Messrs. Johnston and Higgins of New York. Cannot we place in the hands of Canadian brokers the marine insurance that is necessary on our vessels? With reference to the steamer McKee, which is one of the vessels referred to by the minister, the following questions were put by me in the House and answered on April 7:
1.	To whom is the Steamer McKee chartered?
2.	What is the nature of the cargo, the rate of freight per ton, the port of loading and port of discharge?
3.	What is the return cargo, rate of freight per ton, and port of destination?
4.	Is the hull insured? If so, with what company and for how much?
5.	Is the freight insured?

'
1.	To the American Metal Transport Co., of New York.
2.	Cargo of ooal from New York to Chili, rate of freight 3'0 shillings per ton E>.W. per month, and the charterers assume all expenses except wages of the crew.
3.	Return cargo is ore, the rate of freight per ton is 30 shillings per ton D.W. Port of destination, New York.
4.	The hull is insured through Willcox, Peck and Hughes of New York for $336,000.
5.	Yes.
It therefore appears that the Railway Department is using steamers that were built at great expense by the Canadian Government for the purpose of developing American trade. Now there has been a great deal of difficulty of late in selling coal from the mines of Nova Scotia and keeping those mines going, and! yet this boat was chartered to carry coal from New York to the

west coast of 'South America. Why is she not engaged in carrying Canadian coal, which would mean providing work for Canadian miners in the counties of Cape Breton and Pictou and elsewhere in Nova Scotia? I do not know whether the minister is considering this question or not, but if we are going to send out steamers to engage in trade we should at all events consider the question of using them for the development of Canadian trade and not the trade of a foreign country. If there is any justification for the large expense incurred in the building of these vessels, it must be found in their being used in the development of our own trade. I would like to have some information from the minister as to why Canadian vessels are employed in helping the trade of a foreign country.

The steamship to which the hon. gentleman alludes was-chartered to carry coal from New York to Chili. I made inquiries about it and learned that the steamer McKee, while on her way from New York to Prince Edward Island with a cargo of rails, was wrecked and had to be taken to New York and repaired. This was in the winter season and the vessel is a small one, adapted to the navigation of the Upper Lakes rather than to ocean navigation. After being repaired she was chartered to carry a cargo on the Southern route, where she was not exposed to transoceanic risks. That was done in order to keep the vessel employed until the opening of navigation on the St. Lawrence, when it is intended that she shall operate between Nova Scotia and St. Lawrence ports. The Government originally had the Sheba and two other vessels of similar type that were suitable for ocean traffic.
Two of these have been lost since the commencement of the war, one as the result of a collision while on her way from a Nova Scotia port to New York, the other being sunk by a submarine en route to Europe with a cargo belonging to the Dominion Iron and Steel Company.
Was she carrying steel rails?

I think steel rails which were being sent by the Dominion Iron and Steel Company to Europe for war purposes. The Government then purchased the Drummond and McKee, but they are not really vessels suited to ocean navigation. It was for that reason that the charter in question to southern ports was allowed to be taken out. Both vessels will return immediately
and be placed in service between Nova Scotia and Levis at the opening of navigation.

Is it intended to transfer the properties of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited, to the company whose incorporation we are considering, or will the properties of the Canadian Northern Steamships, Limited, be transferred to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited?

When the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway System was transferred to the Minister of Finance, the transfer of the stock of the Canadian Northern Steamships, Limited, to the same authority followed automatically. As the Acting Minister of Justice has explained, a company is being formed under the Companies Act to operate each steamer which is being constructed by the Government. If we were to build fifty steamers a charter must be taken out for each, and the stock represented by each charter would be transferred to the Canadian Merchant Marine, Limited. When we get to that point and there is, let us say, a million dollars worth of stock in existence, that stock can be transferred either to the Minister of Finance or to the Canadian National Railways.

The minister did not understand my question. Will the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited, operate these vessels or will the company that we are now incorporating? In other words, is it intended to transfer the property of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited, to the Canadian National Railway Company so as to form part of that system?

The Canadian National Railway Company that we are now incorporating will control and operate the Canadian National Merchant Marine. It is carrying out a similar policy to that of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The hon. member is aware that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have all their vessels separate from their railway, the stock of the Canadian Pacific Steamship Company being held by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Steamship Company being operated by the board of directors of the railway company.
Who are the directors oi the Canadian National Merchant Marine now?

Of course, it has not been organized, but the directors of the Canadian National Merchant Marine will be practically the same as those of the Canadian National Railways. There might be one or two changes, for this reason. If you have a general manager of the steamship company who is giving its whole time to its management, you might put him on the board of directors of the Canadian National Merchant Marine; or instead of having fifteen directors as on the railway, you might take seven or eight directors and name them as directors of the Canadian National Merchant Marine.
Always forming part of the Canadian Government Railways?

It will always he really part and parcel of the Canadian National Railways. In other words, you cannot very well operate the Canadian National Railways without having a regular steamship line both on the Atlantic and the Pacific, and this is intended for that purpose.
I understand from rvhat the hon. minister says that this is intended for ocean-going steamers?

It might apply also to inland steamers. For instance, the Canadian National Railways may have lake steamers running between, say, Port Arthur and Midland; or it may have steamers carrying coal between Lake Erie ports and Montreal. There is a very large amount of coal used there. So this would apply to any vessels used for that purpose.
At six o'clock the Committee took recess.
After Recess.
The Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

When the Government
took over the Quebec and Saguenay railway, how near to the city of Quebec did the rails of that line come?
The Quebec and Saguenay commences at the terminus of the Quebec and Montmorency, about thirty miles from Quebec, and extends east to Murray Bay or Nairn's Falls.

There are about thirty
miles between the terminal and the city?
We have running rights over the Quebec and Alontmoreney.
When did the Government acquire running rights on that thirty miles?

The chief engineer in
charge of the construction of the Quebec and Saguenay made an arrangement some time last fall. I could not give the date from memory; it was several months ago.

I understand that last
August the Quebec and Saguenay did not have running rights into Quebec. I do not know whether the matter has yet been settled.

I am speaking only
from memory. When the contractor started to operate the railway two rates were charged, one on the Quebec and Saguenay and another on the Quebec and Alontmorency into Quebec. Perhaps I am wrong in stating that running rights were acquired. Anyway, a satisfactory arrangement as to rates was made and approved by the Board of Railway Commissioners.
Under that arrangement, how much does it cost to enter the city of Quebec?

I cannot give that information offhand, but if the hon. gentleman wants to see the agreement I shall be glad to send him a copy of it, and to explain the arrangement that has been made for the carrying of traffic from the end of the Quebec and Saguenay line into Quebec.

I understand that this
arrangement has been made between the Quebec Street Railway Company and the contractor.

The contractor is in
charge of the operation only while the road is under construction. As soon as construction is completed and the road taken off his hands the Government will have to make a permanent arrangement for operating over the whole line into Quebec.
Has the Government considered the question of taking over the thirty miles?

Under an Act passed
three or four years ago we were to take over three roads, the Quebec and Montmorency, the Lotbiniere and Megantic and the Quebec and Saguenay, on a valuation to be made by the judge of the Exchequer Court. But when it went to the Exchequer Court there was some question as to the interpretation placed by the judge upon the subsidies that had been paid and the interest during construction and the valuation of the Quebec and Alontmorency and of the Lotbiniere and Megantic has never been finally decided. A valuation was placed

on the Quebec and Saguenay and we passed a Bill to take it over. Since then the war intervened and we have not considered the matter. At some future time we shall have to decide whether to go ahead with the purchase of that thirty miles, or to aoquire running rights over the Quebec and Montmorency into Quebec. Of course, if we do not wish to purchase the Quebec and Saguenay outright, we can apply for running rights and the Railway 'Commission can decide on what terms and conditions those rights should' be given. From any conversations that have been had-the matter has been seldom mentioned-I understand that there would be no trouble in arranging the matter with those connected with the Quebec and Montmorency. I have been urging the contractors to give me an idea as to when the road will be in operation to Murray Bay, and I am assured that passenger traffic will be handled not later than the first of July.
How many miles would that be?
Murray Bay is about ninety miles from Quebec; about sixty miles will be completed to Murray' Bay.
Has the company made any proposal to the Government with regard to the purchase of the road?
We have not taken the matter up since it was before Parliament.

I am pleased to hear that the train to Murray Bay will be running by the first of July. I think the Government has made a good bargain in acquiring by agreement those running rights on the Quebec and Montmorency. Has the minister any idea as to the time it will take to run those trains between Quebec and Murray Bay, and will there be a through car attached to the daily train from Montreal central station over the Canadian National railways? As I am a summer resident of Murray Bay, and as I know the conditions there, I would suggest that the minister see that arrangements are made to have a through car service between Montreal and Murray Bay during the summer season, because a large number of people from the United States and from the district of Montreal have summer residences at Murray Bay, St. Irenee and Cap a I'Aigle. If such an arrangement be made, the service will be a source of revenue to the railway.

The hon. member, ol course, knows that at the city of Quebec
there is now a union station, namely, the Canadian Pacific, for all railways. The Canadian Northern, I think, runs in there now, and since their station was burned or pulled down, they, of course, being part of the Government railways, will use that station. The summer traffic usually commences about the first of July.
Before that.

I thought that on the first of July trains should be put on the Quebec and Saguenay to take care of the whole summer traffic instead of using the ferry from St. Denis to Murray Bay. In order to do that, a first class train should leave Quebec at night after the arrival ol all the different trains, and go to Murray Bay; a day train might also be put on. We would start out with a service that all would be proud of, and we would show that the Quebec and Saguenay is not such a bad road after all.

During eight months ol the year there is no necessity of having a fast passenger service, but in June, July, August and possibly on to the 15th of September there is quite a large population along that shore, so that a fast service will be required. Alany American tourists and Canadians, too, spend the summer months at Alurray Bay, Cap a l'Aigle and St. Irenee. If you had a train which could reach those points early in the day you would attract more people there.
As regards local traffic, I am quite sure that within a few years from now the minister will be surprised at the quantity ol freight that can be gathered along that shore. There is on foot just now another project which the minister has possibly heard of, and which, if it materializes, will mean the development of the remaining section of the Quebec and Saguenay railway. I understand that another syndicate contemplates building from Nairn's Falls as far as Chicoutimi. If that project materializes it would certainly make a very valuable asset of the Government road.

I cannot remember just now the amount of business Mr. Grant told me a few weeks ago was being done on the Quebec and Saguenay, but I was surprised to know that there was so much. That railway is giving a splendid service, and I have not had any complaints, except that at the start complaints were made about the freight charges. I took the matter up with Mr. Grant and told him to take it before the Railway Commission, and see that rates were made on a basis that the

Railway Commission, would consider fair and just.
Has the right-of-way along the Quebec and Saguenay been purchased and paid for?

When we took it over, there were some few cases that had not been settled, but before the owners get the money they must give us a clear title. The Department of Justice have a firm of solicitors looking at the titles, and they will not let the money be finally paid out until clear titles are obtained. An amount will be kept to cover payment for those cases that have not been settled.
Complete payment has not been made?
The money has been paid into a trust company which is holding it until clear titles are obtained, and then we get title from them.
The minister said he was very much surprised at the report made by the engineer as to the traffic carried on the Quebec and Saguenay.

I said I was surprised there w'as so much traffic. There was an impression that there would be very little traffic on the Quebec and Saguenay, and what I wished to convey to the Committee was that I was surprised to learn from the statement Mr. Grant gave me that there was so much more than I expected.

I spent last summer at St. Irenee on the line of the Quebec and Saguenay, and I could see how the line was being built. I think the minister will very soon have more than a surprise on account of the very peculiar way in which the line is being built. The line at St. Irenee is being built right next to the river St. Lawrence, and when there is a high tide in the fall or in the spring, I am afraid the whole thing will wash out.

I would like to have some information as to the Government's shipbuilding programme. There is a certain degree of uneasiness on the part of the people over the fact that the Government is embarking on the ownership of vessels. It fs a risky undertaking in any event, and in the last report of the Department of Marine and Fisheries I see there is an indication that it is to become a permanent policy. We were told that the building of vessels was a war measure, and then that it was necessary to build ships in order to give employment to our people. As 1

suggested once before during this session, 1 do not think he could have hit on a much worse programme than the building of ships if he wanted to give employment. We are importing the plates from abroad, and the expensive articles that go into the construction of a ship are also being imported; and the labour provided people in the construction of the ships is a bagatelle compared with the expense entailed. I observe in the last Marine and Fisheries report that the Government purpose to build about 200,000 tons of shipping annually at an. estimated cost of about $40,000,000. I can scarcely believe that to be the case.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question asked by the hon. member would be in order only so far as it might relate to ships which are to be constructed or controlled by the Canadian National Railway. But the shipbuilding policy of the Government certainly cannot be discussed on clause 11 of the Bill.

I think it has
already been explained that all ships owned by the Government are under the control of the Railway Department. I do not want to prolong the discussion, but I would like to obtain from the minister a statement as to the policy of the Government in regard to this matter. Is it intended that 200,000 tons shall be built each year, and that large liabilities shall be incurred for that purpose? If it is, I would: like to have a full . explanation as to what use is to be made of. the ships. I can understand why the Government should build certain classes of ships in connection with their railway system, and have a line of ships across the Atlantic to connect with the railway system at Halifax and St. John. But there is no more reason for the Government to undertake the building of tramp vessels than to embark on the ownership of automobiles or trucks on the streets. One can understand their establishing a steamship line across the ocean to carry the traffic of the railways, but as I understand the programme, that is not what they intend to do and is not what they have done so far. What does the minister say?	,

All I can answer for this evening are the vessels that are now being constructed-(I think about fifty in all. These vessels are to be operated in connection with the Canadian National Railway. We have no steamers on the Pacific, and we require a number of vessels to do the business that the Canadian

National Railways will have with the Far East. Then we need vessels on the Atlantic to go to the West Indies and South America. I do not think we can call these " tramp " vessels, and it is in the interests of Canada to do business with those countries. Up to the present time we have had only two of these new vessels. With reference to the shipbuilding policy of the Government. I hope the hon. member will not think me discourteous if I say that that is a matter that can be answered fully by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne), who has just returned. After a few days he will be going on with his Estimates and will, I am sure, be glad to give information in connection with the matter.

I understand that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited, has been organized for the purpose of taking over the steamship end of the Canadian National Railway system, and that this is being done because it is necessary to have a steamship line in connection with the railway in order to compete with the Canadian Pacific Railway and carry freight around the world. As it appears to me, this Canadian Government Merchant Marine Company is only a dummy and the operation and control of these steamships will be under the Canadian National Railway system. That is, Mr. Hanna.who is president of the organization, will see that some one competent to handle steamships will be appointed, like Mr. Bosworth of the Canadian Pacific Railway, to look after the steamship line, which will include both light vessels going through the Sault canal and navigating on the Great Lakes, and ocean-going steamers. If that is so, I do not see why this particular company should not at this time, before its organization, decide where the chief place of business shall be. The only reason seems to be the fact that the Governor in Council would not be exposed to criticism, unless the question were brought before the House and a motion were made to change the place from Toronto to Montreal. I think the main office of the organization which is going to handle the steamships should be at a tidewater port, and if this end of the business is to be in Toronto the minister might as well stand up and tell us so.

The company can have the head office changed at any time. With reference to the matter of having the principal place of business at a tidewater port, the general manager, whoever he is, can be
located at Montreal or wherever it is necessary for him to be in order to do tbs business of the company.
We will no doubt take over the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific and have all these railways incorporated under one Act. The whole railway system will have to be reorganized when we get it together. Then the question of the head office organization must be dealt with. We cannot deal with these matters until we get the whole railway situation settled. Negotiations are going on and I hope they will move with sufficient rapidity to enable us to deal with the matter during the session.	,

Do I understand from the-minister that when the situation is cleared-, up the whole railway system will have to be reorganized? Does he mean by reorganization that he will have to submit to Parliament a new Bill? ;

If an agreement is arrived at whereby we take over the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific, we must certainly come to Parliament. It will be such an immense system and so important that we must reorganize it. When the matter comes up we will be in a position to give much more definite information than we can at present.

I would urge on the minister the advisability of establishing a line of freight steamers sailing from St. John or Halifax in winter and from Quebec in summer. As the minister is aware, the Transcontinental has its water terminus in Quebec. It has been repeatedly urged by the board of trade and other public bodies in Quebec that steps be taken to impress upon the Government the advisability of running a line of steamships such as I have suggested for the purpose of carrying western grain. If my information is correct the Transcontinental railway can do the business of carrying western grain far cheaper than the Canadian Pacific. The grain would go through our own Canadian ports. This has been for some years a matter of great concern to the city of Quebec. I take this opportunity, now that we know definitely that steamships are under the control of the railway, of asking the minister to look into the matter with a view to increasing the business of the Transcontinental railway, taking away the business from rival roads, decreasing the cost of transportation to the western farmer, and in general helping on the prosperity of the country.
I shall be very glad to take this matter up with the head of the road.

Has the minister come to a decision with regard to certain flag stations the establishment of which has been suggested to him along the line of the Quebec and Saguenay railway? Some time ago I sent petitions to his department in regard to the erection of a flag station at Le Petit Debarquement, between Gap Tour-mente and Petite Riviere St. Francois; at Le Ruisseau Jureux, near St. Irenee; and also at Nairn's Falls behind Murray Bay. I would ask the minister to be good enough to let me know what decision he arrived at in the matter. I submitted statements showing the amount of traffic available at these places. I have had no definite answer yet to my request.

I asked Mr. Grant to look into that matter very thoroughly and give me a report. I have not yet received that report. As soon as I get it I will send it to the hon. member (Mr. Casgrain) and discuss the matter with him.

While we are speaking on the Quebec and Saguenay railway, I would like to submit an observation to the minister concerning his department, and it may also concern the Department of Marine and Fisheries. It is the intention to complete the extension of the road to Murray Bay by next season. But there will still be the service of the steamer Champlain which is being operated between the south shore and the north shore or between Riviere Ouelle and Murray Bay. The service of this boat may not be so necessary when the new railway is completed which will take people from Montreal and Quebec direct to Murray Bay. Will it be possible to devise a plan by which this boat will render a double service that will be useful to the people of other parts of the country, such as Cap a L'Aigle, St. Fidele, St. Simeon and Tadous-sac along the north shore below Murray Bay, which places will never have the benefit of the railway if they are unable to have any communication with it. As the service between the north and the south shore will not be so necessary as in the past, the boat might carry on a service between Murray Bay and Tadoussac and then cross to the south shore once or twice a week and make connections for the people who wish to take the boat for Murray Bay and below that point,

The operation of this boat has been carried on by the Depart-J Mr. Power.]
ment of Marine and Fisheries. I will bring the matter to the attention of my hon. friend, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne), and I will also try and get the railway in operation as soon as possible.

The operation of the ferry between Cape Tormentine and Port Borden is under the Department of Railways and Canals. While the Government are embarking on the enterprise of building steamers for traffic, is it the intention to build another ferry to run between these two points? As the minister well knows, the ferry, after being operated through the ice in the winter time, has to go into dry-dock for repairs each. summer, and for a considerable time there is no connection between these two points. While the Government is engaged in building vessels I would urge upon the minister the great necessity of building a twin ferry so that one boat could always be kept in operation. When the ferry service is discontinued between Cape Tormentine and Port Borden the traffic has to cross between Summer-side and Point du Chene, and the offices have to be moved. New buildings have been erected at the junction point of Sack-ville for the purpose of accommodating this traffic, but when the traffic is diverted to the other route they are left unused. I notice by the papers that the vessel has been laid off this week for repairs. This suspension of the ferry dislocates trade, and is very inconvenient for those who use that route.

Owing to the great cost of vessel construction it would probably not be right to consider the building of another ship for this purpose at present. If I remember correctly, the Scotia was operating at Mulgrave and a new steamer was put on in her place. It was proposed at one time,
I think, to fix up that vessel so that she could be used on this route and thus have a spare vessel when the ferry was compelled to lay up for repairs once a year, or might be disabled by accident. The vessel in question is much smaller, but by running more frequently she might meet the need temporarily for three or four weeks.

Such a boat might answer as a substitute for two or three weeks, while the regular ferry is undergoing repairs.
If that were done it would prove of great advantage to the people who use that route for trade purposes.

Clause 11 is very wide in its scope. It reads:
The Governor in Council may from time to time by Order in Council entrust to the company the management and operation of any lines of railway or part thereof, and any property or works of whatsoever description, or interest therein, and any powers, rights or privileges over or with respect to any railways, properties or works, or interests therein, which may he from time to time vested in or owned, controlled or occupied by His Majesty, or such part or parts thereof, or rights or interests therein as may be designated in any Order in Council, upon such terms and subject to such regulations and conditions as the Governor in Council may from time to time decide; such management and operation to continue during the pleasure of the Governor in Council and to be subject to termination or variation from time to time in whole or in part by the Governor in Council.
The minister will admit that this confers upon the Governor in Council very wide powers, under which it can do practically anything it likes with any branch of railway forming part of the system. I think the public should be apprised of whatever action the Governor in Council takes in such matters, and I would therefore suggest that whenever an Order in Council is passed taking advantage of any of the powers granted under this section it shall not go into effect until it has been published in the Canada Gazette, so that the public may be afforded an opportunity of knowing what is going on and given a chance, if any objection is entertained, to remonstrate to the department or the Government.
Hon. gentlemen opposite professed to be shocked this afternoon when I proposed the submission to Parliament of the bylaws which might be passed by the company. I notice, however, that in Australia all such by-laws have to be laid before both Houses of Parliament within thirty days oi their adoption, and, if Parliament is not in session, within thirty days after it shall have convened. The commissioner in Australia is given very wide powers and can make by-laws applicable to every branch of the administration of a railway, but these by-laws must be submitted to the Governor-General and do not become effective until after they have been published in the official Gazette. In Volume 15, Commonwealth Acts, 1917, is the Statute dealing with the Government railways. Section 88 provides:
(1) The commissioner may make by-laws, not inconsistent with this Act, prescribing all matters which by this Act are required or permitted to he prescribed, or which are necessary or convenient to he prescribed for carrying out or giving effect to this Act, and in particular for the following:
Then follows the enumeration of the subjects upon which by-laws may be made, and paragraph (2) of the section reads:
No by-law shall have any force or effect until it has been-
(a)	approved by the Governor General; and-
(b)	published in the Gazette.
And then paragraph (3) reads:
(3)	By-laws shall not be deemed to he Statutory Rules within the meaning of the Rules Publication Act, 1903-1916.
(4)	All such by-laws shall be laid before both Houses of the Parliament within thirty days after the making thereof, if the Parliament is then sitting, and if not, then within thirty days of the next meeting of Parliament.
Now in view of the wide powers conferred by the section in the Bill we are considering, I would suggest adding to the section: Such Orders in Council to be published in the official Gazette of Canada before they take force and effect.

If the hon. gentleman will read the clause he will see that it merely entrusts to the company the management and operation of the lines of railway in question. In the past, so far as the Intercolonial railway was concerned, its operation was entrusted to a general manager, and then a commission was appointed to manage and operate the railway.

"Upon such terms and subject to such regulations and conditions as the Governor in Gouncil may from time to time decide." That is how the clause reads, and we want to know under what terms it is to be carried out.
We formerly had a general manager and all that this clause means is that we propose to do the same thing here-entrust to a board of management the operation of the Government Railway system.	*
No, the powers in regard to management can be restricted or enlarged.

We must trust the board
of management. For instance, if the board of management submits by-laws and the " Governor in Council passes an Order in Council with respect to them, the Government must accept the responsibility of its action no matter what the public mav think. Then when Parliament meets all the Orders in Council that have been passed can be laid upon the Table for the consideration of the House.

That is all I want. I
want the Orders in Council which will be passed under section 11 to be laid upon the

Table within a certain time after Parliament convenes.

It is entirely in the hands of hon. members to have those Orders laid upon the Table. The very fact of it being mentioned in the Bill does not make it any more certain that the Orders will be laid upon the Table-
Oh, yes.

For this'reason the
House is entitled to all Orders in Council, and if they are not laid upon the Table by the Minister of Railways hon. members will ask for them and they will be produced. I do not see that this proposal would afford any greater protection. I do not think we should load the Bill up any more. As was said by the Acting Minister of Justice this afternoon, we are trying to keep away as much as possible from laying Orders in Council upon the Table.

We are trying to keep
away-why?
Because there has been so much complaint about Orders in Council having been passed that one does not want so many Orders in Council as the hon. member does.

The minister does not understand what I am driving at. The clause is clear that these powers may be exercised through the Governor in Council from time to time by Orders in Council. It is not an approval; you have got to enact by Orders in Council. You entrust' certain things to the management, and the words must be written down on the recommendation of the Minister of Railways and then enacted by Order in Council. It is very easy for the minister to have an extra copy struck off every time he makes a recommendation to Council. The Order in Council will say what is being entrusted to the company, and the company is then supposed to act in the best interests of the country; but the Governor in Council can impose restrictions while entrusting this property to the. company, because at line 21 of section 11 it says:
-upon such terms and subject to such regulations and conditions as the Governor in Council may from time to time decide: such management and operation to continue during the pleasure of the Governor in Council and to be subject to termination or variation from time to time in whole or in part by the Governor in Council.
I think the House is entitled to know what parts of the road are being entrusted

to the company and under what regulations and conditions they are being operated. The minister says that we do not want to load the Bill for nothing. It will not load it at all; it wdll just be a reminder to the minister that within a certain time at the beginning of each session all these Orders in Council must be deposited upon the Table of t.he House, and I think the people, through their representatives, ought to he posted in what is going on in. connection with their railway system. I suggested just now that these Orders in Council have no force until publication in the Canada Gazette. I am willing to withdraw my assertion that they have no force, hut I think they should be published in the Canada Gazette so that the people can be kept informed of hhw their railway system is managed. I think it is a sug-
9 p.m. gestion that the minister ought to agree to.

The Commonwealth oi Australia and the different Australian states have had a long experience in state ownership of railways, and it would seem to rpe to be wise for us to follow their custom and have the by-laws pas.sed by the Board of Directors and approved by Order in Council placed on the Table within thirty days from the time they are passed if Parliament is sitting, or within thirty days after the House convenes. I cannot see any objection to that. It would appear to me to be an excellent means of keeping the country in touch with what is being done with its railway property.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no objection to that, Mr. Chairman, but I think it is entirely unnecessary, because all important Orders in Council are 'brought down and laid upon the Table of the House. If any hon. member should ask for an Order in Council relating to so important a subject as this it would be brought down without question. But the section is easily amended, and there is no reason why it should not be if hon. gentlemen think the matter important.

During the debate this afternoon it became apparent that when you apply the rule of Order in Council you do not altogether cover the case, because the directors would have power to make by-laws that are not approved by Order in Council.

But this is the important clause that deals with the handling of property-such orders to be deposited upon

the table of the House within thirty days of the opening of each session.

Under this clause as at present drafted would the Government have the right to acquire any further branch lines, such, for instance, as the Quebec and Oriental Railway and the Atlantic and Western Railway that the member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) spoke of this afternoon? These railways are more or less a continuation of the Intercolonial,, and all their traffic is practically the traffic of the Intercolonial. Some time ago I had occasion, in the Special Committee considering the Railway Act, to submit a communication regarding the present condition of these railways, and although I hold no brief for the companies, I -think they would be willing to -enter into negotiations with the Government for sale of their properties.
Mr. J. I). REID: No, Parliament would have to acquire the roads first, and then the Governor in Council would have the right to entrust their management to this corporation.

Several of the companies enumerated in the schedule have names that indicate they are situated partly or wholly in the United States. It is an altogether new situation, and I would like the minister to give information to the House as to exactly the relation that would arise between a sovereign country like Canada owning and running railroads in another sovereign country.

The stock of these roads is owned by the Canadian Northern System, and therefore by the Government. The American Government are now operating those portions that run through the United States. The hon. member will of course understand that the American Government are also operating some of our Canadian roads. The Michigan Central is an American-owned road. Two or three roads that go through Ontario are part of an American system.
-But they are not owned by the Government of the United States.
The United States Government is operating them; it is hard to say whether they will be taken over permanently by the Government. The Canadian Pacific runs through a portion of the State of Maine.

Are the legal advisers
of the Government of the opinion that the
Government has the right to own and operate railroads in a foreign country? I do not think it has.

The company have a right to operate in a foreign country; the Government is only a shareholder of the company. From this point of view, the legal advisers of the Government inform me that we have a perfect right to do as we are doing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
To meet what my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau) has in mind, I move that the following words be added to section 11:
Any such Order in Council shall be laid before Parliament within ten days after the opening of the next ensuing session, or, if Parliament be sitting at the time such Order in Council is passed, then within ten days of the date of such Order in Council.

Amendment agreed to, and sections 10 and 11 agreed to. ,
On section 12-power to transfer to company the stock or controlling interest of His Majesty in any railway company:
Does this section mean that the directors of the Canadian National Railway Company may, without getting leave, purchase additional stock in railway companies?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, their powers are
covered by section 21. This section merely gives the Government the power to transfer shares to them.

I have an objection to this clause. We know and feel the nefarious effects of that transaction in connection with the Canadian Northern, when we got forty per cent of the stock. If His Majesty is to acquire an interest in any company, he - ought to acquire the majority of the stock so as to be able to have his own board of directors, his own administration and operation. I do not think that His Majesty ought to hold minority stock in any company.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The acquirement of minority stock is not contemplated here. The section says: "acquire the stock or the controlling interest."
If that means " acquire all the stock," why not say so? The wording is not very clear.

It may be true that the reference is to the acquirement of the entire stock, but it might be held that the words "the stock" meant part of the stock. If the word "entire" is inserted before the

word "stock" on line 2, the meaning will be made perfectly: clear.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no objection to that.
Amendment agreed to.

This section seems to contemplate the continuation of these companies in their respective entities. I understand that the purpose of this legislation is to get clear of these outside companies. The Act contemplates that meetings of companies are to be held at which the Government will be represented. I am entirely opposed to that, and I would like some assurance from the minister that it is his intention to get clear of these companies. When will the Canadian National Railway Company he doing business absolutely on its own footing? When will it be absolutely controlling this government property?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I thought I had made that clear. As to the constituent companies named in the schedule of the Bill, the policy is to amalgamate all except those in which there is minority stock outstanding, thus getting rid of the separate entities and of the names. Where there is minority stock outstanding it would not be in the public interest to amalgamate, because other stock would have to be given to take care of the minority stock. That applies only to very few companies. The subsidiary companies do not own or operate railways; consequently, it would not be good business to amalgamate them; they are- better as they are. As to the constituent companies, two at least are American companies and cannot be amalgamated; the policy is to amalgamate the others.

This section says:
The Governor in Council may transfer, or cause to he transferred, such capital stock or any part thereof to the company, or may by proxies or otherwise enable the company or any nominee of the Governor in Council to exercise the voting power thereof at any meeting of shareholders.
Why should the words "or any nominee
of the Governor in Council " be inserted?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The transferee of the
stock could be our proxy to vote the stocks. That could be done, of course, but power is taken to have the stock voted in an alternative way by naming a separate nominee. For example, the Minister of Railways might be named, or the most immediate Government representative on the board, where there is one.

If it is the intention of the Government to give such power to the min-
[Mr. McMaster.j
ister or to any other person whom they may designate, I do not see why that should come into this particular Bill which is a Bill to incorporate the Canadian National Railway Company.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The only way to have the power is by this Bill.

Section agreed to.
On section 13, subsection (1)-application of Railway Aot and Expropriation Act to undertakings of company :
I move that the three subsections of section 13 be considered separately.
Motion agreed to.
WThat Act is meant by "The Railway Act?" Is it the existing Act or the new Bill? .

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It means at present the existing law. When the new Bill passes, it will mean that.	[DOT]
Why not say the Railway Act, 1919?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Interpretation Act covers that.

"Has it been found impossible or too difficult to designate by numbers the provisions of the Railway Act which are not to apply? This form of legislation may be unavoidable, but it is open to criticism. When it is stated that certain portions of an Act are not to apply, it is desirable that those portions should be indicated by the numbers of the sections. When the section states in general terms " all the provisions of the Railway Act excepting those provisions which are inconsistent with this Act " and so forth, that leaves it an open question as, to what portions of the law are inconsistent. Further on the Government seem to have anticipated that very point, because they provide in subsection 2:
In case of doubt, the Governor in Council may declare what provisions and to what extent the provisions of the respective Acts are applicable to the company under this section.
The determining of what sections are consistent and what are not seems to be rather a judicial function. I suppose the matter has been considered, and there may be difficulties in designating the sections by numbers, but if they could be so designated, that would be very desirable.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If the present Act was to continue or if the new Act was already passed, they could be designated without

any difficulty, but inasmuch as both Acts are to apply each in turn, it is difficult to designate; that is to say, the designation which one might now make would not apply when the new Act passes.

There is a very easy way out of the difficulty, unless there are grave reasons why this section should be worded as it is. This Bill is being passed for the purpose of putting the Canadian Government railways as nearly as possible, the interest of the people being protected, on the same footing as all privately-owned railways. Why should the Canadian Government railways, when they require any land for the construction of railways, follow the Expropriation Act and go before the Exchequer Court instead of following the ordinary provisions of the statute? The Canadian Northern railway, before it was turned into the Government, if it wanted to expropriate, went before the courts ol the province' wherein the land was situated and got the land, and I do not see why these provisions of the Railway Act should not apply to the Canadian Government Railway System. If there are any objections, I am willing to consider and discuss them. But this would avoid confusion and it would be fairer to prevent the people from following His Majesty the King, who controls the Canadian Government railways on behalf of the Dominion of Canada, before the Exchequer Court. Why should not in this case the interpretation of the law by a judge of the superior court be as good for the Canadian Government as it is for privately-owned Canadian railway companies operating under the General Act?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is no intention ol going before any tribunal different from the tribunal other railways go before, namely, a board of arbitrators, to determine the arbitration. The provisions of the Expropriation Act in that regard do not apply by reason of subsection (c) of this section which says:
The compensation payable in respect of the taking of any lands so vested in the company, or of interests therein, or injuriously affected by the construction of the undertaking or works shall be ascertained in accordance with the provisions of the Hailway Act, beginning with notice of expropriation to the opposite party.
So that the provisions of the Railway Act as regards the fixing of compensation apply. That was done with the idea that persons whose lands, usually farm lands, are taken are given the right of having the values determined by arbitrators, just as under the Railway Act, instead of being compelled to go to the Exchequer Court. The difference is this, that if the Railway Act altogether applied and no power of the Exchequer Act were invoked, then we would have to file plans with the Railway Commission, and' furthermore, title would not vest with the filing of the plans in accordance with this clause, but taking the powers of the Expropriation Act and embodying them here, we get title on the filing of the plans and thereby avoid the intervention of intermediary parties purchasing lands ahead of us by reason of knowledge of the filing of plans in advance. That is all the difference.
Mr. BUREAU Clause (c) says:
The compensation payable in respect of the taking of any lands so vested in the company, or of interests therein, or injuriously affected by the construction of the undertaking or works shall be ascertained in accordance with the provisions of the Railway Act, beginning with notice of expropriation to the opposite party.
That is when the plans are filed.

There is something wrong here. The Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) says that expropriation and the filing of plans with the registrar gives title. That I think is very summary and autocratic, and it is unfair. I may be wrong, but I think that under the Railway Act we have to serve notice to the respondent in which you must offer him the amount which the engineer or surveyor who signs the notice swears is the value of the land.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That must be done now, too.
What is the use of doing it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is the first step towards getting at the value.

Why not dispose of the whole matter and say that in the case of the Canadian Government Railway System the deposit of the plan will vest title in the company, and that the proceeding of expropriation shall be the same as under the general Railway Act. That would cover the ground and obviate all confusion that might result from this section.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Where information is .given out as to where your route lies an opportunity for intervention by intermediaries arises. The danger time is between the time the information gets out by taking your plan to the Railway Commission and the time of filing the plan.
Why should that not apply to the general Railway Act?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is another question. I am not prepared to argue now that it should not apply.

My whole object is to avoid having two laws regulating railways, whether the Canadian Government Railway or the Canadian Pacific Railway. It would be well if we could eliminate the confusion as to what clauses should apply and what should not and would relieve the Governor in Council of the trouble and responsibility of determining this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There will be no difficulty in saying what clauses apply and what do not apply, as soon as the Railway Act passes. I am advised there is very little need for subsection (2).

The Government will not build roads unless they have a charter, and they generally fairly well indicate where they are going to run. I see there is a section seeking to revive certain charters. The public will know exactly what roads they are and where they lie. I do not see why there should be such a long provision, which is liable to create confusion. If my hon. friend would give me five minutes I would submit a draft amendment to cover the ground.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no objection to giving the hon. member five minutes.
Of course, if my hon. friend will not accept it I will not go to the trouble of doing it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We could not accept any clause compelling us to disclose the exact right of -way prior to the acquirement of title, because that would give an opportunity to others to come in and buy ahead of us. The charter generally indicates the direction of the road, tout it does not give the line. 'So long as only the general direction is known we have nothing to fear, but we do not want to be in the position of having to disclose the exact right of way.

That point is open to discussion. The other railways have to have their plans approved by the Minister of Railways and have to submit them to the Railway Commission. Why should the Government have an advantage over other people who want to build a railway? I do not believe that men who would seek to dispose of their land at fancy prices would be given any consideration by the courts.
I have known arbitration cases in which land was valued, say, at $400 and was sold for $4,000, but the court, realizing that it

was only a hold-up, endorsed the valuation of the arbitration.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I know cases where plans
have been submitted to the Railway Board for consideration and several parties have at once commenced buying lands on the proposed route. They made two or three turnovers amongst themselves and the result was that the railway had to pay considerably more than they should have paid.
Was it because it was held several months before the Railway Board?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is the usual delay.
I think the same principle should be adopted in regard to all railways, and when the Railway Bill comes up we ought to see to that. There is no reason why railways should be held up by speculators as they have been in the past in -many instances. In this clause we are trying !to avoid that so far as the Government is concerned, and if the companies are wise they will protect themselves.

It is not a question of wisdom on the part of companies, but whether private companies shall have the same right as the Government.
Mr. II. A. MACKIE: According to the proposed Railway Act, the notice which is to be served upon the owner refers him to the book of reference and plan which has to be filed with the registrar. You say that the notice for expropriation will give him that information.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It gives him the information that the plan is there filed, and from that he can get the exact area taken. It also tells him what is proposed to be paid for it.

Are we, by this clause, to do away with the filing of plans and the book of reference up to a certain point? He may get information from the plans and book of reference after it becomes impossible, as you say, for speculators to step in? In the meantime he gets notice of the expropriation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Afterwards.
On paragraph 2-porwer to decide cases in doubt:

I do not think this paragraph should pass in its present form. It is not right that the Governor in Council should be at one and the same time a party to a case and the judge in the matter.

Some independent authority should be selected. I would suggest that the paragraph be changed to read:
In case of doubt the Exchequer Court may declare what provisions and to what extent the provisions of the respective Acts are applicable to the company under this section.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Speaking at the moment,
1	rather think that is the law now. A case in conflict would necessarily be decided by the Exchequer Court. If my hon. friend's amendment were accepted, it would be equivalent to removing the sub-clause. If the sub-clause is removed it will have the same effect as if my hon. friend's amendment carries. I do not see that sub-clause
2	need be invoked at all. I would consent to striking it out. I therefore move:
That sub-clause 2 of clause 13 be struck from the Bill.
. Motion agreed to.
On paragraph 3 (now paragraph 2)-(a) signatures to plans deposited; (b) lands vested in the company; (c) ascertaining amount of compensation.

Is there any provision by which we have a president and vicepresident?
Mr. _MEIGHEN: The provision in the Railway Act provides for a president and vice-president.

Under this Bill we have the directors on the one hand and the company on the other. The president of an ordinary company, is usually appointed at a general meeting of the shareholders. I do not see what the Railway Act has to do with the appointing of a president when there are no shareholders to appoint him.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
mistaken. The directors elect the president. Clause 13 of the Bill provides that the Railway Act, except as to certain clauses, shall apply. One of the non-excepted clauses provides that the directors shall elect the president and vice-president. Consequently that clause applies. Our directors will elect the president and vice-president. Section 13 comes in there and its application is clear.
On section 15-actions, suits or other proceedings :

Does this change
the existing law in any way?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. In one sentence
it makes the new corporation liable at law and vests in the new corporation the rights at law of a corporation rather than putting
it in the position of the Crown. A man now to sue in respect to anything done to him on the Intercolonial must have a fiat, hereafter he can sue the Canadian National Railway Company without a fiat. Similarly, the company itself ean sue without a fiat, it can act as a corporation not subject to the restrictions or to the enjoyment of the privileges of the Crown.
Is there any provision for the liquidation of a judgment that may be obtained against the company?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The clause provides
that:
Any defence available to the respective corporations (including His Majesty) in respect of whose undertaking the cause of action arose shall be available to the company, and any expense incurred in connection with any action taken or judgment rendered against the company in respect of its operation or management of any lines of railway or properties, other than its own lines of railway or properties, may be charged to and collected from the corporation in respect of whose undertaking such action arose.
That is what ,1 do not understand.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Any expense in relation to an undertaking is charged against the operation of that undertaking or any judgment recorded in relation to an undertaking is charged against that undertaking. If the undertaking out of which the action arises is in connection with the Intercolonial, the expense is charged against the operation of the Intercolonial and a judgment is charged in the same way.
Mr. MoMASTER: That is, supposing that the company will keep a special record *showing how each undertaking is charged?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

And it is really only a matter of bookkeeping as between different departments of the same railway. The other party will have nothing to do with that. The other party would levy against the property of the whole company if it obtained judgment and, that judgment was unsatisfied.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is right.

I do not understand that this company are to own anything at all. They will not own the railway, they will not own the rolling stock as an ordinary company would, they are a sort of holding concern and are simply operating the railway system which is really owned by the King, as represented here by the Governor in Council. Now when a per-

son has a judgment against this company, and sends the sheriff to execute it, what is he going to levy upon? This company do not own anything so far as I can see.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is not quite correct in his statement. The company is more than a holding company. It is a holding company, but when the power of amalgamation provided for in section 21 takes place the Canadian Northern itself will he amalgamated in this company and will cease to exist as a separate entity. Therefore it is more than a holding company. But even if it is a holding company it has the stock which may be levied on for judgment.
The Minister of Finance holds the stock.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The stock is to be transferred under section 12. The company has to pay its debts, that is manifest, and its debts in respect of a judgment will be chargeable against the undertaking it is operating in regard to which the accident, or whatever it may be that gave rise to the judgment, occurs.

That is perfectly clear, but I want to detain the minister for just a moment longer. Suppose that to-morrow Johnston gets judgment from the Supreme Court of Canada against this company, and they refuse to pay it, and he puts an execution in the sheriff's hands, what can he levy on?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He could not levy on anything until the assets are placed in the hands of the company; there could not be any judgment until such assets are in their possession. But immediately this Bill passes, the stock the Government owns is placed in the hands of the company, and could be levied on. Subsequently roads will be amalgamated with the existing system, and the physical assets of those roads will be the property of this company and may be levied against.

That is a new phase of the matter. I did not think the company were going to be the owners of these properties, and I do not think the House understood that the ownership was vested in this company as such. Then we are to understand the directors are to own these properties?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Upon amalgamation the company will own the direct physical assets.

It is generally understood that there are a great many unsettled claims against the Canadian Northern Railway Company. I would like to have the opinion of the Acting Minister of Justice as to whether a creditor of that company could bring action against these directors in respect of any unsatisfied claim against the Canadian Northern, and if so, whether judgment could be obtained against the directors in respect of it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is in error in stating that there are a great number of unsatisfied claims against the Canadian Northern Railway Company. The claims are pretty well settled up, in fact I do not know that there are any outstanding. But if there were, the judgment now would be obtained against the company, and would be collectable from it. But upon amalgamation the company that absorbs the others is then the company liable and will have to pay any judgment rendered.
I am glad to hear the minister say there are no outstanding claims against the Canadian Northern, because it has been frequently stated in the House that there were numerous such claims.

Section agreed to.
On Section 16-Expenses to be paid out of receipts and revenues.

Some of the clauses that we have been discussing have perhaps not been of the utmost importance, but here is a clause that is worth reflecting on, because I doubt if its gravity has been fully understood by the Committee; certainly its gravity is not understood by the outside public. If there is one principle clearer than another in relation to our financial affairs, it is that every penny of revenue that is collected in any form for the purposes of the Dominion of Canada shall be paid into the Consolidated Fund. Once, in that fund not one dollar of the money can be paid out until it has been appropriated by the House of Commons. That is the basic principle of our system of finance. Yet we are gravely and deliberately proposing to depart from it. We are proposing, as respects the management of one of the greatest of our departments-a department that is a great one now and will be even greater by virtue of the passage of this Bill-to repeal the Consolidated Revenue Act. We are proposing that this company shall be allowed to take into their treasury every dollar that they earn and use it foi

the purposes of the railway system as they think best. There was a discussion, at an earlier stage, concerning one portion of this question. I was not present on that occasion, but I find from a perusal of Hansard that there was a discussion on the question of the deficit, as to whether or not that should he paid without an appropriation. But that is only a part of the issue involved. The broader question is that while every other department of the Government will be held under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue Act, this great department will not be so held. The Minister of Customs, the Minister of Inland Revenue, the Postmaster General, and all the other ministers who collect revenue will be obliged to pay it into the treasury and to await an appropriation by this House; but as respects the collections of this department-and they will run into many millions -they are not to go into the consolidated revenue but into the treasury of this company at whatever point it may have its head office. We shall be told that it is very inconvenient to have any other arrangement. Of course, it is inconvenient. It would be most convenient for the ministers, and I have been one, if they did not have to be bothered by appropriations. The truth is that Parliament is rather an inconvenience to ministers at times. But it is necessary in the transaction of public affairs that we shall have a Parliament. I 'hope that before the Bill is finally passed my hon. friends on the treasury benches will reconsider this matter and see if they cannot, instead of setting the Consolidated Revenue Act at defiance, bring this measure into harmony with it. It was said in the discussion to which I have referred, that you could not make estimates of the probable cost of operating this railway. The answer to that is that for fifty years we have been making estimates for the cost of operating the Intercolonial Railway. I have no doubt it was an embarrassment at times to the Minister of Railways. It was a year ago that he tried to do for that department what he is now proposing to do in the case of a larger scheme. After some reflection and discussion the minister did not press the matter. I do not intend to make any motion on the subject, but I do hope that before this Bill passes the Government will reconsider this matter and see that provision is made for this^ depart-_ment complying with the Consolidated Revenue Act as is done by every other department of the Government.
There is nothing in the argument that you cannot make estimates. If you are
able to make estimates for the Intercolonial, why cannot you do so for these other roads? I remember some reference was made to the difficulty of making estimates because of the great crop in the Northwest. Surely we all hope that the crop will be a great one, and the wise Minister in making his estimates will show that he is hoping there will be a great crop. But I do think that the setting aside of the Consolidated Act in reference to this Department is not wise, and in all seriousness I would .suggest to my honourable friends on the Treasury benches that before the matter is disposed of finally they reconsider that aspect of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Needless to say 1 always pay very great attention and am disposed to give great weight to any observations from my honourable friend (Mr. Fielding) with respect to matters of financial administration in which he has had very wide experience as Minister of Finance. He has pointed out that it may be inconvenient to adopt the method which he suggests, namely, of making an estimate and having all expenditures vouched for in the usual way as is done in the case of Departments of the Government. It seems to me that it is not a matter of inconvenience so much as of practical impossibility. I do not say that lightly, because I agree with my honourable friend that if a thing should be done the fact that there is some inconvenience involved should not prevent its being done. But I would submit, without concluding myself as to the position which the Government will take-because we will be very glad to give my honourable friend's views full consideration-that this railway company of which the Government is the virtual proprietor notwithstanding the corporate from in which its assets are held is not a department of the Government in the same sense that the Railway or Customs or Inland Revenue is a department of the Government. As I pointed out last evening when I spoke upon this matter, there are two ways in which the Dominion Government could administer this great railway system which has now come into our hands and such other systems as may be acquired in the future. One way would be to attempt to administer them as the Intercolonial Railway was administered, by the Railway Department of the Government, which, as the Committee knows, is under the direct control of the Minister of Railways. ~ The other way, both for practicability of administration and for divesting the Government as far
'[DOT]TIM

as possible of control in order that no question of political patronage may enter, is to administer them through the medium of a joint stock company or companies. Take the situation as it exists to-day. The various departments of the Govern-
10 p.m. ment, including the Railway Department in respect of the Canadian Northern Railway, make theii Estimates, and all expenditures are audited by the Auditor General, as my hon. friend has indicated. But in connection with the Canadian .Northern Railway Company, whose stock is held by the Government-just as the stock of this company which we are now creating will be held for the Government-the administration being under a corporation is carried out as corporations carry out their enterprises. The corporation, as such, receives all revenue, and all expenditures are made under the authority of the board of directors, who are directly responsible to the Dominion Government. That is the situation existing today with regard to the Canadian Northern Railway Company, which is owned by the Dominion Government as I have pointed out.
Now, if we had given effect to the suggestion of my hon. friend, the Government during the past year or more that it has owned the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company would have made an estimate showing the entire amount of expenditure which in the opinion of the board of directors and the Government would be necessary, and all expenditures of every kind whatsoever, great or small, throughout the entire system would have to be checked by the proper officers of the Government and vouched by the Auditor General. That would be a very great undertaking. It is a large undertaking as it is. The officers of the company, acting under the authority of the board, receive all the revenue and pay it out under a system of audit established by the company. No doubt a very thorough system of audit should be established, and we have endeavoured to establish such a system. I remember that two years ago we appointed, in addition to the auditors of the company, the well-known firm of Marwick, Mitchell, Peat & Co., a firm of very high standing, and they have been auditing	the	accounts.	In a sense
while the Canadian Northern Railway is not a department of the Government, the directors and those under them and the auditors are Government officials. They are not Government officials in the sense of officials in the several departments, but

nevertheless in substance and in fact, as the Government of Canada owns all the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, its board of directors and their subordinates are Government officers.
I am the first to admit the necessity oi the strictest kind of check upon receipts and expenditures, because if there is one thing that we should have learned in connection with public affairs it is that the strictest check is necessary to prevent abuse of power in the control of money. But I submit that in the present situation, in view of the fact that we hold the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway System, it would be very difficult indeed for the officials of the Government to supervise all the receipts and expenditures of the system. And that has not been done; the company has carried on its business as the Canadian Pacific Railway Companies carries on its business, and as the Grand Trunk Railway System carries on its business-through its officers, and subject to audit, which is continuous and is carried on with great care. The system which we have in contemplation, and which has necessitated the creation of this company, in .accordance with the terms of this Act is a much larger one than the Canadian Northern Railway Company, because we have looked forward to the probable acquisition of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and of the Grand Trunk Railway System itself.
If that should happen, the Government would find itself in possession of an exceedingly large railway system, twenty thousand miles or more, consisting of the Intercolonial, the National Transcontinen-al from Moncton to Winnipeg, the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk Pacific, and, in all probability, the Grand Trunk. These being brought into one incorporation, there would be in Canada two great systems, the Canadian Pacific Railway System, and the Canadian National Railway System of which the proprietor would be the Dominion Government.
