If you have competent directors in whom the people have the utmost confidence; if you have officers of the same standing and integrity as those of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; if you have a proper system of audit and very full annual reports, you have surrounded the system with all reasonable safeguards. The alternative suggested by my hon. friend is that the Government make its estimates in respect of all the expenditures of that vast system and that all the items of expenditure, great and small, be checked as items of Government expendi-

ture in the various departments are now checked, and audited by the Auditor General. I do not say that that is impossible, but it seems to me to be impracticable.
I have very great respect for my hon. friend's opinion on a matter of this kind, but it would seem to be advisable that, if possible, the public interest be safeguarded by the organization of the company and by the checks which are in use in connection with railway systems rather than in the way that we now make estimates and check expenditures of departments of the Government, in the strict sense of the term. I think there is a perfect system of accounts in connection with the administration oi the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; it would seem to be quite as efficient as that which we have established under legislation of Parliament respecting receipts and expenditures of public money. I entirely sympathize with the view that the strictest supervision of expenditures should be exercised in connection with this system, foi this reason, among others: The board of direotors in whom this great trust and confidence is to be reposed will receive all moneys through the officials whom they name; will make all disbursements through their organization, and then come to the Government and to Parliament for any deficit. Parliament, therefore, is immediately interested in every expenditure made by that system. The sole question seems to be one of expediency and of the proper safeguarding of the public interest. If we could be satisfied that this company would carry on its operations as honestly and efficiently as other great railway systems carry on theirs, it would be unnecessary to insist upon a further check and audit on the part oi the officials of the Government and the Auditor General. If, on the other hand, the conclusion should be reached that what I put forward is impracticable and that public loss would ensue, then there is a great deal to be said for the view put forward by the hon. member. I have given the matter careful consideration, and it seems to me that the suggestion, while it should be weighed with great deliberation, is impracticable; and that we can accomplish the result which the hon. member has in mind by a proper system of administration and of audit and by an annual report which would furnish to the Government and to Parliament the fullest possible details of expenditure. I am not concluding, either myself or the Government, with respect to the attitude which we shall take upon this very important matter, but I 108
submit these observations for the consideration of the hon. member and of the Committee.

I take part in the dis.-cussion of this point with some diffidence, because I cannot bring to bear upon it the years of experience in financial matters that may be claimed by the'hon. member (Mr. Fielding) and by the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White). We are face to face with a difficult situation. We are endeavouring so to organize the publicly-owned railway properties of this country that they shall be removed from that partisan influence which has long been the curse of Government-owned railroads in Canada as in other countries. At the same time, we have to retain the control which our fiduciary position towards the taxpayers imposes upon us. Yesterday I proposed a scheme for the first appointment of directors. The argument offered by the Prime Minister in opposition to the proposal was strong enough to convince me that possibly I was mistaken; that there was no way in which the Government could avoid its final and ultimate responsibility, and that, therefore, it had the right to name the entire board of directors. Can we, then, afford to throw aside the safeguards which British constitutional tradition has placed around the expenditure of public moneys? I do not think we can.
Twp points were made by the Acting Prime Minister. First, there was the difficulty of estimating what it would cost to run this great railway system. I grant the difficulty, but I do not believe that it is insurmountable. At the beginning the directors will have to administer a certain number of roads which are now in operation, and the expenditures of last year, with increases or decreases, as the case may be, will form a pretty safe indication of what will have to be spent in the next fiscal year. :I believe that the estimates can be made. True, they will run into appalling figures, but it is just as well that the people should be brought face to face with the importance of this undertaking. The second point is in relation to the audit. I do not see any difficulty in connection with the matter of an audit.
The Acting Prime Minister has told us that an audit will have to be made; that an audit is made now of Canadian Northern RailW'ay operations. Instead of having an auditor chosen in the manner in which this firm of auditors which he speaks about was chosen, the auditor will be the Auditor General, and his staff will make the audit.



I understand the Acting Prime Minister does not do more this evening than express his doubt as to his ability to meet the desires of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), which, I think, are the desires of a large number of the members of this House. I would join with the hon. member in asking the (Government to reconsider very carefully this question, and I think I can say, with those who think with me, that we shall not depart from sound traditional usage which has grown up from generation to generation without the clearest proof and the soundest argument that this tradition can be departed from with safety to the public interest.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In the first place, 1 think there is a misconception as to the effect of this section which has reference merely to moneys received and paid out in respect of the operation of the Canadian Government railways. It has not reference to moneys received and paid out in respect of the operation of the Canadian Northern railway system. It is because it has reference to moneys received and paid out' in respect of the Canadian Government railways that we have to use the term:-
Notwithstanding anything in the Government Railways Act or the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act.
Those two Acts never did provide that money received in respect of the Canadian Northern railway system by the Canadian National Railway Cbmpany should come into the Consolidated Revenue Fund and be paid out of that fund.
Does the minister think it should not?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I will come to that in a moment. What I mean to say is that we are not in any way setting aside the provisions of the Government Railways Act or the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act in respect of moneys that are received from the Canadian Northern railway system at all, only in respect of the Intercolonial. Apparently my hon. friend is asking that as respects all moneys received by this corporation they should go right into the Consolidated Revenue of Canada and should be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue as departmental moneys. Does not this Bill mean that we are attempting to set up a system of corporate management divorced from direct government interference or control, of this great railway system-corporate as distinguished from departmental management? Can you have corporate management of the road and departmental financing? Or corporate management and departmental auditing? Immediately you commence departmental audit through the Auditor General to that extent you have entirely disintegrated the system of corporate management. I would not for a moment contend that an exact, careful, thorough and responsible system of audit, for which we should be responsible, should not apply to the accounts of the Canadian National Railways as constituted by this Bill. It is not a question of thoroughness or propriety of audit, one system should be just as thorough and rigid as the other; but it is a question of whether you are going to have a system of corporate or departmental audit. Can you have management by corporation and departmental audit? To me it does not seem possible. If all the moneys of the Canadian Northern system are to go right into the Consolidated Revenue, and to be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue, how can that be consistent with corporate management of the roads? It appears to be a manifest anomaly.
May I suggest that your whole company is really an anomaly. It is not a real company.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It seems to me to be a very real company. We want to "make it a real company, but it will be a very unreal company if one-half is to be departmental and the other half corporate. I do think that while it is true that this is in reality a Government enterprise, it is equally true that we are trying to operate it as a business concern under corporate management; and every argument that would go to show that we ought to have direct departmental audit would be just as

forcible to show that we should directly manage the road as weir. There is nothing to show that corporate audit by the system now in vogue in that company, upon which we super-impose an audit of our own to ensure that their audit is correct, should not be just as thorough as any audit through the Auditor General's Department.

speechtext: Carried.
I understand, Mr. Chairman, and I think correctly, that the Acting Prime Minister acceded to the request of the hon. member (Mr. Fielding) to let this stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is no
reason why it should not stand for consideration. The system is so large, and is likely to be so much larger, that it seems to me to be a needless duplication of work even if it were practicable. It is a question of safeguardingthe public interest, and the real point is whether the public interest can be safeguarded through corporate administration under which these railways are to be operated. It would appear to me that it can be so safeguarded, but I think the strictest attention should be given to that point. The system should be under the most competent audit from time to time and the Government should be closely in touch with its general finance. I admit that the situation is anomalous, but it is necessarily so. I agree with what my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) said, and I have said the same thing many times myself, though not in the same words, namely, that no matter how the Government or Parliament might try to get rid of responsibility the fact is that this railway system, belonging to the Government and the people, must be administered by the Government subject to Parliament; and it is not possible, nor, in my view, is it proper that the Government should escape responsibility. If it were not for this question of the intrusion of patronage, about which both Parliament and the public hold strong views, whether well founded or not, it seems to me that the logical position would be for the Government to administer the system directly, just as the Intercolonial was administered. We have been seeking to get away from that position, which is the logical one, in order to avoid the influencing of administration in a particular political interest; and to do that we have the expedient not of a com-
mission-which we might have if no question of corporation securities and franchise arose-but of corporation machinery.
But these men are practically commissioners.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am coming to that; I agree with my hon. friend and the point he raises strengthens my argument. We have adopted corporate administration. If it were a commission the Government would appoint the commissioners just as it appoints the board of directors of this system. These men are responsible to the Government in their administration, but we seek to give them independence of action to avoid the evils which I have mentioned. If we have capable men-and I said the other night and say now that the whole success of government ownership is necessarily dependent upon the obtaining of men of the highest integrity in whom the people will have continuing confidence-and if there is a railway administration similar to that of the great systems like the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk, with a continuous audit and the check again upon that audit such as we have in connection with the Canadian Northern, I submit, the public interest is protected although the machinery is different. The Auditor General would audit the accounts to, let us say, an unlimited degree; so can the auditors of a railway system. The system is spread over an entire continent and the audit system would be a very extensive one. If I believed we could not safeguard the public interest in the way the Canadian Pacific Railway Company safeguards the interests of its shareholders by a thorough audit, I would be disposed to give more weight to the view put forward than I do. But we can safeguard the situation. If we were tempted to introduce departmental finance into this corporate system we should be doing what the Acting Minister of Justice suggested a few moments ago-we should be essentially changing the basis of our administration, and should be carrying on a partly departmental and a partly corporate administration. It seems to me that the essence of the question is this: Can the public interest be protected in connection with this system through officials and through a proper system of audit? I think it can. I am entirely willing that this clause should stand until to-morrow if hon. gentlemen so desire.

The
clause has been declared carried and it

cannot stand without the unanimous consent of the Committee.
I would certainly have jumped up before but I understood from the Acting Prime Minister that he had acceded to the request of the hon. member (Mr. Fielding) for further consideration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Does the Committee
consent that the clause shall stand?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the Bill can be finished to-night, I would suggest that the clause be carried now, or later on,-although we would not be disposed to change the Bill in that respect.

It seems to me that there is not only the public interest to be safeguarded but there is also the control by Parliament of the expenditure of public money? During the war the British Government conducted a great insurance department at a very handsome profit, the figures running into millions of pounds. It would be interesting to know whether the premiums that were collected by this department from the shipowners-I think it was a system of marine insurance-were paid into the Consolidated Fund and whether the losses were paid out of that fund.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must insist upon knowing whether this is to stand now or whether it is to be taken as carried.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As I stated, the Government would be glad to give it consideration. Let it stand for the present at all events. I think it very desirable that this legislation should be got through as soon as possible consistently with full discussion. If the Bill is to be finished this evening perhaps hon. gentlemen opposite would be willing that this should go through. I may say that we are not disposed to change our view in respect of it.
We are still considering this clause, are we?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No; it stands.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Stands.
Section stands.
On section 17-fiscal year, January 1 to December 31:
What is the object ol having a different fiscal year from that of the other departments of Government or the other business of Canada?
This is to comply with the provision of the general Railway Act.

That is hardly a suffi
eient reason.

If it were to conform
with the fiscal year of Canada, Parliament would be. able to get fuller information. My hon. friend says that it is to conform with the general Railway Act. Here- is a particular instance in which we should differ from the general Railway Act. It would be better to have the fiscal year of the Canadian Railways conform with the Government fiscal year so that we would know exactly how much we had run behind in any one year. If the Government are going to pay the deficits we want to know each year what is going to be chargeable to it.

The Railway Act provides :
Such returns shall be made for the period beginning from the date to which the then last yearly returns made by the company or carrier by water extend, or, if no such returns have been previously made, from the commencement of the operation of the railway, or other works, or undertaking, and ending with the last day of December in the year, or other interval, for which the returns are to be made, or with such other date as the minister may direct.

If there is any case in
which we ought to make an exception to the general Railway Act it is Ithis, because of all the departments of government this is the one that ought to conform to the fiscal year of the Government so that we would know exactly where to charge the deficits at the end of the year.

When the Minister ot Railways is making his report for the year he will certainly be supposed to report Ujpon this system, notwithstanding that it is under the operation of a company. It is admitted that this system is a part of Government ownership under a different name and the minister will report to Parliament on the operations of this company. Are we going to have two reports instead of one? It is impossible to have a full statement of the operations during the year if one report ends on the last day of December and the other on the last day of March. I submit that the railway year should be uniform with the financial year in the departments of Government. We have nothing as a Parliament to do with the general Railway Act. These companies are not bound to report to this House, and that should not regulate the business at all.

Referring, to the schedule to the Railway Act railway companies have to make returns.
-for the year ending June 30, 19-, required by the Minister of Railways and Canals, showing the conditions of the capital and revenue account of the railways in the Dominion of Canada.
Together with the location and general description of the railways, etc. Those returns, unless the law has been amended, are for the year ending June 30.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Railway Act now applies to the Canadian Northern System, but it does not apply to the Government Railways. The fiscal year now, therefore, under the Railway Act, is the calendar year. It appears as well that this is the fiscal year for all railways, American as well as Canadian, and that returns have to be made. Indeed, this company, must make returns in respect to a part of its system for the fiscal year to the Inter-State Commerce Commission of the United States. It is compelled to do so. Therefore, the company will require to have two fiscal years if you compel it now to change to the 31st March. There does not seem to be any particular object to be served, because the annual) returns would come to Parliament in any event.
Does the fiscal year of the American companies correspond with the fiscal year of their national finance?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I understood that in the United States the fiscal year is the calendar year.
Is their national fiscal year the calendar year?
It ends the 30th June.

The same as our own.
Mr. DAVIS Ours ends the 31st March.
I could understand that the American railways might be obliged to conform to the national fiscal year. If so, that would be an argument why our railways should conform to our fiscal year.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I understand our statistics are given for the calendar year. The calendar year is required in the United States and my information is that it is not their fiscal year. It is their railway year. This company has to comply with that requirement as to its American lines. It would need to have two years, which would be very complicated indeed.

I would like the minister to explain how this change would affect the Auditor General's Report. At the present time we have the expenditure on railways given in the Auditor General's Report up to 31st March. I conclude that the expenditure on the Canadian National Railways will be given in that report. Am I right? In that case, will not some confusion arise in the Auditor General's Report by making the fiscal year conform to the calendar year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I should think not. The Auditor General's Report would, of course, embody a statement of the payments made out'of the Consolidated Revenue Fund, or out of the Dominion treasury, to this company. Such payments made, we will say at the end of the company's railway year, thirty-first of December, will appear as of that date in the Auditor General's Report covering the fiscal year up to 31st March.
Expenditures between 31st December and 31st March following will not appear in the Auditor General's Report for the fiscal year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They will appear if any are made. If there was a deficit the payments would not be made at once, but payments made any number of times, as long as they were in the fiscal year of Canada, would appear in the Auditor General's Report of that year.

The disadvantage of that will be that the books and returns of the Canadian Government Railways are not going to correspond with those of the other departments, and for all purposes of investigation, examination and comparison, the situation will be very embarrassing.

Section agreed to.
On section 18-Works declared to be for the general advantage of Canada:

I understand that all the railways and companies that form part of the Canadian Northern system are enumerated in the list that is printed at the end of the Bill, entitled "Constituent and Subsidiary Companies comprised in the Canadian Northern System." What does this clause mean? Are there any other companies which the Government has acquired, or any companies whose stock is invested in the Minister of Finance for His Majesty, which are not enumerated in the schedule?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As I understand, there are now two companies comprised in the

Canadian Northern System which have not as yet been declared works for the general advantage of Canada. This clause declares them works for the general advantage of Canada, and consequently' makes them Dominion railways. Then the clause goes on to say that any companies hereafter included within this Canadian National Railway System, by virtue of the authority contained in Clause 11, if my memory serves me right, are now in advance declared to be for the general advantage of Canada, so that the whole can be considered national railways.

That is all right, but
it is the last part of the clause that I am alluding to.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The clause does what 1 have explained.

No, wdiat it says is this:
The works of any of the companies comprised in the Canadian Northern System which have not heretofore been declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada are hereby declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada, and the works of any company or companies hereafter from time to time declared1 toy the Governor in Council to toe comprised in the Canadian Northern System are hereby declared from and after the date of the making of such declaration toy the Governor in Council to be works for the general alvantage of Canada.
Now what ure the companies that have not been declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada, what are the companies that are not known to the Government as being part of the Canadian Northern System? My question is, are there any other companies which ought to belong, or which it is the intention of the Government to declare to belong, to the Canadian Northern System, which are not enumerated in the schedule at the end of this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There are two now belonging to the system not declared, but we declare them. There is no other at the present time that it is intended to declare, but there may be at any time, because clause 11 contemplates that any road hereafter acquired by the Crown may be entrusted to the management of this company. Then in section 18 we declare that from the time it is so entrusted, under section 11, it shall be a work for the general advantage of Canada.

A question occurs to
me, although a layman should not set himself up as a legal authority. There is no doubt that under the British North America
Act the Parliament of Canada has the power to declare any railway or other work a work for the general advantage of Canada. But is Parliament to delegate that power to the Governor in Council? That is a legal proposition and I only mention it for the consideration of my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen). He is proposing not only that certain roads shall be declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada, but that any roads which may hereafter be acquired by the Government may be declared works for the general advantage of Canada by the Governor in Council. That is too fine a legal proposition for me to do more than mention it to my hon. friend. That is not my main point, however. I quite admit the difficulty of operating this large railway system unless all the roads shall be brought under a common control, but is there not a possibility, or more than a possibility, of some trouble arising with the provincial governments? For example, one of the roads which, according to my recollection, is under the authority of the local legislature of Nova Scotia, is the Halifax and South Western. I know that originally it was under the control of the local legislature, but it may since have been brought under the general railway system. Has it been?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, that was done in 1914.
What are the two roads to which the Acting Minister of Justice referred a few minutes ago?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The St. Charles and Huron, and the Toronto Suburban.
Both Ontario roads?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: One is a Quebec road.
Have these roads been aided by the provincial government?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

The thought in my mind is this.: If there are cases where a road, having been aided largely by provincial funds, is declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada, some 'people may say Canada should reimburse the local government. As my hon. friend says that in this case the roads were not aided from the provincial treasury that point cannot be raised.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My information is that the St. 'Charles and Huron may have got a land grant, but that is all the assistance that was given to either of these two roads. As to the first point that my hon. friend

(Mr. Fielding) raises, it really is very well taken, tout I fancy that he is a little wrong in this regard: power is not given to the Governor in Council to declare any road a work for the general advantage of Canada. What is done toy this Bill is to declare any road a work for the general advantage of Canada which hereafter the Governor in Council entrusts to this company.
That is practically giving the power to the Governor un Council.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In effect it might be, but still from a legal standpoint the result is different. We do not say to the Governor in Council: "You may declare any road a work for the general advantage of Canada." We say to the Governor in Council: " If the Dominion acquires a road you may then, under section 11, entrust it to this company for operation." Then under section 18 we say: " Since it is so entrusted we here and now declare it is for the general advantage of Canada." I would not like to take the responsibility of saying that even that is within our powers. I do not think I should be called upon to express an opinion on it; it would appear to me at least to admit of some doubt.

This clause does not say that the roads that will be entrusted to the Canadian National Railway Company shall be for the general advantage of Canada, but it provides that the Governor in Council may from time to time declare any road comprised in the Canadian Northern System -to be for the general advantage of Canada. What I want to know from my hon. friend is if there are any roads, in addition to those enumerated in the schedule, which the Government may declare to be part of the Canadian Northern railway. As I understand it, the roads which now form part of the Canadian Northern Railway System are divided into constituent and subsidiary companies and are all enumerated in this schedule.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There are no others that we now have that are contemplated to be turned over at all, but if we should acquire, for example, one of the roads mentioned this afternoon, and turn it into the system, then this clause immediately applies to it and makes it a road for the general advantage of Canada.

Why not turn it over to
the Canadian Government Railway instead of to the Canadian Northern Railway System? The clause sets forth:
-ana the works of any company or companies hereafter from time to time declared by

the Governor in Council to he comprised in the Canadian Northern System lare hereby declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada.
I understand that the object of this Bill is to do away with the Canadian Northern System and have .all the roads consolidated and operated under the name of the Canadian National Railways System.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is right; but immediately it is in the Canadian Northern Railway System, unless there is some outstanding stock, it may be and will be amalgamated under the provisions of section 14. So it all comes out the same.

I do not think it does.
If anything is to be done you are reserving power to do it. After this Bill becomes law, according to the minister's statement, there will be no roads belonging to the Canadian Northern Railway System beyond those enumerated in the schedule. If you acquire a new road why not bring it under the provisions of this Act, and transfer it to the company direct, instead of attaching it to one particular road or the other?
, (Mr. MEIGHEN; Supposing there was some outstanding stock, it would not be wise to amalgamate until that stock was under our control, but it would be wise to put the road in the Canadian Northern System.

You are going to keep
the Canadian Northern Railway System as a separate entity, and the roads will not be consolidated for the purpose of general administration.	,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is just for convenience until it itself is amalgamated.

Section agreed to.
On section 19-Power to abandon line, and dismantle-Or dispose thereof by consent-Consent of security holders.

Would a majority of
the stockholders mean a majority in number or in amount?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Majority in amount.

If it means amount
there may be something in the Railway Act which defines it; but it strikes me that it is open to debate.	.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My impression is that an amendment to cover that point should be made. It should read " a majority in amount."
In value.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: A majority in value.

What becomes of the securities if a road is abandoned? Are they worthless? It strikes me that we are giving very large powers to the Governor in Council and the Railway Commission to abandon branch lines without the consideration of Parliament. As I understand the clause, it empowers the Governor in Council, with the consent of the Railway Commission and the directors of this new system, to close up any railway branch that may be connected with the system, if they think it is not a paying proposition or for some other reason. I submit that that should be referred to Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In so far as the security holders are concerned, their consent is obtained, but their security is not lost. This would only be a small part of their security that would be dismantled and abandoned, and they would see the wisdom
11	p.m. of adopting that course and would consent accordingly. Inasmuch as the whole idea of this measure is the joining together for operating purposes of lines that were formerly under several managements, there will presumably be cases of duplication that may be cut out without injury to the public, and the intention of this section is to provide that that may be done. The Board of Railway Commissioners is entrusted from the point of view of public convenience and safety with deciding what is necessary and whal is not in the way of service. Consequently that is the tribunal, it seems to me. to which resort should be had to determine whether any small part or branch is a duplication or for other reasons may be abandoned.
Are not some of those securities guaranteed by the provincial governments of Western Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If so I presume their consent would be needed also.

Does section 19 govern the last four lines of section 11?
.-such management and operation to continue during the pleasure of the Governor in Council and to be subject to termination or variation from time to time in whole or in part by the Governor in Council.
That is as to roads that come under the operation of the board subsequent to- the incorporation of this company?
Mr. Meighen moved to amend section 19 as follows:
By adding after the -word " majority " in the seventh line on page 6, and after the word
" majority " in the tenth line on page 6, and after the word " majority " in the sixteenth line on page 6 the words " in value."

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
The amendment is "majority in value of the registered security holders;" that is how it will read in the third last line?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think that is quite the proper wording.
On section 20- extension of time for commencement and completion of lines of railway:

I do not think this
section should pass now; it requires a great deal of consideration. It is a further revival of the old conditions against which I wish to protest in the most strenuous manner. We are here authorizing those defunct companies, of which we have heard so much, to start building railways and to get their old machinery in operation again, and presumably we are to furnish funds for such building. Is that the idea? What is the good of talking consolidation if those companies, all of which are hopelessly insolvent, are to be given authority by us to go on building railroads? Why should we sit down here solemnly with all the wisdom we can bring to bear on a question of this kind to perpetuate that state of affairs? I certainly expect this clause to stand over until tomorrow.
Progress reported.	.

While the Transatlantic mails are actually conveyed by steamer direct from Liverpool to Halifax with the soldiers, unfortunately, whilst the soldiers are landed at Halifax, the mails are taken off only at New York whither the steamers proceed from Halifax. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: RULING ON WHAT QUESTIONS MAY BE PUT ON CALLING THE ORDERS OF THE DAY.
speechtext:
The hon. member would certainly not be in order, at this stage, in reading such a letter. It would be in order, on calling on the Orders of the Day, for the hon. member to put a question to the Government with respect to a matter of extreme urgency. Let me say just here that I have noticed a growing tendency in the last few days to ask various questions on the Orders of the Day which properly ought to be put formally upon the Order Paper. In the nature of things, the Government cannot be expected to answer offhand questions of which no notice has been given. Every latitude will, of course, be afforded to hon. gentlemen in asking questions having to do with matters of policy or of great importance, in which the element of urgency is present; but questions of but ordinary importance should be put on the Order Paper, and in no instance

ought correspondence to be read. If the hon. member will summarize his question, if it is of sufficient importance, it may be put-but I. hope it will come within the proper bounds.

subsubtopic: RULING ON WHAT QUESTIONS MAY BE PUT ON CALLING THE ORDERS OF THE DAY.
speechtext: This is a question undoubtedly of great importance not only to the riding of South Renfrew but to the whole Dominion. It has to do with the sale of wheat. This fanner writes that he has on hand 500 bushels of wheat for which he cannot obtain a market in this country.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: RULING ON WHAT QUESTIONS MAY BE PUT ON CALLING THE ORDERS OF THE DAY.
speechtext: That, in my judgment, is not a question which should be asked upon the Orders of the Day. It should either be put on the Order Paper or be raised when the Estimates come up.

subsubtopic: RULING ON WHAT QUESTIONS MAY BE PUT ON CALLING THE ORDERS OF THE DAY.
speechtext: I think the question is of great public interest. A price has been fixed for wheat, and here is a man who says that as he cannot sell the crop he raised last year, he does not know whether he will put in a crop this year.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: RULING ON WHAT QUESTIONS MAY BE PUT ON CALLING THE ORDERS OF THE DAY.
speechtext: I do not think the matter is of such urgency that injustice would be done by requiring this question to be placed on the Order Paper in the ordinary course. I think it is purely a local question, but if it has a wider aspect, the hon. gentleman may put it.

subsubtopic: RULING ON WHAT QUESTIONS MAY BE PUT ON CALLING THE ORDERS OF THE DAY.
speechtext: The kernel of it is this: As this man is unable to dispose of his last year's crop, he has decided not to sow any wheat this year. He claims he has on hand 500 bushels of wheat.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: RULING ON WHAT QUESTIONS MAY BE PUT ON CALLING THE ORDERS OF THE DAY.
speechtext: Will the hon. member put his question?

subsubtopic: RULING ON WHAT QUESTIONS MAY BE PUT ON CALLING THE ORDERS OF THE DAY.
speechtext: The question this man asks is, where can he obtain a market for his wheat? The price of wheat has been fixed, I understand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: RULING ON WHAT QUESTIONS MAY BE PUT ON CALLING THE ORDERS OF THE DAY.
speechtext:
I concur in the view expressed by His Honour the Speaker, that it is very desirable hon. members should give the Government notice of questions of this character. However, it chances that I am able to answer the question. I may say to my hon. friend that although I have had to do with providing the finances, either directly or indirectly, connected with the crop movements of the last two years, this is the first instance that has been brought to my attention of any one being unable to sell wheat. The Government of. Canada did give a guarantee to the banks and to the purchasers of wheat in order that the sale of last year's crop might be facilitated. My

understanding with the Wheat Export Company of Canada which buys the exportable surplus of the crop of last year, is that our exportable surplus of wheat and flour will be purchased provided the Dominion Government is able to find the necessary credits. In order that my hon. friend may understand the magnitude of the undertaking of the Dominion Government in this regard, I may say to him that up to date the Government has paid out over $80,000,000 by way of advances to the Imperial Government for the purpose of facilitating the purchase of Canada's exportable surplus of wheat and flour of last year's crop and that within the last month we have undertaken to provide a sum which may aggregate $90,000,000 more for the purpose of taking care of the entire situation. My hon. friend asks where his constituent will find a market. Not knowing the local situation, I am unable to answer that question, but if the wheat is of the proper grade, it would seem to me that he should have no difficulty in finding a market. Beyond that I am unable to make a statement.
On the Orders of the Day:

I should like to put a question to the Acting Prime Minister to which he may give a Yes or No answer. In view of the unrest which exists throughout the country, due to the high cost of living, no doubt, will the Acting Prime Minister state when he intends to deliver the Budget Speech?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, many novel suggestions are put forward in this House, but this is the first time I have heard it suggested that the unrest in the community was due to the non-delivery of the Budget Speech. I stated some time ago that, following the usual practice, I should be glad to give the House a week or ten days' notice of the date of the Budget Speech, which I hope will not be unduly delayed. I am not aware that public interests are in any way suffering through the Budget not having yet been brought down. To give my hon. friend as reasonable an answer as I can, my expectation is that the Budget may be expected about the middle of May.
On the Orders of the Day:

In view of certain correspondence I have received from interned civilians in Canada, who appear to be British subjects of German

origin, may I ask if the Government has reached any decision regarding the eventual deportation of these people? They naturally address themselves to me, because I have been an interned civilian in Germany. They claim to be British subjects.

speakeroldname: Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Acting Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If there are interned
civilians in Canada who are British subjects, I am not aware of it. I should not like to say, without investigation, that it may not be the fact in individual cases. As to deportation, the matter stands exactly where it stood when discussed in this House about two weeks ago. It is impossible to secure deportation now to any enemy country.
Is it the intention of the Government eventually to deport all interned civilians of enemy origin?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The policy of the Government is set out in an Order in Council which has been laid on the Table-namely, to deport all who from any standpoint are undesirable. That applies, I think, to the great body of the present interned aliens.

The House again in Committee on Bill No. 70, to incorporate the Canadian National Railway Company and respecting Canadian National Railways-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 20-extension of time for commencement and completion of lines of railway:

This is a very important clause and I would like to ask my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) if he has a statement showing how many lines, or portions of lines, are not yet constructed, what are their respective mileages and their approximate cost.

I have not a list of all the lines before me. There are a lot of them whose charters have been kept in existence but which will not be proceeded with. There has been some money-probably very little -expended upon them. It might only be the expenditure for surveying and so on. I thought it would be well, until we really understood the situation, to renew them all. They all belong to the Government now. The common stock is now all- part of the Canadian National Railway system. It struck me that it would be no harm to renew them in this way for the present instead of coming to Parliament with a Bill to revive or extend every one of these charters. There are a large number of lines that have charters. There were two ways of doing this. We could have had a general clause such as we find in this Bill keeping these charters alive until we can take them up with the Railway Committee in the future. Or, we could have a schedule attached to the Bill giving a list of the charters that we were renewing by this clause. I had asked the solicitor of the company to give me a list of those lines that we are really doing work on an'd whose charters it is necessary to renew at once. We can do either one of these two things; that is renew all the charters, or just have a schedule attached and take those that we must have renewed this year. If we do that, of course, the others lapse and would have to be revived by Parliament at a future time. The list that the solicitor has prepared gives all that we will require to do any work on during the present year as far as he knows. The list is quite a long one. I can read it. If the Committee thinks it better to have a schedule attached to the Bill enumerating the companies, we, of course, can do that. I could not see any harm in simply renewing the charters that the Canadian Northern Railway Company has had for a number of years for the reason that they are now all owned by the Dominion Government and work under them cannot go on without the knowledge of Parliament. We must ask Parliament for the money to proceed with construction work. A list of the railways whose construction will be proceeded with will be given when the Estimate for that purpose is reached.
Is it the intention of the Government to complete this year the branch line from Oliver to St. Paul de Metis and the St. Guido line?

The two lines that the hon. member asks about are two that we are renewing the charters for. We are proceeding with work on these two lines. As to the number of miles, or as to the completion of these lines this year, I could not give the hon. member an answer just at the moment, for the reason that I did not expect that a question of that kind would be asked on this Bill. When the Estimates are reached I will be glad to give the hon. member the details he asks for as to whether we intend to complete the lines or how many miles we will construct.

The minister will recollect that one of the lines was provincially guaranteed, but the Canadian

Northern appropriated the money to other purposes than its construction. A large number of people have left the district through which the proposed line was projected, and the minister ought to be in a position to say whether it will be completed this year or not.

I think the Minister of Railways is not giving this question the serious attention which he should. We are conferring large powers on this company, and the method of financing the affairs of the Canadian National Railway System is, in my judgment, rather lax. At all events, the company is made practically free of Parliamentary control, as was clearly established last evening in the remarks of both the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) and the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster). Therefore I think the country is entitled to know what line, or lines, the company intend to build, so that we may have some idea of the amount which will be involved in that construction. The Minister of Railways has a list, but he does not say if it is a list of all the companies which formerly belonged to the Canadian Northern Railway Company.

The list to which the hon. gentleman refers does not include, by a long way, the charters of all the companies that were obtained, and whose stock is held by, the Canadian Northern Railway Company. A large number of such charters were taken out, but allowed to expire on account of the war. If I were to change this clause in the manner proposed it would have to read something like this:-
The times for the commencement and completion of the construction of the lines of railway specified in the second schedule of this Act, which certain of the companies comprised in the Canadian Northern System were authorized to construct, are hereby extended for two years and five years respectively after the passing of this Act.
Then the schedule would only comprise the railways that we really are going to operate and which it is necessary to keep alive. If we were to do that we should have to leave out of consideration a large number of charters that really should form a part of the Government's. system, but are not being proceeded with during the coming year, and would therefore lapse until again revived by an Act of Parliament.

The Minister of Railways should understand that there is such a tremendous expenditure involved in connection with the operation of this whole system that we must be very chary of the 
powers that we now propose to grant to this company, as regards the railways and the branch lines which formed part of the original Canadian Northern System. The least Parliament should exact from my hon. friend is a list of such railways and branch lines; and I think that in view of the novel institution that we are creating in this country a limit should he imposed upon the board of directors, at least for the next four or five years, so that they should not proceed immediately with the huge programme of construction originally proposed to be carried out by the Canadian Northern Railway Company. Some of the branch lines, and possibly some of the sections of the main lines, should be completed, but in all these cases Parliament should be called upon to pronounce upon the policy of the company. I would not leave the company entirely free of control. We are giving sufficient powers to the company; we are practically surrendering all our rights to them, and we are handing to them one, and possibly two, transcontinental railways. Now, by means of this little clause the Minister of Railways will add enormously to the power to spend money which the board already possesses. That is why I say the branch lines, and the other subsidiary lines, of the Canadian Northern with the construction of which the Government intends to proceed, should be clearly set forth in the Bill. Otherwise we shall be entering upon a real carnival of expenditure which the country cannot afford. An hon. member (Mr. Richardson) spoke very disparagingly in a previous discussion of what Lord Shaughnessy, had said on this subject. Well, I am not by any means a corporation man, I am above all a Canadian, and I am afraid of the terrible burden that we are assuming at the present moment; and we must see to it, by a system of checks and safeguards, that the powers given to this board will not in the long run bring us to the verge of bankruptcy. I fear, from my reading of the provisions of this danse, that the board will feel that it is empowered to construct railways and branch lines right and left. This, of course, means that the Canadian people will have to pay the piper, and all that, mind you, Mr. Chairman, without the appropriations first coming before Parliament for sanction. If we give a blank collective charter to the board it may, by virtue of the powers conferred by Clause 17, undertake to build railways right and left. This is a serious danger and Parliament should guard against such a contingency. That is why I say to my hon. friend (Mr. J. D.

Reid) and I am in earnest, that he should state' positively and explicitly what are the branch lines and subsidiary lines which this board, or the Government, intend to build, as well as the expenditure which that construction will involve. I notice by the morning papers that my hon. friend (Mr. Reid) intends to electrify part of the system of the Canadian Northern Railway. I do not wish to switch here on to the hydro question, which has of late set all Ontario aflame, but in that news we have an idea, or a hint, of what is in the mind of my hon. friend.
Mr. J. D. REID Oh, no, in the mind of Adam Beck.
Hear, hear.

Well, let us hear from my hon. friend on the subject. As for Sir Adam Beck, he is not afraid to express his views. It is strange, however, that such a prominent advocate of Government ownership as my friend should be so much opposed to Sir Adam Beck, who is supposed to be the pioneer and the leader of public ownership in the province of Ontario. Let me ask my hon. friend what he intends to do. ' Is it true that my hon. friend intends to electrify either the main line or the branch lines of the Canadian National system? And does he know what expenditure that will entail? The Government should give the Committee all the information it has on the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The section under discussion merely provides for the extension of certain charters that are now owned by the Canadian Northern Railway Company. It provides no power to build. The power to build would, of course, be controlled by the power to get the money to build, and that power is entirely in the hands of the Governor in Council, not in the hands of the company; the company cannot issue a bond without that authority, and consequently it cannot build.
Did you say the authority of the Governor in Council?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Governor in Council must ratify the by-law which provides for the bond issue, but Parliament itself must give the initial authority; so that question really is not under review in this section at all. What the hon. gentleman specifically asks for is that instead of a general revival there should be a revival as to certain definite construction powers that have been granted. That request we can meet in full, and to meet it I move:
To strike out all the words after " construction " in the second line of clause 20 and replace them by the following:
" of the lines of railway specified In the second schedule to this Act which certain of the companies comprised in the Canadian Northern System were authorized to construct, are hereby extended for two years and five years respectively after the passing of this Act."
The schedule which will be printed will give the lines. The work on some of those lines is under way now and will be gone on with this year, and Estimates for that purpose will be brought down. They are branch lines into districts that had been languishing for railways for some time before the war.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Mr. Meighen moves t . strike out clause 20 and replace-
Before that motion is put, Mr. Chairman, should -not we have the schedule before us?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would ask the hon. member to allow me to put the question; then it can be discussed:
Mr. Meighen moves:
To strike out all the words after " construction " in the second line of clause 20 and replace them by the following:
" of the lines of railway specified in the second schedule to this Act which certain of the companies comprised in the Canadian Northern System were authorized to construct, are hereby extended for two years and five years respectively after the passing of this Act."
Is it the pleasure of the Committee to adopt the amendment?
We all appreciate the desire of the minister to meet our reasonable views in connection with this clause, but should the amendment not stand until he brings down the schedule?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The schedule has been brought down.
It was laid upon the Table with the amendment.
I did not know that.

These are companies
which previously belonged to the Canadian Northern System, and which will now be under the Canadian National Railways. We know that some of those charters were very contentious, and were very fully discussed when extensions of time were asked for. I remember one of the rare occasions upon which I had to fight on the same side as my hon. friend the Minister of Railways was in regard to the extension of a charter to the

Canadian Northern Railway-it had slipped from my memory entirely. The minister spoke of Sir Adam Beck; there was quite a lively fight and hon. members were intensely interested, so much so, that Sir Adam Beck wanted to exclude the people from Quebec from taking part in the deliberations of the committee. It is not right that we should pass en bloc the extension of charters to which some people may have objection. We force any other company to come before Parliament and give the people who may suffer from the extension a chance to discuss the matter before the Railway Committee, and they leave that committee to judge whether or not the reasons then advanced are sufficient to justify refusal of the extension asked for. I know I will be met with the answer that the Government had these railways loaded on to it; therefore, it has to protect itself. I am willing that the Government should protect itself to any reasonable extent, provided that it is not at the expense of other interests. But I repeat, it would not be fair to grant any private corporation, say the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, an extension of time on all charters which may have expired at the commencement of the war without knowing what those charters are. The members here do not know anything about the local conditions; there may be reasons existing in certain parts of the country that would justify our refusing any extension of these charters. For instance, there may be rival companies who would be ready and willing to undertake the work the same as in the case of-I forget for the moment a certain charter which had expired and the renewal of which was asked for at the time Sir Adam Beck opposed the Canadian Northern project. I do not believe it is fair to the country to grant an extension of time just by giving the names of a lot of railways the charters of which had expired because the works in some cases had not been commenced within the two years, and in other cases because the works having been commenced were not concluded within the five years. I think it would be fairer that those charters on which the work could not be prosecuted on account of the war should be granted an extension of four or five years in order that the work may be finished.
Go to the Railway Committee?

No, by this Act. When work has been commenced on any of these lines which are the property of the Canadian Northern, and which will become the

property of this company when this Bill is enacted, and such work on account of the war had to be suspended, I do not see so 'much objection to an extension of time if the five years had expired; but I do take exception to the granting of two year extensions from the date of this Bill for the commencement of work under charters which had expired for the reasons I have just stated.
That is the usual clause in the Railway Act.

I know; but under the Railway Act they have to give notice in the newspapers and in the official Gazette that they will come before the Railway Committee, and any person having any conflicting interest has a right to appear before the Railway Committee and argue his case. In the present instance we do not know what objections there may be to the extension of the time for the beginning of work under these charters. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways by citing the case where Sir Adam Beck opposed an extension of time brought to my attention the fight we had on that occasion. As I have said, I do not think it is fair to- grant these extensions of time when interested persons have no opportunity of appearing before the Railway Committee or any other proper authority to state their objections.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In the first place, the one specific instance the hon. member gives of a road in respect of which extension might be objected to is not included in the schedule. Those included in the schedule are all roads upon which work has already been done, except one, from Moose-jaw to Chamberlain, which is the essential link in the line between Moosejaw and Calgary. Furthermore, all these lines in the schedule are west of Port Arthur. It is true that private companies have always had to go before the Railway Committee in order to get extensions, and certain objections have been raised from time to time which so far as my memory goes, have always been overruled. The objection invariably is that the company is seeking a charter, but not building the road. The ground of the objection is delay; it is asserted, perhaps, that the company applying for the charter is trying to forestall another line and is really not itself going on with the construction. No such objection could be urged here. The lines selected are those the construction of which it is least possible to defer. The districts affected have been without railways for years, and a serious

responsibility would rest upon any member of the committee who, if the labour, material, and money can be provided, would oppose such extensions or do anything to delay further the laying out of these lines. But even if one did object, he would have ample opportunity to state his views when the vote was before Parliament. This is merely keeping alive the opportunity for the Canadian National Railway Company to build the lines in question, the money being voted for the purpose.
Will any of these lines be duplications of the Canadian Pacific railway?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

Forty-four branch lines are named in the schedule. If you give to the Canadian National Railway Company the right to build, say, into a district where there is a coal mine, would that be interfering with the building of a railway by those coal interests, whose business interest it would be to develop railway communication in that part of the country long before the Government might be able to find the money to construct the line?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The practice is for the *coal people to go to the company to build the lines. But the primary object is to extend these lines not to coal mines, but to farmers. In every instance it is the farmers who want the roads.
I have not yet heard the objection to having these applications for extensions heard before the Railway Committee.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am at a loss to know why we should go to the Railway Committee to renew charters that are virtually our own. Charters go before the Railway Committee in order that discussion may take place as to whether or not the company really intends to build. We know the intention to build in this case.
Are these forty-four lines to be built this year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The intention is to do some work on all forty-four lines.
Then we should at least know where these lines are, why they are necessary, what is the mileage involved and how much their construction will cost.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot say as to the mileage intended. On a few of the lines no work might be done, but it is hoped that some work will be done on all.

Why not go to the Railway Committee where we may have a map before us and have somebody there to answer questions and to explain why these extensions are asked for? If the Canadian Pacific Railway are ready to build in the same territory, Parliament might rather have the Canadian Pacific Railway build than the Canadian National Railway Company. Why should we not do this thing in the regular way, instead of gobbling up forty-four lines to-day and probably another hundred to-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is a little out in facts and altogether out in principle. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company does not have to come to the Railway Committee in respect of the construction of lines running from the main line. The time to decide in respect of what lines money should be advanced to assist in construction will be when we are in committee on the Estimates. I will tfy to improve on the clearness of my
4 p.m. language, and then I would rather not be told that I have not answered my hon. friend's objection. The only reason for going to the Railway Committee in a case of this kind is to decide the bona fides of the intention to build the line. We surely would not contemplate allowing another company to come in where we have a charter and intend to build, and say: We want that charter, because you do not intend to build. It would seem to me to be an utter anomaly to go to the Railway Committee. If we intend to apply for the charter, surely that is enough; what would there be for the Railway Committee to consider? If Parliament did not wish to build the line, the matter could be discussed when all the Estimates in respect of the lines that it is proposed to go on with are laid before the committee.

Suppose the Canadian
Pacific Railway being ready to build a line into a territory included in these forty-four charters, said to the Railway Committee: This charter has expired, and we do not want you to grant an extension of time that would prevent us from getting a charter for the construction of a line in that territory. Would it not be reasonable for the committee to decide what company they wanted to build the line-the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Grand Trunk,, perhaps some American company like the Great Northern, or the Canadian National Railway Company? I cannot see any objection to going to the Railway Committee.
Are all the railways enumerated in schedule No. 1-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: These are not railways; they are construction powers as to branches.
Are they not railways? They are incorporated.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are not railways themselves; that is to say, they are not companies. They are construction powers or charters taken out by the companies included in schedule 1.

They are not lines of
railways. The second schedule says "The lines of railway," and the minister says that they are not lines of railway. The second schedule says "The lines of railway which the Canadian Northern Western railway was authorized to construct," and then come the lines of railway.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly.
That is what I say. Are the lines of railway enumerated in this list the railways which are being transferred to the Canadian Government railways?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is a difference between a line of railway and a railway company. The list given in schedule 1 are companies, constituting at present the Canadian Northern system, that are being transferred to the Canadian National railways. Those companies took out charters or construction powers to construct lines, and the lines they took out charters for are mentioned in schedule 2 which the hon. gentleman holds in his hand.
Where did they get their powers? I see some of them got their powers from provincial legislatures.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is specified in each case.

Then they do not yet
form part of the Canadian Northern railway system?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Is not the difficulty easily overcome? The Canadian Northern Railway Company have several charters for roads in the West. Some of those roads have been completed, some of them are partially built and some of them are probably yet to be built. The Canadian Government has taken over all the assets of the Canadian Northern railway system. Part of those assets are those unfinished, perhaps untouched roads.

The minister says we
have only the stock; we have no assets and we are not responsible for liabilities.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It will be for the executive management or the board of directors to decide whether those roads will be built or not. If it is not a paying proposition to build those lines or extensions, they will not be built. If they have to be completed or entirely built, we have to come to Parliament for the money, and then will be the time to attack them.

No, the consideration of Estimates is a bad time to discuss those matters. When I raised my objection that, of those lines, the schedule of which is laid on the Table, one alone had not been commenced, and the others, 41 in number, had work done on them, the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) said just now that all the Bill provides for at present is an extension of five years to finish the work, and only in one case is there an extension of two years to begin the work asked for. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My information was
that, of this list of lines, there was just one upon which no work at all was done, and for which an extension of time to commence and conclude had been asked for. My informant tells me now he may not be quite correct in that. In the great majority, in all, perhaps, but three or four work has been done.

.1 do not object so much to the extension of five years as II do to the extension of two years. The Acting Minister of Justice says that we can discuss that on the Estimates. He knows that cannot be done on Estimates the same as it can be done when a Bill is going through the various stages in the House. The minister cannot deny that when Estimates' are being discussed, unless "a very broad question is involved, the discussion is more of a parochial nature, every member being naturally interested in the particular matter that touches his part of the country. I seriously object to the extension of two years, and I would ask the minister to specify the companies for which he is asking an extension of time to begin operation. When operations have commenced, neither the railway nor the public is in the same position. The public cannot, through Parliament, have the work stopped. When, however, a company have not actually begun the work of construction, we can bring them before Parliament to make sure they are going to build. The big-

gest fights that take place before the Railway Committee are with regard to opposing the renewal of charters, when people doubted that the companies were in a position to carry on the construction, but often there are objections of an entirely different character, and I do not think the Government should take advantage of its present position to revive charters without going before the Railway Committee, as has been suggested by the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill), and giving parties interested an opportunity to present their cases.

I understood the
minister to say there was no objection to the section being passed because members would have an opportunity on the Estimates to object to anything in-a charter which is being renewed by this section.
Not to the charter. All you can do is to "object to the money being voted.

When the Estimates are brought down for the purpose of appropriating money for the constructio'n of a line mentioned in schedule 2, can we ask for an amendment of a charter which is renewed by this section?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: One could not, on the Estimates, add anything to the powers contained in the charter.

I wish to make my point clear. In schedule 2, there is a proposed line from Bandeheim to Vermilion in Alberta. Personally, I object to the construction of that line as outlined in the schedule. Instead of the line going as far as Vermilion, I would like it to pass a little eastward of that town, and I would like to have an opportunity of stating my case when that line is-proposed to be constructed. If this section goes through, the only remedy I have is to object to the money being voted. I understand there are forty-two cases of this nature, and I am not prepared to say whether or not every member of this House might have a similar objection to take to the building of one or another of those lines.
Mr. DEVLIN Now is the only time to discuss that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member for Wright knows better than that. What the hon. member (Mr. H. A. Mackie) is asking for is this: He says the charter for a certain line running as far as Vermilion does not suit him, in that it does not run far enough.
109J
It should not touch Vermilion at all; it should go to" the eastward of that town.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The charter would permit of a variation only of a mile. That possibly would not meet the objection?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Consequently, the charter, for the renewal of which provision is made in this section, is not the charter the hon. member would like to see go through. Another charter would have to be taken out for the line the hon. member wants built.
The hon. member objects to the charter that is at present granted, and he wants an opportunity of stating his reasons for objecting to it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He has a perfect right to object to any charter or to the renewal of any charter if he %vishes to take the responsibility.

The minister is simply side-tracking my point. It is not a question whether the line goes one mile east of Vermilion or not. Supposing it is a question of five miles east of Vermilion, am I justified in coming to this Parliament to ask for another charter for a- line duplicating this one?
I am sure the House would not listen to me. It might not be material to Vermilion to have the line run there, but it might be very material to Vermilion to have the railway four or five miles east of there, and one charter would suit the purposes of the whole community. The minister says I can ask for another charter, but the Government would never grant it. It would be duplicating lines only three or four miles apart.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly, it is quite open to the hon. gentleman to oppose the extension of this charter.

This question brings us back to the difficulties involved in multiplying authority. By this legislation and the general Railway Act, we are conferring powers on a body of men, called the directors, to build railways. The point of my hon. friend (Mr. H. A. Mackie) is perti-nenh Why should we encumber this new company that we are creating by any decisions, and possibly wrong decisions, that were made by Mackenzie and Mann? We are starting a new company, which will open up largely a new country. Why should we not give them a free hand to build in

such places and to such an extent as they see fit, in view of the circumstances of the country and the prospects they have in mind? Instead of giving them .a free hand to build as their own judgment may direct, we are placing forty-two old charters in their hands, and saying: "I do not care what you think. Mackenzie and Mann decided some ten or twelve or fifteen years ago to build in certain places. Here are their plans and specifications and charter, and you must build there or not at all." Is not that the position we are putting this new company in? The proper course, to my mind, is this: Every one of those old charters should be wiped out. If the new company decides it is necessary to build roads in certain places, let them do it, but I cannot understand why we should undertake all the promises that Mackenzie and Mann made, I am told that they went through certain municipalities and got concessions and bonds from them on the promise that they would build certain roads. Mackenzie and Mann got the money, but did not build the roads. Why should we be bound by their promises? I do not think that we should be. I do not want in the slightest way to handicap or trammel this new company; I want it to have all the talent we can put into it; I do not want to bind it down to any old charters or any old bargains. I understand that all the powers that could conceivably be required for the building of railways are found in this Act and in the general Railway Act- if I am wrong in that, I should like to be enlightened. I say there is no necessity for these old charters at all.
