Ilf these old companies have any property or have acquired any rights, I would certainly be in favour of assigning those rights to this new company, and let the new company have full control with respect to them. We have a Government-owned road already, without assuming the obligations of all these companies. I should like the Acting Minister of Justice to enlighten me why it is necessary to perpetuate these companies. Why should we pay from the Exchequer of this country a large amount of money in taxes on the properties we are creating under fictitious names-because fictitious names they are; the property will not belong to the company, but to the Government, and the law of the land is that the property of the Government does not pay taxes-why should we pay out millions of dollars all over the country which there is no necessity for us to pay, and especially now, when we should look at every dollar of our money?

I am in favour of putting all the powers conferred on these forty-two different companies in one charter. That would simplify matters, and then ivhen a -question was' asked in the House we should have only one company to deal with, instead of forty or more different concerns. It would be extremely difficult for any one to get into his head the relationship, and co-operation of the forty different companies. There should be only one company, both for the sake of unity and efficiency, and I should like the minister to explain why he thinks it necessary to continue these separate companies.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have tried very hard to understand the contention of the leader of the Opposition. The first thing that struck me to-day was how diametrically he was opposed to the criticism offered by the hon. member for Maisonneuve. That hon. member was appalled at the freedom this clause gave to the company; his leader complains that we are not giving them freedom enough, that we are attempting to make them construct roads on old charters. Both complaints, although diametrically opposed, are equally wrong. We are in no way seeking to impose any obligations on the company; we are simply ratifying charters of companies belonging to the Canadian National railways, which that directorate now runs; the charters must be revived or the roads could not be constructed if construction was desired. The revival of these charters is necessary before we would be in a position to recommend to Parliament an estimate to enable the company to construct. My hon. friend also desires the elimination of these separate companies, wdiether named in schedule 2, as -some may be, or in Schedule 1, as the original constituent companies of the system. I have already assured him, and I repeat -the assurance, that the intention is to amalgamate w'-ith the parent concern, the Canadian National railways, every one of these companies just as soon as -the outstanding stock is got rid of. All these companies can be got rid of at once, except where there is outstanding stock not held by us, and, of course, the American lines.

I do not think my
learned and hon. friend so easily disposes of my objection. It is one thing for the Government, or the Minister of Railways, to approve the plans of a company when the company is putting up the money, taking the responsibility of building the road and financing it. It is another thing for the Government itself, or the Minister of

Railways acting for the Government, to approve a plan wfiere they have to advance the money and where they have to take the responsibility of the venture upon which they are launching. That is a different thing altogether. These- charters which we are asked to revive are charters from this House, some of them, some from other legislatures, to build roads in a certain way and at certain places. They have made their plans, I presume and laid them before the Department of Railways and received the approval of the department for forty or fifty of them. The minister tells us that it is the intention to do some work on every one of them this year but this new company that we are creating now has no choice at all as to whether these roads are to be built, where they shall be placed or to what extent they shall go. The plans are laid down, they have received the approval of the Government and they must be built in accordance with them. What I wanted to say to the minister was that I want this new company when it is starting out to handle the people's money, to have an absolutely free hand as to where these roads shall be built. When the minister puts a charter in the hands of this company, it is merely a construction company in that regard because its powers are confined within the charter that is handed over to it. They must confine themselves to the powers contained in the charter under which they are working and these are the powers that we are reviving. This is imposing a burden upon this new company, which, if they had a free hand, they never would undertake. The minister tells us that they have to take them holus bolus, forty-five or fifty of them, on which Mac- kenzie and Mann are making promises for the last twenty years and we are to furnish the money whether it is good business or otherwise to go on with these works. We are creating this company to build and to operate these roads and therefore they should have a free hand and should not be encumbered by the thoughts and schemes of other people for whose thoughts and schemes they are not responsible; nor is this House.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's
speech, while he puts his position a little more clearly, is encumbered by the very same inconsistency as his last speech. He says this is a new company, and that it is not building with its own money and its own resources, but it is building with the money and resources of the country. Therefore, he says, the same rule does not apply, and from that he proceeds to argue that we should not impose upon them any special conditions of construction, but that they should have a free hand. It would appear to me that the application would be the other way. We should have some control. There should not be.any imposition. There is none. But this company themselves desire the construction of all the lines included in the schedule. Indeed, they would like to construct more. Over that there must be some control exercised by this Parliament of the recommendation of the Governor in Council. There should be that control exercised as expressed in the Appropriation Act or in the Estimates. The company desires the construction of these lines. It is hoped that something may be done on nearly all of them. There may be some on which it may be impossible to do any construction, but for safety's sake it is well to include them in case it will be possible to build them all. But the company desire the construction of these roads because the people demand them. The people in many other localities want construction done there too, but this is the outside list of those we think it would be possible to do any work upon and this is to be done by the company subject to supervision by the Governor in Council and by this House.

What does the minister mean by giving us the thoughts of the company? We are creating the company. It is not in existence yet. This Act is about to bring some entity into being which shall be the company.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
When the time comes that we shall have created the company by this Act the minister with his predestinate, his far-conceiving mind, tells us what this company will be thinking about.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I was thinking about the present directorate.

They are not the company. I have a little keenness of mind, I have been under the tutorship of the minister for a good many years, and when he talks about a company that is not in existence, I feel that we have a right, particularly when we are dealing with a hair-splitter like the Minister of the Interior, to know what he means.

The unusual
thing about a proposal such as this is that we are asked to revive charters granted

by the legislature of Alberta and Saskatchewan and not by this Parliament. That is another reason why the proposal of my hon. friend from Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) ought to be accepted because these charters have never been before this Parliament. There may be a question as to our competence to revive a defunct charter granted by the legislature of Alberta or Saskatchewan. I question if such a proposal was ever made in the Canadian Parliament before. The minister has not given us very much information. We have been discussing this section now for a long time and we have reached the point of being told that it is proposed to build forty-two railways. We do not know the length of them or their cost. These are essential things. We know that one of these railways is 150 miles in length. The length of the others is not mentioned at all, but if they are 100 miles in length on the average, that means 4,200 miles of railway. If these railways cost $70,000 a mile, that means an expenditure of about $300,000,-
000.	I want to enter a protest against the proposal to spend $300,000,000 more in Western Canada in railway building without any provision being made for building branch lines in Eastern Canada. It is a preposterous proposal to ask Parliament to give a blank charter of this sort to expend $300,000,000. We do not know where these railways are, we do not know their length, we do not know anything about them except that there are forty-two of them. If the minister cannot give us definite information he should not expect this section to be accepted by the Committee.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid that (I shall have to say to the hon. gentleman first of all that all of his assertions are wrong from the commencement of his speech to the end. In the first place we are not giving any blank authority to spend a dollar by this Bill.
You are paving the way for it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We are paving the way in this sense, that we have no powers under which to build unless these charters are renewed. We are enabling Parliament later on to say so if Parliament believes that these lines are necessary and if it desires to build them as being necessary. What objection can there be to enabling Parliament, if it sees fit, to build such lines as it thinks are necessary? The next statement the hon. gentleman made was that we did not know what lines they were or where they were.

We know all that from the schedule. We do not know the amount of railway line to be built, but we are not asking for authority to build now, we are simply asking to enable Parliament afterwards to assist in building it. When that time comes all the information will be given that will enable Parliament to come to a conclusion. All we have to conclude now is whether to renew the charters or not. If there is any particular objection to the renewal of any specific charter, this is the time to object.
There is one thing I also wish to say to the Committee. As respects some of these lines the provincial Governments have guaranteed the bonds. Indeed, in certain cases the bonds have already been sold, and the money lies in the hands of the provincial treasurer to be paid out as con. struction advances. The charters must be renewed, and the lines gone on with, in order that the money which lies there for that purpose only, can be used.
Has the minister a list of those charters which are in abeyance until the lines are constructed?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I could by occupying some time give the list referred to by the hon. gentleman. But as to the others, the necessity for the renewal of the charter is absolutely just as clear as in this case, so there is no reason for distinguishing either for the purpose of this section or for the purposes of this entire Bill. There may be such reasons for the purpose of the vote when Parliament is actually deciding whether we should assist the building of the line or not.

I am glad to have heard the minister say that this is the time to discuss any proposed charter, because a few moments ago when the hon. member (Mr. Mackie) suggested discussing a certain charter the minister stated that the present was not the time for that, but rather when the Estimates were under consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, I did not. I said it was the time to discuss whether the charter should be renewed or not, but it was not the time to discuss whether the renewal of a charter applicable to some other place should be taken up.

As I understood [DOT] the hon. member (Mr. Mackie) was offering objections to a certain charter that had been granted, and was proceeding to criticise it when the minister said to him in very clear and distinct language-in language that I

could quite understand without any difficulty-that the hon. gentleman would have an opportunity to discuss the charter when the Estimates were being considered.
Or that there could be a new charter.
You have got to be careful otherwise there will be a paralleling of the line of railway.

In a moment or two the hon. gentleman (Mr. Mackie) will have an opportunity of discussing that phase of the question in which he is more particularly interested. In the meantime I want to .draw attention to one or two other questions which, if ventilated, it seems to me, will help to obviate a good deal of the discussion upon this clause. The hon. member (Mr. Keefer) stated that we owned the constructive rights spoken of a few months ago by the Acting Minister of Justice. On the other hand the latter gentleman said that we do not own them, but we "virtually" own them. I wish to ask the Acting Minister of Justice, as he is in an enlightening mood, to tell the House exactly what the country has purchased from the 'Canadian Northern Railway Company. We have had statements made by the Acting Prime Minister in the past, but we never could really understand, and we do not understand to-day, just what properties the Government have acquired from the Canadian Northern. We know that they have acquired the common stock of the company. We are told to-day by one hon. member well versed in the subject that we own certain lines of railway and the constructive rights that go with those lines. Again we hear the Acting Minister of Justice say: No, we only virtually own these constructive rights. The word "virtually" caught my ear, and that word does not convey to those of us who perhaps do not understand the fine language of the Acting Minister of Justice whether we have both hands, or only one hand, upon these lines. Perhaps if the Acting Minister of Justice cannot do it, the Minister of Railways will tell us just what we own and what we do not own. Do we own simply the lines of railway spoken of in the schedule to this Bill, along with the constructive rights, comprised in the list that has been laid upon the Table? Because the Acting Minister of Justice would not allow a list of constructive rights to be placed upon the Table and lead us to believe that we own them, if we were not the owners, although he did tell us that we only virtually owned them. I know that the hon. member (Mr. Keefer) would not lead the Committee to believe, and I take it he is one of the most enlightened lawyers upon this subject in the House-
I rise to a point of order. I do not think the hon. gentleman is discussing the clause now under consideration.
Would the hon. member please state his point of order?

Certainly. We are now dealing with the commencement and completion of lines of railway comprised in the Canadian Northern system. The hon. gentleman is asking Tor a list of what we own. That has nothing to do with the construction of lines of railway.
The hon. member cannot understand that the words contained in the clause have a direct bearing upon the question I was discussing?
No.
We have been"discussing the matter for the last half hour, so the) hon. member must just have awakened.
He is looking at the stars.

I hope that the Acting Minister of Justice will not 'beat about the bush, but will give us a straight and direct answer-we who represent the people and want to know what we are paying for-and that he will tell us exactly what we have bought. The minister said a few moments ago that the Government intend to build at least a portion of the roads enumerated in the schedule attached to this Bill, or at least that work would be done upon most of those roads.
Forty-four in number.

I presume the construction rights relate to at least thirty to thirty-six out of the forty-two or forty-four enumerated. Now, upon which of these roads will the Government do work, and what will the expenditure be? Will the minister also enlighten the House as to the Government's power to go on and carry out these works when they intend to create, and are creating by this Bill, a company which will have absolute control of the construction' and operation of the Government roads, and of all roads necessary to complete the system contemplated under this Bill? How will the Government go on with that building? Will they dictate to the company what roads they are to build? I trust that the minister will be in a position to enlighten, the House to that extent and then we shall make

greater progress with the consideration of this clause.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has succeeded in the very ingenious art of confusing the issue. He first asks what the Government have bought. As the hon. gentleman voted on the question one would have thought he already understood what we have bought. We 'bought the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company.
The common stock, which is worth nothing.
We paid ten millions for it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As soon as this very interesting interlude is over I will proceed with my remarks.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The ownership of the
common stock, which is now entirely owned by the Government, subject to transfer of some which is pledged and still not paid for by us, means the ownership of the whole Canadian Northern Railway system.
It means control?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
already understands just as well as I can ever make him understand, and he understood before he asked me. Among the assets of the company whose stocks we own are the construction rights or charters en-numeraled in Schedule 2. The hon. member says that I told the Committee we are going to build. If I used the term "we." the more iccurate term would be "Canadian National Railways," which of course he must have understood, because I have a high appreciation of his intelligence. The Government will not directly build any roads of the Canadian National railways.
Only indirectly.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Canadian National railways will build their own roads; but inasmuch as assistance will in all probability be necessary, the Government must exercise supervision as to what is, ventured upon in the way of construction by the company. Upon the company's recommendation it is intended to include in the renewal of charters all those contained in Schedule 2, because it is hoped that undeT most of them at all events some work can be done this year, and what cannot be done this year it is hoped will be done next year and then continued. I think with my limited capacity of language 
I have expressed as clearly as I possibly can what is intended.
Not so much humility.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As to the use of the
word " virtually " I really thought it was very appropriate, but with the hon. members' permission I will change it to " virtuous."
Change it to " scandalously."

Will the minister
allow the clause to stand in order to give us time to study Schedule No. 2?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The schedule is considered after the last clause, so it can be amended then if necessary.
Carried.

No. The lines of railway which the Canadian Northern Western railway was authorized to construct I suppose are under its control and are owned by it the same as the Canadian Government owns the Canadian Northern?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They own the powers contained in the charters.
Therefore the incorporators were the Canadian Northern Western Railway Company?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I suppose so.
Will they form part of the system that is now being consolidated since the Canadian Northern Western Company is one of the constituent companies enumerated?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
These powers of the Canadian Northern Western Railway Company -which I suppose has a federal charter and is for the general advantage of Canada-are granted by the various legislatures?
And declared to be foi the general advantage of Canada.
The legislatures cannot declare them to be for the general advantage of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We did so in 1914.
All these lines?
The charter which the hon. member mentions was a provincial charter, but in 1914 the undertaking was declared by this Parliament to be for the general advantage of Canada.
At the time the stock was being acquired by the Federal Government?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, at the time the Bill went through.
These charters are actually part of the Canadian Government railways.
Of course they are.

And these powers which they are now exercising are derived from the legislatures of Alberta and Saskatchewan, and some, I see, by the heading are derived from this very Parliament. Now, Mr. Chairman, as has been submitted by the hon. member for Edmonton, forty-four lines are enumerated here, there is one copy of the schedule in circulation among hon. members, and yet the minister expects us to discuss the various clauses of the Bill, and at the same time become conversant with the details of this schedule, which is practically impossible. If the hon. gentleman wishes the matter to be understood by us as well as he understands it, he must give us the same opportunity to get posted. Of course we are all aware that anything pertaining to the Canadian Northern Railway system has been the subject of special and profound study on the part of the Acting Minister of Justice, but it has not been so with us. Therefore I think the suggestion made by the hon. member for Edmonton is a reasonable one, and that consideration of the second schedule ought not to take place until we have had time to study it.
The 'CHAIRMAN: I beg to call the attention of the hon. member to the fact that the second schedule cannot be adopted at present, for according to the rules all the clauses of the Bill must first be considered, and the first schedule must be adopted before we can adopt the second schedule. We are now discussing clause 20, and the second schedule will be discussed when the clauses of the Bill have been disposed of.

I have always understood, Mr. Chairman, that a schedule attached to any contract formed part of it, and that when a schedule is attached to one section of a Bill it ought to form part of that section, and ought to be discussed at the same time if it is to be discussed intelligently. If the rule of the House is that any reference to a schedule in one section precludes discussion of it until the Bill has been disposed of, that means a very naked discussion and I would suggest that we form a committee to amend that rule at once.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The ruling of the Chair was not that the schedule could not be discussed; the ruling was that the schedule could not be adopted until the Bill had been fully discussed and the other clauses adopted. May, at page 375 says:
All the clauses of the Bill are considered before any new clauses are brought up and added to the Bill	Schedules to a Bill are considered after new clauses are disposed of.
When the schedules have been considered, new schedules are offered.
Bourinot at page 522 says:
The schedules are the parts of the Bill last considered.

I do not dispute that. I do not care when it is adopted, whether now, to-morrow, or Monday, but I say you cannot discuss section 20 without looking at the charters and knowing what we are dealing with. May says just what I wanted him to say, that we can consider the schedule at the same time as we consider the provisions of the law.
The CHAIRMAN He does not say so. He says they shall be offered after.

We do not want the adoption now; it is just the consideration we are after. We are discussing the various items contained in schedule 2. I was proceeding to say that this is a long schedule with forty-four lines of railway enumerated. We have only one copy of it, and my hon. friend from Edmonton has requested that we postpone consideration of the second schedule until we know exactly what it is. We may agree to the renewal of the charters, except as to certain lines here as stated by him. The Acting Minister of Justice remarked just now that if the line as proposed did not suit the hon. member for Edmonton he would have to get a new charter. If so, that is a reason why the extension of this charter should not be granted. If the charter now does not suit the people to be served by the line, and they want another one a few miles south, east, north, or west, that is a reason why you should not duplicate, and if the other line would better serve the purposes of the people it would be preferable to have a new charter and not renew the old one. That is an argument in favour of not being in too great a hurry to grant wholesale extensions.
We control these railways, but we do not absolutely own them, because there is stock outstanding and the owners of that stock have a say in the administration of the

affairs of the railways. The minister says that moneys have been voted by the Provincial Legislatures in connection with these lines and that bonds have been sold the proceeds of which are to be used in their construction. I had thought that one reason why the Canadian Northern Kailway system was taken over was to relieve the Provincial Legislatures from the burdens which they assumed when they granted advances or aid to that system, and to pay the bonds and the interest on the bonds which had been negotiated and guaranteed by the provinces. That the Government should now ask for aid from the provinces is not-shall I say "dignified"?
Proper.

No, I want a word between the two. We are saying to the provinces: We will build your roads; we will build houses for your people; we will aid your agriculture; we will give you money galore; but when it comes to such a vital matter as the construction of railways we ask you to put up your bonds, sell them and give us the money. I do not think that is sound logic. Let us hold back on the roads and let the provinces do their work. Some of these roads are in Saskatchewan. Last year twenty-five or thirty millions were loaned to Saskatchewan or Alberta; and I certainly object to the Dominion Government now asking the provinces for aid in connection with lines of railway that we intend to build.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's indignation again is wasted.
It is not indignation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Government has not asked and does not intend to ask Provincial Governments for assistance in respect of the building of lines of railway or assistance to the Canadian National railways. But before we had anything to do with it, the Governments of the provinces guaranteed bonds for railway extensions. In some cases the bonds have been sold; the moneys are in the bank, and cannot be used for any purpose except construction. What is to be done? The Government cannot pass an Act and use the money for any other purpose. The only thing to do is to go ahead and construct, and that is what we intend to do.
Will the minister state one case in which there is money in a bank in Alberta for the construction of railways?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Edmonton and
'Calgary-Lethbridge line; there are others as well.

Not the Oliver,
St. Paul and Metis? The Canadian Northern Railway got their money in that case, which is a refutation of the statement of the minister that when money is paid into a bank for the construction of a particular line it must be used only for that purpose. In the case of the Oliver, St. Paul and Metis Railway the bonds were guaranteed by the province; the money was secured and paid into the bank and Mackenzie and Mann used it for their purposes. The Government is now making an appropriation in the Estimates for the purpose of building that line. Since 1909 the people of the district affected have not . been served by a railway. So that it is not always true, no matter what may be the law on the subject, that Mackenzie and Mann caused to be used for the construction of a line, money that had been deposited in the bank for that purpose. What kind of country is traversed by the lines mentioned in schedule No. 2? What is the extent of the population affected or served, and, generally, what are the advantages of the construction of the proposed lines represented by these forty-two charters? If the minister will give me that information, it will avoid my studying the schedule quite considerably.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It might avoid the necessity of the hon. gentleman doing a little work, but it would impose the same work on me. When we are only getting in such a position that we can later on decide what to do, surely it is not necessary to describe the character of the land and the population along each proposed line.
The necessity is not before us 5 p.m. at the present time; when we commit ourselves to capital investment in the matter, then that will be a proper question. The hon. gentleman, being a western man, can arrive at a pretty intelligent idea by studying the schedule, but the information is not at all requisite to the consideration of this clause.

The minister characterizes members of the 'Opposition as obtuse; I may belong to the same category.
I understood the minister to say that if clause 20 goes through now I cannot at some future time, when the Estimates are under consideration, ask that the charters be amended or that the location of any of these lines be changed, and that as a private member I would not be able to introduce a new Bill, and so I would be entirely dependent on a member of the Government for a remedy to my constituents

or to my province. If I am not very obtuse, it seems to me that unless I can make my objections now on the schedule I shall have no remedy except that of asking for a new charter, and if I ask for a new charter which parallels lines or serves a country partly populated or is subject to certain disadvantages from a railway standpoint, then the Government would naturally not grant my request. I note that the minister has beside him Mr. Ruel, who must be familiar with all these lines, as he was solicitor for Mackenzie and Mann at one time. Perhaps he could give us the information we require as to the nature of the country through which these proposed lines run. I do not know why the minister is not in possession of these facts. Only forty-four charters are to be reviewed; the minister should have these things on his finger-tips. .

I think there is good reason why each of these charters should be reviewed separately. The ideals of private ownership are not always the same as those of public ownership. These charters have been granted at the request of the 'Canadian Northern Railway Company, which, after all, had for its prime object its own advantage. Now the system passes to the possession of the public, and the prime object of public ownership is not the enrichment or the advantage of private individuals, but public service.
That being the case, in each instance in the issuing of these forty-two or forty-four charters, the lines of railway were perhaps located according to the private interests of the company that then owned them. Many interests might enter into the location, such as possibly the question of real estate and other matters which 1 cannot, having no knowledge of that, particularize. The location, however, of those lines may presumably have been made more with the idea of advantage to private persons than of service to the public. That is now all supposed to be changed, and as these charters have become the property of the people, it might be desirable to make some changes in the location of the roads. That has already been shown in one case by the hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. H. A. Mackie), and the same thing may be true in the case of many others of these roads. If this blanket power is given just by this one section to all these roads to extend their charters, there is no power in the future to make any change in the location of the roads. While it is true,
as the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) stated, that complaints may be made when the Government asks Parliament for money to build a road, as the hon. member for East Edmonton stated no alteration whatever can at that time be made in the location of the road. That is my reason for saying that if people in any district desire that changes should be made in any of these projected roads, they should have an opportunity of being heard, and the changes, if approved, should be made. Therefore, every one of these charters, before they are renewed, should be considered separately, possibly before the Railway Committee, as has been suggested by other hon. members. I do not believe we can depend upon the men who are now in charge of the system to make any great variation, because nearly one-half of them are the same men who formerly were in control or in the employ of the Canadian Northern railway. When I say that, I have no reflections to make upon them, but 'I do not believe the mere fact that they have been taken from the management of a private road to the management of a Government road has neoessarily changed their ideas very much as to what constitutes services to the public.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: These Charters have their routes all passed upon by the directorate, which directorate is not the old one at all, as the hon. gentleman, as a member of Parliament, knows, or ought to know. Only two out of the eleven were members of the old directorate; nine of the eleven are new. The charters have been renewed on behalf of the Government, and the Government -agrees with the directorate that it ' would be wise to renew them. If any hon. member desires to move that any one of these charters be not renewed he is quite at liberty to do so.

Might not the people of the districts concerned wish to have some voice as to the location of the various roads and if we pass this section now they will have no opportunity whatever of making themselves heard? If each charter has to be considered separately in the Railway Committee, or some other committee of this Parliament, these people would have an opportunity of letting us know their ideas in connection with it. After all, public ownership means the service of the people. The minister's statement, that on the directorate of the Canadian National railways there are only two men of the old directorate, may be true in one sense, but I have just scanned the list of the new management,

and on that list there are at least ten gentlemen who were, if not on the old directorate of the Canadian Northern, at least in the employ of the Canadian Northern.

The challenge of the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) only shows that this: schedule added to the Bill is nothing other than a small, petty, picayune, political trap. This schedule reminds me of those lists of railway subsidies which before a general election, are usually put into the Estimates, many of which railways never see the: light of day except on paper. Who will really believe that the Government will ever have money available to implement the Canadian Northern railway system by the construction of these forty-four lines? The country would be in the hands of a receiver if it was	ever	attempted to fulfil this
blanket promise which, I notice, is made chiefly to western constituencies. Scanning the list of these problematical railways, I notice that the schedule published will include railway schemes for the West only. There is nothing in that list for the East; there is nothing for Quebec. Of course, the support of Quebec is not needed, but the credit of Quebec is of the highest, whilst some of the western provinces were on the verge of bankruptcy because of the guarantees they gave to Mackenzie and Mann. That explains why, before the last general election, we saw so many of those premiers wavering in their faith, because, forsooth, they were promised, if they supported Union Government, that the guarantees given by their provinces would be taken up by the Dominion Government. In fact, no provincial premier came to Ottawa during that eventful period without being met at the station by the wily gentlemen who then controlled the destinies of Union Government. I repeat again that the Government is taking a very serious responsibility in luring the people of this country and people outside of this country into the belief that these forty-four lines of railway will eventually be added to the trunk line of the Canadian Northern. Have lion, members ever thought of the credit of Canada, not only with the Canadian people themselves, but abroad? This country owes some millions of dollars in the United Kingdom and also in New York.
When rhe bankers of the United Kingdom and the United States take up our stock they have regard to the obligations to which we are committed. I say that the Government is lowering the credit of Canada by this political trick, because it is nothing 
but a political trick. It is adding to the schedule forty-four lines to be eventually built
That is not right.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The adding is done at the request of the hon. member himself. He is the author of the trick.

My hon. friend comes before this House with a blanket clause, which reads:
The times for the commencement and completion of the construction of any lines of railway which any of the companies comprised in the Canadian Northern System were authorized to construct, which had not expired at the beginning of the war, in August, nineteen hundred and fourteen, are hereby extended for two years and five years respectively after the passing of this Act.
That was a notice to the country that the Government or board intended to complete the system by constructing these branch lines which originally formed part of the Canadian Northern system. I say that in fairness to the taxpayers of Canada and the creditors of Canada' we should know what railways it is intended to construct.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member is
trying to lead the committee to believe that money is to be voted this year to construct all these lines.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We are only asking
that the charters be renewed in order that Parliament may have the opportunity of voting such money for construction as may be required.

Did not the minister
state that construction would go on except on three or four lines?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is the intention to
ask Parliament for a vote in order that work may be done upon the most of them, and if it is possible, and in so far as it is possible, on all. But that will be submitted to Parliament later. The hon. member was altogether misleading the Committee when he endeavoured to make it believe that a vote for the schedule to renqw these charters, which must be renewed as all hon. members know, was a commitment on the part of Parliament to construct the whole mileage in the schedule.
What will the money voted be used for if not for construction?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: For the purposes asked.

What purpose are you going to ask the money for?

Mr. MEIGfHEN: For doing work on these lines, as II have told the hon. member now for the thirteenth time.
Does not that mean construction?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It does not mean construction of all the lines or complete construction of any one. *
My hon. friend wants to play on words. Let us get down to brass tacks. It is construction and nothing else.

I do not differ with the minister in his interpretation of the schedule and the clause itself. It is a notice served on the country that at some time later on the Government through the board may construct any of those lines. I protest against that. I say the country is not in the mood and has not the resources now to justify notice being served that we may build those lines. It is a crime against the credit of Canada to add to our obligations by the publication of this schedule. The expression may not be parliamentary, and if it is not I will withdraw it, but it seems to me that the Government is going to act like a drunken sailor; but I withdraw that expression. My hon. friend does not seem to realize the extent to which he is committing this country. I certainly find fault with the taking over of the Canadian Northern railway, but it was a necessity, and a necessity which the Government had considerably aggravated during the last five or six years, and God grant that the country may not suffer too much by that awful necessity! But after taking over.this white elephant with its tremendous obligations, to think that in case of a general election the country may be committed to the expenditure involved in the schedule, is something which I cannot understand.
There is another point. By adopting this schedule and renewing the charters en bloc, are we not debarring private companies and the provinces from building lines in the same territory, not exactly on the same routes, but approximately so. These charters have remained dormant-simply paper charters, if I may call them so-for twenty years. Mackenzie & Mann did nothing with them except hold them for their own use; they did not build one mile of railway on any of these charters. Now we are to renew them en bloc and debar private companies and other enterprises, which might eventually wish to build these railways, from doing so.

I should like to be permitted to say a word or two on some of the points which have just been touched upon by my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Leinieux). I must say that as one who had co-operated with him for years in political affairs and had formed an opinion highly favourable to himself, of the breadth of his mind, I was surprised to hear from him what I must describe as so pessimistic and reactionary a speech. I do not know what company my hon. friend has been keeping of late. His views of Canadian affairs and the possibility of Canada's development seem to be absolutely jaundiced. When did he get the idea that railroad building in Canada was bound to be so unprofitable an enterprise? The first two general elections that I fought in this country were on the question of railroad development in Canada, and were in support of the great project of the National road.
Then my hon. friend was an enthusiastic and optimistic young Canadian. I was imported into this country and, I partook of his enthusiasm and believed in the possibilities of Canada. I was surprised to hear such a sort of speech from him this afternoon and I was led to the question: What company has my hon. friend been keeping? Is this the new Liberalism that we are hearing to-day? I think I get some little guidance as to the answer to my question from the remark which my hon. friend made in sitting down. He was not enthusiastic over Canadian National railways, I observe. He gives us in so many words the reason, because he tells us, just as he takes his seat, that this national enterprise, this work of-making a great railway in a great country, of making a Canadian national railway in Canada by Canadians, may interfere with the interests of some private corporation. He mentioned the private corporation-the Canadian Pacific. As a western Liberal who has not abated one jot or tittle of his Liberalism, and who has as much belief in Canada as he had in the years 1904 and 1908, I want to say to my hon. friend that if he is going to take the position that the interests of the Canadian Pacific are more important than the interests of Canada, then my Liberalism is not his Liberalism.
This pessimism in regard to the building of railways in Canada is not an entirely unknown mood on the part of Canadians. When this enterprise, now the Canadian Pacific, was first mooted in Canada, there were pessimists with whom, I suppose, I, along with my friend, had some sort of a traditional connection. These pessimists, T

believe, prophesied that the grass would grow between the rails of the Canadian Pacific and that it would never be a successful enterprise. My hon. friend knows that those pessimists were wrong in their, day and I wonder that the reflection does not occur to him that he may be equally wrong, wide as is his knowledge of and close as is his intimacy with Canada's development and Canada's problems.
He asks what the tax-payers of the country are going to say about this business of having charters put into a schedule and projecting our minds into the future, because that is what these charters do. I submit to my hon. friend the consideration that there will only be one way of paying the taxes, there will-only be one way of building up Canada, there will only be one way of making this the great nation that we all hope it will be and that will be by bringing to our civil development the same spirit which we have just brought as a young country to the doing of our share in this war. I want to assure him that the spirit that was behind westerners in the war is the spirit that is behind westerners in regard to the possibilities of Canadian development in the immediate future. We believe in Canada and in the possibilities of her development. There will only be one way of building this nation up; there will be only one way of paying taxes; that will be by doing business. Two years ago, in our western country, W'e had a surplus crop of 300,000,000 bushels of wheat. We use 60,000,000 bushels in this country in one year. It would just be as easy for the West to produce a billion bushels of wheat if we get the railways to carry it and, by other wise processes of development, find markets to sell that wheat in. We purpose developing that enterprise and we purpose developing Canada along these lines. We know that we shall see other commercial enterprises of all kinds grow up in similar proportion and we expect our railways to develop in the same proportion. In so far as the West is concerned we are grateful to this Government for making an honest attempt at Government ownership of a great system of railways and the West will give them a solid support upon that proposition. Do not let my hon. friend be in all? doubts upon this question.
Just one more point. I want to clear my hon. friend's head of some of the cobwebs that have gotten into it, from, as I suggest, his having kept the wrong kind of company lately-these private interests about which he is so much concerned. We have in Western Canada 300,000,000 nthes

of splendid arable land. I am one of those, Mr. Chairman, who has never shared the opinion that the railway enterprises of the last Government were not justified by the possibilities of Canada's development. 1 am an optimistic Canadian and I hope to die one. There is no pessimism going to get hold of me breathing the clear air of Canada and sharing the stimulating beliefs of the Western Provinces. We have, as I say, 300,000,000 acres of splendid arable land. We have up to now tilled 25,000,000 acres, and no more, of that arable land. Along with the comparable development in other parts of Canada, the result, confining our thought for the moment to railway enterprise alone, has been to build up this very Canadian Pacific railway, about whose interests my hon. friend is at the present time so anxious, and about which other Canadians were so pessimistic, and to put it in a position in which it is rich almost beyond the dreams of avarice. If the other railways are supported with the same faith, the same energy and the same belief in the country it is a simple arithmetical proposition to foretell the possibilities of development. If we have built up one railway system from comparatively small beginnings by the development of a paltry 25,000,000 acres of land in those Western Provinces, it is an easy thing to estimate what will be the position of the Canadian system of railways when we have developed, shall I say, 100,000,000 acres? Then we shall still have 200,000,000 acres waiting to be developed by the next generation.-
These are the thoughts that animate Western Canadians. This is the belief that they have in that country and I want to say to the Government and to my hon. friend that as far as the West is concerned there is no pessimism among the people out there. They believe in' their country and they believe that the best way to develop its wealth is to further the scheme of developing this national railway.
I repeat that my hon. friend's speech has given me the greatest surprise. It is totally inconsistent with his attitude on railway development only a few years ago. Except in so far as he afforded an explanation in the way in which he has done to-day, I cannot understand what has produced the transformation of a very optimistic young Canadian into one who talks blue ruin in the most pessimistic and depressing fashion.
I would really advise him to get back to his former views and become an enthusiastic Canadian once more.

I am not quite clear, Mr. Chairman, as to the connection between

the very eloquent address of the hon. member (Mr. Michael Clark) and the motion before the Chair.
He has to pat the Government on the back.

The ink is hardly dry upon a speech made by the hon. gentleman about two days ago, upon which occasion he solemnly took off his hat, stood up in the House, and warned the Government against any undue expenditure in view of the enormous burden of debts under which the people of Canada were to-day groaning. The hon. gentleman told us then that if he had any advice to give, and if his words were heeded, it would be a warning to the Government to move cautiously and carefully in the expenditure of even ten cents out of the national treasury, except what was absolutely necessary to carry on in the most economic manner the affairs of the country.
Precisely.

To-day the hon. gentleman appears in another role: Saul of Tarsus has become Paul the Apostle, and the hon. gentleman finds a great deal of fault with my friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Le-mieux) because he follows along the same line of caution which the hon. gentleman himself,' [DOT]with all his wisdom and experience, a couple of days ago suggested. If the hon. gentleman, will cast his memory back a couple of days or so he will recall the incident to which I have reference.- No necessity existed for his utterance at that time except that this burden was on his mind and he wanted to get from under it; he wanted to be able to tell this Government, or any other government, that if the crash should come, if the credit of Canada was no longer any good, if our bonds had sunk away down below par, he had warned the people of this country.

I am perfectly sure that my hon. friend does not wish to misrepresent me. He should not put the words " crash " or " sinking below par " into my mouth, when I never used them. I was talking of economy in regard to nonessential expenditure, and I should like to point out to my hon. friend that if you economize on unnecessary outlays you will have all the more to devote to expenditures that are imperative.

The hon. gentleman's position is understandable in this way: His financial training enables him to grasp the expenditure involved in the increase
of a deputy minister's salary-he understands that and it brings him to his feet in protest-but when he gets to a large amount he is entirely at sea; he falls into the current and goes along with it. That is the only possible explanation that I can give of the hon. gentleman's position. If we are to be faithful servants in this world we must be faithful in small things as well as in big things, in order to possess the joy we look for in the world to come. There is no use trying to blow hot and blow cold; no use trying to be an economist in small matters and a plunger when it comes to big things. There is no use trying to get along in that way. I am sure the hon. member (Mr. Clark) would be very sorry if he felt that in this House there were men who would not profit by experience; I am sure he would be the last man to find fault with them for doing as he advises. We have to-day in the hands of a receiver, some three or four thousand miles of railway in the beautiful West which we all admire, and in the advancement and prospect of which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clark) prides himself. So necessary in the Government's opinion was the receivership, and so great was the need for speed, owing to the gravity of the emergency, that they could not follow the ordinary course of procedure but grabbed the railway before it went to Hades and out of sight entirely.
By Order in Council, too.

Yes, by Order in Council, which was entirely irregular; and now this line of railway is in the hands of a receiver who is sitting in this House to-day. Is there anything more discouraging, in connection with any enterprise, than to see that enterprise hopelessly insolvent and in the hands of a receiver? That is the condition of a great stretch of railroad which has been built in the West. Now I ask my hon. friend (Mr. Clark), as one of the custodians of the money of the people of this country, does he not think the exercise of a little care is necessary before we plunge into the expenditure of billions of money in the same territory in which the hapless railroad referred to was built, and which, as a result of its operations, has landed in the hands of a receiver? Supposing the hon. gentleman himself were an English capitalist and a man came to him from the West to ask him to aid a railway similar to the one I have been discussing, would he not say: "Are you not from the same country where a very large system of railways has already been built, and I find that

it is to-day in the hands of a receiver because it did not pay; do I not find the Government of Canada obliged to take over a railway burdened with a debt of $373,000,000 and hopelessly insolvent"? Are not those lessons, Mr. Chairman, that the Minister of Finance of Canada should take to heart? Are not those questions that the ordinary taxpayer, and we ourselves, should consider? And when we say in this House

I would ask the hon.
gentleman if he considered those questions before the expenditure was made on this railway, and if he did not vote for the very expenditure that made the country responsible?

There is all the difference in the world between the situation now and then. My good friend (Mr. Clark) whom I am answering said that expenditure was perfectly justifiable at the time it was made. He was a conservative Englishman, conservative in the sense of being careful; it is only recently that he has become conservative in his politics. My hon. friend was in the swim, he actually believed in, and was enthusiastic for, the building of this railway, and the road went along splendidly under our management. When it was in our hands everything went along swimmingly, but when it got into the hands of hon. gentlemen who did not know how to handle the enterprise it went to smash, and that is the condition we have to-day.

It was knocked by
them.
Mr. McKENZIE; That is why the crash took place; and that is the reason for it. It is perfectly legitimate to put money and property into the hands of men who know how to handle and operate it profitably. Unfortunately the railway fell into the hands of people who are - absolutely reckless and know nothing about proper business management. Ilf the hon. gentle-jnan (Mr. Morphy) wants to know the difference between the building of railways in the days of the ILaurier Government and the building of railways to-day, it is simply that in our time there was competency and capacity in the railway administration, whereas to-day there is recklessness and incompetence. That is what constitutes the difference.
Of course these forty lines of railway would be all right if my hon. friend was Prime Minister.
' Oh, oh.

There is such a thing as committing the unpardonable sin, and such a thing as, a man getting beyond the skill of a doctor. Such a condition in the country's health has been brought about by the men who are in charge of public affairs to-day, that even the best men in the -land might find it difficult to bring that health back to a proper physical state and normal pulsation.
The hon. member is not going to phase me on this question by a sneering reference to what might happen if Cf were Premier. I may never be Premier, but I shall be Premier before the hon. gentleman ever will.
I want to assure my hon. friend that if I seemed to sneer it was furthest from my thoughts.-
But it was on your face.
-But if it will remove his impression that I sneered, I can say quite sincerely that he is by far the nearest approach to a Prime Minister that I can see rwhen I am looking at his side of the House.
And so say we all.

With regard to his prophecy that he will be Prime Minister before I am, I can only fall back upon the saying of the well-known Mrs. Malaprop, giving it, however, in proper English, that comparisons are proverbially odious.
To the man who makes them.

If the hon. gentleman feels the odium he had better move out from the side of the House he is sitting. I think I have made it perfectly clear that we are now at a stage in the financial history of this country when it behooves every man, particularly those in responsible positions, to be careful. And if to be cautious, to sound a note of warning to those who control the expenditures of this country, is to be treated as pessimism, as the expression of a man who has no faith in his country, then we are trying to teach in this House the doctrine that no man shall dare speak his mind at all, and that the whole proceedings from start to finish are to be regarded as a continuous camouflage, until at last the people will come to believe that we do not understand what we are talking about. The hon. member (Mr. M. Clark) wanted to fasten upon my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) the imputation of being in favour of the Canadian Pacific Railway, of being

a corporation man, a man who was trying to deprive the people of the west of their rights in favour of some corporation.
Shame.
I am surprised that a gentleman who is usually so fair should in so short a time be transformed into such an adept at small Tory politics.
Ask him what company he keeps.
Bad company.

As to fault finding and pessimism in regard to building railways. if pessimism it be, I think my hon. friend from Red Deer will be quite satisfied with the company of the Montreal Star, for instance, and perhaps Lord Athol-stan might qualify for communication and communion with him.
Hear, hear.

I think that paper has achieved a sufficiently high standing in this country to be read by most Conservatives, and its readers are regarded as good staunch Canadians. Let me read to the hon. gentleman what that paper says about the very subject we are discussing, under date as late as April 19, 1919:
The annual report of the Canadian Department of Railways for 1918 is a document of startling timeliness. We commend it earnestly to the apostles who preach public ownership as a panacea for present ills.
Canada operated last year a little over four thousand miles of railway-4073.76 miles to be eft a ct.	-
The actual operating cost-not counting in any expenditure that could be charged to capital or any interest on the money invested in the railways, as a company would have to do- exceeded the earnings by over six million dollars-$6,159,503.58.
In addition to the operating costs the Government spent $34,699,416.96, which it charged to " capital account "-a financial camouflage in the main. It all has to be paid some day out of the public purse. So that these public ownership roads cost the public last year over $40,000,000 more than they earned.
There is no consideration in this amount of the annual interest cost which the public is paying on the money invested in these railways. Leaving out last year's charge to capital, this investment now mounts up to the huge total of $378,661,442. With interest at five per cent this means an annual charge of nearly $19,000,000. Adding this to last year's deficit and capital expenditure, the suffering taxpayer will find that his little toy cost him in 1918 close to $60,000,000 more than he got out of it.
It may be of interest to business minds to note that of the actual operating deficit the National Transcontinental contributed over three millions, the Intercolonial over two and a quarter millions, the Prince Edward Island
Railway almost half a million, and the International about a quarter of a million. They all did their little bit.
Here is an interesting problem in arithmetic to wind up with :
The Government railway mileage in 1918 was 4073. Since then the taxpayer lias been handed the Canadian Northern, 9433 miles and the Grand Trunk Pacific 2788 miles. The politicians are now reaching out for the old Grand Trunk which may add 4785 miles.
If it cost us sixty millions to run four thousand miles, how much will twenty-one thousand miles cost?
That is an expression of opinion by a newspaper edited by an orthodox Conservative, a gentleman well versed, no doubt, in the public affairs of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman approve of that opinion himself?

I used the word " opinion. I do not think it is so much an expression of opinion as it is a gathering together of facts. The language in which the editor expresses himself does not make so much difference; the figures are the startling and appalling part which cannot be questioned, because we have had them from the records of the various departments.
While I always want to hear my hon. friend (Mr. Clark) and see him in "line in the House, he must not find fault with anybody who advises caution in view of the fact that in the very early days of the session the Minister of Public Works,-and the building of railways may be considered as public works-told us that we are one hundred million dollars short this year, and he did not know where to look for the money.
Hear, hear.

We are told by every
one who has to do with finance that he is ,at his wits ends to get money. We have to-day a public debt of two billion dollars. Is it not time to pause before embarking on further expenditure to develop this country and proceed with that development only as our means will allow? That is what the Canadian people expect us to do, and there is no man in the West or elsewhere who is so unreasonable as to say that we should render this country bankrupt to build railways. In my part of the country, which has been settled for over 200 years, there are sections which are 110 miles from any .railway to-day. I am not raising any hue and cry on that account. J recognize that we must wait until the finances of the country are in a better position. But that should be a sufficient reason to advance to any fair-minded man in



the West for delaying railway construction. Do not let us have any person, no matter how eloquent, tell the people of the West that some men on this side of the House do not want to give them the railway facilities they require. We gave them what they have got to-day, and their facilities would be in good condition at the present time if we had retained control of affairs.
Hear, hear.

But they got into the
hands of the Huns and Goths and went to smash.
At six o'clock the Committee took recess.
After Recess.
The Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Owing to the turn which this discussion has taken, and owing particularly to the remarks of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) respecting the general railway and financial policy of the Government, I think it proper that I should offer a few remarks.
For the last three days in Committee, and for some days previously, on the resolution which preceded the introduction of this Bill, we have been discussing ostensibly the corporate machinery by which the Government of Canada is to administer the railway system which has come into our possession. But this afternoon-I knew from the trend of the discussion that the stage would be reached-the real issue was revealed which is dividing the two sides of the House respecting this measure. The real issue is not the Bill before the Committee, important as its provisions are; the real issue is whether public ownership is to have a chance for success in Canada or is to leave this Chamber maimed, mutjlated and deformed. What is before the Committee? A Bill incorporating a
tSlr. McKenzie.]
holding company of which the Dominion of Canada, through the Dominion Government, is to be the sole proprietor and shareholder. There are many important provisions in this Bill which should be fully discussed, but it is not too much to say that hours have been wasted upon sections of the Bill which are in the general railway and company Acts and which, had they been before the Committee or the House in connection with a charter of a private railway company, would not have commanded one minute of attention from hon. gentlemen opposite. Who recalls-I do not, although I have been a member of the House for eight years'-in connection with any private railway charter such a discussion as we have had upon insignificant sections with regard to the provisional directors, the appointment of executive committees, or matters of that kind? What accounts for the present attitude of hon. gentlemen with regard to this measure as compared with their attitude towards measures incorporating private enterprises? Mr. Chairman, the real discussion in this Chamber has been between private railway enterprise and public ownership. Every section of this Bill has received from hon. gentlemen opposite the most critical attention, the most anxious solicitude-well simulated, I admit, but the real nature of which is obvious to all on this side of the House and to the press of this country. There has been an influence-I do not say an improper influence-behind the discussion of this Bill by hon. gentlemen opposite, and we all know what that influence has been-private ownership. I do not blame private ownership for fighting public ownership, but I am on strong ground when I blame representatives of the people in the House for espousing the cause of private ownership as against public ownership.
We might have gone through this Bill without the real issue being revealed as it was this afternoon. But during the last two days, watching the discussion in Committee, I have known that this stage would be reached. The member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) disclosed the issue this afternoon, and disclosed it unmistakably. There is no doubt where he stands; he is not in sympathy with public ownership of the railway systems of this country-ownership by the people, and, we hope, for the people. In order that I may do my hon. friend no injustice, I shall quote, from a Hansard extract which I have here, what he said this afternoon. The section before

the Committee was a section reviving charters which had belonged to the Canadian Northern Railway system. They are presumably of value, or they would not have been acquired; and the question is whether the Government of Canada-that is, the people of Canada-are to have these charters for the benefit of the Canadian National railway system-that is, the people- or whether they are to go ttf others who desire to have them. My hon. friend will not deny that he came out unmistakeably to-day against public ownership. I do not see how hon. gentlemen opposite can avoid the charge that as a party, the so-called Liberal party, they stand in this House for private railway enterprises against public ownership of the systems which this Government has to take over and has had to take over. The member for Maisonneuve said:
By adopting this schedule-
Which contains the charters that the Government desires to preserve, not for any improper purpose, but for the people of Canada; and which this Parliament granted to private enterprises.
By adopting this schedule and renewing the charters en bloc, are we now debarring private companies-
His interest is with the private companies.
-are we not debarring private companies and the provinces from building lines in the same territory not exactly on the same routes hut approximately so? These charters have remained dormant-simply paper charters, if I may call them so-for twenty years.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If they remained dormant, they were of some value. The Dominion Government seeks to revive them, for what? For the people of Canada. My hon. friend says: No, do not preserve them for the people of Canada; private enterprise may want them. He says further:
Mackenzie and Mann did nothing with them except hold them for their own use.
Well, if they held them for their own use, it is a fair implication that they were of value for them and for the Canadian Northern Railway system, as they will be for the people of Canada.
Not for the people. The people get nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They will get
something; they will get a good deal out of this system before we are through with it.

They will get the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
says :
They did not build one mile of railway on any of these charters. Now we are to renew them en bloc-
A terrible thing to renew them en bloc for the enterprise owned by the people of Canada. My hon. friend suggests that they are of no value, yet he goes on to say:

and debar private companies and other enterprises, which might eventually wish to build these railways, from doing so.
If they are of no value, why would "private companies and other enterprises, which might eventually wish to build these railways," do so. My hon. friend says in one breath that they are of no value, that Mackenzie andMann had them and did not make use of them; and) in the next he says: Let us not take them for fear some private enterprise in competition with the Government's road might want them.
Does my hon. friend seriously stand upon that ground? As I said, private enterprise and public ownership have been contending during the debate-notwithstanding the form of the discussion in this chamber- upon the provisions of this Bill. I do not mean to say that there may not be a few members opposite with a predisposition, probably inherited from some Liberal ancestor, in favour of public ownership; but if the leader of the 'Opposition had to depend for support upon those on his side of the House who are sincerely in favour of public ownership, he would not command a corporal's guard.
This discussion, so far as hon. gentlemen opposite are concerned, has ostensibly gone along the lines of safeguarding the public interest. Every section of this Bill must be subjected to the most minute scrutiny for fear that the people of Canada might not have adequate machinery to carry out their railway enterprise. Most specious arguments have been put forward. The voice was the voice of Jacob, but the hand was the hand of Esau. Let me put it to the hon. member for Maisonneuve: Are we going to give public ownership a chance for its life, or are we going to strangle it in this chamber, where its friends ought to be, if they are anywhere in Canada? The Government brings down a measure to revive a number of charters which are valuable to-day and which will be more valuable in the days to come, not for any private railway company or enterprise, but for the people of Canada. What chance will public ownership have in this country it, in this cham-

ber, we are going to deny to our own enterprises what we are willing to concede to rival enterprises? Supposing a meeting was held of the shareholders of the 'Canadian Pacific Railway ICompany-an admirably managed institution, one of the best in the world, with a fine list of shareholders, a splendid executive, a wonderfully capable and loyal staff

and the general manager of the company informed the shareholders that during the war a number of valuable charters, which the Canadian Pacific Railway Company had obtained from Parliament, had lapsed, but that he had succeeded in getting Parliament to revive them so that that company had now the revived charters. Can my hon. friend contend that a shareholder of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, much less a director-and he is in the position of a director, not in that of a shareholder- would rise in his place and say: " Really, Mr. General Manager, we should not ask Parliament to revive those charters, because some other railway company in opposition to us may want to obtain them." Does my hon. friend, public man as he is, and member of this House for many years and former member of a Government of this country, contend that?
What's in a name? My hon. friend has often spoken to us in this House as to the true meaning of Liberalism. He is a Liberal, he says. I believe I am understating the matter when I say there is not a row of seats on this side of the House that does not hold more progressive Liberalism than there is on the entire opposite side of this Chamber. If Liberalism means standing for the public interest and the people's rights, my hon. friend, standing here, as he does, for private enterprise as against public ownership, whatever he is, is not a Liberal. He frankly does not like public ownership. If he would express what is down in his heart, he would boldly say: I do not believe in public ownership. He has been too long in politics to do that; -he side-steps. If he had not been so long in politics he would state his conviction, which is against public ownership. If that is his opinion, it is a perfectly proper one for him to hold as a public man, if he avows it. Whether he likes public ownership of railways or not, whether the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) likes it or not, whether all hon. gentlemen opposite like it or not-and they do not like it-we have public ownership of railways in Canada, and it has come to stay. Let me make an appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite. We owned some 4,000 or 5,000 miles of rail-
way, and we have acquired, within the last two years, nearly 10,000 miles more. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company is in the hands of the Minister of Railways as receiver. We are negotiating with the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada to acquire their system. Hon. members know perfectly well the steps by which the Dominion of Canada has become a great railway proprietor, and will become one of the greatest in the world. The situation has been such that, by the inevitable trend of events, the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the National Transcontinental Railway Company have come into the possession of the Government; and by the inevitable and inexorable trend of events, I believe, the other systems that I have mentioned will also come into the possession of the Government-this Government did not go out years ago with a policy of taking over the railways of Canada. Having this railway system, one of the greatest in the world, full of possibilities to any one who has vision for the future, should we not, as public men, take a reasonable pride in the situation and make the best of it?
What is the continual criticism from hon. gentlemen opposite? That roads are bankrupt or in the hands of receivers. Well, that does not advance us very far, Mr. Chairman; this Government did not make them bankrupt. What has produced the railway situation in Canada that has been discussed so often in this House? The railway situation, under which taking over by the Government became inevitable, and a receivership for the Grand Trunk Pacific inevitable-what was it that brought about that situation? Was it public ownership? It was private ownership and politics Huns, Goths, and Vandals, we are called on this side of the House by the hon. leader of the Opposition. Well, " what's in a name," iMr. Chairman? What do the Huns and Goths and Vandals do? Destroy completed and productive enterprises. Has this Government destroyed completed and productive enterprise? If the roads that we took over were bankrupt who made them bankrupt? What are we trying to do with them? We are trying to make them fruitful and productive for the people of Canada. That is our clear duty, and I submit that it is the duty of hon. gentlemen opposite to unite with us in doing it, because the railway policy of this country has been the policy both of Liberals and Conservatives. Both are responsible for the building of railways in this country, and both are responsible, in
