some degree at least, for the situation which I have described. The over-building, the over-lapping, the wasteful expenditure of money-I am not going to make this a narrow party question, that water has gone over the wheel. The policy to-day, if ever there was a time when we should have such a policy, is to make this enterprise fruitful and productive for the people of Canada. What use is there in continually harping on the string that the Government has taken over bankrupt roads? What else could the Government do? I have read in the press, and I have heard in this House, endless criticism of Government ownership of railways. I have never seen in the press that puts out that criticism, nor heard from hon. members of this House who support it, any constructive scheme different from that which the Government has adopted. It was an inevitable policy that we followed, if we were to save this country and its transportation systems which are vital to it. Let me appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite to take pride in public ownership, which alone can save these railway children of theirs.
I have been abused many times in this House on account of my railway policy, and I have often thought: What have I done that I am so abused? I found a couple of half-starved babies on the doorstep of the Finance Department when I went in there, puling, weakly creatures, ill-dressed, dirty. Well, we have them here to-night, and they are not bad looking children.
Who left them there?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will leave that to the imagination and good sense of the House. We found the babies on the doorstep; we took good care of them; and this side of the House is prepared to continue taking care of them until they grow up and become useful to the country. And all we get for it is abuse-and from unnatural parents. I appeal to the patriotism of hon. gentlemen opposite, and to their sense of loyalty to their own railway policy, not to listen longer to the promptings of private railway enterprise, but to stand with us behind the railway system owned by the people of Canada.
It is put forward by hon. gentlemen opposite that these railroads that we have taken over are bankrupt, and we hear of that same old deficit from day to day. Well, let us make them solvent; let us make them fruitful; let us make them the all-important factor that they can be made in the development of the resources of this country. That is the true, constructive, statesmanlike
policy. Any other policy is merely destructive; it will not advance things one bit. I ask the hon. leader of the Opposition how long will it be before the railways of Canada that this Government has been obliged to take over become solvent?-how long will it be before the deficit is wiped out, if we adopt the stand-still policy advocated by him and other hon. gentlemen opposite this afternoon? They are so afraid of the revival of charters. Why, it is a terrible thing that the Government should revive charters for its railway system. Evidently the policy is to stand still and let the deficit continue. I say that if we stand still, the deficit will increase, not diminish. There is no standing still in this world, in transportation or anything else. You must go forward or you will go backward. The hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) took the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) to task this afternoon.

Is there any part of Canada in which you cannot build a railway under the Aot that is now before the House?
-Sir THOMAS WHITE:	i submit, that
is not the point.
I submit, it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If we can build a line in any part of Canada, then we can build five hundred lines, because there are at least five hundred different sections of Canada. All we are asking for is that forty-four charters be revived. So if my hon. friend says that we can build five hundred lines of railway, he should not object to our taking power under only forty-four charters, to go ahead if we so decide.
Why duplicate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All that rwe are doing is to revive these charters to be used if we see fit, that is to say, if the Government, carrying the majority in this Parliament, thinks it in the interest of Canada. We must come to Parliament to get money to build railway extensions. The whole theory of constitutional government is based upon that, and where is the harm in the Government having these charters revived, for construction to be gone on with, if in the public interest it is thought expedient by the Government and by Parliament to do so?
I was saying that the hon. leader of the Opposition attacked the hon. member for Red Deer this afternoon. Well, he is a hard man to attack successfully; but the leader of the Opposition took him to task

for an alleged statement-I emphasize 'alleged',-that at this time, with our great national debt, we must not spend any money. Now, I never heard the hon. member for Bed Deer say that we should not spend any money. I have heard him say on many occasions, both before and since the war, that we should not waste any money; but there is a great deal of difference between spending money wisely and wasting it. I think the hon. member for Eed Deer this afternoon put forward a statesmanlike policy-the only policy for Canada at this time. The leader of the Opposition says: "Why, you have got a national debt of a couple of billion dollars -or you will have." He is so frightened at the national debt that he says, in effect: "Do not spend any more money; close up everything."
If this Government had adopted that pol-[DOT] icy since the 11th of last November, there would have been tens of thousands of people walking around in idleness, and there would have been civil disorders throughout Canada. What policy have we laid down, Mr. Chairman? We have laid down a policy which is unassailable-no money for unproductive undertakings but money for productive works in Canada. How are we going to meet the interest on our national debt and provide a sinking fund for its extinguishment unless we enormously increase the production of this country, rich in natural resources, one of the richest in the world? All that it requires is the application of enterprise, labour and capital. Principal among our resources are our great agricultural resources 

this vast stretch of arable land not only in Eastern Canada but millions upon millions of acres in the great Prairie West extending from Winnipeg to the foothills of the Eockies. The hon. member for Eed Deer spoke of hundreds of millions of acres and of the tens of millions that, by enterprise, could be brought under cultivation and made to yield a golden harvest for the people of Canada. How are they to be developed, unless we have transportation? Are there any members of this House, at this of all times, who will arise and say: You must not have railway extension in the West; you must expand no farther?
The hon. the leader of the Opposition put it forward this afternoon that in his constituency some people were-I think he said-one hundred miles from a railway. My hon. friend, evidently, by implication, was of the view that as long as railways went within a hundred miles of the farm-

ers of the Northwest, or any other part of Canada, there was no cause for complaint. I know a little about farming. If a man has to draw a load of wheat one hundred miles to the elevators to sell it, he has not very much of the value left by the time he gets it there.
Mr. Chairman, at this of all times we must have a progressive, productive policy in this country or else we shall not overtake the effects of this war. We have, in this Government railway system, a wonderful instrument for increasing the productiveness of all parts of Canada, especially the Northwest. Do hon. gentlemen realize what a heritage we have in the West?-to say nothing of the East with its boundless resources; and there are boundless resources in the East. We have the great provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta each of them as large as modern Germany,-in fact, larger; 250,000 square miles each, and modern Germany 207,000 square miles. Have we a vision of the far future? How will it be realized? Will it be realized by a standstill policy under which we will say: No further railway extensions? Or shall we consider the situation from time to time and wisely make extensions which will multiply productiveness many fold for the benefit of the population of the West and for the general benefit of Canada? Is that not the policy that we should follow? It requires courage and imagination, and these are qualities which are necessary in this Dominion, not only for the remainder of this reconstruction period, but for many years to come.
Now, we want these charters. We want them for no improper purpose. We do not desire to give them away or sell them to any rival enterprise. We want these charters for the Canadian Government Bail-ways; that is to say, for the people of Canada. I utterly fail to understand how any hon. member of this House, the Government being the sole proprietor of these railways, can object for one moment to the' Government railway system having the benefit of the revival of these charters to be availed of as may be expedient in the public interest.
Private railway enterprise in this country is apprehensive of public ownership. There is no doubt about that. I do not blame it. But we have our duty to perform, and I submit that our first duty in this House is towards our own railway system. No man in this House will be fairer than I to any other railway enterprise in this country.

They serve a most useful purpose. The Canadian Pacific is the greatest system in the world, and most capably managed. I gladly pay them my tribute of appreciation. But as between any private railway enterprise and this publicly owned railway enterprise, I submit, it is the obvious duty of every man in this House, representative as he is of the people, to support measures designed to promote and make more productive the Government owned enterprise.
Speaking about the West, I was amazed this afternoon-in fact until I saw the extract from Hansard I could hardly believe it-at the attack made by my hon. friend from Maisonneuve upon our three western provinces. My hon. friend may have spoken as a politician, although I can scarcely see the ground upon which he might hope to gain any advantage. At all events, in the heat of his remarks he evidently expressed the deepest convictions of his heart. But to say the least, his remarks were not politic. Let us hear what he says:
Scanning the list of these problematical railways-
So problematical that he was fearful that private enterprise might be debarred from getting them.
-I notice that the schedule published will consist of railway schemes for the West only. There is nothing in the list for the East; there is nothing for Quebec.
Let us see what that means, Mr. Chairman. Nothing for the East and particularly nothing for Quebec! Carry that to its logical conclusion and it is that it has meant nothing, in the opinion of my hon. friend, to Ontario or Quebec that the West has had any railway facilities at all. Why, these railway facilities have made possible the immense production of the West which has enured to the advantage of the whole of Canada, and notably to the East. He says: There is nothing for Quebec. He says by implication clearly:	Any development you
make in the West is of no advantage to Quebec, and therefore 1 am against it. He says:
Of course, the support of Quebec is not needed, but the credit of Quebec is of the highest.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am glad to agree with him. My hon. friend will look over Hansard in vain for any statement of mine reflecting against his province, so we are on common ground with regard to that.
He has only to look through your press if he wants to find out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My press?
Yes, your press, the Tory press, or, if you like it better, the Unionist press.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We practically have all the press now.
Because you bought it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The press of this country is above all things an intelligent press, and it is inconceivable that it should not strongly support this Unionist Government.
But the owners are financial men first.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) says:
The credit of Quebec is of the highest, whilst some of the 'Western Provinces were on the verge of bankruptcy because of the guarantees they gave to Mackenzie and Mann.
Why drag that into a discussion of this Bill. My hon. friend seems to delight to dwell upon the fact,-as he assumes it,-but which I controvert,-that the Western Provinces are bankrupt. He says further:
That explains why before the last general election we saw so many of these premiers wavering in their faith, because, forsooth, they were promised if they supported Union Government that the guarantees given by their provinces would be taken up by the Dominion Government.
Why, Mr. Chairman, the legislation was put through before the general election took place. We took over the Canadian Northern Railway system before the election took place. It is a slander upon those public men-the Prime Minister of Manitoba, the Prime Minister of Saskatchewan, the Prime Minister of Alberta-that an hon. member of this House, the first lieutenant of the Opposition, should rise in Ins' seat and state that they were bribed to support the Bo-minion Government in the last general election. That is what the hon. gentleman says, and it is a pretty serious indictment against leading public men. The hon. gentleman says:
In fact, no provincial premier came to Ottawa during that eventful period without being met at the station by the wily gentlemen-
That is Mackenzie and Mann were waiting down here at the station

-who then controlled the destinies of Union Government.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I think I will leave it at that so far as my hon. friend from Maisonneuve is concerned.
Now, let me say one word with regard to the railway policy with which I have had something to do; with which I have been obliged against my will to have something to do since I have been Finance Minister. When we came into office we found the National Transcontinental Railway line from Moncton to Winnipeg unfinished. I was loyal to the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite, because Government is a continuing thing, and I felt it my duty as Minister of Finance to provide the means of completing that enterprise, and it was done faithfully and well. The appropriations were put in the Estimates. I never criticised them. I felt that that great enterprise, partly finished as it was, should be completed, although I had very great doubt indeed as to its financial success-in fact I felt certain that it would not be a business success. There is not an hon. member in this House on either side who, if he would say what is in his heart, would admit that the National Transcontinental Railway from Moncton to Winnipeg, built at a cost of $200,000,000 and over, could possibly be made productive. If you only take three per cent upon it, to say nothing of four per cent, you have got fixed charges of $6,000,000 per year.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am not going to refer to responsibility for this. That belongs to the past. I want to make the best of the situation. Since I have been minister I have endeavoured, so far as my voice was influential in the Government, to make the best of the railway situation, and the money was provided for the finishing of the Transcontinental Railway-including the Quebec bridge-from Moncton to Winnipeg. There is no man in this House or in this country who would like to see the railway succeed better than I .would; because it is Canadian. I do not consider whether any mistakes have been made or not; the railway is there, let us make the best of it. Take the Grand Trunk Pacific from Winnipeg to Prince Rupert. The leader of the Opposition says the Goths, .and the Vandals, and the Huns-that is, myself and others-destroyed it. Well, we certainly did not destroy it, no matter what else we did. The railway was only partially built. Why, it was only taken put of the construction stage a couple of years ago; One of my first acts as Minister of Finance was to bring down a guarantee of $15,000,000, then a vote of $16,-

000,000, and then successive annual votes of $7,500,000, down to the present year.
Whatever charges hon. gentlemen opposite can bring against me, they cannot say that I did not faithfully, as Minister of Finance, seek to provide the means to carry out this enterprise which they initiated. Now, I am not going to follow my hon. friend in his argument as to whether the railways could have been made productive or not. My hon. friend knows the situation too well. There is nothing gained by reflecting upon your own enterprise-it is a sad kind of business to do that. There is nothing in being pessimistic. Men hate the gloom and love the sunlight. Let us be optimistic *about our railways. A first condition of success in anything is to be optimistic; it spurs your courage. We need courage in this situation.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would like my hon. friend to have a little more of it.
I would need it.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let us look to the future of this country despite the great debt which we have as a result of the war from which we have emerged with the utmost credit to Canada. Thanks to the sacrifices of our men and thanks to the initiative and capacity of the people and of the Government of this country since that war broke out, we have come most creditably and honourably through it. So far as I am concerned, I say that all gentlemen in this House share in that credit and honour; there is enough glory to go round. But now that we are through the war, let us set our faces to the future, and inspire our hearts with courage to meet this reconstruction period, and overcome whatever difficulties it may present. Let us not say: Now we must stop; we must spend no more money, whether productively or otherwise, let us stop. Well, if we do that we will not only stop, but we will go backward. I say to my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition that he will never carry the people of Canada on a destructive policy; his must be a constructive policy, and it must be an optimistic policy, looking to the larger future which this country is destined to have, and which every patriot believes it must have and will have.
We must throw our gates open to properly selected immigrants, and we must develop enterprises, so far as it is the function of the Government to do so; and provide

transportation facilities to the extent that is necessary to promote development in order that we may continually increase our production and make this country the home, not of eight million or ten million people, hut of twenty-five million or thirty million people within the lifetime of those in this Chamber. There is nothing far fetched or visionary in that; I believe it is an understatement; but we can only accomplish it, Mr. Chairman, if we have faith and hope and courage and resource. In connection with our railway policy we must be progressive, we must be enterprising, and we must be able to compete with the other great railway system which is in opposition to us and whose prosperity I have very much at heart. For I believe there is room for both systems. We have heard a good many reflections on public ownership from hon. gentlemen opposite, sometimes in express terms, at other times in a veiled way and by implication or insinuation stating that the railway systems of Canada are bankrupt and consequently the Government should not have taken them over, and that we will not be able to run them or to appoint directors of standing and integrity to ensure that they shall be properly administered.
Now, let me again make an appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite to help in this matter, to have a new outlook with regard to the possibilities of the Government-owned system. And if any hon. gentlemen have it in their minds that the situation could be made different, let me say this to them- and there are not many men in Canada who have devoted more attention to the railway systems of Canada than I have, because I have been obliged to do so: There are just two courses open so far as Canadian Railway systems are concerned; two and no more: One is that the Government of Canada should acquire the railways that must be acquired from time to time following the policy which we have adopted, and that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company should be the other great enterprise, in friendly and honourable competition with the Government, and prosperous, as I know it will be. The other, since the Canadian Northern Railway enterprise and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway enterprise were inaugurated, is that the 9 p.m. Canadian Pacific Railway Company should acquire all the railway systems of Canada. Two great systems -possibly three if the Grand Trunk is not in-one owned by the Dominion Government and the other owned by the Canadian
Pacific; or as an alternative, and the only alternative, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company owning and operating all the railways of Canada. That was the alternative with which the Government was confronted in 1917, and there is no other alternative to-day.
I do not mean to say for one moment that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company could not operate all the railways of Canada with the highest degree of efficiency; I think they could. But when I say that I also say that the public of this country, great as is their admiration for the abilities of those who control the destinies of the Canadian Pacific Railway, would never permit any private corporation to own and operate all the railways of Canada.
I submit that that is the inevitable situation. If I am right, then let us quit harping about public ownership and reflecting upon the railway systems which we have taken over. Let us not go over all that old ground as to what the Liberals and) what the Conservatives did-I am sick of it. Let us face the situation like business men and patriots, and make the best of it, with pride in our Government-owned system. I am sure that that carries the judgment of the members of this. House.
I am a great believer in Canada. I believe in its inimitable resources, I believe in the enterprise, capability and patriotism of the Canadian people. We are destined to a great future; no one in this House . doubts that. Well, let us set our faces to that vision and be constructive in all departments of our Government's activities.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have taken up a good deal of time. I had not intended to say a word more in this debate upon the sections of this Bill, because we have consumed days of valuable time, part of which undoubtedly has been wasted. I am the first to say that there should be full discussion oi a Bill of this kind, but I cannot overlook the fact that much of the discussion has appeared at least to be of a dilatory character. I would not have intervened except that this discussion had taken a turn in which it became necessary in the interests of the policy for which we stand on this side of the House, and in the interests of the people of Canada in connection with their publicly-owned railway system, that I should intervene and express my convictions as to the principles which should govern us in dealing with these great enterprises which have come into our possession.

My hon. friend the Acting Prime Minister derived so little comfort from the report which he had in his hand a moment ago of what I said before six o'clock that he found himself under the (lire necessity of delivering a long and emotional speech just to avoid 'the only point at issue. I suppose the hon. gentleman is not willingly reading into my words a meaning which he could not honestly find in them, but as he proceeded to do so by implication, at least, whilst he was reading the report, I may repeat for his benefit what was the point at issue when I rose. We were discussing clause 20 of the Bill to revive forty-four charters, which were dead and buried long ago. I said that the reviving of those charters, bearing in mind the obligations that the Government was assuming by taking over the main system of the Canadian Northern, was simply another means of deceiving the people of the Western Provinces, and preventing private corporations, if you please; preventing the provinces as well, from constructing railways where there is real need for them. Is there anything strange, anything criminal in criticising a procedure whereby the Government takes a blanket, collective charter and prevents the people of the provinces, east or west, from developing railway construction? That is the result, because the Government has not the means, has not the money, considering all its obligations, to implement that railway construction. That is what I said; that is the only meaning that can be given to my words. My hon. friend derived very little comfort, indeed, from what he read a moment ago. Sir, I am not the promoter or the advocate of private interests in this House; during the twenty-three years that I have sat in the House I have never championed private interests against public interests. My hon. friend said that we must have faith, that we must have hope. Let him have a little charity, too, and give to the words of his opponents the meaning which they obviously intended to convey.

Not charity, but justice.
Mr; VIEN: And fairness.

Well, a little Christian preaching does good under the circumstances. My hon. friend spoke a moment ago of the "legacy of dirty babies" from the Laurier Government. I notice that the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) nods his assent; he is on familiar ground. Norw, this is not precisely Gladstonian language.
I beg to differ; I do not approve of dirty babies. I am very fond of clean babies but I do not care for the dirty ones.

As a doctor, my hon. friend should not approve of dirty babies, and I am glad that he quickly dismisses tae idea of nursing them. But in the heat of the discussion the Acting Prime Minister overlooked the compliment that he paid to those babies and to their nurses when he was fresh from the polls in 1911. When he first came to this Parliament, having served private corporations for some time with great distinction, my hon. friend spoke of the future of the country in a speech which nobody could forget. He referred to that legacy of babies which he had received from the Laurier Government. On March 13th, 1912-on the thirteenth, a very unlucky day for him, but a very lucky one for me

he had hope and faith in the future of Canada. He said:
Despite the serious vicissitudes through which the western wheat crop has passed and the unusual heat experienced fin the province of Ontario during the past summer-
Yes, there was serious heat in Ontario during that summer.
-the field crops of Canada show a bountiful yield and with the high prices prevailing for praotioally all its products the great basic industry of agriculture continues in a flourishing condition. Almost every department of trade and commerce shows expansion. Our mines are wonderfully productive. Our coast fisheries, notably the Atlantic, have enjoyed a good catch and high prices. Our manufacturers are thriving and new industries are springing up throughout the whole Dominion. Railway construction, especially in the West, proceeds apace, preparing a way for settlement in districts not yet opened up and for trade with other markets than we now enjoy. Our increased bank deposits, clearings, and circulation, the amount of public and private building evidenced in municipal and business structures, extensions to manufacturing plants and residences in almost every part of the country, all attest that the general prosperity of Canada at the present time is very great.
" Railway construction proceeds apace " -the Laurier policy of railway construction for the western provinces. At that time my hon. friend was tinged with Liberalism. He remembered the day that he had been a Liberal; he could not completely forget that he had supported the railway policy of the Laurier Government for fifteen years; so he had to praise it when he delivered his first Budget speech. My hon. friend, therefore, who lauded the wisdom of the Laurier railway policy 'n 1911 now makes reference to the " dirty babies " of the Laurier Government. My hon. friend is apt to

change his views. Some years ago speaking in the city of Toronto when the first great fight for the hydro-electric took place, he described the supporters of public ownership as " coveting Naboth's vineyard." You see, I have a long memory. Now, behold my hon. friend extolling the men who covet Naboth's vineyard. My hon. friend will have to again alter his views' on many questions as long as this Government lasts.
My hon. friend was fair to me a moment ago when he put the question squarely: Are you or are you not in favour of Government ownership? Well, I am not like my hon. friend, who was described by one of his friends the other day as living in a fool's paradise-I hope the expression is parliamentary; I will never " rush in where angels fear to tread." I have no opinion to offer with regard to the Government ownership of railways. I do not think I shall be taken to task for not at this juncture stating, ex cathedra, that Canada must adopt Government ownership of railways as against private ownership of railways. There are men who are just as well educated on this question as even the Acting Prime Minister. He referred to the Canadian Pacific railway a moment ago. Lord Shaughnessy is a man of some experience in railway matters, a man who knows whereof he speaks. Speaking in Toronto last September on the occasion of the opening of the Canadian National Exhibition- which, I must say en passant, is a great credit to	Ontario-Lord	Shaughnessy,
though he did not commit himself as being, as my hon. friend would seem to infer, against public ownership, said:
I have covered a great deal of ground in the Quickest possible way. Much of it would stand great elaboration, but on an occasion of this kind long speeches are an abomination. I think probably that you expected me to say something on the subject of transportation. But I would prefer to postpone that until another occasion. It is beyond doubt a very live question, one in which the people of the country are taking a very great interest, but to my mind it is a question regarding which a decision should be reached only after most careful analysis and consideration. We shall, within the next short period, have an opportunity to learn the result of our neighbour's management of the railways of the country and probably have a little experience of our own. I do not wish to have it understood that I am taking an attitude opposed to nationalization of railways. When the Government is satisfied that the people of this country want nationalization, we are a democratic people and we shall have it. But whatever our policy, we should be very sure of our footing or it may become a very serious problem.
The words of Lord Shaughnessy are full of wisdom. Since he made that declaration in the city of Toronto, we have had the result of United States' public railway ownership. Not later than, I think, Monday last, Mr. Mitchell, president of the National City Company of New York, speaking before the -Canadian Club at Montreal, gave in a few concise, pungent words, the experience of the United States as regards public railway ownership:
On paper, Mr. Mitchell declared, the scheme was sound. The country was divided into seven great traffic regions, and for these regions were appointed regional directors, who were, for the most part, the presidents of leading trunk lines. The fact that these operators, however, working to a man to the height of their efficiency and power, were unable to produce satisfactory results, and service deteriorated and morale became constantly lower, is a striking commentary on the general subject of Government operation. The roads were free from hampering restrictions and yet the net earnings fell off $285,000,000, compared with the previous year, the railroads earning only 75 per cent of the amount which the Government had guaranteed them as rental. Notwithstanding the increases in rates, which were far greater than private management had ever dreamed of asking, and which produced greater gross revenue by $865,000,000, the people of our country, after suffering inferior service, were called upon as taxpayers to advance $210,000,000, the amount by which the net earnings failed to equal the guaranteed rental. In other words, the American people paid $865,000,000, more in rates for inferior service and were taxed $210,000,000, in addition, so that the true cost to the people of one year of Federal operation amounted to $1,075,000,000. With these figures before you, I need not repeat that the popular passion for Government ownership and operation has materially cooled during the past year.
Was Lord Shaughnessy not right when he said that, before adopting a policy of public railway ownership, we should be sure of our footing? For my part, I have no solution to offer. I say that we are, under present conditions, obliged to take the main line of the Canadian Northau*, but my objection this afternoon and this evening to section 20 of this Bill is that not only do we assume that enormous burden of the Canadian Northern, but the Government are foisting on that system 44 wrecks-and I have some regard for the credit of my country. Let not the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) think for one moment that I have not, equally with him, the interest of my country at heart. I have the interest of my country at heart just as much as any hon. member opposite.
This afternoon, I referred to the province of Quebec. I did not do so from any desire to force the Government to give to Quebec as much as they were seemingly giving to the West, because I sincerely be-

lieve the West will get nothing out of the 44 wrecks. This is simply another way of deceiving the West on the eve of a general election, as the West will get no relief from the belated tariff policy of the Finance Minister. I referred, and I am glad to refer, to Quebec, for this reason. Out of the nine provinces of this Dominion, at least four were and are on the verge of bankruptcy because of the Mackenzie and Mann system of railways. This is a truth which I am not afraid to state on the floor of this House as I have stated it before during the session of 1917. Sir, the credit of my province on the foreign markets is higher and better than that of the Dominion Government, because the bonds of my province are sold at par, while the bonds of the Dominion Government were sold on the New York market less than three years ago at 93 cents on the dollar. I have reason, therefore, to be proud of Quebec, the only province which did not deliver itself into the hands of Mackenzie and Mann, and we of Quebec have a right to resent the increased expenditure to which we are committing this country, because my province will have to pay its share of that vast expenditure if it is ever expended. That is the reason why, this afternoon, I referred to Quebec.
Speaking again on this question of public ownership, it is a popular fancy at the present time; but really those who favour that new fancy should take the time to read some of the best authorities on the question. I do not know if the Acting Prime Minister has ever read the views of possibly the greatest authority on economics in Europe, and, I should say, in the world, Mr. Paul Leroy Beaulieu, who is absolutely opposed to public ownership. So one might well pause and ponder before committing himself to this fancy. Within a year from to-day many people will regret having committed themselves to the wild policy of the Government which is embalmed in the Bill at present before the committee. It is made to appear as if members were retrograde because they dare offer some mild criticism as regards the wisdom of this policy. Sir,
I could find in the city of Toronto some of the highest financial authorities opposed to this very policy, and they are the best friends of the Government. My hon. friend (Sir Thomas White) said a moment ago that the Opposition was not a unit on this subject. Is the Government of Canada a unit on this question? Let me ask the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell); let me ask my good friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) if

they are as keen as their colleagues for Government ownership. No, Mr. Speaker. We have at heart the interests of Canada, and we are all proud as the the hon. gentleman (Sir Thomas White) stated a moment ago, of the part that Canada and our boys have taken in this war; and the greatest homage that can be paid to those who have survived the great war is for us to serve the country to the best of our judgment and according to out conscience.
In my humble judgment and according to my conscience, the policy of the Government is a dangerous policy, and I speak having regard to the best interests of the country. It is launching the country into a gulf from which it may not emerge., To-day it is a receivership of one of our railway systems. Later on, as is predicted in many reviews and newspapers it may be a receivership for Canada. I do not care for such receivership, Mr. Chairman. 1 want to remain a Canadian. A country may be lost through the economic errors and fallacies of some of its statesmen as well as on the battlefield. Many of our great industrial establishments, many of our railways, many of our commercial institutions in Canada are more or less in the grip of American finance. When this country has no more credit to back its undertakings, I say to my hon. friend: God help Canada and God save Canada. It is all very well for the Acting Prime Minister to come here and deliver orations on a plain question of facts and figures. The facts and figures are staring my hon. friend (Sir Thomas White) in the face. He knows that this country is debtor to-day to an inconceivable amount-nearly two billion dollars. He knows that the credit of our country stands in the balance seriously impaired. He knows that the eyes of the financial world where we have launched loan after loan are fixed on Canada. My friend invites us to have faith and hope. I have faith and I have hope, but I like to have a little common sense with my faith and hope.
Mr. II. A. MACKIE: I rise to a point of order, but before raising the point I wish to state my position in this matter because I feel somewhat under the lash. I took exception to clause 20 this afternoon and I propose to renew my objection until I am satisfied that I am wrong. The hon. member for Maisonneuve started something which I am sure he did not anticipate would lead to the discussion we have reached at this stage. None of the speakers up to the present time have really discussed clause 20, but they have rather

discussed the Government's policy of public ownership. So far as I am concerned, I was in favour of public ownership before private ownership forced the Government to adopt public ownership, and so expressed myself in the province of Alberta, from which I come. My address before this House last session leaves no room for doubt where I stand on that policy. I am entirely in accord with the remarks made by the Acting Prime Minister and also in accord with the remarks made by the hon. member for Red Deer, so far as the spirit of the West is concerned. But it is peculiar what different angles may arise in the discussion of this Bill, and how in one view I may be condemned by the members of the Unionist Government, and how in another view I can partially support the attitude of the Opposition. My objection to clause 20 may be exemplified by a resolution of the Railway Committee of the Edmonton Board of Trade. The territory which is to be traversed by the proposed Bruederheim-Vermilion line is threatened to be invaded by the Canadian Pacific, a private-owned company. The people of Edmonton do not want that territory to be invaded by the Canadian Pacific Railway, and consequently they desire that the location of the Canadian Northern shall be changed to such an extent as to make it impossible for the Canadian Pacific Railway to come into that territory at all. This is what the Railway Committee of tlhe Edmonton Board of Trade has to say on that subject:-
The more consideration that we give to thiis .proposition the more convinced do we become that it is a tremendously serious menace to Edmonton's trade. The road from Cut Knife goes into territory between the C.N.R. main line and the Saskatchewan river. That country is already fairly well settled and is producing heavily in the way of live stock, and present conditions of transportation are not conducive to grain farming, and the country will probably always remain principally a live stock country. The trade of that territory properly belongs to the Government system, which should develop it by something like the old proposed Bruederheim Line, and which they should perhaps bring a little farther north than the projected route of that line, and which should possibly continue eastward instead of turning down to Vermilion.
Now, by clause 20 the Bruederheim-Vermilion charter is renewed, and I have no means of hating that charter amended so .that the location of the proposed Canadian Northern line can be changed, except by blocking the Estimate which the Government brings down for the purpose of constructing this branch line. My position therefore is this:	The Governeroment has brought down to-day, very
suddenly, on the suggestion of one of the members of the Opposition a list of forty-four charters, and we are called upon suddenly to criticise each and every one of these charters without the assistance of solicitors or experienced railway men who have projected these proposed lines; and if the Bill goes through, the second schedule to the Act, which is incorporated in clause 20, will become law without the members of this House having a fair opportunity of discussing each and every one of these charters. I am willing to support the Government in everything that is reasonable, but I am not prepared to become ,a servile follower of the Government or of any minister of the Crown who tells me that I must follow a line of conduct which my conviction tells me I should not. We .are not given a fair opportunity of discussing these various charters. Ilf it were of any use I might suggest, Mr. Chairman, that there are good reasons for being suspicious of the whole Bill. I might suggest, for instance, that Mr. Lash who framed the Bill was formerly a Mackenzie and Mann employee. I might suggest that the counsel, Mr. Ruel, now sitting on the floor of this House, was once -in the employ, of Mackenzie and Mann, and is now in the employ of the Government. To strengthen the suspicion of the Opposition and others I might suggest that the same .counsel at the time he was receiving pay .from Mackenzie and Mann was advisory counsel to Mr. Tilley in the investigation which awarded $10,000,000 to Mackenzie and Mann.
There are circumstances, Mr. Chairman, which do justify to a certain extent our suspicions of this Bill, and particularly when we find some of the personnel of Mackenzie and Mann employed in connection with it at the present time. ^But I am not urging these things at all, I am urging the fact that the Government has brought about an amendment to section 20 of the Act without giving hon. members an opportunity of considering it. Now, I raise my point of order, which is that the minister, in moving the amendment to section 20, has changed the character of the Bill and that this Committee has no power to pass a Bill differing in principle from that which was adopted on the second reading.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Has any hon. member anything to say on the point of order before the decision of the Chair is given? The point of order raised is that the minister in introducing the amendment has completely changed the character and prin-

ciple of a Bill as adopted on the second reading. The. amendment appears to be merely a restriction of clause 20. Clause 20 in the Bill as voted upon during its second reading contained the following words:
The times for the commencement and completion of the construction of any lines of railway which any of the companies comprised in the Canadian Northern System were authorized to construct, which had not expired at the beginning of the war, in August, nineteen hundred and fourteen, are hereby extended for two years and five years respectively after the passing of this Act.
The amendment restricts clause 20 to the lines of railways specified in the second schedule to this Act. It is therefore a restriction and not a change in the principle of the Bill. May, at page 370 says:
Amendments may he made in every part of the Bill, whether in the preamble, the clauses or the schedules; clauses may he omitted and new clauses and schedules added. . . .
On the same page, I find the only exceptions to be as follows:
Amendments cannot he moved which are based on schedules or other provisions, the terms of which have not been placed before the Committee. Amendments are out of order if they are irrelevant to the Bill, or beyond its scope; governed by or dependent upon amendments already negatived; inconsistent with or contradictory to, the Bill as agreed to by 'the Committee; inconsistent with a decision to which the Committee has come upon a former amendment or offered at a wrong place in the Bill.
Bourinot, page 523, says:
The rules of the English Commons provide that any amendment may be made to a clause provided the same be relevant to the subject matter of the Bill, or pursuant to any instructions, and be otherwise in conformity with the Rules and Orders of the House.
In view of these authorities, I rule that the amendment is in order.
Would not the point of order be well taken if we raised the question of the discussion of the principle of the Bill on section 20 after the second reading has gone by?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
A point of order concerning the scope of the discussion would be worthy of more consideration. The debate has not always been strictly relevant to clause 20 which is under discussion before the Committee. The matter has been considered by the Clerk Assistant and myself several times during the afternoon. In view of the scope of the clause and the fact that it relates to the construction of a large number of branch lines extending over the entire western portion of Canada, [Mr. Chairman.[
we have come to the conclusion that the discussion of the public or private ownership of these lines is in order.

Mr. Chairman, I
rise for one purpose and one purpose only. It is not my intention to go back to ancient history and relate what has taken place in this country with regard to railway construction and various other railway matters. I take part in the discussion only because of certain words uttered by the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White). I want to clear up, in my own way, certain misunderstandings under which some people seem to labour. There are gentlemen, the Acting Prime Minister told us in so many words to-night, who seem to believe that to be a Liberal one has to be for nationalization. Liberalism is not socialism, either state or any other kind. Liberalism stands for liberty-liberty of the subject, liberty of speech, liberty of action, liberty of commerce. Liberalism stands for freedom and competition in all lines and spheres. Those who believe that nationalization means necessarily liberty and freedom are mistaken. In many respects it is the very opposite of liberty. Its purpose is to kill competition and erect a bureaucratic state.
That is what they did in Germany.

That is what was done in Germany. But that is not Liberalism; that is state socialism; that is the beginning of Bolshevism-let my Tory friends on the other side not be mistaken about that. I believe that a free trader cannot consistently be in favour of the nationalization of industry.
Oh, oh.

There are gentlemen who speak on certain questions who do not take the trouble to study them. Let my friends read the works of the great freetrader, Yves Guyot; he is against nationalization. Protection prevents freedom of trade and competition in trade. State nationalization prevents freedom of competition in those industries which are subject to it. Do you think that the republicans and radicals of France are lesser Liberals than my hon. friend the Acting Prime Minister and the Toronto magnates who are associated with him?
Sir, the French Liberals at the present time have taken full advantage of the way in which the state has substituted itself for private enterprise and industry during

the war in all directions, and they have just formed an association called " The League of Free Men," to vindicate the rights of private citizens as against the state. Nationalism is a great problem. I do not blame anybody for advocating it, I confess to have an open mind with respect to it, but I deny to any man the right to say that a Liberal has to favour Sifton-I beg the committee's pardon, this is the word that comes naturally when we speak about it; has to favour the system-if he wants to remain true to his principles. Certain gentlemen in this country have queer ideas about Liberalism and Liberal principles, and what Liberalism stands for.
Hear, hear.
Who says " hear, hear?"
We all do.

My friend from Regina (Mr. Cowan) is certainly a good authority to speak for Liberalism. I read quite recently in the Toronto Globe that to be a Liberal a man must stand for prohibition. I am sure the member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) as well as myself will not accept such an absurd theory. Any man has the right to advocate prohibition, but that is not Liberalism. That is the rumour which the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) has circulated in the province of Ontario, but it is not true. Prohibition is a restrictive policy, whereas Liberalism stands for personal liberty of the subject. A Liberal allows his fellows to differ with him on public questions. He is a queer Liberal indeed who believes that he embodies in himself the essence of Liberalism and Liberal ideals. Sir, I claim to be a Liberal in the clear sense and meaning of the word, and I deny the right of the Acting Prime Minister and those who are associated with him to give me any lecture on Liberalism. Needless to say I shall not accept such lectures from him or his associates.

It is not my intention to follow my hon. friend (Mr. Ernest Lapointe) in a discussion of theoretic Liberalism. The hon. gentleman has explained Liberalism as it was expounded in England some fifty years ago. At that time Liberalism was a struggle for freedom, a struggle for religious, economic, and personal liberty. But with the changes that have since come about, due to the development of modern industry, the growth of corporations, the large development of life in the cities, progressive Liberalism has felt compelled to change the point upon which it places emphasis. Progressive Liberalism in England, and in every other country where it touches the social conditions of the people, has felt compelled not to increase personal liberty, but to restrict the power of the strong for the protection of the weak. Modern legislation which the Liberal party of Great Britain placed upon the Statute Books has been legislation to curb the power of the strong, to restrict the power of the great, to control and regulate trade, industry, and commerce, in order that the individual toiler who wa3 unequal to competition in a free, unfettered field, such as my friend (Mr. Lapointe) suggests should be granted-should be protected against the oppression of the strong, whether it be corporate power or large organizations of wealth, and that there should be thrown round him safeguards which would give him a fair chance in life under decent living conditions. So Liberalism has introduced all those great measures of social legislation which have been so characteristic of the administration of which Mr. Lloyd George was such a distinguished ornament, and of which Mr. Asquith was the Prime Minister.
What I rose to refer to was one or two observations of the hon. member from Mais-onneuve (Mr. Lemieux). If I rightly understood his objection to clause 20 of the Bill it was based on two grounds: First, that the proposal to grant an extension of the charters involved an expenditure of public money which Canada at the present time was not in a position to undertake, and second, he doubted the wisdom of public ownership in any case and quoted from Lord Shaughnessy and other authorities on the matter as evidence that it was not a wise policy for us to pursue. Now, first as to the question of the expenditure involved. My hon. friend knows, as all the members of the House know, for it was repeated time and again this afternoon, that this clause does not involve one dollar of public expenditure; the House may vote the money when the time comes if it sees fit to do so. All that the clause does is to extend the period during which these charters may be acted upon, and these branch lines may be built, just as the usual extension to private railways is granted by the Railway Committee of the House, and approved by the House from year to year. Therefore, my hon. friend's contention in that regard fails. He is too good, and too old, a Parliamentarian not to know that there is no just ground for opposition to the Bill on that score. But

in that connection I was surprised when my hon. friend made the statement he did with reference to the credit of Canada. I would remind him that if the situation be as he states-I am glad to think it is not-he is not rendering Canada good service when he rises here as one of the leaders of the people and suggests, on the basis of some magazine article, that the next receivership will be a receivership of the Dominion of Canada. The hon. gentleman knows that there is no country in the world to-day that has come through the war better than Canada has done. All the countries of the world have an enormous burden of debt to carry, but we have come through it probably better than any other country. Certainly no country, unless it be the United States, is in a better position than we are. We have borne the burden in this war in an astonishing manner. As a matter of fact, while the public debt is very heavy, while the public debt is such that we should not unnecessarily increase it, the increased wealth of the people of Canada is greater in excess of the increased public debt. The people of Canada to-day are better off than when the war broke uot.
Will the minister explain what he means by increased wealth? In what way have we accumulated more substantial wealth?
The physical assets of the Canadian Northern.

The millions of money
which have come-into this country and have been spent here for munitions, for all other war supplies, and for food supplies, have added to the wealth of the people of Canada -the money that has come in from the Government of Great Britain, and from other Governments also. My hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) has not done Canada a service by making such a suggestion in reference to our financial position.
Coming to the other point to which the hon. gentleman referred, the question of public ownership, his address has simply made still clearer, if it was necessary to do that, the real situation behind the opposition to this Bill. My hon. friend has clearly stated that he is not in favour of public ownership; at least he holds that he is not bound to commit himself to it, but all of his arguments were against public ownership. And the situation, therefore is this, those who believe in private ownership as against public ownership are entirely opposed to

the Bill; but the people who either believe in public ownership because there is no other course open to us-we have the railways on our hands-or who believe in public ownership because they think it is the right thing in the public interest, are in favour of the Bill, and on that issue the hon. members supporting this Government have no hesitation in taking their stand. My hon. friend quotes from the experience in the United States. How does that help us? We have the railways on our hands, as the Acting Prime Minister has pointed out, and we have either to operate them, or turn them over to another company to operate, and the only other company left to do it is the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I believe the only thing to do is to go forward and operate these railways and make them the greatest success possible. How are we going to operate them successfully and justify public ownership in this country? We can only do it by developing them along the same lines as a private corporation would develop them-by constructing the necessary feeders through the country so the main line may have the traffic which these feeders bring in. Everybody recognizes that there are strong and powerful interests in this country opposed to public ownership. Would my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) expect the ex-President of the. Canadian Pacific Railway Company to be in favour of public ownership? My hon. friend quotes him, and undoubtedly he is an exceedingly able man, but you would not expect him to be an authority on the question. My hon. friend quotes him against it; of course, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company are opposed to public ownership.

What I quoted from Lord Shaughnessy was not an opinion opposed to public ownership, but what he said at the opening of the Canadian National Exhibition at Toronto, that before embarking on public ownership the country ought to be sure of its footing, and should .wait until the experiment of the United States was known.

Mr. Chairman, all I can say is that Lord Shaughnessy stated his position on public ownership more diplomatically than my hon. friend did this afternoon when he referred to the western Prime Ministers.
There is nothing wrong about it. I am against public ownership; I have stated so.

There is nothing wrong about it?
10 p.m. Mr. BUREAU: Certainly not.
But we want to know that the issue is clear and plain: public ownership as opposed to private ownership.
What has that to do with the Bill?
It appears to have a great deal to do with the opposition to the Bill.

I rise to a point of order, Mr. Chairman. As far as I am concerned and as far as I know it has had nothing to do with the opposition to the Bill. The minister is insinuating that members on this side are actuated by motives other than those that should actuate them-or are influenced by the Canadian Pacific Railway, to put it in plain words.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not know what may be in the mind of my hon. friend from Three Rivers, but it is absolutely impossible for the Chairman to impute motives to the hon. member.

I say the minister is imputing improper motives to the Opposition when he says the question of public ownership as against private ownership has influenced the attitude of hon. members on this side of the House. Our criticism of the Bill is not founded upon any hostility to public ownership.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is certainly not a point of order.
All right; go to it.

I do not question the right of any hon. member to oppose public ownership if he does not believe in it. It is his duty to oppose public ownership in that case and his position is perfectly consistent. On the other hand whether one believes in public ownership or not, we have the railways on our hands and we must operate them. But I go further, I "believe in public ownership of this railway system, and therefore I am a hearty supporter of the Bill. I was proceeding to say that there are in the country undoubtedly influential forces opposed to public ownership. They have been opposed to the Government taking over the Grand Trunk, they have been opposed to the Government interfering with the Grand Trunk Pacific and have said we should not do so. In order to make public ownership a real success, I venture to submit, Mr. Chairman, it is the
duty of the Government to acquire or develop such a complete transportation system throughout this Dominion that it can fairly compete with the Canadian Pacific Railway on something like equal terms. Therefore it is not only the duty of the Government to go ahead and take authority for the construction of the necessary branch lines, but to complete and round up the system by acquiring the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk. Then we will have a system of transportation able to compete with the Canadian Pacific Railway. The position of hon. members on this side of the House in supporting this Bill is that it is a necessary measure in order that the best results should be secured in the operation of the system of railways which the Government of Canada owns and which it must operate.
Does the hon. member believe that this company we are creating should be allowed to start out with a free hand? If so, why does he want to foist upon that company forty-four wrecks?

I am dealing with the section, which is simply for the purpose of extending the life of the existing charters which had expired during the period of the war, to enable the company to construct the roads covered by them. The company must come to the House for the money; my hon. friend knows it cannot undertake any construction in the absence of that.
No, there are Orders in Council.

The money has not yet been granted for the construction of those roads, and the company must come to the House for it. My hon. friend referred to the position of the Western Provinces and the relation of Mackenzie and Mann to them; that is all connected with private ownership. I believe that one of the strongest reasons for public ownership in this country is the experience we have had with private ownership o-f railways. That is one of the reasons why I support the public ownership of these railways. One has only to travel through Western Canada and see the rival railways running side by side for hundreds of miles through territory that could only support one line, to realize that there is no justification or excuse for such a waste of public money, that it is a crime to waste public money in this way. That was all done under private ownership. I believe that private ownership of railways has helped to bedevil the public life of this country,



and that is another reason why I want to see a strong state-owned and operated railway system in this country. I am quite prepared to concede if you like, for the sake of argument, that a railway may not be run as economically and efficiently by the Government as by a private corporation, but I would rather that it should be run a little less efficiently and economically so long as it is owned by the people of Canada and operated in their interests rather than owned and operated in the interests of a private corporation.

Because hon. members on this side are not absolutely satisfied with all the clauses of this Bill, would the minister say that they are necessarily opposed to the principle of public ownership? Because, if so, I desire to protest against such an assertion I am just as much a public ownership mdn as any hon. member in this House, and I would go a little further-I would also acquire not only the lame ducks hut the Canadian Pacific Railway as well.

I would not think of
suggesting anything of the kind. The clauses of the Bill should be discussed on their merits, each and every one of them. The hon. member for Maisonneuve, to whom I rose to reply, based his opposition on the grounds which I am answering, and on which I say I am opposed to him and on which I join issue. I stand for public ownership and operation of this railway system, expanded and enlarged until it is made a thoroughly complete system able to compete- on equal terms with the Canadian Pacific Railway.

Will the hon. minister answer my question? We are putting a Bill through this Committee that empowers a body of the ablest railway men we can get to build railways anywhere in Canada. They have authority under this Act to build over every inch of the ground included in those forty-four charters. Why do we encumber this new institution with those wrecks? Because we on this side are opposed to this wreckage being thrown upon the country, we are told that we are opposed to public ownership and to any progress in the West. That assertion is nonsensical, it is without a shadow of truth, and I hurl it back into the teeth of any man who chooses to fling it across the floor of the (House.
Which of the clauses that have been adopted gives the power suggested by my hon. friend?
Every part of the Bill.

We are going through
this Bill clause by clause; which clause that we have passed in Committee gives the power that my hon. friend suggests?

We were given to understand by the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) that this Bill, together with the Railway Act, confers all the power that the company and the Government require to build railways throughout the country. If that is not true, it is not my fault.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman was given to understand nothing of the sort. We come to clause 23 later-and I may add that it is proposed to offer an amendment to clause 23. That has already been made known to the Committee. No clause which has been passed gives the power the hon. gentleman describes, and he ought to know that. I think he does.

This Bill gives power to expropriate lands for the purposes of the beds of railways; what is that for? Does the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid), who knows so much about railways that he does not know whether he'has a manager or not, or if so, what the manager's salary is,-does he tell us that we have been discussing for hours all the machinery necessary to the acquirement of rights of way from the Atlantic to the Pacific, but that the Bill does not enable us to build the roads?
The hon. member knows that we were discussing expropriation after the charter had been granted by this Parliament.

This Bill must be taken as a whole; we cannot read one clause and put another aside. Section 23 gives the company, with the approval of the Governor in Council, power to construct and operate railway lines.
I said yesterday that when we came to- that clause I intended to amend it.
But the clause is in the Bill and we have to consider the Bill as a whole.
We have not reached it yet.

We have not reached it, but must we pass all the preceding sections without giving consideration to the power conferred by section 23? When we consider a given section we may go beyond

it to see what the Bill says; we do not have to accept the dictum of the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell). I will not do it, anyway.
Read section 23, so that the Committee may know what it contains.

This is section 23:
With the approval of the Governor in Council and upon any location sanctioned by the (Minister of Railways and Canals, the Company may from time to time construct and operate railway lines, branches and extensions, or railway facilities or properties of any description. A copy of any plan and profile made in respect of any completed railway shall be deposited with the Board of Railway Commissioners of Canada.
The Acting Prime Minister, in his remarks this evening, either departed from his usual custom or tried to put up a little bluff on the Committee and to scare us from discussing this Bill. I resent the imputation cast upon members on this side that they were opposing the Bill because they were opposed to public ownership. So far as I am concerned, that is absolutely false. I happen to be against public ownership. I stated on the second reading that I was against it; that I was in favour of private ownership and public control. I am just as good a patriot as the Acting Prime Minister and I am as loyal as the President of the Council. My loyalty is not on my lips alone and is not for political purposes alone. I am loyal because I have no other country but this country, because I have no love to send across the ocean or to give to any other part of the world than Canada, where I stand the eighth generation. It makes me sick when I hear the Acting Prime Minister appeal to our loyalty to pass this Bill. Are we to sit here as dummies to prove our loyalty? Are we to take for granted everything that comes from the Government? No, not when we remember the fight of 1917; not when we think of how this Government came to power and how it is holding itself in power. Instead of being rebuked because we criticize legislation that is brought down, we should be congratulated. "No men who can be influenced by outside interests when they discuss public measures here should accuse others of being prompted by any other interest than the interest of their fellow-countrymen. When I get up to speak in this House I get up to speak my mind and discuss questions as I conceive them, and no power on earth shall prevent me from doing so; it is the only liberty left to us on this side of the House. We may be mistaken, but when we are mistaken we
llli
are honestly mistaken, we are not mistaken as the result of calculations or as the result of machinations which might bring ,to us some benefit or even the hope of benefit. I am not going to discuss the relative values of public ownership and private ownership. The Acting Prime Minister tried this afternoon to describe those who did not share his opinions as private ownership people, as people dangerous to the country, as disloyal people. But I have stated my position, and am not ashamed of it. When men in Parliament have no more right to think for themselves and to .express their views, it is high time we dissolved Parliament. We shall be on the eve of Bolshevism when that comes.
The Acting Prime Minister tried to besmirch the policy of his predecessor. He said that when he came to power he found on the door-step of the Department of Finance two dirty babies. That may have been.
We find more than that.

If he had been logical
he would have fired the nurse who had not taken care of those babies. He would have said:	I am going to change this; I
want clean ones; let us clean this baby and make it as it ought to be. But what does he do? He tips the nurse and says: I am going to do better; I am going to give you better treatment; II am going to increase your wages-but I do not care about the dirty baby; let him rot in his dirt. If I came home and found my children not properly taken care of by the nurse, I would fire the nurse and get a better one. Now, I will be candid:
This was, I think, only a bluff on the part of the Acting Prime Minister-pulling the wool over the eyes of the people. The Government know that they have before the committe a poor Bill, a Bill that they cannot explain, a Bill that contradicts itself in a good many clauses-I will not say in every clause-a Bill that we did not oppose because it was vesting in a company power to administer Canadian Government railways but which, ever since it wras brought before the House, we have been trying to word so that the company can be properly administered. This is not a question of deciding policies. !We are saddled with these railways; they have to be administered, and we have given the best of our time and ability to framing a Bill which will give the best results in administering and operating those roads. What we have been afraid of, and rightly so, has been that

politics will not be taken out of the Bill. What we have been fighting for is to vest in Parliament a little more power and to take from the Governor in Council some of the powers which are proposed to be granted by this Bill. I do not think we can be reproached on that account. Some hon. members on your right, Mr. Chairman, may think it is proper that the Governor in Council should run the country, and that Parliament should be convened simply to ratify Orders in Council. We on this side of the House do not think so; we think this country should be run by Parliament and that the administrative part delegated by Parliament to the Government should be taken care of by the Government. Surely we can differ on those questions without its being said that one side possesses all the ignorance and the know-nothings and that the other side is all-powerful and allknowing, able to do everything. I do not believe that; I think God has been kind enough and good enough to endow every man in this world with a little something called brains, and that all the brains are not on the other side of the House. Thanks be to God, there are some brains on this side of the House, and outside of this House also.
On the second reading, I stated that I was against public ownership, my reason being, concisely, experience both with the Intercolonial and in the United States. Last year we were taking our cues from the United States-we had to change our standard of cement; we had to change our standard of weights and measures, because the United States were changing theirs. If those cues were good enough last year, prudence ought to teach us to follow the example of the United States when they have had the experience they have had with public ownership.
I hope to-night, whatever our opinions may be as regards public or private ownership, we shall continue to devote our time to the consideration of the clauses of the Bill. Again I repeat, every time I have risen from my seat has been not for the purpose of opposing the Bill because I am against public ownership, but for the purpose of endeavouring, if possible, to improve the Bill and to protect* the interest of the people, and so much so, that one of my amendments has been adopted by the Acting Prime Minister who thought it was better, although before he thought it was of no importance. . Since then I have met people outside of this House who also thought it was better.

Section 20 provides that all the roads mentioned in Schedule 2, whose charters have expired because they have not been commenced or completed within the time fixed, shall, in some cases, have their charters extended, but mostly revived. What I said was that I had no objection to reviving a charter or to granting an extension of five years for those roads upon which work had been commenced. I also stated that it was not just to grant a revival of a charter without the parties interested or the residents of the territory through which the railway was proposed to be run having an opportunity of being heard before the Railway Committee, or the parties granting the extension. My objection was immediately corroborated by the hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. H. A. Mackie) stating that there was a road, the location of which ought, in his opinion, to be changed. The Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) replied to him: If you want to change the location of the road, you will have to get a new charter. I replied to that: If you should get a new charter for a road to run in the same territory, would it not be fair to cancel . the original charter? As the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) said just now there would then be none of the duplication of railways, two roads running side by side spoken of by the President of the Council. Is there anything unfair in that? Supposing public opinion and public necessity in the part of the country where a deviation of the road was required further than is allowed by the Railway Act without permission being received from Parliament or new plans being filed-or a new charter, being obtained-if you will and some persons applied for a new charter and showed that they were ready to build the road in a part of the country where it would be required, would it not be fair to cancel the old charter, or let it expire, let it die a natural death, and give an opportunity for building, under the new charter, a road which would be promoted by private interests to serve the better, more populous and richer part of the country? I do not see any disloyalty in that. That is how the whole discussion arose this afternoon.
The ministers say: We cannot*go on with the construction of those roads without getting permission from Parliament, and when the estimates are brought down to the House, honourable members can voice their objections. The honourable member for East Edmonton (Mr. H. A. Mackie) objected to that, because there were in

those charters certain points which would require changes; and when an item is put into the estimates, the charter cannot be discussed or changed; all one can do is to say:	I vote against the estimate because
the construction of a line in that particular locality is not required. The better way to serve the public interest and that of the people in the West would be to give them an opportunity to say what lines are of most imperative and immediate necessity and to make any objections or suggestions they wish. Other companies have to make an application to Parliament, to come before the Railway Committee and to go through the usual routine, and anybody who has an objection to offer may cite it. This afternoon I cited a case which brought about the biggest fight there ever was in the Railway Committee. I refer to the Canadian Northern, this very company, and Mr.- Sir Adam Beck, I ought to say, because titles are still under the consideration of the committee-that makes the President of the Council (.Mr. Rowell) smile, I suppose before we get through with this session or before the Committee reports, I shall have the pleasure of calling him "Sir" also.

I am afraid the hon.
member will be disappointed.

The question was, if I
remember rightly, whether the Canadian Northern or the Hydro-Electric Company, should have priority of right of way on a piece of land. The Hydro-Electric declared: We will give the Canadian Northern right of way if we have priority, and the Canadian Northern said:	We will give the Hydro-
Electric right of way if we have priority. Such things may happen at any time, and it is unfair to revive a charter which is extinct, when no work has been done on the line, without giving an opportunity to the parties interested and the people in the district through which the line is to pass, an opportunity of voicing their opinions. I am willing, however, to grant an extension of five years for any line that has been commenced.
