speechtext:
My hon. friend, I know, would not like to leave the House under any mistaken impression. The report of the commission to which he referred declared that the state of things of which he com-[Mr. Sinclair.}
plains had obtained ever since the institution of the Bureau and during the regime of successive 'Governments since then.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: I did not state that the Bureau was not inefficient during the term of the former Government, I do not know that, but it is certainly inefficient at the present time, and this Government has been in power long enough to make it efficient. If my hon. friend (Mr. Burrell) is in charge of the Bureau it has done him very little credit. If he had the courage to appoint a competent foreman at the Bureau, told him to dismiss every man that could not do his work, and replace them with efficient employees, and make that foreman responsible for getting the work done, he would not have any trouble, but he has not the courage to do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: I think my hon. friend does not wish to do me an injustice, and therefore he will permit me to interrupt him and make this remark: I would say that practically within the first two months of coming into charge of the Printing Bureau I did what has never been done, placed this matter in the hands of the Civil Service Commission, who, under the Act which empowered them to carry out a re-organization, appointed the commission referred to, the idea being that the time had come when the Bureau should be reorganized, and this process is now under operation.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
I am very much pleased to hear that my hon. friend has awakened and is going to do something. I do hope he will be successful. All the same he would have done better if he had placed the Bureau under a competent foreman. I was speaking of the matter of government ownership of ships, and pointing out how important it is that we should have efficiency and good management if we are going to adopt the policy of government ownership. The vessel to which I have referred was launched, speeches were made on the occasion, and we were told that she was to be the pioneer ship and that a great development in Canadian trade would be the result. A private owner would have taken . that vessel down the river St. Lawrence before the ice formed and winter set in, but what did the Government do? They sent her down to the city of Quebec and she lay there from the date she was launched in November until about the middle of January. She was fitted out with groceries and supplies in Quebec and lay there until the river was frozen over and filled with ice.

She was then despatched down the river, but only got as far as Father Point, when she was stuck in the ice. The Government sent the Montcalm down to extricate her and the Montcalm also got stuck. Then the Canada was sent to the relief of both vessels, and she got to within fifteen miles of the others when she stuck fast also. A request was then made that the Prince Edward Island ferry should be sent up and liberate the three steamers from the ice, but the Railway Department very wisely refused to accede to the request. However, a storm came and broke up the ice and freed the vessels, and the Voyageur finally arrived in Halifax, where she lay in a damaged condition and finally had to go into dock to be repaired. The other day, when we asked what s'he was doing and where she was located, we were told she was engaged in carrying sugar at a very low rate of freight to New York to help the refiners there to compete with the refiners of Nova Scotia, Montreal, and elsewhere throughout Canada. The Government also informed us that they had purchased another steamer called the McKee. We were anxious to know whether the McKee was engaged in developing Canadian trade or not, and made inquiry. What did we find? We found that the McKee had been sent to carry coal from New York to the west coast of South America, to Chile, for an American Arm, and that she is going to take back fertilizer to New York, being chartered by the month. That is the way in which the Government is developing Canadian trade. We are expending fifty millions this coming year in building ships, we are told for the purpose of developing Canadian trade, and the start that the Government has made in that direction is in the manner I have described.
That shows that Government ownership in the hands of an inefficient government may be a great, handicap instead of a benefit to the business of the country.
We are proposing to unite in one system four great lines of railway-the Intercolonial, the Transcontinental the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern, involving an enormous expenditure of money. What is the Government's idea of the management of that great system? They are handing it over to a man (Mr. Hanna) who made a complete failure of the Canadian Northern system. He and his associates succeeded in getting a lot of money out of the people of Canada through the Government of the day, but they made a wreck of the enterprise in the end. And
the reasoning of the Government seems to be this: That having failed in managing one railway, we will hand over to this man and his associates four railways forming one of the largest railway systems in the world, and we will put that system under their control. The advice of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition was absolutely sound, that we clear up the old wreck altogether, that we get a new name for this system, and place it under new management. Is not that a reasonable proposal after the experience the country has had for the past twenty years of the Mackenzie and Mann people? Why do the Government refuse to follow that advice? Is it possible that my hon. friend the leader of the Government is still doubtful of the success of government ownership? Is he looking forward to the people of Canada becoming so disgusted with public ownership after a few years under such management that the old team will get the property back again? Is that his plan? A few years ago he was not in favour of government ownership. He is a recent convert, I believe, of my hon. friend from South York. He went to see him at night, like Nicodemus, and my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) converted him in a kind of way to government ownership, but he seems to be as reluctant as Nicodemus was to be born again, and I do not believe his heart is in this proposal of government ownership. He is said to have told his friends in Toronto some years ago that those Governments which were taking away from private interests the things that belonged to them were adopting the methods of that old Hebrew tyrant, King Ahab, who expropriated Naboth's vineyard. I do not know whether he has changed his real sentiments or not since he joined his present associates and got his legs under Jezebel's mahogany. Perhaps he may think so still, but that is a matter I would not venture to express an opinion on. However, it looks very suspicious when we see the Government insisting on so much control by the old Canadian Northern Railway management of this new system that we are now proposing to set up.
Now, what would a private concern do if they purchased a bankrupt company? Would they continue the old management? Take the two Ontario banks that are being wound up at the present time, to the sorrow of their stockholders. Would the liquidators maintain in control those who wrecked those banks? I say no, they would do nothing of the kind.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext:

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it has been said that the debate has turned on the question of public ownership of railways. If the advocates of public ownership were to be counted in this House, we would have to come to this side to find a goodly number. Nineteen years ago when we were advocating the further extension of the Intercolonial Railway with a view to extending the principle of Government operation, we were handicapped by the then Opposition, composed chiefly of members from Ontario, every one ol whom was opposed to Government ownership of railways except my hon. friend from South York, who since then appears to have made some converts in his province. During the twenty years that I have been a member of this House, and for twenty years before that time, I have advocated that the Government of Canada instead of paying out money to private interests to build railways should undertake the work itself for the benefit of our people. We have paid excessive bonuses and made extravagant grants of land to railway promoters, and if we had retained those moneys and lands we could have built the railroads and Canada would today be in a better position than she is after her experience of private ownership.
The province of New Brunswick gave a quarter of its timber lands to a provincial company to build a railroad crossing the southern part of the province, and that grant has been a hindrance to the prosperity and development of the province ever since. We gave millions of acres of land to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for tne construction of their very prosperous line, hat I might remind this House that if the Government had now in the treasury the millions of dollars which the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has for the last twenty-five or thirty years realized upon those lands we would be able to build the Canadian Pacific railway and make it an equally prosperous undertaking, provided we had as economical managers as those who have been in control of that company up to the present time, if my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior had to-day in his possession the lands which, are still in the possession of the Canadian Pacific, he would be able to provide for the settlement of every one of our Canadian soldiers, and so give them the chances they are looking for to-day.

I was most amazed when on Friday a couple of hon. members on the other side of the House passed reflections upon hon. members on this side and suggested that we were opposed to nationalization of railroads, although every one of my hon. friends opposite had been opposed to the principle until very recently; they have been converted, they say, by the necessities of the day. We have heard the hon. member for Springfield-whom I regret not to see in his place-say that he also had been advocating the principle of nationalization and that it was due to the maladministration of the Liberal party that railway affairs had come to such a pass-that, figuratively speaking, naked infants had been left on the doorstep of the Government and had to be taken care of. Yet, he himself in 1912, one year after the change of Government, was busy in Winnipeg seeking to bring the country under the rule of Liberal administration. I was amazed at the language of the Acting Prime Minister last Friday night when 1m attempted to defend his case, which he evidently found not sufficiently strong. The member for Springfield had referred 'to the children left in nakedness on the doorstep of the Government. The Acting Prime Minister, who generally uses fair and proper language to express his sentiments, went further and said that these were dirty, filthy babies. Evidently he had forgotten that previous to 1911 he, as well as the then leader of the Opposition and the members of the Conservative party, thought that these children were in a healthy condition and growing sturdy and strong. The best evidence of the prosperity of the country at that time, and therefore of the railroads, was the attitude taken by my hon. friend and the then leader of the Opposition when the Liberal leader and the Liberal party proposed a measure of reciprocity with the United States, with a view to providing greater freedom of trade for Canada. They said, " Do not touch it; let well enough alone ". My hon. friend saw those children then clothed with the mantle of prosperity; to-day he says that they are dirty, filthy babies. Hon. gentlemen opposite say this simply because it suits their own purposes. The Administration that succeeded that of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1911, in the course of two or three years, drew back the country from the state of prosperity which it had enjoyed for fifteen years and put it into a state of uncertainty and retrogression, back to the position in which h had been prior to 1896.

Hon. gentlemen say that the Intercolonial had produced deficits. But it must he remembered that in a country like Canada, with its thousands of miles of territory from one ocean to the other and from the United States to the Arctic, great lines of railway were necessary; and these could not be expected to pay from the start. Neither can we expect this new company immediately to put the railways of Canada in a paying position. But the development of the Intercolonial railway has been good not only for the Maritime Provinces, but for the western provinces as well. During the first years of its operation it was not developing very much the interests of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. It was carrying at cheaper rates the products of the manufacturers of Ontario and the We-t and taking care of trade that would other wise go through New York and Boston. Thus the Intercolonial railway has contributed to the prosperity of the whole of Canada. We do not expect this new corporation to produce immediate surpluses, but it is the nucleus of the nationalization of railroads and we on this side of the House desire that it be placed under the control of the people through the Parliament of Canada. The member for Kamour-aska( Mr. E. Lapointe) moved an amendment to the Bill which would have made the operation of these national railways more democratic in this time of democracy. But instead of trying to bring about more democracy in the administration of our railroads, hon. gentlemen opposite wish to establish an autocratic administration behind the curtain of democracy by placing this company outside the reach of the people. Another amendment was submitted to provide that one or two representatives of labour be on the directorate of the new corporation. But hon. gentlemen opposite professedly devoted to the public interest in the nationalization of public resources, could not see their way clear to accept this amendment. Can we not find in the ranks of labour, men with sufficient knowledge and ability to give the benefit of their experience to the other members of the directorate of this company? To have done this would add to the confidence of the people in the new corporation.
Hon. gentlemen say that we are opposed to the development of the West. I have always said, and I say i't again to-day, that no member of this House, no man in Canada, is more devoted to the development of Western Canada than the modest member for Gloucester. My heart and soul are in Western Canada. I am a member of this
Parliament, but I am also a citizen of Canada. We are not here to be sectional; we are here as Canadians to work for the good of Canada as a whole, and when we advocate the development of the resources of any part of the country it is with a view to the general benefit of Canada. In this Bill there is a list of forty-four charters which are to be renewed, and when we ask for information, it is said that we are against the advancement of the West; that we are not optimistic about the West. No one in Canada is a greater optimist as to the immense resources and future of Canada than I am. For some years before the war things had come to such a pass that the railroads, of which the minister to-day speaks so highly, had practically ceased operation, and one-half of their freight cars were stored away in the divisional points in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. In 1914, conditions became so disastrous that the Government, finding itself going down so fast, was about to take the plunge before the country rather than wait for another year, when war was declared which, from an economic standpoint, saved Canada for the Government. The moment the list of charters was brought before the Committee, the hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. H. A. Mackie) stated that the schedule included a charter for a railway in his constituency, the renewal of which charter might perhaps mean the ruin of that portion of Alberta. He wanted an amendment, but he could not have it; he was told simply that later on, when the Estimates came up, he could vote against the item. But if he voted against the Estimate, his county would be deprived of that line of railway. If he wanted the location of the railway changed, he would have to bring in a new charter, and consequently, there would be duplication. Speaking of duplications, the duplication that has brought Mackenzie and Mann to ruin is a duplication made by this Government from Edmonton to the Pacific coast, a duplication of over 700 miles of railway in the most difficult and expensive portion . of Canada for railway construction. That duplication was made directly after the Liberal Government had, in 1911, refused to grant permission to Mackenzie and Mann to duplicate the Grand Trunk Pacific from the same point to the Pacific coast, a duplication which would have diverted the trade of the Grand Trunk Pacific to the Canadian Northern, a trade, which, in the estimation of our late regretted leader, would not for years to come be sufficient

for two lines. If that duplication had not taken place, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Canadian Northern and the country would have been in a better position to-day, and the Grand Trunk Pacific would not have been in the hands of a receiver.

speechtext:
I should like to read this section:
The Governor in Council may declare that the company shall have a capital stock, with or without shares, to such amount as may from time to time be deemed expedient. All such stock shall, until otherwise ordered by the Governor in Council, be vested in the Minister of Finance on behalf of His Majesty.
It is closely connected with other clauses of the Bill, some of which have been passed. With clause 12, for instance, which grants power to transfer to the company the stock or controlling interest of His Majesty in any railway company; with clause 23, which grants power to construct and operate railway lines; with clause 26, regarding the issue of securities; and with clause 29, granting power to acquire securities of other companies. The Government are seeking very extended powers indeed for the Governor in Council, who may confer unlimited control on the directorate by order in council. I called the Government's attention to these wide powers when the resolution on which the Bill is founded was under discussion.
It seems to me unreasonable for the Government to ask power that the Governor in Council may declare that the company shall have a capital stock. The country will have to ipay for everything, and it seems almost ridiculous to ask for this power. In the second place, if this power is granted, there is no provision in the Bill determining the amount of capital stock which the Governor in Council may transfer to the company. I think this should be named in the Bill. As it is, succeeding clauses give the Governor in Council power to transfer this stock from the Minister of Finance, holding on behalf of His Majesty, to the company to any amount desired, and the company may do almost anything with the stock and with the moneys raised from its sale, transfer or hypothecation. They are given power, with the approval of the Governor in Coun-

cil, 'to construct and operate railway lines and so on. Clause 26 gives the company almost unlimited powers regarding the issue of securities. For these reasons I fail to see any necessity for the section we are now discussing; and even if the stock is granted, I contend that the amount should be named here. We know that the Canadian Northern was capitalized at $100,000,000, on a 60-40 basis, the Mackenzie and Mann interests getting 60 per cent and the people of this country the other 40 per cent. That is quite recent history, and every one knows that as a result of that arrangement this country has had to pay $10,800,000 to obtain possession of the company's holding, nowithstanding the fact that after a thorough investigation the stock itself was declared to be of no value whatever, and that for it not one cent had been paid by the holders.
I think we should incorporate in one section of the Bill the names of the directorate. At present we do not know to whom the management of this great company will be entrusted, and it is only fair that we should know. Extensive reference was made to this point in the press in the fall of 1918. We read in the Globe that the predecessor of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) declared that unless he had his way and secured the appointment he would tear things up by the roots, meaning, of course, that there was trouble in store for the Union Government if they did not carry out the arrangement made in the election campaign of 1917.
I might repeat what I said on Friday night regarding the references made by the leader of the House (Sir Thomas White) and some of his followers to hon. members on this side of the House, which references have been made again this afternoon. I want hon. gentlemen opposite to understand distinctly that they have no justification whatever for saying that we on this side of the House are opposed in any shape or form to public ownership of public utilities.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
I hate at this moment to speak under the regulations of closure. It reminds me of the modern history of some countries beyond the seas, where people are gagged and unable to speak when they wished. Mr. Chairman, we have spent only a few hours on this Bill, and in my judgment every minute employed has been time well spent, because this is a gigantic enterprise for Canada to undertake. We have been spending too much money on railroads and not enough on

harbours, and navigation, and forestry, and fisheries. Let me quote from an Ontario newspaper of 26th April, a despatch concerning a statement the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) made to an Ontario delegation which came to see him about harbour improvements:
Ottawa, Ont., April 26.-That Canada has devoted too much attention to railways and not enough to water transport and that "a horrible mess" has resulted, was the declaration of Hon. F. B. Carvell, .Minister of Public Works, yesterday afternoon. He was answering a delegation from the London district which asked for harbour improvements at Port Stanley and in the course of his remarks said: "I know of nothing in which we are justified in spending public moneys so much as in improving methods of transport and I have to say that heretofore water transportation has been neglected' entirely too much. We have gone ahead building railways and we have 'built too many. I am not saying who is to blame-the whole country probably is to blame. The result is a horrible mess and the Government is compelled to take over lines."
I think we have enough railways and that we should begin to develop other methods of transportation. We have to send our products out of Canada and in order to reach our markets we must have proper water transportation. We have a debt of probably $2,000,000,000, or $250 per capita; and there are 14,000 miles of railways that belong to the Dominion, or one mile to every 300 of the population. In view of these facts, is it not time that we seriously considered the importance of any measure involving the expenditure of large sums of money on further railway development? At one time I was in favour of public ownership of railways, tout my experience of the service rendered by Government-owned lines has been such as to compel me to change my view on this question, While travelling on a Government train one winter we were held up for a couple of hours at an inconvenient place, and in reply to an inquiry as to the cause of the delay the roadmaster informed me that they were having a difficulty with the tanks, which were frozen. They were obliged to dig into the brook, to cut out the ice and pump water into the engine. I asked him why the tanks had not been repaired, and his reply was that they never got satisfaction from the Government. That is one example of the results of public ownership. To give another illustration, I may say that I was recently in the yards of the railway in the town where I live, and there was a train composed of about forty-five or fifty cars with one engine trying to start it from nine o'clock in the morning to three or four in the afternoon. I asked one of the railroad
men why it was that there was only one engine and his remarkable reply was: " We cannot get orders from headquarters."

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: What date was that? Can you give us any information as to when this happened?

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
I may inform the hon. minister that this matter was brought to his attention, and it has been remedied to a certain extent; but I must say that on the International railway to-day there is no possibility of any successful operation under Government ownership. To-day owing to the unsatisfactory operation of the railway it takes three days to receive a reply to a letter mailed to a point six miles distant, I read this morning in the Campbellton Graphic of April 24 an article under the caption "Better Service Needed." It reads:
The mail service along the International Division, C.N.R. serving settlers between Campbellton and St. Leonards, is a most wretched one and should not be longer tolerated; on account ot the poor service on this railway, mail is greatly delayed and the settlers in some districts, send their mail by other routes if they wish to reach Campbellton promptly.
The train service is also deficient and with the change of time, a daily express service should be inaugurated.
Why not restore the service which pertained under private ownership, that is an express over and return the same day. Certainly, there should he a daily express train on this route.
Before I support the public ownership of railways many matters must be explained beyond any question of doubt. Of course, I may be wrong, but so far I have seen nothing but disappointment in the service rendered toy railroads under such ownership. I desire to read some of the remarks of the Acting Prime Minister on Friday in reference to this matter. He said:
I have been abused many times in this House on account of my railway policy,-
Abused, why? Simply because we ventured to debate for a few hours section 20 of this Bill, which involves millions of dollars. Forty-four defunct companies are to be revived, and we were at sea as to how much money would have to be spent on the railroads, and very naturally were seeking; information on the subject. It was denied us, however. And yet the Acting Prime Minister, in the face of this, charges us with abuse of himself. Let me continue the quotation:
-and I have often thought: What have I done that I am so abused? I found a couple of half-starved babies on the doorstep ,of the Finance Department when I went in there, puling weakly creatures, ill-dressed, dirty. Well, we have them here -to-night, and they are not bad looking children.

Well, whatever credit these infants may be to their progenitors, and while they are somewhat dirty, I would like to know who nursed and fed them and what sort of food they were given. Was it Borden's condensed milk? If haply hon. members do not apprehend the point, I beg to say that my meaning is that the Government are responsible for these dirty babies. I do not think it will do any harm to repeat that we cannot afford to spend much more money on railways, and the people cannot bear further taxation.
We read also that there are strikes everywhere throughout this country. Why? Because of the high cost of living. I blame this Government for not taking the proper steps to reduce that high cost now that the war is over. We need a good administration of railways, and I am sorry to gay that the Government in that regard has not pursued the policy calculated to achieve success.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
When the discussion on this Bill began this afternoon we were treated to a very eloquent speech from the hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin) declaiming against the Government for having made an effort to promote the passage of the measure by introducing the closure, and we heard a great deal from the hon. member, in a manner peculiar to himself with regard to the application of the gag and the consequent inability of members to discuss the Bill on its merits. To demonstrate his sincerity in that position the hon. gentleman occupied about seventeen and a half minutes in discussing every subject under the sun but that of the Canadian National Kail-ways, and about fifty seconds in discussing a matter having any reference at all to the clause under discussion. He was followed by member after member on the same side of the House. I listened to all of them attentively, and but one reference did I hear to clause 2, and only an incidental reference to any other part of the Bill, except that made by the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler). There must be a reason for this, and after trying to 'determine what it might be, I have reached the conclusion that hon. gentlemen opposite find they must do something to extricate themselves from the difficult position into which they have brought themselves. The only thing they can do is to throw sand in the eyes of the public by shouting " Gag," in regard to the measure, with respect to which they cannot offer any constructive suggestions or any solu-

tion for the problems with which we are confronted. The Bill is an honest effort to provide means by which the country may relieve itself from the tangle into which men-of whom the hon. members opposite are the official legatees-through incompetence and reckless extravagance, it nothing worse, plunged it in the years that have passed. It passes my understanding, how men can declaim, as they haVe done and are doing, against the actions of this Government, not only in connection with the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Northern Railway, but as regards the men who built and managed the latter system, some of whom are now in the employment of the Government, managing the Canadian National Railways.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Devlin) referred to 'the incidence of taxation that would result from the incorporation of a board oi directors to manage the Canadian National Railways and taking over of railways as has been done and will be done to a further degree. He did not say anything, however, in regard to the incidence of taxation that is resulting and will continue to result from the $500,000,000 that has been wasted in the construction of the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railways. On one or two previous occasions in this House I took the liberty of saying that we were not likely to get very far in the solution of these problems by harking back to what has taken place in the past, but if hon. members insist in keeping these matters before the House there is only one thing to do and that is to answer them.. The situation we are in to-day with regard to railways is the direct result of the iniquitous policy -nothing more or nothing less-that was pursued in railway construction during the regime of men of whom the hon. members opposite profess to be the successors. How are we going to get out of the position in which we find ourselves? We are forced to take over these railways whether we like it or not. It is not a question of whether a man is in favour of public ownership or not, it is a problem that we cannot get away from. I will come to the matter of public ownership in a few moments. We have these railways on our hands, and we must manage them, if they are not going to be a burden that will ultimately sink this country into bankruptcy. The Government is proposing to incorporate a board of directors to manage the railways free from political interference, if that is possible. I believe that it is possible. Notwithstanding what hon. gentlemen opposite are pleased to

say, I believe that we can find in this country men of sufficient public spirit and ability to manage the Canadian National railways and manage them efficiently. The present general manager, or president, and the present board of directors of the Canadian National Railways have been held up to ridicule in this House and all kinds of inefficiency has been charged against them and even their honesty has been called in question. It was stated this afternoon by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) that we were placing in charge of the Canadian National Railways men who had made an utter and hopeless failure of the Canadian Northern. We also have the statement of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) on Friday last with regard to the management of the Transcontinental and Grand Trunk Pacific railways:
If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Morphy) wants to know the difference between the building of railways in the days of the L/aurier Government and the building of railways to-day, it is simply that in our time there was competency and capacity in the railway administration, whereas to-day there is recklessness and incompetence.
There is recklessness and incompetence in the management of the Canadian National Railways and there is lecklessness and incompetence in the construction and management of the Canadian Northern Railway, while according to the leader of the Opposition there was efficiency in the management of the Transcontinental and Grand Trunk Pacific Railways. The Canadian Northern Railway was built simultaneously with the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental. It was just as good a railway, with a much better location, and was built for less than one-half the money that was put into the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railways. Although I may be a few miles out, I think that 9,555 miles is the approximate mileage of the Canadian Northern, and with a reasonably fair equipment it was produced for approximately $400,000,000. On the other hand, we have about 4,000 miles of line, without any branches or equipment worthy of the name, that has cost this country $500,000,000, and to complete it and make it possible to operate., will bring that cost up to $550,000,000. Yet the leader of the Opposition contrasted the men who were responsible for that $550,000,000, or $125,000 a mile, with Mackenzie and Mann, who were simultaneously able to build their line as it is to-day for less than $40,000 per mile, and whose system was managed by Mr. D. B. Hanna.
How can hon. gentlemen square these two statements? I have stated before, I repeat it now, and I challenge contradiction, that there never was in this or any other country a railway of the same character produced or the same amount of money as the Canadian Northern railway. In that railway this country has an asset that is second to none on the American continent -not even to the Canadian Pacific. And that railway system was carried on under the management of the man who is now president of the Canadian National railways. I do not know whether the present president may be the best man-it may be that this Government or some other government may find a more capable man- but until he has been given a fair trial, there is no man in this House or out of it that can raise his finger and point to one thing in the record of D. B. Hanna and say that it has not been in accordance with good railway practice.

Mr. Chairman,
I was just coming to that, and I am glad ' the leader of the Opposition has raised that question. The Canadian Northern railway for the two last years for which an accounting is available paid all its operating expenses and between three and four million dollars towards the interest on its bonded indebtedness, a record that in the same period of time has never before been accomplished by any transcontinental railway in America. What has been the record of the Grand Trunk Pacific road that the leader of the Opposition himself says was constructed and managed economically? Only in the last two or three months, as he knows, the management of that line said: Unless the Government comes forward with ten or fifteen million dollars we will cease operation, because we cannot earn enough money to pay the wages of our employees. Is that right or is it not?

speechtext: I am willing to admit that under the arrangement made for the construction of the Transcontinental the 'Government had very little control- or, at least, if they had any control they did not exercise it; that is certain. If hon. members opposite wish to go into a discussion of what took place in connection with the construction of the Transcontinental, well arid good. I am ready for a field day in connection with it.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: Forty million dollars went into graft.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
I do not know where it went, but I have said before and I repeat it now, a hundred and twenty-five million dollars went into something that was not building a railway.
What we are trying to do is to find a solution of our railway problem, and to that end the Government has brought before the House a measure to incorporate a company to manage our national railways. Let me repeat again, that if D. B. Hanna is not the right man, and if the present Board of Directors are not the right men, there is a means in this Bill by which we can get the right men. What this House and the country must do is to face this issue squarely. Give the management an opportunity to bring the roads all into one system, develop them as they should be developed, and if that is done the Government has an excellent transportation system. It is true that in order to be fair to the railway itself we will be forced to write off the money that we have ourselves thrown away. But that is not a matter that need now concern us. Havin'* read this Bill from start to finish, I can see nothing in it but what is consistent with a reasonable effort to place these railways on a basis where they can be efficiently managed free from political influence. In reading the discussion that has taken place we find that hon. members opposite, one minute demand that the Canadian National railways be taken out of the influence of politics altogether, but in the very next breath they say: We do not want to permit the Board of Directors to pass even a by-law as to how they will conduct their business unless they come before Parliament for the sanction of that by-law. That is the kind of discussion that has been going on all the way through the piece.
CMr. McKenzie.]
Let us see what the situation is. Hon. members have stated that this country is burdened with what the Canadian Northern has cost and will cost. We have a present liability of possibly four hundred and fifty million dollars in connection with the Canadian Northern, and we will be called upon to expend on maintenance and equipment and on terminals possibly an additional hundred million dollars, and we will be called upon to construct branch lines to give the people of the adjacent country an efficient service and gather the traffic necessary to make the railway pay. In order to do that we will again have to spend money, but so long as we keep that expenditure within proper limits in relation to the producing capacity of the railway, which in the final analysis depends on its mileage, the country has nothing whatever to fear. I believe that the leader of the Opposition and hon. members opposite will agree with me that in ten years from now with proper management the Canadian National Railways will not only be paying their way but will be producing for this country a handsome revenue.
One word with regard to public ownership, because that qusetion has been brought forward and there has been a manifest effort to have members declare where they stand on it. My recollection is that the hon. member for Maisonneuve referred to a declaration by Lord Shaughnessy in regard to public ownership, in which he declared himself very emphatically as opposed to it.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: Not in the speech I quoted to the House.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
I was not able to notice that the hon. member quoted anything from Lord Shaughnessy that would show us a solution of the difficulties in which we find ourselves to-day. No man in this House or out of it has a greater regard for Lord Shaughnessy than I have, and for the splendid system of transportation that has been built up under his genius, but when Lord Shaughnessy or any one else comes before the Canadian people and offers a solution for the present railway problem he will be talking about something practical; so long as he simply declaims against public ownership as a theory it is merely so much idle twaddle. We cannot get away from the present condition of affairs. Would the hon. member for Maisonneuve or any one else suggest that we hand over all these lines to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company? Would he suggest in the alternative that we should hand them

back to Mackenzie and Mann and the Grand Trunk, take the burden of a billion dollars of debt and give them the earning capacity of the road? If not, what other solution is there? The only other thing we can do is to take these roads and operate them. If any member of this House will show me a way by which we can get back to the position we were in before the duplicate transcontinental lines, the Canadian Northern and the Transcontinental, were projected side by side, I would say with the hon. member for Maisonneuve; I am in favour of the private ownership of railways. But the hon. member knows as well as I do that that is an utter impossibility. It would be a financial tragedy to put all the railways in Canada under public ownership at this time. The time may come when we shall be able to do that. We now have an opportunity, in this Canadian National Railway Company, of demonstrating our ability to operate publicly-owned railways. There is this saving situation, we have in Canada, without any exception, the finest, the best-equipped and the best-managed railway system in the world.

Now, perhaps I have wandered for a moment from the exact subject under discussion-

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
No one noticed it; even the diligent member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) did not call me to order.
I may be asked: Are you in favour of or against public ownership? One of the members from Toronto who addressed the committee a few moments ago was scandalized at the idea of any one not being for public ownership:	why, public ownership is
thought well of in Toronto; that should close the discussion. But the member for East Algoma who probably knows more about engines and railways than most of us know, says very frankly that personally he is for private ownership, but that we are face to face with a condition under which we are forced into public ownership. I agree with him. We are forced into public ownership and we have to see how we can make a success of it. So let us not have this great vaunting of superior political virtue because we are for or against public ownership. The conversion to public ownership of those whose faces I now look into is of most recent date. It was said that one of the Frankish kings became converted to Christianity and that his armies were converted by regiments and were baptised by platoons. That is very much the condition in which hon. members opposite find themselves in regard to public ownership. If they have all the zeal for public ownership which some of them display, it is the zeal of apostates who have recently turned from another political belief-or I should not say political belief for it is a question not of party politics but of economics. Many gentlemen on the other side, had they possessed the courage and frankness of one of the members for Prince Edward Island, would have risen with him when a vote was demanded on this question.
It has been repeated to me time and again by the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) that we are face to face not with a theory, but with a condition: How can we make public ownership a success? Every man in the House wants to make it a success; yet if it is not a success I do not think anything short of bankruptcy faces the Canadian 
people. What must we do? First, we have to change the mentality of the people in the matter of their rights and their obligations towards the Government. What have we generally found in the past? Let me illustrate by a story. Some years ago a member of one of our provincial governments was fishing on a salmon river when a telegraphic despatch was brought to him. The messenger was treated with all the kindness which kindly men show to those who do them a service, and then he was asked by this provincial politician: "What do I owe you, sir?" The man said: "Well, Mr. Smith, who is going to pay for this, you or thei Government?" If it was the man personally, the messenger charges were to be low; but if it was the Government, the messenger charges were to be high. That, I am sorry to say, has been the mentality of the Canadian people, and perhaps of people throughout the world! That mentality must be changed. The people of Canada, if we are to have an independent, sound, economic existence, will each have to say: What can I do for my country?-rather than:	What can I get
out of my country? It being a fact admitted by all, that example speaks louder than precept, how has .this Government helped to raise the people of Canada to the altitude which I have just indicated? When Union Government was being formed, certain men had to retire from public life in order to make room for others. Did they retire into the modesty of private life? No. One was made a Lieutenant Governor; one was made a Chief Justice; and then we were told that patronage had been abolished.
What has been the attitude of this Government as regards the newspaper press? We would have thought that, when Victory Loans came to be floated the Government might have asked the newspapers, as a matter of patriotism, to give great advertisements for the Victory Loans; the Soldiers' Settlement scheme and so on, if hot free, at least, at low rates. What did the Government do? On the one hand, they presented the newspapers with cheaper paper, and, on the other, they gave them payment for advertisements at higher than ordinary commercial rates.
The next great point and one insisted upon by the Acting Prime Minister was that the people must have confidence in the administration of this great railway. I cordially approve. But what is the basis of confidence? Frankness. Have we had frankness? The other day we asked for information" as to where the Canadian National railway was buying ties, and we were told that it was not in the public interest that

such information should be given us. Not only was it in the public interest that we should have that information, but the information was withheld from us because private interests interfered. Those ties, about which the question was asked, had been purchased by the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid), or those responsible to him, from the Northern Construction Company. Moreover, the Northern Construction Company represents the Mackenzie and Mann interests, and the price at which those ties were bought was higher than should have been paid for them. Because my information is to-day that that construction company is going around from dealer to dealer in ties and getting ties at several dollars less than the stipulated price which they are to get from the Government. It is the same game of the middleman again, making money out of the people of Canada.
We have been told that we should have absolute confidence in this board because they, forsooth, know a good deal about the management of the Canadian Northern in the past, and because the Canadian Northern has, in the past, had a management that will bear investigation. May I just give an illustration which comes under my own personal observation? Some time ago, a firm of Philadelphia bankers,
9 p.m. for which the firm that I was associated with then acted, had bought certain bonds of the Canadian Northern elevator at Quebec, which was a Mackenzie and Mann concern. Those bonds were endorsed by the Canadian Northern Quebec Railway; the money for them was paid over into the hands of the Mackenzie and Mann interests, the Canadian Northern Quebec Railway, and was used in the development of that line. Sir Donald Mann, then just plain Dan Mann, assured one of the Philadelphia bankers that, as long as Mann had one dollar, the interest on those bonds would be paid. The interest on those bonds was not paid; but that is not the gravamen of the offence, because any one is liable to a financial reverse. But when we applied to the Canadian Northern Quebec Railway to implement their endorsement on those bonds, we were told that in endorsing those bonds they had gone beyond their charter powers; and it was not until we had obtained a judgment against them in the superior court and in the court of review, and we were on the eve of having the case tried in the Supreme Court at Ottawa, that they settled. That is one fact I am giving to the Committee, and it is by
reason of such things as this that the Canadian people will not be satisfied until the Mackenzie and Mann control of the past is eliminated from the control of the Canadian National Railways for the future.
There must be economy in administration, but I find no evidences of economy in this Government. I find that they are not cutting down the Estimates as they should. I even find-if we may explain or illustrate a large thing from a small-thaf when the ministers are indoors, they allow their automobiles to go on puffing, waiting until they come back, instead of shutting off the engines and starting them again.
Some hon. MEMBERS; Oh, oh.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
My hon. friends laugh, but let me tell them that while economy is made up of small things, economy in itself is a big thing. It was Bacon who said: "Economy is a great revenue." Well, it is not a revenue that this Government will ever enjoy.
We want to have the management of these roads divorced from politics, and that is quite right, but how are we going to do it? No suggestion has so far been made. We must do it in one of two ways. There will be thousands and thousands of employees of the national system, when it becomes fully developed, who will be sufficient in constituency after constituency to turn the balance. What we shall have to do will be either to introduce proportional representation, in which I am a strong believer, or do as Australia did, create a couple of constituencies in which the railway men would vote-they would, of course, have to vote by mail,-in order that the Government would not have the temptation, on the eve of an election, of raising the pay of railwaymen throughout the country in order to get their votes.
There is another thing in which I think the Government has lamentably failed in spite of suggestions made by hon. members on this side of the House, and that is in giving representation to the workers on the board of directors of the Canadian National railway. This should be done, because experience teaches it, and it is what Great Britain has done 'along the lines of the Whitley report. I offer these suggestions with the best will in the world for the success of the Government railroads, in which we are all vitally interested; and I hope that, although it would appear from the faces of many I see before me that the good seed I am sowing is falling on stony

places, or on stony hearts, there are some who will profit by them.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
For a few moments, I intend to address the Committee as one who believes in public ownership, and most- of all, as one who 'believes in public ownership at this moment and as the means of dealing with the railroad problem now before the people of Canada. Public ownership is in the air in Englishspeaking communities throughout the world. The Mother Country, Great Britain, saw fit at the beginning of the war to take over the railways; she has them now, and she will never part with them. We have it on record that the present Prime Minister is preparing now, with the aid of the Government, for absolute and public ownership of the railroads of Great Britain.
He knows now that the only way to have the loyal support of the railroad men of England to the Government and the railway system is to establish a national'sys-tem of railways. What did the United States do? At the beginning of the war they took over every railroad, and they have them yet, and are now working on a plan, not to give the roads back-that will never be done-but to improve and complete the roads, consolidate and co-ordinate them, supply money for their improvement, and run them absolutely in the interest of the people. They are adopting public ownership, not as a secondary measure, not as something to be resorted to in time of trouble, but absolutely on its merits. Great Britain is for public ownership, the United States is now for public ownership, and our co-dominions, Australia and New Zealand, have had public ownership for many years and are so well satisfied with the system that you could not get them to change it. Wherever public ownership of railways has been tried, the great democracies of the world to-day all insist on keeping the roads public-owned; {hey do not want to part with them. South Africa has been built up on public ownership, and the regeneration of Africa under the leadership of England is absolutely based on a Cape-to->Cairo railway, which will be the property of the Empire for the furtherance of the trade of the Empire and t'he extension of its settlement and influence. Look at all the great countries of Europe. Germany organized herself into the power she was in the war largely on public ownership. She may have lost the war, but she did not lose it by reason of her public ownership; in fact, she got her strength in the war largely from the public ownership of her railways. The evi-fMr. McMaster. J
deuce of all mankind is not that the people of different countries are apologizing for public ownership, but that they are taking to it because it is the one thing absolutely necessary for the settlement of their transportation problems. So I am not coming here to apologize for public ownership, or to be afraid to state my belief, and in particular I am not going to be a bat; and I want to tell the House what a bat is. A bat got into an argument with the other animals as to whether he was a bird or an animal. As occasion suited him, he said he was an animal or a bird. At one time he would say: "I am an animal. Don't you see my nose is like a mouse's?" When he saw things going another way, he would say: "I am a bird. Don't you see my wings?" But all the time he was a bat. Are the public men of this country to be bats? The people of this country want to know where you are, whether you are a bird or a beast, whether you are for public ownership or against it. For heaven's sake, don't be a bat. But that is the case with a large number of men in this House. It is" not the case with the people of this country. They have seen and learned what has taken place in other countries, and are all for public ownership. I should like to see some man get up here and say: I am against public ownership, because of the experience of all the countries of the world that have adopted public ownership in the past and have practised it and found it, as they think, to succeed.
'Coming to Canada, what ought to be our position in connection with the railways of this country? We have heard the question discussed a good deal, but I want to approach it from this point of view. We have the railways, which give the service and are represented by the shareholders; we have the people, who pay for the service, and they are largely interested. But in English-speaking countries-and it is only in English-speaking countries it has come about-in connection with the railroads we have developed not only the shareholders who own the railways, and the people who use them and pay the traffic charges, but, in America, and Canada especially, we have developed what is called the railway magnate. These magnates, or executives controlling the roads, have always been against public ownership, and have tried to persuade the shareholders that public ownership is against them; but they have not been able to prove that. They have always been able to prove, at least they think so, that it was essential that the conduct of the road should be left

in the hands of the magnates. But the United States has got rid of them all, and we are getting rid of them in this country, and the last remnant-I speak with all due respect of Lord Shaughnessy and his associates- the last appearance in this country, of the railway magnate who dictates both to shareholders and the public is in the Canadian Pacific Railway. I give them credit for the way they have run their road, but the Canadian Pacific Railway must bow to its fate. It must be absorbed and I am ready any day, in order fully to achieve public ownership in this country, to take the Canadian Pacific over, and to guarantee just as good management to the public as the Canadian Pacific has given us as a private-owned road. We can get the men to do it. I am ashamed to hear my fellow-Canadians in this House say:	We cannot trust the Canadians; we
cannot trust democracy in this country with the public ownership of railways. I want to tell Lord iShaughnessy and his friends in [Montreal, and that other lord, Lord Atholstan, who is also against public ownership, that they have not got the people of Canada with them. The people of Canada believe in public ownership. They know they can get competent men from amongst our own sons to run our railways. The Canadian Pacific will have to bow to what is coming and come in with the other roads.
Another thing has taken place, and it has been mentioned only incidentally in this House to-day. The largest holder of shares in the Canadian Pacific railway to-day is the Government of Canada. The people of Canada the other day took over, I believe, $20,000,000 of the stock of the Canadian Pacific that had been forfeited because it was owned by German shareholders.
I want to tell the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific another thing:	If they
continue to listen to these magnates like Lord Shaughnessy, instead of looking after their own interests, they will come out at ,the small end of the horn; but if they are wise they will sell their shares to the Canadian people. The appeal I make now to the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific is this: Now is the time to sell and get the best price you will ever get for your road. Come in with the other railways, and the people of Canada will have a great national system with all the railways run for the benefit of the country at large.
I want to speak to my friends from the West. Transportation is the great question in this country, but rail is only one
means of transportation. Lf we go into the public ownership of railways, we must nationalize the steamship lines as well, and until we have done that we shall not have really solved the transportation problem. The evidence of the whole world to-day is that there must be nationalization of transportation not only by rail but by water also. One is the complement of the other. Transportation now is not merely national; it is international, and the real solution of the transportation problem of the world to-day is a joint transportation on an international basis of public control and public ownership. There is no other solution, and the .evidence 1 give to my friends from the West is this: While, by the service of the Railway Commission we were giving to the people of this country, and especially to the people of the West, reduced freight rates, every dollar of reduction that the railroads gave was taken from the farmers of the West by the private-owned steamship lines of the world.
Transportation is a wide and far-reaching question and there is no solution of the problems involved but public ownership. When you have public ownership you are absolute master all the time, and your chief objective is not profits but good service to the people and, after that, good treatment of the men engaged in the service. To this is largely due the progress that is being made in Great Britain to-day in public ownership. The workmen and the coal owners see it, and we must accept it here gladly and not with any apologies. I do not think we should hear any more apologies for public ownership. Can any one go into Ontario and apologize for public ownership there, after the experience we have had with the Hydro Electric? What is Canada deficient in especially in Ontario and Quebec? It is power for the railroads. On the other hand, what is Upper and Lower Canada rich in? It is water-power. And we are allowing that water-power to pass into the hands of private corporations. I think we should keep it for the proper supply of the roads, and when we have public ownership of the roads and of t'he rivers of the country we shall have the cheapest possible transportation. The worst record in the history of the world in railroad matters is the record of the control by the private capitalists and the private executives of the American railroads. They made a colossal failure of it from start to finish. They wrecked and looted the roads and left them in the dust; and if the American nation has to pay to-day for the roads it has taken over it is because

those roads were looted and allowed to run down. They were robbed and were never co-ordinated nor consolidated, nor were they concentrated in the public interest, but were operated for the special profit of the individuals who happened to control them.
Now, we are going to start with the Transcontinental, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern, and we may bring in others. There are a number of lions in the way, or at least so it is said; but we have to approach the problem apart from polities, -and I think the Government are making a fair effort to do so. I have heard them criticised, but still they are making some headway. They are doing what the people of Canada have asked them to do, and if they refuse to do it, there will inevitably be an accounting at the next election When the issue will be:	Are you in favour of public
ownership, or are you opposed to it?
I have in this House for many years expressed as well as I could my views in favour of public ownership, and I have been sometimes discouraged by lack of response in the House. But the response from the people has always been unequivocally in support of public ownership. My advice to hon. members is not to trim on this question but to find out where they stand and to insist that the Government in power shall carry out public ownership on progressive modern lines as is done in other countries. Is Canada going to stand aside after what all the other nations of the world are doing? I have heard a good deal said about the application of the gag, and it reminds me of a little incident in Canadian history. The first Jesuit who spent the winter outside of what is now the city of Quebec had very little experience of the country, but after spending a winter in the woods, in the course of his narration of his experiences he made the following striking statement: "S'il y a du froid, il y a du bois,"-if there is cold there is wood. As regards the gag, all I have to say is that the attitude of the people on that question is summed up in an epigram somewhat'similar to that of the Jesuit: If there is obstruction in the Parliament of Canada, there is the closure. I am not here to justify the closure, but I want to say that the people desire to have this Bill put through. There is nothing else to do but to approach the situation, to vote the money, to stand the loss, and let those who are responsible bear their responsibility. Both parties are more or less worthy of blame in that matter. I know that some
[Mr W. F. Maclean.]
hon. members, at the very beginning of this awful trouble, did put in a protest in the House, and it is on record. Man after man whom I have seen in this country talking in favour of public ownership at one time blocked it; but they have come around, and especially those in the Government to-day are trying to support the measure. Hon. gentlemen on the opposite side may have a good deal of justification for what they say, while hon. members on this side may approve their own recriminations. But that is not the question, and what the people are concerned in is a solution of the transportation problem on the best possible lines, recognizing that transportation is made up of river and rail, sea and land. In France there is a Ministry of Communications, by which they mean railroads, telegraph lines, express and telephone, and all the other systems of communication associated with them. Now, we not only have a national system of railways coming into our hands, but we are going to have steamers and telegraph systems which we must nationalize. We must also have a national express and a national parcel post. And in this connection I would like to know what the Government are doing. For two years I have waited to see some sign of a nationalizing of the splendid telegraph system in their hands. My hon. friend from Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux) had an opportunity ten years ago of giving us an Imperial cable service. It was not carried out although it should have been, and I think it is important that we should have an Imperial cable service to meet the growing demands of communication. We must have a great system of communication in all these things, and must recognize that the underlying principle of all these matters is public ownership, administration and responsibility. Let us make a start so that the world may know that Canada really has faith in public ownership of her communications and transportation.

speechtext:
-and I am always afraid of that, because a doctrinaire may sometimes take his mirage for a reality. However, I am bound to say that on some phases of this particular question of public ownership I am not afraid to take sides with my hon. friend. He has just referred to the State control of cables. I was accused the other evening by the Acting Prime Minister of being in favour of private corporations and standing for private corporate rights in this House. He has evidently forgotten the history of the last few years because when I was in the Government, and since I have had a seat in His Majesty's loyal Opposition, I have always preached in favour of the State control of cables. I had, as Postmaster General, the clear evidence that in this country the consumers of the cable, if I may use the expression-or the users, but "consumers" is perhaps a better expression-were being mulcted by the cable ring, and I advocated in England and in Cafiada, in company with other men-Mr. Henniker Heaton, for instance-the establishment of an allBritish State-owned cable. We have not yet succeeded in that enterprise, but I hope that as a result of this war the Governments of Great Britain and of Canada will see the necessity of having a State-owned cable, with the nerve centre in London, so that the news of the day can be disseminated, without being tainted by foreign influence, throughout the various portions of the British Empire. Moreover I say that as we are going to have a still larger British immigration to our Western Prairies, it is important for these settlers that we should get a cheap cable rate. But that is not the question at issue this evening; we are speaking of the Canadian Northern, and again I wish to state to the Committee that I never, in the discussion that took place last week, pronounced myself on either public or private ownership. I did not offer any solution. 1 admit-with both sides of this House, with my leader, and with my hon. friend who has just taken his seat-that we have to face a condition and not a theory in this matter. We	now	have	theCanadian Northern.	Two	years	ago
we were obliged, after many and many sacrifices made on behalf of that company by the people of Canada, 'to expropriate the company. We had to appoint an arbitration to go into the affairs of the company, and since that arbitration the control of
the Canadian Northern system has come into the hands of the Dominion Government. Therefore we have to face an existing condition, and, nolens volens, we are forced to accept to-day the administration of that system of railways. What I blame the leader of the House (Sir Thomas White) and the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) for is, that they stated on Friday last that this was a fight between corporation interests and public ownership. That is not the case. The objections that were raised against the policy of the Government were two-fold: first, the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) and the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) objected strenuously to clause 16 because in that clause parliamentary control of the expenditure, the vast expenditure of money which the administration of this railway system will compel, is taken away; second, we were shocked, to say the least, when the Government intended surreptitiously to revive forty-four wrecks belonging to the old Canadian Northern Railway without informing the Committee of the mileage involved and of ithe probable cost of the construction of those lines. I do not say that the Government intends to build these forty-four lines, but whether ithe Government, or whether the board, of which Mr. Hanna is president, intends to build them or not, the House is entitled to know the mileage involved and the probable cost of them. I added as an argument, which has not been refuted, because it cannot be refuted, that whether you spend money or not on these forty-four lines, you affect thereby the credit of Canada, and if there is one thing in economics which ought to be sacred to the Government of the day it is the national credit. When you go to foreign markets to borrow money, as you will have to go for that purpose in the future as you have done in the past, the money-lenders will take your ledger and they will say: What are the assets and what are the liabilities of Canada? They will look into Canada's financial position carefully, and they will know the obligations assumed by the Government for the near future. Do you imagine for one moment that if you seek to borrow money from Kuhn and Loeb, or from Morgan, oi New York, that they will not inquire what are rthe assets of the Dominion and the liabilities as well? Sir, I say, as a Canadian and as a patriot, having the interests of my country at heart, the Government should shrink before adding that enormous possible liability to the ledger of this

country. These were the objections that were urged against the two clauses of the Bill, and I see no reason in the world why the Government has imposed the closure in restraint of discussion. No one on this side of the House, and I say it to -my friend the acting Minister of Justice, will recede from the necessity of passing this legislation, but we want legislation that is fair to our own reputation and fair to the people of Canada. I say that Government ownership is not an issue in the House to-day, and it was not an issue last week. That was a bogey raised by the ministers because at the present moment there is a popular fancy in some of the provinces in favour of Government ownership. The Government is anxious to please the great province of Ontario where that policy is popular to-day. The Government also wishes to please the western provinces by lavishly promising the construction of forty-four lines in order to pass its budget without any tariff reduotions such as are called for in the West.
Before declaring myself in favour of Government ownership of the railway system of Canada, as I stated a moment ago-and my record is well known-so far as regards our cable system I am in favour of Government ownership, I wish to say that it is a question of circumstances, it is not a hard and fast rale which you can impose on the people. We must be guided by circumstances and, as wise men, we must be above all guided by the experience of two peoples, one supposed to be the shopkeepers of the old world and the other the keenest business men of the new world. I refer to the British nation, and to the American nation. I am surprised that I, with my French blood coursing through my veins, who am not supposed to be a business man, should have to repeat this elementary truth to a majority of my fellow members who belong to a race of cold, matter-of-fact men, men whose business ability and business honesty have been known from time immemorial. Those business instincts have made both Great Britain and the United States of America the great commercial countries they are to-day-I repeat, I am surprised to have to recall to my fellow members such an elementary truism that before adopting such innovations we should be guided by the experience of both Great Britain and the United States. My hon. friend (Mr. Manion) this afternoon cited the example of France in favour of Government ownership of railways. I . know something of the railway system of France, and I say to the members of this Com-
[llr. Lemieux.]
mittee that that Government system has been a fiasco. But now let us take the precedent of the United 'States and of Great Britain. The other day I gave the House some facts and figures with regard to the United States Railway situation, but let me once more recall to hon. members a few further facts and figures which were given recently in Montreal by a gentleman who is a Canadian by birth, Mr. Mitchell, who has become in the great business centre of New York one of its leading men. Speaking before the Canadian Club in Montreal he said:
Notwithstanding the increase in rates, which were far greater than private management had ever dreamt of asking, and which produced a greater gross revenue by $865,000,000, the people of our country, after suffering inferior service, were called upon as tax payers to advance $210,000,000, the amount by which the net earnings failed to equal the guaranteed rental. In other words the American people paid $865,000,000 more in rates for inferior service and were taxed $210,000,000 in addition, so that the true cost to the people of one year of Federal operation amounted to $1,075,000,000. With these figures before you I need not repeat that the popular passion for Government ownership and operation has materially cooled during the past year.
Now, Mr. Chairman, what has been the experience of Great Britain? We are guided in political affairs by the experience of the Mother of Parliaments. We are guided in commercial matters by the business principles of the British people. Well, Sir, what is the experience of Great Britain? I find this information, not as my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) said this afternoon, in his mild and smiling way, in Le Soleil of Quebec, but in that great Toronto weekly, Saturday Night:
A statement on the condition of the railways of England was recently made in the House of Commons by Sir Eric Geddes. He said that after four years of Government war control the roads are in a semi-paralyzed financial condition and that the Government is now losing $1,250,000 a day in operating them. Further statements made by an authority who has been visiting England are that the railway employees, including the workers in coal mines and industries supplying materials to the roads, have in effect confiscated the properties. The whole English railway system to-day is potentially bankrupt. The burden of meeting the deficit in operation and paying the rental to the owners is being carried by the public treasury. That is, the increased labour cost is being met by the English people through taxation.
This is not my invention, this is the dictum of Sir Eric Geddes, who to-morrow, Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to know, will be the principal of McGill University. What does he say further?
Beginning in October, 1914, and running to November, 1918, there were eight successive

wage increases, varying from three shillings to six shillings per week, and totalling thirty-three shillings-$7.40. Thus was added $275,000,000 to the payroll. At the end of the war, when Lloyd George appealed to the country for a vote of confidence, the railway unions made a renewed demand for an eight-hour day. This was granted. Thus was added $125,000,000 more to the payroll, making a total increase in wages of $400,000,000, or 160 per cent. The payroll had been increased to $650,000,000, as compared with total railway revenue before the war of $680,000,000. In addition, there was a very large increase in the cost of coal, steel and other material, adding $140,000,000 more to the operating expenses.
In all the operating expenses have been increased to $970,000,000 per annum. Including rental or interest on investment, the total cost of producing transportation is now $1,220,000,000 as compared with $680,000,000 before the war, an increase of about 80 per cent.
No increases in freight rates have taken place to offset increased costs of operation, the increase of 50 per cent in passenger fares early in the war being a measure of restraining travel. This increase probably added $100,000,000 to passenger revenue, bringing it to $780,000,000.
