In the United States,
Congressman Aswell, of Louisiana, introduced a resolution for taking over the wire lines. The United States Government has had the wire lines under its control for some time. Here is the published statement of Congressman Aswell:
I am the author of the resolution that was made the basis of existing law taking over the control of the telegraph and telephone wires for the duration of the war. I believed in it heartily and worked for it faithfully, but I am very frank to state that I am greatly disappointed and disoouraged to note the increase of 2'0 per cent, ordered on telegraph rates. I am not yet ready to admit that any such increase is justifiable or necessary.
This' means the death knell to Government oontrol or ownership of telegraph, telephone and railroad lines. I owe it to my people and to Congress to apologize-
Yes, after experience, he has to apologize.
-for my resolution if Government control means increase In rates.
The best means so far has been devised for the administration of our public utilities, for the administration of such a, public utility, as a railway system, is the Railway Commission, which controls the rates and gives ample satisfaction to the people. But the facts are facing us; we must take the Canadian Northern, and, in the name of all that is honest and sacred let us give an administration that will meet with the hopes of the people; let us vest that administration with such powers as will not be above the control of the representatives of the nation in Parliament. It was stated a moment ago that the Liberal Government was lavish in its expenditure in connection with the railway companies. Let me say, in justice to the dead statesman, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, that he ,at least never granted one inch of Canadian land to a railway company, whereas the Tory party .by their subsidies created all the land barons of Canada.

Like all the others on
that side of the House, the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) has wandered far afield. One idea I got from him, howr-gver, was that Government ownership is pot an issue. I am surprised that the hon. gentleman should make an assertion of that kind, because no bigger issue is engrossing the minds of the people than that of Government ownership of the great railway lines, under consideration in this Bill. herself is certainly an issue. The issue is forced because the railways have been put upon the country. I do not propose to go into any avenues of complaint as to how they got there. Mr. H. B. MORPHY': He cannot really understand how any one could say a good word, for the West. their meagre facilities, with their trunk line of transportation crying out for branches. Over four million tons of coal from a country almost unknown from the point of view of coal. Underneath the soil of Alberta which bears the golden wheat there are gold mines in coal, beyond the dreams of any one here. To the West we all look forward as the great harbinger of prosperity in the future, as the real feeder of the Empire in the days to come. Yet the hon. gentleman says: Everything for the West, nothing for Quebec.
The leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) has been much more frank than the member for Maisonneuve, because he has told us where he stands with regard to public ownership.
He has no confidence, no faith in Government ownership as applied to this Bill; he has no confidence in anything this Government undertakes. Therefore, he is willing to risk not only the prosperity of the West, but the success of the scheme, simply for small political advantage, and nothing more. The other night, the hon. gentleman put himself very clearly on record as regards public ownership. He said:
X was never in favour of Government ownership. There can be no mistake about where I stood. I am not in favour of it now; as I think private enterprise will do better in these matters. Particularly in colonization and development, will private enterprise and private energy do much better than Government ownership.
The leader of the Opposition Is decidedly frank. The hon. member for Maisonneuve argues against public ownership, because, he says, if the Government take over the charters, that will prevent private enterprise from building these railroads. While pretending to be in favour of public ownership, he argues for private interests because he says that the taking o-ver of these charters by the Government will prevent private enterprises from building these railways. Thus, we have two members on the Opposition side opposed to public ownership. The hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) says: I have no earthly use for public ownership; I am absolutely opposed to it, first, last and all the time.

A back-bencher from Ontario, the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler)- and I do not see how he can sit on that side on this great issue-tells the frontbenchers they me all wrong. Thus we have, on the other side, the front-benchers against public ownership, the balance afraid to speak, and one voice alone crying in the wilderness scolds them. What a happy family are hon. gentlemen opposite upon this question? I feel very strongly that the people of the provinces throughout the Dominion, including Quebec, are, as one hon. gentleman said tonight, in their very hearts and souls, actually and honestly, in favour of Government ownership as regards this great railway system. Why? What else is there to do? We have the roads placed on our shoulders, and they must be operated by the Government, or, if not, by whom? Will hon. gentlemen opposite, freeing themselves from this destructive criticism, tell this Committee some plan whereby this system, which in the meantime is a great incubus, but which, in time, will, I believe, become a great public project, redounding to the welfare of this country, may be successfully operated under the conditions which confront us to-day? I will give place to any hon. gentleman opposite who will tell us just what alternative there is; I am willing to sit down in order to give him an opportunity to state one. You see, Sir, the fatuity of the situation. Hour after hour, for days, we have been called upon to endure factious opposition, the wasting of the time- of the House and the country without one alternative proposition being given. If hon. gentlemen opposite would even say:	We have a plan, but
we will	not tell you); but they
have not sufficient temerity for that. Here we are as a Canadian Parliament submitting to destructive criticism hour after hour and day after day. What time was there ever before in the history of Parliament when the closure should have been applied to such absolutely futile destructive criticism of hon. members who are not talking even -to the clause before the Committee?

10 p.m. I think it is a pity, indeed, a shame, that the time of this Committee should be so taken up by futile criticism, without one constructive plank in the platform of hon. members opposite, who show by their paucity of resource, their lack of progressive measures, their absolute inability to put some plan forward, that they are not to be taken seriously; and 1 think they should be condemned for taking up the time of the Committee in what is nothing short of absolute obstruction to one of the greatest measures- which the Dominion has ever had before it.

speechtext:
Much has been said as regards public and private ownership. I do not believe that is the real point at issue; but on the other hand, since the-Government is ready and willing to operate, as owners, all railway lines, with the exception of the Canadian Pacific, public ownership is, in my opinion, bound to play its part in the drama. I am far from being ready to vote in favour of Bill No. 70. To begin with, we on this side of the House are only desirous of getting information as to who will be named as directors, what their salaries will be and so forth. It took us about an hour the other evening to learn that Mr. Hanna's salary was $25,000 per annum. Further, I do not believe that by taking over these roads the country will be better off, because the company will demand enormous sums of money to repair the roads and put them into good running

order. Then it will be discovered that we shall have a very heavy deficit every year, and what will be the decision of the Government then? They will say: This is a losing proposition; we will turn the roads over to private enterprise. And the roads will then be turned over to the same monopolists, the Government's friends, and the public will be the losers. We also asked who were the owners of the tracts of land through which the forty-four roads, the charters of which the 'Government wishes to revive, will go. We have been unable to get an answer, but I can safely say that Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann are the owners of thousands of acres alone. I shall state further that Mr. Mackenzie's sons own thousands of acres of land in those districts, and the information given my by the friend of one of the hon. members on your right, Mr. Chairman, who went West to buy land for cultivation was: These loits or plots of land belong to Sir William Mackenzie or Sir Donald Mann or Sir William Mackenzie's son. Why did they and other speculators secure so many acres of land? In my opinion it was simply because they were aware of the Government's intention, and felt absolutely safe in acquiring this land. There is no use asking further questions on this Bill, Mr. Chairman, because since the "infernal machine," the closure, has been set to work "mum" has been the word; on the other side of the House. The Government is very anxious to load up the country with debts even though we now owe over $2,000,000,000. Who are the world's bankers, may I ask? The treasurer of our neighbouring republic recently announced that the' United States has advanced further sums to the Allies as follows: Great Britain, $100,000,000; Roumania, $5,000,000; Serbia, $268,000. This-with previous loans makes a total loaned by the Americans to the Allies of $9,138,829,000, and of this $4,236,000,000 went to Great Britain. Is not this enough to make us sit up and take notice before taking further action? I sincerely hope that it is; but-there is no use in hoping in this case, for the simple reason that the question has been already decided. The closure is working and the Bill will pass whether you like it or not, but I shall certainly take pleasure in voting against it because I consider it against the best interests of the country at large.

speechtext:
I did not intend to say very much in regard to this Bill, but it has involved so much discussion in connection with Western Canada that as a representa-

live of that part of the country I feel it is my duty to say something.
I was very much surprised to hear the arguments which were brought forward by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), complaining about any expenditures which might be made in the West, and I was equally pleased to hear the forcible arguments of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) setting forth the value of that country. We need railway construction there. The province of Alberta is rich in wheat lands, in timber lands, in mineral lands, in coal lands, in asphalt deposits; it is so rich in natural resources that I believe in the not far distant future it will be one of the leading mining, as it is now one of the leading agricultural provinces of the Dominion. An hon. member (Mr. Morphy) from Ontario has referred to the coal production of that province. Although the province of Nova Scotia, from which the hon. leader of the Opposition has the privilege of coming, is one of the greatest coal-producing provinces in this Dominion, and has been engaged in that industry for many years, for decades, yet the province of Alberta in the year 1918 exceeded in coal production every other province in the whole Dominion. It is because of these natural resources that we desire railway construction in the West; and we have other reasons than those. We have the obligations which were assumed by the Provincial Government of that province. We have heard much criticism of Mackenzie and Mann, and no one can criticise them more strongly than I, have criticised them in the past. They have taken to their bosoms Governments from the Atlantic to the Pacific. They have possessed alike Federal Governments whether of Conservative or Liberal stripe, and Provincial Governments; they have done more,
I believe to corrupt public life in this country than any other two men who were ever in the country. Do hon. gentlemen opposite want to allow the administration of one of the great railway systems of this country to remain in their hands, or are they perfectly willing that we should assume the responsibility which has been cast upon this Government? We find ourselves in the position that we must either keep pouring our money into the bags of these railway magnates whom hon. gentlemen opposite all criticise, or we must assume the obligations, put money into the enterprise, and eventually make it a benefit to the people.
So far as the province of Alberta is concerned, the charters which are referred to

in schedule 2 were all guaranteed by the Government of that province. They received their charters, their bonds were guaranteed, and the bonds for three of the lines have been sold and the money now lies in the bank. Hon. gentlemen opposite talk about the credit and honour of this country. Is it more honourable, I ask them, not to construct those lines in the province of Alberta when the bonds have been sold to the English bondholder, than to assume the obligation which was entered into, not by this Government, but by the Government of the province of Alberta? We owe it to the bondholder to construct those roads. We also owe a duty to the settlers who live along or within travelling distance of these projected lines- It has been argued by the other side of the House, when we put through this schedule it will induce people to settle. We have already induced these settlers to come to the province of Alberta. Thousands and tens of thousands have come on the strength of these charters the bonds of which were guaranteed and sold. These settlerls have moved in with their families, and have been crying out since 1911 for railway construction. I submit that this Government owes a duty to those settlers to expend the proceeds of those bonds and give railway communication in that part of the country.
As to the lands through which these lines travel, there iseems to have been great anxiety on the other side of the House as to whether it would be a good business venture. I should like to have the privilege of taking many of my friends through the country which will be traversed by these lines. You will pass through some of the richest agricultural districts in the Dominion-through country which will produce hundreds of millions of bushels of grain in the future and support your ports in the East. Hon. gentlemen opposite complain about this expenditure of money on railway construction in the West, but I hear no complaint from any single man about the hundreds of millions of dollars which have been spent in Sydney, Halifax, St. John, Quebec, Toronto and Fort William on harbour improvements and terminal facilities. We realize they will be an outlet for the produce of the West, and we are now only asking that some recognition of the West be given, so that we can develop our own country by means of railways, and then the produce of the West will help build up the great water terminals which you have here in the East.
My hon. friend from Maisonneuve was very much exercised as to the effect the reviving of these charters would have on the money markets of the world. He says we are bankrupting ourselves and that we will not be able to borrow a dollar because there are charters in this schedule. Does he not know that every railway company in this country has carried on for years branch lines under charter upon which they have done no work and that the people in different parts of the country are suffering [DOT] for want of railway construction? It will not affect the credit of the country one particle to have these lines. The hon. member suggested that these lines were being projected because Ontario was in favour of public ownership, and that it was being thrown out to the West as a sop to satisfy them in connection with the tariff. It must strike him that the tariff and railway construction are two entirely separate problems, and those who are interested in the tariff in the West will not be bought by any promise of railway construction which may be given by this Government. There is no part of Canada that is more strongly in favour of public ownership than the Great West. Perhaps we have been forced into public ownership, but the time is coming when the West will demand public ownership of nearly all its great utilities, the express companies, the telegraphs, the telephones and steamships, and almost every great utility which is necessary to carry on the commercial business of the country. The people want public ownership, and I think we should be fair and not condemn the scheme before it has been tried. Do not let us bring in petty party politics, but let us get together and demonstrate to the world that public ownership of railways and utilities can be made a success. Let us co-operate to the end that every country may point to Canada as the pioneer in this great work. The men who are engaged in the administration of the railway have been criticised in the House. Every member on the other side knows that Mr. Hanna, the president of the company, has the reputation of being one of the best railway men in Canada, and why should he not be employed by the Government? We have also heard reflections on Mr. Z. A. Lash who, as hon. members on the other side must know, is one of the ablest lawyers in Canada. Why should his services not be employed? Now, if hon. members opposite continue to cast slurs on these gentlemen they are just damning public ownership and we shall never get the best

men in Canada to assume positions oi responsibility under such circumstances. 1 think the discussion on the part of the hon. members opposite has been one endeavour to do what they could to defeat public ownership, and they have criticised the Government unjustly and unfairly for purely party purposes. They say they want information on this and on that. Are we going to spend the time of the House in discussing railway ties on the 25,000 miles of railway in Canada, or in talking about section hands and general managers? There is much more serious and important business to be discussed, and we should lay aside these trivial matters and proceed to questions of real importance. There is no fear that there will be any patronage, because the railway employees themselves are so powerful now that patronage in the administration of the railway system will never come into play. I have very great pleasure in supporting the Bill, because it is an honest endeavour, as far as possible, to remove the railway systems from the sphere of politics. The question of public ownership was discussed in England during the last years of the war. This scheme which England thought good enough to consider-and I trust they will adopt it- should certainly be good enough for Canada.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
It has been suggested that this Bill does not propose Government ownership, but rather provides the machinery to operate our Government railways. I think the hon. member for Maison-neuve is more responsible than any other member of the House for the fact that the discussion has drifted to the issue of public ownership versus private ownership. The first day the subject was introduced the hon. gentleman read an extract from the Winnipeg Telegram ridiculing Mr. Hamilton, the representative from Saskatchewan on the board of management. I wish to refute anything that has been said derogatory of Mr. Hamilton's capabilities, and to do this it is necessary that I should refer to what the hon. member read at that time. The article was headed " Making Railway Experts," and was addressed to the editor of the Winnipeg Telegram. It reads: *
Sir:-The West has furnished our Government with two men to fill national railway positions. A short biography of them should provide a tip to President Beatty of the C.P.R., and should also point the way to thousands of ambitious Canadian youths. It should also quiet the disbeliever in Government ownership of railways, as it clearly shows that our prairies turn out captains of industry by the simplest of training.
I Mr. Tweedie.]
Charles McGill Hamilton, in the early '90s, was attending school in Indian Head and later in Regina. About 1902 he settled on a section of land near McTaggart, Sask., a village about ten miles north of Weyburn. He followed this worthy but uneventful career until two years ago, when he was nominated in opposition to the Unionist candidate for Weyburn.
This is a misstatement of fact, for Mr. Hamilton was never nominated in opposition to any Unionist candidate. He was a Liberal candidate for some three years prior to the formation of the Union Government.
This article continues:
A few' months later he was appointed a director of Canadian National railways. Farming a section of land in Saskatchewan is a mighty good training for directing the affairs of a national transcontinental.
You will notice that it is stated that Mr. Hamilton attended school as a boy. This,,
I am sure, no one will find fault with, as it is necessary for every young fellow to attend school. But the writer of this article failed to mention that Mr. Hamilton had continued at school until he fitted himself for a teacher's certificate, which profession he followed for a number of years.
The article stops there with respect to Mr. Hamilton, but I wish to add that besides these qualifications, which I claim are real qualifications, Mr. Hamilton is at the present time and has been for quite a number of years, president of what is known in our province as the Rural Municipal Association. This organization has branches in the -whole of the organized part of our province, and the annual convention brings him in touch with the reeves, secretaries, and councillors of these rural muni- ' cipalities once a year. So that I claim we have not in our province a man better fitted to deal with transportation problems than the same Mr. Hamilton. Why the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) should read this article to the House I cannot understand.
I am confirmed in my belief that he was out to do Mr. Hamilton some harm, because on Friday some other hon. gentlemen to your left, Sir, referred to the management of this road. When the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) interjected the question, " What about Mr. Hamilton?" I want to say to the hon. gentleman, in order to dissipate any fear he may have in this respect, that Mr. Hamilton is one of the coming men of the province of Saskatchewan, one who will do honour to the board of management of the Canadian National railways or any other organizations with which he may be connected. Another gentleman, whom the same article presumes to ridicule, is Mr. Porter. I will not read what the article has to say about Mr. Porter, but I desire

to state that I have known this gentleman for many years and he has qualifications which Mr. Hamilton does not possess, inasmuch as he had been a railroad man for a great many years. As the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) saw fit to read the article in question and to ridicule Mr. Hamilton, 1 thought it well .to point out that the Saskatchewan people are well satisfied with their representation on the Canadian National Railways board, and so far as Mr. Porter is concerned he has been, as a railway man, connected with the Grand Trunk Pacific for many years, and has simply been put into another position; that is all.
There is another .matter that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) touched upon in respect to my province which I thought was not right. In discussing this question he made the statement that many of the western- provinces were almost bankrupt.
I do not know which of the western provinces he referred to particularly, and as he did not definitely say I take it that Saskatchewan was included. For this reason I think I am justified in putting on Hansard a statement taken from the budget speech of the treasurer of the province of Saskatchewan, as given on the 29th of January last. It says this:-
On December 31, 1918, the gross public debt of the province amounted to $29,635,906.26. On a population basis it amounts to a charge of $39.S3 for each individual in the province, using as a basis of calculation the population used by the Dominion Government in calculating .the subsidy to the province. That is the charge per capita, $39.83, In considering the matter, however, the fact that a large portion of this debt is self-sustaining must .be considered. That is to say, the taxpayer of the province as such does not have to pay the interest on it. That portion of the public debt which is self-sustaining amounts to no less a sum than $13,159,090. That amount includes investments in the public telephone system. The taxpayer of the province does not pay interest on the amount invested by the Government in the public telephone system. The public who use the telephone system of the province pay that interest in the form of telephone rentals and toll charges. The telephone system of the province is based on the idea that the people who get the service, and not the general taxpayer, should bear the burden. So that while the province has loaned to the telephone department for the purpose of building our telephone system the sum of $7,184,000 the general revenue of the province is not charged with the interest or sinking fund on that sum, the telephone department, out of its receipts, pays into the treasury annually a sum equal to the interest on that investment and the sinking fund with respect to the loans made for therefor.
Then in respect to the Saskatchewan CoOperative Elevator Company, the Government loaned that organization $1,878,000.
The Saskatchewan Farm Loans Board loaned to the farmers of that province $1,826,000, and there was another small sum loaned in respect of the Regina cyclone mortgage. Now, Mr. Chairman, this leaves the net debt of the province of Saskatchewan at $16,476,000, or a per capita debt of $22.14. This, I think, will bear very favourable comparison with that of any other province in the Dominion.
In respect to the branch lines of railway, as outlined in schedule 2 of the Bill under consideration, much has been said and hon. gentlemen have asked for information regarding them. I will have an opportunity of speaking when that part of the Bill is under consideration, I expect, and I can then give the hon. gentlemen information that I think will be sufficient to convince them that all branch lines to be built under these charters in my constituency are absolutely necessary to its development, and I have no doubt that there are other hon. gentlemen from the Western Provinces who will be able to answer the same for their constituencies.. In this connection let .me point out that while it has been charged that the Government is playing party politics with this Bill, the people of Saskatchewan have got their eye on the Government and on its railway programme. No matter what government is in power in this country, they are looking for a progressive .policy with regard to the construction of branch lines which are so much needed in our province.

speechtext: It is not my intention to make any lengthy remarks on this Bill. When I went to Montreal on Friday last I was of opinion that the measure would be disposed of by the time I returned, but I find that in my absence, after certain speeches had been made by certain hon. members, the Government deemed it necessary to invoke the closure. Now we are trying to discuss the different clauses of this Bill and give our opinions with respect to them, and I am glad to have had this opportunity afforded me to-night. Coming up in the train I happened to read in one of the newspapers, said to be a supporter of the Government, that the Opposition were not serious in their attitude on this question, but that we were just spokesmen, gramophones, so to speak, and tools in the hands of other people who were forcing us to make this fight against the Government in order to prevent it from carrying out the policy upon which it had decided. In this connection the names of Lord Athol-stan and Lord Shaughnessy were men-

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
I purpose offering a
little information with regard to some oi the branch lines mentioned in the notorious forty-four. I do not think any particulars of this nature have already been given. The Government would have been well advised had they brought down certain detailed information in connection with the amendment introduced on Friday. Requests have been made for this information, and as it has not been given, and as I am familiar with a number of the branch lines mentioned, it is in order for me to give some of the details in connection therewith.
During the consideration of this Bill the time has been largely occupied with the discussion of a matter which, so far as I can see, does not enter into the question affected by this Bill, that is, the matter of public or private ownership. I have listened carefully to a great deal that has been said and have read speeches that I did not hear, and I have failed to see in them anything to show me that ithe question of public or private ownership enters into the Bill that is before us.
We in the West who went through the good old days of property fluctuations and inflations a few years ago became possessed of certain properties in the West, lands and lots and so on, and some of us still hold them. That fact might give people the idea that we are in favour of private ownership of land. On the other hand, should we run across some kind, paternal Govern-

ment which is desirous ol purchasing our properties on terms similar to those on which it took over certain properties from Mackenzie and Mann, we would gladly give up our equities-because, as in the aforementioned instance, that is all we have left in them now- to the Government. We might then be said to be in favour of public ownership. And that indicates about the only connection that the question of public or private ownership has with this Bill. We have on our hands certain railway properties; how we got them does not make any difference so far as this Bill is concerned, but we have to deal with them. The fact that we have them might cause people to say that we are in favour of public ownership. I venture to say that if some private corporation should offer us for these railway properties anything like the amount that the Dominion has expended on them, the person here most strongly in favour of public ownership would not objeot to turning these properties over to that corporation. Not five members of the Committee would, if confronted with that proposal, fail to rise in their places and vote strongly for it; in which case we would be looked upon as in favour of private ownership. I do not see how a discussion of the question of public or private ownership is going to settle the matter. The Government brings down this Bill, and. there is nothing in it to indicate that they are in favour of public or private ownership; they are not in any way committed to either. On the other hand, the Opposition make certain criticisms of the Bill. So far as I can gather, they criticise the character of the measure, not the principle of it; there is nothing to indicate whether they are for or against public ownership. If each member voted according to his own firm convictions, a number on each side would vote for puhlie ownership, a number against it, and a number would be neutral, that is, would be in the position of favouring public ownership in certain circumstances and of opposing it in others. So that I do not think we are getting anywhere by discussing this particular question.
So far as I can figure out, the whole controversy now before us in connection with this Bill is with regard to these branch lines, and the question whether their charters should be renewed. I am surprised that some one has not preceded me, and given the information which I propose to give. I am more or less interested in a considerable part of the territory through which a dozen or more of these lines pass, 
mostly those in Northern Saskatchewan and Manitoba. I have checked over the list as it appears in Hansard, and I propose to take up possibly half a dozen of the charters mentioned.
But ilet me first point out the situation generally as to railroads in the West. Most of the roads run east and west. Until pretty far north the settler can go in an easterly or westerly direction without much trouble, but it is very difficult to get across country, that is, north or south. There are, perhaps, only about three locations where there are north and south lines throughout the whole of the West. One line runs from Winnipeg to The Pas-which is only approximately north and south; another from Prince Albert to Begina through -Saskatoon. From Edmonton to Calgary there is one direct line and a couple of lines that are approximately direct. But the vast areas in between have really no means of communication north and south except in a very roundabout manner The aim of a number of these branch lines is to give this north and south communication, not directly, but ultimately. Branch lines will be extended into certain districts where there is considerable settlement, with the idea of accommodating that settlement, and also of bringing other territory just beyond into a position to be settled, and eventually extending into that territory, and so on.
A line is proposed from Craven to Hudson Bay Junction via Yorkton. That would make direct connection, you might say, between The Pas, the terminal of the Hudson Bay railway, and Begina, through a country which is not served at all at the present time. Many settlers throughout that district are not eight or ten miles, but anywhere from fifteen to forty miles from railway communication. The intention is not to complete that railway at once, but to build a certain portion of it, serving well-settled districts at first, and eventualy completing the whole road.
Mr. McKENZIE; What is the length of that line?

speechtext:
It runs from Begina to Hudson Bay Junction; I should say, about two hundred miles. It is already partly constructed at both ends. I am not, however, as familiar with that line as I am with others further north.
One of these charters calls for the construction of a line from Melfort northeasterly to the boundary between Saskatchewan and Manitoba. That line goes through one of the best farming districts in the whole

of Western Canada; the land is uniformly good. A large delegation from Melfort and surrounding country came here about a month ago to press for the construction of that line.
There is at the present time another delegation here from that district to press for the construction of that line. The intention of the Government and of the Railway Board is to grade thirty miles or so, and ultimately to extend the line to The Pas to connect with the Hudson Bay railway. The idea is not to do all that at once, hut it is well in constructing a railway to map it out. with some objective in view and then to do as much each year as conditions demand.
Another project is from Hudson Bay Junction, which is the junction between the Prince Albert section of the old Canadian Northern railway and that section which runs up to The Pas to connect with the Hudson Bay railway. This line is intended to he constructed from Hudson Bay Junction to the southern part of Saskatchewan, via Moosomin. Portions of that line have been built here and there, between Sturgis and Canora, between Canora and Yorkton, and between Yorkton and Melville. The idea is to link up these so that there will be a complete line running north and south from Hudson Bay to the southern boundary of Saskatchewan, to the coal fields.

speechtext: Can the hon. member tell us the length of that line?

speechtext: I am sorry I did not figure out the length of that line, but when it is finally completed, it will be approximately from 250 to 300 miles long. I do not want to be tied down to an exact figure.

speechtext: Is that road partly built?

speechtext: Large sections of that road have already been built and these must be linked up in order to make a complete road running north and south.

speechtext: Where does it go to in the south?

speechtext:
I will confiine myself just to one instance in Manitoba. In the country west of lake Manitoba and between that lake and lake Dauphin, there is a considerable stretch of country a large portion of which is well settled. I know personally that people are hauling their wheat, not as an hon. member Stated a short time ago, only eight or ten miles, but twenty-five or thirty miles. It is the intention of the Governmeent to extend the line from the south up twenty miles. Then there is a gap to Ste. Rose du Lac, and there connection is made with the main line of the Canadian Northern. It is the intention to extend this connecting line farther north, a distance of twenty miles. That means that two particular parts of this general district will be served by those two extensions and that these will be eventually linked up when the territory in between is settled up, but in the meantime, only settled districts are being served. Later the districts a little more remote will be settled up and lines running into those districts will be constructed, and eventually there will be a continuous line from Portage La Prairie to Winnipegosis, which will be a direct line and which will serve one of the best districts in Manitoba.
There has been a great deal of criticism regarding the Canadian Northern management, and particularly regarding the founders of that line, Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann. I do not purpose going over that ground, but while with a good deal of this criticism I heartily agree, I notice that there was no criticism of Mackenzie and Mann respecting the location of their lines. There seems to be a unanimity of opinion in this Committee that the Canadian Northern Railway system passes through a country which is probably the best for railway purposes of any part of the West. We must give those gentlemen who were the founders of this road credit for having made a particularly good selection of their territory, and they selected the particular districts which are covered by * these charters. Therefore, if they were as wise in their selection of these districts as they were in their selection of the territory through which the Canadian Northern Railway system has already been built, it is to the great advantage of Canada that we preserve these charters for the use of the Canadian National railways, and of course, of the Canadian people.
I might say also in connection with these lines that as has probably been noticed, the general trend of a number of them is towards connecting up with the Hudson Bay railway, either indirectly at Hudson 
Bay junction, which is connected with the terminus of the Hudson Bay railway, by a Canadian Northern Railway section ol about ninety miles in length, or directly with The Pas itself, which is the terminus of that railway. I do not purpose discussing the advantage or otherwise of the Hudson Bay railway project at the present time. Probably I shall have something to say about that later on.
But if as much wisdom has been shown in the north as Mackenzie and Mann showed in the rest of Saskatchewan and Alberta, then the connecting up of some of these lines with the Hudson Bay Railway is going to be of great advantage to the West generally, for you will observe that Mackenzie and Mann have had such connections in mind throughout their whole scheme of things.

speechtext: I am not going to agree absolutely with the last speaker. To me this Bill is a public ownership Bill from start to finish. Its title is public ownership, the preamble is public ownership, the first section is public ownership and every other section down to the last. You cannot make anything else out of it. Furthermore, those who oppose this Bill cannot help but oppose public ownership.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: No, no.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
That is my view. I am very glad to hear hon. gentlemen opposite demur, because it again proves to me that they do not know themselves just what they think about it. They have talked on all sides of the subject since they started. Their whole attitude from beginning to end has been an enigma. Some of them have said openly that they were opposed to public ownership. Others have evaded the question entirely and have talked all round it. Even the hon. member for Maisonneuve, for w'hom I have the very highest respect, told us he was in favour of public ownership of cables, but he did not tell us any-

thing about his views on public ownership of the railways. What did he do? He read copious extracts from one or two papers- for what purpose? These extracts showed that public ownership oir public control in Great Britain during a recent period had resulted in a great loss to the Imperial Government. Now, what was his purpose in reading those extracts? Was it to help the cause of public ownership? I fancy not. To me he had only one object in view and that was to do his utmost in opposition to the cause of public ownership. To me it seems that hon. gentlemen opposite have talked in different ways seemingly for a purpose, so that when an election comes they will be able to go to certain people and say, "We oppose public ownership," and in other districts they will quote extracts from their speeches and say, "We are in favour of public ownership." But the fact remains that no matter what they say, they have put every obstacle possible in the way of the passage of this public ownership Bill, and when I find a man putting a lot of rocks on the railway track I must confess to thinking he is putting them there for the purpose of preventing the train from passing, if not of wrecking it. That is the position hon. gentlemen opposite are in.
I have all my life been a believer in public ownership. I have seen it tried in our part of the country in a great many ways, and I have never seen it fail where it was properly handled. Mind you, it has to be handled properly, as any private enterprise has to be handled properly if it is to succeed. I have no doubt whatever that the course now being pursued by this Government in creating this holding company, if I may so call it, is the very best one that could be adopted for the purpose of making a success of the system. A number of hon. gentlemen opposite have pointed to the failures we have had on the Intercolonial, and what political interference has done for that road. I am mighty glad we have had that experience on a minor project like the Intercolonial. It has given us a lesson and taught the Government what it is necessary to avoid in order to make a success of railway management. If we had not had that experience, we should probably have to gain it now in a much more costly way.
My purpose in getting up to-night is more to answer a question which was asked by the leader of the Opposition. He asked why it is that the Canadian Northern has not paid. The answer is very easy to me. Even the Canadian Pacifiic did not pay
the first few years of its operation. I can well recall the time when I lived in that part of the country, thirty-two or thirty-three years ago, when conditions surrounding the Canadian Pacific were very similiar to the conditions surrounding the Canadian Northern or the Canadian National to-day. The country was not then developed; there was no trade then for the Canadian Pacific, just as there is very little trade to-day on the Canadian Northern. The Canadian Pacific had to develop the business, and it did develop it by settling the country. As the country settled the Canadian Pacific became one oi the best-paying institutions in this country. Exactly the same conditions prevail to-day with regard to the Canadian Northern. That road has been built as much as a colonizing road as anything else, and the result is that the farmers have flocked in as the railway has been built. The hon. member knows as well as I do that you cannot go on a farm and produce anything to furnish traffic for a railway for a few years. The first year you break a few acres and have a mighty hard time. The second year is not so hard, and by the third year you are producing a little bit which will furnish traffic, and in the fourth and fifth and sixth years are doing better. The Canadian Northern had just reached the point where the produce of the farmers would furnish paying traffic for the railway company which handled it, and from now on I aim fully satisfied we shall have exactly the same experience with the Canadian Northern as we had with the Canadian Pacific in years gone by. As soon as the country is settled and is producing the railway will pay. As the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Campbell) has said, it is located through the best stretches of country we have out there. I have travelled over a great many miles of it by automobile and buggy, and wherever I have gone I have been satisfied with the location which the Canadian Northern officials have chosen for their lines.
I have no hesitation in saying that in taking over the Canadian Northern Railway the Government has undertaken an enterprise which will be a paying one in a very few years.
In regard to these forty-four "notorious" branch lines about which complaint is made and which have been referred to as "wrecks" I must take exception to any such description of these' lines. I resent the statement that they are wrecks. Twenty-three of them belong to the province from which I come, Saskatchewan, and I wish

to say that we have no wrecks and do not intend to have any in that part of the country. I heartily commend the Government for seeking to renew these charters, and I would condemn them if they did not. Can the Canadian National Railway pay simply as a trunk line? Undoubtedly it cannot. The Canadian Pacific Railway never paid as such, but only when they got branch lines as feeders, and that is exactly what is proposed to be done in connection with the Canadian National Railway. If the Government were so shortsighted as not to build these branch lines what would happen? The settlers out there could not wait forever for railway communication, which they must have in order that they may profitably follow agricultural and other pursuits. To my knowledge thousands of farmers are to-day twenty-five and thirty miles from any railway, and if the Government did not build these lines the settlers would continue an agitation until they secured them. If the Canadian Pacific railway builds into these districts do you think there will then he trade for this government-owned road? Unquestionably the business would go to the railway which furnished the best facilities for handling the traffic, and the result would be that the Canadian National would continue to be a losing proposition. It seems to me that the only thing to do is to revive these charters and to build the lines as soon as the money can be provided and conditions warrant, so as to furnish feeders for our own railway and to stem competition. I think the Canadian Northern have located their lines well. There is no duplication, and the impression that has gone abroad to this effect is absolutely false. There is no duplication at any point in any one of the three prairie provinces. There is a little stretch west of Saskatoon where the lines run probably four or five miles apart, and which might be regarded as a duplication, if any one wished to strain a point. As an old Tory I am going to make the admission that I think the Canadian Pacific Railway was improperly located in the first place. We have been hearing about " a thousand miles of rock " separating the East from the West, but this is only along the north shore of Lake Superior through which the Canadian Pacific runs. There is a magnificent stretch of fertile land which, I am satisfied will hold thousands and thousands of stock farmers. I think the grade and the curves on the Canadian Northern are superior to anything the Canadian Pacific has, and I am satisfied that to-day we have 
an excellent asset and need have no fear of Government ownership. I dare any one to go into our section of the country and advocate private ownership of railways, if he expects to win an election, for you could not win a single constituency in Saskatchewan on the policy of private ownership. In my own city we would not think of granting the franchise to any private company for the street service of Regina. We have made a complete success of government ownership of telephones and believe that the Government can make a success of government ownership of railways, and for that reason we are strongly in support of the scheme. Speaking for a large section of our people, I believe that this matter can1 be conducted without any political interference; and having studied the Bill as carefully as possible, I have come to the conclusion that we shall have as near an approach to government ownership without political interference as can be had. For that reason I give it my most hearty support.

(But when it came to his turn he took the back road and told us nothing at all.
Now I am sure that hon. gentlemen in this House who are willing to take their gospel and their information, their brains, their philosophy and their guidance from the Minister of the Interior, will be surprised when they learn that the drafting of this very Bill that we are supposed to have been obstructing was only completed about four o'clock on Friday. I am sure there will be some amusement in the minds and on the faces of hon. gentlemen who say that we were obstructing the Bill, when I tell them that on four o'clock Friday last, about three or four hours before the closure was applied, the drafting of this Bill was completed, a new section 20 was introduced, and what constitutes in the new -Bill of to-day, five closely printed pages ' of new material were inserted in it. There was no sitting of the House on Saturday, or on Sunday, and we had no opportunity of discussing those five pages of closely printed matter and the new section that were embodied in the Bill, except for the few hours that remained between four
o'clock and about, half-past twelve, when, as I say, the closure was applied. Will any hon. gentleman sitting in this House with reason in his heart and in his head, and who acknowledges responsibility to his electors, say that we were wrong because we found fault with the very short period of time that was given to us for the discussion of a Bill the drafting oi which was not finished until four o'clock last Friday, and the printing of which was not completed until some time to-day? At twelve or twelve-thirty to-day I sent one ol the messengers of the House to see if I could get a copy of this Bill .as newly printed. I failed to do so; I was told that it was not on distribution. The first time I saw this newly printed Bill was at three o'clock when I took my seat in the House, and I venture to say that was the experience of at least ninety per cent of the members who compose this Chamber. At three o'clock to-day, Mr. Chairman, the printed Bill was placed in the hands of members, containing a new section and five pages of new material, and the closure was applied on Friday night! Was it not therefore most extraordinary conduct to apply the closure two days before the Bill was printed?

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: Hon. gentlemen may laugh, but will any member of the Government, or any member of the House, say they ever saw this Bill in its present form until three o'clock this afternoon? And yet, two days before that the closure was applied On the ground that we were obstructing the progress of the Bill, which was yet in tlhe womb of time, and about which we knew nothing. That statement, Sir,-1 think will satisfy you, and satisfy the people, that there was no obstruction in connection with this matter but only a fair and legitimate desire for information. Now, Sir, at four o'clock, this new section was brought down and the new schedule was attached, and we had seven hours in which to deal with the Bill before the closure was applied. Well, there are two hundred and thirty-five constituencies in Canada, but if you divided four hundred and twenty minutes by the number of constituencies, it will give each constituency l-7/9th minutes. Think of it, each constituency in Canada was given l-7/9th of a minute to discuss this Bill!

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
Will any person say
that we were obstructing because we took

more time? The 235 constituencies in Canada took more than one and seven-ninths of a minute in discussing this Bill, and therefore hopeless and reckless obstruction is charged. But is the charge of obstruction well founded when I tell you, Mr. Chairman, and when you know, that a very large body of the Bill did not come t-o our notice until to-day? No, it simply makes the charge more ridiculous. Suppose we had nothing to deal with at all but the forty-nine new clauses, or new subjects that were added to the Bill. Applying the same rule as in the other case gives us the enormous time of nine and a half minutes to each constituency for the purpose of discussion. Think of it! Think of all these constituencies with their population, their intelligence, their want of knowledge and desire for it in connection with these matters,- and nine and a half minutes have been placed at the disposal of each in order to deal with this Bill. We are told that is obstruction, and I can see on the faces of hon. gentlemen opposite-ithose hon. gentlemen who are listening to the impression sought to be published abroad that we are obstructionists-that we certainly are obstructionists, and that we certainly ought to be punished on that ground. Most decidedly- the people of this country ought to know what kind of obstructionists we are when we tell them that one and seven-ninths of a minute was allowed each constituency in Canada to deal with the subject, and that for only a small part of it, nine and a half minutes constituted the limit. If that did not prove satisfactory we had to accept the odium of being men of little sense, and devoid of any desire tp forward the progress and advancement of this country.
The leader of the House (Sir Thomas White), who is not here to-night, went far afield on Friday night to fasten upon us the charge that we were in the hire of some great concern in this country that he suggested, was evidently paying us, either directly or indirectly, to obstruct this legislation, and otherwise that we were putting ourselves up as against public ownership. The hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) undertook to quote to-night what I said about my own attitude on public ownership. I trust the hon. gentleman would like to be fair to me. and fair to anybody, but when he was giving the quotation he should have stated that it was something I said a year ago. Anything that I might say to-day, since even this discussion of to-day, might be tinged with some partiality, or might amount to trimming my sails to suit the breeze at present. But as to what I said a year ago, when this legiisla-

tion was not under discussion at all, surely I was not such *a prophet as to be able to foresee what is happening at the present time. What I said then is clear evidence that I am not now obstructing the Government ownership of this railway system.
I said then exactly what my hon. friend from East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) said tonight. He is a good, staunch supporter of the Government and occupies the first seat in the synagogue when it comes to a question of being a hard, hide-bound Tory. Surely they will not question his confession of faith, they will not deny his orthodoxy? What does he say? Exactly what I said a year ago. He says that we are in this position now, that we have no alternative, we have to make the most of a bad bargain; but if things were at a stage where he could choose between public ownership and private ownership he would be a private ownership man. Surely I may be permitted to walk along the street without any stones being thrown at me when I am in such good company, the hon. gentleman, who is an expert on railway questions-and an expert on most other things that we bring up in this House. When the question was put to me the other night -I said I was opposed to public ownership, and I could only repeat what my record was. I am not in favour of public ownership, because I believe in my heart that the energy and best abilities of people in charge of any work are brought out when they are working for themselves and for private ownership. I believe that the same keenness and ability and the same ambition are not brought to bear upon public ownership. That is my reason, Sir. If wrong I am honest about it. But I did say a year ago to the hon. Minister of Railways, when he was putting his Estimates through: You are in this thing now; I would not be in it if we could have avoided it, but we are in it and we have to make the best of it; we will have to help you along to do the very best you can, and I hope when you come to us in a year that you will be able to present a fairly successful statement. That is what I am saying now.
That the Acting Prime Minister should try to make political capital out of this question is to me very absurd indeed. It shows that things are getting to a very low ' ebb and that everything else out of which capital can be made is getting played out. The war is over and the returning soldiers are damning the Government at every station from Halifax to Vancouver. The Government are finding that they can-

not pass another War-time Elections Act to carry them into power, and they are therefore scouring around for some other breeze to waft them into power. And now they are laughing and saying: "Ha, ha! We have found something new. W^ will say that those chaps across the way are opposed to public ownership, and we are in favour of it, we will start that racket, and with another new franchise and a few other fake issues perhaps we can sail to harfbour once more." The leader of the House told us that he had found dirty babies on his doorstep, and it seems that they are still dirty. I am sorry to say that his babies are not the only things that are dirty in the Administration which the hon. gentleman to-day leads; there are other things almost as dirty. The policy regarding his babies is rather soiled and unsavoury and will afford some work for this Public Health Bill which has been introduced. Then there are other policies- if you will look at the immigration policy policy regarding his babies is rather soiled and its hands needing some bath-tub treatment; and if you look at the finances of the country-well, that is a baby of the vilest, raggedy looking character conceivable.
If the babies were so dirty and unsavoury and so undesirable, why did he pass a paternity order against the Minister of Railways and make him the putative father of another illegitimate child that they brought into the House-and I am told that he is not very well kept or very clean. If the two uirty babies were on the doorstep, and they were obliged to take them in, why pass this affiliation order upon the devoted head of the Minister of Railways to take in another dirty baby? And I find that they are contemplating a regular uaby farm, for they propose to adopt forty-five or other dirty babies throughout the \vest. I also find that the Acting Prime Minister is trying to get a purchaser for some of his land which he had on his hands some years ago when he became administrator of a certain Naboth. It seems that he has Naboth's vineyard on his hands, and it is quite possible that he contemplates founding a home for these dirty babies in the vineyard-and, certainly, if he gets as many of them as he professes to be looking after now, I really am afraid that Naboth's vineyard will not be large enough to hold them all.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I pointed out that we were not dealing with the question of public ownership, that over a year ago I announced what my position was, that I clearly and distinctly understood then the
position that we were in by reason of those roads being in our hands, and that the question was: How best to utilize them? The preamble of this Bill settles that question. It says:
Whereas His Majesty on behalf of the Dominion of Canada has acquired control of the Canadian Northern Railway Company and of the various Constituent and Subsidiary Companies comprising the Canadian Northern System, as specified in the First Schedule to this Act, and it is expedient to provide for the incorporation of a Company under which the railways, works and undertakings of the Companies comprised in the Canadian Northern System may be consolidated, and together with the Canadian Government Railways operated as a national railway system:	Therefore His
Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Canada,-
and so forth. That clearly indicates that we knew we owned those railways and were providing for the best way of managing them. If there should be a difference of opinion between hon. gentlemen to your right and hon. gentlemen to your left as to the best way of managing these roads, does it lie in the mouth of anybody to say that we do not want to have them at all? What would be the sense of saying we do not want to have them when they are already in our possession and we have been operating them now for over a year? I submit, Sir, that it is neither honest nor fair criticism for the leader of the House or any other hon. member on his side to say that we are opposed to, or in favour of, holding those roads, when we are dealing entirely with the question of management. For over forty-five years we have had a Government railway in this country and have been managing it without a corporation of this kind, and a man could be for or against it during that time as he would be now

Mr. ME'IGHEN: One could easily gather from the speech of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) that he was very angry with the Government over this Bill, and also that he was quite anxious to escape from the unfortunate position upon which he impaled himself and his party last Friday. But the most eager listener would find it very difficult to ascertain whether he was opposed to this Bill or whether he favoured it, and still more difficult to learn, if he opposed it, on what ground he did so, and what he objected to in it. For almost several hours to-day I have listened to hon. gentlemen opposite who are osten-

184fi

sibly opponents of the measure and are complaining of their treatment with regard to it; but all through those seven hours not one has pointed to one clause or one word of the Bill which he opposes or which he says is objectionable. Hon. gentlemen opposite say they have not had time to discuss the Bill. The leader of the Opposition gave us a calculation to show us that if every member wanted to speak on each clause, he would have a minute and seven-eighths, or something of that kind, within which to perform the task; therefore he says that when we moved the postponement of the consideration of clause 20 last Friday we took the Opposition short and did not give them a fair chance to discuss this measure. When we moved the postponement at one o'clock on Saturday morning we had discussed for eight hours that day, and for some time the day before, one single clause of the Bill without making any progress, and with the clearest intimation from the leader of the Opposition that we would not be allowed to make any progress. It did not matter what might happen; if everybody wanted to discuss each clause, so long as two or three hon. gentlemen opposite wanted to delay the Committee in order to delay the discussion of one single clause, we could not get ahead. That one single clause was the most unobjectionable clause of the whole Bill, the most absolutely impossible to take objection to. That was the clause which simply empowered the company, if Parliament voted money for the purpose later, to utilize charters which, while the company was in private hands, were the possession of that private company. Have we heard anything to-day to indicate to us why these charters should not be revived? A listener in the gallery or a member who was not here last Friday might gather from this debate that we who were directly responsible for the measure had sat here all day with hardened hearts and obdurate spirit, had refused to listen to hon. gentlemen opposite, refused to give any information, refused even to take kindly suggestions from them, and that, consequently, the spirit of gentlemen on the other side was such that they had to oppose the Bill whether there was any merit in it or not. Well, it would be interesting to inquire what there is in this complaint about lack of information. The hon. gentleman says that we brought down our schedule only Friday afternoon, giving the exact charters covered by clause 20 and asking that they be revived. That is true. The Bill as it formerly stood provided for the 
revival of any charters that had been the property of the private company. For the life of me, I know of no reason why the Parliament of Canada should refuse to revive for public purposes charters that were granted for private purposes. Why was the schedule brought down Friday afternoon? It was brought down at the suggestion of the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Le-mieux) who asked that clause 20 be amended and that we specify the charters we wished to be revived. Because we accepted his suggestion we were met with the most stubborn opposition all the rest of the day and with a refusal to pass the clause in the form into which it had been drawn at the request of the member for Maisonneuve. Now we are complained of because we dared to charge hon. gentlemen opposite with obstruction. We are complained of also because we accepted no amendments from hon. gentlemen opposite. Well, we had not much encouragement to accept any others, because, having accepted this one, we were delayed a whole day and threatened with indefinite delay unless we applied the only rule of the House that enabled us to proceed. What information was asked for that was denied?
