speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
need not think that I would forget that; that was really the most amusing of all these requests. One hon. gentleman asked for a map, and for the mileage. The mileage does not matter, because we are not building the mileage. When we come to ask Parliament to vote money to build the mileage, then all the mileage will be given; an estimate will be given as to the amount per mile. That is when Parliament is interested; 'but we must have the charters, be the mileage long or short. As for a map,
I do not know the value of a map dangling between me and the leader of the Opposition. There are maps in almost every room in the building; hon. gentlemen can go to them and see the direction that everyone

of these lines is to take. All the information is available; hon. gentlemen have had three days and three nights in which to gaze on the glory of the map of Canada, if that is any advantage to them. But the main thing is the matter mentioned by the member for North Renfrew (iMr. Pedlow). Why, he says, we wanted to know the names of the people who own the land along the routes of these forty-four lines. He is quite correct; they really did ask for that. Here is what the member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) said, although he is strangely silent to-night:
There has been deposited on the table a list of forty-four lines, charters for which are to he revived. Now, we want to know where those lines are going-
The schedule itself tells exactly where all the lines are going; that is to say, the general direction-and that is all that is known.
-the counties they will pass through-
*
There are no counties in our part of the country, so they cannot pass through any.
-and the owners of the land traversed by the railways.
Here are forty-four charters sought to be revived; the hon. gentleman asks us to tell him who are the owners of all the lands that will be traversed by these railways. How do you know who owns the land until you have the right of way, until you have a plan made out and accepted by the Minister of Railways? That is not the case here. We know the general direction; we know the lines that are built. But suppose we had the plans; suppose we knew every farm the lines went through, do hon. gentlemen seriously suggest that we should employ every lawyer in Western Canada to hunt up the land titles records and ascertain who are the thousands of owners of lands-for there virtually are thousands-along these rights of way? A more absurd, a more utterly ludicrous suggestion, was never offered to a Committee of this House. Who, it is asked, owns the land along the right of way? Are they friends of the Government? Well, I assume they are. You could not build a line of railway ten feet in Western Canada without encountering friends of the Government. Hon. gentlemen told us last Friday that some friends of the Government have townsites and are going to make great profits; that the roads are no good, but that these people are going to make great money out of the townsites. I challenged them then to come here today with information on that subject-they 1174
would have two days and three nights to think it over. I promised them that they would produce a sensation in the Committee if they gave any such information to-day, and that that information would likely have a serious influence upon the votes of hon. members on this side. Has anybody offered it? Has anybody heard any information as to friends of ours who own townsites along these lines? Well, there has not been very much, and I will tell you why: Ever since the Canadian Northern railway was owned by the Government, the townsites, one and all, have Joeen owned by the Canadian Northern Railway, and therefore by the people of Canada.
That, unfortunately, was not 'the case with the Grand Trunk Pacific. It is the case with the Canadian Northern Railway Company to-day, and it will be the case with regard to all the townsites along the line built under . the charters covered by clause 20. The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) does not know for the life of him how to vote on this Bill unless we tell him the name of every farmer through whose property these lines are going to run.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: Why did the minister not supply that information to us on Friday night when he was asked for it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: The information as to the names of the owners? I have not given it to the hon. member now.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: The minister has answered my question, has he not?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: If the question was to give the names of the owners of real estate along those lines, I have given the hon. member no name at all, but he is apparently quite satisfied. Had I known he was as easily satisfied as that, I would have done so before. We do not know the name of a single owner. For myself, I have never even heard of one and never even suggested one.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: Why did the minister not furnish that information then?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
I really did not think the Committee was so very much interested in the fact that I did not know the name of an owner along those lines. I assumed that the Committee, hon. gentlemen on this side as well as hon. gentlemen opposite, had sufficient intelligence to know that the lines had to run somewhere; that, wherever they ran, tfiere would be owners along the right of way, and that this Parliament was not influenced in the slightest degree by

whoever owned the right of way along those lines. What we are interested in is this, that the lines have been called for by setters for years, and that had it not been for the war they would have been built before this. Any hon. gentleman who made any inquiry at all, would know that there is not one of those lines that has not for years been called for. Governments, whether Federal or provincial, do not grant charters for the construction of lines unless good reason is shown why they should be built. These are charters that have been granted years ago, and that have been allowed to die by reason of the war, and we know that they are needed. Indeed, there are before this Parliament 1,500 signatures praying that one of these lines be built.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) is afraid that, because these charters are revived and made the asset of the people of this country through the people's road, foreign creditors of Canada are going to take alarm and refuse to lend us any money. That is what troubles his soul to-night. He says they are going to look at the debit side of the ledger of this country, and that because they see these 44 charters owned by the people of Canada without any obligations on them at all, they are not going to lend us any money for our future financing. Is it going to disturb a foreign creditor to see that, although we have the railway mileage we have in those western lands, there are still districts in which farmers are hauling wheat thirty or forty miles? It is a good country, but there are no railways to haul their wheat for them. We could not have a finer asset for this country than for the foreign creditor to read in the body of this Bill that there are 44 charters which the Government of Canada deem should be taken up and made the property of the people, because the people are there and need the lines to serve them.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: Will the minister explain how the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Campbell) knows that the Government are going to build 350 miles this year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Nelson has information that I did not have myself, because I have not arrived at the time when the information is necessary. When I come as an hon. member of this House to authorize lines to be built by an Appropriation Act of this House, then I want to know what lines are to be built,

how far they are to be built, and what the rate is per mile.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: The hon. member had no information then. He was guessing?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
I presume he made
some inquiries some time before, but we are not concerned with that at the moment. If it were 350 miles or 3,500 miles, what difference would that make as regards the revival of these charters? Will the hon. gentleman answer me that?

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: I presume that all of these charters cover thousands of miles of railway. The people of Canada might be willing to build 1,000 miles, while they might be opposed to building 10,000.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: Certainly, and they will decide that when they commence to vote the money, but we want the charters whether the lines are long or short, and I vote for the charters, whether the lines are long or short.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: Did the minister ever, in his experience as a minister, see one vote, once put into the Estimates by the Government, knocked out?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: The same thing applies to Estimates that applies to any Government Bill: if the Government is defeated on it, the Government resigns. But parliament is then entitled to the information, because the information should affect the judgment of hon. members. That information affects the issue as to whether we should vote the or not, but it does not in the 12 m. slightest affect the issue as to whether we should revive the charters or not, so that every particular item of information asked for that has the faintest bearing on the issue was given to this committee. No information, whatever, was denied, and hon. gentlemen cannot come to this committee to-day and say, with any reason: Our obstruction was on account of the hard-heartedness of the Minister of the Interior. They obstructed this Bill for reasons very difficult for me to define, but they certainly obstructed it by determinedly opposing a decision of this Committee on a single clause for eight long hours one afternoon and evening.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: I do not want to interfere with the minister's time, but if he will look over Hansard, I venture the opinion that his own side of the House took up more time than we did.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: On Friday evening?

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
To-night and every
other time that the Bill was under fire.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: Who would not do that to-night? We have to go on until two o'clock anyway. On Friday evening practically the whole time was taken up by the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill), the hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) himself, and the hon. member for Three Rivets (Mr. Bureau). We have under discussion this afternoon this Bill that was criticised so much, that needed so much minute examination in Committee in order that every clause might be just right and no clause in it that should not be in, and what do we find? We have had speech after speech from hon. gentlemen opposite, and we find that the leader of the Opposition has discussed government ownership in the abstract, discussed where he stood a year ago, and where 'he stands now, discussed" even somethiing about a sugar refinery-no, I think that was the hon. member for Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux). He also referred to the tariff, as did the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), who had, moreover, something to say about newspaper advertising, railway ties and the puffing of automobiles outside the door of this building. Every subject in the world has been covered except the clauses of this Bill; not one single criticism has been offered of the wording of a single clause, and no suggestion has been made as to any better way of handling the railroads of Canada, with the exception of that made by the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Robb).

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: This is merely a post mortem examination.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
The hon. member may be dead, but I can assure him I am not. We have had one suggestion. We have had a variety of opinions, and if hon. gentlemen opposite are seeking to fit themselves into the peculiar railway beliefs of various sections of the country they have made desperate efforts. We have had all! sorts and kinds of opinions and beliefs as to railway ownership, Government operation and everything else that would satisfy the most fastidious taste in the world. We have the leader of the Opposition, who does not believe in Government ownership as a principle, who boasts that he came to that opinion a year ago. We have the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), who says that the Liberal party were the pioneers of Government ownership in this
country. What does he think of his leader to-day, now that he has hauled down the flag and set up the standard of private' ownership? The Liberal party can no longer, under the leadership of the present incumbent, ever take the stand for public ownership in Canada. Then, also, we have the opinion o.f the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau), who is out-and-out opposed to Government ownership from beginning to end, and against that is the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), who is not only in favour of our operating those railways we already own, but who would lay violent hands on the Canadian Pacific as well.
Against them both, we have the hon. member for Maisonneuve who although he has been in public life for some twenty years comes here and confesses he has no opinion on the subject at all.
Government ownership is wise when properly applied, when the circumstances are such that it is sound principle to apply it, and it gets to be a sound principle proportionately as the competitive element is eliminated and the element of monopoly takes its place-in proportion as the industry is evolved into that stage of maturity in which it becomes a monopoly, and essentially for its best operation must be operated by the State. Here we have this case, the Government of Canada owning to-day approximately one-half the railway mileage of this country. We propose to operate that mileage aside from politics in a separate organization responsible to the Government of this country, responsible to Parliament; operating it, I repeat, aside from political influence wholly and entirely. That is what we propose. We have all the conditions here for Government operation. We have first the condition of necessity; we have every condition that can obtain. The hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon offers the only alternative. He says: Take the offer of the Grand Trunk. They are ready to exchange traffic with you at North Bay, and to run the Canadian Northern at cost. Run the Canadian Northern at cost? What would that mean? Take the railway paid for by the people of this country, every deficit of which must be met by the treasury of Canada, and place its operation in the hands of directors elected by a section of the electorate of England? Place in the hands of men irresponsible to Parliament, irresponsible to the Government, irresponsible to the people, the disposition annually of millions ol money of the people of this country? That is the only concrete suggestion we have

had all afternoon as an alternative to the Bill before the House.
Now, I say, we are going to compete with the Canadian Pacific. The Canadian Pacific has great charter powers and a tremendous organization, and in that competition we shall require the loyal support of every representative of the people of this country. We shall have to hold the balance in our legislative jurisdiction even, between the Canadian Pacific and our own road.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
I do not think it is necessary to go into any lengthy arguments as to whether we approve of government ownership, because the roads have been taken over, and it is now a question of the best ways and means of managing them. I think it will be found that the majority of the people of this country are of my own opinion. I do not think they are in favour of government ownership of roads that can be run otherwise. The experience of England and of the United States and other countries that have operated railroads under government ownership in recent years ought to be a lesson to us, unless this Government is of the opinion that it is very much smarter, and more capable than any of those other governments. Canada has bad public ownership of the Intercolonial for sojne forty years or more, and that road has never been able to pay its way. But we need not debate the question of public ownership, because both the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific are now in the hands of the Government.
The question which seems to be engaging the attention of the House most is the question of renewing some forty-four charters which have been granted to the Canadian Northern subsidiary companies, wisely or otherwise. I believe there are men on the other -side of the House who will agree with me that these charters should go through the regular course before being renewed; they should come before the Railway Committee of this House. The Railway Committee has often had to deal with renewal of charters, and whenever I attended the Railway Committee I never knew of one charter that was not cut down, or remodelled, or revised entirely.
I think one of the things that ought to engage the attention of this House is the reckless granting of charters for the construction of parallel lines. I do not believe there is anybody in this House who has any desire to hamstring or hamper the Northwest or any other part of Canada which is entitled to railroad construction, but I do hope that all hon. members of this House will oppose

the renewing of charters for parallel roads. If these charters came before the Railway Committee, the Committee could decide whether the roads would serve a useful purpose or not. I certainly think it is unwise to renew at one stroke of the pen these forty-four charters about which very little seems to be known even by the Government supporters. It has been insinuated that Quebec is jealous of the other provinces. I do not think that is the case at all. I think that Quebec and all other parts of Canada are in favour of granting charters for the development of any part of this country, but I repeat, these charters should come before the Railway Committee and be dealt with in the ordinary way. Plans and maps should be produced and the location shown, so that the Committee can see whether it is a case of paralleling another road .and whether any useful purpose will be served by renewing the charter. I am satisfied the Committee would deal fairly with these charters, whether they were for construction in the Northwest or any other part of Canada. I can see no reason whatever for bunching them all together and passing them in that form. While I have some confidence in the Government, I have not quite enough to hand over to them the handling of all these matters, about which their own followers seem to know very little.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: Is it not true that these charters have all been before the Railway Committee, and some of them on several occasions?

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
The argument we
have just heard from the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. MeCrea) is not one that I take exception to particularly. He is entitled to have the information that he asks for, but I think it has all been given from time to time before the Railway Committee. Possibly some of these acts were passed by local legislatures, but a large number have been before the Railway Committee and all the information that was required for the passing of the Acts was furnished to the Railway Committee and to this House at the time the charters were first obtained. That, I presume, is all in Hansard and on the records of the Railway Committee, and can be found by any hon. gentleman who has doubts as to the wisdom of the location of the lines or anything of that kind. It has been explained by the Minister of the Interior that when these lines are to be built this matter will again come up before the House and hon. gentlemen can object at that time to the voting of money to the building of them if

they are not thought to be to the general advantage of the people. Many of these branch lines are in territory requiring additional transportation facilities. We have heard from the West and hon. members speaking for that section of the country have made a very strong case as to why railways should be permitted to be built in Western Canada to serve settlers who have been waiting for years and now that the war is over and railway construction is about to begin again, it seems only reasonable that these companies should be rechartered. This perhaps would not be the usual procedure were it a private company but under ownership by the people there surely cannot be any objection. I might remind the leader of the Opposition when he asks whether it is not reasonable that hon. members should have all the information necessary that if he will recall the debates that took place in this House when the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific projects were under consideration the then leader of the Government, the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, said "We have mountains of information with regard to the building of these roads." Now we know what a mess was made in spite of all these mountains of information. Nothing has ever been projected in Canada that has cost the people so dearly and that apparently was so little needed. The hon. member for Guysborough told us this afternoon that they on hi3 side of the House were pioneers in public ownership, and he instanced the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental as evidences of that contention. He says these railways were built for the people. That surely must be news to all hon. gentlemen in the House at that time. No; they were building them for the Grand Trunk and not for the people. The Grand Trunk undertook to pay 3 per cent on the total cost of construction and I think my hon. friend from Guysborough will realize that it was not public ownership that was in the minds of the Government at that time when they constructed these roads, and it was not foreseen at that time we would be faced with the gigantic proposal on our doorstep to-day. I have not Hansard before me but I think the leader of the Opposition must have repeated the words "dirty babies" from fifty to a hundred times in the course of fifteen or twenty minutes. Might I ask him if as a judge of the court he does not think it would improve his vocabulary if he had occasionally referred to them 'as soiled infants.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: The hon. member had better take his leader to task. I was following his language precisely.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
I had not the pleasure of hearing the leader of the Government, but I will venture to say that the hon. leader of the Opposition used the term ten or possibly twenty times where the leader of the Government used it once. However, he repeated this expression until it became nauseating. It appears to me that we do not need mountains of information and the question before us is whether it is proper to place in public hands what has been previously owned in a private capacity. I have been on record for four or five years now as being in favour of public ownership of the great utilities. I believe the municipalities should own all their public enterprises such as street cars, electric lighting plants, telephone systems, waterworks, gas supply, etc., and in provincial matters I believe that wherever railways can be projected to the advantage of the province there should be provincial ownership, and the same principle should apply to national enterprises, which should be under public ownership. This may be a comparatively new thing in Canada but nearly all the nations of the world have recognized it for years. Almost every country in Europe and many of the more advanced of the South American republics, and also Australia, have for a long time been owners of their transportation systems. The only question to be decided is: Are the properties that we get such as we would invest our money in if we had our choice? I do not think that public ownership has had an opportunity to prove its value up to the present time. The Intercolonial Railway which has been held up as an instance has been one of -the greatest stumbling blocks to public ownership in Canada because it has been constantly unproductive and nonpaying. And the reasons are evident. First it was run as a political railway, and secondly its rates were such that no company could afford to haul freights for. Therefore, you cannot hinge a case on the Intercolonial Railway.
The hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) advocated the public ownership of all steamship lines plying to our ports. But I do not think this is an opportune time to bring that forward, and I am not going to put myself on record to-night as favouring the acquisition of any steamship lines at the present time; we have plenty of obligations on our shoulders already. This

has come to us, however, not because we were seeking it; it is a legacy from our friends across the way. They must realize that, and if they are familiar with the history of railway construction in Canada they will know that this was thought to be folly some fourteen, fifteen or sixteen years ago. But the Opposition, at that time the Government, won out. These railways were built and they are on our hands. What are we to do? We have to take them over and make the best job we can of it. We know that the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific were ill-advised undertakings from the start, that they have cost more than double the money that should have been put into them, and they have involved very considerable expenditure, especially in the Eastern section. Hon. gentlemen opposite talk of wanting information in spite of the mountains of information that we had at the time this load was projected. What did we have? We had estimates varying from $13,000,000 up to $60,000,000 for the cost of these roads. Those were the estimates of what the road would cost at that time. Every hon. gentleman knows what the result has been. They have cost the country four, or five hundred million dollars, and the end is not yet. The.Quebec bridge alone, one little link in the Transcontinental, has cost this country $27,000,000. I am glad to see my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) enter the Chamber because he knows that bridge very well. Twenty-seven million dollars is the figure which represents the cost of that enterprise to the people of Canada, and this whole road, as to which we had mountains of information when we started in to build it, has cost the country from three to four times as much as we were led to expect it would at the time the enterprise was projected. Can we, under those circumstances, expect that the roads in this country will pay if we invest in them four or five times what should have been spent? Neither can we make the railways pay in operation unless we set out to handle them as business propositions, and with respect to these roads, now aggregating somewhere in the neighbourhood of fifteen thousand miles, we must have a business administration. We must not pay higher wages than are paid on the ordinary railways of the country. We cannot afford to operate those railways at an excessive cost per mile; we will have to reduce our expenditures to such a point as will justify the freight and passenger charges that are levied upon them. If the wages are not sufficient then the freight and 
passenger rates must be advanced to a point where they will pay, not only all operating expenses, but pay for all betterments and all that sort of thing that is required.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: As a business man, does my hon. friend think that it will be possible to pay the same wages in future as in pre-war times?

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
No, I certainly do not. I hope that wages will never go back to where they were before the war. I believe they will not, and I trust that with the best of administration, and with getting the intelligent labour that we have in Canada, that although we pay our workmen perhaps double the wages we did before the war, that they are justifying that payment by the service that they render to the people of Canada in whatever walk of life they are engaged. I believe that we have an intelligent class of men. I believe we have as good railway men as there are in the world, but it must not be forgotten that we have a very difficult climate in which to operate railways, and you cannot, when the thermometer drops away below zero and there are four or five feet of snow on the ground, get the same results as in the southern countries where they have none of these obstacles to contend with. That is one thing that we must not forget.
Before my time is up I want to make a special reference to my own part of the province of Ontario, in regard to two or three of the charters that appear in this schedule: One is the Toronto, Niagara and Western Railway, and the other is the Niagara, St. Catharines and Toronto Railway. That is a section that is the most congested probably of Tailway enterprises in the whole of Canada. Between Hamilton and Toronto we have only the same rails that we had sixty years ago. It has been double-tracked, but the right of way is the same, and the Canadian Pacific and the Grand Trunk are using the same line. Between those two points there is probably heavier traffic than in any place in Canada. We want another road from Toronto just as quickly as we can get it, and I, for one, cannot understand the opposition of Sir Adam Beck to the project that has been laid down here, and that we have granted charters to the Canadian Northern to build.
I say that we want that road and we want it just as quickly as we can get it. I say that, being a strong advocate of the Hydro Electric, and a strong advocate of radial roads where they can be justified, but I cannot understand the opposition of Sir

Adam Beck to Mr. Hanna's proposal that this line shall be run into the Niagara district. We are not opposed, nor is the management of the National Railways, as far as I understand it, opposed to the radials. That antagonism should never arise, and it would not arise if proper thought were given to it. The radials of Canada and the electric roads of Canada, in my judgment, are quite on right lines, and I hope to see that branch of our railway enterprises very much increased. But I would suggest that instead of running these common trolley cars, which are apparently proposed on all these lines, they start out with electric engines that will draw a train and not simply a car. Shippers in our part of the country do not want to send goods on trolley lines and have to tranship twenty, thirty, or fifty miles away from where they started. They want to run from Brantford, Hamilton, or any place where those goods are purchased for the West-and we ship many thousands of cars per annum to the West-on lines that can carry the goods all the way through without transhipment. We want these hydro-electric roads and these radial roads to be feeders of the great national steam roads too. These might be electrified, which would be a great advantage in operation. I have visited New York State and there I found electric engines drawing fifteen or twenty cars and drawing more rapidly and getting headway much quicker than a steam engine can do. I only throw this out as a suggestion. I believe these radial roads, which are for the advantage of Canada, and certainly are an advantage to the district in which they are planted, should be subsidiary and should be feeders to this great national enterprise. I say, by all means, let us have this proposed road down to the Niagara river just as quickly as it can be built, where it will be able to secure international connection. A bridge should be built for this purpose across the Niagara river. Then this road, having proper terminals, and being in a position to feed itself from all quarters and from all parts of the country, it will be a paying enterprise, and instead of public ownership getting a black eye on the ground that it is no-t a paying enterprise, you will have railways under proper management, with proper freight and passenger charges and I believe you will find public ownership justify itself in Canada the same as it has done in almost every enlightened country in the world.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
Among all the measures that were announced in the Speech from the
Throne, surely the Bill we are now considering was one of the most important. It purposes to consolidate all the state-owned railways of Canada into one company, and to provide for a new system of management. If I were to accept the figures given the other day to the House by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) we have now a liability of over a billion of dollars in respect of these railways. It is to provide a proper system of management for this property, representing a billion of dollars, that we on both sides have been seeking information during the discussions which have occupied the last two or three days.
I do not fear contradiction when I suggest that since the beginning of the session no measure of such importance has been brought down by the Government, and it should by no means surprise anybody if, before committing the country to the policies mentioned in the Bill, we take a little time to study them carefully.
It is surprising, it is even amazing, to see the Government apply the closure at this early stage of the discussion, just to avoid giving information to the House and to prevent free speech in this, the people's forum. The Acting Prime Minister and the hon. member for Red Deer said the other day that there was more Liberalism on the right side of the House than anywhere else.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext: They were boasting.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
They were boasting, Mr. Chairman. Their very act gave them the lie, for at the same sitting of the House they announced the closure. Surely nobody will venture to suggest that that is a Liberal measure. During the fifteen years of the Liberal administration there were protracted debates, but never did that administration impose the closure; on some occasions they preferred to submit to the people the question at issue. The Minister of the Interior has accused the Opposition of unduly delaying this Bill; he failed to see what objection the Opposition had to put forward to the enactment of any of the sections. Sir, I will only say that there was no objection offered by the Opposition to the main features of this Bill, but we studied carefully and conscientiously how we could improve it. We simply asked for information from the Government, and we were sincere in our desire to help the measure along so far as we could do so consistently with public interest. We were blocked on clause 20 of the Bill, granting authorization to build forty-four branch lines, which lines are enumerated in the

schedule laid upon the Table on Friday last. What did we say? We did not ask the Government to withdraw the clause or the schedule, we did not say that we were against the schedule, hut we simply said that we were not in possession of sufficient information to allow us to pass judgment on the clause. Sir, we are asked to incorporate a company and to authorize it to build forty-four new branch lines. The Government says: You have no ground to object to such power being given to the company; we are not asking for power to build, we are simply_asking to revive 44 construction charters given by the various Legislatures or by this Parliament, and never will we go on with the construction unless Parliament is asked to vote the necessary monies. I submit, Sir, that that is not so. The very clauses of this Bill give the lie to the Minister of the Interior and to the other Ministers of the Crown when they assert such a thing. 'They say that even if clause 20 is passed the Government will not be able to go on with the construction work. Let them read clause 26 as enacted. That clause provides that the company, with the approval of the Governor in Council, may issue bonds, debentures and debenture stock from time to time in respect of the mileage of the line of railway which it constructs, acquires, owns or controls to the extent of $75,000 per mile. The Government will he authorized to pledge the whole Government railway system for the building of these additions, and yet the Minister of the Interior and the Acting Prime Minister the other day told the House that never could the Government go on with such construction without asking Parliament for the necessary funds.
I submit that clause 26 of this Bill gives the necessary authorization, and that no further power need be sought from Parliament for construction. The Minister of Immigration and Colonization confirmed my opinion when he said that the construction of many of these lines was going to be commenced in a very few weeks by subsidiary companies of the Canadian Northern System, and would be proceeded with, because by the enactment of this law, particularly by reason of section 26, they did not need any further power, and could issue bonds and pledge the whole of the Canadian Government Railway System for the amount of money so borrowed.
Now, Sir, if the enactment of clause 20 gives to the Government the right to con-
[Mr. Vien.'|
struct 44 branch lines-, and if clause 26, which has been approved, gives the Government authority to issue bonds to the full amount of $75,000 per mile, pledging the Canadian Government Railway system to that extent, we are surely justified in going into the matter very carefully. We have the Drayton-Acworth report, which tells us that we have been overbuilding .^railways in Canada, that this country has the greatest mileage per thousand of population of any country in the world, and that we have been foolishly building railways in the past; and the hon. member for Springfield has used that argument time and again in this House. The Acting Prime Minister the other day said that our railway system was overlapping everywhere, that there was a duplication of lines in many centres. Yet we are now asked to give the Government a blanket authorization to build 44 new branch lines, and we are not allowed the necessary time to inquire whether those branch lines are necessary, or whether they are duplications of existing lines. We are accused of unduly obstructing the work of the House if we ask to be allowed the necessary time to inquire into this matter before we vote upon it. The Acting Minister of Justice, pursuing his ordinary method, ridicules the Opposition because they did not venture to offer any policy or any constructive criticism on this clause. What did we say, Mr. Chairman? We simply asked tha1 the Bill be referred to the Railway Com m u e so as to allow a full investigation of the matter. This was a fair suggestion; this was not undue delay or undue Obstruction. When the minister says that no sound objection could be offered against the proposed law, it is evident that he did not pay sufficient attention to what has been said on this subject. He is wilfully leading the House into error.
