speechtext: Order. .1 must ask the hon. gentleman withdraw the expression, that a minister is wilfully leading the House into error.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
I withdraw the word "wilfully," and I say that he tries to induce the House to believe something that his own Bill contradicts. As a whole, the Bill has some good features. Everybody admits that the present management of the Canadian Government Railway system is poor and inefficient and that it can be greatly improved; in so far as this Bill provides for some improvement in that management, both sides of the House approve of it. But it is only fair that we should not allow the

Government to go on with the construction of these forty-four lines without more careful study and without more information being given to the House. The Acting Minister of Justice says that where these branch lines are to be constructed in the West there is a very extensive agricultural district, the settlers in which have to carry their products thirty or forty miles to reach the nearest railway station. Well, if we are going to build branch lines in every part of this country where the farmers have to travel thirty or forty miles to reach the nearest railway station, the resources ol Canada will not suffice. In many sections of the older provinces there are prosperous farming centres the people of which have to travel longer distances than those mentioned to get railway accommodation. Before we launch upon this policy we should look into it very carefully and be able to express our opinion intelligently, with full knowledge of the facts.
The Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder) said the other day that he was fully conversant with the various charters, because at the time of their enactment by the local legislature ne was a provincial minister. But most members of the House have not had an opportunity of going into the question fully. I wish to point out one feature of these charters which is calculated to cast some doubt upon the great utility, and the imperious necessity of building these branch lines. These construction powers were enacted by the provincial legislatures or by this Parliament some years ago, but they have elapsed. Although the provincial governments had held out the inducement of bond guarantees, the interested companies did not think that the traffic possibilities and the conditions generally in the district where these lines were to be built justified the construction of the roads. And now, suddenly, without giving due warning to the House, the Government comes down with legislation and tries to hurry it through without giving sufficient time for members to go into the matter. They want us to give a blanket authority to revive forty-four charters, although the private concerns who originally got the construction powers did not see their way clear to build the lines, and to take advantage 'M the grants of money that had been offered to them. We are asked to undertake the construction of these lines without taking advantage of these provincial grants. The Minister of Railways said the other night that in connection with the construction of these branch lines they would not call on the provincial treasury to make
the grants of moneys even though the provinces would benefit by the building of the roads. The Canadian Government Railway system will depend on Federal resources only.
Section 16 of the Bill provides that all the expenses of the company shall be paid out of the receipts and revenues of the railway, and that deficits will be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund. That is to say, the company will have the right to apply to all the purposes of the railway, even to the purchase of subsidiary companies, all the revenue and income of these railways, and if there -is a deficit they will obtain from the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada the necessary amount to cover it. Moreover, they will wait until next session before coming to Parliament to get authorization for and sanction of the payments already made by the minister under this section.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
Some of my hon. friends on this side of the House are very candid and naive. For instance, having left the House at eleven o'clock on Friday night, I was not present when the Acting Minister of Justice decided to play his favourite part, and dressing himself in the garb of chief executioner moved the application of the gag. Some of my hon. friends whom I met the next morning seemed to be surprised at what they thought was a very unusual incident. I was not surprised, however, at hearing the news. I thought the action of the Acting Minister of Justice was perfectly natural, and thoroughly in line with the spirit of the weathercock combination which at the present time the people of this country have to suffer as a Government. Why, Sir, if you consider that the Tory element of this Government has never failed yet in the high art of side-stepping issues, and in finding some camouflage or other to hide their spreading sores; if you remember that in 1911 in order to win the election they prevented the people of this country from deciding on the reciprocity issue by branding as disloyalty the simple idea of trade with the United States; if you look back at the conscription policy of 1917, when instead of letting the electorate vote on that issue alone, the Government wilfully and purposely unchained the devils of racial and religious strife;-remembering these things, you will not be surprised that in the year of our Lord 1919 the same element, true to its principles which had proved so effective in the past, is trying to abate the threatening storm of the western demands for lower tariff by fabricating for themselves a cloud of rails and locomotives which will burst at their will at the proper time and flood the western prairie.
This Bill is for the building up of a tremendous machine that will enable the Government to distribute millions of the people's money without the constitutional safeguards to protect the taxpayer against illegal expenditure. Clause 20, and the schedule annexed, will allow the Government or its namesake, the Canadian National Railway Company, to revive forty-four charters which their petitioners have not seen fit to utilize, for the building of railway lines of which we have no particulars and which may involve the spending

of enormous sums of money. And because, as tihe representatives of the people, sent here for the special purpose of seeing to the proper expenditure of public funds, we insist on having details before voting, we are not only refused the opportunity of giving an intelligent vote but are branded as obstructionists, and the gag is applied.
Sir, it was because the kings of France prevented the voice of the people from being heard that the monarchy went down in blood. The horrors of Bolshevism were caused by the choking of the representatives of the Russian people. When will this Government realize the dangerous unrest in this country? When will it avoid further irritation which may light the match that will start the fatal conflagration?
If the Bill we are now studying had a momentous object, if we were discussing in the hour of danger and stress a question which necessitated an immediate solution, probably we could realize the anxiety of the Government. But, Sir, we are asked not only to deliver without inquiry into the hands of the Cabinet unheard of powers, but to engage upon a policy that will bring Canada into the hands of a receiver. The United States are losing a million dollars a day by Government operation of their railroads. The earnings so far this year have been lamentably below even the guarantee to the companies. In England the gross receipt for last year were $440,000,000 less than the cost of producing transportation, including return on investment.
I am not going to take up the time of the House by reading articles that have been published recently, even so late as to-day, in the Montreal Star, on the question of Government ownership of railways; but yet I should feel guilty if I resumed my seat without giving this House the benefit of the opinion of the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) on Government ownership.
Speaking in the session of 1917 the minister said-page 4266 of Hansard:
My opinion has always been that if a man has opinions of his oiwn he had 'better assert them and try afterwards to convince the public that he is right. If he is not right, then he can let the public do what they have a mind to do about it. That may he a very independent attitude, hut I have always taken that view. I do not believe in public ownership of any kind. I do object to the Government going as far as they are going in respect of the proposed ownership of the Canadian Northern Railway system. The Minister of Finance stated that it was the intention to appoint a Commission
[Mr. Archambault-1
that should be subject to Parliament not to the Government. Well, if the Government can do that, it is a wonderful step in the right direction. But no jrnan who has lived in the Maritime Provinces all his life as I have done can honestly say that he is in favour of the public ownership of railways. I know that in Ontario there is a fetish in respect of public ownership. Men are worshipping the public ownership of everything. But it will not be many years before they come back to sound business principles. We had an illustration of that in the House the other evening. In Ontario they have had public ownership of utilities in the way of electrical energy-the greatest administration of electrical energy which the world has known. There is no doubt that the Hydro-Electric Commission of Ontario has done wonderful woTk. But (they are commencing to get up against the wall. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) was compelled to call upon his supporters to vote for an amendment to the general railway Act of Canada absolutely to put out of existence a competitor to the Hydro-Electric because it stood in the way of this Juggernaut. You would not find a better illustration in the records of Canada, from Confederation down to the present time of the failure of public ownership.
At page 5148 he said:
Many of my friends from Ontario and the West have been captivated by this public operation fad. I want to point out to them that it is the greatest farce and fallacy that ever was brought forward in any country. It is useless to talk about the Government operating railways or telephones, or electric light systems, or anything else as cheaply and economically as they can toe operated by private enterprise. Such a thing is not reasonable. Some of my friends from the West believe that if they can get this road operated by the Government, in some magic way they will get better service and better results. Possibly they think they may get a reduction of rates. No greater fallacy was ever held out to anybody. They cannot beat the roads down below what Is a reasonable business 'basis. Remember, you have another railway there, and you cannot cut the rates down below what is fair. No Government in Canada can operate a railway system in the Weist and make it pay with any lower rates than are being charged by the Canadian Pacific to-day. If the Government carried on the road for the next ten years at the same rates as the Canadian Pacific are charging to-day, instead of paying a ten per cent dividend as the Canadian Pacific is paying, it would go behind fifteen per cent or twenty per cent every year. No man knows this better than my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) who has had the longest experience in this House, with one exception, and who has lived in the Maritime Provinces. He has seen all the bungling and all the mismanagement, he knows exactly 'the condition of affairs, and he knows that every word I say is the truth. I am rather surprised that he has sat here as long as he has without raising his voice in opposition to the scheme.
Listen to the following sentence, Mr. Chairman:
Of course he may have been overmastered and overpowered by his colleagues.

Shall we say to-night to the Minister of Public Works that he has been overmastered or overpowered by his colleagues? I am awaiting his vote at 2 o'clock. It will enlighten us on the matter.

subtopic: DISCUSSION IN COMMITTEE UNDER CLOSURE RULE.
speechtext:
The hon. member (Mr. Ar-chambault) has presented a very dismal and pessimistic view of the nationalization of these railways. He says it is a fetish in Ontario where they have more or less adopted the principle of public ownership. I may tell him that the principle is not so new after all even in Canada, because it is recorded as early as the year 1850 at the time the Grand Trunk Railway was being built that the Government obtained permission, if they desired, to build the railway as a government railway. It appears that the opposition to this Bill is largely in keeping with the policy constantly pursued of obstructing and opposing every measure that is brought forward by the Government. The leader of the Opposition gibes the Government because it undertakes to provide, as he says, a home for these forty-four babies. Well, under ordinary circumstances that would be considered rather a philanthropic work, and I would suggest that the Opposition might well establish a school for the co-ordination of Liberal policies. Throughout this debate we have had demonstrated to us the fact that their policy is rather of tae Heinz variety-mixed pickles. There are so many different opinions and different policies that there seems to be no hope of co-ordination. The hon. member for Charlevoix-Mont-morency said this afternoon that the Government in 1914 were not justified in giving the assistance they gave to the Canadian Northern, and that the object was to protect the Canadian Bank of Commerce and the bondholders and other friends of the Government. In this connection I desire to quote the leader of the Opposition at that time, the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He said:
I said a moment ago that my intention was simply to summarize my views and the policy *which we have laid before the people on this question, and I summarize them in a few words. We must carry on this enterprise ; we cannot allow it to go by default; we cannot allow anybody or anything to come in which would imply anything detrimental to our credit in England; this enterprise has to he carried out; but, instead of carrying it out in the way proposed, we propose that we should carry it out hy other means.
That we should take absolute control of the enterprises and for that purpose I beg to move, seconded by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) : That the said Bill be not now read a third time, hut that it be resolved that
under existing circumstances no assistance should he given to the Canadian Northern Railway Company unless at the same time it is provided that the Government have power, within a reasonable time to acquire the ownership of the entire stock of the company at a price to Ik* fixed by arbitration, but not to exceed thirty million dollars.
On August 8, 1917, when the matter of the Canadian Northern was further being considered by the House, Mr. German, a member of Parliament at that time, gaye expression to these sentiments:
I wish to state, however, that I would have been in favour of a broader and more courageous policy, one which would have gone further in the way of public ownership of these railway systems than this proposition goes. Whatever we may have thought in the past in regard to public ownership of railroads, we must change our opinion at the present time, if we are to keep pace with the opinion of the public, because it is an undoubted fact that the wheels of democracy are revolving very rapidly. The democratic Juggernaut is advancing rapidly, and those who stand in the way will be crushed under Its wheels, whether they 'are lords, barons, knights or premiers.
	and I tell the Government they must
not stand in the way. The people are determined to have public ownership of these utilities, and it will come.
Sir, it would be possible to quote from Hansard for a period of some years back, as this subject has been frequently discussed in the House, showing inconsistency and variation in the opinions of hon. gentlemen opposite. I therefore can realize how difficult it is to believe that they are sincere in enunciating any policy-and in fact they have enunciated no policy in reference to the subject under discussion. I have not observed, during the few years I have been in this House, that the Opposition have been really from time to time endeavouring to assist by any constructive policy, the work of the Government. On the contrary, it has been their accustomed policy, on every occasion, to consistently oppose everything that the Government proposes; and the only reason that they are not to-day standing unanimously for the principle of public ownership is because the Government of the day has adopted that policy, and, consistent with the course which they have followed in the past, the Opposition are simply opposed to this measure.
We point with pride to the very great success that has attended the management of the Canadian Pacific railway; we are proud of that road, a id gratifled at the development which it has effected. The Canadian Northern railway, in the opinion of those who know the western country
i860

well, has within it the possibilities of success on its merits, and a prospective earning capacity equal to that of the Canadian Pacific. That road has now been taken over, and the Government ot the day is committed to its operation and is interested more closely than ever in its success as a national enterprise. As to these branch lines which have been provided for in connection with the future operation of the Canadian Northern, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the members from the West, those who have a personal knowledge of the different lines, and to the evidence which they have submitted with respect to the importance of the lines in question as feeders to this great system. Hon. gentlemen from Quebec have referred to the large expenditure that has taken place on the railways in the West and to the fact that their province has contributed a considerable portion of the cost. As a man from Ontario, I want to inform my hon. friends that our province, like theirs, has contributed its quota to the national development of our railways; but I desire to say to our friends from the West that we do not begrudge any expenditure, or any effort, that has been made with a view to developing that great western country. Sir, the possibilities which the further development of the West holds for the future lend every hope and every justification to the expansion of our railways-justifying the construction of the laterals, as it were, of these roads running north and south that have been spoken of to-night-until the various parts of the rich prairie lands of the West are provided with that railway accommodation necessary for the sending of their grain down to the trunk lines where it can seek the necessary outlets. I wish to quote some observations made by Mr. E. B. Biggar, a couple of years ago, when he was writing to the press a plea for the nationalization of Canadian railways. He said at that time: :
To allow matters merely to drift, while immigration is at a standstill and traffic arising from new construction in cities and settlements has largely ceased, and while long stretches of the new main lines are unable to live on local traffic alone, will simply invite a panic whose extent no man can measure. No Government charged with a responsibility for the commercial stability of the country can permit such an outcome.
There are two other main alternatives-further aid to the private railway companies now in difficulties, or the nationalization of the steam railways of Canada.
As to the first alternative, there is a deep-seated conviction that the people of this country have already been too grievously taxed to

pay for roads which have been extravagantly built, unwisely located from the standpoint of the general interest, and yet remaining to-day inadequately equipped and deteriorating in that equipment, not to speak of over-capitalization and the evils of railway corporation influence on legislation and on the public morals. Any further aid that would be sufficient to place the suppliant companies in the position that would be deemed safe from their own standpoint will raise a tide of public resentment, which, when added to the burdens involved in the war, will bring about the defeat of the party who imposes those burdens, and if the duration of the war is accompanied by a single bad harvest, this defeat will be all the more disastrous. No amount of blame thrown upon the other party for its past railway maladministration will excuse the error by which the last straw is placed on the camel's back.
Reasons For Nationalization.
The only way out which promises complete justice to the people, which insures a more patient resignation under the load of taxation which they will have to bear, and the method which will tend to the purification of public life by removing the greatest source of our political corruption, is by the immediate nationalization of the steam railway systems.
The following are some of the reasons.
The trend of modern opinion the world over has been steadily in the direction of the State ownership of and operation of railways, until out of the sixty-five countries in the world that have railways, no less than fifty-one have already adopted state ownership.
The character of this movement is remarkable in three respects:
First, the rapidity of the change-up to 1880 the world's mileage showed 10,000 miles under Government ownership, whereas now there are 230,000 miles, not counting military lines built since the war began.
The second feature of the movement is that during all this progress there has been no backwash towards private ownership. There are only three cases in the world of even partial abandonment of State ownership, and these are Peru, Cuba and Newfoundland. In the case of Peru, however, the Government takes the option of resuming possession at the end of a stated period.
The third feature of the drift towards State ownership is that it has been brought about in countries with the most diverse forms of government and types of people-from the absolutism of Turkey and the autocracy of Russia to the republics of South America, the referendum-governed country of Switzerland and the self-governing Dominions of the British Empire. Of the seventeen British Crown colonies and protectorates, no less than twelve operate their railways under direct Government ownership, while of the self-governing dominions, all outside of Canada have state ownership of all but a fraction of the total mileage.
A War Example.
A study of railway history will show an unprejudiced investigator that England, as the pioneer in both railway building and locomotive engineering, gave the world a false start in the direction of private ownership only because the men who composed the British Parliament in 1830 were, with few exceptions, obstinately blind to the possibilities of steam transport and, more pitiful to state, were careless of the needs of the common people. This defect of legis-

18G1
lative Insight is full of solemn warning to our own legislators in the present crisis of Canadian railway history. However, Great Britain has at last accomplished complete state control, as hy a miracle, and it is a certain deduction from the marvelous accomplishments of this State control, not yet revealed to the British public, that private ownership there has ended now and forever.
What happens when a people really wake up to perceive the true purpose of a railway in the national life is well described by A. G. Gardiner in " The War Lords ": " We have talked for generations about the nationalization of railways and have found the scheme too vast to tackle. We woke up one morning to find that the companies had been dispossessed of their control, and that the twelve hundred directors had been sent out to play, and that the whole railway system of the country was subject to the Government. And the transition seemed so natural and proper that no one even ' wrote to the papers about it.' At the impact of a great occasion the whole theory of railway ownership and control collapses without a murmur. It is seen that the sole ultimate function of the railway is to serve the State, and that anything that interferes with that function in a time of emergency is brushed aside as lightly as a feather. The lesson will serve for future use. By a flash of lightning, as it were, it has revealed the true relation of the railway to the community, and that relation is as applicable to conditions of peace as to conditions of war."
The Private Stronghold.
With this transformation in mind, it may now be said that among civilized nations of any importance they are but two remaining strongholds of private railway ownership in the world 

the United States and Canada. In the case of the United States, it does not require any profound study of railway literature or the drift of economic and political thought to convince an inquirer that the ever-tightening control of railways exercised by the Interstate Commerce Commission and the various State Commerce Commissions must find its logical conclusion in Government ownership; and the change is likely to come sooner than most people expect. This observation about the United States is, of course, only a forecast, but the statements regarding the other countries of the world are not speculations but accomplished facts, and if the forecast of the United States proves to be an accomplished fact, where will Canada stand? At the very tail of the procession struggling through a financial cataclysm due to the exploitations of its public resources by private corporations or struggling upwards to complete representative government and the unfettered exercise of its own sovereign functions?
Is it necessary to remind ourselves that the operation of a railway is a function of sovereignity? The public roads in times past were dedicated to the State, and hence the expressions King's Highway and Queen's Highway.
Those observations were made in the year 1916 on the railway situation, and the figures given there, which I presume are correct, show that the nationalization of public utilities is not a feature peculiar to the province of Ontario, but is spreading throughout the world. I do not want to say to my hon. friend from Quebec, when he speaks of our experience in the province of Ontario, that we have no regrets for having adopted the principle of public ownership of public utilities. I have no knowledge of any instance where it has not been an undoubted success; and there is no reason why under capable management it should not be a success. This management must be entrusted to the Government, and is fairly well provided for in the Bill. My hon. friend stated all the dire consequences that may follow on public management. The Government must manage our national system side by side with the Canadian Pacific Railway in the closest competition, and they have got to manage it efficiently or they cannot succeed. If they do not manage it efficiently we must appeal to the country, and the country will return those who will make Government ownership a success. I admit that it is a most difficult problem, but it is not the only difficult problem we have before us. Let me repeat a definition given by Murray Butler of the word " difficulty":
Difficulty is a mere word indicating the measure of effort necessary to attain certain objects -a bugbear to children and fools, but to men an incentive to greater exertion.

Section agreed to.
On section 29-power to acquire securities of other nmpanies:
Mr. CRQNYI ; I would suggest that the words which were struck out " and disposed of " at the end of the second line be restored, so that the clause will read:
The Company may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, acquire, hold, guarantee, pledge and dispose of shares-
It is quite possible that this company will acquire, or has already acquired, certain undertakings which later on it may desire to sell, and it would very much limit its efforts in that respect if these words were not contained in the Bill.
Mr. MEIG'HEN: I am disposed to think that the hon. member is right. He has drawn this to my attention, as has also the hon. member for Three Rivers. The latter gentleman, however, felt that the words " and dispose of " if introduced should be made applicable only to bonds, notes, securities and stocks. What the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn) has in mind i3 the desirability of providing that this company, should it find itself in possession of certain undertakings, such for example as hotels, might very conveniently dispose

of them, with of course, the consent of the Governor in Council, by selling the shares. Certainly the words " and dispose of " should be restored, and therefore I readily withdraw my amendment, which will leave the clause as it was originally. .
Amendment withdrawn.

The Government can revive forty-four charters, can undertake the construction of an endless number of railway lines all over Canada, and we are told that our security against extravagance or reckless undertakings will be the fact that they will have to come to Parliament for the money. But this company is vested with the power to issue stocks, bonds, debentures and every form of security known to the devices of an organization of this character; with these they can get all the money they want, and, upon the advice of the Governor in Council, invest it where they please without coming to Parliament at all. What assurance, then, have the people of Canada that these amounts will be put in the Estimates and voted by Parliament, and that the information for Which we .have been battling for the last four or five days will be given? We shall know nothing about these expenditures until, perhaps, years after the money has been spent and misspent, as much of the money of the people has been misspent in the past.
We on this side have been severely taken to task because we say it is unnecessary to revive these charters. I say now that it is unnecessary to revive them, and that there is no need for them, unless it be the promises that have been made by the Government to members all over the country that roads are to be built. The cat came out of the bag to-night when the member for Nelson (Mr. Campbell) told us that 350 miles were to be constructed this year. How does he know that, if the matter has not been discussed? This thing has been understood; the places where politics are to be played by the Government have been laid out, and members know it. The good, honest member for Nelson gave it out. The Minister of Interior (Mr. Meighen) tells us in one breath that the revival of these charters is a mere harmless thing, and in the next breath that work is to be done on every one of them this year. In Manitoba, to which, of course, the member for Nelson naturally gives most of his attention, there is evidently the promise that at least 350 miles will be built.- If as many miles will be built in the larger provinces, there will be at least 500 miles in Saskatchewan and as many more in Alberta. If the promises

are distributed anything like fairly, the Government will undertake to build this year about 1,300 miles of railway. I suppose they intend to sell these stocks and build the roads with the money they get from them, while Parliament will whistle and have nothing to do with it.
The Liberals of this country have always been anxious for development in the West. I have been in this House nearly fifteen years, and during that period most of the money that was expended in the West has gone through Parliament. I have yet to know of any Liberal who voted against the expenditure of one dollar of the millions that have been necessary for the development of the West. We have never refused anything for the development of that country. Besides what we did in the building of railways, we took our lives in our hands in 1911 and went down to an honourable defeat in a fight for freedom of trade for the people of the West. The policies and the principles of the Liberal party to-day are what they were then. The policy of the Liberal party to-day is honesty and integrity and proper administration of the country's affairs. In the conduct of the great chieftain, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who has been laid to his rest, during the years that he led the great Liberal party from 1911 down to the day of his death, what was there to show that he was for anything but for advocacy of the principles that he put forward during the many years that he was in power? Did he, as a leader, depart from those principles in any way? Not at all. He was a Canadian from Scatarie to Vancouver. He was not a sectional man, and we are not sectional men to-day. We are pot for Ontario against Quebec or for the West against the East; we are Canadians, from one ocean to the other. If there is necessity for building railways in any province of the West and we have the means, we are here to do it; but we want to know what we are doing; we want to know where we are going to build them, what provinces they will be in, and whether they are going to meet the needs of the people. But the Government is putting on camouflage. We are told:	You shall not know where the
roads are to be built; it is not our policy to be honest with the people; it would not do for the people to know what is going on. Instead of standing up manfully in this House last Friday night and doing as he should have done when this information was asked for, the leader of the House talked about " dirty babies " and about everything else except the question that we were discussing. He tried to create a camou-

flage by saying to the people:	I am for
public ownership, but hon. gentlemen opposite are not. He seems to forget his own record, when, by his own will and by his own wrong-doings, perhaps, he became an administrator and had that little property in his hand, like Naboth he was absolutely and entirely for private ownership. My hon. friend is everything by turns, and nothing long; he is godly when godliness pays. It does not worry him very much to change from public ownership to private ownership and back again if that is necessary for him to steer the head of the ship into a safe harbour. I agree with him that the ship is water-logged, that the sails are torn, that the compass is out of order and that the craft is absolutely unseaworthy and should take no further cargo on board. I am not surprised, therefore, that the minister is shifting from one leg to another in order to avoid telling the people what the situation really is.
Why, it is provoking, at least to an old member of the House like myself, who has been voting consistently, whether in Opposition or supporting a Government, for everything that was necessary for the general development of this country from .one shore to the other, that we are to be told by the leader of the House, because we questioned closely into the methods under which they are going to handle the railroads of this country: Why, you are opposed to public ownership altogether and we are going to raise that issue in the country and to censure you on your narrowness and lack of intelligence and vision in this great country. If there was vision, if there was intelligence, if this country has become the great country that it has, it was by the vision and energy and foresight and policy of development of the party to which I have the pride and honour to belong.
In 1896, the Conservative party handed us a country that was bankrupt at every turn of the road. We have developed that country in its every policy; we have bettered its railway policy, its financial policy, its immigration policy. We have built it up; we have driven the prairie rabbit and the buffalo out of the country, and we have substituted men, and government, and provinces in their place. If hon. gentlemen are out of their element now until they get back the prairie rabbit and the buffalo, we cannot help that, but we purpose, whenever we have the power and the right to do so, carrying forward that great policy of the Liberal party which
we created when we took power in this country and which we carried forward to its very fullest in 1911, when there was no1 criticism from hon. gentlemen opposite except to leave well enough alone; that every phase of business in the development of this country was going on as well as could possibly be expected; that nothing further could possibly be required, and that we were not wise in trying to better conditions. Every condition for which we fought at that time and every condition which was strenuously opposed by hon. gentlemen opposite, have since been admitted by them to be all right. They admit now that our policy on the trade question, that "truck and trade with the Yankees," was a most excellent thing, and they could find no possible fault with it. They are taking it to their bosoms and their hearts now, and they are obliged to go down to the Yankees to get the money which they cannot get elsewhere.
The particular point with which I wanted to deal was about the revival of those charters. It has been continually pointed out that there is a necessity for those charters. If local charters of this kind, or whatever they are, were necessary for the building of roads in the West, I would say: Certainly, revive them. But we have the Government Railway Act, chapter 36 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, which gives every conceivable power to the Government of this country to build a railway anywhere in the whole land from ocean to ocean; we have chapter 37, which is the Railway Act, which gives further power to companies and Governments to build railways; and we have this Bill which we are putting through the Committee now, with sections 13, 23, and 26, all providing for the building of railways by the Government and under Government control, where the Government thinks proper, after Government engineers have laid them out and given us information. What is the matter with that? Why should we be dragging along with us those 46, or 48, or 50, old charters with bargains and encumbrances about them with which we should not be bothered at all? If whoever are going to take charge of this work are going to make a success of it, we must start them out with a clean sheet. If the old management is an encumbrance to them, let us cut out the old management. Mr. Hanna is, I believe, a very excellent man, but circumstances make men, and ii it is necessary to have other men and to cut loose from Mackenzie and Mann influence,

surely we can find in this country men who will take charge of the work and do it as well as anybody trained in the school of Mackenzie and Mann. It is a stigma upon our railroads with which we have been dealing for fifty years if we have not one man as experienced as those trained in the school of Mackenzie and Mann. The old saying is: If thine eye offend thee, pluck it out; if thy hand offend thee, cut it off; it is better for you to go to heaven with your hand off or your eye out than to go to hell with your eye in and your hand on. That is what I say about the influences and combinations and ramifications of Mackenzie and Mann;- cut them off. We are to-day, I am told on the best authority, buying coal from Mackenzie and Mann upon old contracts that were made ten years ago between the Canadian Northern and themselves. One branch of Mackenzie and Mann owns coal; another branch owns a railroad; and Mackenzie and Mann railroad was buying Mackenzie and Mann coal, and we have taken over the contract which they had with themselves. The Minister of Railways shakes his head wisely and says: It is not in the public interest that we should tell that we are getting coal from Mackenzie and Mann. Perhaps it is not. It is certainly not in the interest of Mackenzie and Mann to disclose those things. We should cut off those things and give the new combination of men that are going to take charge of the Government railways a clean sheet. So doing, we should not embarrass them, we should give them no reason for excuses. Otherwise, they will come back here in a year or two and say: This is a failure because you encumbered us with 44 lines of railway which we had to build, which we could not use; we were compelled under an old contract to buy ties at three prices and to buy from Mackenzie and Mann coal that was no good and to pay three prices for it and to haul it hundreds of miles further than we should. We do not want excuses of that kind. Give them a free hand; start them anew, and if they make a success, God be with them.

Hon. J. A. CARDER (Minister of Immigration and Colonization) moved the second reading of Bill No. 52, to amend the Immigration Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, when this Bill had its first reading I explained to the House very briefly the effect and purpose of the amendments which it proposed to the existing law. As these amendments are submitted for the purpose of carrying out certain policies which the Government have agreed upon, I think I should ask the indulgence of the House while I discuss in a general way the immigration problem which confronts Canada. Since the outbreak of the war in 1914 our people have had ample time and opportunity to consider a great many of the problems with which we are confronted, and one of these problems in which our people are particularly interested is the problem of immigration.
I think it will be generally conceded that in the past a great many mistakes have been made. Our people generally agree that in regard to the admission of people to this country for many years past there have been mistakes made and that care should be taken to prevent these in future.
We have a great many complicated problems on our hands to-day. We have many social, educational and industrial

questions. These in a very large measure, to my mind, reflect the policy which has been pursued in this country for twenty or thirty years. If the Canada of to-morrow is to be what it should be, the first essential is that this House should very carefully consider and weigh what our policy is to be in the future.
Since I have become Minister of Immigration and Colonization a great many suggestions have reached me from people throughout the length and breadth oi Canada; letters and petitions have poured in from many sources. All sorts of suggestions have been made. To my mind this indicates very clearly that our people are taking a deep interest'in this matter and that they are anxious that this Parliament at this session should review the whole situation with the object of strengthening our immigration laws in order that we may avoid in the future the mistakes which have been made in the past.
The suggestions which have come to me may be roughly divided into two large classes. In the first place, there are those who hold that Canada should be reserved for Canadians-for Anglo-Saxons. They maintain that this is a British dominion, that it must remain British and that only those who are British should be permitted to knock at our doors and enter. There are many who hold that view. On the other hand, there are those who hold the view that we should maintain the open door, not as wide open as in the past, but that there should be certain clear-cut and definite restrictions. They say there should be restjictions applicable to all people as regards health, mentality, earning power, character, and matters of that kind. There are those who hold that, in so far as certain nationalities are concerned, they should be absolutely excluded. Then again, some contend that, as regards still other nationalities, they should be admitted to Canada only in limited numbers; in such numbers as the country is able to absorb and assimilate. In reference to these three suggestions, I am sure that there will be very divergent views in this House and differences of opinion as to the policy that should be pursued. I am sure that every hon. member recognizes that throughout the country very divergent views are held on these points. The problem is an exceedingly complicated and delicate one. It is not one easily solved; nor is it easy to satisfy the great majority of opinions on account of the very great diversity of thought that exists with respect to what should be done.
Just for a moment or two I would like to speak of the necessity for increased population in Canada. I am sure it must be selfevident to every one who understands our economic situation that our greatest need is population. I might cite only a few reasons-in the first place, we all know that as a result of the war we have piled up, to say the least, a very considerable national
debt.	.
It means increased taxation, but as to our being able to take care of the burdens which have been placed upon us as the result of this war I have no doubt whatever. The other belligerent nations have similar debts, and our position in comparison with their position is favourable. Our debt is no larger in proportion, and when we consider our vast resources and the opportunities presented for their development, I have no hesitation at all in saying that we should be able to take care of that burden.
The question, however, arises as to how that burden can best be taken care of. We have been preaching economy, increased production, thrift, and all those things will help very materially. But notwithstanding all the talk about thrift, to what extent have our people been saving during the last two or three years in order that this situation might be met? So far as I can see there has been very little done in the way of saving, and it seems to me that if our war burden is to be taken care of it can best he done by an increase in our population and an increase in our production. Every additional person who comes to Canada will help to lift the burdens of those who are now here. During the course of the next few years an extra one or two million people will in a large measure make the situation very much easier in so far as taxation is concerned. Therefore I think it is essential that our efforts should be directed to a large extent during these coming years to attracting as many settlers as we possibly can.
During the last few days we have had a discussion on the railway situation. The burden the nation is carrying in that respect is a colossal one. There is no doubt that our transcontinental lines are over developed. We have more railways in a sense-I am speaking of transcontinental railways-than we actually need at the present time. I do not say that they should not have been built. Do not misunderstand me. I have faith in Canada and in the future of these lines, and the time will come in my opinion when every

one of them will pay. But at the present time they are a burden on the country. We are called upon to pay out millions of dollars every year in excess of earnings, and that condition will continue for some years to come.
What is the solution? There is only one solution in my judgmenG-tpeople and production. We must create traffic for these lines, and that traffic can only be created by filling up our vacant spaces, thus insuring increased production of all the various commodities which this country can produce. We have had some discussion in reference to branch lines. Branch lines are very essential throughout all sections of Canada, in my view, if we are to secure the increased production to which I have referred. In Western Canada production has been retarded enormously, simply because we have not sufficient branch lines. Undoubtedly, if our enormous railway obligations are to be properly taken care of there is only one way to do it, I repeat, and that is by increasing our population, which will be naturally followed by increased production.
There is another reason why we need population. In addition to the obligations which the Federal Government is carrying, our provinces and our cities are carrying very heavy obligations, more particularly our cities. In Western Canada, and I am sure the same is true of Eastern Canada, most of our urban communities have mortgaged their future; they have made civic improvements and carried on large undertakings ahead of their actual requirements, and they are feeling the burden of taxation. There again I think we can look for only one solution to that problem-unless the lands back of these cities are settled, which settlement will bring in its train increased production, these cities will have to continue to bear their present heavy burdens. So for that reason it is very essential that we should see that our rural population is increased just as rapidly as possible.
I might refer also briefly to the situation as it exists in respect to our manufacturing and industrial concerns. One of the main reasons why our industries are not established on as firm a basis as they should be is because we have a very sparse population, and consequently our home market is very restricted. If we had a gresfter population we would have larger markets for oui products at home and abroad-
Hear, hear.

-and these industries
would be established on'a sounder basis. 
In the case of our smaller industries their overhead charges are excessive and on account of the smallness of their output they cannot compete with larger industries. So the more people we bring to this country the larger home market we will create to say nothing of a more extensive foreign market all of which will tend to place out industries on a proper basis.
Are you speaking of the farming industry too?

I am speaking of all industries. We all know that we have enormous national resources of all kinds the products of the field, the forest, the mine, and the sea. These^have been developed to a certain extent, and I think it can be said generally that they are developed in proportion to our population. We have billions of dollars, lying dormant in our natural resources, and if those resources are to be developed for the good of the nation, there is only one way to develop them: we must in the first place have the necessary capital, and in the secondi place we must have the necessary people. At present we are all busy in various directions, and these natural resources will never be developed as they should be until the necessary population is brought into the country. Our population at present is too 'sparse.
Has my hon. friend any idea of the approximate population of Canada at the present time?

We invited those people here; we sent across the seas our agents who went into their communities and explained to them the possibilities of this country of ours; how they would be welcomed here, how well they could get along and all that sort of thing. And when we brought them here, and scattered them throughout Canada, we left them entirely alone. Our policy in that regard has been nothing short of a tragedy. We have done very little to familiarize them with our laws; we have no policy in our country to Can-adianize them; we have simply let them drift, and, therefore, we should not blame them. Thousands of those people came to Canada with the very best of intentions, and we know that they left their homes across the sea because they looked upon this democratic country as one in which they could make their homes and become Canadian citizens. But what have we, as a people, done to familiarize them with our institutions, to improve their habits and customs, to increase their earning capacity, their productive power? We have done practically nothing.	.
Let me give a very simple illustration. There are in this House men who know whereof I speak. We have in Western Canada somewhere in the neighbourhood of fifty or sixty or seventy-five thousand people called Galicians, of whom hon. members have heard, and who are sometimes called Euthenians or Ukrainians. They come mostly from Austria where we sent our agents and spent large sums of money in inviting them to come here. We brought them to Canada, carried them on our trains away out into the West and dumped them down on the prairies, giving them homesteads. Those people were absolutely unfamiliar with our laws, our customs, our mode of living, our methods of carrying on business. They did not know how to farm; they knew nothing about farm machinery; they knew nothing whatever about our municipal and school systems. What did the Government of Canada do to help those people? Again I say,, practically nothing. I was in their settlements in the early days, and many of those people were exceedingly poor, most of them in the early stages living in mud houses. Some of them actually dug holes in the ground and lived in those holes until they got a little ahead and were able to put up mud houses. They struggled along without any assistance from any one; nobody went near them. Instead of being helped, protected, advised, and assisted, they were the prey of every shark in the community. They

were simply allowed to drift. The wonder is that they ever got along at all, that they ever succeeded. It was only by hard work year after year that they eventually did succeed, but no credit for that is due to the people of Canada who invited them to come, to this country to be Canadian citizens. That illustrates the policy that has been followed for the last 25 or 30 or 40 years, by all Governments in this country as regards those foreign-born people, and it is no wonder that we have trouble on our hands at the present time.
The proper policy that should have been pursued in the past and that must be pursued in the future if people of that class or of any class coming from foreign lands are to be assimilated, is that we must see to it that every possible assistance is given to them to become Canadian citizens and that steps are taken to make them familiar with our laws, customs, municipal, and school systems.
I do not wish to leave a false impression upon the House. During the course of the past few years our people have wakened up to the situation, and some work is being done. In Western Canada the whole situation has, in some respects, been changed during the last three or four years. The war in its very early stages brought home to our Governments, our municipalities, and our people in the West that they had a real problem on their hands and that they had to get down to business if that problem was going to be solved. As a consequence, steps have been taken, and measures are now in course of preparation that will go a long way towards Canadian-izing the foreign-born people settled in Western Canada. When we go into Committee on the Bill, I shall, if the question is raised, be only too glad to give to the House some information that I am sure will be quite new to hon. members who are not familiar with the existing situation in the West.
Do I understand the minister to say that the Galicians have not made good citizens?

I did not say that.
When one considers the handicaps under which these people have laboured for a good many years, the material progress they have made in the way of production is amazing. Thousands of them have made good settlers, from the purely material standpoint, but from the standpoint of good citizenship the situation is very largely a failure.

I come now to the question: where shall we look for our immigration in future? "What people are we to admit to our citizenship? That is not the easiest question in the world to decide. No nation lives absolutely to itself: all nations are more or less inter-dependent upon each other. The flow of trade and commerce and the relationships that exist between the various countries of the world are such that it is not an easy matter to close the door absolutely against any class, no matter how much we might wish to do so. Hon. members know that all nations are very jealous of their citizenship, and of the rights and privileges of their nationals wherever they may go. Moreover, all nations claim equality; they claim that no nation should be specially favoured over other nations, and that element naturally enters into any discussion of this problem.
I had intended to bring this Bill down earlier, as I know the interest that is taken in it both in the House and in the country. There was a possibility, and there still is one, of the question of immigration being considered by the Peace Conference and of certain conclusions being reached by that Conference. I had intended not to bring down this measure until we knew definitely what the Peace Conference was going to do in connection with this matter. But from my reading lately I do not think there will be' anything in the Peace Treaty regarding the question of immigration. Apparently, it is to be left to each nation to determine its own policy. Our people have been, shall I say impatient. They have been very anxious for the Government to get busy on this question, and with reason. I should like to remark, however, that there is just a possibility at the present time of our being swayed and perhaps swept off our feet by our feelings. I think we should endeavour to avoid that at all costs. We should approach this question in the broadest possible way, and whatever conclusions we may reach we should endeavour to see that they are sane conclusions. I think that is very important, because otherwise we might make mistakes that would have far-reaching effects. Let us bear that in mind throughout all our discussion, and let us try to make a law of such a nature that it will not give unnecessary offence to the people of any country in the world.
Would my hon. friend explain why there has been such a pronounced objection, at all events in the press, against the admission into Canada of the Hutterites?

I shall come to that in a moment. I was going on to say that . in framing our immigration policy the underlying principle should be briefly this: We should have the absolute right as 4 p.m. a nation to determine for ourselves what our future citizenship shall be, and while we lay that doctrine down for ourselves we should be prepared to concede it also for every other nation. We should know best what classes of people we need in this country and what classes we can best assimilate. We should know best what numbers of these people we can take care of. We should not be asked to throw our doors wide open to receive any number of any class of people who may desire to come to Canada. We cannot afford to do that. If we are to protect our citizenship we must be most careful not to attempt to absorb more of these people than we reasonably can. I would also go this far: We should not be tied down by any treaties or agreements that may exist of which we have had no knowledge or to which our consent has not been given. If there are any such treaties or agreements in existence, it seems to me we should endeavour to get them out of the way just as quickly as possible. For this is a domestic question affecting Canada, and we, and we alone, should determine the class of people that we are going to ask to become citizens of this country. I do not think anything should be allowed to stand in the way of our carrying out that policy.
But we are not bound by the treaties of Great Britain?

Yes. I say that if
any treaties or agreements of that nature-
I know of none-stand in the way, we should endeavour to have these treaties or agreements removed in order that we may determine this question for ourselves. That doctrine was agreed to when we were dealing with the Hindoo question at the conference last year. The British Government and all the Dominions assented to the proposition that this was a domestic problem, which the self-governing Dominions should have the right to determine for themselves.
My hon. friend might go further. Some years ago we had Great Britain denounce certain treaties curtailing the rights of Canada.

Bearing these things
in mind, the Government has endeavoured

to determine what shall be our immigration policy to meet the existing conditions ' in this country.
In the first place, as regards all nationalities and races the world over, including Great Britain and the Dominions, our existing law and this Bill provide for the exclusion of certain prohibited classes, which include persons suffering from some loathsome disease, or who are otherwise unhealthy, and those of weak mentality, or of bad character, and criminals and others of that kind. The existing law, and it has been extended by this Bill, provides for the creation of prohibited classes, and we think that so far as all nationalities are concerned these undesirable people should be excluded from Canada. I do not think that any objection can toe raised to that. We purpose to extend those provisions and to establish the necessary administrative machinery to ensure that that law shall be effectively and efficiently carried out. This is going to cost some money. One of the reasons why in the past some have entered the country who should not have come in is simply because the necessary money was not expended to provide the machinery adequate to keep them out. If the law in this respect is going to be properly effective then this country must be prepared to expend money for the purpose. We must provide the necessary machinery and the necessary experts, and we must have a sufficient number of inspectors and other officers to see that the doors are properly closed [DOT]against the prohibited classes. It is the intention to extend to five years, as is the case in the United States, the time during which undesirables who may get into the . country, or who may prove to be undesirable after they have entered, may be deported. Heretofore the period has been only three years, but I am sure the House will agree that the extension is proper. We are going to adopt that five-year period here, not because they have it in the United States, but simply because we think it is necessary that there should be a longer period than three years in which to ascertain whether or not many of these people who get into the country are desirable.
A very large portion of the Bill is taken up with provisions for greater responsibilities so far as transportation companies are concerned. We are increasing the responsibilities which rest upon them and the penalties to which they will be liable.
Do you provide for adequate health inspection on the other side ti the water?
That is a matter I should like very much to discuss in Committee. There are two sides to that problem. -

My hon. friend will understand that when an immigrant is brought over the Atlantic to Canada if he is not acceptable to the health authorities on this side it is a hardship to send him back. It is better to prevent the evil than to have to cure it.

As the law exists it is
not very hard to send them back. There is no trouble in sending them back, because if a transportation company brings a person of that class to Canada, and we stop him at the border, or if he enters and it is discovered that he is undesirable, we throw upon the company the responsibility of taking him back. They are doing that every day.	_

But it is a hardship you can prevent.
GMr. CALDER: It is a hardship to the transportation company.
Mr. LEMIEUX nnd to the emigrant- you separate him from his family.
That is a question we may very well consider in Committee. The best method of dealing with that phase of our immigration problem is a question worthy ot serious consideration.

I do not wish to infringe on the rules of the House, but the reason I call the minister's attention to that particular phase of the subject is that I once saw in Quebec a case of great hardship. 1 saw a family composed of several members, two of whom had tp be deported because they could not be accepted by the health authorities, and it was a heart-breaking scene.

We can go into the details of that in Committee. In addition to prohibiting the entry of undesirables, we must take steps and we have taken steps to protect ourselves against increased unemployment conditions in Canada. At all our ports of entry since the armistice we have been discouraging the entry of skilled and unskilled labour. We have been shutting them out on every pretext and righthly so. Some months ago an Order in Council was passed prohibiting the entry of skilled and unskilled labour from Asia to British Columbia. That Order in Council is still in f tree and it is proposed to keep it in force.

What about the land grants that were given to the Canadian Northern Tailway for the purpose of building the branch lines of that system? Now that the railway system is the property of the Government, do I understand that these lands will become a part of the public domain and be available for immigrants?

These lands, I understand, are still handled by the railway company. They are, It is true, the property of the people of Canada, but the railway company has its own lands department. They are handling these lands and seeking settle-, ment for them. They are settling these lands just as was done by the railway company but 'they are doing it for the people of Canada.
Practically the Government?
Practically the Government. The lands have not come back to the Government itself and they are not administered by any department of the Government but by the railway company.
These lands have reverted to the Dominion of Canada?
They have in a sense; they are the property of Canada.
Should they not be under the administration of the Department of Immigration?

That is a question of
policy and it is one that might very well be considered and discussed. These lands are being held by the company itself for settlement purposes. Whatever moneys are derived from these lands that are sold will

belong to the people of Canada. The question of whether the land shall be transferred to one of the departments and administered by it is one that might very well be discussed and considered.
I desire to point out as briefly as I can what the position is because I find there is a great deal of misunderstanding in the country regarding some features of our existing law. Many people have a very erroneous idea in regard to this and for the information of the House I would like to give some information along these lines.
When the armistice was signed an Order in Council was put through, under section 38 of the Act, prohibiting the entrance of all persons from enemy countries-Germany, Austria, Bulgaria and Turkey. That order is still in force and it is intended to keep it in force.
I have already pointed out that an Order in Council is in existence prohibiting the entry of skilled and unskilled labour from Asia; at least skilled and unskilled labour is not permitted to enter our British Columbia ports, which means that, in so far as this class is concerned, we are excluding it. I will come in a moment to the Japanese and Chinese. The prohibition that now exists enables us to shut out all nationals of all countries who do not come directly to Canada from the country of their origin. That is the existing law. I might explain that by means of an illustration-a man we will say, leaves Portugal, comes to the United States and then desires to enter Canada. We can stop him from doing so because he does not come direct to Canada from Portugal. Recently-and we intend to continue that system-we have been shutting out people of that class. All persons of enemy nationality residing in the United States, and who have not become United States citizens, are shut out under that order because they do not come direct to Canada from the country of their origin. Consequently, nationals of enemy countries have not been entering Canada during the war or since the armistice has been signed. It is intended to keep that Order in Council in operation.
At the present time the department is carrying on propaganda, or publicity work only in two countries-Great Britain and the United States. Some very exaggerated reports have appeared in the press in relation to the work which we propose to carry on in the United States during the present year. I have seen it repeated time and again that we proposed spending a million dollars on advertising in the United States. There is not a word of truth in it. We are

not proposing to carry on our work there to any greater extent than has- been done in the past.
Why not in Belgium?

As far as the continent of Europe is concerned, we, early in the war withdrew our agents and closed our . offices. The question has been asked: Why [DOT]should we not re-open them now? The answer is very simple. We might go in there and carry on publicity work to educate those people as to the advantages and possibilities of Canada, but I think there is very little possibility of getting them to come to Canada for many months yet owing to shipping conditions. There are thousands upon thousands of British people who would like to emigrate to Canada if they had the opportunity, but conditions are such as to make that absolutely impossible. Until our soldiers and their wives and children are brought home we must utilize all available ships for the purpose of bringing them home. It is estimated that there are in the neighbourhod of 30,000 soldiers' dependents still in Great Britain; we have brought home about 15,000; so you can understand the problem that we have on our hands.

The answer given
by my hon. friend is quite plausible, I am aware that shipping conditions would not at present permit of any exodus from continental Europe. But the reason I mention Belgium is that I gather from a report made by the agent for the province of Quebec that there is a possibility of a very strong tide of emigration from Belgium to America, and that many Belgians are ready to settle in this country if they are offered proper facilities; and, as my hon. friend is aware, they are a good farming class.

Yes. I am quite
sure in so far as the northern countries of Europe are concerned we will be able, if we so desire, when the proper time comes to secure many thousands of first-class settlers, but I think my hon. friend will agree with me that the time is not yet ripe. We will have to consider shortly what we will do in the way of carrying on publicity work in those countries, looking to the future rather than to the immediate present.
Will the hon. minister say why he has not extended his publicity work to Ireland? Is it because of the Sinn Fein movement there just now?
No. I mentioned we were carrying on publicity work in-
Great Britain.

Ireland is part of
Great Britain. As a matter of fact we have two important offices in Ireland, one in Dublin and one in Belfast. I mentioned the fact that we have closed all our offices and withdrawn our agents from continental Europe. There is a desire on the part of a good many thousands of British soldiers to come to this country, and I think they will make very excellent citizens. The problem, however, of placing them upon the land will be somewhat difficult. Many of them will not have had previous training in farm work, and on account of the provision made for our own soldiers I am inclined to think that until we have succeeded in placing a larger number of our men on the land, we must go a little slow with the other problem.
Mr. LEMIEUXc Lord Grey some years ago had a plan for settling British sailors in British Columbia. I wonder if the department has acted upon that plan.

I have not heard of
it at all. The House is aware of the fact that some years ago an arrangement was made whereby a limited number of Japanese would be permitted to enter Canada. I have gone into the situation very carefully, and I can tell the House that the agreement has been lived up to by the Japanese Government, to the letter. As a matter -of fact, taking the figures for the last four or five years, there are in the neighbourhood of 400 or 500 fewer Japanese in Canada to-day than there were in 1914.. Recently I have been in constant touch with the Japanese consul here, and he is very anxious to co-operate with the Government in every way possible in order to prevent the situation on the Pacific coast becoming any worse than it is. In fact, he has taken the matter up with his Government in order to insure that as few people as possible shall come from his country during our period of reconstruction.
In so far as the Chinese question is concerned, personally I am inclined to the view thait a very great mistake was made in arranging for a head tax. It seems to me that by so arranging we have simply commercialized the business of bringing in Chinese immigrants, and I believe we would have fewer Chinese coming in if that head tax had never been imposed. As it is, individuals and companies have become interested in advancing this head tax to young Chinamen desirous of coming to this country, and, if my information is
correct, these young men live in semislavery here until such time as that head tax is paid back probably twice over.
That is true.

When we go into
this matter it may be found advisable to abolish that head tax and do what has been done with the Japanese Government, endeavour to make some arrangement whereby the number of their nationals coming to Canada can be restricted. That can very well be considered when we get into Committee.

I notice the Bill excludes immigrants who believe in the overthrow of the Government of Canada. I do not know how far the country is ready to endorse that, but my purpose in rising is to ask the hon. minister: how is he going to ascertain what a man's political belief is?
I think that question can be best considered when we come to the clause in the Bill.
Would the hon. minister-
