I just wanted to say that if the clause in question is directed against Irishmen, every Irishman is "agin the Government."

The hon. member for Maisonneuve sometime ago referred to the question that has arisen recently in Western Canada with reference to the admission of a class of people known as Hutterites. The matter has interested a very large number of our people, not only as regards that sect but other peculiar sects, such as Mennonites and Doukoboxs, and the Government has given a good deal of attention to that problem. It appears to me that the policy to be laid down is this: We should be free to shut out any class of people that we do not think can be readily assimilated.
If there are any peculiar peoples the world round whose customs and beliefs, whose ideals and modes of life are dissimilar to ours and who are not likely to become Canadian citizens, we have the right to put up the bars and keep them out, Without discussing the matter further, I may tell the

House and the people that the Government proposes to do that so far as these peculiar classes of people are concerned.
Mr. TWEElDIE: Since the signing of the Armistice, Western Canada has been agitated about the coming into Canada from the United States of Hutterites and Men-nonites. What does the Government intend to do with regard to those who are now in the country, and will they take action immediately by Order in Council to prevent any more of these people from coming in?

Briefly, the position is
this:	Unless we take action under the
War Measures Act-which we might do- there is no power under the existing law, as I understand it, to exclude these people at this time. As soon as this Bill is approved by the House we propose to put through an Order in Council under section 13 which will provide for their exclusion. Those who are now in Canada have come in under existing law, and I do not think the hon. gentleman will advance the idea that under those conditions they should be deported. That is a matter upon which there may be differences of opinion, but personally I do not think that people who have come'into the country under existing laws should be excluded simply because some new law is to be enforced against people of that class.

These people are coming in, and I think it is the duty of the Government, pending a settlement of this question, to take action under the War Measures Act with a view to preventing any more of them from coming in.

That is a matter which
will be taken into consideration, and a decision can be reached with reference to it.
I have covered the situation in a very general way, and I have suggested some of the proposals that the Government has in mind. 1 simply repeat, in closing, that for some years to come, it seems to me, our policy should be directed along two lines, first, towards increasing our agricultural population; second, towards providing, under the existing law and under the Bill now before the House, for the exclusion of certain classes of people who cannot readily be absorbed into .our population at the present time. We must protect ourselves so far as the future is concerned. We have a very large problem on our hands now, and its difficulties should not be unduly increased. What the policy of this country will be two or three, four or five, or ten years from now, can be settled by the Parliament of those days. For the present, the Government be-
lieves that we should put up the bars to a very considerable extent. I am quite sure that when we get into Committee and hon. members who know the situation in Canada have opportunity of thoroughly discussing the matter, the view which I have presented will be the majority view of the House. I move the second reading of the Bill.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.
The House went into Committee on the Bill, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On Section I-definitions:
While I thoroughly agree with the remarks the minister has made, it seems to me that the principle upon which our Immigration Act is based is wrong.

Order. I will have to ask the Committee to give its unanimous consent if the hon. member intends to discuss the principle of the Bill upon Clause 1. If the Committee are willing to give consent, I have no objection.
Some hon. MEMBEES: Go on.
I had thought that some hon. gentleman on the opposite side would speak on the second reading. When the motion was put I was not prompt enough to rise, and it was declared carried.
The minister made such a fair explanation of the Bill we thought the sooner we got into Committee the better.

I shall try not to delay the Committee. The system that this country and perhaps every oth,er country has adopted is to start out by saying that the country is open to the world, that any one is welcome to its shores, and then immediately to raise bars excluding this nation of that nation. That method produces at once in the mind of the nation debarred a feeling of irritation; it has from time to time given rise to difficulties, and it may in future produce international complications. I prefer to see the positive method adopted. Let Canada state that she is prepared to admit the people of such and such races, nations, or countries; and when others desire to enter it will be their privilege to make application and have their claims for admission duly considered by this Parliament.
As the minister has said, the subject is of importance, Canada is in reality entering upon a new era, and is able, even by the proposed amendment, to remedy some of the defects of our former legislation. The

minister so far as I can recall his remarks did not mention the clause to which he had special reference when he spoke of the powers of exclusion, but if section 13 was that to which he referred, it seems to me it would be wiser, instead of vesting the power of exclusion, as set out in that section, in the hands of the Governor in Council, to settle the question by the Bill itself. I hope at the appropriate time, to have the Committee consider an amendment to that end.
The point of view- from which we consider this question is of importance and has already been stated by the minister. It is, unfortunately, a matter of almost tragic import-perhaps those words are too strong -that the arguments in favour of unrestricted immigration appeal with particular force at the present moment. As stated by the minister, our financial, transportation and industrial problems demand an immediate increase in population, but must we not in spite of these pressing needs, have regard to the future, to the end that the welfare of this country may not be imperilled in generations to come?
It may be interesting to consider for a moment or two the figures regarding immigration in the past. For a term of ten years prior to the war, there entered Canada over 2,500,000 immigrants, of whom about 1,000,000 came from Great Britain, 850,000 from the United States of America and 675,000 from other countries. While this total figures out at an average of 250,000 a year-enough considering our total population-as a matter of fact, the tide was a rapidly rising one. For instance, in 1905, the total in round figures was
146.000.	That total rose five years later to
311.000.	The next year, 1912, it was 354,000, and, in 1913, we reached the top of the wave with 402,000, although, in 1914, the number was nearly as great. Of the 675,000 coming under the classification "from other countries"-and in that list nearly fifty races are specified-the leaders are Austrians with 150,000, Italians with 100,000, and Russians with 80,000. It is significant that in the last year of the decade the leaders above quoted very largely increased their entries. Speaking from memory, in 1914, of Austrians, 28,000 entered the country, of Russians, including Finns, almost as many, and of Italians, over 24,000. It is, therefore, well to remember that the inflow of immigrants from Southeastern Europe is a rapidly increasing one.
The figures as regards immigration into the United States of America correspond
to those just quoted. During the same period of time about 10,000,000 immigrants entered the United States. When we compare the relative population of the two countries, it will be admitted the effect on Canada of this onrush of new peoples must be far greater than the entrance of evefn four times the number into the United States. In the year 1914, the year the war started, eighty out of every one hundred immigrants into the United States came from European countries, and as many as sixty of those eighty were from three countries only, namely, Italy, Austria-Hungary and Russia. In 1914, Italy sent 295,000, Austria-Hungary, 286,000, and Russia,
262,000.
Has the hon. member the figures for Germany?

I doubt if I have the German figures available. German immigration fell off quite markedly in the last five years of that decade. The figures are in tabulated form in the report of the Commissioner General of Immigration. It would delay the Committee too long to add them up, but they are strikingly smaller than they were in prior years. Indeed, that feature is most noticeable when one looks into the question of immigration into the United States. There is plainly running through the history of this subject a distinction between the old immigration and the new immigration. Up to 1880, or 1882, the bulk of immigration into the United States came from Northwestern Europe. Speaking in a general way, about three-quarters of the immigrants from Europe up to that time came from Northwestern Europe and one-quartei from the Southeast. Since that date, and particularly for the last ten years prior to the war, the situation was completely reversed; three-quarters of the immigrants coming from Southeastern Europe and only one-quarter from the Northwest. This condition has brought about in many respects an unfortunate state of affairs in the United States, and it would be well for us, in considering this Bill and our own situation, to endeavour to profit from the experience of our neighbours.
If we are to continue our present policy of allowing European nations generally to enter Canada, we shall undoubtedly experience more and more the very result from which the United States has suffered, and for that reason I believe we should most carefully consider a strict limitation, at least for a period of years, of immigra^ tion from certain sections of Europe.



After all, the main reason for immigration nowadays is purely an economic one. The condition of the immigrant in his own home country and the hope held out to him of an improvement in that condition by coming to a new country is beyond everything else the main motive for his move. Provided times are good on this continent, immigration takes place from Europe without much regard to the conditions there, and it is a curious fact that the curves of imports and of immigration into the United States correspond with wonderful regularity. Then, too, the situation has been taken advantage of by many agencies, chief among which are the steamship companies and the labour agents, to stir up and exploit this movement. The result is that instead of attractingr as in the old days, the man of adventure and independence prepared to face the hardships of a new land, the way has been made to appear easy and the unfortunate immigrant has been deluded, with deplorable results in the end.
The minister has referred to what, to my mind, is one of the gravest results, and that is the overcrowding of our cities. The figures obtainable from the census department of the United States are striking in this respect. Their last census was taken in 1910, and shows that while forty-six per cent of the total population of that country was to be found in the cities, almost three* fourths of the foreign-born population was so located. New York being the port of entry for the greatest number of immigrants, naturally shows this concentration in a more striking degree than any other city. The Commissioner General of Immigration for the United States, in his report published in 1916, says of New York:
At the taking of the last census it contained as much as one-seventh of all our foreign-horn population, in contrast with only one-nineteenth of our total population. This one-seventh represented 1,945,000 foreign-born, of which more than one-half (52 per cent), came from Russia, Italy and Austria, the three combined having a total of more than one million. The amazing growth in the population of our cities has been predominately in the foreign-born element and their children, while the slight increase of the native-born population of native parents in cities is hardly observable.
The next striking feature of this enormous tide is its effect on the industries of the United States. The latest authority on the subject, F. J. Warne, quotes the following figures:
More than four-fifths of our recent immigration, which is most largely from Italy, Russia and Austria-Hungary is going into the north Atlantic states. Of the total increase of more
[Mr. Cronyn.l
than three million in our foreign-born population in 1910 over 1900, approximately sixty per cent went into these north Atlantic industrial and manufacturing states. Thus the Slav, Hebrew, and Italian, is being drawn by the industrial development of the country into manufacturing and mining and is settling in the larger industrial centres. This flow of recent immigration into the industrial states is as striking as was that of the earlier immigration into the agricultural sections.
Another striking and unfortunate feature is that the bulk of this new immigration is composed of single men, and less and less [DOT]as the years go by do the married
5 p.m. immigrants attempt to bring in with them their wives and children. It is quite true that families which at first are left behind are brought across to join the immigrant if he prospers. Here again the figures of the United States are enlightening:
In 1914 as many as two-thirds-as many as 799,000

were males between the ages of 14 and 44, one-half of whom were unmarried.. Even among those who were married, large numbers left their families at home and came only for temporary stay.
And that temporary stay is perhaps the next feature of the new immigration to be noted, because the ' birds of passage as they are termed, have become in some ways an all-important part of the incoming and outgoing tide. Speaking from memory, in the ten years up to 1910 some 9,000.000 immigrants entered the United States; that is a million less than the number entering that country in the ten years prior to the war. During the same period 3,500,000 immigrants left the United States, and the statement is made that two-thirds of those who returned to their native country never revisit America. As the same writer puts it:	,
They do not come with any intention of making this country their future home. This characteristic development of recent immigration alters completely the essential meaning to us of immigration as conceived in the past, although the word name of the economic phenomenon is the same. In consequence, immigration to-day requires a different avenue of approach if we are to understand its true significance to the American nation. This significance lies in the fact that a large volume of our immigration does not come here to be assimilated into our national life.
The report of the Commissioner General of Immigration on the next phase to be considered-the mentality of the immigrant -'should be brought before the House. He says in his report for 1914:
Medical science had demonstrated that many if not all, of these serious mental dteficiencies are handed down from generation to genera-

tion, with steady increase in the strain; so that the importance of rejecting and expelling aliens of this class, even to the extent shown to have occurred, can hardly he overstated. The law on this subject should be even more strict; and the bureau urgently recommends that legislation supplementary to the excellent provisions of the existing law be enacted at an early -date, so that the people of this country may be fully protected against the introduction here from abroad of additional strains of latent but none the less dangerous cerebral deficiencies, as well as against the introduction of such strains actually developed into acute stages. Why should our difficulties on this score, already sufficiently great, be increased by immigration ? "
I take the liberty of reminding you that there are more insane in institutions in this country than there are students in colleges and universities. There are more insane in the country than there are enlisted men of the Army, Navy and Marine Corps; and in addition to these, each year, there is being added to this great army, an army practically equal to the army of the United1 States, approximately sixty thousand new cases every year. The cost ot conducting these institutions 'Sn which this vast number of persons is cared for is so great that in several states it is exceeded only by the amount expended for education.
The effect on the standard of living by the injection of so vast a number of people is the last feature to which I shall refer. To examine into the question of immigration the United States Government some time ago appointed a commission which sat for four years affd at an expenditure of $800,000 produced a report contained in forty volumes. On the standard of living the commission says:
The measure of the rational, healthy development of the country is not the extent of its investment of capital, its output of products, or its exports and imports unless there is a corresponding economic opportunity afforded to the citizen dependent upon employment for his material, mental, and moral development.
The majority report states that evidence presented to it is a basis for the following findings:
1.	The immigration policy of the United States has oreated a number of our most difficult and serious industrial problems and has been responsible in a considerable measure for the existing state of industrial unrest.
2.	The enormous influx of immigrants during the past twenty-five years has already undermined the American standard of living for ail workmen except those in the skilled trades, and has been the largest single factor in preventing the wage scale from rising as rapidly .as food prices.
3.	The great mass of non-English-speaking , workers, who form about one-half of the
labour force in the basal industries, has done much 'to prevent the development of better relations between employers and employees.
President Samuel Gompers of the American Federation of Labour has presented this view quite clearly. He says:
119J
The American-born wage earners and the foreign wage earners who have been here long enough to aspire to American standards are subject to the ruinous competition of an unending stream of men freshly arriving fro >
foreign lands who are accustomed to so low a grade of living that they can underbid the wage earners established in this country and still save money.
And the various organizations of labour including the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers, the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen, the Order of Railway Conductors and the Brotherhood of the Railroad Trainmen emphasize their views by resolutions which they have passed from time to time. The farmers also, as organized in the Farmers' National Congress, the Farmers' Educational and Co-operative Union, the National Grange, and like associations have .stated 'that they .are '"unalterably opposed to the present foreign influx from southeastern Europe and western Asia, and to its proposed distribution and diversion to the South and West."	[DOT]
I have taken the liberty to put these facts on record as briefly as I could, so that when we come to the sections in question, there may be some basis in support of the limitations which I trust will be put in the Bill. Happily our experience has not been that of the United States, or at all events it 'has not been so acute, and we are now fortunately able, with proper thought, to	safeguard our	future-

You speak of three and a half million people coming to the United States and going back. Have you any idea of the length of time they remained, or the amount of money they took away when they- returned for good?

I do not recall having seen any statement as to the length of time they remained. A computation was made by the commission of the amount of money which they sent away. It was in the hundreds of millions. I am speaking again from memory.

May I make a suggestion to my hon. friend? Assuming that all that he has proposed is wise-and with nearly everything ' that he has said I heartily agree-I think it would be very much better if he could give us a revised Immigration Act rather than the Bill that is presented. The amendments here are very numerous. Where there are a few amendments to a large Aot it is desirable that we should have an amending Act, but where the amendments are very numerous it might be the wiser policy to give us a revised Act, instead of having numerous

amendments striking out a few words here and putting in a few words there, and striking out a clause here and substituting a new clause somewhere else. If we have to have this measure and a general Act also there will he a danger of confusion, and the wayfaring man, though he be a member of Parliament, will have some difficulty in following the law, while the immigrants coming in will certainly never understand it. I think we might discuss the Bill in its present form in the light of the minister's speech, and he might instruct the proper officials to embody these amendments in a consolidated Act, so that before the matter is concluded here he might present a substitute Bill which would not require further discussion.

I gave instructions to draft the Bill in such a way that the House would have the least possible difficulty in .understanding it. A reading of it will show that there are very few sections in which, as suggested, a few words are struck out and others substituted. In the main, whole sections have been struck out and others substituted even where the changes are very slight, the object being that hon. members may clearly grasip their purport. I think the House will have very little difficulty in following the provisions of the Bill. On the other hand, I quite agree with the view expressed by hon. gentlemen that we should have a consolidation of the Act. The intending emigrants, of course, see very little of the law. They have very little opportunity of reading it. They do not obtain their information in that way; but for the use of our officials who have to carry out the administration of our law, I think a consolidation should be made in order that the provision might be very clearly apprehended by every one. I have no doubt that measures of this kind are usually consolidated by the department when an amending Bill goes through. I do not know what the practice is here, but I know that in our own legislature, when we amend a Bill we have an office consolidation of the law so that the consolidation will be available to every one interested. If the Committee wishes it I will give instructions that a consolidation shall be proceeded with at once so that members may have the advantage of having it before them. On the other hand, I think there will be very little difficulty in following the provisions of this Bill. If thought advisable I will have a number of copies of the existing Act brought to the House so that, if we find it necessary, 
we can refer to the provisions of the existing law.

I would not suggest
that there should be any delay in regard to the consideration of the matter. I agree that we can discuss the Bill very intelligently with the minister's explanation of it before us. But I think that, before we dispose of the matter finally, for the information of the officials, and of the public generally, there should be a consolidation of the Act. A man who is asked to become a settler in Canada may say:	I
would like to have a copy of your Immigration law, and if you are able to send him a consolidated Act it is more convenient, not only to the intending immigrant, but to the officials of the department.

Mr. Chairman, I have a
few observations to make on the general tenor of the Bill that should have been made earlier, and I am afraid I shall have to ask the Committee for the same indulgence they gave the hon. member XMr. Cronyn). The substantive part of this Bill is contained in the three or four first sections; the remainder deals mostly with the way in which the Act is to be put in force and is more for the guidance of transportation and other companies than for the information or the immigrant. Therefore, it will only ' be with the first few sections that the House will have to deal.
I must congratulate the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder' upon his excellent address. I have not much fault to find with anything he has said, nor with the Bill as a whole, with the exception of perhaps one or two sections, which ought to be amended radically or struck out completely. I will refer to them in a moment or two. The minister stated in his address that things have happened in the matter of immigration in this country which should not have happened if the previous Governments had been alive to the entire situation. I am sorry the minister did not see his way to tell us what the particular things were that had happened and which should not have happened. We know that under the Liberal Administration of this country, from 1896 to 1911, we had a vast immigration and that the foundation , of the prosperity of Canada was the immigration which came in at that period. Whatever may be said about Sir Clifford Sifton, no one will deny that his policy of immigration was the right policy at the time, and that if we have had this large immi-

gration into the country it was entirely due to his foresight.
I would judge that the test whether immigration would or would not be satisfactory to the country would be the reports from the various penitentiaries, insane asylums and houses of correction. By reading those reports we can judge whether immigration is or is not proper for the country. I have not the figures from these institutions before me, but I think I can state without fear of contradiction that the figures will show quite clearly that this country is relatively ahead of any other country on this continent in regard to the small number oi people detained in these institutions. I think you will find that the population in the insane asylums is very much less than it is in the United States, in England or in other countries per capita. So it is with regard to the jails and penitentiaries. Speaking for my own particular race, I can point with pride to the Montreal jail, where you will not find a single person of the Jewish race at present incarcerated. The poor chaplain, who has been paid a small stipend of $300 or $400, fears he is going to lose his position unless something is done. So it is in regard to the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, where conditions are nearly as satisfactory. Of course, some of the people who are opposed to Jewish immigration take the ground that it is because these people are too clever to be caright, but I do not think there is very much in that. Our police forces and other departments are capable of looking after all classes.
The open door policy to which the minister referred incidentally is one which I think ought to commend itself to the people. Canada is not at present in a position to pick and choose. We must absorb into this country very large numbers of immigrants before we can begin to pay the interest on the debt which we have upon our shoulders at the present time. I have figured out that every man, woman and child will have to pay something like $50 per year in taxes to pay the interest on the debt which we have rolled up. It does not require an arithmetical problem to demonstrate the fact that if 7,000,000 people are required to pay $50 per head, 14,000,000 would pay just half that amount, and so on. So long as we can assure ourselves that the people brought into this country are law-abiding citizens, healthy, and able to take part in the work of developing the country, that is all we require. Whether they come from alien countries, or from
other countries, amounts to little. It is-of no significance to this country. The-alien enemy of to-day will be the friendly alien of to-morrow and possibly the friendly alien of to-day may become the alien enemy of to-morrow. I doubt very much, from the point of view of international law, whether, when we have made a durable ' and lasting peace with the countries with which we have been >at war, we can legally say to the peoples of those countries: You cannot come into this country because at some time in the past you were our enemies.
I question that very much. Tit seems to me that so soon as peace has been signed we have no longer any quarrel with these people and we cannot, on the ground that they have been alien enemies in the past, refuse to allow them into this country or bar their entrance. The minister made the point that some people whom we had brought into this country-Galicians-were living in the same conditions in which they had been living in Galicia from time immemorial.
I did not say that.
I understood the minister to state they were living in Canada in the same conditions as they had lived in in their own country.

As a matter of fact, the Galicians or Ruthenians who are residing in Western Canada, and who settled there fifteen or twenty years ago, have made very substantial progress in so far as their habits and customs are concerned.
Did I understand the minister to say that it was at some time while they were here that those objectionable conditions prevailed?
I stated that after their arrival in Canada they were left to struggle for themselves without any assistance or advice of any kind.
They made good subsequently?	,
Yes, from the material standpoint, and I can also say that from the social standpoint they have made considerable progress.
I understood the minister to say that they lived in mud huts and in a way not consistent with civilized conditions.
Originally.

If they are not doing so now it seems to me that is one of the very

best reasons why we should take men who live in mud huts and make good citizens out of them. That is the white man's burden. Those Galicians have worked out their own salvation in this country and have certainly become an asset. They came from Austria, and if they had not come in their thousands from that country they would have been fighting our own soldiers during the wrar that has just 'been concluded. We have taken them out of Austria and made most of them fairly good citizens, and I have no doubt that many gave a good account of themselves on the field of battle when fighting for the Allies. It is part of our duty to assume some of the burden, which Kipling says the white man must shoulder, in regard to those who are less advanced than we are. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the Government is making a serious mistake when it presumes to legislate to keep out people from different countries simply because their habits before they come here are not quite the same as ours. We ought to encourage them in every possible way, not only for their own sakes, but for the saxe oi ourselves, and in that connection I am reminded of a story told to me some years ago by Commissioner Coombes, of the Salvation Army. He instanced a case in nondon where a man the back of whose shirt was badly tom used to carry crippled people across the street in wintry weather. Commissioner Coombes congratulated this charitable individual, but received for reply, " That is no charity at all. While I carry them across the street they warm my back." That was the object, and both parties were benefited. I do not say that we have got down to those, straits yet, Mr. Chairman, but I mention the incident for the purpose of illustrating that while we are doing the other man good we are at the same time benefiting ourselves.
It is part of our duty to teach these people our laws and customs in order that they may become good Canadian citizens. We may not be very successful with the parents, but through our public schools we can reach the children, and the second generation will develop into citizens as good as many of those who belong to the so-called better class. I have only to cite a case in the history of my own race. You will remember that when the Israelites left Egypt they escaped from slavery and they wandered for forty years in the wilderness. Not one of those who left Egypt was permitted to enter the Holy Land, but their children did, and the Bible tells us these made good. The same thing applies in
[Mr. Jacobs !
the present day. You cannot expect to do very much with people who come to this country in the matter of changing from the old manners and customs of Europe, but with our magnificent public school system we can teach the second generation our Canadian social life, and they will develop into citizens as capable and efficient as the descendants of those who have lived here many generations.

Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question, because it goes to the very heart of the situation? In Western Canada, more so than in any other part of the Dominion, the prevailing opinion is that the number of foreign born is so great in proportion to the balance of the population that it results in a difficult social and educational problem. Does the hon. gentleman advocate that we should keep our doors wide open in order that thousands upon thousands of these people shall have the privilege of going in there to intensify the problem of those Western Provinces? Or should we endeavour to keep a balance between these foreign born and our own people, in order that we may grapple with that problem as it exists from time to time? He can readily understand what might result if we were to follow his policy. We could probably arrange to carry on propaganda work in Europe which would bring hundreds of thousands of these people to Canada. Does the hon. gentleman think it advisable to do so under the circumstances I have mentioned ?

If they are decent, respectable people, why not? Take the state of Wisconsin. I< understand that practically the whole state is peopled by Scandinavians. Take the state of Louisiana, that originally was settled exclusively by the French. Why should foreigners coming here grow up in ignorance when we have such a splendid educational system? As the hon. minister pointed out, a few years agio these Galicians were living in mud huts; to-day they form a very important part of the community. In fact, they were considered so important that when the War-time Elections Act was passed a provision was inserted withdrawing their franchise rights.
With regard to the peasantry which you must expect will immigrate to this country, you cannot get any but the poorest class from Great Britain or any other part of Europe, for it is their poverty which causes them to emigrate. Who ever heard of a man of wealth leaving his home in Europe and coming out to Canada either to live in a large city or to go on the land? I't

is the poverty of the peasantry and other classes in Europe which promotes emigration, and you cannot expect to receive any other class of immigrants. They go to the West and have to scratch the earth for a living ;they have very little means and cannot engage in agriculture on a large scale like the American immigrants, they cannot buy tractors and other up-to-date agricultural implements; they must continue to live in a primitive style until such time as they are able to make enough out of the soil to improve their position. Therefore it seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that it is a shortsighted policy on the part of the Government to simply restrict immigrants because they happen to come from this or that country, or because they do' not happen to have the means which immigrants from the United States possess.
I regret that the Government should have decided at the present juncture to introduce a Bill of this character, because it is bound to create considerable discussion among the people of this country. The returned soldier problem is upon us. The returned soldier who has failed to find a job will consider every immigrant as coming here for 'the purpose of taking away employment which should go to the soldier, and in that way we may accentuate a feeling against the newly arrived which would not exist were this Bill bro-u^ht down a year or two hence. I do not believe there was any particular urgency for this Bill. We have in the Immigration Act many of the provisions which are incorporated in this Bill, and we could have got along with it very well, particularly as the regulations under the Orders in Council carefully see to it that only a good class of immigrant is permitted entrance.
I have had a good deal to do with the Immigration Department, and I must say that its work is being done most efficiently; all the officials, from the highest down, are interpreting the Act with intelligence. When a case of hardship is brought to the attention of the department, an appeal is had, and when the matter is finally disposed of the immigrant receives justice. That being the case, I cannot see why this Bill should be introduced, unless it be for the purpose of barring the alien enemy. 1 shall certainly oppose the section which introduces that provision into our law. !t is undemocratic; it is wrong in principle; I have very grave doubts as to its legality under international law. For these and many other reasons I think the section should be left out.
The provision under which we debar alien enemies from entering Canada is a regulation under the existing law. The purpose of this Bill is not to exclude the alien enemy.
But the alien enemy is excluded under the War Measures Act?
No, I think it is Section 38 of the present law which provides that the Government, by Order in Council, may exclude any persons of any nationality, race, class or occupation.

It was right and proper that that should be so. But it is wrong to introduce into the substantive part of a new law a clause to provide that every person belonging to alien enemy countries shall not be permitted to enter Canada.
There is no such provision in the Bill.

Paragraph (p) of Section 3 says:
Enemy aliens or persons who have been alien enemies and who were interned in any part of His Majesty's Dominions or any allied country on or after the eleventh day of November, one thousand nine hundred and eighteen.
That refers only to interned alien enemies.

What distinction does the minister make between a man who has been interned in any part of His Majesty's Do' minions and a man who comes direct to Canada from Germany, Austria, or any other enemy country? I do not see that there is any distinction. A large number of persons who came from alien enemy countries reside in Canada. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) in answer to a question I put to him the other day, said that 2,117 alien enemies only had been interned during the war. This shows that thousands of them were considered good and valued citizens and were in no way molested or interfered with.
Another clause to which I intend to take serious objection is that which provides for a literacy test. That clause does not appeal to me at all; it is wrong to debar a man from this country because he cannot read. If that rule had been applied in the United States in the time of Abraham Lincoln, Lincoln's own father and mother would have been debarred from entering the United States because they could not read. I do not know where the minister got his warrant for introducing a rule of this kind. We want all the immigration we can get. If a man is respectable, industrious and

honest he should be permitted to come into this country; if he is unable to read, that is not his fault, but his misfortune. In the remote parts of England, Scotland and Ireland, the countries from which you expect to get your best class of immigration, I venture to think large numbers of the people of the older generation cannot read. We know the difficulties'* under which people labour in Europe. Many men have not had a chance to go to school and learn to read or write; they have been ground down by poverty and heavy work almost from the days when they could scarcely walk. Now, when they want to improve their position and come to a new land, they will find they cannot come here on account of this misfortune of being unable to read. The House should not concur in any legislation which makes a distinction as to entry in Canada between the man who can read and the man who cannot. You are not going to keep out Bolshevists by such a provision; the Bolshevists and people of that ilk are able to read and write. You are keeping out the poor man who, through no fault of his own, has been unable to secure even an elementary education. If people who cannot read and write are permitted to enter Canada, the minister will at least have the assurance that they will not commit forgery; so that one thing would be guarded against at all times.
On the whole, were it not for these two clauses I would be heartily in favour of this Bill, particularly as I know that the law will be administered with intelligence by the very capable department over which the minister presides. I trust that before the Bill is through the Committee stage the minister will see his way clear to strike out these objectionable passages and give satisfaction to all elements of the community.

The greatness of a country must be measured by the standard of its people; a nation's greatest asset is the people of whom it is composed. In view of the immigration restrictions which are being imposed by the United States, it is important that legislation of the nature of this Bill should be brought down by the Canadian Government. Otherwise, Canada would be the Mecca for the outcasts of Europe to wham access to the United States is refused. But to my surprise the hon. gentleman (Mr. Jacobs) has made a plea for the alien enemy, for the people with whom we are at war-because peace has not yet been declared.
May I correct the hon. gentleman? I said: the people with whom we "were" at war.

That is exactly
what I said. We are still at war with those people, and yet the hon. member makes a plea here to-day that we should grant them concessions and that we should forget the things they have done, and forget the principles to defend which some of our men are still overseas waiting for peace to be declared before they can return to Canada. The ink was not dry on the signatures to the armistice before we heard the leaders of the Liberal party in Canada apologizing for the things that had been done by alien enemies during this war and referring to the Germans as one of the noblest races in the world. We heard from the Atlantic to the Pacific about the so called iniquitous Dominion Franchise Act which disfranchised people of alien birth in this country during the war. But to-day I think the limit has been reached when an hon. member makes the plea In this House for alien enemies; that we should not exercise any precautions with regard to ourselves as against those people coming into Canada under our immigration laws. To my mind the matter is so serious that a statement of that kind should be considered an unpardonable offence. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Jacobs) may smile, but the brave men who have been offering their lives for the cause for which we have been contending during the last five years will not smile at the statement I make. Since the signing of the arm- istice we have been told by some people that we should forgive and start over again. There is, I admit, much to be forgiven, and personally I have not yet reached the stage when I am prepared either to forget or to forgive the horrible offences that have been committed.
I am a better Christian than the hon. member.

I am not boasting as to that, but I do not think the hon, member's attitude is very much evidence a^to his Christianity.
1 should like to say a word or two with regard to the exclusion under present conditions in Canada, of skilled and unskilled labour of a desirable class. It has been pointed out that Canada needs population; that we have great undeveloped resources in this country, and that our hands are practically tied, because we have not the people to develop those resources. Some people anticipate a very unsettled condition

of affairs in the labour market, because those hundreds of thousands of returned soldiers will again have to take their place in civil life.
The Government have made a reasonable provision, although perhaps not as liberal as it might be, to take care of those men at least for a short time after their return, and I have not the slightest doubt but that, in a short time, there will be in Canada a great demand for labour both skilled and unskilled. I cannot conceive of a country, with the resources which [DOT] Canada has, being in any other condition than short of labour, and I want to issue a warning to the Government that many of those measures that are on foot with the object of restricting desirable immigration, are not in the public interest. Some labour unions have been taking the stand that legislation of this kind should be enacted. The minister has pointed out the necessity for getting men on the land in order to develop our agricultural resources, and I quite agree with him in that regard; but how are you going to meet the demands of the country in that respect unless you permit desirable immigrants to enter. Because, by reason of the labour organizations fixing the hours of labour and regulating the scale of wages, if a man can get a greater remuneration for his services at some other occupation than farming, he is going to engage in that occupation instead of working the land? That is the very thing that is taking place throughout Canada at the present time, and has been for many years, that is the chief reason why, notwithstanding all the great natural resources we have at our disposal, the cost of living is bound to remain very high in this country. The policy of the labour unions as regards hours of labour is, in my opinion, a very short-sighted one. I may seem somewhat reckless in making such a statement, but I am quite sincere in making it and I do not believe they will gain the end they have in view by organizing along those lines.
Agriculture in this country is suffering to such an extent that it is simply deplorable that something is not being done to stem the ravages and depredations that are being made upon our resources as a result of bad farming. The result of bad farming is evidenced on every hand throughout the country, and as the years go by, it is becoming much worse, and, unless there is a material change in labour conditions I see no prospect of its becoming better. It will be found that ia feeling has been engendered against the people cd the rural districts
by the people in the towns and *cities; indeed, that feeling exists Tight here in Ottawa. The citizens are calling meetings and passing resolutions with a view, they claim, to bringing down the cost of living, by bringing into competition with the legitimate business of the agriculturists of this country something that will meet their selfish purposes, but they lose sight of the fact that agriculture is going to suffer to a great extent if they succeed in carrying out the views they express. This may be getting away from the Bill somewhat, but what I have in mind and what I wish to emphasize is this; that the Government must be very careful in not excluding from this country desirable, industrious immigrants, even although they have not one dollar in their possession.
The hon. member (Mr. Jacobs) criticised the minister because, although he said that mistakes had been made in the past, he did not point out where those mistakes had been made, but simply condemned them in a general way. He also eulogized Sir Clifford Sifton and what the Liberal party had done in peopling the plains of the West. The Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder) has lived in Western Canada for many years, and I have no doubt that he, being of an observant nature, has followed the question of immigration in the West as a careful student would.
It is not very many years since we witnessed in the Parliament of Canada an effort to find out who it was that was bringing out to Canada from the alien enemy nattiorris of central Europe hundreds o'f thousands of people under bonus. It was claimed that it was done by a certain corporation but you coud not find out by hook or by crook who constituted the notorious North Atlantic Trading Company. That company located these people on large blocks of land in Western Canada, and instead of these people being assimilated, the people of British birth who did not wish to live close to them moved further away, and the boundaries of those alien settlements were extended. But that is a thing of the past, and I should not have referred to it had it not been mentioned by the hon. member (Mr. Jacobs). I believe it was not good policy to permit thousands of people of foreign birth to congregate in settlements in Western Canada and maintain there the language and traditions of the country from which they came. If we want Canada to become a great country within the Empire, we must both feel and act as if we were a part of the British Empire, and the
1S86

people who come here should be made to observe British laws and institutions. But that is not being done in many places in Western Canada to-day.
Just imagine hon. gentlemen opposite, with peace not yet declared, saying that we should not debar these people of alien enemy countries, many of whom are now interned in Canada.
Mr. JAiOOBS:	Those interned are here
already.

But they will go
out just as soon as it is possible for us to get them out, and I hope they will be kept out for the rest of their lives. We have had that menace to contend with, and we have not received much sympathy from hon. gentlemen opposite in dealing with questions of this kind during the last few years. But our boys from overseas will soon be home and they will see to it that never again in his counry shall such a condition of affairs exist as has been the case in this Parliament during the past few years.
