The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Militia and1 Defence-Allowances-Active Militia, $50,000. *

Major-General MEWBURN: In preparing these Estimates it was very difficult to determine just how far to go in getting back from war to a peace basis. These Main Estimates were prepared on the same lines as last year, as we did not 'then expect the armistice. In the Supplementary Estimates, therefore, there will have to be included some amounts in addition to those now before the Committee. The question of what is to become of the active militia in the future is a matter that will have to be given very serious consideration, probably at a later session. In the Supplementary Estimates there will be a larger amount in connection with certain grants, in one or two items which I will explain later on. In the Estimates now before the Committee there is a total reduction of $26,130 as compared with the previous year, the expenditures having been cut down to the lowest minimum possible. Some amounts that have been previously charged to war expenditure will now have to come out of the Estimates by vote. It is proposed to recruit the permanent corps as a temporary measure up to 5,000, which is the number laid down in the Militia Act. It is considered essential that that force ahould be built up, at least, to the number mentioned.
Mr. MeKENZIE: What does this $50,000 cover?
Major-General MEWBURN: That $50,000 covers allowances for general purposes for all militia units throughout the Dominion. During the war that amount was required t° keep the active militia units in some semblance of an organization. It was distributed among all the various units in Canada for the care of arms and for matters pertaining to the active militia regiments including all branches 6f the service. The pre-war vote in connection with that was something over $100,000. During 1017-18 it was $70,000 and last year $50,000. I do not think it is possible to manage with an amount less than that. In the Supplementary Estimates there will have to be a vote if it is considered necessary to train the militia or any part of it this year. Whether that is advisable or not I am not prepared to say, but we have to make provision.

To whom is this money usually paid?
Major-General MEWBURN:	It goes to
the officers commanding the militia units, to the credit of the units, ,for command pay,

care of arms, drill instruction, postage, and so forth.

And salaries?
Major-General MEWBURN: No. There are no salaries at all. The militia units have not drawn a cent of pay practically for four years.

What is the command pay?
Major-General MEWBURN:	The command pay is estimated on the basis of 60 cents for each man actually trained. A very large number of militia units in Canada have retained their organization and have actually trained their men. In one military district there are over four regiments of infantry that have kept up their regiments*-men who were over age or medically unfit. These regiments trained in the spring and fall and never drew pay. They were kept as a nucleus. A great many of them spent enormous sums of money out of their regimental funds. One regiment, the 48th Highlanders in Toronto, spent over $23,000 in connection with recruiting for the overseas units, and that organization is magnificent to-day. The same is true of the 5th Royal Scots and the Victoria Rifles, and the 65th, the 8th and 9th, Quebec; and in Winnipeg the 90th and the Grenadier Regiment, and one in Vancouver.

What advantage is this to the country?
Major-General MEWBURN:	There is
every advantage, and I do not think that the country would be satisfied to have the militia units wiped out of existence.

But of what advantage is it to keep the units?
Major-General MEWBURN: I think it is absolutely essential that the militia units should be kept up. It is not for me to say whether their services will be required again or not. If it is the intention to wipe them out of existence that is a matter for Parliament, but I cannot for a moment imagine that they have not been of advantage in the past and may not be of advantage in the future.

The minister misunderstands me. What do they do?
Major-General MEWBURN: During the war they were the backbone of recruiting for the Canadian Expeditionary Force, and I think that the units, if they are kept on a peace basis, are very essential in aid of the civil power.

Will any definite policy be formulated with regard t'o the future of the Canadian militia?
Major-General MEWBURN: No definite policy has been formulated but considerable thought has been given to the matter.
It would be premature for *me even* to suggest at this time what will be done; I have felt that until the Canadian Expeditionary Force is demobilized it would be unwise to state any definite policy. We organized and sent overseas a very large number of units. In the infantry we recruited in Canada something like 258 battalions. I shall not criticise the way in which it was done but a large number of - them were broken up. A large number of units that were at the front are now coming back and are being practically disbanded, and the only thing we have on the statute-book is what is known under the Miliita Act which provides for a permanent and non-permanent force. There is the nucleus of a committee that has been giving a great deal of consideration to this matter and it is proposed to add to that committee some officer or officers who have served with distinction at the front representing the permanent corps-those who were neither in the permanent or non-permanent but served with distinction at the front. It is proposed that the committee shall visit the eleven military districts in Canada to get the views of the various officers who have served in the war as to the situation, and also to consult with people in certain centres who have been behind the militia in the past. Probably at a future session some proper scheme will be laid before the House as to the reconstitution of the militia, as a great many people feel strongly that these fighting units should be perpetuated. The 16t*h Battalion was a regiment that was raised originally in British Columbia and has now become a Manitoba battalion. There are others: The 15t*h which was ostensibly fathered by the 48th Highlanders in Toronto, the 13th and the 5th Royal Scots. There is considerable feeling that these units should be perpetuated, and I think there is reason for the view, as they have made splendid history for Canada and I would like something to be done to continue them. I am not prepared *to say how far the country intends to go in the future in maintaining a military organization. It is premature at present to lay down any far-reaching policy until we know what our responsibilities and cares

will be, but in the meantime it would be wise to try and keep the units in existence.

It is pleasant to know that at times, Mr. Chairman, I can agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux), and to realize that the. gulf which separates this side from the other is not one that at all times cannot be bridged. I am pleased to associate myself with the hon. gentleman in his remarks in regard to the cadet corps, and we will have an opportunity to discuss it more fully, I suppose, on the next item. But I want to say one word in regard to the active militia. I do not know whether there will be any annual camps this year or not; I heard it intimated that there would not be.
Major-General MEWBURN: This amount does not provide for them.

It is quite true that in recruiting men for the front, the old militia those men who went out to camp year after year, did splendid service; a great many of those who were associated with the militia joined up and went overseas and did their part nobly. There were some, however, who for years had been connected with the militia but who never showed any disposition to enlist for active service. I know some men in my own part of the country who used to strut about with all the gold lace and brass buttons they could decorate

themselves with, who for a great many years used to go out to the annual camp for fourteen days and take all the salutes that those under them could give, priding themselves on their rank in the militia, but who did not go overseas and did not want to go overseas. In any reorganization of the militia it would be a very great mistake it those gentlemen were given their old rank; that would be something which the country generally would resent very strongly. The hon. gentleman who has just spoken stated that fourteen days' annual drill was too short. In my judgment, if you have that annual drill conducted by men who have had experience overseas, you will get more benefit from the fourteen days' training under their guidance than you would get in four years under the old system. I would cut off every one of those men who pa-raded as militia officers, but did not prove themselves of the right calibre when the testing time came. The men to carry on the instructional work are the men who went overseas and did their bit, not those who were content to remain at home and who now, no doubt, will again haul out their uniforms from the dusty closet and strut about just as gloriously as they did for thirty-five or forty years before the war began.

I have little experience in military matters, Mr. Chairman, but I would like to express strong support of the attitude adopted by the Minister of Militia, which I understand to 'be this: He does not intend to launch a scheme of general reorganization of the militia until the present situation clears up. The great statesmen of the world have been working for months past in Paris to s^e whether the scourge of militarism can be removed from the civilized nations of the world, and on their success or failure will depend very largely whether this country, with other countries, will have to look forward to the burden of maintaining military establishments, or whether a reign of peace and harmony can be established throughout the world. I am hopeful for the future because the present situation is so awful. Possibly we have not realized it on this side of the Atlantic as much as the people have on the other side, but I fear the crushing weight of military establishments will be found too much, along with the tremendous load of national debt heaped up during the war, to be borne by a world which has been impoverished by four, aye, almost five, years of hitter conflict. I believe we are fortunate in having at the head of the Militia Department a
gentleman who, although a general in the Canadian army, is of an essentially civilian turn of mind, and who is not desirous of seeing great military establishments formed in this country. May I be allowed to ask the House to approve and support the idea which he has set forth? I think we should not allow our militia organization to fall fo pieces, I am quite at one with him there; but I would reduce the expenditure on the upkeep of our militia to the smallest point consonant with the maintenance of a skeleton organization. The load of debt which we have in this country does not for business reasons permit us to do otherwise. But there is something much greater than business reasons-the heart of humanity is crying out for release from mitilarism. In so far as we can do so consistently with national safety we should endeavour to meet that demand, which is uttered by the whole human race.
Major-General MEWBURN: I am delighted to hear the remarks of the hon. gentleman opposite. II have been pressed to lay down some immediate policy regarding our militia organization. We have been keeping very closely in touch and endeavouring to get information from Paris as to the future military organizations of the -world We are also getting information from a commission which is sitting at the British War Office to-day dealing with post-bellum war conditions and reorganization of the British army, on which we have one of our most distinguished officers, General Me-Brien, who has been an outstanding figure throughout the war. He has been transmitting to us a lot of valuable information. Also we have been keeping in close touch with the reorganization in the United States. They started out with the idea of maintaining a permanent standing army of some 500,000 men, but I think they are modifying their views. I have felt, as I have already stated, that it would be very foolish for us in -Canada to launch into a big military scheme at the present moment, and therefore we came to the conclusion that this suggested committee should go into the matter very carefully and get the views of various parts of the Dominion on the matter, and next session the whole matter could be fully considered.
I take issue with my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) in his reference to members of the militia who, he considers, have not done their duty. No doubt in many militia^.units throughout Canada there were men of that calibre, but I think I can safely say that of most of the militia units that were in exist-

ence in 1914, every officer, non-commissioned officer and man who was of military age and medically fit has served at the front or is over there now. I speak particularly of the city corps. The peace establishment of an ordinary city battalion was something like 445. Not an officer, non-commissioned officer or man drew one cent of pay from the Government. The pay they got for annual training went into their regimental funds and they paid out of their own pockets for the extra uniform and equipment to keep these units up to their establishment. I believe most of the men of these city corps, without one exception, served at the front. The officers took a great many military and staff coui'ses, paid their own expenses, gave up tlieir holidays in order to train. The money devoted to these city corps really came back into the coffers of the Government for the benefit of the country. They maintained their own bands and other organizations at their own expense. I do not wish to speak boastfully, but of my own battalion in Hamilton some 124 officers and 3,800 men went overseas; 20 officers were killed; 12,000 men from Hamilton went overseas. While these men have been overseas the organizations have been kept up so that when the men come back from the front they have a home to go to. That is creditable, so it is advisable to keep up the nucleus of these organizations. But it is premature for us to launch into some big military scheme now; the matter will have to be given very serious consideration.

We have had almost a
love feast here this evening. First the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) congratulates the minister; then the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster); and now I have my word of endorsation to add to what the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) had to say. I agree with the member for Frontenac that there have been in Canada during the last three or four years a large number of militia officers who should have gone to the front, but did not. They have walked around in uniform for several years, and I do not think they should be in a position now to hold high commands in the militia. If the militia is re-organized, it should be the business of the minister to see that men who have been at the front are put in charge of the battalions. Further, if a man did not go overseas because he was medically unfit, but still remains in the militia, he should be retired, because if he is not
[Major-General Mewburn.]
fit to be a soldier in France I do not see what use he can be here.
Major-General MEWBURN: In the present reorganization, the senior officer in the militia unit concerned who has seen service overseas, will take command of the regiment and will make his recommendation with regard to new officers in that regiment. This will eliminate all those who have not been overseas.

When officers who were in the militia units and who proceeded overseas, return and are demobilized, what will be their rank?
Major-General MEWBURN: That is one of the policies that we have not definitely settled. What we have done is this: In many cases officers who held the rank of lieutenant in militia regiments went overseas and rose to the rank of lieutenant-colonel. As these officers return from the front and are struck off the strength, they are placed on what is called the Canadian Expeditionary Force Reserve of Officers, with the rank that they held overseas or obtained at the front. Of course, they may still appear on the rolls of the old militia units, because, as we have not yet settled upon a definite policy in this regard, we are not in a position to disband those militia units.

What would be the rank, say, of a major who reverted to go to the front and did not succeed in regaining the rank which he originally held?
Major-General MEWBURN: The rank which he originally held would be restored.

What is the scope of the inquiry which is to be conducted by the Sir William Otter commission?
Major-General MEWBURN: Sir William Otter has been requested to organize a commission or committee to go into the matters of which I have spoken. As yet he has done nothing beyond collecting an enormous amount of data in connection with headquarters here and compiling a lot of information. In the meantime, he is awaiting the return to Canada of some officers from overseas. The commission will inquire into and report upon the future reorganization of the militia. A great many people in Canada-I frankly say that I myself am in favour of it, although I do not know whether I shall live to see it- advocate universal military training in this country. My hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) spoke of the Swiss system, which is undoubtedly one of the best systems in the

world, the cheapest and most satisfactory system ouside of conscription, in all the continental countries. Personally I think that the youth of this country should be induced in some way to put in a certain amount of training; it would be better for the youth, and better for the country. How far the country will care to go in (hat regard I cannot say. But this Committee will be able to give an expression of opinion from other countries as to what should be done.

I am in favour of universal training. Apparently General Otter's commission will inquire only into the best method of consolidating or co-ordinating the militia units overseas and at home on the old basis of pay. To my mind that is not the most advantageous system for Canada. Canada's soldiers should serve without pay; it is because pay has been attached to the service that many of our troubles in the past have arisen, and that difficulty has been experienced in getting men of the proper spirit into the militia. I would not like this item to pass without having had the minister say that this matter will be thoroughly discussed at the proper time when his other Estimates are up. I am delighted to hear the expressions of opinion which emanated from my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux). I am sure that my hon. and gallant friend from Quebec East (Mr. Power) will take part in this discussion to the great advantage of the Committee and of the country. The trouble is that during the last couple of years a difference of opinion has arisen between Ontario and Quebec on the questionof "conscription." As regards universal training of young men from eighteen to twenty-five, of whom there are some 336,000 in Canada, if they would train voluntarily, that is, receiving nothing more than mere pocket money, that would be of great advantage to their physical and moral well-being. Speaking of that, which I purpose advocating at another time, I think it is not unnatural that expressions of opinion in favour of it coming from hon. gentlemen opposite, should come from those living in Quebec, because that province first gave Canada the idea of universal service. As long ago as 1808, that province passed the first Militia Act which made every man then fit to carry arms in the province of Lower Canada a member of the militia. The only members of the militia to-day are those who are full of an ardent military spirit or who take the annual training for a holiday or for the money that is in it,
That was not, however, the case with the men of Quebec in the early times. They joined because they felt it was their duty as well as a pleasure to do so, and I am quite sure the spirit which animated them in passing that Act still exists in Quebec to-day, and when we come to discuss this question, I am sure we shall have many supporters from that province.
If one looked through the militia list, one would find page after page, for almost hundreds of pages, of names ' of'members of cadet corps established in the schools and seminaries of Quebec, a greater proportion in Quebec than in any other province, so that there must have been that idea prevailing throughout Quebec in the last few years. Those things all conduce to the idea that we can get rid of the pay system in the militia, which system has been to its detriment, and for which before the war in 1914, we paid $10,000,000. We can escape a great part of this enormous expenditure and get a much more efficient, loyal and better trained army of citizen soldiers as they have them in Australia, South Africa and New Zealand and as they are now to have in the United States. We cannot be behind the United States of America in this great idea because, if we are to live beside them in our present friendly manner, we cannot say to the world: We are going to drag behind and have no efficient force and be, to a certain extent, under an obligation to our great neighbour to ithe south. That would be beneath the pride of Canada. In the state of New York a system of universal training has been adopted for boys up to nineteen, and a boy cannot only not get a graduation certificate from a school, but he cannot get employment unless he has a certificate to show that he has been trained. That measure was passed in 'the state ol New York last year after thorough debate, and I believe the same idea which made the legislature of that state come to that conclusion will be found to exist in Canada. Similar legislation is now before the United States Congress at Washington, with very good prospects of being passed there. Therefore, we are gradually accustoming our young men to the idea that as they pass through life they must recognize that some military force is necessary. We cannot do without it altogether, and the best way will be to accustom every man to think that not only must he go to school to educate himself in the ordinary rudiments of learning, but that he must look forward to taking part, if the call should come, in the defence of his

womankind and his country, although we hope that he will never be called upon to do so. He will not be a paid soldier, a mercenary; he will be a man who is full of the best patriotism, and who will be willing to give a few weeks a year in order to take up arms if arms are necessary.
Cadet services-for pay of instructors, expenses of, teachers qualifying; at military schools, and contingent expenses, $75,000.
Major-General MEWBTTRN: I am sorry the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) is not in the House just now. I agree with everything the hon. gentleman said as regards the cadet corps throughout Canada, which have a wonderful record. I have here a memorandum which I have not been able to complete, but for the benefit of the committee I should like to give these figures which are much less than the actual numbers, because we have not the returns from all parts. The figures I have show that the number of young cadets, that is, members of cadet corps in Canada, who enlisted in the Canadian Expeditionary Force for overseas service, was over 40,000. Of these, 2,319 were killed in action; 11 obtained the Victoria Cross; 857 received other decorations; and 401 obtained commissions. The record' is a most creditable one. The vote of $75,000 is just the same as last year. The pre-war expenditures in 1913-1914 for cadet services was $392,000. Personally, I should like to see the appropriation increased a little this year, and I may ask later on in the Supplementary Estimates for an increase. The present vote is barely enough to keep the organizations going, and even now many of the schools throughout Canada are anxious to continue their cadet corps and build them up again.

What is this money expended on? For instructors?
Major-General MEWBURN: For pay of instructors, expenses of teachers qualifying at military schools, and contingent expenses.^ It includes the pay and allowances and transportation of all the organizers and inspectors, and also an instructional allowance of one dollar each for the first fifty cadets, and fifty cents each for the excess over fifty, in each corps. They furnish their own uniforms.
. Mr. POWER:	Is that amount per
annum?
Major-General MEWBURN: Yes. A certain amount is paid for physical training instructors.

Is the cost of rifles and
other arms included in this vote?
Major-General MEWBURN: No.
Engineer services and works, ordinary repairs and works, Halifax defences, Quebec defences, Esquimalt defences, $430,000.
Major-General MEWBURN:	This is for
all the care and upkeep of the various armouries and general engineer services. It does not cover the extraordinary amounts. That would come under Public Works.

Does this cover building
the armouries?
Major-General MEWBURN:	No, that
would come under Public Works.

Is this not a large item
for ordinary repairs and works?
Major-General iMEWBURN:	No, it has
been pared down. The pre-war expenses ,ran over a million dollars.

What has been done to
the citadel at Quebec?
Major-General MEWBURN: There is a re-vote of $20,000 for that. The whole vote was not expended.

What is it for?
Major-General MEWBURN: The upkeep of the walls of the citadel.
Grants to associations and bands-for grants to artillery and rifle associations, military bands and military institutions, $25,000.

Does this cover grants to rifle associations?
Major-General MEWBURN: Yes.

I was not aware that any grants had been allowed during the last four years, but I see that the same amount was in last year's Estimates.
Major-General MEWBURN: Only about $5,000 of last year's vote was spent, but we expect to expend the money this year. We have already had applications from several rifle associations, which want to reorganize and to go on with both Dominion and provincial rifle association matches. Even the Bisley matches are going on again in England, and the authorities overseas are anxious that we should send a team over, and it is suggested that some of the men who have been overseas should form a team. A number of civilian organizations would like to organize again.

Is it in order for rifle associations to send in applications for grants as before the war, and for rifles and other equipment?

Alajor-General A1EWBURN: It is quite in order, and we would be very glad to take the matter up.

This year?
Major-Genei'al MEWBURN r I hope so. I would be very glad to encourage rifle associations in every way.

Are rifles available now if asked for?
Major-General MEWBURN:	Yes, there
would be no difficulty in getting them now.

What military bands are included in this item?
Major-General MEWBURN:	Regimental
bands of the various city corps. A maximum amount of $180 was given to city corps for bands. I think I am safe in saying that nearly every city corps in Canada kept its band in some sort of organization, and many bandsmen went to the front. Quite a large number have come back and are going into the regimental bands again. They have, indeed, been a perfect God-send to the troops coming back, and many of them are turning out to welcome the returned soldiers.
This does not in any way maintain the organizations, as they are maintained by the regiments themselves.
Headquarters and District Staffs, $225,000.

What staffs are these?
Major-General MEWBURN: The Headquarters staff here, and the staffs at Military Districts Nos. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12 and 13. The staff includes the officer commanding the military district, general staff officer, the Deputy Assistant Adjutant and Quartermaster General, the officer in charge of administration, and the district intelligence officer.

Does the vote pertain to the headquarters staffs in the military -districts where men are being demobilized?
Major-General MEWBURN: The bulk of those are only temporary appointments, changing almost every day. They come under the war vote.

At the proper time I wish to say something about these staffs in the different military districts, particularly in the province of New Brunswick. At the present time there is a sort of guard at St. John, N.B.
Major-General MEWBURN: Those men are all drawing Canadian Expeditionary Force rates and allowances.

I want to call the minister's attention again to the fact that in these headquarters' staffs for the military districts there are a large number of men who did not see service overseas. These good staff positions should undoubtedly 9 p.m. go to the men who have seen service at the front. I drew the minister's attention to this matter last year, and he promised that at the earliest opportunity he would see to it that the overseas men were appointed to important positions on the district staffs. Shortly after that I put a question on the Order Paper asking who were employed on the headquarters staff at Alilitary District N^. 5. There were twenty officers, if I remember correctly, only four of whom had seen sef-vice at the front. The amount paid out in salaries per month was $4,000, of which something like $800 was paid to returned soldiers, and the general in charge of the staff also drew his salary out of that $4,000. Obviously, the returned soldiers of that district were not getting the positions to which they were entitled. At the beginning of this session I put another question on the Order Paper with reference to the headquarters staffs, but through delay from some cause or another, I have not received an answer yet. From the information that I have obtained here and there, however, I have come to the conclusion that most of the district staffs are in the same position as Quebec. There has been a slight improvement. I am told, since last year, but not to the extent there should have been. I do not like to bother the minister about this all the time, but I really think that the people of this country expect good staff positions to be given to returned soldiers.
Alajor-General MEWBURN: Since I have been Alinister of Militia and Defence I have not made any permanent appointments in the Militia Department, and so far as I am concerned every appointment that is made will be given to a man who has seen overseas service. With respect to the officers who have been employed and are employed to-day on district staffs through the period of demobilization, I am only too glad to retain the officers who have done faithful work during this war. A large number of officers have been unjustly abused for holding down what is called Government or militia jobs who were unable to go overseas. In the early period of the war a great injustice was done to some of our Canadian soldiers. When the

war broke out some of the officers and noncommissioned officers of the permanent corps were prohibited .from going overseas; they were held here, and rightly so; and these men felt very keenly because they could not go. They were willing to take their chances, and it was not cowardice that kept them back. If we had not had officers and non-commissioned officers in Canada we should not have had troops in France. It was absolutely necessary that they should do the work which had to be done here, and I think all credit is due them. Some people say that because they have not been overseas they should get out. That*is not the proper spirit. I know hundreds of officers in the country were disappointed at not being allowed to go overseas, and before and immediately after the signing of the Armistice I received the resignation of many officers who wanted to make room immediately for officers from overseas. YVe have had the greatest diffioulty in getting officers to stay and help in the problem of demobilization. The work that is involved to-day with the return of the troops is of great magnitude. We have to deal with 40,000 to 45,000 troops every month, and every man has to be dealt with individually. We cannot simply let the men go home, but every account has to be made up as well as the paysheets and it is like a run on a bank. I think that the people will appreciate, even if they do not say so, the loyal faithful w'ay in which these officers have done their work. As regards permanent appointments all these districts staffs will be reduced to the minimum, and in some districts there will not be more than four or five permanent positions which 1 hope will be filled by officers from the front. Officers coming back are not anxious to take up civil life again, and I have made. it a ppint to see as far as possible every officer returning to Ottawa and urge him for his own good to get back into civil work, because military jobs will no longer exist for many of them in two or three years' time, and it will be much harder then than it is at present for the men to resume civil occupation. Every important position in the Militia Department should be given to a returned man. But why should this not apply to all the departments-Customs, Post Office, Railway and everything else? And if it is suggested that those in the Militia Department who have not been overseas should get out, the same principle should apply to the other departments. We have an organization of railway troops, the Canadian engineers, the [Major-General Mew-burn.]
finest that the world has ever known, men of outstanding deeds in the war. In the United States the army engineers take charge of public works, and why should the engineers not take charge of public works in Canada and build canals and highways. We all say we w'ant to give the returned soldiers jobs. Well, why not let them carry on the public works of Canada? I believe the country would save money and get better work and the returned soldier would get a better show.

Has the department
disposed of the rifle ranges at Rockcliffe?
Major-General MEWBURN: No.

In my opinion these
were the most magnificent rifle ranges in all Canada. Some years ago the department bought a farm in the county of Carle-ton and new rifle ranges were built. I happened to visit them three or four years ago with my hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Murphy), and I observed that there had been a vast expenditure of money at that place. Of what use is this rifle range to the department at present? Is it intended to make use of it in the future?
Major-General MEWBURN:	An hon.
member asked me last year about the Connaught rifle ranges.

He will accept the answer now.
Major-General MEWBURN: The Connaught rifle range was a property bought by the Government about five miles from Britannia. It is probably one of the finest rifle ranges, I was going to say almost in the world. It was laid out for a very large range, and considerable work was done on it. It was never quite completed, all the work having stopped with the war, but it could be completed with a very small expenditure. It is within a mile of the train. The Rockliffe rifle range is a beautiful place and if shooting develops as in the past, and a great deal of interest is taken all over Canada in the Dominion Rifle Association, it wflll come into being. The Connaught rifle range would be the proper place to carry out rifle shooting. It is a magnificent property. It could also be utilized for camp purposes. But during the war it has lain dormant and no use has been made of it.

Might I suggest, in view of the expenditures which were made for the acquisition and equipment of these ranges, that it would be in the interest of

the country to sell the other property as a pure venture in real estate? I can assure my hon. friend that the Rockcliffe rifle ranges are worth money. You could get a very fine price for that property, ami in that way recoup yourself for what has been spent on the Connaught ranges.
Major-General AIEWBURN: I quite agree with my hon. friend. I understand it was the. intention that the Rockcliffe ranges should be put on the market. But during the war and up to 1917 the Rockcliffe ranges were used far instructional purposes for officers going overseas. If the Connaught ranges had been completed, I understand the other would have been on the market.
Is the land comprised within the Connaught ranges cultivated land?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If hon. gentlemen would allow us to pass the vote now under consideration, this discussion would be perfectly in order under the next item, which concerns rifle ranges.

The hon. gentleman brought
this question up himself.
Air. NiICKLE:	I happened to be up in
the Railway Committee so I am not aware of what may have taken place since this item was called. There are one or two points to which I would like to draw the attention of the minister, as I come from one of the military district headquarters in Ontario. I quite agree with what the minister has said that there were a number of lacn on the district and headquarters staffs who would have been glad indeed to have gone overseas if the opportunity had offered, but the necessity of undertaking the mobilizing and training of the men who volunteered and who were subsequently called under the Alilitary Service Act obliged them to remain in Canada, and without doubt they did good work. In the progress of the war very many men in connection with the district and headquarters staffs attained, as was natural, very rapid promotion, with the result that the emoluments of their offices were very largely increased. At the present time they have the exalted rank incidental to war activities. It occurs to me that when Canada returns to a peace basis it would be well that the minister and his deputies should be active to see that there is a readjustment of the staffs, so that the Consolidated Revenue Fund is not unduly called upon to meet large expenditures for men of exalted rank who will be discharging duties of no very
120| S'
onerous character and involving no very great responsibility. In other words, what I am asking is that the minister should proceed as he has been doing in connection with the demobilization, as promptly as possible, to clear the service of all superfluous officers of high rank, unless these gentlemen are prepared to accept much less remuneration than that to which theii present rank would now entitle them.
I believe the people were quite willing to give remuneration in proportion to the responsibilities borne during war time, but I do not believe that they will be content, particularly when the strain of the war debt comes upon them, to have a large number of men of high rank engaged on the district and headquarters' staffs paid salaries-unless the suggestion I am making, to the minister is put into effect-not commensurate with the duties that they will then be called upon to perform.
Major-General MEWBURN: I explained that pretty fully before the hon. gentleman (Mr. Nickle) came in.

How many officers
are there at the headquarters staff at Halifax, district No. 6?
Alajor-General MEWBURN:	There are
on the actual headquarters staff only five officers. There are in addition the officers in connection with the hospital situation there, the dental service, and the officers in connection with the fortifications that we are closing up. There are also in connection with demobilization the dispersal areas and the army service units. They are all temporary appointments.

How many are
there altogether?
Alajor-General AIEWBURN:	I would
not like to say. There is a garrison regiment, the discharge depot, and the officers in connection with transportation and disembarkation at Halifax and who are temporary.

In the event of an officer
of high rank, who had served in the army and who in the olden times had belonged to the permanent force being assigned to a military district, I presume that his salary would not be reduced?
Major-General AIEWBURN:	That is a
difficult problem. There is no provision in the law for dealing with a case of that kind. Take the case of a Alajor General commanding a division in the field, or a permanent corps officer; when he comes home the only appointment he can get is

at headquarters here or command of a military district. I am afraid that such men will have to come and take the salary of pre-war days unless Parliament 'is willing to increase these salaries. They would not receive the Canadian Expeditionary Force pay and allowances, because the pay and allowances will cease at the conclusion of the war. I appreciate the position of a lot of these officers who have attained high rank at the front, who have rendered distinguished services and who have commanded divisions in the field.

There are only three or four such cases?
Major-General MEWBURN:	There are
to my knowledge, three who have been Generals in the field and they are entitled to the first consideration. But there is no provision in the Militia Act authorizing us to deal with their cases. To-day they are drawing the pay and allowances of the Canadian Expeditionary Force.

At present the commander of a military district is engaged for only three or four years?
Major-General MEWBURN: The usual tenure of command is four years. There is nobody in any military district who has a permanent appointment.

Is there no special allowance for a G.O.C. of a district?
Major-General MEWBURN: His pay and allowance covers everything. The Canadian Expeditionary Force pay and allowance overseas are greater than those of peace times here. In the permanent corps there were certain allowances.

Is it possible for some of the medical men in the Canadian Army Medical Corps to be released in order to procure the positions which are going to be created in connection with the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment? I believe that most of these appointments are being made from amongst civilian practitioners for the very good reason that others are not available.
Major-General MEWBURN: That is one of our most difficult problems. I would not like to make the positive statement, but as near as our estimates can indicate we figure that we ought to be pretty well through with our hospitalization work in connection with the soldier patients about next February. I would not like to state that positively. The Civil Re-establisbment work will go on for a great many years. At
[Major-General Mewburn.]
the time of the armistice our casualties overseas were 45,000. We brought back a large number of patients for treatment in our hospitals, and it was a most difficult problem to figure out our requirements. We estimate that some time about the first of May 18,000 Canadian patients will have been brought back to Canada. That indicates that the number is being reduced very rapidly. After that I do not think there will be more than 14,000 to bring back. They are gradually recovering; in fact, they are recovering more rapidly than we expected. They are coming out of the hospitals and going back to civilian life. Therefore, the medical profession, those magnificent men who went overseas, and even those who served in Canada in the hospitals, giving up their private practices in order to do so, are naturally anxious to get back and pick up their practices or to get some employment with the pension commissioners, or with the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment Commission, which will be of a more permanent nature. We are endeavouring to cope with that situation and to release these medical officers as rapidly as it is possible to do so. We do not want to retain a medical officer one minute longer than we must. A large percentage of the medical officers and members of the dental profession are staying on out of a pure sense of loyalty to duty, in order to look after the patients in the hospitals. It is a most difficult problem, and it is most embarrassing for us to have to ask these men to continue. They are working for a mere pittance compared with the emolun^eats of their private practices, and although they are most anxious to get back and pick up their work, they are staying on the job simply because they think it is their duty to the returned soldiers who have been wounded.

Does that include the Connaught rifle range?
Major-General MEWBURN:	I do not
think that has anything to do with the rifle ranges.

I find here:
For grants to artillery and rifle associations,-
Am I out of order?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No, sir.

The Connaught rifle range is one of the finest properties in that section of the country, and I suppose that about half a million to a million dollars has been spent on it. At the present time it is used as a cattle range. There are some-

thing over 2,000 acres in this property let at a rental of 50 cents an acre. That is a very small sum of money for such a large piece of land. I only discovered that after a great deal of trouble. I also discovered that the department employs a caretaker to look after the property at $1,200 a year, and as it is only getting about $900 in return it seems to me not to be a very paying speculation. I do not think it is very much to the credit of the country to keep such a large tract of land for the benefit of a few cattle dealers. That property could be laid out as one of the best rifle ranges on the North American continent. Why does not the department rent the land to some farmers? A farmer tried last year to rent it, but he was turned down. Those few cattle dealers have been making a fortune fattening cattle on that range, and I think it is time something was done to stop this mismanagement, But that is not the worst part of it. I went several times to try to get some person a job and was asked: Was he a returned soldier? If not, he could not get the job. Is there a returned soldier on the job now?
Major-General MEWBURN: No; there is to be one.

Why does not the department put a returned soldier on it? It is giving a man who is not a returned soldier $1,200 a year for doing nothing. I was turned down last year on this item, I was told I was out of order, and I was beginning to think I would be out of order tonight, but I was determined to press my question. I hope the gentleman in charge of the department will see that something is done to improve this condition of affairs.
Major-General MEWBURN: I understand the range is let for grazing purposes. I did not appoint the careteaker, but I gave instructions some time ago for the appointment of a returned soldier directly the present man's contract is up. I am very glad the hon. gentleman has drawn my attention to the matter, but it had been already dealt with and the change he suggests is going to be made.

What are you doing with the timber?
Major-General MEWBURN: I do not think there is any intention to cut the timber. We do not know for what purpose we may require the property.

Some timber was cut down for firewood last winter.
Major-General MEWBURN: A certain amount of fallen timber was taken by the Militia Department last winter and used in various barracks for fuel.
I have it on the best authority that a hundred cords of good green standing trees were cut.
There are some fine farms over there.

I could not hear all my hon. friend (Mr. Boyce) was saying, and he might have been giving to the minister the information I want to get. What money has been expended so far on this rifle range?
Major-General MEWBURN: I could not give exact figures now, but I think about 1780,000 up to 1916.

And the work was not completed, was it?
Major-General MEWBURN: No. I think the balance of the contract at the time work was stopped was something like $40,000. It was stopped in 1916.

Has the land been cultivated by any person, and have any returns been received by the department from the sale of crops.
Major-General MEWBURN: I understand the only revenue derived is about $960 for grazing rights; there is no land cultivated.

Was it let by tender to one individual or more?
Major-General MEWBURN: I understand" three or four tenders were received. The highest tender was accepted.

How many years has that been going on?
Major-General MEWBURN:	Two years
ago I believe, and the rights have been renewed.

I have not exact figures,
but I understand a large quantity of valuable timber was cut and carried away by others than the Militia Department or any other department of the Government.
Major-General MEWBURN:	I understand that the only timber cut was cut and utilized by the Militia Department in connection with one or two camps. I do not know that any good sound timber was cut.
That property includes 500 acres of the finest land in that part of the country, and I think advantage ought to be taken of it.

I would like to know if there is any correspondence in the department with regard to the mismanagement of this property?
Major-General MEWBURN: I would not say there is none, but none has been brought to my personal attention.

Mr. Chairman, how
many rifle ranges are maintained in the Dominion? A range was established a few years ago at the instance of the Megantic Rifle Association. It is situated in my own riding, although the members of the association live in the county of Compton. I attach special importance to this range, because on the day that it was opened I was invited by the members of the association to be present, and, although I never before had held a rifle in my hand, I demonstrated, by recording a bull's-eye at six hundred yards what a simple art the handling of a rifle is. Is this range still being maintained?
Major-General MEWBURN: I cannot say off-hand: probably it is a regimental rifle range. There is a range in every military district, in some cases mare than one. In some parts of Canada rifle-ranges are organized in connection with militia units and maintained on leased private property.
Permanent force, $2,575,000.

Is the permanent force not now part of the Canadian Expeditionary Force?
Major-General MEWBURN: The permanent force pay and allowances have, during tne war, been paid out of this vote.

Was not an Order in Council passed last summer or autumn to the effect that every unit in Canada was to be part of the Canadian Expeditionary Force?
Major-General MEWBURN: They are all part of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, but the permanent force has always been kept on separate pay and allowances.

Is it intended to keep up the permanent force as it has been during the war?
Major-General MEWBURN: We hope to be able to build up a permanent force of 5,000. If that is done, the amount of this vote will have to be increased in the Supplementary Estimates.
[Major-General Mewburn.]

I assume that the pav 'and allowances of the permanent force would include pay and allowances to permanent officers located in Ottawa?
Major-General MEWBURN: It would include a few of them here.

It is said that some of these officers who were too old to go overseas, or who, at all events, were required here, changed their uniforms to khaki when the war broke out and began to receive subsistence allowance, field allowance, and so on. Perhaps there is a good explanation for that, but it does not occur to me.
Major-General MEWBURN: During the war these men got this extra field allowance. A great many of them should have had their pay doubled, considering the hours that they worked. The men at district headquarters worked day in and day out, Saturdays, Sundays and nights. Last week the staff at headquarters worked until midnight Saturday night, and all day Sunday without going home to lunch -and they do not ask extra duty pay. There is very little criticism of officers working on Canadian Expeditionary Force rates of pay and getting this field allowance.

I have no doubt that these men were doing practically double the work that they did in peace times, and were entitled to more pay. Perhaps this was the proper way to give them increased remuneration; it does not strike me that it is the proper way. For instance, the Department of Justice wanted to increase the pay of a certain man connected with the department, and they could think of no other way of doing it than that of making him a lieutenant and having him draw a lieutenant's pay as well as the salary of his official position in the department. That looks like a roundabout way of doing the thing; it looks as if there was an attempt to cover something up. If a man deserves an increase in pay, give it to him in a straight und above board manner. I do not say that these officers were getting more than they should, but I do not see the necessity of giving them consideration by sending around a roast of beef or bag of potatoes and calling it rations or subsistence allowance or something of that kind. It looks to the ordinary layman as a way of getting graft.
Major-General MEWBURN: The practice which has been followed, has prevailed in the army for a great many years.
Yes, and there has been a certain amount of graft in the army for a number of years, too.

Do I understand the minister to say that we have a permanent force at the present time of 2,000 to 3,000 ?
Major-General MEWBURN: The strength is a little over 3,000, and we hope to build it up to 5,000. the establishment authorized by the Militia Act.

Under present conditions, a permanent force of 5,000 men for Canada is the least that any one should contemplate. I do not know what our responsibilities may be in the matter oi the league of nations; perhaps the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) can tell us. I understand that the United States have announced that they are prepared to organize a standing army of 500,000 men, if necessary, in order that they may ,ake upon themselves their share of the responsibility of policing the world. Canada may be called upon to do a little of that from time to time, and surely the modest estimate the minister gives for the permanent force should be attained in the very near future. We have excellent material coming back from overseas at present, and amongst those men and officers will certainly be found some who desire to follow soldiering as a career. I trust the minister will get at least 5,000 men as soon as possible. and that they will be maintained as a permanent force in Canada, so that we may preserve our self-respect as a very humble member in the great League of Nations that is being proclaimed as practically the millennium of the world. After all, whether the League is an ideal, or something of a concrete formation, its ultimate resort will evidently be physical force, and we cannot expect to maintain the position of Canada in the League of Nations unless we have at least a few men upon whom we can call, who are, at any rate, ready for eventualities, I am heartily in accord with the prospect that the minister holds out, that we shall have 5,000 officers and men in the permanent force in the near future-and in my judgment it cannot come too soon.

Will the minister explain the procedure as regards purchasing provisions and supplies?
Major-General MEWBURN:	Everything
is done through the War Purchasing Commission.
Salaries and wages-for pay of caretakers, messengers, barrack labourers, boat crews at
Halifax, engineers and firemen for the drill halls, and all other civil employees in the districts not provided for elsewhere, $2.60,000.

What does this cover?
Major-General MEWBURN: It covers salaries and wages of caretakers, messengers and so on in the various military districts, at the dock yards at Halifax, and also in the barracks and hospitals throughout the Dominion. For instance, it includes all the caretakers at the rifle ranges.
Surveys, $35,000.
Mr. CAS'GRAIN: What are these surveys?
Major-General MEWBURN:	They are
military topographical surveys made all over Canada. The item has been gradually cut down, and we hope to get the work completed eventually. Salaries in connection with this work amount to about $24,500; transport and sundry expenses in the field and maintenance, $3,700; freight and express, $130; miscellaneous, $870.

On what scale are the maps?
Major-General MEWBURN: One inch to the mile. The total area surveyed amounts to 28,000 square miles.

What is the purpose of these surveys?
Major-General MEWBURN: To prepare a regular military topographical map, showing the water features; the boundaries of counties, townships and cities; the timber, and other features of military value. The maps, while ostensibly for military purposes, are most complete and can be utilized for almost any other purpose.

Are they sent out promiscuously?
Major-General MEWBURN: No.

Are they filed in the department?
ATajor-General AIEWBURN: It would not be in the public interest to distribute them, but they are always available.

I cannot see what advantage they are to military officers if they are filed away in the department, and if the maps are of public importance they ought to be made public.
Major-General MEWBURN: It certainly would not be in the public interest to distribute these military maps.
Transport and freight, $25,000.

Can the minister explain wliv the transport of the staff is estimated

at $15,000 and the transport of the permanent force, which would include the whole permanent force except the officers, at only $10,000? Apparently it costs more to transport the officers than the rest of the army.
Major-General MEWBTJRN: We have cut the item down by $10,000. It is to cover travelling and other expenses in connection with transport between the different districts. A lot of shipments are made between the different districts.

But my point is this: How does the minister figure out that it is going to cost more to transport the officers than the rest of the army?
Major-General MEWBUBN: The men are not moving from one station to another as the officers are.

It does not include the transport of a battalion to a training camp?
Major-General MEWBUBN: Oh, no. Training- areas, $35,000.

In what district are these training areas?
Major-General MEWBURN: We do not propose spending very much this year. It is estimated that $900 will cover the cost of the site at North Sydney required for defence work. The site at Beau-10 p.m. mont was selected early in August, 1914. This item is mainly to cover unforeseen expenditures in connection with the training areas, and there will be no particular expenditure on the training areas themselves.

I judge from the minister's answer that the department does not intend to buy any more property around Valcartier camp.
Major-General MEWBURN: No.

Is that camp going to be closed down?
Major-General MEWBURN: I would not like to say it is going to be closed. I hope it will come into being again, because it is one of the best camps in Canada.
Miscellaneous-amount required to pay Consular officers abroad for services, $300.

Is this to pay our own
Consuls? I understand we have Consuls now.

No, Canada has not her own Consular officers. This item is simply to cover the expenses that may be incurred by a Consul in some foreign country in 
procuring information requested by this Government. This item is similar to last ye-'11' s. It is to pay the Consular officers appointed by Great Britain to whom we might write to procure information on certain specific matters, the procuring of which would entail some small expenditure.
If they are officers of the British Government, should not the British Government pay them? Wiry should we add to their salary?

I speak from a very general knowledge of the matter, but I understand that this is not compensation for their services, but to repay small expenses they may have incurred in procuring information for us.
-Can the minister give the House a concrete example?
I cannot to-night, but I shall be glad to get one. How'ever, the item is very small.

But the principle seems
to be bad. For instance, if the Canadian Government has certain work to perform through the British Embassy in Washington, would the minister maintain that this Government should pay for services rendered by officers of the British Embassy?
No. I have already said that that was not the character of the expenditure. It is simply to provide for the payment of expenses incurred by a Consular officer at our request.

fl think there ought to be some reciprocity between the two Governments. Suppose we obtain information for the British Government, do we charge them for the expenses incurred? They would only be trifling amounts.

This vote is only for a
trifling amount.

The point I wish to make is this:	If the British Government asked
us to procure certain information we would surely do that without exacting from them the small outlay entailed.

There would be no charge for services rendered, but if an expenditure was made by us at the request of the British Government I presume an account would be rendered. If the British Government incurs an expense at our request,
I presume an account would be rendered, and it would be paid out of this small appropriation.

But the minister must
have some facts on "which this estimate is based. Why should we vote this $300?

It is the same amount
as last year. If my hon. friend wishes the item to stand I am willing, and I will get him a concrete example.
Mr. Beland carried.
Salaries and expenses of the Paris Agency, $28,000.

Canada is represented in Paris by a Canadian Commissioner, Mr. Philippe Roy, who has charge of the office there and is rendering very efficient service. I think it was wise to open a Canadian office in Paris, and I believe it is being very satisfactorily administered by the present commissioner. Owing to the increased cost of living I expect it will be necessary to bring down a supplementary estimate making some further provision for the expenses of the Paris office. The vote is the same as last year.
What was this Order in Council?

Under the treaty between the United States and Great Britain under which the International Joint Commission was appointed, the commissioner is authorized to investigate and consider questions relating to boundary matters between the United States and Canada. Mr. Stewart is one of the experts of the department here and is entrusted with special duties as adviser. to the Canadian Section of the International Joint Commission. In regard to a question which arose last year with reference to water-power, Mr. Stewart investigated the whole matter on behalf of the Canadian section of the commission in order to inform them of the facts from the engineering and scientific standpoint. I am advised that he is a very capable man, and is rendering efficient service in protecting Canadian interests in this important regard.

Would the minister be
good enough to lay on the Table as soon as possible the award or judgment which was rendered by the commission on this question of the St, Lawrence water-power? He knows what award I am referring to. Yesterday I brought up the question, and the Minister of Railways stated that the arrangement was that the company in question would be allowed to exploit that waterpower during five years after the war. I do not object to the exploitation of that waterpower on a basis which would be acceptable to both Canada and the United States, but I would not like any particular industry to have a monopoly of the power. The judgment, which I think has been published in book form would be very useful for future reference.

I shall endeavour to lay
it on the Table to-morrow. My present recollection of the judgment differs slightly from the view given by the Minister of Railways and my hon. friend, but it is no use discussing it until we have the actual order here.

Is Mr. Stewart a regular
employee of the Government?
I believe he is, although I am not familiar with the particular branch of the work he is engaged in.
Mr. W. J. Stewart was a distinguished graduate of the Royal Military College, and for about thirty years he has been engaged in work of this nature.
What department is he working in?
I am told that he is in the Department of Naval Affairs, but I am not sure.
This is a special allowance. But what does he do, and what is his regular salary?

In the absence of the Minister of Naval Affairs I cannot say what his work in the other department is. 1 can only speak as to his work in this department, which is undoubtedly very important and valuable. All those who have to do with Mr. Stewart have spoken in the highest terms of the service he is rendering on these important questions.

I have no doubt of that, and I am willing to accept the statement of the minister and of the other hon. gentleman in regard to this distinguished man. But that does not give us the information we desire. If this man is well paid by the Government for doing regular work and this is in his regular work, I do not see why, because he is distinguished, we should vote an extra allowance. If he has done extra work for which he is entitled to be paid, let us know what it is and we will be prepared to consider the question.

This is not a new allowance. On the general principle I am in accord with what the hon. gentleman has said; I think it is wiser that officials should be paid one salary only. But here is a case where an officer has been in receipt of a salary from two departments. He has been dividing his time between the two. Had he not been receiving these amounts from these two departments, and had he been devoting himself to the work of one department only I have no doubt that his salary would have been increased. The practice has been for each department to pay him a certain salary.

Has this been done for more than one year? What my hon. friend says may be absolutely correct he may be getting a salary from both departments. But I feel that we should call a halt in regard to a system of this kind. Every once in a

while we have some minister getting up and slipping through a $1,000 for a man here, and $500 for another there, and we know nothing about it. Members of the House should' have some information in regard to twhat these men are getting from the public treasury. If officials are not paid enough, I do not believe there is a man on this side of the House or the other but is perfectly willing to give them what they are entitled to.
Why has the minister delayed the payment of this item since 1912?

My hon. friend is not correct in that. The payment this year is the same as last year. This is the allowance he gets for the service he renders to this department each year. According to the Civil Service list he gets a salary of $4,000 in the Naval Service department; with this $1,000 his total salary is $5,000.
He has been getting this salary since 1912?
All I can say is that he got it Iasi year. I understand he has been getting this salary for some years.
Why is this not included in the Estimates of the Naval Service Department?
Because this work is not done for the Naval Service Department but for the International Joint Commission which comes under the department of External Affairs.
Does the Government pay the cost of that commission?
It pays the cost of the Canadian section.
The appointments to the commission, I understand, are made by the British Government.
The appointments are made by the British Government on the nomination of the Canadian Government.

One of the last acts of
the Laurier Government was the appointment of Mr. Aime Geoffrion, K.C., as one of the commissioners. The recommendation was made and sent by the Canadian Government to London in order to get the ratification of that nomination by the British authorities. Meanwhile a storm passed over Canada and, unfortunately for this country, the Government which my hon. friend and myself supported so strenuously in 1911, was defeated. That was a very sorry day for

Canada. A new Government came into office. The first thing that new Government did was to nullify the Order in Council recommending Mr. Geoffrion as one of the commissioners. His Majesty's Government was informed that the recommendation had been made in a moment of weakness, and they recommended Mr. T. Chase Casgrain, K.C., as commissioner. The Home Government accepted the recommendation of the Borden Government and Mr. Casgrain, who later on became Postmaster General, acted as commissioner. Then, when he was sworn in as a member of the Cabinet, he had to Tesign and his successor was Mr. P. B. Migneault, K.C., who was appointed to that same position following the same appropriate procedure. Then Mr. Migneault was appointed a few months ago a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada. Since that time there has been a vacancy on the International Waterways Commission. I am informed that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), on behalf of the Canadian Government, offered the appointment to Mr. F. J. Bisaillon, K.C. Mr. Bisaillon is one *of the leading King's Counsel in Canada. He has been engaged in all the big legal *cases and is well known throughout the country as a man of great ability. He certainly would be a credit to our country on that commission. It appears that the Minister of Justice informed Mr. Bisaillon that be had been recommended by this Government to the Home Government in succession to Judge Migneault, but since then nothing has been done and the vacancy is there. I hold no brief for Mr. Bisaillon, who Is a political opponent, and than whom no [DOT]one certainly is more deserving of recognition by the Union Government because he has always been
May I interrupt the hon. gentleman? This Government has abolished^ patronage, and such an appeal as this is absolutely beside the point and rather insulting to hon. gentlemen opposite.

This is not an appointment by this Government; it is an appointment by the British Government on the recommendation of the Canadian Government. Mr. Bisaillon was one of the lonely old Conservatives who in the last general election gave a generous support to Union Government. He was told that he had been recommended by the Minister of Justice, and that the recommendation had been forwarded to London, yet nothing has been done. Could my hon. friend enlighten me on the subject?

My hon. friend, I think, has been misinformed. No recommendation has been so far made to the Imperial Government to fill the vacancy due to the resignation of Mr. Justice Migneault. 1 imagine that none will be made until the return of the Prime Minister, as it is a matter for the Department of External Affairs.
I would like to know how many sittings took place last year of the Commission and what kind of work the gentleman did for whom this vote is asked, and how long he was engaged on it?

This gentleman is not a member of the Commission; he is its technical adviser. I cannot state how many sittings of the Commission were held, although I recall a number. His work consists of looking into any question that comes before the Commission, and it may involve a large amount or a small amount of work, depending on the character of the question; but if he is not working on this branch he is working on the other. His total salary is in respect of his position with the Naval Department and his work on this Commission.

We are paying this gentleman $4,000 a year in the Department of Naval Affairs, and $1,000 a year in this department. I would like to know exactl\ what he did, to be entitled to the $1,000. If he was working exclusively upon naval matters he was getting $4,000 a year, and was not entitled to a cent more. If he was working all the time for this Commission, and got only $1,000, he was not getting enough. But you cannot have a man in two positions if he can only occupy one at a time. I would like to know whether his work is done in Ottawa of in \\ ashington, and how much time he devotes to it every year.

Of course, my hon. friend will understand that I cannot give him those details to-night, but I can tell him the general character of the work. I know during the past year this gentleman made a study of the St. Lawrence power situation and reported on the application of the American company to build a dam, and attended hearings of the commission when the matter came up. That came under my personal observation. Any other matters of a similar character he would advise upon and would carry on his work whenever the necessities of the case required. I imagine that the-matter I spoke of involved his visiting the site of the proposed dam

and looking into the situation, and attending a hearing in Washington and a hearing in Montreal. When not engaged in this particular work he was engaged in work for the other department.
Can the minister tell us what particular work he does for the Naval Department to earn $4,000?
His title indicates the character of the work he is doing. Personally, 1 have no knowledge of his work there.

If the vacancy on the International Joint Commission which has been referred to still exists, how it it possible for the commission to carry on its work? I understand the personnel consists of three American and three Canadian commissioners. It would 'be manifestly unfair if this commission sat with only two Canadian members in attendance as against three American. Have any sittings been held since Mr. Justice Migneault retired?
Mr. .ROWELL: I believe some sittings have been held, but no matters of a controversial character arose where there might be a division of opinion.
Sittings have been held with three American and only two Canadian commissioners present, although three Canadians were appointed?
Yes; but, as I say, no question of a controversial character has come up where full representation was necessary.
Could the minister tell us when the vacancy will be filled?
I have already stated that it will be filled when the Prime Minister returns. I do not expect it will be dealt with until then.
Is the absence of the Prime Minister the only reason why it is not filled?
It is in the Prime Minister s Department and is a matter for him to deal with.

The Prime Minister at the present moment is just in the place where the appointment is to be made. I understand it is made from London.
Amount required to meet expenses of the Lake of the Woods Technical Board and the Lake of the Woods Control Board, $6,000.

This is a board constituted as a result of an investigation carried 
on by the International Joint Commission to regulate the waters of the Lake of the Woods in order to conserve the interests of navigation and to prevent the waters falling below a certain level. As my hon. friend is aware, the Lake of the Woods is an international waterway, and people living on the American side have rights in it. We have to maintain the level, but as that level is influenced by the outlet, which is wholly in Canadian territory, and is not the work of an international commission, we regulate the level in our territory, but we are doing it pursuant to the orders of the International Joint Commission.
Who are the commissioners?

The commission consists of two members appointed by the Dominion Government and two appointed by the Government of Ontario. Its duties are to look after the level of the waters of the Lake of the Woods and the proper conservation and control of the waters in the interests of navigation, water powers, etc., and to make regulations for the control of the same. The members of the commission appointed on behalf of the Dominion Government are: W. J. Stewart, who is chairman, and J. B. Challies, secretary.
Is that the same Mr. Stewart?

Yes. This is not for salaries; it -is for expenses in connection with the work of the Commission.
^ Mr. CANNON: How much did Mr. Stewart get last year as a member of this-board?
Nothing. The Commission was not constituted until January of the present year.
How much of this vote' goes to Air. Stewart, and how much t( the-secretary?
None of it goes to Air. Stewart. As I have said, this vote is purely for the expenses of the Commission.
What expenses?
They must do this work: through men employed for the purpose.
Who are the men?
I cannot give my hon.. friend that information at present.

When this item was prepared by the officers of the department

surely they knew exactly what it covered. The minister should have this information and give it to the Committee.

If my hon. friend thinks it important to have the details, I shall be very glad to get them from the officers of the department.
Item stands.
Canadian War Mission and Representation at Washington, $50,000.

When this item was up before, the member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) and the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) asked for some information. If the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) desires it, I will let this item stand, as the time has come when I said the Committee would rise.
I do not want to obstruct my hon. friend's Estimates, but he does not seem to be as well informed as usual, and he might as well take a little more time to go over the items.
I can give my hon. friend information with regard to this one.

We will have the happy anticipation of getting it at the next sitting.
Progress reported.
On motion of Hon. Mr. Rowell the House adjourned at 10.40 p. m.
Wednesday, April 30, 1919.

2.	If so, what are the names of the generals?
3.	What has been the outlay in connection with these portraits?

2.	If so, from what date?
3.	Why was Separation Allowance not paid wireless operators from the commencement of the war?

1.	Yes.
2.	1st November, 1918.
3.	The Wireless Branch oi the Naval Department is a permanent organization undertaking in peace time a commercial service and providing aid to navigation, and in war time providing wireless service for naval purposes.

To represent the Government of Canada in connection with the purchase and distribution of Canadian agricultural products and manufactured articles by governmental agencies appointed by the United Kingdom and other allied nations; and to keep the Canadian Government and its departments more directly in touch with such activities; and to render important service generally with the purpose of securing for the agricultural and other productions of Canada their appropriate share in the markets of the world during the period of reconstruction.

House again in Committee on Bill No. 52, to amend the Immigration Act, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the Committee rose yesterday at six o'clock we were considering clause 1 of the Bill, and the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) had the floor.

When the Committee rose at six o'clock yesterday I was dealing with the remarks of the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) with reference t-o the alien enemy within our country. There are several thousand such alien enemies interned in Canad-a at the present time, and the hon. gentleman thought that on account of that fact no danger was to be apprehended. On the other hand I made the remark that I thought it would be in the public interest if these people could be sent back to the country from which they came as quickly as that could be arranged for. Under present conditions some difficulty m-ay exist in that regard. I would point out, however, that this question is one that affects the country to such an extent that it is very important we should have a proper conception as to whal the effect of this Bill is going to be on the future of Canada.
