If you contaminate a stream -at its source that stream will he polluted throughout its entire course. The next few years will undoubtedly see a great many people coming into Canada from other countries, and therefore I am glad to see that the Government has taken steps to meet the conditions which will confront us in future by establishing a separate department of the Government, with a responsible minister in charge, to take care of the stream of immigration that is likely to enter the Dominion.
A Department of Public Health ha3 also been established with a view to preventing

Ihe lowering of the standard of our people through undesirable immigration and otherwise. We cannot pay too much attention to questions of this kind. Many people who have come here in the past h'ad little or no means; in fact I believe that in many instances assistance was granted to them by the provincial governments to enable them to reach this country. Ultimately they became good citizens. During the next few years the Government should see that immigration to Canada comes from Great Britain in so far as is possible. We as a part of the British Empire must have people who are actuated by the motives that actuate the people of the British Empire; our educational insti-tutipns must carry on wdth that object in view.	,
I was surprised at some of the remarks that were made with regard to the foreign element which have established themselves in large colonies in Canada, particularly in the Western Provinces. The minister told us that no effort had been made by previous Governments to do anything for these people after they came here. The member from Montreal (Mr. Jacobs) contended that with our splendid educational facilities, there should be no difficulty in taking care of the foreign element wdro come to this country. Unfortunately, our educational institutions are not of a uniform nature; in one province certain regulations prevail, and in another province we have something entirely different. If we are going to remain a part of the British Empire we should have national schools; children should not be permitted to attend schools where a foreign language is taught, and in which the fundamental principles of ithe British Empire are not properly set forth. So far as the constitution permits, the policy which I suggest should be adopted and carried out in its entirety.
That is altogether nonsensical.

Some reference was made to an Imperial policy. No doubt a policy will be formulated as a result of the negotiations which are taking place between the representatives of the various colonies, and the Motherland. It is not possible to anticipate v'hat will be done, but this Bill will enable the Government to put into effect the conclusions arrived at as a result of those negotiations.
Reference has been made to the splendid reforms that have taken place among the people who have come into some of our provinces. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Jacobs) said that if the Austrians who have settled in Western Canada had not come here and become established in these communities they might have fought against us during the war, and that it was a. splendid thing to have brought them here and thus to have prevented them from joining the ranks of the enemy at the front. If you stop to consider, you will be able to form an estimate of the deplorable influence exercised upon the standard of our citizenship by the attitude of those who are not and have not been in sympathy with us during this war. I remarked at the outset that the standard of a nation's greatness must be measured by t.he character of their people. Canada, with her tremendous undeveloped resources and her great possibilities for the future, must see that none but the most desirable people are permitted to come within her bounds.
The hon. gentleman also complimented the late Liberal Government upon the work which they did in the matter of immigration. I have my own opinion with regard to what was done in this respect while hon. gentlemen opposite were conducting the affairs of the country.
I do not know that I could better illustrate the methods pursued by hon. gentlemen opposite than by reading a letter written by the notorious W. T. R. Preston, an officer of the then Liberal Government, who was at the head of the Emigration Department in the Old Country, with headquarters 17 Victoria street, London 8.W., on October 18,	1901-a time when the
peopling of Western Canada and even of Ontario by immigration was at its zenith-to an official of the Ontario Government, then a Liberal Government, The letter is as follows:-
Private.
My dear Southworth,-I have your letter of a late date on emigration to Ontario. You incidentally say in the letter that you are opposed to indiscriminate emigration. Well, in that respect you agree with everybody else. I do not know any one who suggests, or who would propose, that there should he' indiscriminate emigration to that province. Whatever is dona must be done carefully, and any who are sent out must be well-selected emigrants. But don't run away with the idea that only well-to-do people, or those with money, are going to emigrate. If you are going to keep up a population in the old parts of the province you must he satified with sober, energetic and industrious emigrants. I know all you people are terribly afraid of the foreign element. Upon that point I don't agree with you, and have no hesitation in saying that a good class of foreigners scattered about the old parts of Ontario will do very much more towards preserving a proper agricultural population than those from England for instance. Politically

speaking I believe the introduction of a hundred families or so into some of those close ridings with the connections which could be had and maintained here would' easily preserve for us many doubtful seats in that province. I know the anxiety or nervousness of the minister upon this question. Confidentially, I may tell you, I fear it bears some slight resemblance to one of courage. You know enough about politics to know that courage always beats. However as we don't agree upon that phase of the question we won't discuss it. Etc.
(Signed.) W. T. R. Preston.
This was the opinion of a man in the employ of the Government that, the hon. gentleman says, did such wonderful things for Canada. Large numbers of people were being brought from Central Europe by officials who 'were endeavouring to place people in Ontario for political purposes. When you realize the influence they would have over those people after placing them here, you can form some idea of the cause of the resentment and the outburst of indignation that swept through their ranks when they found that so many of their alien enemies had been debarred from polling their votes	in the wartime
election; they would not be able to exercise that control which they sought and which they had exercised for so many years. I need not say anything further in that regard, but I want to emphasize this, that we cannot permit those people in those communities of Western Canada to carry on their language and to teach in their schools whatever suits them, and at the same time expect that we are going to *overcome the difficulties confronting us.
Reference has been made to the recruiting that took place in Ontario, and it was pointed out how well the people of Ontario volunteered. La'st night when the Minister of Militia (Mr. Mewburn) had his Estimates before the House, an hon. gentleman opposite (Mr. Lemieux) pointed out that this was due to the military training they had. It was due not to the training they had along military lines, but to the *fact that the old stock in Ontario was of British origin and, therefore, the people responded quickly to the call of duty when danger threatened this country. Danger may threaten this country again, because the menace with which we have been confronted during the past five years may again threaten. We must look to the future, and Canada must be built up on a sure and sound foundation. We are not going to take any chances in that regard, and I, therefore, compliment the Government on having established a Department of Immigration with a respon-

sible minister at its head, and on having brought down a Bill which is going to ensure that in the future people who are not desirable will not be permitted to come within the borders of Canada, and consequently, the purity of the stream of our immigration will be maintained as it should be. The influence of the stock that came out here years ago and peopled this country will be felt in the future, and we must .not jeopardize it in any way by permitting an indiscriminate flow of undesirables, as regards which it was stated last night by an hon. member opposite that no bars, no hindrance should be placed in their way, and that this Bill was introduced with a view to barring out the alien enemy. We are still at war with the enemy; peace has'not as yet been declared, and we cannot read what the future may have in store for us. But we would be blind to our interest and our duty, if precautions of this kind were not introduced and placed before Parliament.
I do not know that it is necessary for me to say anything further on the matter, in view of the fact that we are in Committee on the Bill and that this discussion is really out of order, it being only by permission of the Chair and the House, because, owing to an oversight of some hon. members who intended to take part in the discussion, the Bill received its second reading without any discussion on the principle. Before sitting down, however, I would again refer to the urgent necessity, particularly during the next few years when reconstruction will be taking place, that nothing should be permitted in this country that would make possible such a condition of affairs as is now being experienced in many European countries; that nothing must be done to aggravate the situation at home. We must take great care to see that our returned men are given every possible opportunity and advantage to become reestablished in civil life. That being done, we must then see that only people of a,, desirable character are allowed to come into this country to develop the resources which have been placed at our disposal.

The question before the Committee at the present time is probably of more importance to Western Canada than to any other section of the Dominion on account of the fact that we are looking for people to develop the West. But I think experience has taught us that we should in the future be very careful in the selection of our citizens, and we should benefit from the mistakes that have been made in the

past. It is true we want countless peoples to come to the prairies to cultivate the soil and produce wealth, but at the same time, we want more than that; we want people who will make good Canadian citizens, and the qualification of production of crops, production of wealth, is not sufficient in itself. Undoubtedly, some people have settled in 'the West who are not assuming the obligations of Canadian citizenship, although probably at the time they came to Canada it was not recognized that their characteristics were contrary to Canadian citizenship, and that they, to a greater or less extent, separate themselves from other communities and live by and for themselves alone. Since the commencement of this debate, mention has been made of the Hutterites and the Mennonites, and I feel my responsibility, as member for a district in which many of those people have been settling during the last year, to make some observations with regard to those two classes of settlers. I intend to argue that they are not desirable citizens, although probably not on the same ground as is defined in the Bill itself. I look upon a desirable citizen as one who comes into this country prepared to associate with the rest of the people and to assume all the obligations of citizenship. If immigrants fail to do 'that, then I do not look upon them as desirable citizens, and we should refrain from allowing such classes of people to enter the Dominion of Canada. For many years we have had Hutterites living in practically all sections of Canada, and I always understood that they lived in individual homes, although in communities, but the so-called Mennonites that have been coming into my district in the last year, do not live in what we would call individual homes. All ithe families live together in one large house; they all eat in one building, and all sleep in another. I do not think people' of that type should be allowed to come into this country. Further, they want their own schools, and want to teach their own language, which is almost wholly German. Those of you who have followed the dispatches in the press will know that in Saskatchewan and Manitoba the authorities have had a great deal of difficulty in compelling some members of this sect to support the public schools and send their children to them. On the contrary, they want to maintain their own schools, have their own teachers, and perpetuate their own language. I object to that because I think that the only way we can develop good citizens in this country is for the newcomers to acquire a knowledge of the English language in order that they may mingle with the other elements of the population and become good British subjects.
I have another objection to these people -and I am going to class the Hutterites and the Mennonites together, although there may be some distinction between them- and it is that their property is vested entirely in one individual, who practically controls the situation. In South Dakota,
I understand that an effort was made during the war by the authorities there to break up these organizations and force the property into the hands of individuals, and probably as a result of that action a great many Hutterites and Mennonites left South Dakota and came to Canada. Now, we have had experience with one_ class of people with a form of Government very similar to that of the Hutterites; I refer to the Doukhobors, who are also under the control of one head, in whom all the property is vested.
Another objection I have is this: When an effort was made in South Dakota to break up these organizations, evidence was adduced to prove that these people were prepared to admit that under certain circumstances their own laws were above the laws of the State, and that they would refuse to obey the laws of the State if they came into conflict with their own laws. I do not think we should admit people of this type into Canada. Some of them have come in already, but I think we should prevent immediately the entrance of any more of them.
We know what the attitude of these people is with regard to military service. There are many people who are quite sincere in their opposition to military service and to war; but the particular classes of whom I speak are not prepared to assume any obligations whatever in connection with war. They refused to contribute to war funds and war loans, though I understand that in my district they did contribute in some instances to the Red Cross by subscribing to the Victory Loan and allowing the interest to go to the Red Cross. At this time in our history, I think it is extremely important that we should only allow into this country, people who are prepared to assume all the obligations of Canadian citizenship, who are prepared to bear all the responsibilities, acquire a knowledge of our language, attend our own schools, and assimilate with the rest of our people. I maintain that these people are not prepared to do any of these things, and consequently I look upon them

as undesirable citizens. We know that in the United States they did object to contributing to war funds, and objected to military service; and largely on account of the feeling of their neighbours in South Dakota they were forced to leave, and have come to Canada. I do not see by what right they have earned a place in this free country, and as it will take some time for this legislation to come into effect I would urge that an Order in Council be passed immediately, under the War Measures Act, to prevent any more of these people coming in. If we do not do that, they will continue to come in as they are doing at the present moment and have been doing for months past.
I do not represent the feeling of merely one class in my part of the country. I believe that all classes of our people desire that no more Hutterite's and Mennonites shall be allowed to settle in Canada. Of course the agitation is strongest with the returned men, and I fully appreciate their point of view. They went across the seas and risked their lives, and they dislike very much to see other men who were not prepared to risk their lives or their money for the freedom and liberty they possessed come and buy land and settle in this country and enjoy all the privileges and protection of Canadian citizenship, and especially as these people are nearly all of German origin and want to perpetuate the German language in Canada.
But apart from the returned soldiers, a number of Canadian clubs throughout Western Canada have declared themselves, *against the entrance of these people into [DOT]the Dominion. Now the Canadian clubs, as I know them, are supposed to represent a very high type of citizenship; they want to perpetuate the very best ideals of our citizenship, and if after mature consideration by men of all parties and of all creeds, the Canadian clubs in Winnipeg and elsewhere in the West declare that it is not in the interest of Canada that these people should be allowed to settle in this country, I think their views are worthy of the attention of [DOT]this Committee.
By reading the press and the statements made by public men and leaders in all important movements, I find that the feeling *is unanimous in the Prairie Provinces that these people should not be allowed to come into Canada. The women's organizations of the province of Alberta and I think the same remark applies practically to the whole of Western Canada, lpok upon these people as *a menace and' are urging their exclusion. I do not want to be classed as an individual

who wants to discourage people coming away from oppression to a land where there is freedom. I am' prepared to welcome to this country all classes of people who we are satisfied will assume all the obligations of citizenship when they come to this country, but I want to place myself on record as opposed to the entrance into this country of people who are not prepared to assume all the responsibilities of citizenship and who desire to live by themselves under their own form of government, who want their own schools, and if possible to use their own language exclusively. That is my reason for asking the Government to take immediate action to prevent any more of these people from coming not only into Western [DOT]Canada,- but into any other part of the *Dominion. I believe it is in the welfare of Canada that they should be kept out.

I desire to say a few words on this Bill, not because it affects Western 'Canada, but because the introduction of undesirables is a matter that affects the whole Dominion. This is a period of reconstruction. We have heard a great deal in the last few months concerning reconstruction, and I wish to congratulate the Government that in this Bill they are preparing to ensure that we shall get a better class of immigrants in Canada. Perhaps we in the West may be in a position to speak with more knowledge on this question than people in the East. Possibly Western Canada offers greater advantages to farmers, in that they have less trouble in breaking up new lands and establishing themselves upon the land. In the province from which I come the natural resources are not only very great, but are very easily accessible, and the climate appeals to people coming into a new country. In the past we have experienced difficulties in regard to Oriental immigration. I am not going to deal so much with the question of Oriental immigration, because it has been threshed out in this House and by the people from time to time and is fairly well understood. The hon. member from Montreal (Mr. Jacobs) yesterday eulogized Sir Clifford Sifton on his immigration policy. In the main I endorse that eulogy of Sir Clifford Sifton, but I want to tell the hon. member that Sir *Clifford Sifton informed me himself that he made a mistake when he brought the Douk-hobors to Canada. No one who
4 p.m. knows those people can deny that they are sober, industrious and hard working. But they live in communities. Their families all live together, eat together, and have their buildings together,

and they do not allow their children to attend the schools provided by the country, nor do they comply with the necessary regulations for the registration of births, deaths and marriages. They speak their own language, and as a class they are not even educated in their mother tongue. I do not think we would ever be able to assimilate these people so long as they are allowed to remain in these communities, and we should not allow the Doubhobors, Hutterites and Mennonites or any people of that sort to come into Canada and live under their present customs. If we are going to build up a united Canada we must have people whom we can assimilate and who eventually will join the family of Canadian life. The people I have mentioned are not of that kind and I wish it were possible in this legislation not only to debar any more from coming in, but-and I hope the Government may see its way to make this possible-to deport those who are living in communities, as well as interned aliens, and to send them back to the countries from which them came, Russia or wherever else it may be, where they will be more at home among their fellowmen. In this reconstruction period 1 think we should see to it that the necessary restrictions will be provided so that we may not be flooded with an influx of people whom it will take generations to get rid of or to assimilate. I do not think that any one should advocate the giving of the privileges of Canadian citizenship to interned alien enemies belonging to countries that vve have been fighting and with which we are still technically at war. These men who were interned were not peaceable, law-abiding citizens. They were interned for some breach of the laws of the land; and at this moment, it seems preposterous that we should advocate, just because peace is about to be declared, that they be taken in as full citizens of Canada. One of the great troubles in the past has been the laxity of the naturalization law.
I do not know whether they have experienced any trouble in the East, but in the. West we have had traffic in naturalization papers, and I venture to say that it is not all over yet. Under the new law, however, this matter will be more easily dealt with than in the past. Under the old law a man was only required to live two years in the country, and if he made his application and it was vouched for by some one, even if proper notice had not been given to the public, he was accorded the full rights of citizenship. Under this Bill he must have five years' residence, and there are many
restrictions in the Bill to-day that were not in the old law. I wish to again congratulate the Government on the introduction of this Bill, and I hope that when it is completed it will not only keep out of Canada those aliens who are not desirable, but will enable us to deport those who have proved to be undesirable while living amongst us.

If the general discussion
is to continue I think we might bring ourselves in order by taking one of the sections of the Bill which will provide for a discussion such as this. Section 13 will, I think, be found wide enough to cover a discussiorr such as that which has been going on. If action is to'be taken at an early date or immediately to prohibit the entry of certain of these people to Western Canada I would like to have an expression of opinion from this House on this particular section. 1 concur in the view that has been expressed that it will probably be ten days or two weeks and possibly more before the Bill is eventually through the House. But owing to the feeling that exists in the West, it seems to me that it may be desirable to act at once so far as these particular classes are concerned. I move that we proceed to the discussion of section 13.

Just a moment. With regard to clause 1, subsection (a) as to the position of the minister and the deputy minister. As I understand it, there is no deputy minister of immigration at present. Is it the intention under this Bill to provide for a deputy minister?

The department provides
for the appointment of a deputy minister and the Estimates do. as well. Provision is already made in the Act to create a department with a deputy minister.

I understand that the
Deputy Minister of Immigration is also the present Deputy Minister of the Interior. Is it the intention to divide the two positions so that we will have a Deputy Minister of the Interior and a Deputy Minister of Immigration, separate and distinct?

That has been the intention. As the hon. gentleman no doubt was aware, during-the past year, the volume of immigration has not been very excessive. We thought it advisable for the time being to ask Mr. Cory, who is the Deputy Minister of the Interior and who formerly had the administration of this Act, to act as deputy minister in the meantime for the purpose of getting ready for the immigration which we expect to come. That matter, however, has not been considered or decided. Unless there is an amalgamation

of these departments again, or an amalgamation of this department with some other department, I think it would just as well to let the matter stand as it is now.

Section agreed to.
Mr. Calder moved that the Committee proceed to the consideration of clause 13 of the Bill.
Mr. RICHARDSON': I have a very few words to say on this Bill. I wish to take issue with the minister's statement that nothing had been done by the people for the vast number of Ruthenian and foreign immigrants who have been brought into the country in past years from central Europe. A great deal was done for these people. They were pretty thoroughly debauched very shortly after getting into this country by the politicians of both sides in the Northwest. I think it is just as well that we should be frank in regard to this question. In Manitoba the Ruthenians and other immigrants from central Europe were organized into clubs and herded in the cities and towns of Manitoba and they were supplied with whisky and beer. I see my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) raise his eyebrows in wonderment. I imagine he has never heard the words " whisky '' or " beer " used in this House before. He ;seems to be quite horrified that I did not make a distinction as between the poli-icians of the different sides but that 1 placed the blame on both. The manner in which these people have been debauched became a public scandal throughout the West. Their votes were bought, they were herded into political droves, members of their own class were given offices and they were used as political bosses. I do not think this country has perpetrated any greater crime upon any portion of the population than it has perpetrated upon the foreign population that has been brought to .the country.
Was that in connection with provincial elections?

My hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) suggests that this has occurred in connection with provincial elections. I fancy that if my hon. friend will confer with the hon. member ifor Maisonneuve he will probably get a satisfactory answer to his question. It is a great satisfaction to me to know that in this Bill that is now before the House provision is being made which will prevent the importation into this country of undesirable settlers. We have Doukhobors, and Mennonites and now we are getting a portion of the Hutterites.

I think all are undesirable. The Mennonites who were brought in when Alexander Mackenzie was in office under certain guarantees have proved very good settlers so far as agriculture is concerned. But they have not become assimilated with the other peoples to any extent up to the present time. I would like to testify to the fact that in connection with the Victory Loan, the Patriotic Fund and other subscriptions for the purpose of carrying on the war the Mennonites acted very well and subscribed a large amount thus showing their sympathy with the ideal of liberty for which the enlightened 'nations of the -world were fighting.
Did they volunteer?

They did not volunteer at all; they believe in the scriptural injunction: "Thou shalt not kill." They have a firm conviction that they should not participate in war. It is a matter of conscience with them and I never felt that I should blame them very much for adhering to their conscientious convictions in that respect. I represented the constituency of Lisgar in the old days and a great many Mennonites are located in that constituency. I found them a very agreeable and law-abiding people. It is true they do not patronize our schools.
Did the first Mennonites come from the United States or from Russia?

From Russia I understand. I want to say, in case I should be misunderstood, that a new policy is being adopted in regard to the Ruthenian population in the province . of Manitoba. The present Manitoba Government, for which I hold no brief, is pursuing an excellent policy. When these people were controlled by politicians, all sorts of promises were made to them and in many cases they were allowed to conduct their schools in their own way and use their own language. That has all been done away with under the administration of the Norris Government. Manitoba has, in the person of the Hon. Dr. Thornton, an excellent Minister of Education. It was recently my privilege to visit the constituency which I have the honour to represent in Parliament and in which there is a very large Ruthenian population. I visited some of these schools in company with the Minister of Education and Mr. D. A. Ross, the local member of the Legislature, and I found that marvellous pro-

gress was being made by the children of foreign parents. They are wonderfully bright and progressive; in fact they make almost greater progress than the children of the Anglo-Saxon population. In these schools nothing but the English language is taught; nor will be allowed to be taught.
I believe that since partisanship has been abolished, or abandoned to a great extent, a better spirit is coming over the dreams of the foreign settler of that province and higher ideals are taking hold of our foreign population. I agree with the Minister of Immigration that we should follow the foreign population, endeavour to set the highest example and lead them along the right path particularly in regard to becoming British citizens. In my constituency, as I say, there is a very large foreign population. Under the War-time Elections Act, which prevailed when the last election was held, this population was not, of course, allowed to vote. I regret to have to tell the House that I have received from time to time lately very disturbing reports in regard to certain portions of the foreign population of Springfield, Winnipeg and other adjacent districts. It is even said that they expect an uprising and indeed that the day has been set for such uprising. I took the opportunity of letting the members of the Government know in order that measures might be taken to put a stop to anything of that kind.
To what population do you refer when you say that there is danger of an uprising?
To the population brought in from Central European countries.
In what portion of the West?
I was referring to Manitoba especially in my remarks.
Can you give us any authority for that statement?

Yes, I have among my papers upstairs a letter from Mr. D. A Ross, member of the Provincial Legislature of Manitoba in which he infers that there is danger. The night before I left for Ottawa last week, after visiting my home about eight days ago, Mr. Ross called me up by telephone and asked me to warn the Government that there was grave danger in the situation; that he had returned from a tour of the constituency, and that throughout it, as well as in the adjoining districts, foreigners were talking of rising
at a certain time. I think he said the date fixed was some day in the ensuing month of May. I do not know why this is, but lie states that the spirit of Bolshevism prevails and that these people have got the idea that the profiteers in Canada have made immense sums of money-
Hear, hear.
-that that ought to be taken away from them, and that certain other measures of retribution should follow.
Hear, hear.
I cannot tell the Committee just what views these people hold with regard to this matter, but if my information is correct their views are radical and dangerous.
How long have they been in the country?

I should think for ten, twelve, or fifteen years. They are very industrious and quite prosperous. They have taken up lands in small areas in that country and carry on market gardening, small farming, etc., and the progress they have made along agricultural lines is wonderful. If these people are properly handled even at this juncture there may not be much to fear. In this connection Mr. Ross tells me that Bishop Budka, of .whom members of the House must have lreaid a great deal from time to time-
Hear, hear.
-is behind this agitation, and criticism has been indulged in that the authorities have not dealt with Bishop Budka as he deserves to be dealt with.
Is Bishop Budka the same bishop who is behind a Bill at present before the House having reference to certain Ruthenian children?

I am unable to give the hon. member any information in that regard.
Sir SAA1 HUGHES: I will give it.

I have no personal
knowledge of the actions of Bishop Budka, but Air. Ross, the local member for Springfield, assures me that he is a very dangerous man. I noticed in the press of Winnipeg that the returned soldiers propose to deal with Bishop Budka, and you may be sure, Air. Chairman, that if the . returned soldiers undertake to deal with him he will be treated in a summary manner. I ob-

serve, however, in a despatch in the morning papers that action has been taken, I think by the Dominion Government officials, probably as a result of the information 1 laid before the Government, to summon Bishop Budka before the authorities to show cause why he should not be deported. 1 presume that this action is a result of measures taken by the Government to see that justice is done, and I want to congratulate the Government upon its promptness. As I said before, I have no personal information to convey to the House, although I learned from quarters that I do not doubt are perfectly reliable that a rather dangerous, if not a menacing condition of affairs, exists in that country.
Will the hon. member for Springfield lay on the table of the House the letter which he states contains the statements referred to?

The hon. member
for Springfield will do exactly as he likes about that matter. I rose for the purpose of giving the Committee the benefit of any information that has been conveyed to me, and I hope that the situation will be dealt with by the Government in such a manner as it should be. I took the first opportunity on my return from Winnipeg last week to lay a statement before the members of the Government, 'particularly charged with this branch of the administration. I then learned that action had been taken; that word had been sent to interview Mr. Ross, to collect all possible information, and to make such an investigation as would result in the prevention of any such incendiary outbreak as any portion of the population might have in 'contemplation.

In saying a few words on this subject, I regret that I shall not be able to take quite the view that is entertained by the Government. I regret that the more sincerely because I know I shan't get any credit from a certain section of this House for differing from the Government. I listened to considerable portions of the speech of the minister (Mr. Calder), and I could not quite appreciate his point of view from the necessity which usually exists of having a coherent policy from the Cabinet. My hon. friend spoke very enthusiastically of Canada's need of increased population. Well, in ordinary times we should all feel just that way, and should use my hon. friend's language but we are not living in ordinary times, and where the policy of the Government,

as a Government, appears to lack coherence is in this: That in its policy, as brought out in some of the measures which were mentioned in the Speech from the1 Throne, and in some of the measures which we have discussed here, there is an apprehension that we shall not be able to handle, without considerable difficulty, for the next few years the inhabitants we already have. 1 do not think, Mr. Chairman, that is a misrepresentation of speeches that we have heard in this House in support of certain measures. The Government has taken extraordinary steps, and has taken credit to itself for those steps, to prevent unemployment in this country in the years of difficulty that are immediately ahead of us, and that we all hope will not be numerous. Now I, for one, cannot see the coherence or consistency of a policy which on the one hand is directed to relieve the population we already have, and on the other to increasing that population by means of an immigration policy
Hear, hear.

And I should be glad if, approaching this matter with no other thought in my mind except to take the wisest steps for Canada, the minister, or other members of the Government, can meet my difficulty on that particular point. My general position in regard to making a distinction between ordinary times and the present time, applies equally to some of the remarks which fell from my goodnatured friend from Montreal

1 forget
his division.
Good nature is no distinction as regards members from Montreal.
It is, I think, the hon. member from the St. Lawrence division, to whom I refer.
No, the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier.
I heard a warble from another region which tempts me very much to tell a story, but I will not do it at this time.
Let us have the story.

I agreed with the spirit of the remarks of my hon. friend from Montreal (Mr. Jacobs) as to ordinary times, when he said that our enemies of to-day will be our friends of to-morrow. Everybody who knows British history will recall the period when Englishmen never referred to Frenchmen except as " frog-eaters," and when Frenchmen never re-

ferred to England except as " perfidious Albion," and that proceeded for some years after the great wars between England and France.
Mr. LEM1EUX: Some centuries.

Well, not quite for centuries; it proceeded for some years; but as my hon. friend indicated would be the case now, those feelings passed away to such an extent that the two countries were allies in the recent war. Still, it took some time, and I think that my hon. friend, in his remarks, was not sufficiently careful to remember that fact.
There were other remarks of my hon. friend that I could not quite see the force of as encouraging a vigorous immigration policy. He reminded us that the race to which he has the distinction-I use the words very sincerely-to belong wandered for forty years in the wilderness, and when they got to the promised land there they made good. Well, the record of what they did when they got to the promised land was that they killed off all the native inhabitants, and if that is my hon. friend's idea of how immigrants made good, I hope there may not be many immigrants into Canada of that particular type. However,
I repeat that with the general tenor of his remarks I agree, because they were based upon well-known historical facts. I do not think that these race asperities will last forever, by any means, or else we have fought the vainest war ever fought in history.' I understand that the League oi Nations, about which most of us are enthusiastic, is to put an end to war and to put an end as fast as possible to that hate in the minds of men out of which all wars must come.
Having said so much, I return to the ground of the present condition of Canada and to the immigration policy of the Government as I learn something about it from the speech of the minister. There are other grounds than the fact that we have just come out of this war and that there are great misunderstandings between the various races of the world why we should go very carefully about promoting immigration at this time, or-shall I say?-about how we handle the immigration question. Before the war began at all there was considerable emigration out of Western Canada. That was being stated in this House; it was never contradicted in this House, because it could not be contradicted. We may have an opportunity of discussing at considerable length before this session closes the economic reasons why that was
taking place before the war. Of course, since the war began we have lost a large number of inhabitants from Western Canada; I do not want to go into numbers on that question, but it is notorious that that has happened. I quite apprehend that there might be an explanation of that in the early years of the war connected with the war itself. However, the fact is there, both as to the time before the war and since the war began, and that fact would lead one to look at this immigration point of view from a different angle than the enthusiastic one of the minister when he seemed to want to bring men in in great numbers. He said* indeed, that we had been to blame because we had done nothing for our immigrant population in the past. From one point of view, there is a great deal of truth in what he said, although I believe the very first reason he gave for wanting to get more men in shows that he is going to do something to them now, because he said that we needed more taxation. He is going to improve on our having done nothing for our immigrants in the past by now taxing immigrants when he gets hold of them. Well, that is perhaps too liberal an interpretation of what my hon. friend said. I simply point out, however, that that is not a reason why we should endeavour to flood the country at the present time with a certain class of immigrants, to say the least of it. The people who take up homesteads and the people who take up land on a small scale are not a very taxable quantity in the first years of their settling in Western Canada. That remark applies to the various other lines of national activity in which the minister said that, an increased population would be useful to us. If I am right in saying that we were losing inhabitants before the war and losing them from the lands of Western Canada, then it is more necessary, to promote the best interests of Canada, that we should see what was wrong with our government of the West; what was wrong with 6ur methods of taxation for instance; what was wrong with our trade policies; what was wrong with the life of the people in the West, that was making our inhabitants leave the country. That would be a more fruitful line of Government activity than the introduction of a Bill or the making of a speech in this House at this particular time to promote immigration upon a large scale.
We have arrived at a period in our history when, if we govern our country properly, we do not need to go over the world

seeking to give inducements to people to come and live in Canada. I am one of those who can speak with the feelings and experiences of an immigrant myself, upon this question, and I think I know that no country in the world offers to a man such an opportunity of advancing his position in life and enjoying a rational and a free existence as Canada does-if Canada is properly governed. A great deal hinges on that. If we frame our laws so that equal opportunities are afforded to all sections of our population, then no country in the world offers the inducement that Canada does to people from more crowded lands to come and reside within our borders. But I should like to guard myself further-though I have been trying to use very guarded language, Mr. Chairman-by saying that the "if" that I have used is one of considerable size, and has been under all Governments, so far as I have been able to study economics in the direction of enlightenment. I do not think that we need to hurry about getting fresh inhabitants at this time. Canada has arrived at that period in her history when it is emphatically true that the best immigration agent is a successful colonist.
Let the Governments of this country in the immediate future get that thoroughly into their heads, and they will do a great deal to settle the immigration question so far as getting suitable and proper inhabitants into Canada is concerned.
When I rose I said that I viewed this question in a slightly different way from the Government, and there are in the Bill points which we shall, perhaps, discuss better when we come to them, but I would have approached the question from an entirely different point of view from that which seems to have guided the Government. They seem to be largely concerned about the people they are keeping out of Canada. I would have approached the question from the Canadian point of view entirely and said:	What would be the general policy that would, under the peculiar after-war conditions in which we find ourselves, be the best for Canada? We did enormous things in this war; we sent an enormous number of our inhabitants overseas, and our very first problem at this time is to re-absonb into our civil life, and to place thean in a good position when they have been re-absorbed, the boys who went across the seas and fought for us. Our first duty above all things is so to rule our country and direct our policies that we do the right thing by those citizens, primarily, because it is a duty that we owe to them, 
but scarcely secondarily, because it is obvious to everybody that, if we do well by those men, we have laid the basis of a population which will be second to none in the world if the men can only get women of a similar type to marry, and I do not think they will have much difficulty. On those two grounds I think the overwhelming primary duty of the Government for the next three years would have been to devote their attention to problems connected with our returned soldiers in connection with the immigration question. This consideration was evidently present to the minds of the government of the United States who have a longer national experience than we have, and that Government have, I understand, taken a step in regard to their immigration policy, rather different from that taken by this Bill. Before that announcement was made as to the Government of the United States, I had been in the West saying to my intimates that I personally would be in favour of closing the borders of Canada absolutely for a period of three or four years to everybody except carefully selected citizens of allied countries. I would support that policy-and I want the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) to apprehend my point-not along the lines of hostility to any people on earth. I want to repeat that I agree with the general principles he laid down, and I can and will exemplify the sincerity of my belief by saying that within thirty miles of my home there are Germans, born in Germany, who have lived as long as I have in Western Canada, whose conduct has been perfectly correct during the war, with whom I have been on friendly terms during the whole of the seventeen years that I have lived in Western Canada, and with whom I hope I shall live on the same friendly terms in the years immediately in front of us. I do not hesitate to say that, however much it may be misunderstood in certain quarters. That is my point of view on this question. I do not advocate our imitating or following the policy of the United States from the point of view of exclusion, but I advocate it from the point of view of governing Canada in such a way as to make her a desirable country to live in for the best men in the world who are not satisfied with the countries in which they are living at the present time. That is all the contribution I have to make to what would, perhaps, have been a debate better conducted on the second reading of this measure.

During the recent recess, it was my privilege to attend, at Win-

nipeg, a very large meeting comprising, I think, the Rotarians, the Kiwanis, the Canadian Club, the Women's Canadian Club, the Great War Veterans, the Imperial Veterans, the Army and Navy Veterans, Orange lodges and perhaps some others.
It was estimated that at least 35,000 citizens of Winnipeg were represented at that meeting. It was pointed out 'by the chairman that, with the exception of the Canadian Club and the Great War Veterans, whose views on the subject of the entrance of those Hutterites were well known, the others had been invited without knowing to what they were coming. There was a free and open discussion without any strings attached to it, and there were present at that meeting at least four members of this House. Speeches were delivered by gentlemen who had evidently made a very careful study of the subject under discussion, and I am only too sorry that they cannot deliver them here to-day, because they covered the ground from the early days down to the present. It was pointed out, amongst other things, that the Hutterites were known to have been in existence for something like 400 years; and that to-day the community was very small, numbering only a few thousand; that during this time they had owned their property in common, and that if a man did not agree with them, he was thrown out on the stre'et. Cases were cited of men 56 years of age who were destitute after having belonged to that colony for twenty years.

Like Government
ownership?

So far as I could
gather, the Hutterite community, as an institution, was not looked upon as a very serious proposition there, except in so far as it was related to the entire alien problem in Canada. The Hutterites are not numerous as they have produced only a few thousand in 400 years, so that they have not been a success under modern conditions. So far, however, as the Hutterite community is related to the present alien problem, the unanimous opinion of that meeting was that they must be stopped at once, and that the whole subject of citizenship in this country must also be tackled immediately. A considerable amount of criticism was expressed at the slowness with which the Government had tackled this problem; and it was hoped that no further delays would be permitted, and it was stated that if further delays were permitted, they could not be responsible
for the results. There is in the West, a very high feeling with regard to a certain class of aliens. It is so strong that it cannot be played with, and I say that advisedly. The minister in moving the second reading of the Bill yesterday pointed to the mistakes of the past. There is an old aphorism which runs "A man who never makes mistakes never makes anything else," which can be applied with equal force to governments as to men. As an old-time western man who had been out there for years among our undeveloped resources-and the Indians had been there years before me-
I know we w'ere all mighty glad to see these foreigners coming in under the old immigration policy, for we needed a little help in developing our country. As has been pointed out by my hon. friend (Mr. Richardson), who knows whereof he speaks, the mistake was not so much in bringing them in, as in the treatment they received after they got here. I sometimes think that the old-time western Canadian was too much of a trapper; he had a tendency to skin his capture as soon as he got it. I well remember those sheep skin coated men coming in, and fine husky men they were. The following winter they would go to the bush armed with small hatchets which they brought from the old land. One would get on each side of a tree and peck it down like woodpeckers, then they would cut it in four-foot lengths and after piling a cord, which it would take two men a whole day to do, all they received was thirty cents. A little later when an election came on, somebody thought that if these men could be taught to make a cross they would be able to vote, so they were sworn in as good citizens, and then a little later on came the bottle of white whisky. I am sometimes surprised that we have not had more trouble with our foreigners. But we have come to the jumping-off place now. Our returning soldiers have had the fact driven into them by six-inch shells that citizenship is a question of vital importance, which must be settled. It did not take John Bull or Canada two years to wake up. If it had, we would have been licked. I do not wish to be understood as saying that those men who enlisted early in the war had more courage than those who enlisted later, because as a matter of fact I am convinced that it took more courage to join up in the later stages, but it was the spirit of those men who sprang to arms in 1914 that saved the show; and I think we all realize that in the future the thing that will count is not our great railways not our enormous

resources or our millionaires, but Canada's honour, and we must breed and bring up in this country men who at the drop of the hat will spring to arms in its defence.

I fully agree with other hon. members that we should not adopt m our immigration policy the principle of hostility to any nation or race. History records that eventually our enemies may become our friends. While that is true, and should be one 6f our guiding principles, it must be pointed out that the war is not yet over, and that the feeling in Canada, especially among the returned soldiers, against people of German blood and German tongue is very intense; and I could not imagine any better way of accentuating that feeling of hostility than to allow people of German blood and German language to come into Canada at this particular time. I think that if we wish to cure this feeling of hostility towards the German people, which undoubtedly does exist, we should see that the feeling of Canadian soldiers and Canadians generally is not irritated by an influx of people speaking the German language, if not of German blood. The \\ ar Veterans of Canada have taken a positive stand against the immigration of Hut-terites and Mennonites into Western Canada. The hon. member for Lethbridge this afternoon gave in my opinion .sufficient reasons why it is not desirable to admit these people into Canada. I do not think it is the policy of this country, and I hope it never will be, to exclude people from Canada on account of their religion; we should never act on that principle.
Does the hon. member mean that positively or negatively? A great many people have been brought in because they were of a certain religion.

I do not mean it either positively or negatively. I simply state that religion should not enter into the discussion of this question. In. addition to the reasons which the hon. member for Lethbridge gave, I should like to point out another characteristic which is very unfair to the other citizens of Western Canada, and that is their method of purchasing land. They will buy a certain area of land, four pieces, perhaps. close together, and at once the other people on the circumference of that circle desire to leave. The value of their land goes down, no one but these organizations will take it, and in that way the colony spreads, to the detriment of the citizens settled around, and

who, of course, have a right to live in any part of the country they please.
I am very pleased that section 13 of the Bill empowers the Government to remedy by Order in Council just such situations as these as they arise. The feeling in Western Canada during the last few months has been so intense-and this is not unreasonable when it is remembered that in that part of the country we-have just as great a proportion of foreign-born people as we can possibly stand, and having regard also to the fact that we wish our people to live up to British ideals-the situation in the West is so serious that I think the Government should not wait for the Royal assent to this Bill before passing an Order in Council excluding Hutterites and Mennonites, but should exclude them now by passing an Order in Council under the War Measures Act. I do not think it is necessary for me to say that it would be quite proper to pass such >an Order in Council under the War Measures Act, because the situation is one of the results of the war.
The soldiers of Canada do not wish to force their views upon the rest of the people, but the opinions which they have on this subject have been gained under circumstances which, I think it will be admitted, place them in a position to speak with knowledge. Their right to these opinions and their right to set them forth on all proper occasions must always be conceded. They have no uncertain voice on this question and have been asking that the Government should take some steps in regard to it. Now that the Government have enunciated their policy, and having regard to the fact that the situation is extremely critical and that these Hutterites are coming in even now while we are speaking on this Bill, and that it is difficult to know exactly what may happen if this stream continues, I think the Government would be well advised to take advantage of the provisions of the War Measures Act and pass an Order in Council to exclude the Hutterites, Mennonites and Doukhobors until such time as the Bill may become law.
Mr. W.HIDDEN: With regard to clause 13, if the context is as good as the text which we have here there should he no trouble in having a very unanimous support.

Will the hon. member
permit me to interrupt him a moment?
I intend to suggest to the Committee a new clause 13 before the discussion on this

clause proceeds any further. It is proposed to amend clause 13 by striking out all the words after the word "nationality" in the sixth line and replacing them with the following:
or race or of immigrants of any specified class or occupation, because of any economic, industrial or other condition temporarily existing in Canada or because such immigrants are deemed unsuitable having regard to the climatic, industrial, social, educational, labour or other conditions or requirements of Canada, or because such .immigrants are deemed undesirable owing to thear peculiar customs, habits, modes of life and methods of holding property and because of their probable inability to become readily assimiliated or to assume the duties and responsibilities of Canadian citizenship within a reasonable time after their entry.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.

I am satisfied that the clause as now amended will meet the views of fighting men returning to Canada from overseas. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Red Deer, we must think of these people in their relation to the developing of Canada, and we must also consider what they think about other people in relation to our developing country. Whether all the men have thought correctly with regard to the Hutterites or not, I am not prepared to say, and I do not think any of us are, because we are not omniscient. But the general attitude of the men returning from overseas and of their families in Western Canada has been a sanely expressed view of this whole matter. I am sure that there is no desire on the part of any of us, as the member for East Calgary (Mr. Redman) has said, to exclude the Hutterites simply because of their religious views, but because embedded in the very heart of those religious views there is a false political philosophy, a false conception of their relation to the state, which makes it impossible for them to become other than a people in Canada, and what we need to-day is not more people, but more Canadians. We need just as many new people as we can assimilate, hut only as many as we can assimilate. Numbers are not the greatest consideration at the present time. These people may bring money with them and may buy some of our best lands, but if they are allowed to come with their peculiar and. to us, false views we may be able to tolerate them, hut it would be only toleration. They pay iheir debts well, I understand; they are good farmers and have good bank accounts. But so far as I can learn, the Government of South Dakota and generally the people.residing there found that they were very loath to purchase, or even to consider purchasing, Liberty bonds. I am glad that the Minister of Immigration and the Government have been willing to consider seriously the taking of steps to relieve me present situation, and will make it possible to give the Hutterites a fair deal before they cross the line and, above all, to give the Canadian people a fair deal now and permanently by excluding the Hutterites.
1 believe this Bill is one of the most important that will have been before this House during this session because it affects more than conditions to-day; it may affect conditions in Canada for many years to come. I am glad to see in the Bill evidence of more practical and scientific regulation of immigration, and a realization of the necessity of a national policy-that is a dangerous term to use, but I repeat it, a national policy-of immigration involving the preparation for nationalizing all people who come into our country. And I hope that, associated with this Bill, legislation will yet be brought down for the purpose of doing away with colonizing and of making impossible the growing up of classes of foreigners who have come into Canada in ignorance of the significance of Canadian institutions, Canadian laws and the Canadian spirit.
In other words, provision must be made, in some way or other, apart from the public schools of the several provinces, for simple machinery whereby the education and naturalization of aliens now in the land or who are yet to come in, may be taken eare of, so that we may have more Canadians. I would like to submit before sitting down, four simple statements which, I believe, are involved in this Bill and most of which are either involved or implied in this clause. We should be slow to make statements, at least without considering all phases of the question, such as were made yesterday in regard to letting down the bars and making Canada an asylum, a place of refuge, for all who desire to come here. That may be a good church policy; it is not the way to built a nation. It may be desirable that missionaries of one kind and another shall have the spirit which was suggested by the words of the hon. member (Mr. Jacobs) who spoke yesterday,- I do not mean political missionaries. But certainly, the preaching of that gospel in this country at the present time and the creation of machinery which would make it possible for that gospel to be accepted, will not give us a united Canada or an in-

telligent Canadian people. It will give us a group of Canadian states-Balkan states if you please-throughout the West. Canada should-and I believe the hon. minister has this in mind-so regulate and, if necessary, restrict immigration that only so many of each race of people shall be admitted as can be wholesomely Canadian-ized.
Would it not be possible to so arrange matters, provincially and federally that each such immigrant would become a citizen of Canada rather than remain a member of a foreign state?

I am satisfied that it could be done. The presence in Canada of races who have become Canadianized will afford the best basis of a -measure for the further immigration of other members of those races. I am satisfied, without giving very much consideration to the matter, that without any hate in our hearts at all towards certain alien enemies, that principle will settle the matter and will not let them come into Canada immediately peace has been signed. My third point is that Canadian standards of living should be protected from the dangerous economic competition of immigration whether from Europe or Asia. Such provision should be made for the care of aliens residing in our country as wil most rapidly and genuinely promote their being Canadianized, and thus maintain intact our democratic institutions and real national unity. Let us then, Mr. Chairman, support the minister and the Government if they have the carrying out of these principles in their minds, as I believe they have, and see to it that immigration is regulated proportionately in a ratio based upon the possibility of assimilating foreign peoples, taking as the basis the number of these different peoples that we have in our country at the present time -five per cent of a given people, ten per cent of another, three per cent of another, and 15 per cent of another. Let there be no indiscriminate letting down of the bars. To use the term employed by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), let us get a selected immigration of the peoples from the allied nations in the immediate future. Let us also have a Federal distribution bureau. We should arrange in some way or other for a distribution of settlers which would be fair. In addition to all the educational plans and programme in our respective provinces. I submit that some provision should be made for a Federal bureau for the general education of all immigrants and [DOT] settlers from non-English speaking
[Mr. WhicIden.J
countries who may yet come into Canada
in elementary Canadian history and civics.

I neglected to say in my remarks that I was thoroughly opposed to the Hutterite immigration. Lest my silence may be interpreted as indicating that I am in favour of it, I would like to make this explanation, because in the West, and particularly in Winnipeg, it is a very acute question. I am opposed to Men-nonite, Doukhobor and Hutterite immigration in its entirety.

Clause 13, I think introduces a new era in the development of an immigration policy for Canada, an era which is going to be characterized by the fact that Canada has at last determined to select her immigrants. That seems to be the characteristic principle of this clause -the selection of immigrants. In the past we have to a great extent opened our arms to every immigrant who, for his own purposes, chose to select Canada as the countrv to which he would go. In the future that policy must be reversed and no man allowed to come into Canada as an immigrant except such as Canada wishes to receive.
We have been neglectful in the past; from the point of view of citizenship we have been almost criminally neglectful. Let us now, as Canadian citizens and as a Government, modify our policy in that respect and realize that every immigrant who lands on our shores is, as it were, a ward of this Government, for a certain length of time at least, and that the Government owes an obligation to that man to educate him and to train him into Canadian citizenship. I hope we shall never see in Canada again what we have seen during the past four years: The spectacle of men who have come to this country as immigrants, who perhaps could not be objected to very much in time of peace but who, when trouble arose and danger threatened Canada, showed that their sympathies were with the enemy. If that occurs again it will largely be because this Government has not done its duty to those men in educating them in the privileges and duties of Canadian citizenship. Without going into the matter at length, I believe one of the first duties in making Canadian citizens of the immigrants who come to this country is an insistence, if necessary, that within a very short time-within a very few years at least-that before they are granted the rights of citizenship they shall, to a substantial extent, acquire the English language. I believe that if we studied the cases of those whom we speak of as for-

eigners and who have not assimilated with the rest of the population, we should find that one of the main reasons is that they preserve their native tongue and make no effort to learn English. I would not object to any man preserving the language which he brings with him. But when he comes to Canada-where English and French, if we wish to unite the two, are the languages of the country-and decides to become a Canadian citizen, he should have it impressed upon him that before he becomes naturalized he must show that he possesses a substantial knowledge of the English language. Because when they acquire a knowledge of the English language these people will see that their families are also taught it; and as they get to know the language of the country they are able to associate more freely and with less hesitation with those whose language is English, and in that way, almost unconsciously, acquire the customs and the thought of the English people by whom they are surrounded.
1 am glad that the Government has decided to modify this clause so that there shall be no exclusion of a religious sect. We have heard to-day a good deal of criticism of the Mennonites, and if the clause . under consideration stood as originally ' drafted it would exclude, providing the Government passed an Order in Council to that effect, all Mennonites. I want to say that there are Mennonites and Mennonites, and if the estimate that has been made of the people of this community who are going into the Canadian West is correct, they are entirely different from many Mennonites whom I know that are located in the province of Ontario. I feel in duty bound to say a word for at least a section of Mennonites who are citizens of Canada and located in that province. I know many of them very well, and I must say there is no better class of citizens-perhaps I should say residents-in Ontario to-day, from many points of view, than the Mennonites. They are splendid farmers, they are an industrious people, their family life is above reproach, they are a moral-living people of a high type, and they are devoted to their church. Let me say also, what perhaps cannot be said of every class of people, that although the teachings of their church may be regarded as rather peculiar in some respects, you will find the Mennonites practising what is preached in their church. The only objection, I think, that can be taken to them is that they are not in favour of military service-they are opposed to war. They are opposed to war in their 122
church teachings, and they religiously live up to that just as they live up to all the other teachings of their church. They have brought that teaching down from several centuries ago, when they suffered from oppression in Europe, and were glad to be free from that oppression. They obtained refuge in the United States, and from the State of Pennsylvania came over to Ontario, for the same reason-to escape the war service which was being imposed upon them during the great revolutionary war there. Let me say further that the Mennonites are not pro-German in sentiment. There may be some. I believe there are some, who may feel that way; but throughout the recent war their sympathies were largely with Britain, because-while they know little perhaps of British life and of Britain as a country-one of the teachings of their church is that every member of it shall be loyal to the country in which he lives, and they emphasized and illustrated that to a very large degree during the past four years. It has been said that some of the Mennonites will not contribute to the Victory Bonds. Let me give an illustration of how some of the Mennonites, those in my own neighbourhood, contributed to Victory Bonds last fall. A congregation of 160 families, living near the town in which I reside, contributed to the Victory Bonds at that time the sum of $39,000, almost $250 for each family in the congregation. At the time they were being canvassed for Victory Bonds, they were also being canvassed for contributions for the Belgian Relief Fund, and their contributions for that purpose amounted to nearly $5,200. I say this in justice to a class of the community in Ontario who are respected by every person, who are held in high esteem, who are absolutely honest, who live up to their religious doctrines, who are perfectly law-abiding-in fact, they do not believe in going to law at all-who live a high moral life, and who have adopted our public schools. Such great advocates of education are they, that they probably give their children a better public school education than does the average citizen of Ontario. They did nothing under the Military Service Act, I think the Mennonites of Ontario were exempt from military service. They are intensely opposed to military service, there is no doubt about that, but the Order in Council, which I understand has been passed, providing that no Mennonite coming to Canada hereafter shall be exempt from military service, obviates any difficulty in that regard. I am glad that the Government has brought down this Bill, and has



inserted section 13. I hope that as the discussion goes on the necessity for selecting our immigrants in the future will be further emphasized.

I cannot see eye to eye with those who criticise the immigration policy followed in this country up to 1914, because the immigration policy of the late Liberal government was the cause of the great prosperity which prevailed in Western Canada for quite a number of years. I live in a section of the country in which there are large numbers of the settlers referred to as alien enemies, and I must pay this tribute to them: during the war, in spite of the fact that they felt aggrieved by the War-time Elections Act, which deprived them of their franchise, they behaved in almost every instance as good Canadian citizens should behave, true, their nationality was that of the people whom we were fighting, and blood is thicker than water; but their public conduct was as good as, if not better than, that of a great many other people with whom we were, one might say, on neutral terms. There were branches of nationalities in Western Canada, with whom the allied armies were not fighting who showed stronger pro-German sentiment than ever was exhibited by Austrian, German or Bulgarian in Canada.
One criticism has been that certain nationalities which have been brought into Canada during the past twenty years have carried out their own ideas of education and language. In Alberta we have not that condition. The Provincial Government maintains absolute control over educational matters, and no particular section of the community has endeavoured to teach its own language and preserve its own national traditions. That criticism, therefore, is not fair, at least in its application to a great proportion of the people in Alberta. I have also heard adverse criticism of the Mennonites. The member for Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan) said that Mennonites in his section of the country lived in communities, had a sort of common household, and were communistic in their ideas and apparently socialistic in their method of carrying them out. The Mennonites that I have any knowledge of in Alberta live the same as any other men, in many cases it would be difficult to discern their nationality. In their methods of life, their habits, their industry, and in everything that goes to make up a good citizen-with possibly one exception-the Mennonites in Northern Alberta are a model citizenry.

But they do object, on religious grounds, 1 believe, to military service. From my own knowledge, that objection took the form only of a refusal to serve as combatant soldiers. When it came to subscribing to patriotic funds, buying victory bonds and taking part in Bed Cross and other war work, these people, my information is, contributed as generously as any other section of that community. So that it is only fair to say that this particular class of people should not be classified as they are in Southern Alberta.
I wish to draw the attention of the minister to the clause of the Bill pertaining to naturalization. Immigrants have been brought into Western Canada from different sections of Europe. Prior to the adoption of the new Naturalization Act of 1914, these men could be naturalized quite easily and without much formality, but it is a fact that when the war broke out there were men of foreign nationality who, though they had been residents of Canada for ten, twelve or fourteen years, had not been naturalized. That condition should not be permitted. If these men wish to take up their homes with us and obtain the benefits of Canadian citizenship, the 'Government should insist that after a reasonable length of time, say three years, they formally signify their intention to become citizens of Canada. In the United States it is necessary that an immigrant, after three years residence in the country, should signify his intention to become a citizen of United States. If in five years an immigrant does not signify his intention of taking out naturalization papers, I take it that he is not a desirable citizen and should be deported. Population is what we need above everything, but I do not think it is right that we should allow foreign people to come here, partake of the benefits that this country affords to any man who wishes to earn a competence, and yet not assume and live up to the obligations of Canadian citizenship. The minister will be well advised to look into that phase of the question and, if possible, to make some provision in the Act to compel people coming into the country to signify their intention of really becoming Canadian citizens and of adding to the wealth and prosperity of the nation with which they have become affiliated.

If I understand my hon.
friend aright, he states that in the United States there is provision of law whereby an alien who has resided for a certain length

of time in that country is compelled to make a declaration of his intention to take out naturalization papers. That is not the case.

I did not intend to convey that impression. I understand that he must signify his intention within three years if he intends to take out naturalization papers within five. We could go further and insist that he signify his intention of becoming a Canadian citizen.

The minister in explaining the Bill made a statement with which I heartily agree. I do not give it in his own words, hut he intimated that as a result of the war the mind of the people .at large is, perhaps, not quite normal and that unless the feeling of Parliament is well controlled we may do injustice to others as well as to ourselves. Without a doubt, the war has brought about a great many prejudices and has bred racial hatred. This, probably, is not to be -wondered at. But, in reference to that, I should simply like to throw out this suggestion, that after all those prejudices and hatreds will not last forever, and at this particular time it should be borne in mind that, while those feelings are quite natural and to be expected as the result of the events of the prolonged war which is now coming to an end, those feelings are not a safe guide for those who are legislating for the best interests of Canada. .
What, impels me to rise just now particularly is the speech of the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) and that of the hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. J. M. Douglas) with regard to the Mennonites. 1 am glad to endorse much that those hon. gentlemen have said.
