I haive read, with a good deal of regret, some statements by public men published in the press with regard to the Mennonites. I desire to say at the outset that I know nothing whatever of the Hutterites, but they have at times been described as Mennonites. I know very little of the Mennonites in the West; I know there is in Manitoba a sect of Mennonites which immigrated into Canada in 1873 or 1875, and that they were accorded certain privileges. Criticism has been made of those Mennonites and others living in the Canadian West: that they do not yield themselves to tne customs of uie country; that they will not permit their children to attend the ordinary public schools; that they have their own schools in which they teach German and other languages; that they do not live as ordinary Canadians do 122*
and as well-living citizens ought to live. 1 want also to make the point made by the hon. members for South Perth and Strathcona that there are Mennonites and Mennonites. In the county, the northern part of Which I have the honour to represent, there are a large number of Mennonites; in fact, one township is inhabited almost entirely by people of that sect. They did not come from Russia, nor from Germany; they did not come from any enemy nation at all; they immigrated into Waterloo county about one hundred years ago from the state of Pennsylvania. I am not sure that some of them did not come from Germany into Pennsylvania a long time before that, but I know many of them claim that they came from Switzerland. For -many years these people and their descendants have lived in the northern part of Waterloo county. Some of them have settled in Perth, some in Huron and some in Bruce, but the central settlement of the Mennonites is in my county. They are considered amongst us as being of our very best citizens,-and I use the term "citizens," although I think the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) rather qualified his statement with regard to that. They are the best of farmers, understanding farming well; they are clean in their living; they do not live in communities; each family lives by itself, and they have never to my knowledge raised the slightest objection to having their children attend the same schools as are attended by all the other -children in our county.
Are any numbers of that class of people immigrating into Ontario at the present time, or have they been immigrating during the last few years?

I know of none at all. In fact, the immigration- of Mennonites into Waterloo county and, I presume, into any other county in Western Ontario, has been an accomplished fact for many years. Whether those people were at the time of their entering into Canada a hundred years ago of the same character and class as those with whom so much fault is found in the West, I do not know. It may be that they were, and if they were, there is at least reason for hope that, if a considerable number of those people have already entered the Western provinces, it will be found before long that they are after all pretty good citizens and an asset to the Dominion of Canada. We should take cognizance o-f those people. The reports that have begn spread abroad as to the Mennonites generally will

be found to be untrue and not founded in fact. It is true they live to some extent' *to themselves. They do not very readily intermarry with the other people in the county, but they are absolutely respectable, hardworking, responsible people. Their word is as good as their bond, and in my county it is a fact that any iman would almost sooner take the word of a Mennonite than that of anybody else. That is a strong statement, but I believe it to be true; and a3 I said before, you cannot find the same fault with the Mennonites of Western Ontario as is apparently to be found with those of Western Canada. They do not ask for schools of their own in which they may teach a foreign language. There is no distinction whatever as regards education between the children of the Mennonite of Western Ontario and those of any other class.

They are absolutely
loyal?

They are absolutely loyal. They cannot be anything else, because all their traditions are Canadian. They did not come from a European country; they came from the United States. It would be a great pity and injustice if, at some time, their friends and relatives in Pennsylvania -and they have many relatives in Pennsylvania whom they visit occasionally-who happen to belong to the Mennonite sect, should be excluded from Canada. I do not think they should. For many people a basis of objection to permitting the entrance of Mennonites into Canada is that dhey do not believe in war. They take the Bible literally; they are entirely conscientious in their attitude; they refuse to go to war because of conscientious objections. I think we all hope that we shall not again have a war, and if that be the case, it may be after all that the objection which is raised to the Mennonites will never again become a practical one.

I should like to point
out to the hon. member that this section governs immigrants; that it would not prevent persons residing in the United States from temporarily entering Canada for the purpose of visiting here. I think in section 44 of the Act as it stands there is a general power given to the minister, notwithstanding any provision in the law, to allow any particular person to come in on humanitarian grounds, or on any other grounds. That is a section which we are called upon to exercise quite frequently, because, as hon. members can understand, there will be many
 '
cases where a power of that kind should be exercised on purely humanitarian grounds. I wish to make it clear that there is in the present law sufficient power to deal with cases of that kind, should they arise.

The minister states that
there is provision in law whereby those people could come into Canada for the purpose of visiting. I would like to ask him, if Mennonites from Pennsylvania, for example, and they are of the same class as our own, should desire to locate in Western Ontario, whether the proposed measure would exclude them. If it did, it would not be a just law nor one in the interests of our people.
There is power to exclude.

But would that mean
the necessity of excluding those Mennonites? If such a clause is added I think it is desirable that the minister should be given discretionary powers to decide in individual cases.
I understood my hon. friend to say that the Mennonites object to military service on conscientious grounds. Do they object to others fighting for them?
They object to war altogether.
It must be obvious that if this class of people were in Canada in sufficient numbers they might very seriously affect our policy in defending ourselves.
If all of the inhabitants of Canada were Mennonites, Canada would never be at' war.	-
But should we not be under the domination of Germany to-day?

No aspersions can be cast on the loyalty of the Alennonites; they are true Canadians. I know of Mennonites helping to-day to rebuild France. They have no objection to performing noncombatant service, but they do believe it is absolutely wrong and sinful to destroy human life.
Is not that a limited loyalty?
The hon. gentleman may put his own construction upon it.
It is not one hundred per cent loyalty from my point of view. Does the hon. member consider it one hundred per cent loyalty?
I am not responsible for my hon. friend's opinion.
What about yours?
Should I be in order, Mr. Chairman, in discussing one or two other clauses now?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It would be much more in order if my hon. friend would wait till the particular clauses are called. By the unanimous consent of the Committee a great deal of latitude has been allowed to hon. members during the past two days, but I must draw attention to the fact that there has been a tendency in the House of Commons for some time to discuss the principle of a Bill in Committee instead of on the second reading. The discussion which has taken place to-day, while very interesting, should have taken place on the second reading. The minister has moved for the consideration of section 13 and I think hon. members should confine their remarks to the subject matter of that section.
It was not my intention to speak at any length on the other clauses. I had only one or two remarks to make.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The trouble is that the moment one hon. member makes even one remark on some other clause, an answer is made by an hon. member on the other side of the House and a very lengthy discussion may ensue. I must ask the hon. member to adhere strictly to the rules of the Committee.
I think the wording of the section would be improved by substituting the words "by reason of" for the word "because" in the seventeenth line.
May I suggest that this clause be allowed to stand for the present? I have not seen a copy of the amendment, and it is therefore quite impossible for me to judge whether it meets the case.

We all know the objection that has been taken to doing things under the War Measures Act while Parliament is in session, and' the only reason I suggested that this section be considered at this time was that I might have the approval of the Committee before taking action under the War Measures Act. If the Committee agrees to the principle, I think we might very well take immediate action under the War Measures Act to prevent these people from coming into Canada.

May I suggest that if immediate action is necessary it could be taken under the present Act, which provides that you can prohibit for a stated period or permanently the landing in Canada or the landing at any specified port of entry in Canada of immigrants belonging to any race deemed unsuited to the climate or requirements of Canada or of immigrants of any specified class, occupation or character. Surely we can specify the Hutterites as a class of people unsuited to Canada? 1 think any lawyer, in fact, any member, will agree that the minister has power to take immediate action under the law as it now stands.

I understood the Minister of Immigration to invite an expression of opinion as to the advisability of taking immediate action for the exclusion of these people who are seeking entry into Canada at the present time. In my opinion, and I think I am speaking for every one of my constituents, the Government should take immediate action by Order in Council, or any other expeditious means, to prevent the entrance of Hutterites, who, I believe, are of the same class and kidney as the Men-nonites and very similar to the Doukhobors. The hon. member for Kitchener would like the bars let down and these people now living in Pennsylvania to come and settle in Western Ontario. He has made the remarkable statement that these people are absolutely loyal. What does he mean by absolutely loyal? I would take the qualifying word "absolutely" to mean that they were loyal in every sense of the word. These people who would not lift a hand to save this country from being placed under the heel of the Hun, but were willing to let others go across the seas and fight and die for principles that we hold dear, are in the opinion of the hon. member absolutely loyal. That may be his idea of absolute loyalty, but it is not mine.
We do not want in Western Canada or in Ontario or in any province in the Dominion people who are not prepared to assume their full share of the responsibilities of citizenship. If there are in the United States or Europe people of any class, whether they be called Mennonites, Hutterites or any other kind of " ites," we do not want them to come to Canada and enjoy the privileges and advantages of life under the British flag if they are willing to allow others to do the fighting for them while they sit at home in peace and plenty. We certainly do not want that kind of cattle in this country. Indeed not only do we not waht that kind of cattle, but I would go further and support the view that we should deport from Canada others of the same class who were allowed to come in by mistake.
I rise to a point of order.
I would say, Mr. Chairman-

I had not the hon. member for South Renfrew in mind when I made the remarks to which objection has been taken. I certainly had no thought of the Quakers, although I would include the Quakers with the Mennonites or Doukho-bors or any other class in this country who would object on conscientious or any other grounds to assuming their full responsibilities as citizens. When I used the word "cattle" I did not notice any hon. member on the other side of the House with horns or other characteristics of these four-footed animals enough to call the word to my mind. If I had looked more closely, however, I might have deemed it proper to use another word describing a different class of four-footed creatures that are more distinguished for the length of their ears than for horns. On section 13:

I just want to add one or two remarks before this clause is disposed of. I got in wrong with certain hon. gentlemen by using the word " cattle " in reference to certain people that I thought were an undesirable class to have in this country, or to be allowed to come in to any great extent. My use of the word-I am not going to withdraw it-had special reference to Doukhobors and such people as that. I had no reference whatever to Quakers or conscientious objectors. May I remind the Committee of a little incident that took

place in this country a few years ago when some of these people-the Doukhobors they were called-went on a tramp, or march, through the country, men, women and children, absolutely naked. Is that the kind of people we want in Canada? I was perfectly right in offering my apology to the cattle when making a comparison between them and people of that kind. Cattle are pretty high priced now; they are valuable. That is not the class of people we want. It was a mistake that they were ever permitted to come in. It is a reflection upon the intelligence of the people who were administering the affairs of this country that they were allowed to come in under special conditions. It emphasizes, in my opinion, the mistake which has been made along immigration lines by every Government in Canada from 1867 down to the present time. One hon. gentleman spoke about the success that had attended the immigration policy during the Laurier regime. In my judgment, instead of estimating the success of our immigration policy by the number of immigrants we have obtained, in looking back over past history, we might take the number of immigrants as an indication of the lack of success which has been achieved, or the lack of thought which has been given to our immigration policy; for, just to the extent which we have been successful in point of numbers, in my judgment, we have been unsuccessful from the proper standpoint of getting people into this country.
Just one word in regard to another class which may be considered as being mentioned in clause 13-those who come under the designation of the conscientious objectors. I need not emphasize now what I said in that regard before six o'clock.
I said then, and I still maintain, that we have a country here sufficiently attractive to people of other countries in Europe, or other parts of the world, that we can select the class ol people that come to this country, and we should select them. If a man comes here, no matter from where he comes or what he may call himself, to take advantage of our splendid resources and to share in all the privileges that go with citizenship, we must .make him understand distinctly that it will be part of his duty as a citizen to take his full share of the responsibilities of citizenship. If our country is in danger, if its fights have to be defended, or if we find it necessary to go to war, every person, no matter what he calls himself or to what sect he belongs, whether he is a conscientious objector or anything else, should come forward and do his full share and take his full part in the fight. Why should we open the doors of our country to all classes from the continent of Europe, to the people that have governed the continent with their doctrines and with the leprosy of their political ideas? What do we want them here for? Are we to consider that a man is a desirable immigrant because he weighs so many pounds and gives evidence of being physically able to work? Is that the only thing we are to go by?	.
One hon. gentleman objected to a reading or writing test. We are perfectly justified in requiring that a man should be able to read some language before he comes into this country. Fancy a community in a part of Canada-hundreds of them-who can neither read nor write. We are appealing to all classes of the agricultural community to farm along the best lines. We are spending hundreds of thousands of dollars getting out agricultural bulletins. For what purpose? They are got out to send to people who are engaged in agricultural pursuits in order to give them the advantage of the results of scientific research that has taken place at our agricultural colleges, farms and schools. What is the good of getting out these bulletins if a considerable proportion of your population cannot read or understand them?
The minister called attention to the fact that we had not done our part in trying to make citizens of these people. He said that we had failed in that respect. I think the hon. gentleman was perfectly right in that. We are not going to help any by allowing those people to come in here regardless of whether they can read or write any language. How are we to instruct these people or to give them the knowledge that we expect to give them along patriotic lines, how are we going to give them any idea of the British institutions under which we live if they cannot read? We are perfectly within our rights in insisting upon an educational standard at least to the extent that they should be able to read some language before they come into this country? We have been over anxious in trying to fill up the country. We have lots of space, lots of agricultural land, lots of opportunities for people, and we have thought that perhaps the larger our population the more we could divide the burdens of taxation and the public debt. That probably is all right. But we are in a peculiar position in Canada at the present time and would like to get the right class of people here to help in carrying through our period of reconstruction. In my judgment, we do not want
COMMONS *
in this country, ifor many years to come, an inferior class who will only increase our difficulties and troubles, so far as the labour market is concerned, without assisting us to any material extent in bearing the burden of our national obligations. For years we have placed restrictions upon certain people entering Canada. We have placed restrictions upon the Japanese, only a certain number of whom are allowed to enter Canada, and we have also placed restrictions upon Chinese immigration, and that has apparently been accepted by both parties in the Dominion as a proper policy. Noiw, it does seem to me that we have been illogical, to say the least of it, in placing restrictions upon the entrance into Canada of a progressive people like the Japanese, and a decent people such as the Chinese have shown themselves to be-at any rate all that I have seen coming into the country -and throwing our doors wide open to immigrants from, countries in central Europe whom we have been fighting for the last four and a half years, and with whom we shall practically still be at war until peace is signed.
I am in entire accord with the idea of placing restrictions upon immigrants coming to this country. There is no necessity for us to cheapen Canada in the eyes ol the world. We believe that we have the very best country on the face of the earth, and we can with confidence invite immigrants to come here. But I do not think it should be necessary for us to spend a dollar in inducing them to come. Our country is sufficiently advertised in the countries that we want immigrants from, so that we need not spend any more money for that purpose. Where do we want immigrants from? Principally, from the British Isles, from the United States, and from France, Belgium and Italy, the countries which have been allied with us in this war. If these countries have people to spare let them come, because we have tested them as they have tested us, during the past four and a half years of war. We know what these nationalities are like, and we know that we can depend upon them in a crisis or in an emergency; they will not hide behind any conscientious objections to military service, nor behind any Douk-hobor or Mennonite doctrine; they will fight if necessary for the liberties of the country in the future as they fought for liberty along with us in the recent war. That is the class of people we want here. You do not need to advertise Canada to them because they know what it is like. The money we needed for the purposes of immigration, 
in my belief, should be devoted to a rigorous inspection on the other side of the Atlantic, before the immigrants board ocean steamships destined for Canada, supplemented by a further inspection on this side, to see that we exclude from the Dominion a class of people who have shown themselves to be troublesome in their own country, and from whom we can expect nothing but trouble if they are admitted here. Let me say emphatically that we do not want that class of people here at all; we have too many of them at the present time. In the past we have allowed things to drift, we have been too lax entirely. There has been too much compromise with -these people, and too much compromise in the western provinces, in the way' of allowing these people to settle in colonies and communities by themselves, to retain their own languages and their own customs, and their own ideas of how people should live. They have brought from Europe their own ideas of how a country should be run, and their ideas are not our ideas, and they are not the ideas, I venture to say, of any member of this House. Therefore I say we are perfectly justified in taking steps to maintain the high standard of civilization that we now have in this country. If there has been any lowering of that standard it is not due to our native-born population, or to immigrants from the British Isles or the United States. Any lowering of the standard of civilization in Canada has been brought about by our lax immigration laws in permitting the entry of people who never should have been allowed' to come here, people who have shown themselves to be absolutely unfit for the privileges and liberties they have enjoyed here, and who refused to come forward and fight for those liberties and privileges. That is not the class we want in Canada, and I for one will support the Government in the most drastic legislation it can bring forward to restrict and prohibit that class of people from coming into Canada. I will go further and say I will support the Government in any move to debar from Canada those people who have shown themselves to be unreliable when the test came, and proved themselves to be an undesirable class of citizens.

The position taken by the member for Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan) is the position that I also desire to take in this matter as a member from the province of Alberta. I intend to speak on one of the points that

has befen brought up this afternoon when the Franchise Bill was introduced, but as I have been subjected to attacks in the press of Canada in that regard I deem it advisable to discuss at some length what has taken place and to refute the charges that have been made in several newspapers in reference to myself. This afternoon the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) laid a charge against a population of three hundred and fifty thousand souls residing in the West, basing his charge on statements contained in a letter from D. A. Ross, a member of the Manitoba Legislature. I do not believe the rumours referred to, and I will give the Committee the grounds for my belief in a few moments. With the intention of assisting the member for Springfield I asked him to lay upon the Table the letter upon which he based his accusations, and the abrupt Teply I received was that the member for Springfield would do just as he liked. I want to tell that hon. gentleman to-night that whenever he, and his friend from Kingston (Mr. Nickle), move resolutions, and amendments to resolutions, in this House, and line up the members behind them, and then secretly enter into a compact with a member of the Government that they shall withdraw such resolutions and amendments, and place members in a difficult position and force them to vote against their convictions so as not to give a slap in the face to the Government-I tell that hon. gentleman the next time I shall vote as I please, and I am sure that in saying so I am voicing the sentiments of a large number of my colleagues in the House. The hon. member was unfortunate in most of his irresponsible statements this afternoon, and unfortunate also in the choice of his language. In the Evening Telegram of October 8. 1918, there is an article written about me appearing in special correspondence from G. C. Porter.

Why not send for the
hon. member for Springfield?

speechtext: Order.

He will get it. The heading of the correspondence referred to in the Telegram is as follows:
To restore vote to Aliens.-Hon J. A. Oalder makes move.-H. A. Mackie, M.P., Admits Appeal to Premier Borden on behalf of Ukrainians.
(In this article they make an attack upon the Minister of Immigration and Colonization and upon me, saying that we were endeavouring to restore the vote to those who were the enemies of the country. They
conclude the article by saying that " Mr. Mackie, who has been chosen to carry on the negotiations with western members of this province, is a native of Quebec, a French Canadian Catholic." I shall be pleased, with your permission, Mr. Chairman, to file this article so that it may be published in Hansard. I do not blame the Evening Telegram, because the article in question is the special correspondence of Mr. Porter of Winnipeg.
If the hon. gentleman wants any article to appear in Hansard, he will certainly have to read it.
Read it.

I did not like to take
up the time of the Committee. It is as follows:
(Special Correspondence to The Telegram from G. C. Porter.)
Edmonton, Alta., Oct. 8.-Intrigue is rampant through the west to have the Dominion Elections Act disfranchising electors of alien enemy races abolished at the approaching session of Parliament. Hon. James Calder last week laid the plan before the Great War Vet-erns' Executive Committee, of Edmonton, and this week will take the executive at Calgary into his confidence. H. A. Mackie, M.P. for East Edmonton, has been selected to communicate with all the western members to see how they feel on the subject. He said to-day that he would move the resolution when Parliament opens. He admitted frankly that he has wired the Prairie members the following:
Seek Revision of Act.
" Local Ukrainian Association want revision of War Times Election Act relative to disfranchisement with a view of doing non-com- . batant work at soldier's pay and taking a share in the war. Their bishops and priests favourable. All western members are being canvassed. If Government is favourable will you concur? "
This is supposed to be a telegram which I sent. As a matter of fact, the statement is not correct. The article continues:
Mr. Mackie said he had already received some replies, both favourable and unfavourable. He defended his position very vigorously, saying this would solve alien enemy labour question of the prairies. He limited his observations to the Ukrainians.
Veterans to Oppose.
But Hon. J. A. Calder, in talking with the Soldiers' Committee, referred to all alien enemies disfranchised. The returned soldiers are individually bitterly opposed to the idea, and it will come up for discussion on Thursday night. The members are greatly excited, as this coming at the time of the immigration^ of so many German Mennonites into the prairies, has provoked the returned soldiers to desperation.
Not Wanted.
Tom Dace, Alberta's representative of the Dominion Great War Veterans' Executive, said

he would not express an opinion until after the meeting to he held following the Calder suggestion of suspending the Disfranchisement Act. It was so serious that 2,000 members here should first he permitted to discuss the subject before he spoke. He did, however, say that he and all other soldiers were 'bitterly opposed to these Mennonites coming in here with their German schools and exemptions. As he put it: "We don't want any of these people being spewed out of the U.S., and the 2,000 returned members here and the similar number in Calgary are a raging volcano on the subject of the preferred treatment the alien enemies are and have been receiving from the Government."
He added that the soldiers' executive put the Mennonite menace up-to Hon. Hr. Calder at the meeting here as they did to Hon. N. W. Rowell.
Where was that meeting supposed to have been held?

In Edmonton. I will refer to it; I know what he means. I just want to give my friend Porter something that is coming to him in a few minutes:
-and' neither faced the question squarely, and the soldiers were much disturbed by their equivocating demeanour. Bach said he would have to take the subject up at Ottawa before making definite reply.

Bishop Budko, of the "Ukrainians, was in Edmonton last week in connection with the scheme to get his people's franchise restored, and has been working quietly all over the prairies for some time in this direction. He is now in Ottawa. This is the same Bishop Budtoa who was charged with sedition at H-afford in July, but acquitted, and it was Budka who issued a pastoral letter to his flock advising them to return to Austria and fight for the fatherland. He escaped serious consequences because the document was issued prior to Britain entering the war.
EDITOR GETS THREE TEARS. Ukrainians are mostly Austrians, and there are from 70,000 to 100,000 of these alien enemies in the prairies. The editor of the chief Ukrainian paper at Winnipeg was sentenced to three years in penitentiary for seditious utterances.
There was intense excitement among G.W.V., Next of Kin British Citizenship League and sons of England over the Mennonite menace, that the latest disclosure of the intrigue to give the alien enemy back his franchise, has enormously increased the feeling of alarm among patriotic societies, and feeling is general that the Act is likely to toe suspended unless the greatest energy is displayed to convince the Government of its unpopularity.

Mr. Mackie, who has been chosen to carry on negotiations with western members for this purpose* is a native of Quebec, a French-Canadian Catholic, and in his constituency there are two thousand alien enemies. His majority in the last election was 600, exclusive of the soldiers' vote, which gave him nearly 2,0'0« majority. He said he opposed the dis-
franchisement of these ipeople last fall'until he learned that the Imperial authorities' did not want them sent overseas as soldiers.
The statement made by Porter with regard to the Minister of Immigration and myself is absolutely false and manufactured from his own immoral imagination. A meeting was held in the Macdonald Hotel, Edmonton, at which the Minister of Immigration and myself were present, along with a number of civilians and soldiers. We made a protest against the entry of Mennonites into Canada; not a word was said about the Disfranchisement Act, nor did I have any communication with the minister in connection with this matter, good, bad or indifferent, except that I stated to him that I was sending a petition to the Government asking that the War-time Elections Act be rescinded so that the Ru-thenians who are British subjects could be conscripted for non-combatant work in Canada. This man Porter comes into my office and says: "I understand that you are to present a petition to the Dominion Government asking for the recision of the Wartimes Elections Act." He passes off as my friend; his zeal began with hypocrisy and ended with treachery. He says: "I am your friend. You are doing a -great deal for the soldiers." I assented to all these remarks, and then when I told him what I was doing he began to ask me whether I was a Mason or a Roman Catholic or a Protestant. I resented these remarks and told him where he was "getting off at." Before he left he asked my permission to publish the interview and I granted it.
Was that before the election?

This was in October, 1918. What I told him was this: That the Ruthenian Association had asked me to send a petition to the Dominion Government asking for the rescision of the War-Time Elections Act so that Ruthenians, British subjects, could be conscripted to do non-combatant work in Canada.
I told him I thought that was the proper attitude to take. I did not see how I could reconcile my views with those of the Government who had disfranchised those people, because, even although they were not wanted overseas and their opinions might not be taken seriously in war matters in the Dominion of Canada, they could have been recruited for non-combatant work. Those are the views which I held then and which I hold at the present time. He spoke of Bishop Budka. I never met Bishop Budka until the month of February

of this year, when I was on my way from Edmonton to this House, and in the presence of the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Blake), I told the reverend gentleman that if what was being circulated about him was true, I would be one of the first to ask for his deportation. In that regard the hon. member for North Winnipeg put upon the Order Paper a certain number of questions which were answered by the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen), and I shall refer to that very shortly.
This report of Porter makes out that I am allied with Bishop Budka, and I do not know what purpose he has in view when he says that I am from Quebec, a French Canadian and a Roman Catholic. Again, Mr. Porter is not stating what I told him, and it is quite evident that he intended to do me an injury, one that I could not repair by correspondence through the press. I wish to point out to the press gallery here the power that they have in destroying men in public life by writing such articles as this, if they emanated from them directly. Not very long ago, the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) had to complain about the Globe, and may I tell my friend, Marchington, that he had better pay a little stricter attention to the truthfulness of his premises. There is only one member of the press gallery that is safe, and that is Ford, because he never transmits anything West. This man Porter came to me as a friend; at first he deceived me and at last he betrayed me by a most brazen and audicious falsehood. But that is not all.
We come to Jack Canuck, of January 11, 1919. I do hot purpose putting Jack Canuck on Hansard. This paper that lives and thrives on carrion meat, is the scavenger in the political and social life of Canada and does not deserve anything more than a passing reference from me.

Is that a Government
organ?
I do not know. Ii it is, the Government should blush for it. It is published in the holy city of Toronto.
Is it an Opposition prgan?

It may be an Opposition organ. Some parts of it, I imagine, came from them. The hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Blake) put the following questions to the Government:

The answers were the following:

speechtext:
1.	Yes, but the charge was subsequently withdrawn.
2.	He has been accused of disloyalty on several occasions.

I see by to-night's paper that the reverend gentleman is brought to answer a charge before some local authority in Winnipeg by virtue of an Order in Council passed by the Local Legislature on 12th February, 1919. It is quite evident that Premier Norris is not a member of the Federal Government, or he would be able to write out a better Order in Council than the one which I hold in my hand, which says: Wheras this and whereas that-
He has not'had the practice.

That is what I say.
That pursuant to and under the provisions of the said charterand so forth.
-a board to be known as the Alien Investigation Board of Manitoba with powers to investigate the whole situation.
That is the Order in Council constituting a board consisting of certain gentlemen in Manitoba to investigate the whole situation. What is the whole situation? What is the effect of this Order in Council except to foster a political move?
And what the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) said this afternoon is quite true, namely, that we have done nothing for these people, whom we have brought to this country, except to exploit them. There is, indeed, exploitation. I know, as a matter of fact, that a politician in the employ of the Norris Government has a room in Labour Hall, and he gets these people to come and report to him and he tells them: " Now, here is your exemption card from deportation; you are all right; keep that in your pocket or you will be deported, and the Norris Government is preventing you from being deported, by virtue of an Order in Council
