which is bound to investigate the whole situation." Are these people being treated fairly? Have they been treated fairly in Saskatchewan or Alberta, where, for instance, in a constituency I know a local member, a man totally incapable of broad and generous thought, who has three political organizations, English, French and Russian, that go forth with three political war-cries: "Long live the British Empire," " Long live Quebec," and " Russia forever?" And here, lo and behold, the Norris Government comes along with an Order in Council that is passed by virtue of some statute in Manitoba authorizing .a committee of three men to investigate the situation, and the Rev. Bishop Budka is being investigated at the present time. If it be true that he has done anything against this country, I believe the Dominion Government, and not the Provincial Government of Manitoba, will have to take steps to deport him.
On what side was that provincial member at the last election?
He is a member oi the local Legislature'of Alberta, and since the creation of that province there has been only one political side and I believe they are about to stick there for a longer time.
Who are the members of that board?

Judge Myers, a member of the Great War Veterans, and the name of the third I do not recollect. Adverting again to the article which was written against me and which was trying to link me up with the Rev. Bishop Budka, who was supposed to be guilty of seditious utterances and to be a traitor to this country, let me point out what I petitioned the Dominion Government to do, because this is the only place in which I can at least explain my conduct and give any publicity in the Dominion of Canada in refutation of articles which are absolutely untrue. On October 16, 1918, I forwarded this petition to Sir Robert Borden, and I shall read only portions of it, as it is rather long:-
Recent representations were made to me by the local Ruthenian Association that the " War-time Elections Act '' ought to he rescinded so as to permit the Ukrainians in Canada to render non-combatant service. To ascertain the feeling of the western members I wired all but two in the four provinces. The replies are enclosed herein. Some disclose that the member is not familiar with the law. Others show an open mind, and still others are decidedly against that proposition	

We now consider the advisability of rescinding the War-time Elections Act in so far as the foreign population, whose citizenship has been suspended, so that every one may render a non-combatant service at soldier's pay for the balance of this war, since we are forbidden by the Imperial authorities to take them for
combatant service	
I have the assurance of the Ruthenian Associations here that they. Supported by their clergy, are prepared to instruct their people and explain why their franchise was suspended and why they should serve, if allowed.
Is that what Porter said? The statement I gave to him is the statement I have just read, hut the statement he gave to the press links me up with Bishop Budka. For the purpose of feeling the pulse of the Western members, I wired them, because they were all as much interested as myself and I felt that they would support me in having the Act rescinded so as to ensure a large number of these people doing war work in Canada. I stated to the Prime Minister some of the objections that were raised:
Objection is taken that their non-combatant work would interfere with labour and their organizations. Non-combatant workers need not disturb economic conditions. The present equilibrium can be maintained and the surplus value of earnings can ibe diverted to a fund for returned soldiers.
That is what I was asking for, and what I told Porter, that the Act should be rescinded so that these people could do non-combatant service in Canada at $1.10 a day. And I said: Let the surplus value of their earnings go to a fund for returned soldiers. That was the request I made of the Dominion Government.
In 1916 a letter was addressed by the Ukrainians of Northern Alberta to Mr. R. B. Bennett, president of the National Service Commission, Ottawa:
A recent political development in Europe, namely, the establishment of the independent kingdom of Poland and the promise of infernal autonomy Ifor the kingdom of Galicia, are principally responsible for the present letter addressed to you as Chairman of National Commissions, to secure your consent and support in adopting a certain new policy in our recruiting campaign.
This letter points out that the Ukrainians were willing to do national service, and they asked Mr. Bennett how best that could be brought about. On page 7, the letter says:
The method of securing recruits should be gone into fully by the writer who is in a position to know what would be the best way to reach thes-e people and to make them understand the reason why they have an interest in the present war. I should at all times be ready and willing to give you the assistance necessary in forming the plan.

May I call your attention also to the advisability of undertaking the recruiting among the Buthenians of the western provinces by stating that it would very materially assist the undertaking of the Government to raise 500,000 troops in Canada?
I would1 like to point out to you that in the 218th Battalion, commanded by Lieut,-Col. Cornwall, there are a large number of Ruthen-ians who have volunteered to enlist and have been accepted and Lieut.-Col. Cornwall informs me that they are of the very best material in his whole battalion. Lieut.-Col. Cornwall also informs me -that the Ruthenians in his battalion have shown a remarkable ability to learn the English language and that they understand the commands given in English just as well as any English speaking soldiers.
I should be very happy to read at your earliest convenience, that your Committee has given this matter their earnest consideration, and I trust that you will come to the conclusion that the Ruthenians in the Dominion of Canada are able to serve Canadian interests; that we are willing to become better Canadians if you will assist us; and that we realize fully the justness of the cause of the Allies in the present war.
In 1916, therefore, these people were asking to do national service, but the Government did not see fit to adopt their suggestion. What do we find at the present time? Let mg_ read a petition that was addressed by the Ukrainian Council of Canada to the Dominion Government by these people who were alleged this afternoon to be uprising in Manitoba and creating a Bolshevik movement. I shall not read all the "Whereas" clauses, hut I shall be glad to show the petition in its. entirety to any hon. gentleman who cares to call upon me.
I might explain that the Ukrainian Council represents 350,(MX) people, not 70,000 or 100,000, as has been stated. The Ruthenians do not all come from Galicia. Some come from Bukowina, Hungary, and the little Russias, so called. They are all the same people; they are Ruthenians, but they call themselves Ukrainians because it is the Ukrainian family in language, literature and ideals. The chances are that the Ukrainian republic will be established by the Peace Conference in Paris, which will furnish the key to the eastern -situation. What did the Ukrainian Council ask the Dominion Government to do? The petition reads in part:
Whereas such politicians are advocating indiscriminate deportation.
Whereas, Ukrainians in Canada realize they have not become Canadianized as rapidly as might have been expected.
Whereas the Ukrainians' are of the opinion that Canada cannot be a nation until a.system of education is evolved whereby all people shall learn to suffer alike and to love alike, to revere the same great historical figures and to interpret the meaning of the flag in the same way.
Now therefore be it resolved that we on behalf of the Ukranian people of Canada, humbly petition the Canadian Government:
(a) To establish a national school as -a remedy to the evils enumerated herein.
(b)	That the Canadian Government do deport from this country all enemy aliens who have committed an offence against this country or the British Empire during the time of the war.
(c)	That the Canadian Government do amend the Naturalization Act so as to make education a test, providing that no one shall be naturalized from now on unless he is capable of reading and writing the English language, with the proviso, however, that the Supreme Court judges or the Superior Court judges of this country shall take into consideration, such cases, for instance, of a man who is of an age and so situated that he could not be expected reasonably to acquire more than a smattering of the English language; trusting that such judges stand historically and traditionally as a great body of men who come between the legislative and [DOT] the executive of the state and the public, and your petitioners shall ever pray.
What then do we find these people doing who, the hon. member for Springfield, seeking cheap notoriety, says, are uprising?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think I shall have to ask the hon. member to withdraw the expression that an hon. member made use of his place in this House to seek cheap notoriety.

If the expression is not parliamentary I gladly withdraw it, but I still believe it is true. These people in their petition to the Dominion Government asked that the Ukrainians in Western Canada be permitted to serve with the English and French forces to put down Bolshevism in Europe.
In conclusion, I say that before hon. members make a statement which has a tendency to stigmatize 350,000 citizens of Canada they should first take pains to find out the facts.
Mr. LEMilEUX:	Speaking of this Mr. Porter, my hon. friend said that he attempts to link his name with Bishop Budka, and before that my hon. friend referred to the accusation of sedition brought against the Bishop. Will he explain that point, because there are so many rumours about Bishop Budka?

The difficulty that has arisen in Western Canada regarding Bishop Budka is a religious one. There is a difficulty between the Greek Orthodox and the Greek Catholic. The Greek Catholics recognize the Pope, but are not subject to his authority, instead of recog-

nizing the 'Czar of Russia who was a religious and a political leader at one and the same time. So far as I have been able to ascertain a meeting was called prior to the declaration of war by Britain and the reverend Bishop attended and exhorted his people to advise their friends across the seas not to think of coming to Canada any longer because there was a question of labour and they were not in a position to take care of them. Is that the explanation that the hon. member wishes?

The charge of sedition
was referred to.
Mr. H. A. MAC'KIE: Yes, there was a charge of sedition against the Bishop. He was tried and acquitted. Other rumours have been circulated about his attitude, but so far nothing has come out of them, and the Acting Minister of Justice replied to the question which was put to this House by the hon. member for North Winnipeg. Under the Order in Council the whole situation is now being investigated and the Bishop will either be requested to get out of Canada or will once more be excused.
I wish to say, in conclusion, that Porter could not have had any intention other than to create a feeling of antagonism against me at the hands of the returned soldiers, or to create a religious prejudice against me. It is true that I come from Quebec, but that is not the way Porter intended the remarks. I do not blush when I say that d do come from Quebec, which has given to the political and social life of Canada a Mercier, a Chapleau, a Lafon-taine, and last but not least, a Laurier. And if hon. members will press me I will say why I prefer to come from that province than from any other part of Canada. The returned soldier is full of speculative ideals and he would like to see society differently constituted. But the time politician is the man who will 9 p.m. make the most of the material he finds in the country. A disposition to preserve and an ability to improve taken together form what in my opinion is the essence of true statesmanship in the matter of immigration.

May I ask a question of the Minister of Immigration, in regard to the question that was brought up by the hon. member for East Edmonton? Will you deny that you are associated with the telegrams with which our country was flooded, after your visit to Edmonton-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will have to ask the hon. member to address his remarks to the Chair.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I will speak to the minister through you. At that particular time our section of the country, or at least a great many people, condemned the Minister of Immigration because they believed, and it was generally asserted, that he originated the telegrams which were sent out by the hon. member for Edmonton stating that the War-time Elections Act wras to be repealed on condition that these men would go into non-combatant service.

This is the first time I have had any inkling that that question has exercised the minds of persons out West. I had nothing either directly or indirectly to do with the origin of these telegrams. I have never discussed the matter in any shape or form with the member for Edmonton. It originated entirely with himself, and I did not know that the matter was of any concern to any people in Western Canada. I may say this too:
I am fairly well acquainted with Mr. Porter, who has written and said a great deal about myself, and I ceased long ago to pay any attention to anything he either writes or says.

About twenty years ago the Ruthenians began to come into the district for which I am now the sitting member. At that time there was about a township and a half immediately south of the southwest corner of the Riding Mountain Reserve which was wild land heavily wooded and hilly, with a ravine separating it on the east side from the English settlement. It lies about fifteen mile3 from the town of Neepawa. These people came in and took up that section of the country. They have now about 60 per cent of it clear and about 25 to 30 per cent under cultivation, and they have been there from fifteen to twenty years. I have had a great deal to do with these people generally. They do not attempt to cultivate a whole quarter-section of land, but as a rule divide it into smaller areas, 40 or 50 acres, and as you go along the roads in one of their districts it is much like one of the river settlements in the West, a continuous village. The houses generally are built of logs, very neatly plastered-which work the women generally do-and are a story and a half high, roofed with shingles, or even thatched. The farm buildings are of log, and they are generally thatched with straw The people start out clearing a very small bit of land for a garden or a small field, and the men go into the harvest fields every season for labour, and this has been the source of our labour in the West. The older men who are grown up when they

come, except those who have been out in employment hired by the year, very seldom get any command of the English language, and I regret to say that very few of the children have any knowledge of English. It will be understood that, due to political conditions into which I need not enter now, prior to 1915 in the province of Manitoba we had an abominable abuse of the bilingual situation which was first created in 1897.
Owing to that, the Government there permitted young Kuthenians to go to the Normal school, obtain certificates as teachers, and then go into schools to instruct the pupils. There was a stipulation, or a regulation, that these men should be able to speak English. I will tell you how far they were able to speak English. I have had three of these teachers at different times come into my office to do business, and they have had to go out and get an interpreter in order to talk to me. Yet, from a source like that, we were expected to get teachers who would have some command of the English language. That was the situation down to 1915. I, with many others who were interested in politics, I suppose, was to blame for having got these people naturalized as speedily as possible. I have paid $30, or $50, at a time for naturalization papers for them, and I suppose half of them knew practically nothing about the political "situation. But we were all doing it and it had become a common practice in the West.
Sometimes we talk of these people being put into settlements and segregated. I do not know just how you are going to deal with that situation. A number of these people come in, they get their friends from the Old Country to come, and they buy land in a neighbourhood. <The English-speaking people in that settlement get out, and for a very sufficient reason. In a settlement like that there are not too many people at any time to support a church organization or the social activities of the community. When people have different ideals and different languages there are not enough of them in a district to support those institutions, and the English-speaking people quite naturally * get out. Besides that we find that we have a difficulty in regard to English-speaking schools. The Englishspeaking people find that with teachers such as they have, their own children are not getting proper instruction in English. Ih consequence, you have this segregation. You are going to have segregation as long as you are getting in these foreigners in large numbers. This will repeat itself despite almost any regulations Parliament may make. As
a consequence of what I have told you, we have very few children of these people who are able to read and speak English with any fluency whatever.
What would you do to meet that situation?
I have outlined to you the development and history of a typical community. There are hundreds-yes, thousands-of these scattered over our great West. The deduction I draw from that situation-and which I think any sensible man will draw - is that we cannot continue bringing in these people, increasing the area of such settlements and not only the area of the settlements which have begun but increasing the number of them. We have to call a halt until we have assimilated that population which is now out of hand largely owing to the mistakes we have made in the past. It is we who have sinned rather than they.
I wish to say >a word or two for them. I know that many of these people have been willing in the past to enlist. They have been willing to do service according to their light, and they have in some cases contributed. But they have also committed errors. The accusation has been made, and,
I think, in some cases rightfully, that when there were victories by the enemy they put up their flags and celebrated. They have not been Anglicized and they are not British citizens although they, in many cases, hold our naturalization certificates. We are very largely to blame. But the time has come now when we must check the further encroachment of this situation upon the opportunities and prospects of the Canadian West. If we do not do it the time will come when we shall not be able to control the situation.
You have seen in the province of Ontario 15,000 or 16,000 people every year going from your farms into the cities. The same movement was almost threatening before the war in the West. We found our English-speaking men going off the farms and into the cities. We saw a great many of them leaving the country. The consequence is that these people of whom I have been speaking are spreading very rapidly. There has been some evidence of that in my own district. They have been making money during these times. The constituency of my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Crerar) lies right west from mine and from the constituency which I now speak of clear across to the other side of the Riding Mountain reserve and almost to the western side of the constituency-that is on the north side of his constituency-there is a

population of a character similar to that of which I have spoken. These people have been making money and buying farms down in the English settlements. It is curious to note the encroachment there. It was a subject of remark in my town within the last year that a splendid quarter-section two miles north of the town and right in the heart of an English-speaking settlement was bought by Galicians. They have been buying first-class farms. In my district we have a rather hard piece of land contiguous to the railway and facilities for shipment, and yet, because of its rough character, the English settlers had avoided it. Tnese foreigners entered upon, that and they have made good. But farther west we have a settlement in the constituency of my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture which is better land. The settlers there made very rapid progress and many of them have farms which aie worth 315,000 to 320,000. They have their Hudson cars. They have been making money. But they have not become Anglicized. We have perhaps a more difficult situation to deal with now that they have money, are able to organize and have leaders amongst themselves than we would - have if they were poor and more or less helpless under our conditions.
I thought I should explain the situation to the Committee. There are many men in the East and, I think, some in the West, who have not been out through those districts as I have been. Time and again I have had occasion to go through these particular districts, and I thought it would be instructive to the Committee to understand the conditions of these districts industrially and in the way of settlement and also what has been the result of the effort to induce these people to become British subjects.

Just before we pass on I have a few remarks to make in regard to section 13. We have heard considerable discussion to-day in regard to the various classes of people who should be allowed to come into Canada, and it seems to be pretty generally agreed that great restrictions should he imposed upon future settlers, especially upon those from European countries. I have listened with pleasure to the remarks of the hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. Mac-kie) in regard to the Ukrainians and Ituth-enians, and also to the remarks of the hon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Davis) respecting the Ruthenians in his district, and despite the arguments of these hon, gentlemen I think we must conclude that the

people referred to are a class that we do not want to settle in this country. Both gentlemen have shown completely that although these people have remained in the Dominion for a great number of years, and although they have become iCanadianized to the extent that they have amassed considerable wealth, have acquired great areas of land, .and have purchased their automobiles, still they have not become Cana-dianized or Anglicized to the extent that they can become part and parcel of the social and economic life of this country. I believe, further, that there are a great many settlers in Canada hailing from European countries who are absolutely out of sympathy with Canada and with tne British Empire, and while these people may be naturalized and enjoy the benefits of our laws and the proteeti ;n of our institutions, I think we must bring them to a full realization that there cannot be granted in the future, as there has been in the past, any concessions by reason of any political affiliations. We have received petitions from many people in the West, since Parliament assembled, asking concessions in regard to, for one thing, the use of their language. W e have heard bitter complaints from many because the authorities have seen fit to deprive them of the use of the German language in their schools and in their press; but I do not believe that this Government, or any government in Canada, would be justified in allowing these people to conduct their commercial, social, religious, or educational life in the German language, or any medium which savours of that tongue, and in my opinion it is the duty of all governments, 'both federal and provincial, to see to it that that instrument of intercourse is curbed to Fhe greatest extent in this country. It is very difficult for me to believe, and doubtless it is equally difficult for any member of the House to-night to believe, when a man uses as a means of intercourse the German language, that he is not so closely allied with the German race and the German people that his sympathies are German. While we curb the people who are already in the country in that respect, we must use the greatest caution and care to see that Canada is not settled for a long time to come by any class of persons who use that tongue as a vehicle for communication. In view of the agitation which has recently arisen in the West in connection with the Hutterites and the Mennonites, it may appear to some eastern people that there is over-anxiety or over-excitement in that country in regard

to the matter. But we find that one of the things in connection with these people is that they have been brought up and taught to use the German language. They have been using it in South Dakota, and other parts of the United States, whence they come to our country. They now desire to use that language in Canada; they have been asking the privilege of carrying on their schools in the province of Alberta in the German language. Their sympathies are not -with Great Britain or with Canada, but are first with the German people and then with the Hutterites and Mennonites, who, in the true sense of the word, are Hutterites themselves. We do not want these .people in Canada at any time; and I trust that this Government will take immediate steps to prevent the entrance into Canada of any one single person of that class. Why do we not want them in this country? Some person will say they are good farmers, they can herd cattle, and their efforts will tend to the agricultural development of this great country and of Western Canada in particular. I admit that is perfectly true, 'but their social and economic status, their mental attitude and their ancestral affiliations are such that they can never become part and parcel of the true Canadian people. As" has been pointed out by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan) this afternoon, we find that they are in one sense, and a broad sense, communists. What does that mean? They have been driven from South Dakota by the operation of the laws of that state. Following the doctrine of Jacob Hutter, they formed their various societies, which they call religious denominations, and through their medium operated in the state of South Dakota. An investigation was conducted by the authorities, and it was found that they were carrying on trade and commerce under the guise of religion. The state authorities at once put the law in force and are now bringing actions to dissolve these organizations. But the difficulty with the organization, so far as our economic system is concerned, is that the individual in it has no rights. If there is anything upon which we pride ourselves in this country it is our individual liberty, our individual freedom, and the right to enjoy and to hold property. These Mennonites and Hutterites wlao are now coming into this country as individuals have no power to enjoy any such rights; the property which they acquire as the result of their industry and of their labour becomes the property of their association or organization. The women 123
toil, the men toil, but as a result of all that labour they are not the owners or the possessors of one dollar's worth of personal or real property-it all becomes the property of the organization. The result has been that in South Dakota, where actions are being brought in the courts for the dissolution of some of these organizations, we find there are men well on to fifty years of age. who have toiled all their lives for these organizations, who are now turned out- they have not a dollar. We find again another case in which a man left behind him two wives and fourteen or fifteen children who have been thrown upon the mercy of the public. We find that every man who disagrees with that organization is, if possible, kicked out into the street, and receives no share of the profits that have been accumulated. Hutterites and Mennonites, so- far as their organizations are concerned, are introducing into this Dominion the greatest possible form of bondage and slavery. It is a condition which is inimical to the best interests of our agricultural and our economic life, to the best interests of the individual, and to personal liberty.
Then if we turn from the economic side of the question, and consider it from a personal point of view, there is the character of their social life to be borne in mind. These people all live together. They live under conditions which are not suitable to our people, and which would not be tolerated by Canadian citizens. They live under conditions in which Canadians would not associate with them. They converse in the German language, they carry on their own trading amongst themselves, and they desire to have their own schools if the law will permit it.
Is this country to be benefited by that class of people? When they form their small colonies the English, Scotch or Canadian settlers round about them are gradually driven out because their form of life is inconsistent with ours and wholly incompatible with our customs and ideals. What we want is immediate action; we do not want one more Hutterite or Mennonite to cross the boundary from United States into Canada. The Government would be justified in passing an Order in Council under the War Measures Act dealing with this matter pending the operation of this proposed legislation. If this is not done there will be great unrest throughout Western Canada. Having excluded these people, the future policy of the Government should be to exclude from Canada all classes of people who have communistic ideas. Com-



munism as practised by people of certain European countries is incompatible with the economic and industrial life of Canada. One of the best sections in the Bill is that which places in the hands of the Government power to exclude from our country people whose ideas and notions are wholly inconsistent with ours.

As the minister knows, a head tax of $8 is irpposed by the Unitedi States Government upon Canadians visiting United States, the amount being refunded if the visitor returns within six months. The money is collected by the railway and steamboat companies, and sometimes it takes one, two or three months to get it back, even if the visitor remains in the United States only three or four days. Many Canadians who live near the border have relatives in the United States, and often illness or death in the family necessitates their making a trip to the American side. In many cases they can ill afford to deposit this head tax with the United States Government. The law is not aimed particularly at Canadians; it was originally intended to apply to entries at the ocean ports. Nevertheless, it affects our people. I am convinced that ninety per cent of the people of the United States have no knowledge of the law; it should be brought to their attention. The best way to do that would be to place a similar tax upon persons entering Canada from the United States, the amount to be refunded if the country whence they came accorded a similar privilege to Canadians. Is any progress being made in securing the removal of this head tax?

No progress has been made in the direction of having this head tax removed; that is a matter for the American Government, which may see fit to impose a head tax against any peoples entering their country. However, we have taken the matter up with the United States authorities; the head of their Immigration Department is here to-day and the officers of my department have had another opportunity of discussing the matter with him. The head tax is not imposed on all Canadians visiting the United States; it is imposed only in cases where the United States immigration officers think there is good reason to disbelieve the statements made by those who enter their country from Canada. From the negotiations that have been carried on, I think that this law will be administered a little more carefully than it has been in the past.

Section, as amended, agreed to.
On Section 2-domicile, etc.

A slight change might improve paragraph (vi) of Subsection 2. It reads:
Members of dramatic, artistic, athletic, or spectacular organizations entering Canada temporarily for the purpose of giving public performances or exhibitions of an entertaining or instructive nature and actors, artists, lecturers, priests and ministers of religion, authors, lawyers, physicians, professors of colleges and commercial travellers entering Canada for the temporary exercise of their respective callings.
I would suggest that it should read:
Members of dramatic, artistic, athletic or spectacular organizations entering Canada temporarily for the purpose of giving public performances or exhibitions of an entertaining or instructive nature and all persons entering Canada for the temporary exercise of their respective callings.
We have dealt with ministers, circus managers, lawyers and so on, but possibly we have left out some, and if we make the clause read in the way I suggest, we shall cover every occupation and calling.

We have left out one
class that was in the old clause, namely, musicians. Why that was omitted, I do not. understand.
Would the hon. member (Mr. Jacobs) suggest that persons whose business is spreading seditious utterances should be allowed to enter Canada?

If that is a calling, it
would be for the minister to use his discretion under section 38 of the Act. We are dealing here with a certain specified class of people, authors, lawyers, physicians, professors of colleges and commercial travellers, and so forth. That does not exhaust the entire list of occupations and callings, and to cover those which we may not have in mind at the moment, we might say " all persons entering Canada for the temporary exercise of their respective"-and if my hon. friend would wish it-and respectable callings." That might improve the matter.

The officials of the department have had a good deal of trouble in connection with the administration of this Act, and if we throw it wide open as the hon. member has suggested, it might lead us into serious trouble. I should, therefore, like to have a full discussion with the officials of the department before I would agree to his suggested amendment. As regards the inquiry from the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn), the term "musician" has been dropped from this sec-

tion mainly because we have a very large and excedingly troublesome class of strollers called musicians who we think should not be admitted under this section. The only way in which we can properly deal with . them is to exclude them from the provisions of this section.
If it is a profession?

If the musicians belong
to a dramatic, artistic or regular theatrical society that is coming in for the purpose of giving dramatic or musical performances, they are readily admitted, but the single musician who comes in can hardly in many cases be classed as an artist, and it would be just as well for us to watch him carefully.
What about Paderewski? He is a musician first.

The department would
class him as an artist, not as a musician.

Before the minister agrees to this amendment, I sincerely trust he will give very careful consideration to the possibility of an injustice being done in the border towns by 'the adoption of the suggestion of the hon. member (Mr. Jacobs).
I know that in the riding from which I come there has been considerable discontent owing to the fact that American orchestras have come in, alleging that they were dramatic companies, and have interfered a great deal with Canadian orchestras. There is a conflict, more or less acute, between the provisions of this Act and those of the Alien Labour Act, and I would be exceedingly sorry to see the provisions of this Act so widened that orchestras, which certainly would come within the language of the amendment suggested by the hon. member (Mr. Jacobs) would be admitted as not being considered an immigrant class. I trust the minister, before changing this clause, if he has any idea of so doing, will look carefully at the Alien Labour Act and see that the two Acts are made to harmonize.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Jacobs) presses his amendment, I will certainly ask that this portion of the section be allowed to stand until such time as I have an opportunity of looking into the side of the question mentioned by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle).

I would suggest that it be allowed to stand for the moment. Before the clause finally passes, I should like to say a word or two with regard to section 2, paragraph (ii), which at present reads:
Canadian domicile is lost, for the purposes of this Act, by a person voluntarily residing out of Canada not for a mere special or temporary purpose but with the present intention of making his permanent home out of Canada.
That is to say, a man may have come to Canada and become a British subject. He leaves Canada with the intention of residing elsewhere for the purpose of improving his position, and then he finds, if he has not improved his position and wishes to return, that he cannot return to Canada, although a British subject, because of this section which says that the domicile governs and he has changed his domicile.
I do not think that is quite fair.

I scarcely think that is the interpretation to put upon this clause. The purport of the proposed amendment is briefly this: If a person retains his Canadian domicile and he leaves Canada temporarily, when he attempts to enter Canada again, having retained his domicile, the provisions of the law against prohibited classes do not apply to him. Let us assume that a man has retained his Canadian domicile, and he goes to the United States and remains there for a short time. He contracts some loathsome disease, or tuberculosis, or he becomes insane. We cannot shut him out from Canada as long as he has retained his domicile. But if he leaves the country with the intention of leaving the country, and he loses his domicile, then we have the right to shut him out.
Even although he be a British subject?

Yes. We shut out people from Great Britain noiw if they belong to the prohibited classes. For instance, we shut out any one from Great Britain if he is of unsound mind, or if he is liable to become a public charge, or if he belongs in any way to any of the prohibited classes. If a man has come to this country from any part of the world and leaves this country with the intention of leaving the country, and during his residence outside of Canada he comes under any of those prohibited classes, why should we admit him?
Assuming that in every other respect he is qualified to come in?
There would be no question about his entering. He would have a perfect right to enter.

A distinction should be made between a British citizen and a citizen of another country. We ought to give some protection to the British citizen who

has shed his old citizenship and has acquired his British citizenship. He goes away to improve himself in business, and then he comes back and finds the doors are closed to him.
Only if he belongs to a prohibited class.
That is not so stated in the section.
That is the purport of it.

Suppose a man comes to Canada, becomes naturalized and has his domicile here, then goes to the United States with the intention of remaining there. Now, we could not shut him out within the prescribed time of his domicile if the United States immigration authorities wanted to deport him on account of insanity.
If they deport him, we must accept him.
It does not make any difference whether he is in a prohibited class under our law. If he has his domicile here they can ship him back.

I see no provision in subsection 2 for the admission of farm hands or harvesters. In recent years the farmers of the Vvestern Provinces have been very glad to get harvest help from the Western States. The harvesters work in the fields of Kansas, move on to the Dakotas, and then come to Canada. Apparently they would not be admitted under this Act.

If there is any defect in the law in that respect it certainly has not been used against these people during the last ten years, for they have been coming in every year. The department itself has been responsible for bringing them in to help in the harvest fields. There is now a provision in the law whereby the minister may admit any person for any cause if he deems it advisable. I do not anticipate any difficulty over the harvesters.
Perhaps they will be admitted as members of athletic organizations.
How will paragraph (a) read as amended?

With this amendment the law will read as follows:
Persons afflicted with tuberculosis in any form or with any loathsome disease or with a disease which is contagious or infectious or which may be dangerous to the public health. . . .

What would happen in
the case of a person, not a naturalized British subject, who contracted tuberculosis in Canada, and, having been to Denver for treatment, attempted -to come back to Canada?

I think he could easily
establish that he went to Denver purely for a temporary purpose. He could apply to the consular agent, if necessary, for a certificate to the effect that he went to Denver for the purpose of a cure. He would not lose his domicile.

The law is being very well administered by the department. I think the Department of Immigration is handled with more intelligence perhaps, than any other department of the "Government; at least, that has been my experience. The Minister of Agriculture looks surprised. I think it would be well for us to make the Bill as clear as possible, because even ministers of the Crown sometimes change, and a king may arise who knows not Joseph, and who would apply the law more rigorously than at present. Many of these sections are satisfactory if handled intelligently, but I think eases of very grave hardship might arise if they were interpreted by a department not sympathetic to the immigrant.

Subsection agreed to.	*
On subsection 5-beggars and vagrants:

The law at present reads as follows:
Professional beggars or vagrants or persons likely to become a public charge.
The phrase " or persons likely to become a public charge " is transferred to another part of the Act, and is put in a substantive section reading as follows:
Persons who in the opinion of the board of inquiry or the officer In charge at any port of entry are likely to become a public sharge.
On subsection 6, paragraph (k)-psychopathic inferiority:
What is meant by "constitutional psychopatic inferiority"?

Can we deport those in Canada suffering from this disease?
Mr. CALDER. Yes, if they get in.
(a) Enemy aliens.

I think the Committee
would like to have from the minister a clear interpretation of the meaning of this section.

I must admit that when
I first looked at the section I took a wrong meaning from it myself, but if it is read carefully the meaning will be clear. One would suppose that the mere mention of enemy aliens in the first line would indicate that hereafter all persons who are enemy aliens are to be rejected. That is not the purpose of this clause. The clause says: " Enemy aliens or persons who have been alien enemies." Once the peace treaty is signed, those people who are now interned and who will not be deported until after the war is over will not then be alien enemies, because the war will be at an end. So that the section as I interpret it is this:	Enemy aliens who have been
interned or persons who have been alien enemies who have been interned. That is, it does not mean that enemy aliens shall be prohibited, but enemy aliens who have been interned.

Would it not be better
to strike out the words " or persons " and say " enemy aliens who have been interned in any part of His Majesty's Dominions"?

But some of them may
be interned after the war is over and they will not then be enemy aliens.

I must confess that the
section appears to me to be rather obscure and I think it would stand re-drafting. For that purpose I would suggest that it be allowed to stand.
What will happen to those-who are enemy aliens who have been interned and have been let out on parole?

I did not know that any were let out on parole.
Mr. CROiNYN: I am told that there are many hundreds.

As was explained by the Acting Minister of Justice, in the early part of the war some thousands were interned, not because they were dangerous or had committed any overt act of any kind, and not because of disloyalty, but. simply on account of conditions existing at that time. At that period employment was very scarce and many of
10 p.m. these people were interned merely to take care of them. To provide that these people shall be deported simply because they happened to have been interned in the early part of the war would be a great mistake.
I do not think it would do any harm to make the clause comprehensive enough to cover all those who. should be dealt with.
I think we might let the clause stand. I am not quite satisfied with the drafting of it, and possibly its intention might be made just a little clearer.
Does this clause refer only to those who have been interned, or also to possible immigrants after the war?
This refers only to those who were interned.
Is it the intention of the Government after the war to debar absolutely those who are now alien enemies?

They are now debarred and have been ever since the armistice. An Order in Council has been put through debarring all persons who are nationals of Germany, Austria-Hungary, Turkey and Bulgaria, and it is certainly the intention to keep that Order in Council in force for some time.

I am not raising any objection to that. I am merely asking for information. I have not Hansard before me, but I have a copy of the Globe of to-day in which the minister is quoted as saying

that there was no provision in the law to -debar alien enemies.
Section 13, which we were -considering all afternoon, gives the Governor in Council power to prohibit the entry of people of any nationality or race.
I missed that, and would have liked to make a suggestion when section 13 was under discussion. Would it be in order for me to make a suggestion now?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It would be out of order to discuss section 13 now. Paragraph (p) of section 3 is being discussed.
Will there be another opportunity?
ilf the hon. gentleman merely has a suggestion to make, I think we might hear it, Mr. Chairman.
If the law is absolutely prohibitive without any discretion on the part of the minister or the Government, it should be changed. There should be some provision for the minister to make exceptions.

There is a provision in the Bill whereby the minister may, under permit, allow any person to enter Canada. I explained that this afternoon. In addition to that, in the Order in Council which we put through, there is express provision for the minister to admit any of them. There are very exceptional cases arising that must be dealt with on humanitarian *and other grounds.

In view of the uncertainty *as to the application of this clause and the fact that there is already an Order in Council dealing with the matter which the Government intend to keep in force, would it not be wise to delete this section altogether?

Clause (p) deals waith persons of enemy nationality who have been interned in any portion of His Majesty's dominions.
Mr, JACOBS: Or in any Allied country.

Or in any Allied country. Persons who were interned in the United States or in any of His Majesty's dominions are shut out as being of the prohibited classes who have no right to enter Canada; whereas our general order applies only to persons who are living in enemy countries.
What does the minister intend to do with the interned alien enemies in Canada? Are they to be deported?

An announcement has already been made to the House on two or three occasions by the Acting Minister of Justice to the effect that all those aliens now interned who are thought dangerous or undesirable will be deported. An arrangement has already been made by the British authorities whereby a hundred will be deported-if they have not already been deported-just so soon as shipping can be arranged and the countries to which they belong are open for their entry.
So that we will deport 2,117, the number of interned aliens during the war.
No; there were 8,000 or 9,000.
The return brought down by the Minister of the Interior the other day stated that there were 2,117.
That is the number now in the internment camps, but during the war there were about 8,000.
Then the Minister of the Interior misunderstood my question because I wanted to know the actual number interned during the war. I was told that it was 2,117.
The others were out at that time.
As I understand the minister it is only the intention to deport those that are regarded as dangerous? (He does not purpose deporting all aliens who have been interned?

I think the fact that those spoken of by the Acting Minister of Justice are still interned, after some three or four years of war, is an indication that there is a very good reason for keeping them there. If I am not mistaken, the great bulk of those, unless some very good reason can be shown, will be returned to their own countries.

Many of them were sent to farms and made to act as farm help and others were put on railway construction. They were under the supervision of the Government but they were not actually interned in the sense in which we understand internment.
I do not know that.

Many of them were employed on public works. I do not know about the 2,100 you have now. Certainly many of them were interned and then afterwards

employed. What are you going to do about them?
Do you mean those who were interned during the war?
Yes.

There has been a large internment camp in North Ontario. At one time there were 2,000 interned aliens in one camp. But they have been weeded out. Those that were considered not dangerous and not regarded as a class that it was necessary to intern, were allowed out. Those who are still in camp are men of a dangerous type who could not be safely permitted to run at large.
That is what I have been trying to find out.

We have in Northern Ontario many hundreds of men who were interned in the early days of the war, but who after a careful investigation by the officers of the Militia Department, weTe found to be perfectly harmless. They were allowed out. But they are still reporting month by month. There are several hundred still interned who are recognized as dangerous enemies.

Some people were considered at the outbreak of hostilities as being alien enemies who have since become our Allies. What will the Government do in connection with these people? For instance, Germans who were living in German Poland were enemies and now not only are they not our enemies, but they have become our Allies, and I see by the papers they are going to sign the covenant of the League of Nations with Canada, Great Britain and other allied countries. Is there any provision made in this Bill for this class of people?

The Order in. Council to
which I have referred excludes all people from enemy countries; that means Austria, Germany, Bulgaria and Turkey. It is quite true that, particularly in Austria, there are some of the people-Poles, Czecho-Slovaks and Jugo-Slavs-who were more or less opposed to the Austrian Government, and new nations are going to be set up under, I presume, a democratic form of government. But until these conditions are settled and we know where we are we feel that this prohibition should be maintained against ' people residing in that part of Europe. If I followed the discussion this afternoon, it is evident that there is a feeling in this House
and in the country that, with conditions as they exist in Canada at the present time, during the reconstruction period, we have pretty nearly all on our hands that we can take care of without inviting people from these portions of Europe whether they are friendly or not.

Under this Bill, will the Government be in a position to consider these people as living in these countries according to the boundaries as they existed at the time of the war, or according to the boundaries as they will be limited and defined at the Treaty of Peace? That is a very important question.

Under section 13 the Government is left free to consider this question from any standpoint it chooses. That section gives the Government very large powers. The Government is empowered at any time to prohibit the entry of any class or section of people or people of any occupation and coming from any country. So that we will be able to deal with the people of such areas from time to time according to the conditions as they prevail.

If Poland is set up as a new kingdom, if that kingdom is friendly to Great Britain and the Dominions over the seas, and if it signs the Treaty of Peace and the different covenants that are going to be entered into at Paris as an Ally friendly to this country, will the Government, aocording to international law, be allowed to treat the inhabitants of that country as enemy aliens now or later, or as a people who cannot enter Canada, or will they be justified in so doing?

We would not treat them as alien enemies at all. If the hon. gentleman had been in the House and had heard the discussion, that has taken place he would have learned that the members of the House and the people have come to the conclusion that in so far as the admission of any people to Canada is concerned, we should have the right to determine that for ourselves. There is nothing in international law that I know of that would prevent us from exercising that right. But while we exercise that right of determining for ourselves what people shall enter Canada, we must be prepared to bear the consequences of the exercise of that right.
That is, if we say to the people of any nation, " Your citizens shall not enter Canada," we must remember that that nation has the power to take action against us, in some other direction it may be, and we

must be prepared to suffer those consequences no matter what they are, so long as the action upon which it is based is within international law. Again I say, I think the hon. gentleman is mistaken in holding that there is anything in international law to prevent us from making a prohibition against any class of people, the world around, whom we do not wish to enter Canada.

Reference has been made on one or two occasions to what happened at the Imperial Conference in 1918, and it might be well to place upon record the actual resolution that was unanimously passed at that time. The Imperial authorities, of course, were represented at that conference, and representatives from the Dominions. as well as from India, were there as well. This is the first clause of the resolution which was introduced in 1917, and passed in 1918:
It is an inherent function of the Governments of the several communities of the British Commonwealth, including India, that each should enjoy complete control of the composition of its own population iby means of restriction on immigration from any of the other communities.
That does not, of course, deal with foreign nations, but it is, I submit, a very admirable precedent on which we can act in dealing with nations outside of the British Commonwealth.

That is as between the
British Colonies?
Paragraph (p) allowed to stand.
On paragraph (q)-persons guilty of espionage with respect to His Majesty or any of His Majesty's Allies:

What is the object of that at this time? As I understand, when the war is over, espionage automatically stops, it is no longer in force. This is liable to give rise to a great deal of misconception, and perhaps considerable activity sometimes on the part of the Government.

The paragraph, as I understand it, simply means that any person who has been, found guilty of espionage during the war, or at any time should be placed in the prohibited class and not allowed to enter Canada.
Espionage in what respect?

I am presuming, of
course * the expression has a well defined legal meaning.
[iMr. Oaldor. ]
It has a well defined meaning in time of war, and has probably a different meaning in time of peace.

Paragraph agreed to.
On Paragraph (r)

Persons guilty of
conspiracy against His Majesty or any of His Majesty's Allies, or guilty of assisting His Majesty's enemies.

What is understood by
"persons found guilty of conspiracy"? Does it mean that he be found guilty by a court of justice, or deemed guilty by the department?
No, he must be found guilty by a court.

I think it would be well to make the meaning clear by amending the paragraph so as to read:
Persons found guilty in any competent court of justiceand so on,
-against His Majesty.
The paragraph does not say that the man is "presumed guilty," but that he be "guilty."
Found guilty by whom? A person may be guilty and yet not be found guilty.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Under our law a man is always presumed to be innocent until he is found to be guilty.
This is a different case. This is a statutory enactment, and I think it is well to be as clear as possible in framing the language.
How would the word "convicted" do?
"Convicted of conspiracy" would be better.
Instead of "guilty"?

Is there such a crime as "conspiracy against His Majesty"? I presume that conspiracy against His Majesty would be sedition and treason. It would be well to have a definition, because I do not remember such a crime in the Criminal Code as "conspiracy against His Majesty."

The drafting was done by our law counsel, and I presume he has used the proper legal phraseology in describing these crimes. However, if hon. gentlemen think there is any question about it, I will have the matter referred to him again.
Suppose we let the paragraph stand?
What is declared here is that a person must be guilty of the crime of conspiracy. If conspiracy constitutes treason, then he is guilty of treason.
I do not think there is such a crime as conspiracy against His Majesty defined in the Criminal Code. As far as I know that is treason and should be defined as such.

To save time and discussion, if there is any question about the matter, because I want to get the wording right, I am quite prepared to let this paragraph stand in order that we may have an opportunity to look into the question of the appropriateness of the phraseology used.
Paragraph allowed to stand.
On paragraph (s) Deported conspirators.
That ought to-stand also.

I do not know how we are going to conclude the consideration of this Bill if everything is to stand on an objection raised by the hon. member. As I understand the meaning of "conspiracy" no one person can be guilty of it. It is a crime entirely different from sedition. One man may be guilty of sedition, but one man cannot be guilty of conspiracy, two men may conspire, and although their object may not je attained, one or both of them may be found guilty of conspiracy. I am sure the hon. member will understand that is the law.
That is the very reason why I asked that this paragraph should etand, so that we might have a chance to straighten out the difficulty.
I do not see any difficulty at all. It is so plain to the average lawyer that there should be no argument upon it.

For example, the paragraph in question reads:
Persons who at any time within a period of ten years from the first day of August, one thousand nine hundred and fourteen, were or may be deported from any part of His Majesty's dominions or from any allied country on account of conspiracy against His Majesty or of any of His Majesty's allies, or for assisting His Majesty's enemies or because such persons were regarded as hostile or dangerous to the allied cause during the war.
By -whom were they regarded as hostile or dangerous?
By the parties who deported them.
It is not so stated. We ought to be particular in a matter of this kind.

The clause we are considering only refers to persons who have been deported. Those persons would be deported oy the state within which they were interned, and the authorities of that state must have regarded them as hostile or dangerous, otherwise it would not have deported them. Take the case of persons interned in Canada to-day. Some person must decide whether they shall be deported or not. Eventually they will be deported, and this prohibition will prevent those people from again entering Canada. Now, we will assume that there are certain persons interned in the United States, who will be deported because the authorities there regard them as hostile or dangerous to the Allied cause. The paragraph in that case obviously refers' to the authorities who do the deporting. We can take it for granted that if the governments in allied countries have thought it advisable to deport these people we should not admit them to Canada.

To return to my objection of a few moments ago, I am quite convinced there is no such crime as conspiracy, and I therefore raised the question in order to make the matter clear. I understand, in reply to the question raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs), the minister said that the person to be refused admission must be convicted of the crime of conspiracy. But if there is no such crime, and you cannot indict a man for conspiracy, I do not see how in the world you are going to prevent him from entering Canada.
Conspiracy is an agreement between two or more persons to commit an unlawful act.
If there is no such thing as conspiracy, no one will be affected by this clause; so why bother your head with objections?

I have a great deal of respect for the good name of the House, for the Minister of Immigration, and for the officers of the Department of Justice, and I would hate to see things that are of absolutely no use put into our statutes. This crime should be defined; we should ascertain exactly what offence will render a man liable to exclusion from the country under this provision.
Why should we, in this Act, define crime ot conspiracy in this country when the clause has reference to conspiracy in some other country?
Conspiracy in His Majesty's Dominions.
If certain countries do not know better than to have such a thing as conspiracy and a law against it, persons convicted under that law should not enter Canada.

I am perfectly willing to let it go through, because we may be called upon in our legal capacity to interpret the law for the benefit of the Government or of others, and in that way make a handsome fee.
If two men conspire to commit sedition, that is conspiracy.
Conspire to do any unlawful act.
To commit the crime of conspiracy against His Majesty; to be guilty of sedition or treason. The provision is quite plain.
Conspiracy is not a crime, but conspiracy to commit treason is.

This is simply a category of prohibited classes; the officials of the Immigration Department will interpret these definitions. There will be no recourse against them if they decide, on the information that they have, that a person who has teen engaged in a conspiracy in some other country is not a fit person to be admitted to Canada. I do not see how the hon. member (Mr. Jacobs) can get any law case out of that. If a person is refused admission to Canada he cannot sue the Government to secure permission to be allowed to come into the country.
Yes, he can; I have done it myself. We take out a habeas corpus and bring the party before the court, sometimes with splendid success.

The clause would cover the case if it was made to read: "Conspiracy to commit any crime against His Majesty." Hon. gentlemen will search Section 74 of the Criminal Code, which enumerates all crimes against His Majesty, in vain for any such crime as conspiracy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is a kind of conspiracy -conspiracy against His Majesty.

The Government wishes to keep out of the country any man who

has committed an offence against His Majesty; that is all right. But the clause should be correctly drawn. There is no such crime in our law as conspiracy, but there is a crime called "conspiracy to commit an unlawful act."

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Would you want to exclude a man who had conspired other than against the Crown?
No, I would say: "Conspiracy to commit any crime or offence against His Majesty."

I see no objection, in order to make these provisions perfectly clear, to adopting the suggestion that has been made. I move that the words "to commit any offence or crime" be inserted after the word "conspiracy" in paragraphs (r) and (s).

If we are going to limit this provision to conspiracy to commit a crime, we should include in the definition the words set out in the Criminal Code, in which are enumerated certain things which constitute a crime against His Majesty. 'But under the section as it stands it is possible to exclude from this country people whom we could not exclude if we confined the section to the literal meaning of the Criminal Code. An offence committed against a Sovereign in a foreign country might not constitute a crime under our Criminal Code; yet persons guilty of such offences in other countries might conspire to commit the same offences against our Sovereign. A man who commits what is a crime in his own country and under his own law is a very undesirable man to have in Canada, because he may conspire to commit that which is a crime under our Criminal Code. I submit that the wording of the section is better as it is, because they may conspire beyond the jurisdiction of the Dominion of Canada against our Sovereign, in a manner which does not constitute a crime, and consequently we could not exclude them, because we have this interpreted by the words of the Criminal Code. The section is better as it stands. It gives wider jurisdiction to the immigration officers; it gives them power to exclude people from other countries who conspire against His Majesty, but who do not commit an offence under the Criminal Code.

This clause applies only to people who have been deported within ten years from Great Britain or a British colony or an allied country. Great Britain and the British colonies have all the same

law as we have, that is the English criminal law, so that there cannot be any mistake as to that. If we are going to draft our statutes now to meet the Italian or the French or the Montenegrin or the Bosnian or the Grecian law, how far will we go? For instance, I understand that in Italy treason goes far further than it does in Great Britain or in Canada, and acts that are in no way criminal in this country or in Great Britain are considered in Italy to be highly criminal. Are we going to load our statutes with clauses to meet foreign laws? That would be an altogether new and very dangerous departure. When we are called upon to enact legislation in this Parliament, we enact it according to conditions existing in this country and to traditions given to us by the English tribunals. I am satisfied with the English law and with the fair play that exists in England, and I do not want to have in Canada laws that would be drafted to meet conditions existing in Italy or Greece or Montenegro, where people are put in jail for hardly anything. The hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Tweedie) says the Act might be a crime in those countries. Is he sure of what is conspiracy against His Majesty in Montenegro? Does he know anything about the law in Greece, or in Italy? I do not, and I do not claim to . know. I know the British law and I am satisfied with it, and I want our law to be the same as the English law. We shall be better 'satisfied if we stick to it than if we have adaptations from Italian or Greek legislation.

My hon. friend takes this position then, that some person in Italy who was regarded by the authorities in charge of the administration and welfare of that country as unfit to remain there, is fit to remain in Canada?

Yes, otherwise, Garibaldi would never have been allowed to enter England, and Garibaldi was the saviour and founder of United Italy. And some of the leading Italian patriots would never have been allowed to enter England, for instance, Giuseppe Mazzini. The leading revolutionists of the past were deported from their countries and they sought refuge on the free soil of England and America where they were well received. Therefore, if we were to pass a law such as this, and if at some future time the laws of a foreign country are such that freedom is no longer enjoyed, are we to be debarred from receiving men of the stamp that I have mentioned? I do not think we should be.

On looking at section 74 of the Code quoted by the hon member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon), I notice how closely the clause in question reads to the wording of the Criminal Code which the hon. member says does not contain this sort of crime. Subsection (e) of section 74 provides against:
Conspiring with any person to kill His Majesty or to do him any bodily harm tending to death or destruction, maiming or wounding, or conspiring with any person to imprison or restrain him.
A little further down, subsection (g) probably brings it closer to the intent of this Bill:
Conspiring to levy war against His Majesty with any such intent or any such purpose as aforesaid.
So that, in this respect, the Code clearly and distinctly recognizes conspiracy against His Majesty in the very words of this Act as a crime.
Conspiracy, to do something against His Majesty.

I am sure we have all but the one desire, and that is to have the Bill perfectly clear. From the discussion we have had, I can take the matter up with the law officers of the Crown and have them inquire into the point which has been raised, and if necessary I will bring back re-drafted clauses to the House.

[DOT] I would suggest that the insertion of one word would meet the objections raised by hon. gentlemen opposite, and I think it would be an improvement upon the amendment proposed by the minister if the clause were to read:
Persons guilty of ' criminal ' conspiracy against His Majesty.
Then it is a crime, and the crime is defined.
Every conspiracy is a criminal conspiracy.

One might conspire to see that His Majesty gets a good brand of cigars or whisky. I fancy the hon. gentleman would agree that was not a crime; but if he says "criminal" conspiracy, then I suppose crime is defined by the Code.
The hon. member knows the proverb, "Sutor, ne supra crepidam."

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The clause is quite plain. It says "conspiring against His Majesty."
Amendment stands.
Clause as amended stands.

On section 3, subsection (6), paragraph ( t)-illiterates:

This is a clause about
which I had occasion to make a few observations yesterday. I feel sure that the minister could not have given much attention to it, because, if he had, I am positive his sense of justice and fair play would have caused him to pause and consider before he submitted to the House the section as it is. I do not purpose going into the matter any further now, but merely wish to add that a clause of this kind cannot appeal to the good sense of justice and equity of this Committee. It is not right that a person who, through no fault of his own, but only through misfortune is unable to read, should be debarred entry into this country. If this had been done in the past we should have kept out of this country many people who have come here and made good and became assets to the community.

And many that
we would be glad to be rid of now.

I think if we were to make a list of those we want to get rid of, we should find in the list more people who can read and write than who cannot. I pointed out yesterday that this test would exclude people not only from Europe proper, or what we are pleased to call the better parts of Europe, but immigrants from the British Isles in large numbers. In the remote portions of the British Isles there are many people to-day who have not had the advantage and blessing of being taught to read, and yet these people would make splendid material for this new country.
Where are those remote portions of the British Isles?

I would say the Hebrides, the Orkney Islands, the Isle of Skye, and places of that kind where people earn their living from five or six years of age in fishing and mining, and consequently have not the time to learn to read; they have neither the opportunity nor the schools if they want to improve their condition. Now these are the very people who might want to come here to improve their condition, and are we to bar them out simply because they have not been taught to read? I have no doubt that this clause was inserted with the best of intentions, but I very much fear that it will not have the result the Government expect. We want to keep out undesirable classeis, and page after page is devoted to describing these undesirable classes. Surely a man who is un-
able to read, if he has no other disqualifications, ought not to be debarred from entering this country. I appeal to the minister to strike this clause out entirely. I should like to have an expression of opinion from the House on this matter, as I am confident the majority of hon. gentlemen are opposed to the inclusion of a provision which would be a blot upon a statute which is in many other respects very good.
iMr. A. E. FINLEY (Souris):	II think
this is a very important section, because it is a very well recognized fact that illiteracy and crime have always been very closely allied. I received a letter a day or two ago from a statesman who has given a great deal of thought and attention to this very subject, which I should like to read:
As the subject of immigration will come before the House shortly, I wish to bring to your serious attention some considerations of great and vital importance to our national welfare.
The policy which has obtained during the past, of establishing communities in special colonies, and- of granting special privileges to various sects and communities, has proved most unsatisfactory from the point of view of our Canadian national life; it is highly desirable that no special privilege should be given to any individual or community in the future, and steps should be taken to limit, -and if possible, terminate, the arrangements that have previously been entered into.
The request by any community or individual for special concessions, such as exemption from military service, is a clear indication that these people do not wish to accept the general laws and institutions of this country, that they do not intend to become Canadian in spirit, -but wish to retain their own institutions and customs. Their presence gives rise to many difficult problems in our community life, affecting municipal, social and especially school affairs.
The history of these settlements is that their proximity is resented by the neighbouring settlers, who finding it impossible to mend matters, sell out their holdings to the newcomers, sometimes at considerable sacrifice and move elsewhere. Thus the truly Canadian citizen is driven from his home; thus the colony spreads in extent and influence to the detriment and ultimate extinction of the true Canadian community.
Last year a colony of Hutterites was established in Manitoba, thirty-five miles west of Winnipeg. They left Dakota to escape from the obligation of military service. Already the selling out process has begun in this neighbourhood.
I am reliably informed of negotiations nearing completion for settlement of two similar colonies at other points in this province. Steps should be taken to prevent at once the entrance of any such, pending the passing of any necessary legislation. A definite and decisive policy should be adopted to exclude as undesirable immigrants, all persons or communities who will not accept unreservedly, all duties, burdens and responsibilities of citizenship or residence in Canada.

This could be acpomplished by requiring of each prospective immigrant before his entry into Canada, a sworn statement that he is prepared to accept all responsibilities of citizenship in Canada, including military service if necessary.
