This letter was written by the Hon. Dr. Thornton, Minister of Education in Manitoba, who has studied this question very thoroughly indeed. In that province we have some thirty odd different nationalities, with whom Dr. Thornton has come in very close contact. I thought the letter was worth putting on record.

I sincerely hope the minister will not consider altering or in any way amending this section. It is of the greatest importance that it should form part of our law, more particularly as it has been the law of the United States since 1917. If we do not follow their example, the ineviable result wijl be a larger percentage of illiterates seeking entrance into Canada. The hon. member for George Etienne Cartier asked what warrant the minister had for including suoh a proviso. I do not know that there was any warrant, if such were needed, but I am quite certain that if the minister and the department have taken cognizance, as I am sure they have, of what has happened in the neighbouring republic they could not help being impressed with the need of a section of this kind. I am not instancing what has been done in the United States as something that we must of necessity follow, but because it is evidence of a striking nature. Their experience in immigration has been on a very much larger scale than our own and has extended over a longer series of years.
What is termed the literacy test has been the subject of nineteen votes in the Congress and Senate of the United States, every one of which favoured it. Three times a law to this end passed by both Houses was vetoed by three different Presidents, and in each case either the House or the Senate failed by a narrow margin to overcome that veto. But in 1917 the literacy test was included in the law of the United States and has been in effect since that time.
All of the nine members but one of the Commission on Immigration, which, as I said yesterday, sat for four years and most exhaustively studied the whole subject, recommended the imposition of the reading and writing test " as the most feasible single method of restricting undesirable immigration." Of course, we know the inability to read very often arises from lack of opportunity, and neither this test nor any other that may be devised can prevent some undesirable immigrants from entering, whereas, on the other hand, it may possibly prevent a desirable immigrant from coming to Canada. The classic case of Lincoln has been quoted on the other side of the line until it is threadbare. It really does not touch the subject. We are dealing with a mass of figures and a vast volume of immigration, and, in my opinion, this test is one of the most valuable we could have.

I just wish to say a word in regard to this section and in reply to the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs). He made the statement that in the remote parts of the British Isles the people could neither read nor write. I am sorry that he made that statement. I have lived in some of the remote parts of the British Isles and I presume I know just as much about the subject as the hon. member does. I did not know in the Orkney Isles, at the time I lived there quite a few years ago, any one person of my own age who could neither read nor write. They have the finest public schools I know of in the British Empire. They have compulsory education and truancy officers who see that the children go to school. I cannot speak with any great authority in regard to the Hebrides or the Isle of Skye, but I do not know that I have met a Highlander who could not only speak the English language, but could also speak the two tacks. I hope that this clause will be accepted in its entirety. Canada to-day does not need to go begging for a second or third class immigrants. We want the very best immigrants who can at least read and write in theii own language.

The most important part of this clause I think is the provision that those who cannot read the Eng-
11 p.m. lish or the French language, or some other dialect shall not be admitted into our country. If the clause simply restricted the class to those who could not read English or French I would support it, because it would mean that no one would be admitted who could not read one of the official languages and who would therefore be unable to become a true Canadian. The clause goes too far by including "some other language or dialect." Suppose a man comes from the remotest part of Russia and knows a dialect which is spoken by say five hundred people. He would have a right to be admitted and the Government could not exclude him. He could ask for a printed paper in his dialect and if he could read it would certainly have the right to be admitted. Would that tend to the advantage of Canada? Would you, Mr. Chairman, compare a Russian who was able to read a dialect spoken by five hundred people, with a clever and intelligent Irishman who, unfortunately, could not read English? Would it be contended for a moment that an Irishman who could not read or write English would not be as good a citizen as the Russian, and in all probability a very much better one?
Where would you get your immigration from?
If the qualification is only ability to read any language or dialect it is just as well to have no clause at all, because it is of no value.

I think it would meet the case if we took care not to exclude any from the British Isles or British countries.
I practise law and I know it is not an unfamiliar thing to have Old Countrymen who cannot sign their names come into my office, men of the finest type. You very seldom see this inability among the Scandinavian races. I think we should provide for the admission of British subjects.
We have had a fairly good day of it and I doubt very much if we would be able to agree upon this clause to-night. I suggest that the Committee rise and report progress.

Before that motion is put; can the minister give us a fair idea of how many dialects there are and how many officers he expects to have standing with slips in their hands to test the ability of these people to read-about 3,000 or 4,000?
I doubt very much whether you will find those dialects in the form of printed languages.
I think the clause is unworkable.

He has to provide for agents to meet thousands of different kinds of people that come in. It is not very easy to find or to apply them. In Great Britain a oommittee of lawyers of the British House of Commons was appointed to consider English law upon the subject,. and in the United States a similar committee performed like duties there. The result in the United States is that a new law has been passed by Congress. The law officers of the Department of Justice consider it doubtful whether the present sections of our Criminal Code adequately provide for all questions which might arise at this particular time, and it

Mr. H. M. MOWAT (Parkdale) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 82 to amend the Criminal Code (Electrocution).
Explain, please.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is to provide that the mechanism of capital punishment shall be made more in accordance with present day public opinion. The law now is that the condemned man shall be taken back to the local jail and, after a sufficient delay to enable him to make peace with his Maker, that he shall be hanged by the neck until he is dead. The hanging is often inefficiently performed. The sheriff is the executive officer, but not being practised in such duties, he employs the public executioner, whose services are sometimes not available with the result that when a substitute is employed bungling has occurred. In the United States since 1889 execution by electric process has been well tested and has proved very efficient, the death sentence being carried out painlessly and instantaneously. A hundred years ago executions were public and they wrere made the occasions for wassailing and rioting by the people, but eventually with the advance of enlightenment these gruesome exhibi-124
tions have ceased and the sentence is now carried out in private. Those who are familiar with the Ingoldsby Legends will remember that my Lord Tomnoddy's appetite for sensation was so jaded that to revive his spirits his friends could suggest nothing better than an execution. This Bill provides that the execution shall not be in the local jail, as is now the practice, but it shall be in the nearest penitentiary of the province, the reason for that being that condemned men have made their escape from local prisons. Only this month in a certain city of the province of Ontario the death watch allowed communication between the condemned man and his paramour, and the convict escaped and is still at liberty. This Bill provides that a special room be set apart at each penitentiary for the purposes of the execution.
Is this a government measure?
No.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

On the Orders of the Day:

Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called I desire to bring to the attention of the Minister of Militia a matter of national importance. From the items in the public press and -the number of letters 
that come to my office and what I hear from other members, it is apparent that there is a great scarcity of farm help throughout Canada, and farmers are becoming restless for the return of their sons, some of whom are no<w in France, and some in England. I should like to know if the Militia Department cannot arrange a preference for the return of farmers' sons.
Major-General MEWBURN: This matter has, ever since demobilization commenced, been given most serious consideration. The British army attempted to work out a scheme of demobilization by pivotal or occupational groups, but immediately after the armistice that was found to be impracticable, and the British authorities had to abandon it immediately. It created great trouble and dissension in the army, and a great lack of discipline and a very bitter feeling throughout the whole corps. After a great deal of correspondence with the overseas minister and with the corps commander, it was found that giving priority of return to any individual or class created a very embarrassing situation and a great deal of trouble within the corps. It was, therefore, decided that it was found impossible to bring back any man in priority except on strictly compassionate grounds.
I have the utmost sympathy with members of Parliament who are and have been receiving applications from their constituents for the return of soldiers. Those applications, which have been forwarded to me, have been coming in in very large numbers ever since November, and I have endeavoured to the best of my ability to deal sympathetically with each case. On the 29th of January last I sent a circular notice to every member of Parliament and every senator, explaining the situation and pointing out what men could 'be brought back only on compassionate grounds, and that medical certificates had to be procured from the districts from whence the -men came.
As to demobilization in Canada, we met the situation and demobilized all men whose services were not urgently required, giving particular attention to that class.
As regards the corps, the men are being brought back as units, and I think the hon. member will readily understand, if in one unit one or two individual men are pulled out and brought back in priority to their comrades, the feelings of the rest of the men who are held back. Hundreds upon hundreds, in fact, thousands of applications have been received, not only from farmers, but from all classes for the return of relations and friends for whom posi-

tions are awaiting here. I spoke to many officers who came back and they all said that the giving of priority of return created a frightful situation, and that the only way to deal with the matter was to carry out (the policy that has been laid down and that is sound and workable. Demobilization is proceeding more rapidly than was expected; the strike at Liverpool is now over, and the whole of the troops will be coming (back at a very early date.
As regards individual men in England who are not with any of the units, they have been given priority 'in accordance with length of service, the married men being returned first.
Mr. WILLIAM D. EULER (North Waterloo) : Could not the Minister of Militia consider the discharge of all farmers who are very badly needed in Western Ontario and elsewhere, who are still held at militia headquarters in the various districts? I think there are still some at London, Ont., and possibly elsewhere. Could not an exception be made in those cases?
Major-General MEWBURN: We have already given that most careful consideration, and, as I have stated, as regards demobilization in Canada, we have released every man possible. It has been absolutely essential, in every military district in Canada, to keep the smallest staff possible to carry out demobilization, which is of much greater magnitude than many people realize. We have also found it necessary, for more reasons than one, to keep a very small garrison unit in each district. We have given priority, as I have stated, and in connection with that I sent out a circular giving these instructions:-
Certain Units of the Canadian Expeditionary Force must be maintained in a state of efficiency ; such as, Canadian Garrison Detachments, Canadian Medical Corps, Canadian Army Service Corps, and certain administrative units; 'but the personnel is being reduced as fast as possible, taking the following as a basis for priority of discharge.
Those who can be spared and who are desirous of discharge:
(a)	With overseas service.
That is, the men who have had actual overseas service are entitled to priority.
(b)	With dependents. This class will be determined by eligibility to receive separation allowance.
That is, married men have been next allowed to return.
(c)	In low medical category and unable to render fully efficient service.
(d)	In occupations required u for economic reasons as indicated by Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment.
These men will be released as speedily as possible. It was felt that some of these men who had not been overseas could afford to devote some time to cleaning up the enormous work of demobilization, but I have, in every instance that has been brought to my attention .tried to meet sympathetically every specific request of any hon, member and I shall try to do so as far as possible.

House again in Committee on Bill No. 52, to amend the Immigration Act, Mr. Boivin in the (Chair.
On section 3, subsection 6, paragraph (t) -illiterates:

I beg to move that this
paragraph be struck out of the Bill.
Amendment negatived; yeas 37, nays 75.

I would suggest that discretionary powers be given to the minister

to permit, in cases where he deems it advisable, the landing of such persons as are pientioned in this paragraph, so that it would not be necessary to have these cases brought before Council or dealt with in .some other way under the Act.

I wish to record my
dissent from this very unnecessary and unworkable innovation in the Act. It is absolutely impossible to carry out this test. There are thousands and thousands of different dialects in the countries from which we receive and expect to receive immigrants and it is proposed that slips containing between thirty and forty words in the dialect of the person attempting to enter shall be placed in the hands of our officials, who can neither read nor understand that dialect. If the immigrant can mumble over these thirty or forty words he is to be allowed to enter, althouth the official cannot tell whether he has read them correctly or not. The test, on the other hand, will debar the honest British subject, the stalwart healthy Scotsman, (Irishman, or Englishman, who would make a desirable citizen in every sense of the term simply because he is honest enough to say that he did not have the opportunity in his early days of being taught to read and write. I submit that that is not a test at all; it is not British; we have never had such a test before. An army of officials would be required to carry out this test, and when carried out, I submit that it would be absolutely no safeguard. I am quite willing that all reasonable precautions be taken to secure a desirable class of immigrants, but I submit that if a man is healthy, physically and mentally, and complies with all the other requirements of the Act, he should not be debarred simply because he did not have an opportunity in his youth of learning to read and write. I am very sorry the minister has thought it necessary to put this unworkable barrier in the Act.

The Committee will agree that there is something in the contention of the leader of the Opposition whose viewpoint I can see quite clearly. However, I do not think we will have the difficulty in administering the law which he anticipates. A very similar law has been in force in the United States for two years and it was only yesterday that I had an opportunity of discussing the matter with the chief official responsible for the administration of this law there, Mr. A. Caninetti, Commissioner General of Immigration, Department of Labour, Washington, whom I think many members in the Committee know,

tells me that they have had very little difficulty in administering this law. While it is true that there are in all countries in the world some thousands of dialects, many of them are not in the form of written or printed languages. As a matter of fact, as I stated to the Committee yesterday-
Does the minister say, thousands of dialects?

I am repeating what the leader of the Opposition says. He told us that there were some thousands of dialects and for that reason we would have all sorts of difficulties in administering the law. In the United States there have been some hundreds of thousands of people seeking entry every year, and the authorities have found it necessary to make use of only some thirty-five different languages. I do not expect it will be necessary to create an army of officials in order to administer this law. Very few officials will be needed, and there should be very little difficulty in training them to administer the law in a reasonable way. I agree that there is a possibility that under a law of this kind we may exclude some very desirable people; but on the other hand I am quite convinced that the great majority of the people in Canada have made up their minds definitely that this country is not going to be flooded with illiterates. That is unquestionable. It might be advisable to add a rider to this clause giving the minister, under proper regulations approved by the Governor in Council, some discretionary power in the matter. I can understand that persons who have not had an education may seek entry from Great Britain, but it seems to me that if that power is given every precaution should be taken to see that it is properly exercised. I think that before any persons desiring to come to Canada from Great Britain left it would be well that our officers there should thoroughly examine them and ascertain whether or not they would be desirable citizens of Canada, and report the facts to the -department before the granting of permission for them to come. If the Committee thinks fit, we might add a rider placing some discretion in the bands of the department, and I would be quite prepared to have a clause drawn accordingly. When we consider that this law has been in force in the United States for two years, if we did not have similar laws here the tendency the world over on the part of people of this class would be to come to Canada, and we might have conditions that would be very undesirable indeed unless there were some check.

I would support the suggestion that the minister have a discretionary power as regards letting in people who cannot read or write. There are people who come from the British Isles and are unable either to read or to write, but who, nevertheless, might make excellent citizens.
I think that if there is one thing more than another that we require in Canada it is ordinary labour, and a great many of these illiterates from the British Isles would make splendid ordinary labourers. As an occasional employer of labour to a limited extent, I have frequently met persons who could neither read nor write but who were good and successful citizens and acquired farms of their own. I think the trouble is that a good many of the people who come can read and write too well and do not want Jo do anything else. Many of the clauses in the Bill prevent people of bad character from coming, but I think that the suggestion is a very good one that the minister should be given some discretion in the admission of people who might be desirable although they cannot read or write.

As there has been considerable discussion on the question of illiteracy in the British Isles, it might be well to put on record a table covering a period of ten years which the United States Immigration Commission published after a long investigation. The average illiteracy during the period from 1899 to 1909 among all European immigrants was over 26.6 per cent, and it is interesting to note the striking difference between the illiteracy displayed by what are called the old immigrants and that displayed by the new immigrants. You will remember that on a former occasion it was pointed out that the old immigrants came chiefly from Northwestern Europe and the new immigrants from Southeastern Europe. This table of the percentage of illiteracy is based upon the inability of the immigrants to either read or write, so that it is a severer test than that proposed in this Bill. The table is published by the United States Immigration Commission and is quoted in Professor Fairchild's work on immigration at page 198. I was just going to comment on the fact 'that Scotland does not appear in this list at all, for the reason, I suppose, that there were no illiterates. They are like our friends' the Acadians, who, we were glad to hear yesterday, had no illiterates amongst 'them. I want to draw the attention of the Committee to the great difference between the Italians of northern Italy with 11.8 per cent illiteracy and the Italians of southern Italy with 54.2 per cent.

The table just quoted by my hon. friend (Mr. Cronyn) is of very great significance to any one who has had anything to do with the foreign peoples that have come into this country. You will note that of the Scandinavians 0-4 per cent were illiterate, while the Rumanian percentage was 34. I have lived for thirty-five years amongst a people in which all classes of foreigners are very thickly mixed. In the town in which I have lived for that period we have had a large number of foreigners. We have them yet in Northern Ontario and the foreigner that is giving us trouble, and that is giving this country trouble to-day by adopting a Bolshevik attitude, is the educated foreigner. There are three families living in the little town where I reside who came into this country and the fathers and mothers of whom were absolutely illiterate. They have lived there now for 34 or 35 years, their children have grown up, they have attended the public schools and have become good citizens. The mothers and fathers themselves have learned to read and write English and can converse freely in that tongue.
But when you get the educated Scandinavian who has been referred to, you get the class of man who is creating all the agitation amongst his fellows and trying to break down the ideals for which Canadians stand. I related an experience to one of the members of the House that we had this past winter with 500 Scandinavians. Nine or ten years ago, if you had asked a man who had paid any attention to public affairs in Northern Ontario what, in his judgment, was the best class of men that you could get into that country in order 
that it might be properly developed, on account of its rigorous climate and long winters, he would tell you the Scandinavian. That was our experience when we had a small number of these people but they have come in large numbers and since they became saturated with the ideas of the educated agitator they have become difficult to deal with.
At the present time in the town of Sudbury there are eleven men awaiting trial at the next sessions, not one of whom is an illiterate. They are men in the same class as that referred to by the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt)-the man who does not want to do anything but read and write and circularize his fellow men of the same nationality in order to '	4 p.m create unrest in thq country
and to break down the Government and the ideals of Canadian citizenship.
I have had something to do with many foreigners and with a very considerable number of Rumanians. This is the class of people who seem to be more willing than any others to enter into our citizenship, and 1 say that with all due deference to other classes, and notwithstanding the possibility that I may be misunderstood, of the Rumanians, and a number of people who were formerly citizens of Austria. _,A large class of men who were interned as enemy aliens in the early days of the war and were afterwards let out on parole have always been recognized as peaceful, law-abiding citizens in Northern Ontario. They belonged to countries that were part of the Austrian Empire and many people of these races are now citizens of the Allies. These are facts that cannot be gainsaid and any one who will go through the country and investigate conditions as they are cannot fail to come to the conclusion that an educational test on the basis of a man having been educated in the country of his origin, and for the country of his origin is not right. If the ideals that have been taught to him are not right, submitting him to this test gives us no assurance that we are going to get the right kind of citizen for Canada.

If the Committee approve I would suggest the addition of some words at the end of the clause. The clause now reads:
The provisions of this paragraph shall not apply to Canadian citizens and persons who have Canadian domicile, or to persons in transit through Canada.

1 would suggest that these words be added:
-or to such persons or classes of person^ as may from time to time be approved by the minister.
The Committee will understand that this places a very large discretion in the hands of the minister. It may not always be administered wisely, but that will be a matter for the minister and the Government of the day, whoever it may be, to look after. It is just a question as to whether or not the Committee thinks it advisable to place that discretion in the hands of the Government.

As those who are undesirable are debarred under some other section of the Act, it would not impose a great responsibility on the minister, because if the immigrant was not debarred on that ground the probability is that he would be debarred on some other.

He would be debarred for other reasons and not on account of illiteracy. The clause would then read in this way:
The provisions of this paragraph shall not apply to Canadian citizens and persons who have Canadian domicile, or to persons in transit through Canada, or to such persons or classes of persons as may from time to time be approved by the minister.

We have a situation in my part of the country as between ourselves and Newfoundland, which ought to receive consideration. Hundreds and thousands of people go back and forth pretty much all the time between Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, landing at North Sydney. They are the best men that we have in connection with our coal and steel works, and *we could not get along very well without them. I am afraid that this test may keep a great many of them out. In many parts of Newfoundland they have no very great educational advantages, and while they are a splendid people, good workers and desirable citizens, I am afraid that this requirement that they shall be able to read and write may keep many of them out of the province. We are very anxious to have them come in and go out as they want to. The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer) suggested last night that this rule would not apply to Great Britain and Ireland. I wish to add Newfoundland. I do not think we would be running any risk by saying that this rule should not apply to the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and Newfoundland. Let it apply to those who are really foreigners
and let our own people come in if they are otherwise desirable. The probabilities are that most of them can read, but let us not put any obstruction in the way of the others.

It seems to me that if we follow the suggestion which has been made by the Minister of Immigration we wil, throw wide open the question of the literary test in regard to the immigrants that enter Canada. The arguments of the hop. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) and the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) were not confined to cases of extreme hardship. As far as the immigrant himself is concerned, the hon. member for North Oxford points out that we require people oi that class to come into this country for the purposes of labour. He says that we bring them in as illiterates, and being here, they are more contented while they are in that state. Therefore his argument practically means that we must permit the admission of ignorant people for the purpose of having quietness amongst the labouring class. My opinion is that if we throw the burden upon the minister of determining who shall be admitted he will be at once flooded by requests and petitions from all classes of employers in this country who will say that we need a certain class of farm labour. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Douglas) suggests that we need another class of labour to operate the coal mines. It will also be suggested that we need others to work as section-hands on our railways; in fact, that we need for labour purposes generally throughout Canada the admission of ignorant people. I deem it right at the present time to face the issue squarely and say whether or not we are going to apply the literary test to immigrants coming to Canada, or whether we will allow the law to remain as it is. To make the minister the judge would, in my opinion, impose an unfair burden upon him, and he would be more than human if he could resist the many requests having for their object the evasion of this section of the law. I think we should apply the literary test and require the immigrants brought to .this country to have a certain amount of education, so that even if they cannot speak the English language they may, through the medium of their own tongue and their own papers, become familiar with the conditions that exist here. We should not, as in the past, permit the entrance of a great many illiterates of foreign birth who cannot read in their own language, let alone read, write,

or speak the English language, and who have no way whatever of familiarizing themselves with the prevailing Canadian conditions, except through such representations as may be made to them. The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) charged last night that the illiterate immigrants that have been brought into this country in the past have been made the victims of political trickery, and have been imposed upon by the politicians of both parties. Well, if we wish to avoid that condition of affairs which no doubt has existed in this country in the past I can see no better way of making a start than by requiring the immigrants who enter Canada to be able to read and to write in some language. As far as regards the percentage of illiterates who would come from Great Britain it is certainly very small. I think we should either stand by the principle of the clause as it is now, and not place in the hands of the minister power to permit the entrance of any class of illiterates, or else we should wipe out the literary test entirely, and let the law remain as it is at the present time. Personally I am in favour of the application of the literary test, and I would be very sorry to see any such broad power placed in the hands of the minister.

The hon. gentleman has misquoted what I said. I did not maintain that it was necessary to bring in an illiterate man for labour purposes. What I said was that I would not bar his admission because he was illiterate, provided he was otherwise qualified. The hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn) further said that no illiterate 'Scotchman had come to Canada in the last ten years. I have personal knowledge of a Scotchman who has come to this country in the last five years, who is illiterate and has a very broad accent.
He was an Irishman.

He was not an Irishman. but it would not hurt him any if he were. I personally am inclined to leave it to the judgment of the Minister of Immigration in certain cases to permit the entry, in his own judgment, of certain classes of immigrants. I am not afraid the . present Minister of Immigration would ever abuse that discretionary power, or that he would not carry it out with ability, and I hope that in the future no Minister of Immigration will be appointed in whom we could not repose equal confidence.
