I would like to point out the exact effect of this section. It will be noted that it says:
The following persons shall be prohibited from entering or landing dn Canada:-Persons over fifteen years of age,-
and so on. Then it says:
The provisions of this paragraph shall not apply to Canadian citizens and persons - who have Canadian domicile or to persons in transit through Canada.
That is to say, it exempts those who Have acquired a Canadian domicile, or those who are simply passing through Canada as tourists or travellers. What the section means, if it passes, is that every person over fifteen years of age who cannot read shall not be allowed to land or enter Canada. As I understand the situation down by the sea, every year there is a fairly large number of people who come over from Newfoundland to work in the coal mines.
Yes, and in the steel works.

That is, these people are engaged in seasonal occupation, and there seems to me no reason why in that particular instance discretion should not be used for the admission of these people to engage in such seasonal occupations. Again, it has been pointed out that on account of the conditions existing in Western Canada from time to time we must send to the United States and engage some thousands of labouring men to work in our harvest fields. Well, if the section remains exactly in its present form we must see to it that such persons are admitted to render that harvest help. It appears to me that, taking everything into consideration, some discretion should be permitted under this section whereby we might be able to meet the labour conditions that arise from time to time in this country.
, Mr. H. A. MACKIE (Edmonton East): W'hat would happen in the case of these people desiring to remain in the country permanently?
I think we should provide that the section shall not apply to .those people who enter Canada for the temporary purposes referred to, but if they wish to remain then the test will be applied.

How would the minister deal with a case such as I am about to mention, of which I have experienced two or three in the last few years? The father has come to 'Canada and is providing, or is in the way of getting, a home.

He obtains a good occupation and later op sends for his wife and chidren whom he left behind in the Old Country-I am speaking now particularly of persons who came from Great Britain. In one of the. cases there was a wife, and I think six or seven children, one of the children not being as bright as doctors thought she ought to be. The parents were faced with this condition:	They either had to abandon all
their arrangements and the whole family remain in England, or else come to Canada and leave the one dull child behind, although it was demonstrated she was not able to take care of herself. It appears to me that where the parents are prepared tc guarantee that a child of that kind will be looked after and will be no charge to the country, it is scarcely charitable, to say the least of it, to break up a family circle and upset the plans of six or seven people wishing to come to this country because ,one of the number may be considered not as bright as she should be. I want to ask the minister if he has any discretion in dealing with a case of that kind?

There is discretion under the law as it now stands to deal with cases of that kind, and the department is from time to time handling such cases. Usually we require something in the nature of security from the relatives that a child such as the hon. member speaks of shall not be a public charge, and the child is then allowed to enter Canada under a section of the existing law. All of those cases are gone into very carefully, and every precaution is taken to see that the person admitted does not become a public charge.

I think perhaps it might be pertinent to ask what is the object of the reading test for immigrants? The only object of such a test that I have been able to gather was indicated by some words of the minister, to the effect that we have not done our duty in times past in our efforts to Canadianize those foreigners who have come to this country. So I assume that one of the objects is to enable us to impart information to them which they jshould have in order to know something about oui institutions, customs and ideals. It must be clear to every person that if the immigrant is unable to read there is no opportunity of imparting such information. If that person comes from a country other than Great Britain, say from Italy or Rumania, and he can read his native language, we are in a position to place in his hands reading matter printed in his Own tongue which will convey to him some
idea of our national ideals, customs and institutions, and in that way we can carry on a campaign to Canadianize him. If that is true there is not the same reason to impose a reading test on an immigrant from Great Britain as to impose it on persons coming from foreign countries, because we can convey to a Britisher by word of mouth our ideals and customs in fact, coming from the British Isles he understands them pretty well already.
It occurred to me that the real object we had in view in applying this reading test was to enable us to carry out our work of making these foreigners Canadian citizens, and I repeat, if they are illiterate there is no possible way of imparting to them the necessary knowledge of our ideals, customs and instructions. Therefore I think the reading test is consistent with the idea of the minister that we should be more particular and more energetic in performing our duty of turning these foreigners into Canadian citizens. But I do not think there will be any very great hardship in applying the reading test to persons coming from the British Isles. I think there is a smaller percentage of illiteracy among those people than amongst our native-born population as I understand the figures. In Scotland particularly the authorities have been giving very close attention to the subject of education, and I do not think immigrants from England and Scotland would have any trouble in passing a reading test, especially those coming from Scotland.
If an immigrant is under fifteen years of age the reading test does not apply, but if any boy or girl who has lived in the British Isles until the age of fifteen is unable to read the English language, I do not think it is desirable to allow such a youth to entet this country. Any boy or girl who has not had enough ambition, with the opportunities available in Great Britain, to acquire that reading knowledge had better stay at home for a few months longer until able to read.
I think the idea of a reading test is very good and is perfectly logical and consistent with the attitude taken hy the minister all along. I might add that this fact has been very strongly impressed upon the people of the United States during the last three or four years. I was very much interested in reading a summary of a report presented by Secretary Lane to the President of the United States in regard to this very matter. I will not take up the time of the committee by referring to it in detail, but he impressed on the President in the very strong-

est language possible the great importance to that country-which we do not regard as illiterate by any means-of taking very vigorous measures to enforce attendance at schools, that the population might be better educated. He calls attention to the large number of illiterates in the United States and the very serious effect it has upon the country. So when the United States is taking energetic measures along the line of selection of their immigrants, it does seem to me that it would be unwise for us to be lax in this matter wherein, I think, we have in times past been altogether too negligent. I think we should have some test along the lines of enabling ourselves to carry on a propaganda of instructing immigrants, if not in our own language, then in their native language, by means of pamphlets and other reading matter.

I do not agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards), because what we want is immigrants, and a man may be a very desirable immigrant although unable to read or write. We all know that we have had men from the British Isles wlyD have made good citizens, and a great many of them have not had the advantages of an education. I know an old man who was not able to read or write, but he was a skilful farmer and a progressive man and gave his children a good education.
It is a good while ago since he came to Nova Scotia, but his grandson is now principal of a great university in the United States. It would be foolish, I think, to exclude that class of men who are so unfortunate as not to have had educational opportunities. There are not as many of them at present as there were years ago, but there are still a certain number, and why should we exclude them? They are in no way dangerous citizens., and I take it that the purpose of the minister is to exclude undesirable people, and a man cannot be said necessarily to be undesirable merely because he is unable to read. The question raised by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) is important in Nova Scotia, and I do not see how the minister can very well deal with every separate case, because that would keep him pretty busy. In the spring of the year, when fifty or a hundred men, who are not able to read, arrive in Sydney from Newfoundland every day, they will not be allowed to land, !and they will have to return home until permission for them to land is obtained from Ottawa.

I do not think the hori. member rightly understands the wording of 
the proposed amendment, which is that the minister may allow persons or classes of persons to enter Canada. If it were adopted, provision would have to be made that those seasonal workers from Newfoundland be put in a class that would be allowed to enter.

If the minister will have to make a regulation to apply to such cases as that, it might as well be inserted in the Bill. The minister should consider the advisability of not applying this regulation to the British Isles, or for that matter to the self-governing Dominions, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and Newfoundland. I am not moving this as an amendment, but I submit for the minister's consideration that these words be inserted:
Or to persons being British subjects emigrating from Great Britain or Ireland or from any of the self-governing Dominions of the Empire.

I am afraid if we attempted to deal with this in the Bill in a specific way, we shall only land ourselves in trouble. If it is to be dealt with at all, discretion must be given to deal with such cases as they arise from time to time.

I should like to support the minister's proposal by way of amendment to add these qualifying words which will tend to soften the previous clause and to guard against a possible injustice, at all events, against a possible harshness of administration. It is not generally desirable that we should confer too much power upon any individual minister, but it is, from time to time, necessary to allow a minister a discretion. I quite agree with the minister that it will be better to leave the matter in a general way as he has proposed in his amendment than to adopt words specifying those who might be admitted. I know enough about the case of men from Newfoundland, referred to by the leader of the Opposition, to see the force of his representations. Yet, if we were asked to specify Newfoundland, that would seem to be an unfortunate discrimination against other portions of the British Dominions, and if we adopt the suggestion of the hon. member for Anti-gonish and Guysborough (Mr. J. H. Sinclair), mentioning several Dominions, that would still leave out other portions of the British Empire. I hope that the thing can be worked out as the minister proposes in his amendment, and I certainly think to go beyond that and specify particular countries might get us into trouble.

I! the amendment " that discretionary powers be left in the hands of the minister " is to be included in the Bill,
I will certainly support the Bill, because I would not be in favour of excluding British subjects, even if they were unable to meet the requirements in respect to reading and writing. That would be doing an injustice to British citizens if they met the requirements of the Bill in every other respect. It would be working a hardship on the people of England, Scotland, Ireland, and the rest of the British Empire.

1 was rather surprised and somewhat startled at the figures which the hon. member for London (Air. Cronyn) gave us with respect to illiteracy. Quoting from Professor Fairchild's book, he gave us a list of the percentages of illiterates from various countries in Europe, and amongst those, he told us that Hebrew illiteracy was about 25 per cent. This is the first I have heard of there being such a country as a Hebrew country in Europe. These men come from certain specified countries in Europe, and a classification of some according to nationality and others according to race and religion would require explanation.

This is the heading of
the table as I read it: "Percentage of illiteracy of immigrants of the specified races."

I think I know probably as much about Hebrews as Professor Fairchild, and no doubt more than .my good friend from London (Mr. Cronyn). I can safely say that, in my experience, covering quite a number of years-and I have been the president of the largest Hebrew philanthropic institution in Canada-there never came under my review the case of a single Jew who did not know how to read his own language. In fact, such a thing is absolutely impossible. I have only to turn to the biblical command to prove that Jews must know how to read their own language, otherwise they cannot become members of the Jewish community If my good friend wants to accompany me to my room where I always have a Bible, I think I can show him the text. That being the case, I cannot understand why those figures should have been given by Professor Fairchild, unless it be for this reason that these Jewish people coming from various countries were unable to read the language of the country from which they came. But I question whether, if the test were put to them with regard to their own language, they would be found unable
to read that language. Such a thing is absolutely impossible, and my object in rising was to put this clearly before the House. Furthermore I understand that an impression has gone abroad that I have strenuously opposed this Section because it is going to debar Jews from this country. The reasons already given by me would indicate that I have no such idea at all. My object is rather one of endeavouring to assist others who, not so fortunate as the Hebrew people, have no injunctions of that kind in their religious cults. I would be satisfied with the clause as accepted by the minister namely, that we give discretion to the minister. I would have been more satisfied if the clause had been entirely struck out, but half a loaf is better than no bread. I trust, that with the intelligence which characterizes the department, no real hardship will be suffered by those who wish to enter this country, who are desirable citizens, but who may be disqualified by their inability to read.

I hope the hon. member will accept my assurance that in quoting this table I had no feeling against any race therein mentioned. His explanation may have hit the truth; there is nothing in the context to show. The table did include both reading and writing, and it might well be that the test was in the tongue of the country from which the immigrant, came.

I should like to know when these definite and well-defined arrangements will be made. I have in mind particularly people from Newfoundland coming over to Cape Breton. If a boat-load of these Newfoundlanders went to land at North Sydney, are we to infer that they would have to lie off North Sydney until Ottawa had been communicated with and it was ascertained whether they could come in? Or is it proposed to put the regulations in the hands of the immigration officers at North Sydney and other places, so that they can decide whether the men shall be allowed to land? There was almost a riot in our town last year on account of some regulations that had been passed, inadvertently, I believe, by the Department of Immigration. Three or four hundred Newfoundlanders were held up at North Sydney in consequence of this regulation, but after a few days we managed to reach an understanding with the department and they were allowed to land. These Newfoundlanders are the most loyal type of British subject; they have'shown themselves to be excellent soldiers in this war and they are

very sensitive of any obstructions placed in the way of their entry into any other part of the British Empire. I trust that whatever arrangements are made, they will not create any ill-feeling or misunderstanding between the colony of Newfoundland and ourselves.
Mr. >OALDER : This section does, not come into force until the first day of July, so that we shall have ample time to consider the situation down by the sea. My intention is to refer the matter to the officials of the department immediately, so that the necessary regulations may be framed and our officers in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island made thoroughly acquainted with them before the first of July. The same is true of immigrants from Great Britain. We shall endeavour to frame regulations and give our officials over there ample notice. It can all be done in ample time before the first of July.
Amendment agreed to.

I desire to move the addition of a further subsection to section 3. If the Committee are weary of the number of times I have risen on this Bill, I may urge in mitigation that heretofore this session I have not occupied much of the time of the House. Last week we had a prolonged and strenuous debate, but on that occasion I think I had some balance of time to Spare over the one and seven-ninths of a minute which it was calculated was the allowance of each member. We heard then a good deal about figurative babies and imaginary wrecks. It seems to me this Bill is fraught with potentialities which will affect many real babies in the years to come, and may possibly bring about many human wrecks. It is in fact the resumption of one of the great biological and sociological experiments that we are considering in this Bill. My amendment, which I shall read later, proposes to prohibit for a term of years immigration from southeastern Europe. It may be urged that under section 13, which has already been passed by the Committee, power is given by Order in Council to accomplish the same end. Perhaps I share with certain other hon. members of this House some apprehensions with regard to Orders in Council. At all events, if the Bill is passed in its present form, no member of the House should afterwards raise objection to Orders in Council affecting immigration passed under section 13.
There are divers views regarding the general subject of immigration, and I do 
not desire to detain the Committee by discussing these at length. There is the broad view of the man who may be termed a sentimental monogenist-the man who says "Are we not all brothers in this world?" and who points out that the great war was fought for liberty and mankind, and urges, therefore, that no country should shut its doors against any race. Of course, if he be logical, he must allow the entry of the natives of Asia and Africa as well as those of Europe, and while there are advocates who are prepared to go to that logical length, I fancy that few of them will be found in this country. The hon. member for George Etienne Cartier spoke of the white man's burden and Kipling's gospel thereon. Now, my memory of that gospel is different from his, and I shall take the liberty of calling the attention of the Committee to what Kipling actually did say. I shall not read the whole poem, because it is too lengthy. One or two stanzas will show that what Kipling was speaking of was the missionary effort of Great Britain to the less enlightened nations, and not of opening the doors of Britain or her colonies to these races:
Take up the White Man's burden-
Send forth the best ye breed-
Go bind your sons to exile
To serve your captives' need ; '
To wait in heavy harnessi On fluttered folk and wild;-
Your new-caught, sullen peoples,
Half-devil and half-child.
Take up the White Man's burden-
The savage wars of peace-
Fill full the mouth of Famine And bid the sickness cease;
-And when your goal is nearest The end for others sought,
Watch Sloth and heathen Folly Bring all your hope to nought.
Take up the White Man's burden-
. Ye dare not stoop to less-
Nor call too loud on Free'dom To cloak your weariness;
By all ye cry or whisper.
By all ye leave or do,
The silent, sullen peoples
Shall weigh your Gods and you.
Opposed to that general argument in favour of unrestricted immigration, there are those who believe in selective immigration. I shall not now delay the Committee to give the reasons which may be urged in favour of such selection. They are in a sense all covered by a word which has been frequently used throughout this debate-" assimilation." What does assimilation mean? The Century dictionary gives it as: "The act or process of making or becoming like or identical; the act or process of bringing into harmony." So that

assimilation involves identity. There ^ is one final test as to whether assimilation will be efficient in connection with race, and that test is the free intermarriage between the races. If marriage can take place between any man and woman in a country without reference to ethnic origin, then true assimilation has been found. But you may well say: You are talking of European immigration; no question arises in your proposed amendment regarding the white or black races. I therefore desire to say one word on the situation in Europe. Those hon. members who have at all been attracted by the recent discoveries in anthropology will know that the distinct trend of present scientific opinion is to the effect that Europe contains three main races which have nothing to do with national boundaries, languages, or religions, but come out of the womb of time, and the characteristics of which have been fixed, according to some scientific writers, by millions of years of growth. These three races of Europe are known by the names, Nordics, Alpines, and Mediterraneans. One could spend some time in describing the variations that distinguish these races, but I am afraid the Committee might be impatient if I went that length.
Go on.

These races shade into each other at different points, and the dividing line is indistinct at other points. Speaking in a loose way the Nordics occupy the extreme northwest of Europe, the Alpines are found in the west'and central portions, and the Mediterraneans in the south.
The proposed amendment is to exclude for a time immigrants from southeastern Europe, and while I do not wish to repeat any of the remarks I made in the opening of the debate, I would like to summarize once again the objections against allowing these people free entry into Canada at the present time. In the first place, should we do so, they are likely to arrive in large numbers, judging by the past. Now it is well known that if you introduce into the body of man or beast an inordinate quantity of food, particularly of a new and strange variety, digestive disturbances arise and toxins are produced. And so with the body politic. If you introduce a large mass of strange people who cannot be assimilated, poisonous currents are set up which pro- duce results similar to those mentioned yesterday by hon. members from the West. The second reason is that these immigrants
flock for the greater part to the cities and rarely become occupants of rural districts.
I gave the percentage on a former occasion and need not repeat it, -but it is somewhat alarming to learn that in the case of certain of the races from that portion of Europe over 90 per cent stay in the city and cannot be persuaded to go on the land. The third objection is that so many of them are but temporary visitors to this continent. It will be readily understood that if a man is here to make money he will economize to the greatest extent in his method of living, and will decline to be interested in the social or political problems of this country. A good deal more might be said in that regard, and striking instances could be given of what happens in Canada to-day with that class of worker, but I must hurry on. The fourth objection is the great percentage of illiteracy among these immigrants. We have already dealt with that point and so I pass to the fifth objection, which is the lowered standard of living that must follow the introduction into the country of so many people of this type. I shall now read the proposed amendment as sub-paragraph (u) of section 3:
3. (.U) the following persons, unless otherwise permitted by existing treaties, shall also be prohibited, for a period of five years from the first day of July, one thousand nine hundred and nineteen, from entering or landing in Canada:-
(i)	Aliens from the Continent of Europe whose domicile is situate south or east of a line drawn from the Atlantic Ocean east along the forty-second parallel of latitude to the fifteenth meridian of longitude thence north along said fifteenth meridian to the fifty-fifth parallel thence east along said fifty-fifth parallel to the twentieth meridian thence north along said twentieth meridian to the sixtieth parallel thence east along said sixtieth parallel to the thirtieth meridian and thence north along said thirtieth meridian to the Arctic Ocean.
(ii)	Aliens from the North American Continent of European birth who are not citizens of the United States of America and whose domicile dn Europe was situate south or east of the above described line.
It may be objected that the above is a wholly artificial boundary. I wish some hon. gentleman would try to find some other way of getting at what I want to accomplish. With the map of Europe in flux it is a difficult matter to describe under any other method the boundaries which I suggest. Starting at the 42nd parallel of latitude, which is the southernmost latitude in which Canada lies, the 42nd of very close to it, being the latitude of Point Pelee, we are just above the northern boundary of Portugal. We cross the northern portion of

Spain, past Corsica, just north of Rome to a point where the line bisects the 15th meridian of longitude. The line then runs north leaving to the west of it almost the whole of Germany, a great part of Austria and what is called on this map, Czecho Slovakia. I have no hesitation in leaving these alien enemy countries within the favoured area because of the declaration oi the minister that provision has already been made for the exclusion of alien enemies as immigrants. The 15th meridian bisects the 55th parallel in the Baltic sea whence the line goes east to Konigsberg, north along the 20th meridian to the gulf of Finland, then east along the 60th parallel to a point north of Petrograd 5 p.m. and then clear north to the Arctic ocean. To the north and west of the boundaries so defined and thus within the favoured area will be found the British Isles, Norway and Sweden, Finland, Denmark, the Netherlands, Belgium, France, Switzerland, the northern portion of Spain, the northern half of Italy, and, as I say, some of the enemy countries. These boundaries are crudely placed but I could find no other method of arriving at my object.

Your object is to exclude the Latin races?
_ Mr. CRONYN: My object is to exclude immigrants from Southeastern Europe for a period of years.
Does that exclude people from any portion of France?

The whole of France and part of Spain are taken in. Portugal is left out. As a matter of fact, in eighteen years, we have had exactly 110 immigrants from Portugal; so that omission is not a serious matter. Southern Italy is left out. It is somewhat remarkable that all the American articles on immigration point to the difference between the inhabitants from Northern and Southern Italy. So great is that difference that the American immigration tables always show the inhabitants of Northern Italy separate and apart from those of Southern Italy. The Southerners come almost entirely from the provinces or departments of Abruzzi, Campania, Calabria and the island of Sicily. *

In what part of Italy
is Naples?

It is of course well to
the south. This map does not give the departments; I am speaking from memory as to those. It may be of interest to the 
Committee in passing to learn that I was unable to obtain a wall map of Europe from any department of the Government to which I applied; nor could I buy one in any book store. With the discussion which we may have later about the Peace terms, L took the opportunity of suggesting to the geographer of the Department of the Interior that he should have a supply of these maps on hand.

You are going to distinguish between places bounded by certain degrees of longitude and parallels of latitude. These lines divide many countries that you propose to exclude immigration from. What is to hinder people from moving from one side of the meridian or parallel to the other? It seems to me that there will be a very great mix-up.
Mr. 'CRONYN':	The words used are
" whose domicile is situate." The word " domicile " is interpreted by: the Act as follows:
" Domicile " means the place in which a person has his home, or in which he resides, or to which he returns as his place of permanent abode, and does not mean the place where he resides for a mere special or temporary purpose.
I take it that the immigration authorities would demand, if this were put into force, a certificate from some proper officer of the country of origin that the immigrant had his domicile at such and such a point.

Many people of this
character are nomadic in their habits and they move from one place to another. They do not have the same idea as we have about holding real estate, they have no permanent abode and it seems to me that they cannot be lined up very closely.

That after all would be
a matter of detail. I am bringing the amendment before the Committee more to present the general idea than in any hope that it will be accepted as the final working clause.
Would the hon. member explain in plain and less technical language from what portions of Europe he would exclude immigrants?

I am sorry I have been using language that any member of the House cannot understand; I had no intention of doing so. The lines drawn would exclude all Portugal, the southern three-quarters of Spain, the southern half of

Italy and the Island of Sardinia, all of Greece, Turkey, the Balkan States, Bulgaria, and the whole of Russia in Europe.
Would the hon. gentleman exclude people from Malta and the other British possessions?

So far as any inhabitant of Malta is not a British subject. I am using the word "alien" in a technical sense. As defined by the Act, an alien is a person who is not a British subject. British subjects either in Europe or the United States of America, would be free from this prohibition.

What would happen in
the case of territories over which Great Britain has established a protectorate?
Perhaps the hon. member will inform me what places in Europe are under a British protectorat?
Take the case of Egypt. Great Britain has a protectorate over that country.
This clause is confined to the continents of Europe and North America.

Then emigrants will be
admitted from non-European countries if Great Britain has a protectorate over them?

I did not attempt to deal with emigrants other than those from southeastern Europe and North America. This is a temporary expedient at best, and for a period of five years I think we can take it for granted that there will be little if any emigration from other continents.

Shall the amendment
carry?

If the hon. gentleman insists upon the amendment I think it should stand so that we may have ample time to consider it. His proposition, in many respects, is a novel one, and ~how it can be worked out in a practical way I cannot at the present time see. Therefore, I should like to have ample opportunity to carefully consider the amendment from every angle. There are difficulties in the way of carrying out what is proposed. I cannot, for example, see how we can for a period of five years exclude Russians who live in Europe, and not exclude people of that nationality if they are domiciled across the Ural mountains. It seems to me there would be very little logic in that position. Neither do I see how we could exclude people from the continent of Europe, whom
we regard as undesirable, and not exclude people from the continent of South America, or from the continent of Africa. The method proposed of applying geographical boundaries so as to exclude certain classes of people for a period of years will, I think, have to be looked at very carefully before the House commits itself to the principle.
I would suggest that we proceed with the other clauses of the Bill and allow the proposed amendment to stand. It will be printed in Hansard, together with the discussion which has taken place on the proposal, and we will all have a full opportunity of considering the suggestions at our leisure.
I understand the hon. gentleman, by his amendment, proposes to exclude the Greeks and the Portuguese?
The Greeks and the Portuguese.	,
That is to say, a portion of Portugal?
All of Portugal.

That immediately raises a question in my mind for the simple reason that these people are our allies in this war, which will not be concluded until peace has been signed. The Greeks and the Portuguese are still our allies in every sense of the word, and I question the advisability of this House excluding, or going on record as being willing to exclude, the soldiers from other countries that have fought alongside our own men and helped to win this war.

I have no objection to following the course suggested by the minister and allowing the amendment to stand, ihe suggestion made is, perhaps, novel, although not quite so novel as might appear to the -Committee. The method followed in this case has already been adopted by the United 'States -in connection with the entry of Asiatics into that country-that is to say, the method of using lines of latitude and longitude to define the boundaries of areas whence emigration shall be prohibited. I would much prefer-as I said in opening the	debate-that the entire
Act should be recast. I would like to adopt the positive instead of the negative method. Let us say, for instance: "We will accept immigrants from the countries of all our Allies," or from certain of them, and then consider the admission of emigrants from other countries. Unfortunately, the

whole trend of legislation for many years has been the other way, and we are forced to hold the wrong end of the stick unless we are prepared to upset all that has gone before.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It has been moved that further consideration of this section and the amendment submitted in connection therewith be now postponed. Is it the pleasure of the Committee to adopt the motion?

Motion agreed to.
On section 4-Titles of officers.

The hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) is not in his seat, or he certainly would object to proceeding with this clause, which the Committee will observe opens up the whole question of titles, concerning which the House has pronounced so recently. I suggest that the clause be allowed to stand until the Committee appointed to deal with the question of titles has had an opportunity to report.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the clause carry?

I do not think the objection is entitled to very much consideration. The jocularity of my hon. friend from Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) completely carried me away, but I was going to ask, is it intended to appoint more officials at the different immigration statiohs? For instance, in my own town, there is a doctor and an immigration agent both engaged in the handling and examination of immigrants who land there. Is it intended that such a staff [DOT]as that shall be increased under this Bill? Possibly the only immigration stations we have in the Maritime Provinces are at Halifax, St. John, North Sydney and Sydney. I would like to know if it is the intention of the minister to re-arrange those stations so as to increase the staff to any perceptible extent.

I have had a thorough
examination made of the Outside Service fiom ocean to ocean, and as a result our staff has been cut down to a very considerable extent. We have no present intention of increasing the staff; it will be increased only as actual requirements make such increase necessary. I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. McKenzie) is aware that we also had an inquiry made into the administration of our quarantine stations. I have a report from those who made the inquiry, but I purpose to hand it over to the new Health Department, to be created shortly,

and leave to the minister in charge of that department the making of any changes that may be necessary.
The minister would require under this Bill, I understand, interpreters for thirty-five different languages.

No. Sometimes we have been able to get interpreters with a knowledge of as many as ten languages, and I think we will be easily able to get them again. These interpreters are required at the eastern ports of entry, St. John. Halifax, and Quebec, where most of the people land from Europe. I think probably five interpreters would be quite sufficient to handle the great bulk of that work.

The different provinces
also have immigration commissioners, I understand. Is it the intention of the minister to make arrangements with the provinces for co-operative effort? Sometimes in the past there have been clashes between provincial and federal officials.

The work of the provinces is entirely different from our work. They have nothing whatever to do with the matters covered by the Immigration Act and by this Bill. If they have commissioners of immigration those commissioners are interested in colonization work, and there is no reason in the world why the two sets of officers should not co-operate in every possible way.

For instance, supposing the province of Ontario has a commissioner to promote settlemeht of certain portions of Ontario, and this department has a commissioner to promote settlement of portions of the western provinces, how would those two commissioners work?

Some provinces have
agents who are carrying on propaganda and publicity work, which they have a perfect right to do; there is nothing in our Federal laws to prevent them. But we have the right to decide at the port of entry whether those people who are so attracted to Canada shall be permitted to enter.

Section agreed to.
On section 7-Board of Inquiry:
The section provides "for the summary determination of all cases of immigrants." I understand that an appeal would still lie to the minister?
Yes.
What happens when there is not a sufficient number to constitute a board of inquiry?
That is provided for in the next section, I think.

Section agreed to.
On section 8-Officer to exercise powers of board:
My own port is a very important port of entry, but we have only two people there who have anything to do with immigration.

That is covered by section 22, subsection (1):
Where there is no Board of Inquiry at port of entry, or at a neighbouring port to which a person detained under this Act could conveniently be conveyed, or to which a case for decision could conveniently be referred, then the officer in charge shall exercise the powers, etc.
Is that an old section?
Yes, it is the first subsection of section 22 as it stands now in the Act.

Section agreed to.
On section 9-Inspection of immigrants:
I heartily approve of that particular provision and hope that the inspection will be made as efficient as possible, and so prevent a great deal of trouble on this side.
Hear, hear.

I xdo not wish the House to be under a misconception as to the purpose of this section. Numerous suggestions have reached the department, and it has been mentioned in Committee-, that we should provide for the inspection of all intending immigrants before they get on board ship. That is not the purpose of this section. This section provides that we may make regulations for the inspection- we may do this if we think it is advisable. I am sure the Committee will readily understand what our difficulty would be. Imagine that we are back in normal times, say five years hence, with conditions settled, the country growing and prospering, and we are reaching out for immigrants in many countries; if we were to undertake medical inspection of those people in their home lands. I can assure the Committee that it would be a veiy big problem and a very expensive one as well We may, however, find it advisable, at certain ports of entry, where those people
would come from very largely, to have medical inspectors to see that the work of medical inspection is properly carried on by the ship authorities, and in the case of Great Britain by the officers of the Board of Trade upon whom certain responsibilities are thrown under the English laws. While we are purposing to take power to have certain of this work done on the other side of the line and on board ship, I would not like the Committee to think that we intend to see that every immigrant who, hereafter, purposes coming to Canada shall be thoroughly examined from the standpoint of health before he ever gets on board ship, because, from the investigations I have made, I feel quite certain that, if we ever undertook that work, it would cost this country a very large sum of money. On the other hand, under the law as it now stands, and as modified by this Bill, we throw upon the transportation company which brings those people to Canada, the full responsibility of ascertaining whether intending immigrants are up to the required standard of health and mentality. Personally, notwithstanding all that may be said on the other side of the question. I am convinced that that is where we should keep the responsibility. We should compel those transportation companies, through their medical officers, to continue to do that work, just as it has 'been done in the past. I am perfectly aware there are two -sides to this question, but from all the information I have been able to gather and the study I have made on this subject, I -believe it will be much safer, wiser and more economical, and the administration will be better conducted if we leave the law in the main just where it stands at present.

While I would not suggest that there should be many places specified from which intending immigrants could start for this country, I do not think it would be any great hardship on them to say that there would -be certain specified ports in Europe from which they would have to start, and that at those ports we would have our machinery for proper examination. Immigrants would have to come to -those places by rail or otherwise, be examined and receive the proper certificate to permit them to commence their journey to Canada. Doctors and examiners are human like the rest of us, and I can well imagine, if I were a doctor in an office at Halifax and a man came to me who had paid his passage and had arrived in this country, my mentality towards that



man would be very different from what I would feel if he were in his own town iD some part of Europe to which he belonged. I would say to myself: This young man has come across here; after all, it will be all right, and it would he a desperate situation to dump him back aboard this vessel and send him home to his own country. That is the human side, and those are considerations which you cannot dispel from the minds of officials, because we are all human; we are all subject to those humane feelings, and it is a good thing that we are. That is why I am particularly anxious that such considerations should be removed from the mind of the officer, so that he would 'be dealing with a man at his home where those sentiments would not come in at all, and so that the man would be coldly and eooly told: You have no business to attempt to come to Canada, because you are not within the class of people we want there; you must stay at home. At the same time, I would not in the slightest degree lessen the responsibility which we put upon transportation companies which bring immigrants here. My purpose in emphasizing the desirability of this investigation and examination and of certificates being obtained by immigrants before they leave their homes is as a further precaution and one that is taken at the very beginning where no responsibilities are assumed at all.

Section agreed to.
On section 10-medical examination of passengers.
Are these medical officers to be on this side of the Atlantic, or are they to conduct examinations at the European ports from which the intending immigrant may sail?

This refers to medical
officers on this side.

This clause touches one of the most important matters with which the Immigration Department will have to deal, namely, the examination of immigrants by medical officers. As an evidence of that, I have simply to point out what has been going on in the past, and to illustrate to the Committee what has been occurring in connection with our immigrants in past years, let me point to one fact, which will be sufficient. In Ontario, in 1914, out of 1,451 patients admitted to the hospitals for the insane, 545, or 374 per cent had been born outside of Canada.

That is an enormous burden to be laid on our country.
Could the hon. gentleman give us the proportion of the number of people in Ontario who were born outside of Canada.

I could not give the hon. member that information. Through the immigration offices in Canada there had been admitted up to that time 545 persons who, in one year, were committed to hospitals for the insane in Ontario. How many were admitted in the other provinces, I have not the statistics to show. But I think we shall find that a very large number of such people are in our hospitals for the insane throughout the country, a burden that is laid upon this country, that will continue for years to come and that will grow in cost to Canada, because we know that these feeble-minded people, if they are not confined in some institution, multiply very rapidly, and statistics show that about eighty per cent of their offspring are also feeble-minded. Therefore, when we are putting to intending immigrants tests, such as those mat have been already discussed, the literary test, the exclusion of some on account of the country in which they reside, the exclusion of certain classes and so on, let us remember that, in any of the classes that are admitted under the Act, there may be immigrants who themselves appear to be all right, but who will produce children that would be undesirable citizens. The mental condition of the parents is so little removed from the normal that it is very difficult to detect. If the parents are admitted, their offspring may be in the feeble-minded class and be a burden on our country for years to come. For that reason, 1 think it is most important that much greater attention should be paid to the medical examination of our immigrants, and I have no doubt the minister sees the importance of that. I think we all know that medical examinations in the past have been exceedingly lax for many reasons, but particularly for the reason that the men appointed for this work were not fully qualified. Only men who have the expert training in detecting feeblemindedness are capable of detecting it. The ordinary physician may be an excellent man for other work; he may be able to detect tuberculosis, trachoma, and the contagious and infectious diseases that will debar an immigrant; but he might be quite incapable of detecting feeble-mindedness. For tha't reason I think we ought to have ex-

perts for this work. Although they might cost the country a good deal in salaries they would save the country an immensely greater sum by excluding the feeble-minded class. To illustrate this, let me mention this fact. Among [DOT] the immigrants desiring to land at New York in recent years prior to the war, 4 out of every 1,000 were found to be in the feeble-minded class, and were rejected. If the same proportion prevailed with respect to the 400,000 immigrants that were coming to Canada in the years before the war, it means that 1,600 feeble-minded persons were seeking admission into Canada every year, and we did not reject anything like that number. Many of them are in this country to-day, and are multiplying our feeble-minded population. That is apparent in every municipality from one end of Canada to the other. I would urge the minister to make every effort to have our immigrants thoroughly inspected for feeble-mindedness. It matters not where it is done, but it does matter that men properly qualified for this work are appointed to do it.

I want to
support the remarks made by my hon. friend. In my judgment this is, perhaps, one of the most important clauses of the Bill, because it deals with the health of the people who will in future come into this country. The figures which have just been given and .the percentages quoted are, of course, absolute and accurate. I have no doubt if a poll were taken of the inmates of the insane asylums and hospitals in Canada a similar condition would be disclosed; that is, a very large percentage of the inmates would be found to have had .their origin in countries other than our own. It is an exceedingly difficult thing to detect mental incompetency on a ship or dock as these people arrive. It requires very considerable eixperience and ability ini the medical man to do this work properly, and I would urge the minister, when he is picking his medical men, to secure men who have been trained in this particular branch of the profession. If he does, I can assure him the country will be well repaid by the services these men render, no matter what the cost may be. Too often in the past medical men have been selected-both political parties have been guilty-more for their political affiliations than for their fitness for the work. As I have said, this particular class of work requires a man of very considerable experience and ability. But he should have other experience; he should be an expert in venereal diseases. These 125i
diseases have been imported into our country in the past, and no doubt will be in the future. Knowledge of these diseases is being acquired daily by the medical profession, and competent medical men at our ports could prevent a very considerable number of these immigrants from coming in. This is a very important phase of the work. I would again impress upon the minister the necessity of selecting high-class medical men for this work. Another very important disease we should be on our guard against is pulmonary tuberculosis, ordinarily known as consumption. A string of sanatoria stretches across Canada from Prince Edward Island to Vancouver for the treatment of this disease. I have had some experience in this particular work; I have been in practically every sanatorium in Canada, certainly in the majority of them.
As a visitor.

Yes, fortunately, and one of the things that has impressed me in talking'to the patients in these institutions is the fact that many of them were born outside of Canada. A number of immigrants suffering from tuberculosis would be turned back at our ports if we had competent medical men to examine them. That is another reason why we should have high-class medical men at the ports through which these people come.
My hon. friend has also mentioned trachoma, a disease of the eyes, which is perhaps not so difficult to detect as incipient disease of the lung, venereal disease, or mental incompetency, but which nevertheless requires considerable ability to detect. I am sure that if the minister selects high-class medical men for this work, the future of this country, so far as our stream of immigration is concerned, will be more rosy.

Section agreed to.
On section 11-no clearance if Act not obeyed, but deposit may.be allowed:

There is a word here which I think is not well chosen. There is no such thing as the consignee of a vessel. There is a consignee of cargo, but you do not hear of a vessel being consigned. I think it would be better if the word "charterer" were used instead of the word "consignee," so that it would read: "No vessel shall be granted clearance if the master, agent, owner or charterer violates or refuses or neglects to comply with any provision of this Act." I know a good deal about shipping and I have never heard of the consignee of a vessel.
If the term consignee is not applicable, I must confess I am not familiar with shipping terms. I think we might make it "owner or charterer."

I do not think the hon. gentleman's point is well taken. There is a consignee on this side of the water or on the other side as the case may be. It seems to me that in our province trust companies are assigned to special work-they administer estates.
They can, but they do not generally do so.
And they can act as trustees in bankruptcy under this Bill.
But it is a special venture to which generally they are not assigned.
There have been a number of cases where they have been constituted receivers for the purpose of winding up insolvent estates.
They do not do it much in our province.

I do not see why a trust company should not be put on the same plane as an ordinary trustee. It may not be a difficult matter for a trust company to provide the necessary security; it probably would be a more difficult matter for the individual trustee to do so. While it may be said that I was a party to the drafting of this particular section, still I am willing to admit that the argument of my friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) seems to me to be pretty strong in favour of seeing that no particular advantage is secured by the trust company over the private individual. It will not be a hardship on the trust company to furnish security, and that being the case, why not put them all on the same plane?

It seems to me there is quite a difference between a trust company acting in this capacity and a private individual. If my friend from Brome wanted to start a bank he would not be able to do so; banks have charters under which the Government impose certain restrictions before they are allowed to receive money. Trust companies likewise are obliged to live up to certain requirements, and their bonds are looked upon as a proper investment for trust funds in many cases, which seems to indicate that the law recognizes that the security of trust companies is such that it cannot be questioned,

because any violation of trust is a very serious matter for anybody.
Take the case of the Dominion Trust Company.

I can quite see that the private individual is going to be somewhat at a disadvantage, but if he follows this as a business, once he gets his $10,000 bond underwritten by a bond company- and most men of any integrity can get that done-he will not be obliged to go on multiplying that security indefinitely. Presumably he will be in a position to pay the necessary premium on his $10,000 bond. But the trust company will not have to do that, because it is in a superior position financially, and is so acknowledged by the Government of the province. I think my friend from Brome. who is also a member of the Committee, will remember that we thought there was quite a difference between an individual, so far as security was concerned, and a trust company subject to very special laws and regulations which it must live up to.
Do these trust companies have to be appointed by the Governor in Council as official trustees?
I said it was open to them to be so appointed.
They cannot be appointed trustees of an estate unless they have been previously appointed ,by the Governor in Council.
Certainly not.

That is a very good provision, because recently a small company was incorporated in New Brunswick for some particular purpose-I do not know why; in other provinces small trust companies have been incorporated; therefore it would be necessary for the Governor in Council to be very particular before appointing trust companies as official trustees to see that they have proper assets and also authority under their charters to act as receivers or trustees.

In Ontario the Committee will see that the trust companies are those approved according to the laws of the province. In practice these trust companies are on a list approved by the province, and the province sees to it from year to year that they do not give guarantees in excess of the security which they put up; they have to keep bonds on deposit with the provincial government commensurate with the liabili-vties under their guarantees.

Does that occur in
all the provinces?

I do not know, although I assume it does. If there is any practice that a trust company should be approved by the province, this does not apply. The idea of the Committee was to give the public the impression of security; we were not thinking of benevolence towards young chartered accountants.

I do not want benevolence; I want justice, and it is fundamentally unjust, when you come to distribute professional trustee work, that the professional man, individual or in a firm, is obliged to put up security, while a trust company which is going to do the same work through its clerks or employees, is not obliged to do so. I quite see that, as a rule, a trust company should, just because it is a trust company, give a guarantee of security, but that does not always happen. There has, during the last few years, been a very striking failure of a trust company, and many people lost money through it.
A straight failure?

I did not say "straight failure," I said a very striking failure. These trust companies are not, I think, obliged to put up deposits with the Federal Government, which is relying upon other jurisdiction, and that being the case, would it not be better to put the chartered accountants and the trust companies on the same level? Some provinces may not be as careful as they should be with regard to trust companies. I cannot say, because I do not know.
British Columbia, for example.

They may allow trust companies to operate in unbusinesslike fashion; that is, they may allow them to issue more security bonds than they are able to guarantee. Therefore, instead of having the Department of the Secretary of State or the Federal authorities depending upon nine different jurisdictions for the security which is to be given to the creditors, why, on this ground as well as on the ground of fairness, should not the trust company and the ordinary man doing this trustee work be put on the same level?

The Government of
Ontario has that deposit already, so why require the company to put it up again? The company has to be approved by the laws of the province.

The deposit which the trust company has made with the province of Ontario is not for this specific purpose, but in connection with other activities of the company. This is to secure another activity of the trust company, and I do not see why we should make the distinction.
The security is in proportion to all the business done by the trust company.

A trust company is no more honest than the people composing it.
A year or two ago, we had the instance of the Dominion Trust Company of British Columbia which went to the wall and caused the loss of large sums of money to the public who put their faith in that institution. I still believe, with the hon. member for Brome (McMaster), that this clause should be amended, and I therefore move:
That in subsection (6), of section 14, the words " notwithstanding the provisions of this section it shall not be necessary for trust companies approved according to the law of the province to provide such security " be struck out.

I will ask my hon.
friend to allow that motion to stand until the Bill comes up for consideration tomorrow, and I will come to some conclusion in the meantime. I am not by any means wedded to the present clause. It is, however, following the general practice, and to strike it out would be an innovation.
I would not like this Bill to go forth with a slap in the face to the great trust companies of Canada. I would like it to go forth with the accepted usage of measures dealing with trust companies.
If that is the only slap in the face they will get, let it go at that.

Our people are educated that investment in the funds of trust companies is a wise and proper thing. I believe that to be so, and I would not like it to be said that we have no faith in trust companies. We are dealing here, on a very important measure, with what appears to be a very trivial matter.
I do not consider it a triviality to do what I believe to be justice to individual professional men.
I do not think the case will arise once in a year.

The Governor in
Council has the power to appoint a trustee and they will not appoint a trustee whom
they do not regard as solvent. Therefore, by selecting a trust company, the Governor in Council shows that that company is deemed to be solvent. It is rather a reflection on the party selecting the trust company that an insolvent company might be selected. We really come back to the former position, that the selection of a trustee who will carry on his duties without a bond must be made by the Government, and in exercising that selection they will take into consideration whether or not the company is solvent.
Amendment stands. Subsection stands.
Progress reported.
On motion of Hon. Mr. Reid the House adjourned.
Friday, May 2, 1919.
The House met at Three o'clock.

speechtext:
I have no doubt plans were filed in the case before the International Joint Commission, but the Government

is not in possession of any plans" so far as I know.
Before this motion is carried, Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to draw attention to a provision of the minutes of Council stating the oase of the Government of Canada? I do so in order to correct what appears to be a misunderstanding .outside this House as to the position of the Government in reference to the development of power in the St. Lawrence river. I will just read this extract:
It is with this purpose also that the Canadian Government deems it appropriate to refer here to the proposal made in the Order in Council of the 2nd September, 1918, that the two Governments should take immediate steps jointly to prepare and carry out a scheme looking to the mo9t economical and comprehensive development of the waters of the St. Lawrence River in the interests of the people of both countries. Even though the utilization of only a portion of the whole capacity of the river can be immediately contemplated, yet the endeavour should be to design at the outset a complete scheme into which successive developments might be fitted from time to time as and when the occasion might demand. Without some such scheme there is always present the great danger that the ultimate possibilities of St. Lawrence navigation may be neglected or even irreparably injured; for it must be borne in mind, not only that navigation is the paramount national and international use of this great highway of commerce, but that the possibilities of the stream in this respect have been as yet by no means fully developed. On the other hand it Is certain that the .subordinate and incidental but important use of these international boundary waters for power purposes can never be rendered as efficient and productive through a policy of simply permitting a haphazard series of unrelated private enterprises as through a carefully considered and comprehensive scheme of development carried out under public auspices by the two countries; and obviously it is only by agreement and concerted action between the two countries that such a development can be undertaken.
But, as already intimated, this is not all; there .is, in addition to the economic advant ages, the much more important consideration affecting the status of the treaties and conventions between the two countries. For the adoption of the proposed joint project as an international policy would, it is conceived, be calculated to obviate many occasions for public dissatisfaction and misunderstanding that on the one side or the other might otherwise arise from time to time in respect of private exploitations of the uses of these waters. Unquestionably these uses are becoming more and more regarded as public uses, and it follows that the responsibility for their development should be undertaken, and the benefits of such development enjoyed, by the public. Indeed, for this reason and in view of the other considerations here adduced the Canadian Government is trongly convinced that nothing should be allowed to prejudice the chance of such a comprehensive power development of the St. Lawrence waters, and so far as its consent may be necessary, it will, therefore,

toe unable to sanction further private enterprise of this nature.

REPATRIATION OF CANADIANS IN IMPERIAL SERVICE.
speechtext:
A number of young Canadians who enlisted in the Imperial service under an arrangement with the Canadian Government are now being discharged from the Imperial service in England. I received a letter this morning in connection with one case where a young man went over from Canada in 1915, was wounded early in 1916, and went back to his regiment after his recovery. The regiment was sent to India and the young man arrived back in England late in March, was discharged on the 8th of April, and left England on his own resources. No provision has been made for his getting back to Canada; he may return as best he can, and without any remuneration for the delay. It seems to me that this is a situation that should call for some action on the part of
the Government with a view at least to doing justice to these young men.
Major-General MEWBURN (Minister of Militia):	About ten days ago I learned
that some Canadians who had joined the Imperial forces were desirous of getting back to Canada and were unable to make the necessary arrangements for transportation. These included some flying corps officers. I transmitted a cable to the overseas minister requesting him to arrange with the War Office for the immediate repatriation-at the Canadian Government's expense, the cost to be charged back to the Imperial account-of Canadians who were in the Imperials for discharge. I also transmitted to the War Office a request that Canadians who had joined the Imperials and had been granted commissions-a large number of men from our universities got commissions in the Imperials-be given the privilege of taking their discharge and returning to Canada; and that arrangements be made for their repatriation. The overseas minister replies that he has 'taken the matter up with the War Office and will use every endeavour to see 'that this request is complied with.
