speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the Committee rose last night, we had reached clause 14, which was being considered subsection by subsection. We had reached subsection 6.
On section 14, subsection 6-security:
Amendment (Mr. Jacobs) agreed to.
Subsection as amended agreed to.
On subsection 7-security to be kept in force:

Did I understand the minister to state yesterday that he had received no complaints against this Bill 
from boards of trade, municipal councils, or Provincial Governments? Is it not a fact that the premier of the province of Quebec sent in a communication objecting to this Bill ?

No protest from any Provincial Government has come before me. Copies of this Bill, as it left the special committee last year, were submitted to the Provincial Governments, and it is possible that the premier's objection may have been sent to some other department of the Government. I will make inquiries about it.

What certainty have we that these bonds will be kept in force? A good bondsman to-day may be absolutely worthless as a bondsman to-morrow. I think we should provide that the security shall be continuous.

The intention certainly is that the security shall be continuous. Subsection 4 provides:
No authorized trustee shall accept any assignment or trust or execute any duties under this Act unless and until he has given security to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council, hy bonds or otherwise, executed to His Majesty as represented by such departmental officer as may be designated by the Governor in Council, for due accounting and' for payment over and transfer of all moneys and (Property received by him as such trustee.
No trustee is permitted either to accept or to execute any assignments unless the security is there. I assume that the officer who is designated will see to it that the bonds are kept renewed from time to time. A trustee would not be entitled to act if he was in default of his security. I do not know that it is usual to provide that the security shall be continued in force, but perhaps a clause might be added that if for any reason the security lapses the trustee shall be disqualified. But I think the inference that the security must be maintained is very plain.

I certainly think that the courts of the provinces would be able to handle this better than the Governor in Council. I do not know what definite knowledge the Governor in Council could have, of a bondsman in British Columbia or the Yukon, for instance. The Governor in Council would not be able to get the information from a remote place as expeditiously as the courts. I do not wish to interfere very much with this Bill, but it does seem to me that if any function at all in connection with this Act is to be discharged by the courts, it is the approval of the bonds. In case of default, the most expeditious and convenient way would be

to apply to one of the judges of the provinces to have another bondsman substituted, so that this machinery might be kept in proper shape.

I do not quite agree that that would be the most convenient way. I am satisfied that there is some official of the Government to-day who deals with the approval of security much more expeditiously than any court could. I do not know just what department of the Government looks after this work, but securities are being passed on almost daily. Under subsection 4 some official has to be designated for the purpose of examining and accepting the security if approved. I fancy he will be familiar with all classes of security. I am satisfied that in practice the security will be that of a guarantee company. It may be that in some cases a private bond will be submitted, but I doubt very much whether the Government would accept a private bond. The Ontario Government does not. It used to, but now it will only accept the bond of a guarantee company. That has been found much more satisfactory, and I think that practice will be followed by the Dominion Government.
Why, then, does not the minister specify that it shall be the bond of a guarantee company?

The Bill does not insist on that. It says the bond shall be to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council. I am not sure that the Governor in Council has prescribed any particular form of bond in regard to the public service of Canada, but I know that in the vast majority of cases the security is in the shape of bonds of a guarantee company. In Ontario the only security that will be accepted in these cases is the bond of guarantee companies. What the rule is here I am not prepared to say at present, but it must be to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council. I have no doubt that the official designated under subsection 4 will see that the security is in proper form.

In the drafting of the Bill we thought we were making assurance doubly sure by providing in the next subsection that there shall be a double security-not only the original security of $10,000 but the security of each individual estate. I think the security has been made absolute.

Would not the fact that the Governor in Council is the custodian of the security indicate that the Government is the proper authority to release the security when it is assured that the obligations of the trustee have been fulfilled? It appears to me that the security is quite safe when deposited with the Governor in Council.
But the bond may or may not be good.

The Bill provides that the security will be absolute. It will be a trust company or bond company whose credit is beyond reproach. If the suggestion of the hon. member were followed the court sitting in the district would give orders to the security holders in Ottawa to release the funds, and we would have the anomaly of the smaller commanding the greater body. The fact that the security is with the Governor in Council seems to me to lay the onus on the Governor in Council to see that the bonds are not released until all funds have been paid over satisfactorily.

My hon. friend does not quite understand my objection. If the

minister will see that it is to be a guarantee company or some form of security that is absolutely permanent and secure, I have no fault to find. But my objection is that the Governor in Council may be imposed upon to accept a bond signed by two or three bondsmen who are not good, or who, though they may be all right to-day, may be insolvent themselves to-morrow. If I were looking for a bondsman in the town of Brantford I would very much prefer the hon. member's judgment than that of the Government as to whether or not that bondsman were satisfactory, because he would have specific knowledge.
I can assure the hon. member that the Government will see to it that the security is absolutely good and permanent.

I do not see anything in the Bill providing that in the event of the trustee's failure to carry out all his undertakings the security given to the registrar is to be turned over at once to the substituted trustee. iSubsection 8 has no reference to this matter. Perhaps it is in another part of the Bill, but II think it is the intention of the Bill that this security should be turned over to some person acting on behalf of the creditors.

I do not understand what my hon. friend means. There is a provision for the removal of a trustee. Section 15 provides:-
An authorized trustee may be removed and another substituted or an additional authorized trustee may foe appointed for cause, by the court.

That is not the question. The trustee when appointed is obliged to give a second security by bond or otherwise to the registrar that he will carry out his undertakings. Should he abscond with all the assets of the estate there is no provision whereby the new trustee can make application to the registrar for the payment of any security which the absconding trustee has put up.
It is to be assumed that if there is a shortage or default the registrar can enforce the bond.
For the benefit of the creditors?
Yes.

That is the spirit of the Bill, but I do not see any clear provision to that effect. Of course, it is clearly understood that the creditors have no interest in 
the first security of $10,000. That will be turned over to the Secretary of State or some proper official and will form part of the consolidated revenue" fund for that year. It is with regard to the second security I am inquiring.

Does my hon. friend
suggest that the clause should go further, and say that the registrar shall enforce the bond for the benefit of the estate?
Yes.
That is a necessary implication. We need not express it in language, but I have no objection to doing so. Otherwise there would be no object in the bond.
It properly comes under subsection 8.

I think that the position taken by the Solicitor General is absolutely correct. These official bonds are given to the officers of the court and the officers of the court, on default, by order of the court, will sue on the bonds for the moneys which, upon recovery, are paid to the credit of the estate. That is the practice in regard to official bonds of that description. We have very many cases of that kind and there has never been any difficulty in working it out in a practical way. It would not be necessary to add the clause suggested by the hon. member (Mr. Jacobs). It seems to be sufficiently stated in the clause in the Bill. The bond can be enforced by the officers of the court subject to the direction of the court.

We might add the words:
And the said bonds shall be enforceable by the registrar for the benefit of the said estate.

The section specifically says that the bond:
For the due accounting and payment over and transfer of all moneys and properties received or to be received by him as such trustee in respect of the estate of such debtor.
You might as well put a clause in stating that in the event of default you should have power to collect the bond. It is absolutely unnecessary.

But the registrar is the
officer of the court and if the money is recovered by him, without any specific instruction, he may be obliged to turn it over to the provincial government or to the court proper. I think the suggestion made by the Solicitor General will be satisfactory.
Subsection agreed to.
On subsection 8-additional security to be given by trustee:

The amendment proposed would have to be made to this subsection and I think we had better let it stand until I have drafted the amendment.
Subsection 8 allowed to stand.
On subsection 9-meeting to be called if security not given:
Read.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If it be the desire of the Committee that I read the clauses, I am quite willing to do so, but, as the Bill consists of some 66 pages and has already been considered by a special committee, I do not think the Committee will ask the Chairman to do more than he is required to by the practice and the rules. According to May, page 369, the practice in England is:
The Chairman proceeds to read the number of each clause, which is thus brought under the consideration of the committee.
Bourinot, page 522, says:
The chairman usually calls out the number of each clause, and reads the marginal note, but he should give the clause at length when it is demanded by the committee.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It must be demanded by the Committee and not by one individual member. I am quite willing to meet the views of the Committee, and if the Committee so desires, I shall read the clauses.
We like to hear your voice, Mr. Chairman.

After the consideration of this Bill was commenced, I noticed that six or seven clauses were disposed of inside of five minutes. This is a very important Bill and the members have the right to have the clauses read in order that they can follow them properly. It is important legislation.
-The CHAIRMAN: Is it the desire of the Committee that the clauses shall be read?
Yes.
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: In my opinion the nays have it.

As the Chairman is not reading the clauses, I suppose the members will have to read them in the presence of the Committee so that we will hear what the clauses are and have some conception
of their consecutive order and effect. It is impossible to enact laws by reading the numbers of clauses or the marginal notes. We are warned in the Interpretation Act that no Act is to be interpreted by the marginal note. It is almost impossible to understand a clause, paragraph, or subsection by reading the numbers 8, or 7, or 5. While I fully agree with the Chair that he should not always read the clauses, I think that when there is a specific demand for the reading of any one clause, the Chairman should exercise his discretion and read it. This clause is:
Unless the creditors, either at the first meeting, or at a meeting convened by notice-

That is subsection 8.
We are now at subsection 9.

Very well; subsection 9 reads:
Should the trustee be unable or fail to give the security required, in the manner and within the time hereinbefore provided, he shall within ten days from the expiration of the said thirty days, by notice in writing, convene a meeting of creditors for the purpose of appointing a new authorized trustee, and should he neglect or refuse to call such meeting, he shall be guilty of an offence and subject to the penalties provided by this Act.
That seems to be all right.

Provided the
trustees fail to perform that duty, who is punishable; what is going to happen?
There are penalties.
There are penalties, but penalties will not help matters. Is there any other provision for calling a meeting and electing a trustee?
Yes, there is provision for calling the creditors together and electing a new trustee.

On subsection 11-security surrendered:

I understand that under our constitution this Parliament has the right to legislate as to insolvency and bankruptcy, but the right of the 'Federal Parliament is limited to anything outside of civil rights. Everything that appertains to civil rights is given by our constitution to the province^, and if this Parliament should legislate concerning civil rights in Quebec I do not think the law would be constitutional.

The hon. gentleman was not in the House last night when I gave the leading authority on the question at issue. It has been held by the judicial 
committee of the Privy Council in a number of cases that while it is to some extent an infringement upon the rights of property and civil rights in the various provinces, the fact that power has been conferred upon the Federal Parliament to pass legislation in respect to bankruptcy- and insolvency, confers upon it the further -right to take any incidental steps that may be necessary, or to infringe upon civil rights or property rights in so far as it may be necessary to give effect to bankruptcy and insolvency legislation, but no further. The case that is the leading case on the subject arose thirty or forty years ago in the province of Quebec, and it was specifically decided when, under the Insolvency Act of 1875, the defence was set up in a particular case that certain provisions of the Act were an infringement upon property and civil rights in the province of Quebec. On section 40, subsection (1)-remuneration of trustee:

Provision is made in the Act that general meetings may be called by the trustee at any time he thinks fit, or by order of the inspectors. In the notice calling the meeting, it is not necessary for the trustee to specify the purpose for which the meeting is being called. A couple of creditors attend and vote whatever remuneration to the trustee they see fit. In such an important matter as this, proper notice should be given to the creditors of the purpose for which the meeting i3 called. I would ask the Solicitor General to consider' this subsection with a view of drafting an amendment to provide for such notice.

At the first meeting of creditors there is generally a fairly good representation of creditors, and general directions are given for the management or winding up of the estate. At that time no one knows what the estate is going to realize or what amount of trouble the trustee will have; consequently, the remunere tion of the trustee is seldom fixed at the first meeting of creditors. The difficulty is to get an attendance of creditors at all at the next meeting; the dividend as a rule, i3 so small that there is no inducement to them to come. In general practice the first meeting is the only meeting of creditors; the subsequent meetings are meetings of inspectors. This section provides that the creditors, or, in default of the creditors, the inspectors, may decide the amount of the trustee's remuneration. This provision is almost identical with the Ontario Act in respect to assignments and preferences. If we were sure that the creditors would attend and that a majority would vote the salary or remuneration, all well and good; but they will not attend.

Subsection (2) provides that the remuneration of a trustee shall be limited to five per cent. If he wants to get more than five per cent he should get it at a meeting at which a majority of the creditors are represented. If he wants to get that extra remuneration he must arrange that the creditors be present at that meeting in person or by proxy, and those creditors should know what they are to vote for. Otherwise, he will get the remuneration fixed by the Act.

This matter dealt with in this clause has been the subject of a great deal of-shall I say-malfeasance in office by assignees and inspectors. In my experi-

ence, assignees and inspectors sit down and simply vote themselves a large remuneration. The creditors, as the Solicitor-General has said, in anticipation of a small dividend, do not pay much attention to the matter. We hould curb the generosity to themselves of these gentlemen. The words " or of any creditor " should be struck out so that the subsection will read:
The trustee in bankruptcy or in authorized assignment proceedings shall receive such remuneration as shall be voted to him by the creditors at any general meeting, or by the inspectors in case the creditors fail to provide therefor, subject to review by the court upon application of the trustee.
I would like to see the court review the remuneration which the trustee is to get.
Why should not the creditor apply for a review by the court?
In practice, the creditor does not apply, and we have to protect the creditor against excessive charges oil the part of the trustee or his inspectors.
That is what this clause proposes to do. If the creditors vote too much to the trustee, a single creditor may go to the court and say that it is too much.

I want to put the boot on the other foot. I want the trustee to satisfy the court, whether the creditor takes any action or not, that the remuneration which he votes to himself or receives by the assistance of the inspector is a proper one. The remuneration should have the approval of the court before it is payable, for the very reason suggested by the Solicitor General- that the creditors do not pay any particular attention to the estate after the assignment has been made. It is all left to the inspectors, and the inspectors are very often appointed by, the trustee himself, in this way:	The trustee, or the assignee as we
now call him, . having a majority of the' creditors' claims in his hands, writes to the creditors or gets their proxies and appoints John Brown and William Smith, friends of his, as inspectors. Very often it is a conspiracy between the assignee and inspectors to pay themselves large fees which they have not earned. I want the trustee to satisfy the court, in the absence of any action taken by the creditors themselves, that his remuneration is reasonable.

Suppose the creditors or the inspectors say to the trustee: " We are going to give you a very small amount." Why should he not have the right to go to the court? The creditors may give too much or too little. I think the remedy 
should be reciprocal; if either party is dissatisfied, let him have the matter reviewed by the court. I do not anticipate any difficulty, because the next section, I think, will be the guiding section.

The point made by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. McLean), I think, is well taken. Many creditors may not be present at the meeting at which the remuneration is fixed, as they may not have known the matter was coming up. Would it not be well to provide for notice being given that the matter of remuneration will be considered at the meeting?

I quite agree that the notice should state that the remuneration will be considered at the meeting, but I would not like to see the trustee bound to get a majority value of the creditors there, because in many cases it might be impossible. If they took any interest in the matter, the notice would bring them. I think the majority of the creditors present should have the right to fix the remuneration. As to the contention that the creditors should not be allowed to appeal to the court, I think they should; the trustee should also be allowed to appeal if he thinks his remuneration unsatisfactory.

I do not know that the inspector should have anything to say about the remuneration of the trustee. I think the subsection would be improved by striking out of line 20 the words " or by the inspectors in case the creditors fail to provide therefor."

There is another reason why the trustee, in the absence of any action taken by the creditors, should satisfy the court that his remuneration is reasonable. This Act is passed in the interest of the debtor as well as the creditor. Now the debtor is not protected unless the court passes on the remuneration.

The amendment seems quite satisfactory except that it does not provide for notice being given that the matter of remuneration will be discussed at the meeting. All hon. members seem to agree that that should be included.
I honestly think we are making a little too much out of this. The remuneration fixed by the creditors is subject to review by the court upon application of the trustee or of any creditor.

Our experience has been that in a number of cases, estates have

When the House adjourned on Wednesday preceding the Easter recess, it was understood that on going into Supply on the Post OflSce Estates we would discuss the principle of the motion I had introduced earlier in the session concerning certain amendments to the Post Office Act, the desirability of which is only too apparent. In order that my hon. friend (Mr. Rowell) may appreciate the situation, I shall first of all read what the

hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), minister of I don't know what department, said on that occasion in answer to my hon. friend from Antigonish (Mr. Sinclair) and myself :
I should like to have the opportunity of giving consideration to this matter and of bringing it before my colleagues and if my hon. friend will bring up the subject again, say on the Post Office Estimates, I should then be in a position to give the view of the Government.
So I avail myself of this opportunity of discussing with the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) this important question of enacting more drastic legislation respecting the daily and the weekly press, periodicals, etc.
This question came up on various occasions before the western conventions last year and two years ago. Indeed, the resolution which I put on the Order Paper was simply a copy of the resolution which had been adopted by the Grain Growers of Alberta, if I mistake not. It read as follows:
That in the opinion of this House all newspapers, magazines, trade journals and other periodicals publishing articles designed to influence public opinion shall be compelled from time to time to publish sworn statements setting forth the names of the owners, managers, editors, stockholders, bondholders and of any other person having an! interest in such newspaper magazine, trade journal or other periodical.
We all realize that the press in this and every other country wields an enormous power. Indeed, when one can control the press, he may to a certain extent control for the time being public opinion. The weapon is a most dangerous one. It may constitute a beneficent power provided it is not corrupt. Unfortunately, in this country, as in the United States and in some countries of Europe, not excepting England, the press has not always lived up to its primary function, which is to enlighten public opinion and to exercise a proper control over the several constituencies. The other day when I brought this matter before the House I gave as an example of the evil influence of lax legislation in regard to the press the camouflaging of a paper by its proprietor in such a way as to make it appear to be speaking for one party whilst it was really speaking for the opposite party. That has actually happened in the good city of Montreal in the case of the Montreal Herald, a century-old paper, which has had for its directors and editors the most remarkable writers of the English-speaking minority in Lower Canada,-a history of the last century could not be made complete without referring to the files of the Montreal Herald. It so happened that during a period of at least fifty years the Montreal Herald was the accredited organ of the English-speaking Liberal minority in the .province of Quebec. It had, besides, a large constituency outside of Montreal, and with the '.exception of the Montreal Witness, which was by far the most respectable paper we had in this country, it wielded perhaps the greatest influence.
Unfortunately it fell into the hands of a certain Mr. Brierly, who obtained control of it through tricks that were mean and ways that were dark, and after the elections of 1911, as it was perhaps easier to swim with the current, he made a bargain with the managers of the Tory party, into whose hands it passed, although for a while it kept the appearance of its primeval honesty and virginity, and the change of ownership was known but by few. It was heralded as the organ of the Liberal party in the district oi Montreal. Some of us know that some very prominent gentlemen in the Tory party had control of it, but the paper masqueraded as a Liberal organ. Finally it passed directly into the hands of Mr. McGibbon, a prominent Conservative in the district of Montreal, who had some tramway and power schemes of his own. But he thought it was more profitable for him to sell the paper outright to Lord Atholstan, then Sir Hugh Graham. Sir Hugh Graham, who is a keen business man, did not want in the field any rival of the Montreal Star, and therefore considered it politic to maintain the Montreal Herald as an ostensible rival, the Herald getting the skim milk and the Star the cream. The Star was the organ of the Conservative party and had a large circulation, while the Herald was as insignificant as a paper could be. It published four pages, while the Star issued twenty-five, thirty and forty pages. Yet that lean and insignificant journal, the Herald, was represented as the organ of the Liberal party. Some of us, though only a few, knew perfectly well that the Herald was the property of Sir Hugh Graham. But, sometimes the saying "there is honour -among thieves" is falsified, and a case before the criminal court in Montreal gave us the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, and it was proven that the -Star and the Herald were the property of Lord Atholstan and that the Herald was kept in the field merely as a camouflage, and that it was not the organ of the Liberal party but the instrument by which Lord Atholstan endeavoured to pre-

vent any other enterprising journalist from establishing a paper in the interests of the honest Liberal party in Quebec. I may say that since then the Herald has been released, so to speak, and has become the property of Mr. Leitbead, who wrote me the other day protesting against the suggestion that the Herald was the property of any other person than himself, and affirming that it was now really an independent journal. I must give him the benefit of his declaration; I believe it is now an independent paper. I have read it since Mr. Leithead became the owner, and I do not think it has any more connections with its former proprietor, Lord Atholstan. This merely to show the tricks that can be played on the public by some enterprising gentlemen, and how dangerous a weapon a newspaper may become in the hands of an unscrupulous editor.
I have another case in mind. In 1904 my hon. friends' friends, Mackenzie and Mann, undertook to defeat the Laurier Government, and the first thing they did was to obtain the control of a certain paper in Montreal having a large circulation, which fact was pretty well known. But this evil is not peculiar to Canada. I am sorry to say that in England it prevails and has been detected. I have a pamphlet published in the United States, and it should not be necessary to refer to it because the facts to which I shall allude are well known to every member of the Committee. We all know that during the last general elections in Great Britain the great " dope " or Cellulose scandal was uncovered, and a close investigation of that scandal might perhaps have caused some heartburnings in Great Britain on the part of several gentlemen of world repute. The London Chronicle was one of the old standard papers of Great Britain. Its influence, moral and otherwise, was very great, and its editor Mr. Robert Donald-a good Scotch name-enjoyed the highest reputation throughout the continent. Indeed, his articles and reviews of current events were read in every Chancellery on the continent. But one morning the world was apprised of startling .facts. On October 5, 1918, the London Globe announced that Lord Beaverbrook, whose friends were hopelessly involved in the scandal, had been trying to buy the Chronicle for some time, and that the alleged purchaser, Sir Henry Dalziel, represented him and others. The immediate resignation, October 5, of Mr. Robert Donald, who for twenty years had been managing editor and for seven years managing director of the Chronicle, follow-

ing his exposure of the Walter Long-Colonel Grant Morden, or Marden, letter and its bearing on the "dope" scandal, astonished all Fleet street, yet no reference to the " dope " scandal has been published in America in connection with the sale of the Chronicle.
The New York Times, October 5, the date of the sale, published the following comparatively innocent cable dispatch from London:
Commenting on the sale of the Daily Chronicle, the Westminster Gazette points out that the sale of the newspaper cannot he considered on the same level as the sale of a butter business, as men who can command millions have learned how they can use these millions to sway public opinion. The London Globe says widespread regret will be felt beyond the confines of Fleet Street at the news of the sale. We do not even know who the new proprietors are, though some time ago it was stated that the ubiquitous Lord Beaverbrook was endeavouring to acquire our contemporary.
We nevertheless sincerely regret the transaction because under the editorship of Robert Donald the Daily Chronicle has acquired a remarkable position as a fearless and independent organ representing the best side of liberalism, while rigidly avoiding infection and defeatism, and subordinating every minor issue to victory.
The Chronicle has been fearless in attacking financial scandals in which prominent politicians were implicated. The National News sees in the transfer a disquieting attack on the influence and independence of the press.
The Editor and Publisher (New York), October 19, 1919, in a statement dated London, October 16, declares: "Announcement of the purchase of the London Daily Chronicle coming without any preliminary indication, caused the biggest sensation in Fleet Street since the announcement of Lord Northcliffe's coup giving him possession of the Times. Negotiations for the transfer were conducted so quietly that even Robert Donald was completely surprised by the announcement. He resigned immediately."
You can see that even in old merrie England, so Conservative in her traditions, so honourable in her transactions, there are, as unfortunately there have been in the United States and in Canada as well, editors who will sell their pens for a mess of pottage. I drew the attention of the House the other day to the evil influence which to my mind such a state of affairs can produce in the country. It creates demoralization and it certainly leads to revolution. If the plain people of this country begin to realize that the press can be bought, as it has been bought, they wall also believe that the public men can be bought and can be controlled. It is an evil day for Canada when that impression gains ground and, unfortunately, it has gained ground.

I have said fearlessly and I repeat this evening it was a scandal that on one given day, and before the elections of 1917, the whole of the Liberal press in the province of Ontario made at right about turn.

Oh, oh!
Mr. LEM I El iX: There are honourable exceptions. I have one in my mind especially; the London Advertiser remained true to its traditions, and there are others. What has disgusted the public, Mr. Chairman, and made it apprehensive and what has caused it to believe that this is really a true state of affairs, is that at the same time Sir Clifford Sifton and Mackenzie and Mann were closeted at the Chateau Laurier here in Ottawa and Parliament was rushing through the Canadian Northern deal. It was passed under closure because these things must be expedited, and they were expedited.
The hon. gentleman mentions the change in the press of Ontario. Does he want the Committee to understand that it was due to corruption?

My hon. friend has listened to what I have said. I think I have been more severe even than the statement he is making now. I think he is very mild. Would you believe, Mr. Chairman, tnat in a certain city not far from Ottawa, where certain papers had in their constituencies Liberals and Conservatives alike, Liberal candidates were obliged to pay for the report of a political meeting? At that particular moment the whole of the press of Canada was plastered with placards insulting the late leader of the Liberal party, and insulting his native province, in order to stir up the feelings oi the people of Canada for the " unity " of the Dominion. Who paid for these advertisements? Who paid, Mr. Chairman? We know just half of the truth. My hon. friend who sits beside me (Mr. J. H. Since August 4, 1915, and before 1917. We only know half the truth yet. We do not know what has been paid by Order in Council. We do not know what amount has been spent by the President of the Privy Council in his new department.
Will the hon. gentleman give us a specific instance of the wrong advertising which ha.s been carried on so that we may get a clear grip of the situation?

I have a collection of the placards which were so freely plastered in all the newspapers of Canada with the exception of those of one province. I keep those placards as a memento for future generations and for future reference. If my hon. friend, who is fair-minded, were to read to-day what was published in the press of Canada during the months that preceded the elections in 1917, he would blush with shame for his country, because he loves Canada as I do. Do not believe, Mr. Chairman, that it is a pleasure for me to bring this matter before the Committee and before the country. I am doing my duty as a public man and doing it fearlessly, knowing that I shall probably receive, as I have already received, an avalanche of attacks from the press of this country. But we are not here to exchange bouquets only; we are here to speak the truth and nothing but the truth; and I want the Canadian Parliament to do what the United States Congress has done, in order, if possible, to put a stop to such a state of things in the interests of the good name of Canada. Now what is the privilege enjoyed by the press of Canada? By chapter 9 of the Statute 45 Victoria, we give the newspapers and the periodicals of this country a very great privilege. Let me read the preamble and the first clause of that statute:

To encourage and facilitate the dissemination of useful information in Canada, Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:-
(1) On and after the first day of June in the present year one thousand eight hundred and eighty-two, newspapers and periodicals printed and published in Canada, mailed by the publisher in the post office at the place where they are published and addressed to regular subscribers or news dealers in Canada, resident elsewhere than in the place of publication, shall be transmitted by mail to their respective addresses free of postage: Provided, that in order to be entitled to such free transmission, the publication for which it is claimed must conform to the following conditions:-
1.	It must be known and recognized as a newspaper or periodical in the generally received sense of the word, and published regularly at intervals of not more than one month:
2.	The full title, place and date of publication, and the distinguishing number of the issue must be printed at the top of the first page, and also on any paper purporting to be a supplement to it, and sent with it:
3.	It must be addressed to a bona fide subscriber, or to a known newsdealer in Canada.
In 'the same Statute the powers of the Postmaster General for preventing an evasion of the said conditions are enumerated. It will be apparent that ,the press obtains at the expense of the public exchequer a very important privilege. If we wish to mail a newspaper to a friend it will cost us one cent-during the period of the war that postage has been .two cents-but a newspaper can mail a paper to one of its subscribers free of postage. Now let us see what that privilege means in dollars and cents. My hon. friend (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) put certain questions on the Order Paper not long ago, and those questions were answered as follows:
1.	What was the gross postal revenue derived from newspapers for the year 1918?

2.	What is the estimated expenditure for the same year in so far as newspapers are concerned?
A. The department has no data on which a close estimate of the expenditure involved in handling newspapers can be made, except that newspapers make up about sixty-five Per cent of the bulk of the mails. The total expenditure for the carriage of mails and the cost of mail bags during the fiscal year 1918 is $8,293,515.24.
3.	What is the average daily weight of newspapers carried in the mails?
A. 239,731 pounds.
Now, sixty-five per cent of the total cost amounts to $5,390,784, and we only received from the newspapers $291,539. If this sum is subtracted from the other amount it will be seen that the press of Canada is very heavily indebted to the exchequer of this country, and we therefore have the right

to expect that that press will re-
9 p.m. spect the privilege which is given to it by this Parliament. What has been done in the United States, where they have suffered from -the same evil? In the country to the south they have adopted the following law, of which my resolution is practically a synopsis:
That it shall be the duty of the editor, publisher, business manager, or owner of every newspaper, magazine periodical or other publication to file with the Postmaster General and the postmaster at the office >at which said publication is entered, not later than the first day of April and the first day of October of each year, on blanks furnished by the Post Office Department, a sworn statement setting forth the names and post office addresses of the editor and managing editor, publisher, business managers, and owners, and, in addition, the stockholders, if the publication be owned by a corporation; and also the names of known bondholders, mortgagees, or other security holders; and also, in the case of daily newspapers, there shall be included in such statement the average of the number of copies of each issue of such publication sold or distributed to paid subscribers during the preceding six months:
And there is a proviso that this drastic law shall not apply to religious, fraternal, temperance and scientific publications. But the United States Congress went even further and exacted from every newspaper editor that:
All editorial or other reading matter published in any such newspaper, magazine or periodical, for the publication of which money or other valuable consideration is paid, accepted or promised, shall be plainly marked " advertisement." Any editor or publisher printing editorial or other reading matter for which compensation is paid, accepted or promised, without so marking the same, shall, upon oonviction in any court having jurisdiction, he fined not less than $50 nor more than $500.
Those, Mr. Chairman, are the two amendments which were made to the post office laws in the United States to cure the press of that country of the gangrene which there, as here, was infecting its vitals. Is there any fair-minded gentleman in this 'House who has the honour of his country at heart, and respects his fellow citizens of whatever creed, race or political affiliation, who will object to similar legislation here?
In my younger days I was a journalist myself, and I compare an editor to a school teacher-and when I look at my good friend from Toronto (Mr. Hocken) I am inclined to say that I compare him to a preacher, for, indeed, he was a preacher during the last general election. The editor of the Orange Sentinel was not satisfied with writing vitriolic, evangelical editorials against French Canadians and Roman

Catholics, but he had to take the pulpit and preach to the faithful in the name of the Lord in order to retain in power the masters of the Administration,-Sir Joseph Fla-velle, Sir Clifford Sifton and Mackenzie and Mann. I remember an incident men-, tioned in the history of the French Revolution, Mr. Chairman. A lady who played an important part in that revolution, Madame Roland, was, like many others, sent to the guillotine-as perhaps, if the wave of Bolshevism reaches Canada many editors will he. On her way to the	guillotine as she passed
near the statue of Liberty she stopped for one moment, and, bowing reverently before the statue, exclaimed, "O Liberty, how many crimes are committed in thy name!" And when I read that the editor of the Orange Sentinel and my good friend the member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol), addressed the faithful from the pulpit in Toronto, I paraphrased the words of Madame Roland: O Religion, how many crimes are committed in thy name! Indeed, the press and pulpit during the last general election were strong for the Tory party, but I notice of late that some of the millionaire Methodists of Toronto are protesting against the Methodist church issuing a political platform. Mr. Parsons delivered an address the other day and said: "I will take my religion from the conference, but not my politics on the tariff issue; and if I am going to be lectured by my minister on the tariff issue, w ell, I may not continue a member of the church." It is the old story, Mr. Chairman,-the chickens are coming home to roost.
But I am asking seriously if any one would oppose the amendments which I suggest by this resolution. Once more I say that the editor is to be compared to the schoolmaster. The school-master is surrounded by the most drastic legislation so that he may be worthy of his class and his students imbibe what really education should give to them. And the editor should be as closely safeguarded by Parliament-protected, so to speak, against himself, and thereby his constituency, the larger class, the public, also protected. The United States have declared that the backers of newspapers shall be known; and if we had had similar legislation here, when Lord Atholstan got control of a newspaper in Montreal the public would know that it was he and not Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his party. I hope the Government will accept my resolution and will bring down during the present session the necessary legislation to cure an evil
which, unfortunately, exists in Canada to-day.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. SINCLAIR (Antigonish and Guysborough):
speechtext:
I had the honour of seconding the motion when this question was up for discussion in the House a few days ago, and I may be permitted to say a few words in reference to it. What is asked for is publicity, and it seems to me that there can be no reasonable objection to the acceptance of the proposal of the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux).
We were crowded for time to discuss this question when it was brought up just before the Easter holidays, and the acting minister then suggested that the present would be the appropriate time to deal with it because it would involve an amendment to the Post Office Act. The chief reason, I suppose, for making the proposed regulation an amendment to the Post Office Act is the convenience of enforcing it. The owners or publishers who refused to comply with 'that regulation could be deprived of the use of the mails. I do not say that the press of this country is mercenary; I have a little more respect for it than that. But some very sudden conversions have taken place especially in Western Canada and have not been clearly explained. We have it on the authority of an ex-minister of the Crown, a very prominent man in this House and in this country who has had large experience, as a member of this Government, that there is such a thing as "sweetening" the press. In Nova Scotia, at the last general election, we had a fund which was popularly known as the "slush fund." It was in the hands of a prominent gentleman in Halifax who supported the Unionist movement and was available to any newspaper in Nova Scotia that would publish Unionist propaganda in its editorial columns. Large rates were offered to the newspapers for this purpose, and while some of the old Liberal newspapers remained true to their allegiance, others of them yielded to the temptation and accepted the money. This fund, I understand, was not confined to Nova Scotia; it was common to the whole Dominion. It would be very interesting to know where this "slurti fund" came from and how much it amounted to-but we have not yet been told. I do not think it can be successfully denied that a great many of the newspapers have abandoned their time-honoured place of the defenders of the interests of the public and have become mere organs of the present Government. They are no longer newspapers but merely party

organs, they do not even tell the public the things that happen. If you read the accounts of what takes place in this Chamber, you will find that very 'little is made public that reflects on the Government, and that many things are omitted that ought to be reported. Of course, that may occasionally be accidental, but it is very marked in the case of certain newspapers that are supporting the present Administration. I think it was last autumn that some ministers made a trip to the Pacific coast and certain things happened out there, at Vancouver and elsewhere, that found no place in the eastern newspapers. We discovered them later, but they were not among the press despatches. Very little publicity was given to the disclosures that were made at St. Johns Quebec, last summer; they were hardly mentioned in many of the prominent eastern newspapers supporting the Union Government. The speech of my late honoured leader at London, Ontario, was not reported in the eastern papers; and that was a very marked incident. A few weeks after that, an interview given by Hon. Walter Scott in which he announced that he was withdrawing his support from the Union Government did not appear in many of the eastern papers. Now, there was a time when things like this did not happen; when these items would be welcome as a matter of news, but at the present time in many newspapers matters of that kind are suppressed.
There also appears to be a great reluctance on the part of the Government to give to the members of the House information in regard to money that has been paid to newspapers. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) drew attention to the fact that during the last few years over $2,000,000 had been paid out to Canadian newspapers in advertising-and that is not at all a complete statement. He mentioned also the fact that the country is every year contributing some $5,000,000 for carrying the newspapers in the mails. We are contributing $50,000 per year to the Press Association. The statement was made by the member for Sherbrooke (Mr. MoCrea) a few days ago that a million and a half dollars were being contributed to the publishers by the manufacturers of paper under some regulation made by the present Administration with regard to the price of print paper. So that it would appear that we are making very large concessions to the press, and that gives us a right to demand publicity in regard to the ownership of the newspapers.

I said that there was a great deal of reluctance on the part of the Government to give information in regard to the payment of money to the newspapers. When an hon. gentleman asks a simple question regarding the amount of money that has been expended for any special purpose, he naturally expects a prompt answer; but he does not get that kind of answer when the question relates to the amount of money paid to the press. Let me give you a few instances. On March 31, the member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx) put the following question:
During the year ending March 26, 1919, what amounts were paid by the Government for advertising to the following papers: Dundalk Herald, E'lesherton Advance, Markdale Standard, Durham Chronicle, Hanover Post, and Grey (Durham) Review?
Now, that is a very simple question, and you would expect the minister to instruct one of his clerks to find out how much money had been paid to these small newspapers, and to give the answer. But he does not do that; he puts it down as an order for return. That is only a sample brick. Some time ago the member for Fron-tenae (Mr. Edwards) asked the following question:
What amount was paid to the Ottawa Journal and the Ottawa Journal-Press for Government printing, advertising and job work from 1S96 to 1911 inclusive?
What amounts were paid to the Ottawa Journal and the Ottawa Journal-Press for Government printing, advertising and job work in each of the years: 1912, 1913, 1914, 1915, 1916, 1917 and 1918?
That also was put down as an order for return. Then, take another. On March 19, the member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx) asked the following question:
What amount, if any, was paid by the Government to the Halifax Herald for printing, advertising, joib or other work for each of the following five fiscal years: 1914, 1915, 1916, 1917, 1918?
That also was put down as an order for return. The same day the hon. gentleman (Mr. Proulx) asked what amount had been paid by the Government to the Toronto News for printing and advertising; this also was put down as an order for return. He inquired also what amount had been paid by the Government to the Toronto Mail and Empire for printing and advertising during five fiscal years, and that also was put down as an order for return. The Orders of the Day are full of cases of that kind. Information regarding the amounts paid out in connection with the Victory Loan was also, denied to the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It must be quite obvious to my hon. friend why information of this kind should be submitted in the form of a return rather than in the form of a question. It involves replies to a series of questions concerning all departments of Government, of which there are a great many, covering a number of years and requiring a great deal of time to prepare. The information has not been delayed unnecessarily at all, but rather expedited. The answers to the questions with regard to the Halifax Herald and Mail have already been laid on the Table. I am sure my hon. friend will recollect that the practice in Parliament has always been in cases of this kind to ask for an order for a return.

I do not think my hon. friend will say that it is- purely a coincidence that every one of these questions has been put down as an order for a return. Some of these returns come very slowly. Questions were asked last session, more than a year ago, which were put down as orders for returns and have not been answered yet. Some of the questions asked covered a period of years, and others one year only; but in every case the Government denied us the information. The only explanation I can think of is that the Government are aware they have been paying altogether too much money to the papers. They have been attempting to corrupt the press-I do not say they have succeeded- and they are very anxious to conceal the facts. But I do not propose to discuss that phase of the question further.
My main purpose in rising is to ask the minister to consider the reasonableness of the proposal of my hon. friend from Maison-neuve. There are many reasons that could be urged in favour of accepting this proposal, and there is no strong reason against it. The proprietor who is conducting a respectable newspaper is doing a splendid work, and he will be glad to let the public know that he is the owner of such a paper. The man who is conducting a yellow journal that he is not very proud of, and which takes a course that cannot be approved by the public, will naturally want to conceal his identity; but we are not interested in a man like that. The proposal is a progressive one and ought to be accepted by the Government. It will increase the respect for truth. Slipshod exaggerated and untrue statements do more than anything else to destroy confidence in the press. If the ownership were made known, I submit that it would be a strong additional inducement to the
proprietor to exercise care. It would tend to eliminate the influence of the mercenary press, or at all events to make it harmless, by removing the mask of secrecy and showing the proprietor in his true colours. It would elevate the tone of the press, and place an additional handicap on what is known as yellow journalism. I submit, therefore, that it is in the public interest that this proposal should be adopted by the Government, and I respectfully invite the minister now in charge of the Post Office Estimates in this House to give the proposal his most serious consideration.

I should like to express my appreciation of ithe very high tribute paid to my versatility by the hon. member for Maisonneuve. He classes me as editor, school-teacher, and' preacher. Now that is a pretty wide range of public activities for one individual, especially when he happens to be also a member of Parliament. I make no pretensions to being a preacher, Mr. Chairman. If I were in some isolated spot where a real preacher could not be found I might make a few moral remarks for the benefit of the inhabitants, but that is not my forte; it is something I have never cultivated. Perhaps my hon. friend will be pleased to know that on that single occasion when I did occupy the pulpit after the regular service I made quite a hit with the congregation, who told me afterwards that my remarks were very much to the point, and. that as a consequence they thought Union *Government would get more votes. That, brief experience was not altogether unsatisfactory .to myself, however the hon. member *may regard it. Unfortunately, the collection was taken up before I spoke; they might have got a 'little more if they had; not taken it up till after.
What was the text?
My text was the preservation of civilization'and liberty.
By the Orange Sentinel.

It is a text that might *inspire any man, be he preacher or editor. I might say that I endeavoured to the best of my ability to use that text on the platform as well, when I had the assistance of the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol) who is no more adept at preaching than I am myself. I was interested to learn from the hon. member (Mr. Lemieux) *that $2,000,000 had been spent in advertising by the Government.

Mr. LEMIE'UX:	More, from what we
"know, but that is only half the truth.
IMr. HQCKEN: Perhaps he has forgotten that through the expenditure of that $2,000,000 this country was enabled to raise hundreds of millions of dollars in war loans, and to educate the people in regard to food *control and many other things. It was a perfectly legitimate expenditure, and I deny absolutely that it was of such a character as to influence any newspaper one way or the other. I do not think it had the effect 'of " sweetening," as the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) puts it, any newspaper in which these advertisements appeared. The hon. member for Maison-neuve couples that in a way with the expenditure in connection with the political campaign which is not altogether a fair thing to do, because they were from entirely different sources. I think those who were conducting the campaign prepared the copy for the newspapers, and it appeared very plainly as an advertisement. That was a commercial transaction in respect of which no complaints could be made against the newspapers; it was a perfectly legitimate and proper thing for the newspapers to do. In fact, some papers in our province printed one page favouring one party and another page favouring another-an amazing impartiality that perhaps other newspapers would have been just as willing to exercise if they had been offered the copy. There have been newspaper transactions in the city of Montreal, well known before they were revealed in the criminal court, which every person must condemn.

Hear, hear.
Mr. 'HOCKEN: No person will condemn them more vigorously or more sincerely than the men who are actively connected with the press. The purchase of one newspaper by another newspaper proprietor, and the continuance of that newspaper supposedly as the mouthpiece of the party to which the proprietor is 'opposed, can only be described as something discreditable. At least it is something that no decent newspaper man would attempt to condone for a moment.
Puck and Judge are both owned by one man.

But they are not influencing political opinion in the same way as the paper mentioned by my hon. friend. My friend from Maisonneuve about three weeks ago made some general remarks about the newspapers of Ontario, and one
,
of the principal papers there challenged him to name one Liberal journal in Ontario which declined to support the party in the last election and which had been bought. He has not named one, and will not. He will not name one outside of this House, and that is the test after all. 1 know that in my city the two principal Liberal newspapers-in fact there are only two daily Liberal newspapers there-are conducted by men of as much integrity as any hon. member. I know the men who publish both those newspapers, and up to 1917 they were as ardent Liberals as any man in Canada had been, and had rendered splendid service to the Liberal party. Their defection was not due to any "sweetening" nor to any purchase, but to the fact that they believed there was involved a principle which they had to maintain on their conviction. Any man who stands up and condemns a newspaperman for making a change of that kind because his convictions compelled him to do so, is guilty, 1 think, of an offence as bad as misrepresentation on the part of a paper.
Will my hon. friend permit me to say something here?
Yes.

I do not care to name any editor, but my friend is an hon. gentleman and whenever it pleases him to receive my confidence I will give him the name of a very prominent western journalist who, at the very time when the whole press was veering round, came to Sir Wilfrid Laurier's residence on Sunday and in my presence declared, with tears in his eyes that he had to quit the paper with which he was connected. That paper was published in the West, was a very prominent one and for many years had supported the Liberal party, but had just been acquired by a certain organization, and this man was told that unless he agreed to write against his leader and his party he would have to quit. I will give the name of that gentleman to my hon. friend whenever it pleases him to receive my confidence in this matter.
Mr. (HOCKEN: I do not know everything about the West-
I have given the precedent of the Herald.
-but I am speaking for the newspapers of Ontario. Some things may happen two 'thousand miles away of which I do not profess to know everything.
Distance makes no difference; there is the telegraph.
Was it the city of Toronto?
No, sir; not in the city of Toronto.
Winnipeg?

Winnipeg, says my hon. friend. Now, Mr. Chairman, we are all intelligent men; at least we are elected as such. What will the ordinary elector of the West think when it is known that Sir Clifford Sifton is the owner of the Winipeg Free Press, which supported Reciprocity in 1911, when Sir Clifford Sifton was the principal instrument in the defeat of reciprocity? What will the ordinary elector think of the association of the two names? That is precisely why I am advocating this change in the law.

I know that the defection of the principal papers in our province from the Liberal party in the last election was due absolutely to principle, and my information is that the same is true of practically every Liberal paper in Western Canada. We must remember that in the last election there was before the people of the country a question of principle that exceeded in importance any other in our history, and it is unjustifiable to condemn these men for a change in party allegiance at that time because they followed their patriotic impulses. The hon. member for Guysborough complains that the London speech of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier was not printed in the East. I do not know how far east of Ontario it was printed, but up our way the friends of the late Liberal leader complained that it was being printed too much. It was not only printed but reprinted in its essential parts, and its laudation of that noble race the German people, at the time they were devastating France and committing atrocities unparallelled in history, was something that the people in that part of the country did not want to see in print quite as often as it appeared. So that while my hon. friend from Guysborough may have a complaint against the papers in Nova Scotia I do not think he has any ground for complaint on that score as regards the papers in Ontario.
Is my hon. friend opposed to the proposal to amend the Post Office Act as indicated by the resolution?

I thought I would leave that for my peroration. I want to say a word for the newspapers, because there are
not many newspaper men on the floor, and we are a very respectable guild as a rule.
I do not like to see the newspaper men attacked without some reply, however inadequate it may be, from my lips. Complaint is made about the amount of money sipent in advertising. The value received from that advertising was two to three times what it cost, and some of these great public movements could not have been carried out without advertisement. It was only in this great emergency that the Government learned the truth of the old saying, which I am sure the hon. member for Maisonneuve has heard before, "It pays to advertise." It certainly paid the Government to advertise the Victory Loans, and the amount of advertising used brought results that any commercial man would be delighted to have at the same cost. Just a word to my hon. friend from Guysborough in regard to his complaint that these returns are too long coming down. I discovered among other things that in connection with a return which covers the different departments of the Government, it took three clerks seventeen days to get the information for that return from one department. That will indicate the amount of work there is in going through the files to get out every item asked for by a question that is on the Paper. I believe the Government is not to blame for that. As to the principal proposition that was laid down by the hon. member (Mr. Lemieux), I am quite in accord with it. I think the public interest would be served by something of that kind.
I thought that a. good preacher would come to my views.

I am not speaking now in my ministerial capacity but in my capacity as an editor. I think that while there have not been many abuses of that kind in Canadian journalism up to the present time, undoubtedly there have been some, and the way is open for a great many more. We are not rich enough in this country for that kind of thing but abuses of that kind have occurred in the United States. Personally, I would not object to seeing a law of that kind enacted; in fact, I would go further and I would make another suggestion for the consideration of my hon. friend. It would not be right for me to resume my seat without taking cognizance of further remarks by my hon. friend. The hon. gentleman has deliberately challenged the integrity of the press of Canada, and he has deliberately challenged the integrity of the press of my province. I want to hurl that challenge back to my hon. friend, and tell him that he dare not repeat outside this House, where proceedings could be taken against him, that challenge against the integrity of the press, or say there that

one of the leading Liberal papers of the province of Ontario was bought at the last election.

I was not dealing with what the hon. member for Red Deer said. I hold my hon. friend responsible for the words he uttered in this Chamber to-night. *He challenged the integrity of the press of Ontario. He said it could be bought and that it had been bought.
By advertisements.

I do not care by what means, I say the statement is absolutely false, and there is not a shadow of foundation to support it. There is no more upright press in this country than the press of Ontario. I want to say this for the whole press of Canada, and I will include in the statement the press of my hon. friend's province: No finer contribution has been made by any class of the community to the cause of Canada and the cause of civilization in the recent war than has been made by the press and by the public journals of Canada. From the outbreak of the war the press, more than some of 10 p.m. the public men of this country, realized the magnitude of the issue which faced the Canadian people. They did not hesitate to set clearly before the people the character of the issue and all that was involved in it. During the whole period of the war their columns have been filled with news gathered at great expense, because telegraphic and cable news was particularly expensive, in order that the Canadian people might be kept posted on 'the events occurring in the theatres of war, as well as in all the countries with which we were brought into touch by reason of the war. From the very commencement of that great struggle the press of Canada has served a most valuable public function in forming and shaping public opinion in the Dominion, and giving the news, without which public opinion would not have sustained the carrying on of the war. And a public man is not doing credit to himself, or to this House, who challenges the integrity of that great medium of public opinion, the 'Canadian press.
One or two words further with reference to the situation. My hon. friend (Mr. Le-mieux) said that at a given date the whole 
of the Liberal press of Ontario underwent a right-about-face, with the single exception of the London Advertiser.
'Mr. LEMIEUX: I said with a few honourable exceptions.

My hon. friend specially mentioned the London Advertiser. I say that statement is equally without foundation. The Liberal press of Ontario, for months prior to the date my hon. friend mentions, had been urging upon the Government of Canada more active and aggressive measures for the prosecution of the war. They had been urging that compulsory military service should be introduced in Canada, for without it we could not secure the necessary reinforcements. They had been urging upon the Government that the time had come-in fact, that the time had come long before-for the formation of a union or a national Government to unite the people of Canada for the vigorous prosecution of the war. When my hon. friend charges that the press sold itself I say there is no grander evidence in the history of this country, or in the history of any other country, of fidelity to high public purpose and noble national aspirations than was displayed by the Liberal newspapers of my province.
They stood by their principles, they stood by their convictions, they stood by what they believed to be the national interest to their own loss-because it meant the loss of subscribers and supporters when they could not necessarily carry all their friends with them in the course they took. They did not change their position. They declined to go back on their convictions, they declined to go back on the policy they had been advocating for months because the leader whom they would have been glad to support was unable to see his way clear to support the policy which they believed to be right. And, instead of charging those papers with having sold themselves, one should pay tribute to their fidelity to the national interest in the service they rendered the country in those critical times.
My hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) has given certain illustrations of cases where the owner of the paper entertained a different view from the policy which the paper was advocating, and he suggested that the public might be misled. I was under the impression that the public knew that Sir Hugh Graham did control the Montreal Herald. I certainly have seen it stated in the press repeatedly, and, almost immediately after the transaction took place it was published in the press. Of the other case

to which my hon. friend refers I have no knowledge. But I wish to point out that he has used those cases to justify him in attacking the advocacy by the Liberal press of a particular policy during the last general election, a matter that has nothing whatever to do with the resolution that he suggests the House should adopt. Does he mean to imply that if these newspapers had published the names of their editors and proprietors the course they pursued would have been different? Not one particle. I think it might have much strengthened their position if the public had known that the strong solid Liberals who held stock in those papers were back oi the policy which was being advocated in support of the national interest.
My hon. friend has referred to the amount of advertising done. I think the answer made by my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) is perfectly complete. I have absolutely no apologies to make for the money the Government has spent for advertising since I became a member of it. I believe that it is the bounden duty of the Government to keep the public fully informed as to its acts and policies.
The Government of this country is of concern to more than the members of the Cabinet, it is of concern to more than the members of this House-it is of concern to every citizen of the country. Every citizen is deeply and vitally interested in it, and the Government is serving the cause of the people in keeping them as fully informed as possible in connection with its policies . and courses of action. My hon. friend has not ' suggested, and he cannot truthfully suggest, that the advertising which the Government has paid for was in support of any party or of any political activities. The Government was advertising the Victory loan; the campaign for greater production; matters in connection with food control; outlining the procedure being adopted in connection with repatriation. That money was wisely expended in the public interest. Every dollar expended that helps to give additional information to the citizens of this country in reference to the action of the Government in matters in which they are deeply and vitally interested is sound expenditure, if that information is useful and should be given.
But I want to say further that there was no discrimination in connection with that expenditure. All journals, irrespective of party, race, or creed, received the same advertising. My hon. friend knows that. The Government has been attacked from this
side of the House because it gave advertising to Le Devoir and certain other papers in the province of Quebec. The Government may be open to criticism as to that, but it has treated the press of Canada alike irrespective of their political views, the racial origin of their editors or proprietors, or their religious faith, because in administering the affairs of the country we are trustees for the whole people and we went on the principle that every citizen is equally entitled to the information, no matter in what section of the country he lives, or what be his political leanings. My hon. friend referred to the bringing down of returns. That matter has already been fully explained and I shall not take time going into it.

I desire to say a word with reference to the position of the rural postmaster. It is true that since the last session of Parliament there has been some relief given to the rural postmasters but I am confident that an investigation of the situation in which they are placed will show that they are not being fairly treated. They are not being paid for the work they are expected to perform.
