It is now 50 per cent on the first $1,000 and 25 per cent on the balance. The old scale was 50 per cent on the first $1,000 and 30 per cent on all over $1,000. Leaving that aside altogether, when every other class of man in the country has had his rate of remuneration increased from 100 to 150 per cent, the rural postmasters, who are asked to perform a most important service for the public and the rural communities in particular had an increase of five or ten per cent in the rate of their remuneration.
In the constituency I represent there are dozens, yes scores, of postmasters and post offices that must be maintained-some one must be there all the time

where the remuneration would not pay for the services of a boy or girl of fourteen or fifteen years of age. The postmasters have to take all the responsibilities that go with the situation, and conditions are such that it is becoming almost an impossibility to get people of any reputation whatever to fill these offices. I have urged upon the department the importance of the post office service to the rural communities. One of the things that the Government of Canada can do to build up a contented rural community is to give them an adequate postal
service, and yet in many parts of the country they are not getting it.
There is another point, to which my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Cowan) has referred, and that is supervision.	I have
received a letter on that subject with a request that I read it to the House. I am not going to detain the House by reading the whole of the communication, but I will give some extracts that will emphasize the point to some extent. The letter also has relation to the question of salaries and the investigation which has been made by a commission with a view to re-classifying the public service, and the first paragraph that I will read relates to that:
Men with experience should have been consulted by the experts appointed for the purpose. We suggested this to the commission months ago, but did not get even a reply; and [DOT]when one of them was here he did not see, so far as we are able to learn, any mail clerk on a route perhaps the most important in Canada, as it is the trunk line where bulk is broken both ways for all Canada.
Then the writer says this with regard to supervision:
The other nieht practically all the letter mail for the West-
That is the whole of Western Canada.
missed the train, and was delayed twenty-four hours because the transfer man failed to make the proper connections. The main trouble with the Post Office service is that there are only privates and generals. For instance, in my opinion, the most important post office official in Toronto is the chief transfer man at the Union Station, and yet he ranks only as a transfer man with the nominal pay of a letter carrier. We have no traffic experts to correlate the business. Clerks on this route have almost begged the department to re-arrange the running so that the work would be more continuous and better done, but there is always a No, no, without even an enquiry. The department does not seem to realize that all other railroad service has outstripped the railway mail service, which Just stands pat until there is a public protest	The post office service is the backbone of business, and it might pay business men in Parliament to have a committee authorized to call in for consultation a few of the field men who do the actual work.
I will not take up time by reading the balance of the letter, but the extracts I have read give some idea of what is in the minds of the men who are actually doing the work. I know some of these men and they have drawn to my personal attention the conditions that exist in connection with the mail service. I will go further and say that to my personal knowledge the mails going North and West out of the city of Toronto during a large part of 1918 were delayed, not once, but sometimes four and five days a week, for twenty-four hours, for

the reason which has been stated in this letter-the lack of proper supervision. I question whether any commercial institution in the world would undertake to have a business of the importance of the Post Office Department carried out in the way that the mails are taken from the post office in large cities and placed on the trains. All over the Dominion this work is performed by a messenger without any one to supervise the manner in which it is done. If it was simply a matter of a few bags of mail it would not be so serious, but when four, five, six and sometimes seven carloads of mail matter have to be placed in such a way that it can be properly handled and properly distributed to all points in Western Canada-and the same applies to other parts of the country, but I am only speaking in regard to something that I am personally familiar with-you have a business that requires expert attention. You cannot go out on the street and hire some boy, and say: Take all this mail matter and load it on the cars and have it in such a way that the mail clerks can distribute it. The contention made by my hon. friend from Eegina (Mr. Cowan) is perfectly correct. The Post Office Department will give more efficient service and in the end save money by getting experts to supervise the work that is being done; by calling into its councils some of the men who 11 p.m. are actually doing the work.
The railway, mail clerks-these are the men I know most about-are giving good service, but they are handicapped in the performance of their duties because they are working along the same lines as thirty years ago when transcontinental trains first began to run from the East to Vancouver.
Mr. TOLMlIE: Is it the intention of the Government to consider the feasibility of carrying mail by an air service? This is a matter of great interest to some of us on the Pacific Coast. It has been taken up by our boards of trade out there with the suggestion that this method of carrying the mails be adopted, if it is found to be possible. We have a number of aviators, very expert men, in this country, who have returned from the war, but who, on account of their inability to find occupation in their particular profession, are now leaving Canada and going to other places where they can make profitable use of their knowledge *and experience.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: I did not at the time understand the question put by the hon. member (Mr. Lemieux), but I have since learned what it was. I may say that I am, and have been for some years, acquainted with the law in regard to members of Parliament accepting business from the Government, and there is no danger of my being disqualified any more than other members of the House who may be shareholders in a newspaper, or any other company, except, of course, those engaged in public works.

The matter to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Tolmie) refers has been under the consideration of the Post Office Department for some months. Last summer certain trial trips in carrying mails from Toronto to Ottawa, and from Toronto to Montreal, were made, the result of which was satisfactory so far as expedition in the carriage was concerned. The whole question of an air service for Canada is a very large one, and affects a good many of the Government departments. Consideration has beerl given to it by the Department of Militia and Defence, the Department of the Naval Service, and the Department of Mounted Police. The Chairman of the Cabinet Committee on Reconstruction has been devoting particular attention to the subject, and has introduced a Bill into the House of Commons providing for the creation of an Air Board.
It is really a question of practicability, having regard to the distances to be travelled. I quite agree with hon. gentlemen that in view of the present situation in Canada very great benefits would accrue if we could establish at not too great a cost the transport of mails by airplane, particularly to bridge the great gap between east and west, as it would really contribute to the unity of the country. But at the present time, as my hon. friend is aware, airplanes are expensive to purchase and to operate, and the whole matter will require the greatest care and consideration, and that is one of the objects of the appointment of an Air Board as suggested in the Bill now before the House. I agree with my hon. friend that in view of the magnificent part which our Canadian boys have taken

in the air service abroad-they have been unsurpassed in their work, and individual Canadians have distinguished themselves, above all others I was going to say, but certainly equal to any-we would like to maintain their splendid traditions in some form by developing an air service here. The matter will receive the most careful consideration of the Government.

I desire to draw to the attention of the House, the laxity of the postal department in answering communication of postmen and hon. members during the postmen's strike last year. I think that strike could have been averted if the deputy minister, or whoever was in charge of the department, had been prompt in answering the communications of the men. The department was to my mind, certainly lax when the strike broke out, in withholding any information as to what the men were claiming and what wages they were receiving. No information on the matter was available in Winnipeg until the Minister of Labour arrived there and the strike had made considerable headway. I have had to wait as long as a week'for an answer with regard to an inquiry I made of the department. I think the department might well look to their laurels and answer inquiries more satisfactorily, not only when communications are addressed to them by the postmen, but also by hon, members.

I have listened, Mr. Chairman, with a great deal of interest to the discussion in connection with the Post Office Service. There is perhaps no public service that comes home more closely to every individual than the service rendered by the Post Office Department; and accordingly the discussion that we had a few weeks ago on the question of whether the minister in charge of such .a public service should sit in this House rather than in the Senate comes very much to the fore to-night. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Rowell) in charge of the Estimates to-night for the Postmaster General is a good lawyer of wide experience, and as such he knows that hearsay evidence is not evidence at all, and that no judge will listen to it. My hon. friend (Mr. Rowell) gathered this hearsay evidence very industriously and very cleverly as he was going along, but it would have saved a good deal of trouble if the deputy minister, or the other assistant who is here, were permitted to furnish information direct, rather than put it through the unnecessary machinery of being chewed out to us by the President of the Council.
It strongly emphasizes my point, that such a popular institution as the Post Office-I say popular because it deals with everybody- should be represented in this House by its head, the Postmaster General. I sat for many years in this House with the distinguished senator who is now Postmaster General, and far be it from me to say anything about him except that he is a first class man in every sense. But he is not in this House and cannot get a proper impression of public sentiment-and every public man must be governed to a very great extent, if not altogether, by public opinion. I said a few days ago that in this democratic country the head of every department should be represented in this House as far as possible. Of course, the hon. gentleman who was giving us this second-hand evidence to-night was doing very well, and possibly no other member of this Union Government could do very much better. Nevertheless, we cannot help feeling when we see a minister, I care not what department he is representing, casting about for information to support his Estimates, that he is not seized of the matter himself, and really has no opinion of his own. I submit, therefore, that it is highly desirable, as I have already stated, that questions of this kind should be dealt with by ministers sitting in this House, and I trust that the day is not far distant when this very important department will be so represented.
The management of the department seems to me to be somewhat extravagant. The ordinary revenues, of course, go into the coffers of the department, and are supposed to be used to carry on the operations of the mail service. We find that in 1911 and for a few years thereafter there was a very substantial surplus, but according to the figures given to-night we then struck deficit upon deficit, and I venture to say that if the department was confined during the past year to its own legitimate revenue we would have rather a striking deficit as a result. On the operations last year, stamps which were sold, not for the purpose of carrying the mails, but for other purposes, had found their proper channel, there would be a deficit of something like $4,000,000. That does not speak well for the management of the department, in view of the fact that the war has brought a great deal of additional revenue to it on account of the hundreds of thousands of men overseas to whom their parents and relatives were sending letters and packages.



Possibly larger subsidies had to be paid for carrying these mails across the water, but I do not believe that the number of employees in the post offices have been materially increased, or that additional amounts have been made to mail couriers throughout the country on account of the war. 1 do know, however, from the experience in my own town, that an enormous amount of mail matter went through the post office which would not have been transmitted had there been no war. I reason, therefore, that had not the extraordinary revenue of the war, direct and indirect, gone to the credit of the post office, the showing of that department would not be satisfactory; indeed, the deficit would perhaps be the largest we ever had.
Occupying the position that I do, I should be careful in entering upon this discussion about newspapers-whether newspapers were bought or whether newspapers were sold. We have passed through a period of very deep agitation. There has been a strong and striking division among the people, intensified by a situation which we hope we shall never again meet or have to deal with. Our attitude should be, I think, that every -man and every woman in this country was earnest and honest in the course that he or she pursued in connection with the war and that the division that took place among friends on the question of conscription was of the most honest kind. That is the only way, as I understand it, in which equity, fairness and justice will be extended to all. The war has been won; we Canadians are engaged in advancing the best interests of the country, and I see no good purpose in perpetuating the division that arose over this question. So far as I am concerned, I will be no party to any such feeling. But apart altogether from any such accusations as that against newspapers, before as well as since the war-election the member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) made very strong insinuations- not insinuations, but statements-along the line of the observations made by the member for Maisonneuve. Hon. gentlemen sitting to your right, Sir, had equal provocation then to stand up in their places and deny those accusations. Whether a charge of corruption against a newspaper comes from your right or from your left, Mr. Chairman, makes no difference; but it is a striking fact that nothing was said about the matter by hon. gentlemen opposite when the member for Victoria made the statement that the press was " sweetened;" that the money of this country was being used to corrupt the press and to create a favour-
able public opinion for the Union Government. Sir, I hear no strenuous denials of that statement. I am not saying that I lost any sleep in pondering its truth or otherwise; but if it was necessary for hon. gentlemen opposite to make vehement, denunciatory denials to-night, it was equally proper and just that they should have made them then. All of us were children once, and we shall always have some more or less childish sentiments. If one child hears another accusing his fellow of something, and it is not denied, that child assumes that the accusation is true. An accusation was made by the member for Victoria, and there was no denial of it; it was allowed to pass as true. It is only the instinct of childhood, therefore, for us on this side, in our innocence, to believe that the accusation is true; and if we repeat it we are only repeating what was stated by an ex-minister and a very prominent member of the Conservative party.
I need not emphasize the importance of a clean and untrammelled press, a press which is faithful to its duty to the people. I was surprised to hear the President of the Council even suggest to-night that it was necessary to pay the press in order that the views of the Government might reach the people. What is the press for? Do I pay for a newspaper merely for the sake of getting a piece of paper with some print on it? I pay for a newspaper as I pay my preacher, or as I pay a teacher who instructs my children. I pay for that newspaper because it is its business to gather news, to gather opinions, and to publish them so that I may read them. Is it to be said that, apart from what I am paying for my newspaper, the man whose opinions are worth having must always pay for having them published in the paper? That is the doctrine that is preached here tonight. Over two millions of the money of the people-who had no two millions to throw away-had to be paid to the newspapers in order that views of the Government and of public men should find their way into the press. That is not my view of public service as it should be rendered by the press.

My hon. friend certainly misunderstood what I said if he thinks I said anything like what he is attempting to answer. What I said was that the people were entitled to know of the activities and of the work of the Government, and that the principal money spent along this line was in connection with Victory Loans, in-

creased food production, and other campaigns' of that kind.

What my hon. friend said will appear in Hansard. I might go further and say that it will appear in print generally, whereas very little of what I say will appear. When a man on this side of the House tries to put his views before the people, a very meagre, indifferent and unsubstantial portion of what he says appears in the press, whereas the minutest details of the professions of hon. gentlemen who sit on the Government benches are lapped up with delight and glee. That is the striking difference. But we know that what we say will at least find its way into Hansard, and that we may, through some strenuous work, get it out here and there before the country.
We should like to reform the press so that it would convey to the people the views of everybody as expressed, without any painting of tainting, so far as may be worth while, and let the people judge for themselves. The people are the great jury in this country; let us put the evidence before them, and let them judge whether they shall serve Baal or whether they shall serve God. If they wish to serve Baal, that is their business, and the blood will be on their own heads. We have had a good deal of talk but, if the Chairman will excuse me, it has been quite germane to the subject under consideration. We are talking about a public service; we are rendering assistance by means of one public service to another public service. Newspapers may be private-owned, but they are a public service because their product goes through the public channels. You can buy your groceries from any store you like and nobody knows anything about it but yourself, but -a newspaper is not confined to any individual; when it is published it is available to the whole country. It is therefore a public service, and it is important to us all that it should be conducted along proper lines, in a truthful manner, without any improper influence being brought to bear upon it, and without any contamination of the real fountains of truth. For these reasons it was quite proper for the hon. member for Maison-neuve to bring these matters to the notice of the House. An hon. member of this House is reproached if he says anything here that he would not say on the street. That should not be the case. It is possible for a man to go too far in that line, of course; the law does not always recognize the protection of this House. If a man says 109}
anything here that is malicious or slanderous or which cannot be justified, in the ordinary sense of the word, his shelter in this House does not protect him. The protection of this House is to afford an opportunity for fearless and open expression of opinions which if expressed outside, might possibly be slanderous in the eyes of the law. If a man makes use of that protection to bring before the public questions which he thinks are in the interest of the body politic, but which, if expressed outside, would drag -him into court, he is simply making use of a protection which the British constitution has afforded to members of Parliament from time immemorial. If he uses that protection properly, for the purpose of getting the people to think of what is going on, I submit he should not be reproached or accused of taking improper advantages of the privileges which the law throws around a man sitting in this House.
As a last word, let me say that we were told by the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) perhaps not more than twenty days ago in this House, that this Government was owned body and bones by a certain gentleman residing in the city of Toronto. I heard no denial of that statement; I hope it is not true. I only mention it to show that there is an opinion abroad that wealth cuts too much figure in this country, that corporations have too tight a hold on the Government and can influence the press, that big money ha-s greater influence than the individuality of any single man. Those are the things that we are trying to bring to-night to the attention of the President of the -Privy -Council and the Government, so that they -may guard against them. It is only a few days ago that I read in a newspaper that ordinary people in this country must not expect newspapers to be free from outside influence so long as they are not willing to pay for their newspapers. " You must expect," says that newspaper, " that the men who pay for the advertisements will have a certain influence on the editorial opinions of the paper." I was surprised to find that in a newspapei, but I suppose it is true. If it is the case that a newspaper is influenced, not by public opinion, but by the weight of advertising which comes into its business office, is it not time that we should receive with some degree of caution the expression of opinions -as we find -them in those newspapers? When a man becomes editor and launches into the newspaper business he must expect to be criticised and his cenduct to be closely scrutinized as is the

case with all public men. For myself, and I am sure I am speaking for every hon. member of this House, when we put ourselves in the hands of the public we are quite willing to be properly and legitimately criticised. The same holds true of a newspaper. It is better that we should sometimes tread upon the corns and hurt the feelings of a newspaper man than that, through any laxity upon our part, the people of this country should suffer for lack of purity of opinions or honesty of publication upon the part of the organs which have the best opportunity of expressing public opinion.

My hon. friend spoke of the extra cost of administering the Post Office Department having regard to the revenues, and I think it is only right to point out in what respect that increase arose out of the war. The Post Office Department has, I think, approximately 1,500 employees who have gone overseas to serve at the front and who are paid by the department. The department has had to engage other employees to do their work here. Hon. members have only to stop and think to realize what a very large sum of money that amounts to. The second factor is the war bonus to the employees of the department, and the third is the increased cost of supplies. The three together more than make up any possible deficit which would arise if you deducted the revenue derived from the sale of the war-tax stamps.
Lest my hon. friend should on some other occasion say that he suggested that, a certain gentleman was the owner of this Administration and I did not deny it, may I say that he is no more the owner of this Administration than is my hon. friend or any of the others whose names have been coupled with it on different occasions.
With regard to the 1,500 employees who went overseas, is it the policy of the department to give them back their old positions?
Yes.
Is it being done?

My information is that all permanent employees have been given back their positions. I know there are cases of hardship where there were temporary employees who retired from the service and went overseas and other temporary employees are now filling their positions, and the Civil Service Commission has been called upon to consider these cases. I know of cases of real hardship, and I hope the Civil Service Commission

will find it possible to give to these temporary employees who enlisted and went overseas positions in the service.
I am very glad to know that consideration will be given to such cases, and when the acting minister said that positions were being given to these men I thought he was not well informed.
To the permanent employees. I understand they are getting their positions back, but the others I mentioned belong to the temporary class.

Some postmasters have small offices and their salaries are anywhere from $1,000 to $1,500 a year. They enlisted in the earliest stages of the war and other postal employees who had not offices enlisted at the same time. These employees received their full salaries as provided by Order in Council for civil servants who enlisted at the first of the war, but the postmasters who had these small offices were compelled to employ and pay postmasters to do their work. They gave up their positions and have lost their civil salary, which nearly all the other civil servants who enlisted at the same time receive. I would like to know whether it is the intention of the Post Office Department to adjust the claims of these postmasters and have'them reimbursed to the extent which they have paid out to others to perform their duties while they were overseas. This matter has been before the Post Office Department, the Militia Department and the Civil Service Commission, and yet these men have been unable to get any satisfaction.

I understand my hon. friend refers to men who are not in the Civil Service. The rural postmasters are not in the Civil Service in the sense that the regular city officials are. The rural postmasters are paid a percentage on their business plus whatever minimum they get. So far as I know the matter has not been before the Government for consideration. It has not come to my notice, and I am sure it has not come before the Post Office Department.

My informant advises
me that it had been before the Post Office Department and had been taken up with the Deputy Postmaster General and had been referred to the Militia Department.

I will see that it is
brought to the attention of the Government.

I want more than having it brought to the attention of the Gov-

eminent. I want to see some measure of justice given these men. These men technically may not be civil servants. Their yearly salary is determined on the past year's earnings, and I think it is an absolute injustice to let them leave these offices, enlist and go overseas, and tell them they will not get a cent, while employees in other branches of the Civil Service get their full salaries. They are equally good men, and it is unfair to crowd them through some hair-splitting technicality. The number in the whole of Canada is not very large, and it would he only fair on the part of the Government to reimburse these men.
Does the minister intend to give the House any information as to the reduction of the rate of postage? Is it not a favourable time to return to the two-cent stamp instead of the three-cent?

That question was asked in the absence of my hon. friend from the Committee. I said that it had been asked this session and that the answer was that any announcement affecting the revenue would be made in the Budget.
It is now 11.40 o'clock, and we have had a good deal of discussion. I would suggest to the minister that we might let the first item go through and adjourn. We could let the second item stand.

I thought possibly we
could let both go through because the Post Office comes up again under the Supple-mentaries. However, we will pass the first one.

I would like to have this
vote explained-Superintendent Mail Contracts, Controller Railway Service, Controller Postal Stores and Superintendent Staff Bran eh, $4,000 each. It seems to me before we let that vote pass we should have some discussion on the different items. What is the reason for these increases?

The increases have been given because it is felt that these public servants hare earned them and should receive them. All Deputy Ministers are being increased from $5,000 to $6,000. Now in regard te these other men who are getting increases, not one of them has been in the service less than twenty-five years, and they run to thirty, and one over forty years of efficient public service. These public servants are simply receiving small increases having regard to the important positions that they fill.	I

If all these officials
deserve an increase, certainly, there is an army in the post office department in the country who also deserve increases.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I allowed a great deal of discussion on the Outside Service on the understanding that both items would be considered together. I see now that the second item concerning the Outside Service it to be considered as if it had never been discussed. I therefore must rule that the discussion concerning Outside Service salaries is absolutely out of order.

I have listened with a great deal of pleasure to the explanation given by the minister in regard to the reasons why the salaries of deputy ministers and others should be increased. I haye no objection to that, but I .notice that messengers, packers and sorters do not get any increase.
I wish to call the attention of the minister to a circumstance that happened in Quebec some time ago. A mail clerk was killed in an accident on the Intercolonial.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, that has noth-i*g to do with the Inside Service.
Certainly it has to do with the pest office.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That has to do with the Outside Service. All the clerks in the Quebec post office are in the Outside Service.
That can be dealt with when that item is up?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.
I think the discussion was very much wider than this item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The discussion was very wide on the understanding that the two items were to be discussed and passed

together. Objection has been taken to the .passing of the second item, and therefore H must keep the Committee to the first.

Then I will discuss the first. The minister mentioned, a moment ago, that fifteen hundred employees of his department had gone to the Front. The Postmaster-General went over to the Front also, and I would like the minister to tell me when he came back.
According to my recollection, he returned about the month of July or August, 1918.
While the Postmaster-General was in France or England, was he drawing his salary as a minister?
So long as he was Postmaster-General, I assume he drew his salary, but I have no personal knowledge.
Is the minister in a position to tell me if the Postmaster-General drew his pay as a Lieutenant-Colonel?
I cannot say.

These are very important matters and the public ought to know the facts. The Hon. Mr. Blondin is a member of the Senate, he is not here to give us the information, and I think the item should stand. The next time it comes up before the Committee the minister may be better informed.

I cannot consent that the item should stand. It is already agreed that it is to be passed to-night. I understand that there was a question on the Order Paper, and the answer given was that Mr. Blondin only drew his salary as Postmaster-General.
Did he net draw his salary as Colonel?
I have no personal knowledge.
While Mr. Blondin was in France, England or Italy, which department paid his travelling expenses, the Post Office Department or the Department of Militia and Defence?
I would assume that it would be the Militia Department; the Post Office Department certainly did not pay them.
That is only an assumption?

I say that the Post Office Department did not, so I assume that it must have been the Militia Department.
[The Chairman.]
Will the minister say whether Mr. Blondin was accompanied by Mr. Laflamme, what Mr. Laflamme did, and who paid him?
Mr. Laflamme accompanied the minister. I assume he drew his ordinary salary. I could give my hon. friend that information when we take up the next item.
I shall not be able to discuss this with my hon. friend because the next item deals with the Outside Service.
My hon. friend can put a question on the Order Paper and he can get an answer at once.

I have a right to get an answer now. Now is the time for the minister to give me the information to which I am entitled. The minister has no right to tell me to put a question on the Order Paper. I will do that if I think proper, but if I wish to put a question verbally it is the minister's duty to give me that information, and if he cannot, I think the item should stand.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
Carried.
With the understanding that when we go into the Post Office Estimates again this information will be given by the minister.

Quite so.
Progress reported.
On motion of Hon. Mr. Rowell the House adjourned at 11.55 p.m.
Monday, May 5, 1919.
The House met at Three o'clock.

speakeroldname: Hon. N. W. ROWELL (President of the Privy Council):
speechtext:
I beg to lay on the table of the House copy of a document received from the Secretary of State for the Colonies, being the terms of the Armistice concluded between the Allied Governments and the Governments of Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Turkey; also .copy of the revised draft of the League of Nations Covenant as approved by the Peace Conference in plenary session on April 28, 1919. In view of the importance of the League of Nations Covenant and the desirability that members of the House should have copies in their possession, I move, with the consent of the House:

That one thousand copies of the revised draft of the League of Nations Covenant, as adopted by the Peace Conference in plenary session, laid on the table of the House on May 5, be printed forthwith, and that rule 74 be suspended in relation thereto.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: This motion requires unanimous consent.
Motion agreed to.
On the Orders of the Day:

subtopic: PEACE TREATY-CONDITIONS OF LABOUR-THE EIGHT-HOUR DAY.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Hon. NEWTON WESLEY ROWELL (President of the Privy Council):
subtopic: PEACE TREATY-CONDITIONS OF LABOUR-THE EIGHT-HOUR DAY.
speechtext:
The hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Blake) on Friday asked if the Government had any information as to whether provisions for an eight-hour day had been incorporated in the Peace Treaty, and I promised to give an answer to-day if possible. On Monday last, the 28th of April, on motion of the Prime Minister of Canada (Sir Robert Borden), the following clauses relating to labour were unanimously approved for incorporation in the Peace Treaty:

The high contracting parties, recognizing that the well-ibeing, physical, moral and intellectual, of Industrial wage-earners is of supreme international importance, have framed a permanent machinery asking that of the League of Nations to further this great end. They recognize that difference of climate, habits, and customs of economic opportunity and industrial tradition make strict uniformity in the conditions of labour difficult of attainment. But holding as they do that labour must not be regarded merely as an article of commerce, they think that there are methods and principles for the ratification of labour conditions, which ajll industrial communities should endeavour to apply so far as their special circumstances will permit.
Among these methods and principles, the following seem to the high contracting parties to be of special and urgent importance:
First-The guiding principle above enunciated that labour should not be regarded merely as a commodity or article of commerce.
Second-The right of association for all lawful purposes by the employed as well as by the employers.
Third-The payment to the employed of a wage adequate to maintain a reasonable state of life as this is understood in their time and country.
Fourth-The adoption of an eight-hour day or a 48-hour week, as the standard to be aimed at where it has not already been obtained.
Fifth-The adoption of a weekly rest day of at least 24 hours, which should include Sunday whenever practicable.
Sixth-The abolition of child labour and the imposition of such limitations on the labour of young persons as shall permit the continuation of their education and assure their proper physical development.
Seventy-The principle that men and women should receive equal remuneration for work of equal value.
Eighth-The standard set by law in each country with respect to the condition of labour should have due regard to the equitable economic treatment of all workers lawfully resident therein.
Ninth-Each State should make provision for a system of inspection in which women should take part in order to insure the enforcement of the laws and regulations for the protection of the employed.
Without claiming that these methods and principles ore either complete or final, the high contracting parties are of opinion that they are well fitted to guide the policy of the League of Nations and that if adopted by the industrial communities who are members of the League and safeguarded in practice by an adequate system of such inspection, they will confer lasting benefits upon the wage-earner of the world.
That, I think, succinctly answers the question of the hon. member for North Winnipeg, as it appears that not only an eight hour day, but a weekly day of rest, a living wage, the abolition of child labour, equal pay for men and women for equal work, the right of the association for all lawful purposes, are declared to be the standard for which all nations should work. It is a matter of gratification to the House and to the country that the Prime Minis-

ter of Canada was permitted to move the adoption of those clauses which will in the future be looked upon as the Magna Charta of labour.

speechtext:
On the motion of Hon. A. K. Maclean Bill No. 80 to authorize the appointment of an Air Board for the control of Aeronautics was read the second time and the House went into Committee on the Bill, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section I-Short title:

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: Has the minister given a general explanation of this Bill?

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: I really cannot say anything more than is stated in the Bill which I explained briefly on its first reading. Obviously there must be some development in commercial aeronautics in the immediate future. During the war the development in aeronautics related almost entirely to military and naval affairs. Private and commercial aeronautics was prohibited altogether and consequently there was no development along these lines. It is necessary, in view of the probably development of aeronautics, that there should be some governmental control of such matters and it is proposed to establish a Board which shall have entire control of any Government or commercial service. If my hon. friend will look at section 3 he will see there set forth the duties of the Board which will cover fully, I think, all the probable activities in aeronautics. Section 4 is the other important clause and that empowers the Air Board to establish regulations for the control of aeronautics.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Air Board; chairman and vice-chairman; representatives of Militia and Defence and Naval Service Departments; term of office; salaries.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext:
It is not proposed to establish another department to administer this Act. I would suppose that most of the members of the Board would be selected from established departments of the Government. The administration of the Act will be largely in the hands of the vice-chairman of the Board who will be the chief executive officer. It is necessary, of course, to have representatives of the Naval and Militia Departments upon the Board for the reason that heretofore they have been very much and practically in-

terested in aeronautics. Consequently it is proposed that they shall have direct representation on the Board. It might be urged that the Post Office Department, the Interior Department, the Dominion Police and some other departments should be represented on the Board. However, there was a reason at the moment existing for the representation of the two departments I have mentioned and it is not deemed advisable that other departments which may possibly be interested in aeronautics in the future should all be represented on the Board. But, it will be understood that this measure is of a temporary nature. I have no doubt that in the working of it during the coming year weaknesses will develop but experience will enable us to pass legislation which will be more satisfactory.
Mr. (MORPHY:	I have listened to the
statement of the minister and I would judge from it that his intention is to set up a theoretical Board rather than a practical one. Otherwise, he would have stated the fact that we have a large number of the finest Canadians who have ever done service for their country many of whom have returned to Canada after real practical service on the battlefields of Europe. While there may be men who have been employed with the military and naval services in Canada this is a very opportune time of recognizing the boys who have been fighting for their country, and doing good practical work, and of calling to the service of the country some of these young men who fought for it. I will leave that with the minister. I think that there should be some recognition given to these boys who have done their duty overseas.
Mr. A. K. iMAOLEAN: Doubtless the class to which my hon. friend refers will be represented on the Board.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: Has there been any consideration given to the question as to the salaries that will bs paid as to those who serve on this Board?

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: No consideration so far has been given to the matter. It is impossible to give any information to my hon. friend which will be at all reliable at the moment. Possibly the chief executive of the Board will be one who is now employed in some department of the Government. The other members may possibly serve without pay. The development will be largely commercial and perhaps it will not be very extensive for a time. I am hopeful that all the members of the Board will not be paid.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: Is any provision being made in the Estimates this year for this service?

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: There will be in the Supplementary Estimates.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: You could give us some idea from that.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext:
The Committee
will have some idea of the probable expense when the Supplementary Estimates are brought down.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: Will the minister kindly state if it is in the mind of the Government that this Board shall at an early date undertake the commercial development of aeronautics, not with the idea that it is to be merely an adjunct of military and naval development but with the idea of taking up definitely the commercial development?

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: If my hon. friend is inquiring whether the Government intends entering into the field of commercial aeronautics, I am bound to reply that it has not yet considered the matter from that aspect. The operations under the Act will, of course, largely relate to commercial activities; I would expect that for the next few years, at least naval and military activities in aeronautics will be very limited, indeed.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: I do not think the minister has given the Committee very much information as to the functions which this board is to perform. I have not got any clear idea as to whether it is simply to manage aeronautics in connection with private enterprise, or whether it is to embark upon some large scheme of its own.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: The remarks of the hon. member will be in order when we take up the next clause.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: Has the Government any idea with respect to its future policy on the subject of aeronautics?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: The remarks of the hon. member will be more in order when we take up clause 3.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: Before we pass this clause I would like to ask if the operations of the board to be created under this Bill are to be centered at Ottawa?

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: It will be an organized body under the supervision and control of some department of the Government?

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: Is it intended, in connection with the operations of this hoard, to establish an institution or school where practical and theoretical instruction in aeronautics will be imparted so as to render a man thoroughly competent to take charge of an aeroplane?

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: Up to the present moment it is not the fixed or settled policy of the Government to establish a school for the purpose indicated. Speaking generally, the Government has no settled policy in respect to aeronautics. The Militia and Naval Departments, during the period of the war, carried out a programme, but it has now practically ceased. It was necessary to first enact legislation before any fixed policy could be adopted by the Government in respect of any form of aeronautical activity. Many applications have been received from commercial companies for the establishment of aeronautical routes throughout Canada; and, as I said a moment ago, it is open to the Government to embark upon various forms of aerial activities, such as the conveyance of the mails, the survey of forest, fire protection, patrols by the mounted police, and so forth, but at the present time, the Government has reached no definite policy in respect of any of these matters.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: What will be the real function of this board after it has been organized ? What will it start out to do?

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: The immediate purpose of this legislation is chiefly to control aeronautics in Canada, established by any Government department or by private corporation. For example, it is not within the right of any individual to fly in the air with aeroplanes or hydroplanes, or any other machine of the kind, although there is no statutory law which directly prohibits it.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: It is entirely unknown to the common law.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext:
It is unknown to both the common law and the statute law. Consequently, nobody can legally engage in flying to-day, and in none of the provinces, nor in Canada, is there any statutory authority for any body to grant licenses for the purpose. This board must establish aerial routes, or to put it in another way: If a commercial company desires to carry on an aerial service between, say, Montreal and Toronto, their route should be first established and that would be one of the functions of the board. The machines used should be licensed and inspected just as a TMr. A. K. Maclean.]
steamer is. The pilots and the crews must also be licensed, and that will be another function of the board. Furthermore, regulations must be enacted, compelling flying machines to use telephonic or wireless apparatus, and in relation to many other matters which do not occur to my mind at the present moment. I think a very close parallel to the control of aerial navigation is the control which we exercise over shipping, with, of course, the very notable difference that one operates on water and the other in the air. Generally speaking, the object of the legislation is to put ourselves in a position to control aeronautics, chiefly commercial, as that is the form we shall likely have in the immediate future in Canada.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext:
By this Bill, according to the minister, Parliament is establishing its authority over aerial routes and all matters concerning air craft. But does my hon. friend think that if a company, for instance, established a line between Montreal and Quebec, to operate exclusively within the limits of that province, it would be a provincial matter, and that the company in question should not come under the authority of this Parliament unless its undertaking is declared to be for the general advantage of Canada? My hon. friend classifies aerial navigation with marine navigation, but article 92 of the British North America Act declares that a provincial legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to the matters coming within the class of subjects "hereinafter enumerated," and article 10 of section 92 sets forth:
Local works and undertakings other than such as are of the following classes:-
Lines of Steam or other Ships, Railways, Canals, Telegraphs and other Works and Undertakings, oonneoting the Province with any other or others of the Provinces, or extending beyond the limits of the Province.
Therefore if such a company were operating exclusively within the limits of one province it would be a provincial matter, and I do not think this air board could fix the route, or control the license to pilots, and other matters in connection with it.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext:
The constitutional question, of course, arises in connection-with this matter, and had it been pointed out to the Fathers of Confederation that we might possibly have this aerial development in later years, it would be difficult now to say whether it would have been placed in clause 91 or 92 of the British North America Act.
Clearly, the legislation, if enacted, would cover interprovincial aeronautics, and con-

sequently to that extent the Federal Government would have control. Whether it has control over purely provincial aeronautics is a question open to very much doubt, and possibly it will have to be settled ultimately by the courts. There is a clause in the British North 'America Act which in effect states that subjects not assigned to the provinces fall within Federal jurisdiction. Aeronautics were not placed in the list of subjects assigned to provincial jurisdiction, and therefore it is arguable that the suhject falls within Federal jurisdiction. However, any doubt we may entertain on the point does not affect the competency of Parliament to pass this legislation, although later it may be held by the courts that it is only intra vires in so far as it affects interprovincial aeronautics.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: I do not know if this development of transportation was known before Confederation, hut two of the greatest poets of the 19th century, Lamartine and Tennyson, predicted that some day we would see argosies floating in the fair blue sky.	[DOT]

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: And Jules Verne also.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: Yes. I think the objection of my hon. friend from Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) was well taken. It seems to me that as the Government is so anxious to have Government ownership of all kinds of transportation, it should not lose this favourable opportunity of furthering that project. There is no incubus attached to aerial as there is to railway transportation, and the Government should take control of this new industry, which no doubt will develop to a very great extent in the near future. The British Government have already organized an aerial postal service and have mapped out three routes, one for freight, another for passengers, and a third for some public service, I think the postal service. The United States also have organized a postal service between Philadelphia, Washington and Baltimore.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext:
And New York.
Perhaps we would save enormous railway subsidies by organizing an aerial postal service.	[DOT]
I regret sincerely that the Government did not take over the magnificent plant which the Imperial Munitions Board erected at Camp Borden during the war. Unfortunately the whole plant was sold to an enterprising Yankee, and Canada lost thereby an excellent opportunity. If it is not too late, I would urge upon the Government the necessity of taking over that plant and giving Canada the benefit of it. We do not lack enterprise in aeronautics. During the war our young men showed that they were equal to the best among the Allies in that particular sphere. I need name only one of them who is world famous- Bishop. We have not only the men, but we have all the elements that constitute the material part of the industry itself. During the war the Imperial Munitions Board found in British Columbia the timber which was best suited for the construction of aeroplanes, and I understand they went even as far as to subsidize very heavily a branch line several miles in length an order to tap the district where that special timber was obtainable in large quantities. It seems to me that the Government should be extremely careful in its legislation,- more careful than it appears to have been in the present instance,-so as to start this industry in the right way.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.

speechtext:

tween Ottawa and Montreal they might ignore the specified landing places around Ottawa and lease for a trifling sum landing rights on any field within a reasonable distance of the city. Airmen are now ready to leave Newfoundland for England; they have all decided to start at about the same place.
