maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext:
The only thing I can say in reply to my hon. friend is that the Government have not in mind the granting of exclusive privileges in respect of certain routes to any individual or company which may be organized. But we must be guided largely by experience in this matter. While at the moment it may seem undesirable to grant exclusive privileges to any person or persons, still a limitation of licenses granted to individuals along certain routes may be necessary. It might, for instance, be perfectly proper to grant a license to twelve or twenty-four persons to fly between Ottawa and Toronto, but, in the light of experience, it might be considered improper, possibly dangerous, to grant licenses to several hundreds or several thousands. As I have already indicated, the policy of the Government in this matter is not yet fully considered or matured. We shall be guided very largely by efforts which are made to develop aeronautics commercially by individuals or corporations. My hon. friend might suggest the propriety of our establishing a mail service between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. That might strike one as a very desirable place to experiment

in aerial mail service. I should not like to speak for the Government at the moment and say that they propose establishing such a mail service, but naturally, in the course of time, the Government must develop a policy in respect to these matters. If there is great activity on the part of private interests and private capital, it might be well to allow such interests to do a great deal of-experimenting.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-duties of Air Board:
Major-General MEWBURN: I was glad to hear the remarks of the member for Mai-sonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) with regard to our taking over some of the property at Camp Borden. The Imperial Munitions Board spent a large amount of money in Canada in connection with the Royal Air Force. They had a school of aerial gunnery at Beams-ville, on lake Ontario, which we did not consider it advisable to touch. They also had large buildings at Deseronto and large aerodromes and plant at Camp Borden where they spentc millions of dollars. When the armistice was signed I immediately took the matter up with the Imperial Munitions Board and all that plant and machinery was transferred to the Militia Department.
It was difficult for us to determine from a military standpoint what should be done as regards the air force. I realize what wonderful work the Canadians did in the Royal Air Force, and while it seemed to me that we could not utilize that force in Canada for training purposes, I thought it my duty to protect, as well as possible, their property and equipment. Therefore, the buildings and all the equipment there were handed over to the Government for a mere song, and they are on our own training ground, Camp Borden, which is recognized as one of the best training grounds on the North American continent and which has been used for training American fliers. We also had handed over to us, free of cost, a large number of airships and also a quantity of maps and so forth, and we have retained a very small staff there to protect them. Some of the buildings we expect to utilize as hospitals, thus saving the erection of hospitals. At Long Branch, on lake Ontario, where the rifle ranges are, the Imperial Munitions Board erected a number of buildings which have been handed over to us, but other properties which were on leased ground were scrapped. All the property I have mentioned is intact, and we have the facilities for continuing training and developing an air force in the

future. When my Estimates were being discussed the other night, I was discussing the reorganization of the militia, and if we have to reorganize the militia for defence and other purposes, no doubt an air force will form part of it. That, however, wms one of the subjects that we decided the commission would deal with, and as regards the Air Board, I sincerely trust the magnificent men who have made such a name for Canada in the air will have the first opportunity of being recognized in this. Many of them are coming back and are now talking of the commercial side of the industry which is being developed in England. We have a large quantity of information both from France and England as regards air forces, and I sincerely trust that our men who have made good in the air from a military standpoint will be able to make a success in the air from a commercial standpoint.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext:
Were there any Canadians associated with the American who bought the whole of the aerial property in Toronto?
Major-General MEWBURN: I do not know that there were. Col. Bishop told me that he expected to be interested in some British machines for which he was offered the agency, and while he had not worked out just what he was going to do, he hoped to be able to develop in this country some commercial enterprise, possibly in conjunction with the postal service. This Air Board is only a temporary one to study the question, and the Department of the Naval Service is represented on it merely to keep in touch with a view of developing something in the future.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: I cannot agree with Shakespeare's lines: What's in a name? I would suggest that the minister have Col. Bishop on the first aerial board in Canada.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext:
I should like very strongly to second the suggestion of the hon. member. Col. Bishop is a native of my town and is a son of my former legal partner. I have known him from the day he was born to the present time, and he is to-day the world's champion living airman, having brought down seventy-two aeroplanes. He is a boy of whom any country might be proud, apart altogether from his ability and record as an airman. I would respectfully suggest that anything that can be done by the njinister to secure his services on this Air Board would be one of the best moves the Minister of Militia could make.
I understand he served for a time on the Administration Board in connection with the air service in London, England, and wrould be admirably qualified for the position, though I do not know if he would accept it at the present time.
Major-General MEWBURN: I do not think any salary the Militia Department could offer Col. Bishop would induce him to take such a position. I have had many consultations with him, but at the present time he is making something like $30,000 a month under contract in the United State-.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: I am sorry, because I would like to see a " bishop " associated with the present Government.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: Under subclause (b) of section 3 this Air Board can travel throughout the whole country studying this question, without let or hindrance on the part of any one. They may go even into other countries, as they see fit. Under subclause (c), they have power to construct and maintain all Government aerodromes and air stations, including all plants, machinery and buildings necessary for their efficient equipment and upkeep. In these two clauses, the approval of the Governor in Council is apparently not necessary, and I should like to know whether or not it is the intention of the Government to give such wide powers to this Aerial Board.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext:
The purport of subclause (b) of section 3 is merely a direction to the Air Board to take cognizance of and to study aeronautical development in all countries of the world. It does not imply that the board is to travel as a body to do research work in connection with this matter. It might conceivably at some time be desirable for a member of the board to visit some countries to study the development there taking place, but I do not anticipate that much in the way of travelling will be done by members of the board for a considerable time. I think, however, it is a very proper provision that members of the board be directed to study the development of aeronautics in all countries in the world. Section 7 says that all the moneys proposed to be expended under this Bill must be voted by Parliament, so that Parliament will have control over the matter.
The purport of subclause (c) is to place in the hands of the Air Board the absolute control of the construction and operation of any air service owned by the Government. If the Post Office Department should de-

cide to establish a service between Halifax and Newfoundland, or (Halifax and Charlottetown or Halifax and St. John the control of the service would be in the hands of this Board. The Board will also control any services which originate in either the Naval Department or the Militia Department, and this clause places in the hands of one body all matters relating to aeronautics. I trust that this will commend itself to the judgment of my hon. friend. For the time being it seems the best thing to do. D and E are similar in character to C: it simply gives the Board the control and management of all aircraft and equipment necessary for the conduct of any of His Majesty's services. Possibly the Government may establish other services of its own, but in any event, such services when once established, and so long as this legislation stands upon the statute books, will be under the control of the Air Board.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext:
I would not like my hon.
friend to think that I am raising any objection to the passage of the Bill. My only object is to get some information in regard to it. The minister suggested that the possibility in the near future of a postal air service between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. Suppose a private individual started such a service, would this Board have the right to designate the landing places on the island and on the mainland and undertake the expenditure of public money in regard thereto?

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: If it were a Government service, yes; and if it were a private service, still in some respects the Air Board would have control. For instance, it might very properly designate the route to be followed by the service, and should certainly have the right of licensing machines and naming the landing places. In the case of a private concern, the Government, of course, would not expend any money in securing the landing places; that would be done by the companies. There is in contemplation the organization of private corporations which will shortly approach the Government for subsidies for the carrying on of a mail service between different points in Canada. It was necessary that we should have this legislation in order that private companies might be in a position to approach the Government for assistance to carry on public sendees or to conduct any form of commercial aeronautics themselves.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext:
I quite agree with the minister that such legislation should be passed at this session. Aeronautics are only in the 
experimental stage and it is but right that opportunities should be given to develop this service if it becomes of commercial value to the country. I would suggest, however, that we surround it with adequate safeguards, particularly in connection with the expenditure of moneys. I fear that if money is expended without the approval of the Governor in 'Council a very much larger expenditure will be incurred than the Government or this Committee foresees at this *moment.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext:
The Governor in Council will exercise a very critical control of expenditures. Clause 7 of the Bill reads:.
All salaries mentioned herein and all expenses incurred under the provisions of this Act shall be paid out of such money as may be appropriated by Parliament therefor.
The authority of Parliament must therefore be obtained before any money can be expended.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext:
If it is good in this case, why not in the railway case? My hon. friend says that companies are already petitioning the Government to establish aerial mail services, and he gives us .a gentle hint that the Government may favourably consider the request made by these companies. He has mentioned possible routes -Halifax and Sydney-
Mr. A. K. (MACLEAN: The Magdalen Islands.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: My hon. friend has struck the nail on the head. The Magdalen Islands are the only group of islands inaccessible during several months of the year. Navigation closes at the beginning of January and is hardly open on the first of May, and it would be highly beneficial if a mail service could be carried on during the winter months between, say, Pictou and Prince Edward Island, and the Magdalen Islands.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: I have no doubt that mailer will receive the attention of the Air Board. They would have to study very carefully the atmospheric conditions, the affect of altitudes, etc., before it could be definitely decided how practical these questions are. But when one is thinking of the practical uses to which aeronautics may be applied in Canada in public services, one immediately thinks of Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, the Magdalen Islands, the Yukon Territory, across lake Superior, Jaimes Bay and many other routes.

maintopic: CONTROL OF AERONAUTICS-APPOINTMENT OF AIR BOARD.
speechtext: And the bruising of our forests.
Yes, the cruising of our forests.

The Conservation Gem-mission is very anxious that such a service should be established, and I note with pleasure that the province of Quebec has secured two aeroplanes to cruise the forests there.
Major-General MEWBURN:	They can
also be used for photographic purposes in the making of surveys.
'Mr. LEMIEUX: Yes. The great enemy at present is- fire, and according to statistics published lately the losses are colossal.
I see in the establishment of an aerial service a great boon for Canada not only in the matter of defence but commercially and industrially.
I see in the American papers that the United States Government have been experimenting in the locating of schools of mackerel by aeroplane. Possibly aeroplanes might be useful in that direction.

I have seen that in the papers but I do not think that any experiments in that direction have been really made. I know of something analogous to that, though. The seal fishermen in Newfoundland were endeavouring some months ago to secure the services of an aviator-I do not know whether they succeeded or not-to fly out over the ice floes to ascertain the location of the seals and the openings for sealing vessels and steamers. That is easy of accomplishment if atmospheric conditions permit.

You can see deeper into the water from above, and schools of mackerel can be located in that way. By this section the Departments of Militia and Naval Affairs are associated with this Board. Which department will it come under?
Both.

What minister will be responsible for the administration of this board?	.
Major-General MEWBURN: That is not settled. There will be a representative of the Militia Department on the board.

The service to
which my hon. friend (Mr. A. Thompson) refers is one of the many that it is intended shall come within the purview of the board. Just how practical a service the aeroplane might render on the coast is one which, of course, will have to be determined by experience. But at least I can inform my hon. friend that that is one of the subjects which will have the attention of the board when it is established.

With regard to clause 3, which with clause 4 is the chief operating clause of the Act, I would say that the draughtsman has done his work well, but there is one thing that he has not had present in his mind in connection with the matter and that is as to the question how aeronautics is going to interfere with the property rights of the public. I would suggest to the minister that he consider that point before the Bill goes through. According to the law, as it has stood for many hundreds of years, the right of the property owner exrtends usque ad caelum ab inferno,

that is up to the heavens and down beneath the earth. That is his property. It may be that we have arrived at a stage in the world's history in which a machine has come which will suddenly be launched across his property. While a flier may be far up in the air and could not be said to do very much harm to a man's property, sometimes aeroplanes come very near to a man's house and they do make a great deal of noise. You may have claims made by certain property owners who do not want these things coming over their houses or property. There is nothing in the Act which enables the Government to say that aeroplanes shall have the right to pass over a man's property or to define the conditions under which that right shall be exercised. I do not share with the minister the doubt that he seems to have as to his power to enact this legislation as having reference to the point raised by my hon. friend from Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe).
As to provincial service only.

Quite so. Property rights will be provincial. You have the right to legislate with regard to that because you have the exhaustive clause of the British North America Act which says that anything which is not provincial is Dominion. You_ have besides that, the Post Office service, the naval service, and the military service, and, last, but not least, the service suggested by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. A. Thompson)-the geological service. That brings it into the Interior Department. With all these uses in the different departments of the Government to which the aeroplane might be put, there seems to me to be a preponderating case in support of the contention that these are Dominion matters and would naturally come under the control of the Dominion authorities. How could an air man know where the exact position of the provincial boundary was? When he starts out on his journey he must have some rule or regulation which will carry him to the end of it in Canada without regard to what particular province in Canada he may be in. I doubt if any one will raise the point that this is a matter for exclusive provincial jurisdiction. If any one does, it behooves the Dominion Government to fight for Dominion rights with all the power they have.
I agree that it is a good general purpose Bill. It is impossible to foresee all the things that will come under it but its provisions are expressed in general terms and it the minister will consider the addition 
of a clause which will give the right to go over properly either with or without compensation-I do not care which-he will be making a Bill which will do for the time being and until we know more about the subject. It seems to me that the Bill should pass at this session even if it is not wholly adequate to provide for all cases so that the world may know that Canada, is, as usual, in the van in regard to improvements in science.

As my hon. friend (Mr. Mowat) in closing, referred to the necessity of legislation at this session, I would like to emphasize the statement a little farther and say -that I am very anxious to have the Bill become law at once and that I shall probably ask His Excellency's assent to this Bill long before the closing of Parliament. I do not desire to amend the Bill with a view of abrogating any of the common law doctrines in respect to property rights in the air. In view of recent developments, the point is one for the courts to determine but I doubt very much if that doctrine would be held to have much validity under the circumstances. I would refer my hon. friend to paragraph (i) of section 4 which reads as follows:
(i) the institution -and enforcement of such laws, rules and regulations as may be deemed necessary for the safe and proper navigation of aircraft in Canada or within the limits of the territorial waters of Canada;
The subsection 3 immediately below reads as follows:
(3) All regulations enacted under the provisions of thi-s Act shall be published in the Canada Gazette, and, upon being so published, shall have the same force in law as if they formed part of this Act.
The important thing to have in mind in aerial navigation is the protection of life and property, and I have no doubt the board will provide by regulation that no flying machine shall approach the ground, or approach a building, within a certain number of feet. I have heard the story frequently, and I assume it ds a fact, of somebody when flying in the city of Vancouver entering a bedroom where a patient was being attended by a -doctor; the machine and pilot landing in the bedroom. We will .seek to avoid the repetition of such a discourteous act as that by providing a regulation that -the flight of -the airplane shall be of a certain height in order to safeguard, so far as is possible, the safety of property and person. I submitted the Bill to the Justice Department before introducing it, and was told that the measure

*was' perfectly constitutional and about the best that could be done to meet the situation for the time being.

I rise to support the suggestion of the hon. member for Maison-'neuve (Mr. Lemieux) that this is a good opportunity to really consider Government ownership in connection with aeronautics, and I bring the point up under subsection (11) of the clause under discussion. I _ would urge upon the minister, when preparing the regulations considered necessary for the control or operation of aeronautics in Canada, to make those regulations so drastic for the time being that the Government will .be able to keep that control within its own hands. I think one of the tests to be brought to bear on the question of public ownership is whether the particular business under consideration has become, or is likely to become, a natural monopoly; and while it is impossible for us to foresee, as was instanced -in the case of the Bell Telephone Company, to what extent aeronautics may become a monopoly, there is some danger of it. Some months ago I overheard a discussion in New York about the formation of a wealthy syndicate to acquire the landing places around the great cities in the United States* and thus to completely control aeronautic operations, or aviation between those points. It is evident that unless an aeroplane can come close to the heart of a city to make a landing its speed avails little, because the time consumed after the landing is made to reach that centre, takes so much off the time gained between cities that the aeroplane comes then into competition with the railway. I might also be permitted to point out to the minister that Mr. Rudyard Kipling, many years ago, drafted a code of aeronautics. Following his wonderful tale which, I think, is called "The Night Mail,'' he' as a matter of tour de force of the imagination, prepared a series of rules. I have not read them for many years, but in those rules Mr. Kipling covers some of the very points we have been considering this afternoon.

I think it is only fair when we are dealing with so practical a phase of the development of aeronautics as the present, that I should suggest to the minister that he would-in connection with this board and in connection with any legislation on this subject-enlist the sympathy and help of the father of aeronautics in this country, I refer to Dr. Bell, who has a home at Baddeck, N.S., although he sometimes resides in Washington. I had the pleasure in September 1896 of being present in the machine shop experimenting office of Dr. Bell in the town of Baddeck, when it wras considered a great achievement in aeronautics that he could cause a certain machine that he had in his laboratory to rise three or four inches from the ground.
It is gratifying to know that we have today reached such an advanced stage of development in aeronautical science. Dr. Bell is a Canadian, born in Brantford in the great province of Ontario and is well known, and he spends about ninety per cent of his time at his beautiful home in the neighbourhood of Baddeck in the county which I have the honour do represent, and I think it would be only fair on the part of the Government to recognize his great services, the great research he has displayed, and what he has done for this science. The first airship that was ever built in Canada was constructed at his workshops at Baddeck, and did considerable flying. It was operated by a Baddeck boy, young McCurdy, who was famous afterwards as a flier and who was in charge of some of the works at Toronto or Camp Borden in the early stages of the war. I do not know where young McCurdy is now.
Major-General MEWBURN: Long Branch.

He is the young man s*who took charge of the first flying machine that was built in Canada, if not on the continent of America, under the direction of Dr. Bell. He was assisted by another young Canadian, also well-known to fame-or at least his progenitors were, young Baldwin, the grandson of the famous Canadian statesman of that name. Mr. Baldwin is in charge of Dr. Bell's works at Baddeck, where not only flying machines, but machinery of the most advanced type in connection with transportation, are turned out. I therefore suggest to the minister that it would be a proper and well-deserved compliment, and a mark of recognition on the part of the Canadian people and Canadian Government, to Dr. Bell to enlist his sympathy and utilize as much as possible his great knowledge in connection with the enterprise in which Dominion authorities are now about to engage. As to landing places, if it is desired to take advantage of possibly the greatest site in the world, let me point out to the minister that his own native town of North Sydney is the place that was selected by both the United States and Canadian Governments while the war was on, and when they were

looking for the very best location for the starting of an aerial service. At that time North Sydney was chosen as the best place on the east coast of America for the purpose. A large amount of money has been expended on the station there, and very extensive buildings erected which are now owned by the Government. Large areas of land were also acquired for the purpose of carrying on experiments, and I would suggest to the minister that the board to be appointed under this Bill are the proper persons to take charge of that property and see that it is not lightly thrown away, lhere is an idea that a portion of this land is to revert back to some of its original owners, and if that should turn out to be the case the Government may not again acquire it as cheaply as they did in the first instance. Those works were constructed, at the nearest point to Newfoundland, and there at least forty or fifty machines were ouiit and put in operation last summer. We Sot so used to flying machines last summer in North Sydney that it was no more a novelty to see an aeroplane in the *air than an automobile on the street. I am bringing these matters to the attention of the minister so that he may not forget to *make use of the knowledge and experience of those great men who are to all intents ,and purposes Canadians, and of the development that has already taken place in connection with the use of aeroplanes and hydroplanes for commercial purposes. [DOT]

The property at Sydney will, of course, under this Bill, come within the control of the board, and it is not the intention of the Government, so far as I know, to part with it. I quite agree with my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) that it is a very desirable property, particularly in connection with trans-Atlantic operations. I am also grateful to him for caning the attention of the Government to the pioneer work of Prof. Graham Bell. His very valuable services in the science of aeronautics ought to receive proper recognition, and I shall be very glad to submit to my colleagues the suggestion of my hon friend.

The clause now before the Committee affords a good deal of scope for the imagination of hon. members in defining the duties of the Air Board. When we contemplate the great strides that have Leen made in the science of aeronautics during the last five years and the possibilities of the future, I think we may well realize that this is likely to become a very 
important service. I do not feel very much concerned about the danger of not having sufficient landing places. If there is one thing we may claim to have in abundance it is sufficient room for that purpose.
The question raised by .the hon. membes for Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) and other hon. members is, I suppose, a constitutional one, but to the ordinary layman it seems inconceivable that any province should claim a monopoly of the air. This is a case where provincialism should not creep in, and certainly it ought to be within the jurisdiction of the Federal Government. It seems to me that the Government have shown good judgment in promptly bringing a measure of this kind before Parliament. No doubt the Air Board will keep in touch with changing conditions and report to the Government from time to time, and I think this section should be made as broad as possible in order to give the Board the fullest control of the air service. But with regard to the disposal of certain machines which were in service during the war, those machines might be all right for training purposes, but a very different type of machine will be needed for commercial purposes.
I do not altogether agree with the view that the Government should exercise too rigid a control over the service. I think something should be left to the ingenuity or individual initiative if this service is to develop as we would like to see it develop.
Our Canadian boys made an enviable record in the air at the front, and the Government would certainly be lacking in their duty if they failed to retain in our air service as many as possible of those splendid men who made such brilliant records overseas. When we consider the 5 p.m. immense undeveloped resources of this country, and what can be accomplished through such an air service I think it is very important that instead of restricting the powers of this board we should extend them as- far as possible. Practically the whole northern part of Canada is unexplored, and we have as yet no idea as to the value of our resources in that vast territory. This service can render very valuable work in the way of exploration and fire protection.

I think the Government
is to be congratulated on taking this progressive movement and in recognizing the splendid work done by our air men at the front. In a country like British Columbia this service can be very usefully developed in connection with the handling of forest fires, and also in exploration work. But I

hope one of the first things to be taken up by this Board will be to thoroughly investigate the possibilities of using the service for rescuing shipwrecked people. We have had many serious wrecks on the Pacific coast, some of them almost within a stone's throw of shore, such as the Princess Sophia recently, and the Valencia wreck on the coast of Vancouver Island a few years ago. The latter boat was within a few hundred yards of the shore, but owing to the shallow water and the steep cliffs it was an utter impossibility to rescue the passengers, and they dropped off the rigging one by one and only a few were saved. In such cases an aeroplane could render valuable help by carrying a cable to the ship by imeans of which those on board might be brought safely to shore. 1 trust this will be one of the first things investigated by the Air Board.
Section agreed to.
On section 4-powers of Air Board to make regulations with approval of Governor in Council.
In the matter of penalizing a person who violates the rules, has the minister given attention to the question of jurisdiction? Where will the offender be tried and the penalty be imposed?
Such a case would be comparable, I suppose, to a case against an offender engaged upon a ship; he would first be served by a process of the court.
How about the customs laws?
Section 5 provides that the board shall have power to control the places in Canada where a landing may be made from a foreign country. .

Section agreed to.
On section 5-officers and men:

The purpose of this clause is to provide for the control and discipline of those employed in connection with the Government service. F^r instance, if it was an air service in connection with national defence, the Air Board would acquire these powers, which are somewhat similar to the powers enjoyed by the Naval Department and the Alilitia Department. If the service had something to do with policing the unorganized territories of Canada, it would probably be necessary to house and clothe our men. The powers are very general, but important and necessary.

Section agreed to.
On section 7-payment of expenses, etc., under Act.

Is it contemplated to have a certain number of aeroplanes reserved for the exclusive use of ministers of the Crown? It would mean a great saving in time-and time is precious just now, as is evidenced by the fact that we are interfering with the ordinary course of the sun to gain some of it. To have some aeroplanes reserved for ministers would afford them an opportunity, when they travel in that way, to see very much more of the country which they govern. Further, it would avoid the repetition of the fearful plight in which my hon. friend (Mr. AlcCoig) found himself at the station in Toronto the other day, when he was unable to get a sleeper because of the fact that three private cars were attached to the Ottawa train.
Alajor-General AfEWBURN: You would not want to see the ministers any more up in the air than they are now, would you?

Section agreed to.
Bill reported.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.

speechtext:
On motion of Hon. T. A. Crerar (Minister of Agriculture), Bill No. 75, to amend The Live° Stock and Live Stock Products Act, 1917, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Air. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-selling and buying rights of other persons preserved:

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: This clause makes some slight changes in the Act which was passed in 1917. I notice that it gives the farmer, drover, or other person the right to " buy his live stock at any stockyard ". Why is the word " his " there?

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext:
The clause as it formerly stood, read:
Nothing in this Act, or in any regulation made hereunder, shall take away, or in any manner limit, the right of any farmer or drover to sell his live stock at any stock yard.
The main change in the amendment is to provide that any farmer may buy as well as sell in any stockyard. My hon. friend direct? attention to the fact that the term "other persons" is included, and he desires to know what is meant by that. It merely broadens the scope of the amendment.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext:
I was not objecting to that. I was drawing attention to the last line:
Or other person to buy his live stock at any stock yard.
Why is the word "his" in there? Why would a man want to buy his own stock?

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: I think there is an error in the printing of the Bill. The word "his" is not in the amendment as I have it on my notes here. And I would move that the word "his" should be struck out.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Why not also strike out the word "his" where it occurs before? A man might want to sell his neighbour's live stock as well as his own.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Yes. I would move that the word "his" in the tenth line, and also in the twelfth line of subsection (2) of section 1 be struck out.
Amendment agreed to.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: If the ordinary construction that lawyers put upon matters of this kind is applied to the term "other persons" in this section, it will not have the effect that the minister says; it will not widen the scope of the section. rt means simply "other persons" of the classes already mentioned. The minister should be under no misapprehension, and if he intends that anybody at all can go there, that should be made clear.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: "Any person of the classes mentioned" is what is intended.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-manner of inspection may be prescribed by regulation, also size of packages of wool.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext:
I can, perhaps, make this clear by reading the clause as it stands in the existing Act:
The manner in which live stock, meat, poultry, eggs and wool shall be graded and branded or marked, and what shall be the size of packages containing meat, eggs and poultry, the kind of package that may be used, and how such packages shall be branded, marked or labelled.
The amendment provides that regulations may be made as to the manner in which these shall be inspected, and it adds wool to the other articles mentioned that are subject to regulation as to size of package. The request for this has come from probably 90 per cent of the wool growers in Canada who.desire to have their commodity standardized and subjected to regulations the same as the other articles.

Section agreed to.
[Mr. Crerar. 1
On section 3-requirements for shipping.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: The minister should explain where the inspection will take place. Must farmers have their stock inspected before it is shipped? Very wide powers are given to the inspectors as to the regulations they may prescribe, and I should like to know what the minister's policy is.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: This provision is not intended to be applied in the manner suggested by the hon. member. It is rather for the purpose of giving shipping companies power to refuse shipments if they think the Act has not been complied with in respect to inspection and grading. A similar provision exists in the Meat and Canned Foods Act. It is not intended that a farmer shall have his stock graded before he ships it from the farm. This is not intended to apply to live stock at all, but rather to live stock products such as hides, wool and similar commodities.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: In connection with stockyards, could the minister give us some information about the proposition to build a cold storage plant at Montreal to some extent under the guidance and supervision of his department, and is it 'the policy of the Government to build cold storage plants in other parts of Canada. In the Maritime Provinces there are no cold storage plants for chilled meats, and very strong pressure is being brought to bear upon the department to extend to those provinces the same privileges as are being given to Montreal in the way of cold storage plants.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext:
The cold storage warehouse to be erected at Montreal will be under the control of the Board of Harbour Commissioners for that port. The purpose is to erect a plant on the water front, to provide facilities for transhipment of perishable commodities. At present, the existing cold storage warehouses in Montreal are located at some distance from the water front, and it has frequently happened that deterioration has occurred in moving foodstuffs from the cold storage warehouse to the vessels for shipment. I know on some occasions last year, for instance, in the shipment of frozen beef, carloads of beef had to be sent back from Montreal to Toronto to be refrozen and put in proper condition for loading on the vessel to be carried in its refrigerated space across to Europe.
The development of cold storage and refrigeration in the shipping of perishable commodities, has been very remarkable in

recent years. I urged on the Government the necessity of having such an equipment at the port of Montreal in order that we might have all the facilities for developing an overseas trade in this respect. For example Great Britain, I am informed, imports annually two hundred million dozens of eggs, of which large quantity Canada, I believe, supplies two or three million dozens. If we are going to take advantage of that market we must provide proper facilities for reaching it, and to that end it is essential that there should be proper cold storage facilities at the point of shipment, so that a carload of eggs, or beef, butter, or cheese, as the case may be, which comes into the port of Montreal and has to wait for a week or ten days or possibly two weeks for a vessel will have propeT storage and be readily transferred to the vessel on its arrival. As to the policy of the Government, I am not in a position to speak, but I can express my personal opinion that this aid to the development of trade in these commodities is one that should be encouraged by the Government. That is only my personal opinion. I think that other ports such as Halifax should, as soon as opportunity offers, and it is possible, be provided with such facilities.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Will the proposed cold storage plant have railway trackage so that cars can be run into the building or alongside of it in order to preclude depreciation in unloading? In what part of the city will the construction take place? I understand that a new cold storage plant is proposed, a short distance west of Mile End on the Canadian Pacific Bailway tracks. It is intended to unload western frozen commodities there, and when they are ready for shipment overseas they will have to be reloaded in cars and sent to the dock to the steamer. I think it is important that the cold storage plant should have railway trackage to enable the cars to run either into the building or alongside. This would greatly facilitate loading on the steamer.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext:
The Government is assuming to itself all the virtues in connection with government ownership of all the great utilities of the country, and I might suggest that this is a field into which the hon. minister might extend his jurisdiction and his usefulness by announcing a policy of ownership of cold storage plants in Canada. If you will permit me some latitude, Mr. Chairman, I will point out to the minister what is regarded as a great
curse to the ordinary people in the private ownership of cold storage concerns. It is said that five or six million pounds of butter is being held to-day in cold storage waiting for higher prices than the extraordinary prices we are now paying. If these facilities were held by the Government and foodstuffs such as butter, etc., could be put into cold storage and controlled, and only a fair profit allowed, we would not have the condition that exists to-day of butter which was bought for about 40 or 45 cents a pound, as I am informed, being held for higher prices which in some places have reached 75 and 80 cents a pound. Such a condition should not be permitted, when such a useful article of food as butter can be allowed to remain in storage in immensely large quantities until the price soars from 45 to 80 cents and over. In some parts of Canada butter is selling at one dollar a pound. I have read that Dr. McFaul, the representative of the Labour Department, who has been inquiring into this matter, has suggested to the Government that some immediate action should be taken in regard to these large quantities of butter now in cold storage. I would like the Minister of Agriculture to consider this matter and to see if anything can be done to relieve- the situation. The Government should release this food so that people may have it at reasonable prices.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: It puzzles me to know why Canadian butter is cheaper in London to-day than it is in Canada, and my hon. friend will be doing a great service if he can reduce the cost of living by giving us at least as cheap butter in Canada as in London. We are taking very necessary precautions against Bolshevism, and it is right that we should do all in our power to prevent any revolutionary wave from sweeping over Canada. But I would remind the Committee that revolutions are primarily caused by empty stomachs. The French revolution began at the bakeries, and when the French-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Order. I must call the hon. gentleman to order. I hope the Committee will not impose upon the indulgence of the Chair.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext:
I understand that the cold storage warehouse which the minister says will be erected on the property of the Harbour Commission of Montreal will be controlled by the Harbour Commission. If the Government are going to subsidize the Harbour Commission, they should be careful to make such regulations as will

compel the Commission tc handle these products on a fair basis, and not such as will create the same arbitrary conditions as now exist in the grain trade. Grain that is sold locally pays more than grain for export. It is unfair to the people of Canada who are putting up the money that they should be taxed a higher rate than when grain is exported. The minister should be careful to see that the regulations will provide that on products for domestic distribution people will not be charged more than is charged on goods going for export.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: I shall gladly keep the suggestion of the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Eobb) in mind'when the regulations are being prepared. I want to make it clear to the Committee, however, that the main purpose of the plant to be erected in the harbour of Montreal is to facilitate the export of perishable agricultural commodities. As to the points that the leader of the Opposition has raised, of course they are very important, but they are not intimately related to the clause under discussion. The cause, mainly, of the high prices of butter at the present time is the great demand and the shortage of supply. The dairy herds of Europe have been depleted enormously by the war. Recently the dairy commissioner of the Department of Agriculture had an inquiry from Denmark" to purchase Canadian butter. It is a well known fact that Denmark has, in the past, been one of the largest exporters of butter in Europe. The demand is so great and the supply so limited that the inevitable result is higher prices. To what extent the farmers of Canada should be controlled in the prices they are getting for their dairy products is another question. I quite agree with the leader of the Opposition that, if cold storage warehouses and butter speculators are cornering supplies of butter with a view of reaping a golden harvest, through the sale of it, there should be some method of formulating regulations which will reach such people. But from all the information I have been able to get, I really believe that in the main-practically altogether- the excessively high prices are due to the reasons I have stated. The tendency in the last few weeks has been for butter prices to come down. I believe that in Ottawa to-day first class butter can be secured for fifty cents a pound, and the dairy commissioner tells me that the Montreal price had dropped ten cents a pound during the last two weeks.	.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: I do not like to let the remarks made by the leader of the Opposition, as to the prices of butter being so exorbitantly high, to pass without being Challenged. The papers to-day say that on the Montreal market on Saturday choice creamery butter is quoted at 51 cents per pound. I do not know of any other foodstuffs that are quoted at any more reasonable price than butter at 51 cents a pound, and when you talk of butter at a dollar a pound

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: If the hon. member would allow me to interrupt him; the only fault that can be found with his argument is that you cannot buy butter at 51 cents a pound.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: I am speaking about what the producer has to sell it for, and if it cannot be bought for that price I am unable to understand why. There must be some medium between the producer and the consumer, and there is room for complaint if, as the leader of the Opposition says, butter is now selling for from 70 cents to 80 cents and a dollar a pound. But you will see from the market reports that butter is not unreasonably high considering the cost and everything bearing on the production of butter.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Let me say to the hon. member (Mr. Sutherland) that I have a right to believe the records as they come to us from the Labour Department. If he will look at the last Labour Gazette which gives the prices he will see that the price of butter at Sydney and Halifax was 75 cents a pound, and at St. John 80 cents. There are some other places where it went as high as $1 a pound. I am sure that my hon. friend, who is always very anxious to make a point against the leader of the Opposition, sometimes perhaps justly, but often wrongly, is wrong again to-day. I was calling attention to the fact that these orders were sent overseas; that they were sent back; that when the manufacturers began to carry out their part of the contract they found that since the signing of the armistice ocean rates had increased from fifty to one hundred per cent and in many oases more. The result has been that notonlyhave the manufacturers' profits been

wiped out, but a great deal of additional expense has been incurred, and unless conditions are very materially changed we are liable to have a very serious interference with the development of our trade with other countries. In 1913, Sir Henry Drayton was appointed by this Government to go overseas and interview the Imperial Government on the question of joint control of ocean rates. He went, and on his return made a report in which he favoured joint control. In 1916, he made a further report in which he emphasized his position in that regard. His report was a very full one, and I wish to read only a paragraph or two of his summing up:
The whole discussion is predicated upon conditions and .practices existing before the war, and I am firmly convinced that, with a situation such as we have had it-with agreements between the carriers-with the absence of competition, a proper measure of sane and constructive Government control is necessary. That of itself, however, will be insufficient to oope with the situation arising on the proclamation of peace.
On the one hand, there has been a large destruction of mercantile tonnage, made up in part, doubtless, by new construction, but resulting in the whole in all probability in a largely decreased tonnage. On the other hand, there will exist) producing centres glutted with commodities they produce and oversea markets most urgently requiring these commodities.
He shows that he is definitely in favour of government control of ocean freight rates. In 1912, the British Government appointed a commission on natural resources, trade and legislation in certain portions of His Majesty s Dominions. This commission travelled throughout the different dominions of the Empire and made their final report in 1917. Their report, presented by command of His Majesty to both Houses of Parliament, includes the following as part of its-summing up:
Our investigations have satisfied us that in normal times the combination of shipowners is strong enough to limit the freedom of shippers, whose varied and detached interests moke it difficult, If not impossible, for them to combine in any effective opposition, ana that, therefore, in principle, it is not desirable that the operations of the steamship companies should remain longer without some measure of Government supervision.
Following this, the commissioners state:
We are, however, unanimous in thinking, as we have indicated in the preceding paragraphs, that some measures of supervision are needed.
In our opinion, the line which should be taken is as follows:-
And they give a number of pages of suggestions as to the lines along which they would advise joint control between the

Dominions beyond the seas and the Imperial Government. I respectfully urge upon the Government the necessity of bringing about a permanent joint control of ocean freight rates. I need not tell the Committee how urgent it is that this matter should be dealt with at the earliest possible time.

speechtext:
I suppose, the door
being open to this discussion to all, it is necessary to give a little further attention to it. The subject brought to the notice of the Committee by the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) is very important and one that was brought to the notice of the Government on several occasions. But the reasonings and warnings that were uttered, fell as the old saying has it, like water on a duck's back-there was nothing done. The question of shipping has been before the House for quite a number of years, more especially in 1910, when the naval policy of the Laurier Government was announced in this House and heartily supported by the Opposition of that day, led by Sir Robert Borden, as it was going to bring about the happy condition that we in Canada would own our own shipping and be able to handle our own goods and control, to a very large extent, our transportation freight rates. It is unnecessary for me to point out how that scheme failed by reason of the fact that some plan other than what was agreed upon at that time was devised, for political purposes, by my hon. friends opposite, thus defeating the scheme.	*
I wish to bring to the notice of the Committee, and incidentally to that of the hon. member for East Lambton, the fact that this Government, about the time of the signing of the armistice, took no steps whatever to secure shipping for Canadian business. A great many ships from Nova iScotia were commandeered by the British Government. The ships that carried our coal to Montreal and our other goods to many parts of the world were taken from us and used in connection with the war, and we had no complaint to make. But immediately after the signing of the armistice every Government in the world, every business agent in the land, was trying to get hold of shipping as rapidly as possible. One would naturally have expected that the great army of representatives that we had in Great Britain, ministers and missionaries in the shape of trade missions, as they are called, would waken up and look after Canadian interests. Such, however, was not the case. Canadian vessels were sent to Australia, and when shipown-131
ers in Nova Scotia looked for their ships, they found them chartered by the British Government, practically after the war was over, to concerns shipping wheat and other commodities from Australia to England and other parts of the world. Our Government were evidently absolutely indifferent about the business, and we have no ships at all. To-day, the hon. member who speaks about the trade that we are trying to create with Belgium and Roumania, will find, when the time conies for the delivery of the goods, that we have no ships. He will find that this Government started, as an eleventh hour matter, a death-bed repentance matter, to build ships at a time when they will be absolutely useless. The Government will find their ships coming in at a time when ships are plentiful and not in great demand. They are building ships at a time when they are costing 400 per cent more than they should cost, and are 400 per cent less useful than they would be if they had been built at the proper time.
That is the kind of action the Government is taking in connection with the building of ships and looking after the general interests of the country. I am pleased that there is some one behind the Government who has been enterprising enough to bring up this question, and I trust we shall have from the Government some constructive policy in connection with shipping. Yet, indeed, I cannot hope so; it is impossible now. The day is past when something could be done. But I hope that the hon. member for East Lambton will be able to infuse some life into this inertia that is passing itself off as a government.

speechtext:
The speech to which we have just listened is a good illustration of the unwisdom of departing from the rule that requires one to confine oneself to the subject under discussion. However, out of respect for my hon. friend 1 will say a word or two on the matter he has mentioned, and then suggest that the proper time for discussing the question will be when the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has his Estimates before the House. Then my hon. friend can discuss the matter at any length he desires. In reference to the question raised by the hon. member for East Lambton, he is in error if he assumes that the Government has not taken any action in this matter. The question he has brought up is an important and urgent one, and the Government has been active in regard to it. So long as the war was on all the shipping was controlled directly by the Controller



of Shipping in London, and it was essential that the shipping of the Allies should be mobilized and used to the greatest possible advantage in the carrying of troops overseas or to the various theatres of war, and in the transportation of necessary food and war supplies to the centres where they were needed. Under these conditions, the bulk of the ocean-going shipping of Canada was commandeered, and as long as the attention . of the British authorities was centred on the problem of transportation in the interests of the war, it was difficult to get them to consider the question of controlling ocean rates in times of peace. Notwithstanding that fact, however, the matter was brought up at the last Imperial Conference held in July, 1918, when this resolution was passed:
That, In order to maintain satisfactorily the connections, and at the same time encourage commercial and industrial relations, between the different countries of the British Empire, this Conference is of opinion that shipping on the principal routes, especially between the heart of the Empire and the Oversea Dominions, including India, should be brought under review by an Inter-Imperial Board, on which the United Kingdom and the British Dominions and Dependencies should be represented.
2. That for this purpose an Imperial Investigation Board, representing the various parts of the Empire, be appointed, with power to inquire into and report on all matters connected with ocean freights and facilities,-
The very question my hon. friend has mentioned.
-and on all matters connected with the development and improvement of the sea communications between the different parts of the Empire, with special reference to the size and type of ships, and the capacities of harbours; the board to include, in addition to representatives of the Governments concerned, persons with expert knowledge of the problems involved, including representatives of the shipping and trading interests.
The Government has recently been in communication with the Prime Minister and his colleagues overseas, as well as with the Canadian High Commissioner, to get into touch with the British Government in order to work out this very problem. Hon. members will realize that no one Government can deal with this problem of shipping, as it affects international communication; it can be done only by joint action of the Governments affected. This Government is not unmindful of the importance of the question, and is using its best endeavours to see that satisfactory action shall be taken. At the present time it is pressing the matter upon the attention of the British Government. The hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) said the Government had not taken any action to get

ships for Canadian shipping. Just so soon a3 the armistice was concluded and the urgent necessity for the mobilization of shipping for war purposes ceased, the Government did take up with the Imperial authorities-as did also the Canadian Pacific Eailway and other companies controlling ocean transport-the matter of the release of these vessels, to have them restored to Canadian trade. Everything that the Government could do has been done in that respect, and having regard to the difficulties of the situation and the very great demands upon the world's shipping, I think the Imperial Government on the whole have met us in^a fairly reasonable manner. They certainly had every desire to do so, and it has only been the difficulty of the shipping situation the world over that has prevented us from getting a larger use of our own tonnage. I hope that if there is further discussion it will be confined to the subject matter of the item before the Committee.

speechtext:
When this item was called some three or four weeks ago an hon. member-I think it was the member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau)-asked for a statement as to the work of the Canadian War Alission and as to what was proposed in this representation. The reason for the establishment of the Canadian War Mission was briefly this: When the United States entered the war the whole situation -was changed so far as it related to trade between the United States and Canada. The Committee are well aware of the enormous development: in the trade between the United States and Canada in recent years. To-day our volume of business with the United States, imports and exports, is more than 50 per cent of the external trade of Canada. For the fiscal year ending 31st Alarch, 1919, Canada's total trade in merchandise was $2,124,057,238. Of that trade no less sum than $1,201,860,679 was with the United States. The Committee will therefore realize how important a part our impo*t and export trade with the United States plays in the whole industrial life of Canada. When the United States entered the war and commenced to produce munitions and war supplies on a large scale she found that she had not sufficient of the materials which are the bases for that manufacture to supply her war industries and carry on domestic manufacturing enterprises at the same

time. Canada was largely dependent upon the American market for the maintenance of many of its industries, in the supply	of raw materials or	partially
manufactured materials basic	to those
industries. To meet the situation the United	States established	a	licensesystem	for export trade,	and to
regulate and control this licensing of exports, they created what was known as the .War Trade Board. Not a single article could be imported from the United States into Canada without first obtaining a license from the War Trade Board in Washington. Not only that, but the United States realized that if they were to get their war supplies produced within the time required it was essential that war materials should have priority in manufacture. They therefore established a scale of priorities whereby certain classes of contract were to have priority in point of manufacture over others. One could not expect to get a contract filled by a plant in the United States for the manufacture of any supplies unless he had a priority order from what they called the War Industries Board.
Then the question of - transportation in the United States became exceedingly urgent, the railways were congested, they could not transport upon their railways all the war supplies required and at the same time maintain their domestic system of transportation. The United States railway administration therefore imposed an embargo on all freight traffic except under permits authorized and issued by the car service section of the Railway Administration. This embargo was imposed on the 24th January, 1918. If a Canadian manufacturer required to get speedy delivery of the articles that he had purchased in the United States he had to get a permit to transport them over the American railways. So this was the position-the 'Canadian importer had to get a license to export from the War Trade Board in the United States, he had to get a priority order from the War Industries Board, and then he had to get a shipping permit from the Railway Administration. One could readily see that, under such conditions, with American institutions, strong and powerful themselves, pressing for priority orders and shipping facilities, it became necessary for the Government of Canada to step in and protect Canadian industries and the development and maintenance of our industrial life. In order to do that it created the War Trade Mission at Washington and the Canadian War Trade Board here at Ottawa, the two working to-131*
get-her to meet the situation. That was the reason why the mission was created. It was created under an Order in Council-
