maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: By any Government. If my hon. friend could tell me any -way by which it could be created except by Order in Council I would be glad to hear it.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: By Parliament.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: If my hon. friend will refer to Orders in Council a little later I will be glad to give him all information upon them. I do not wish to break the continuity of wdiat I am saying in reference to the Canadian War Mission by discussing Orders in Council. I say that by Order in Council the War Trade Mission was created, and Mr. Lloyd Harris became chairman of the mission. Subsequently three or four other members were added and they carried on their work in Washington so long as the war lasted.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext:
Who were the other
members with Mr. Harris?

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Frank A. Rolph, Toronto; Mr. Ross H. McMaster, Montreal; Mr. Arthur H. Scott, Montreal, and Mr. J. Allan Ross, Montreal. Mr. Young of Montreal was appointed secretary of the mission and he filled that position until Mr. Harris went to England. He accompanied Mr. Harris to England. In addition to the work I have mentioned, and which constituted a very important part of the Canadian War Mission work, an opportunity opened up for Canadian manufacturers to secure munition contracts from the American Government. In the latter part of 1917 the demand by the Imperial Government for munitions fell off. The Imperial Government had been steadily enlarging their own facilities in Great Britain for the production of munitions, and as these facilities were enlarged and as they were producing what they themselves needed, they desired to discontinue to a substantial extent the production of munitions in Canada. Our industries were faced either with the question of largely curtailing their operations and throwing a large number of men out of employment or of getting contracts elsewhere. The Imperial Munitions Board, being then in touch with the conl

ditions, thought there was an opportunity of securing contracts in the United States. To that end they opened negotiations with the Ordnance Department of the United States. Mr. Harris had already gone to Washington. He went in January, 1918, I think, as the representative of the Imperial Munitions Board to endeavour to secure contracts from the Ordnance Department of the American Government in order to keep our munition industries in operation. Therefore when the Canadian War Mission was constituted, it acted not only on behalf of the Imperial Munitions Board in Washington to secure contracts for Canadian industries but also in connection with the other matters that I have mentioned in association with the War Trade Board in Canada.
I am sure the House and the country will be interested in knowing-and so far it has never been made public-the extent -of the business that the Canadian War Mission secured from the American Government. From the time it was constituted in February, 1918, up to the date the armistice was signed, the Canadian War Mission secured for Canadian industries contracts to no less a sum than $231,045,544-a magnificent contribution to the industries oi Canada, to work for the workmen, and at the same time a splendid contribution to the prosecution of the war by providing the American Government with munitions and supplies. I think it is only fair to say that so successful were the manufacturers and working men of Canada in producing the munitions required, and so excellent was the quality of the product, that the American Government was glad to avail itself of the facilities our plants offered to have munitions turned out and turned out satisfactorily. There was a certain period during the summer of 1918 when more shells of an important class, used by the American army at the front, were being turned out for the American ordnance department in Canada than were being turned out in the plants in the United States. Canada made a splendid record in the production of munitions and in the ramifications of industrial war work. When the history of this war comes to be written there will be no finer page than the record of the splendid achievements of the manufacturers and workmen in the production of munitions, to the success of which work the Imperial Munitions Board so largely contributed.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext:
The minister has referred to the magnificent record of -the Canadian manufacturers of munitions, and the dire 
necessity existing in the United States for these munitions. Why was it necessary to create this commission and expend public moneys getting these orders?

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: I did not say there was dire necessity in the United States, but I believe there was real need. My hon. friend, I am sure, is quite well enough acquainted with the business men of any country to know that they are not anxious to have business go to another nation if they think they can get it themselves. The only way Canadians were able to get the business, and it is one of the evidences that the Union Government was on the job, and the country is getting the benefit of it-was by going after the business. They knew that we had the plant and the working men who could turn out the munitions, and they knew it was a good thing for the American Government to get the work done here, and so we secured the orders. It so happens that peace came earlier than was anticipated, and necessarily many of these orders were not filled, but were cancelled. I think possibly one-half of the total amount consisted of orders that were cancelled, and settlements have been made from time to time with those manufacturers whose orders were cancelled.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: The minister stated a moment ago that there was $1,200,000,000 worth of trade between United States and Canada?

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Of that amount what part consisted of imports to Canada, and what part of exports to the United States?

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Our imports from the United States were $746,937,511, and our exports were $454,923,170.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: In view of the figures showing that we were importing to such an extent over our exports, would it not be advisable for us to retain the commission in the United States that sold us the goods instead of the commission that sold our goods to the Americans?.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: I am afraid my hon. friend does not understand business. I assume we only buy goods in the United States that we need. In view of the tariff against them, those goods would not be brought into Canada unless they were needed here.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext:
The minister says that Canada was buying goods that she needed. Does he wish to imply that the United

States were buying goods from us that they did not need?

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: I did not say so. I said the United States needed these goods for the war. The war is now over but the United States still needs certain of our goods. She requires our nickel and many other commodities. We are selling those to her, but we cannot now sell munitions to the United States or the particular goods that were being sold to that country during the war. I have pointed out the success of the commission in securing this laTge number of orders. Then allusion must be made to the success achieved in securing licenses for export.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Before the minister leaves that point. I understood him to say that this board had secured contracts amounting to about two hundred and thirty odd million dollars on munitions. Was that correct?

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Two hundred and thirty millions for all purposes. The munitions consisted of S188,000,000.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Then do I understand the minister to say that about one-half of those contracts were cancelled when the armistice was signed?

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Yes, I should say that one-half, or a little more than one-half, were cancelled when the armistice was signed. Practically all the orders that were not filled, or were on the way to being filled, were cancelled, and the American Government made such compensation as they considered right, or as was agreed upon.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: While the minister is on that point, will he state just what the duties of the board will be in times of peace? We all understand it was very useful to have the War Trade Board in Washington because there were many things there which they had to attend to. Could the minister now tell us how they have succeeded since November 11th in securing orders for Canada, or has anything been done in that direction? [DOT]

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext:
The War Trade Board is winding up the business; there are no orders which can be secured at the present time. That matter has been carefully canvassed, and so far as business between the United States and Canada is concerned, it is now back to its normal channel. Canadian business men must obtain orders from
the United States if they can, and American business men must secure business in Canada if they can.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Is it intended to wind up the board altogether?

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: It is intended to wind up the board, but the item provides for representation at Washington because the Government intends to continue representation there. It is not necessary that I should elaborate this matter, it is obvious from the statement I have made how essential the work of the board was. In order to illustrate the character of that work, let me state that they had ten thousand applications for export, and in the case oi each separate application, the War Trade Board had to be seen and a permit obtained. There were no less than 2,765 applications for priority, and we know how pressing the American manufacturers were in that regard. The Board had to take up and meet these applications and I think the country is indebted to them for rendering an exceptionally fine piece of public service. The board had to employ a staff who were paid, but the members of the board themselves served without compensation. I wish to say that not only in connection with the work of the Imperial Munitions Board in dealing with the question of munitions for Great Britain, but also in connection with their work in assisting in securing munition contracts for Canada from the United States, the country is deeply indebted to them for the services they have rendered. The American Government chose the Imperial Munition Board as the medium through which they distributed their orders in Canada, and the board acted in that capacity.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Will the minister kindly give the names of the members of the War Trade Board?

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext:
The Minister of Trade
and Commerce was chairman, and the other members were Messrs. Frank P. Jones, J-W. McConnell, Montreal; J. H. Gundy, Charles B. McKnight, and Joseph Gibbons, Toronto; Mr. C. A. Magrath, fuel controller, and Sir N. H. Laporte, chairman of the War Purchasing Commission were ex-officio members of the board. I was going on to say that not only are we indebted to the Imperial Munitions Board for the work they did in that respect, but for the splendid contribution-

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Will the minister give us the names of the Imperial Munitions Board?

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext:
The chairman was Sir
Joseph Flavelle.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext:
My hon. friends say,
"hear, hear." I want to say to the Committee that when the history of this war is written, and Canada's contribution is summed up, it will be seen that no single man in the industrial life of Canada, no man [DOT]outside the military forces, has rendered more conspicuous service to this country in the successful prosecution of the war, and in assisting the Imperial 'Government, than did Sir Joseph Flavelle by his work on the Imperial Munitions Board.
That what I have stated is true I will give my hon. friend the proof, because I anticipated that some of my hon. friends would say " hear, hear." At a gathering held in Ottawa in November last, when the heads of the different branches of the Imperial Munitions Board met to say goodbye before the work of the Board was dissolved, the following cable from Mr. Lloyd George was read. I would draw the attention of the Committee to the fact that the Imperial Munitions Board was constituted by Mr. Lloyd George himself while Minister of Munitions:
Now that hostilities have ceased1, I am anxious to send you, on behalf of myself and my colleagues in the War Cabinet, our congratulations on the great work of the Imperial Munitions Board for three years, which has been of such signal assistance to the British Empire and to the Allied Cause.
It is a great and varied achievement for your Board, not only to have produced so great an output of munitions, representing no small proportion of the shells used by the British armies, but also to have built over three hundred and fifty thousand tons of shipping for the Ministry of Shipping, to have assisted to so great a degree the Royal Air Force in Canada, and to have developed the great output of Aeroplane timber which has been essential for ouir Air Service.
As the Board was appointed by me when 1 was Minister of Munitions, it is particularly pleasurable to me to recognize the success, efficiency and value of its work and to thank you, and through you, your staff, the Canadian manufacturers and the great army of workers who have so splendidly assisted you, for the great services so rendered.
Mr. Lloyd George would not pay that tribute if he did not know that it was deserved, and undoubtedly he knew the value of the work done by the Imperial Munitions Board.
Mr. ARCHAMiBAULT:	May I ask the
minister the date of that cable?

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: November 22, 1918.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Was Sir Clifford Sifton in England at the time?

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext:
I do not know. My
hon. friend knows very well that Sir Clifford Sifton had nothing whatever to do with the message. Mr. Lloyd George does not move at the behest of any particular man; he gives praise where he believes it to be deserved.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Not always.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext:
Well, possibly my hon.
friends would prefer to hear what the then Minister of Munitions, Mr. Churchill, had to say. He cabled:
As the Armistice with Germany has now been concluded I wish, as Minister of Munitions, to congratulate you and, through you, your staff on the splendid work of the Imperial Munitions Board during the last three years.
You have carried through a work of the greatest magnitude with uniform success and efficiency and I wish to pay my personal tribute to the great ability, energy and organizing power you, as Chairman, have shown.
Canada's remarkable output of munitions has played a large part in the munitioning of the British armies and will remain a testimony to the high value in that great struggle of the work of the Board and of all those, whether manufacturers or work people, who have shared the burden with you.
With these statements of Mr. Lloyd George and Mr. Churchill I am in most hearty accord.
When I was in England in 1918 I heard from the Minister of Munitions and from Lord Weir of the Air Service nothing but words of the highest commendation for the character of the output of Canadian manufacturers and working men and of the fine work of the Imperial Munitions Board. In connection with aeroplanes Lord Weir told me that in his opinion there had not been a finer aeroplane factory anywhere in the world or one that had done better service than the factory operated by the Imperial Munitions Board and situated in Toronto. Our manufacturers and working men made as creditable a record in their sphere as did our gallant soldiers in their particular sphere; they all did magnificently.

He was vice-chairman
for some time then he went down to Washington to become chairman of

speechtext: Mr. Vaillancourt.

speechtext:
Yes. All the members of the board worked together harmoniously and very effectively.
As to the future, while the several British ambassadors at Washington have rendered admirable service to Canada, our business with the United States is now on so large a scale that the Government is convinced that our interests can only be adequately protected by a Canadian representative resident in Washington. While ordinarily the Government would wind up the affairs of the War Commission-and they are being rapidly wound up-yet in view of the decision to have permaneent representation at Washington, it does not deem it desirable to have an interregnum between the closing up of the War Mission, and the opening of the office of our permanent representative. Therefore it has been decided to continue the War Mission until permanent representation is arranged for.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: How will it be arranged?

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: That is being taken up with the Imperial Government. It is one of the matters the Prime Minister has under consideration.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext:
Would the minister
point out what proportion of this $50,000 is required to wind up the present situation, if I may so term it, and what amount is proposed to be spent on the continuation of the mission for the next year?

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext:
The present expenditure
in connection with the mission is between $4,000 and $4,500 a month. We do not anticipate that the expenditure in connection with the permanent representation will exceed that amount. It is impossible to figure the exact amount; the estimate is the best the Government could make of the probable expenditure.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext:
I am pleased to learn that Canada is to have a permanent representative at Washington. If it is right that Canada should be represented in London, Paris and other large centres, surely the interests of Canada demand that we should also have a representative at Washington. Previously, matters arising between Canada and the United States were so managed as sometimes to cause heartburnings on the part of Canadians. For instance, if anything happened to a Canadian in business on the other side of the line which resulted in international complication, the negotiations had to be carried on via London; the Canadian Government could not,

according to international law, go directly to the British Embassy at Washington. The Canadian Government, through the Governor General, would first address himself to the Colonial Office; the Colonial Office, through the Foreign Office in London, would address itself to the British Embassy in Washington; and matters which were the subject of correspondence or discussion might not be settled before many months. Some years ago, thanks to the common sense of the then Governor General, Lord Grey, a series of conversations began between the Canadian Government and the British Embassy at Washington, and the roundabout method of dealing with such matters was avoided. But this is all against international law. Subject always to British control, it is better to have, as far as possible, direct communication through our agent in Washington. During the war the Government took Sir Charles Gordon from the Imperial Munitions Board and sent him to Washington. I have the honour, as has the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) of being very well acquainted with Sir Charles Gordon. He is a Montrealer; he is one of the most progressive Canadians of the day; he is a credit not only to his native city, but to Canada as well. With his knowledge of business methods and his keen intellect. Sir Charles Gordon has been able to render very valuable service to Canada and to the Mother Country as well. About the year 1898 Sir Wilfrid Laurier, then Prime Minister, had almost decided to appoint a very distinguished Canadian to the high position of representative of Canada at Washington. I am not free to disclose the name; perhaps I will some day. At all events, the appointment by the present Government will be a welcome innovation. Most of our business, except that which we engage in with Great Britain, is with the United States;	and now	that
we have been allies in the great war our trade relations and our other relations should become closer every year. The appointment of a prominent Canadian, well versed in business, who will be in a position to build friendships for Canada in that great country, is an excellent departure. It is an indication of Canada's growth. Besides, it will tend to remove old prejudices which since the time of the United Empire Loyalists have prevailed in our country. The United States and Canada are bound to be close allies in future, and I hail with satisfaction the announcement 
that Canada will be represented in the great capital of United States.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Will this representative at Washington deal merely with trade matters or will he have a diplomatic mission as well?

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: I heartily agree with all that my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) has said with regard to the importance of this appointment and the close character of the relations that must exist between Canada and the United States. If this representative is to be truly a Canadian representative, his functions must have a wider scope than that of merely dealing with matters of trade. The condition creates the need; the need undoubtedly will be met when the arrangements are completed. Moreover, Canada has a unique opportunity of being the means "of keeping more closely together than they have been-in the past the Mother Country and our sister nation to the south. We understand the Americans better than the Old Country people do, and we understand the Old Country people better than the Americans do; we may be interpreter between the two. I am sure, therefore, that the appointment of a Canadian representative at Washington is in the interests of the Empire as a whole as well as of Canada.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Will the appointment be made by the Civil Service Commission?

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: No, I think that will be beyond the scope of the Civil Service Commission.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: How will this representative be useful to the farmers of Canada?

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Any man who is useful to Canada as a whole is useful to the farmers of Canada. I am not one of those who believe that the interests of any one class are best served by ignoring all other classes. The greatest progress and success will be made in Canada when each recognizes that the other has a part to play and we seek to unite rather than to divide along any lines.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext:
Doubtless this man will be useful to all parties in Canada, but he will be more useful, under existing conditions, to the manufacturer than to the farmer. The minister has told us that in the last year there is a balance of trade against Canada of something like $300,000,000, and that condition could, to a large

extent, be relieved by the Canadian Government adopting the reciprocity agreement and reducing the tariff on certain goods that are imported into the United States. That would be much more useful to the people of Canada as a whole than the appointment of a trade commissioner at Washington. Has the minister in view the early adoption of the reciprocity agreement?

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.

speechtext: The hon. member knows that the question of the reciprocity agreement is a fiscal matter and could be dealt with only in the Budget. He knows, even if we were considering it, I could not make an announcement on it to-night.

fortunate if he would continue to act as her permanent representative. That, however, is a matter for the future.

maintopic: LIYE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK ' PRODUCTS ACT AA1END-AIENT.

speechtext:
Is the establishment of new relations between this country and a foreign country, although that foreign country is a neighbour, not of such importance that it should be dealt with by Parliament, and that tire will of the people as represented by Parliament should be ascertained upon such a question? Is it to be said .that a government of this country, without any mandate or authority from the people, are going to open negotiations of this kind and establish a new institution, entirely foreign to our former relations with the United States, without bringing down 
legislation with a view to establishing that position and defining what the powers and functions of the plenipotentiary shall be? We are already represented in the United States as a part of the British Empire by a British plenipotentiary. We are going to depart from that position and have a representative of our own.
It cannot be said that the appointment of a new man will not in any way influence the old status. It must necessarily do so. These are serious matters upon which there should be no doubt, and the relations between the British ambassador and the official whom we are going to appoint should be of such a character as to make any clash or misunderstanding impossible. Our representative might conceivably make certain representations to the United States Government, while the proper representative of the whole nation and of the British Empire might make others. It is not such a simple matter that a mere Order in Council, by which the Government appointed a Trade Commission whose duty was to secure contracts for munitions factories in Canada and to provide for rapid transportation over the railways of the United States, should be extended to create an institution to conduct the diplomatic relations between two countries. These relations are of such an important character that the wdiole policy of the Government should be embodied in concrete legislation and thoroughly threshed out before being put into force. I am not opposed to the idea involved. The closer the relations that exist between ourselves and our great neighbours to the south, the better pleased I am. I am in favour of the freest relations between the eight millions of people in Canada and the one hundred and twenty millions of our kinsmen across the way, and I only hope that this step will be taken in such a way as to ensure that the will of the people will be constitutionally carried out, and that there will be no rule-of-thumb arrangement that may afterwards be found to be inoperative and not based upon broad and well founded constitutional principles.

When we were on
Mail Service and Mail Contracts last year the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), who is now absent, was Acting Postmaster General. The question of mail contracts was fully discussed, particularly contracts which were made before the war. The phase of it which we specially discussed was the cost of living for horses, if I might use that expression, and the cost of vehicles and everything else, which had gone up about 400 per cent. It was contended that those who took contracts under normal conditions were losing money and could not reasonably be expected to carry out their undertakings. At that time the Acting Postmaster General said that he would look into the matter, and we hoped for some relief for these people. I am told that nothing was done to relieve the situation, and I would suggest to the minister now that if it is not intended to supplement these contracts or pay a little more money to those who were obliged under security to perform the contracts, new contracts should be called for, so that the work might be performed under conditions as they exist now. The war came on suddenly and everything doubled and trebled in price, and it is entirely unfair that these poor men should be compelled to carry out the mail contracts under such circumstances. As a lawyer my honourable friend knows that when parties enter into a contract they are supposed to be cognizant of every consideration that affects the contract, but they are not supposed to make provision for extraordinary circumstances that they cannot possibly foresee. At the commencement of the war when men were entering into contracts for the carrying of mail for four years they could not know what effect war conditions would have upon the different elements that enter into the performance of that contract, and the Canadian people have no right to expect, nor do I think they do expect, to receive their mails in the regular course at the expense of suffering mail contractors. The Acting Minister last year thought he
could deal with the subject, but probably found it impossible to do so.
I admit it is a difficult thing to revise these contracts and add anything to them. But if nothing else can be done, I think that such a percentage might be added to these contracts as would bring them into proportion with increased costs at the present time. But if that cannot be done I would certainly expect that people who are suffering by reason of being bound by these contracts should be relieved and new tenders called. I have not heard of anything being done by the department to meet the situation, nor have I heard whether the promise which was given by the Postmaster General last year has been implemented. But if not I think the earliest opportunity will have to be taken to relieve these people from the distressing situation in which they find themselves by reason of the conditions which exist now as compared with thpse which existed at the time they entered into these contracts. -

The matter which the
leader of the Opposition has raised is one of very great interest and importance not only to the mail carriers themselves but to the service which they render. I presume there is not a member of the House who has not amongst his constituents people who are concerned in this matter. Last session the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) moved the following resolution:
That, in the opinion of this House, Parliament should provide that the Postmaster General shall have power to revise rural mail carriers' contracts not yet fully executed in order that the service may not suffer from conditions bearing unfairly on the said carriers arising from sudden rise in prices due to unusual circumstances and unfairly affecting the rate of remuneration contracted for.
That expresses in another form the idea which the leader of the Opposition has been expressing to-night, and it undoubtedly represents a condition which exists throughout the country. There is no doubt that contracts which were let before the war were let on a basis of prices and conditions radically different from those which existed during the war and particularly in more recent years. I have turned up the statement of the Acting Postmaster General to which my hon. friend has referred and I find that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Doherty), in speaking to this motion, made this statement:
It is not impossible-it is, in fact, highly probable-that there are cases (quite a few have been brought to the attention of the department) where it is contended, and in many

of them it may be true, that conditions have so changed by reason of circumstances quite unforeseen as to make the prices of the original tenders and the prices of the contracts made upon them inadequate. But it hardly seems to rhe that the proper remedy in those cases is to empower the Postmaster General to revise the contracts and enter into new contracts with the individuals at present holding them. It would seem to me that the proper method of dealing with these cases, if the conditions of the contracts to-day are, by reason of unforeseen circumstances, inequitable, would be to cancel the existing contracts and call for new tenders, which tenders would be made in view of and under the existing conditions of to-day. I may say that where it has been made clear to the department that there was serious loss resulting from entirely unforeseen circumstances, in not a few instances the contracts have been cancelled and new tenders called for, and I think I may say we are inclined to continue that policy. It does seem to me that it would be an unjustifiable procedure simply to modify the conditions of existing contracts in the direction of increasing the prices; that in effect, would be making a new contract, and where there is a question of making a new contract the proper thing in the public interest, in order that the best price obtainable under existing conditions should be had, and the fairest course to those who may seek to do this work would appear to be to proceed as I have suggested. The department is quite prepared to aid in that way whenever a case is made showing that there is serious loss on the part of the contractor.
Members of the Committee will see that the policy outlined by the Acting Postmaster General a year ago v. as that where complaint was made by a rural mail contractor that the price at which he had taken the contract was such that he could not carry it out except at a loss, the contract should be cancelled and new tenders called for. He then would have an opportunity of securing the contract at a higher price in open competition with .others. The policy thus outlined has been carried out by the department during the year. When application for an increase in salary, or relief from a contract, is made to the department, if the contractor can establish to the satisfaction of the department that to insist on the performance of his contract will cause him serious loss, tenders are called for with a view to making other arrangements. If a reasonable offer is forthcoming, a new contract is entered into and the contractor is released. The old contractor submits a tender and competes on equal basis with the others. That principle has been applied to all contracts entered into prior to the first of January, 1918. In reference to contracts entered into since that date, the view of the department has been that any man who made a contract after that date made it in view of the existing conditions and that conditions had not so radically 
changed since 1918 as to justify the cancellation of the contract.
Mr. MeKENZIE:	Certain people who
have contracts have written that their routes have been put up as many as three times since they have had the contracts and that the department found the tenders too high and continued the poor victims under the old contract, continuing them in harness and making them do the work. If I am put to the test I can produce written evidence to the effect that it is true. One man says: My route was put up for the third time, and each time the Government refused to make a new contract saying the price is too high, and I am compelled to continue the work.

I am only expressing my own opinion as a member of the Government but I would think that in a case like that there should be some method of relief.
I would think that some additions should be made to the contract. If the Government cannot get anybody else to take the contract at a figure which they are willing to accept, there should be some measure of relief to the existing contractor. I will take the matter up with the Postmaster General and make representations to him in connection with it.
Mr. MeKENZIE: I see a good deal of force in what the Acting Postmaster General says about contracts that were entered into in 1918. ' Of course, conditions have not changed so very much. The people had notice as to the conditions. But I am advocating relief for people who had before that time entered into contracts. There must be a great many of them. I have onl v mentioned a few.
But there are a great many who have had contracts for quite a period prior to 1918. I know personally that around the island of Cape Breton tenders have several times been called to replace contracts now existing, but they were not accepted because the department regarded them as too high. Of course, the department could call upon the man who already had taken the contract, and given securities, to continue, and in some cases that has been done. That may be regarded as economy, but it is economy at the expense of the poor man and economy that the Canadian people do-not want, if I judge them aright.

I have a distinct recollection that about a year ago certain of the city mail carriers were brought under the Civil Service Commission, but the rural mail couriers were not. Could the

minister give us any figures showing the average stipend paid to rural mail couriers as compared with the wages paid to the carriers or postmen in the cities and towns? It was only a short time after the House prorogued last year that the postmen in the city of Toronto went on strike. They demanded higher wages than they were then getting, and their deman was acceded to. As to the rural mail couriers, some of them, who had taken contracts several years ago, have carried on, hut others have bitterly complained that they were not able to do so by reason of the increase in the cost of living. It must be remembered that the rural mail couriers have to furnish a horse and rig in order to carry out their contract, whereas the postmen in the cities and towns are relieved from any such expense, and in addition are furnished with uniforms. I think that such a comparison of cost as I have 'asked for will be very useful to the House and to the country at the present time.

I do not quite understand what my hoh. friend refers to when he speaks of mail carriers having recently been taken under the Civil Service Commission. If he means the city postmen or letter-carriers, they have been under the Civil Service Commission for several years. I do not see how it is possible to make a comparison between the wages paid to postmen in cities and towns and the amount paid to a rural mail contractor. In some cases the contractor works all day, and in other cases his working day is short, depending entirely upon the nature of the route. The conditions are so entirely different between the two classes of employees that I have no figures upon which to base a comparison such as the hon. member (Mr. Sutherland) has asked for.
In answer to the leader of the Opposition, I intimated my own view that if a rural mail contractor took a contract before the war at pre-war prices, and if new tenders have been called for and the department cannot get one at a price it is willing to accept, the existing contract should be readjusted so that the contractor should not be compelled to carry out his. duties at the old figure. If, however, the department, in calling ior new tenders, should receive a tender at what it considered a fair price, I believe it would be its duty in the public interest to accept it.

I do not see why it is not possible to make some reasonable comparison between the wages paid to the
postmen and the amount paid to contractors in the rural mail service. The average route for a mail courier is from twenty to twenty-five miles, which surely involves a day's work, now that the country is getting down to an eight-hour day basis. The rural mail courier has to provide a horse and rig, as I have already explained, and if a comparison such as I have suggested were made, I think it would be found he receives much less than is paid to the postman in the towns and cities, who is not obliged to make any such outlay, and is supplied with a uniform.
Comparing 1919 with 1915, I would like to ask the minister what he considers should be a fair increase in the remuneration now paid to a rural mail contractor?

I confess that I cannot answer the question, because there are so many conditions involved that would have to be considered. One would have to know what the actual contract was, and the conditions under which it was entered into in-1915 as compared with 1919. That, I think, would be a matter for the expert advisers of the Post Office Department.

We are told by the acting minister who had the affairs of the Post Office Department in charge last year, that he considered fifteen per cent a very fair increase, and that both the rural mail courier and the country should be satisfied with it. I think it would be a good business policy to cancel the existing contracts and call for new tenders, in view of the inadequacy of the present remuneration. I have in mind a case where a rural mail courier received $1,000 for the work which he per-.formed. It was suggested to him that he should relinquish this contract and put in a fresh tender. He did so and re-tendered at what he thought was a fair price, viz: $1,250. He was the only tenderer, and months passed without the contract being renewed with him. Then there appeared upon the scene a representative of the Post Office Department who made a canvass from house to house, and eventually succeeded in getting a retired farmer to accept the contract for $950. The departmental official described to this retired farmer what a delightful occupation mail carrying was, describing that he was out in the early morning listening to the birds singing, but he did not enlighten him about the snowdrifts through which he would have to drive in winter, or anything of that nature. Now the repre-

sentative of the constituency in question is being urged by this man to secure for him an increase of at least $400, so that he can meet expenses. I consider the tactics of the department were decidedly unfair in the case I have mentioned.

In the ease the hon. gentleman has alluded to the official was perhaps over-zealous in the public interest is his desire to keep down expenses. If the increase was only what my hon. friend mentions I would have given the man the contract.

Then I wish the minister would bring the facts to the at-of the Postmaster-General, who has not the honour of a seat in this House, and that he would see that this man receives a proper increase in his remuneration.
Am I at liberty, Mr. Chairman, to refer to the salary items for the Post Office Department under the heading "Civil Government," and to ask the minister a question with respect to them?
We will have to come back to this item, I suppose, because I have something to say about it also.
The hon. gentleman will ^be quite in order in referring to the salaries of the deputy minister and the assistant deputy minister, which items have not yet been passed.
That will afford me the opportunity I want.

I have a request to present on behalf of a very large population in the district along the Transcontinental between the city of Quebec and Edmund-ston, N.B. The Canadian Government Railways are running two trains daily, one in each direction. There is a mail car attached to the train leaving Quebec in the afternoon, but that car goes only so far as Monk in the county of L'Islet, about a hundred miles from the city of Quebec, and then it is attached to the return train. The population between Monk and Edmundston is asking that the car be retained on the train to deliver the mail on the whole section of the line. Petitions were sent to the department last fall and winter asking for this improvement. It is a very important section and a large business is transacted by lumber companies. There are among others the important settlements of Pohenagamooke, Blue River, River Ulanie, Lake Long, St. Eleuthere, Escourt, and Baker Lake.
The district is in the counties of Temis-couata, Kamouraska and L'Islet for the most part, with a portion in New Brunswick. I do not understand why the department is not operating this mail car on the whole route instead of only as far as Monk.

My hon. friend's question involves two considerations: the public to be served and the cost of the service. One of the reasons why, up to date, full postal facilities have not been provided on certain sections of the line is because of the cost of the service. Generally speaking, railway service depends on the volume of business, and the service is increased as the volume of business increases. With reference to the particular section that my hon, friend mentions, and certain other sections of the National railways, the whole matter, as I
mentioned on Friday night, is under consideration by the Post Office Department.
A number of requests have come in for increased postal service, and the department is now reviewing them to see what can be done to meet local needs, at the same time conserving public interests and not imposing too great a tax on the exchequer.

Going back to the subject of contracts, I have a letter here from a place called Boundary Creek, in the province of Alberta. It is from a contractor who is an old servant of this department, his contract dating from 1911. He writes me that he has been making desperate efforts to be relieved from his contract, but the only relief he can get from the department is in the form of threatening letters to himself and his sureties that unless he carries out the terms of his contract the law will be enforced upon the bond. For the last three years, I understand, they have had hay and oat crops failures in the part of the country where this man lives, and he has to haul his hay and oats from a long distance in order to perform his contract. The man's name is Stuart Selby. He is an entire stranger to me, and I suppose he wrote me because I am leader of the Opposition and in the hope that I would bring this matter to the attention of the department.
His route is from a place called Carston to Boundary Creek and back; it is a thirty-mile Toute. This man appears to be in desperate straits. According to a letter he writes me, the amount which he gets from the department does not begin to pay for the upkeep of his horses; but he is bound under a bond, and can do nothing in the matter.
In my part of the country there is a mail route from a railway station at a place called Christmas Island to the head of East Bay, a distance of about twenty-five miles each way. The mail contractor, a man named McIntyre, has had the contract for a good many years. He has applied for some relief, but so far has received no consideration, and he is still performing the service faithfully and well. There is another contractor in the northern part of Victoria county on the mail route between Englishtown and Path End, or Ingonish Ferry, at the foot of Cape Smoky, a distance of thirty-five miles each way. This man, whose name is Mclnnis, is in the same position as the others who are claiming that they cannot perform the contract on the allowance that they aTe getting-though, if they get no relief, they will have to perform it whether they are ruined or not.
Were all these contracts entered into prior to January 1, 1918?

Yes. The McIntyre contract is much older than that, as also is the Mclnnis contract. There is a mail service from Christmas Island to East Bay three times a week. A,t the head of East Bay the courier connects with the Sydney route which runs from the city of Sydney to East Bay, and letters for the north side of East Bay were formerly carried by the Sydney courier and delivered to the East Bay-Christmas Island courier at the head of East Bay. The East Bay-Christmas Island courier would take this Sydney mail back to Christmas Island on his return trip and distribute it, so that the people along that route got mail every day, alternately from Christmas Island and from Sydney. But about a year ago the lady who kept the post office at the head of East Bay refused any longer to distribute this mail on the ground that she was not paid enough for doing so; consequently the people on the Christmas Island-East Bay route are deprived of the service that they had for thirty years. The amount of money that this lady asks for distributing the mail cannot be very much, but rather than pay it the department has thought fit to drop the service and deprive these people of a daily mail. I have taken the matter up by correspondence several times with the minister and with the inspector, but the only answer I get is that this woman refused to do the work. I was never asked to find out how much she wanted, but I am sure that a woman living in a country house would not be unreasonable in her demands. She should be paid a reasonable amount so that the people of that community may be served as they were for thirty years; the expenditure of a trifling sum should not stand in the way of giving them a good service.

I will have all the cases mentioned by my hon. friend looked into carefully and will report to him with regard to them. If the member for North Renfrew (Mr. H. J. Mackie) will give me the particulars of the case which he has mentioned,
