The minister knows about the letter carriers' strike which occurred last summer and which caused a great deal of trouble and considerable loss in the city which I represent. A war bonus was granted and the delay in its allocation caused a strike. That bonus expired with the last fiscal year. Has it been renewed, and is their remuneration satisfactory to the men-because we wish to avoid another strike this year?

All the bonuses to which the hon. member referred continued until the 31st March of this year. The Government have now a Supplementary Estimate

before the House continuing the bonus for three months more, that is, up to the first of July, and the men are being paid the bonus now just as they were during last year. Much before the first of July, the Government anticipate the re-classification of the Civil Service will be brought down, upon which Te-elassification there will be submitted to the House for approval a new salary schedule and a new system of bonuses which will take the place of the old salary and the old bonus entirely.
What salaries are the letter carriers receiving now?

The salary, apart from the bonus, is a minimum of $2 and a maximum of S3 per day, with an increase of 25 cents a day per annum. In addition to that, there is a series of bonuses and allowances totalling $350 'for the East and $o00 for the West, which has 'to be added to the salary in each case; and in addition there was $180 extra living 'allowance in the West.
What would the maximum salary be?
It is $939 for salary and $350 for bonus, or a total of $1,289.

As regards the renewal of contracts of mail carriers, the Government has adopted a very wise and just policy in allowing those who made their contracts previously to the first of January, 1918, to be, if they so desire, released from those contracts. But in cases where, after advertising, it is found impossible to get any one else to put in a tender for carrying the mail on a route, the Government should take the impossibility of getting tenders as evidence of the fact that the price paid has been too small; and while the Government must allow the service to go on and hold the original carrier to his contract, he should be held only for a reasonable time after the Government has exhausted its efforts to get tenders, and some consideration should be given to that man on his contract. He should not be compelled to carry it on because it is found impossible to get any one else to tender for the same kind of work.
There is another matter that I want to call to the attention of the Acting Postmaster General (Mr. Rowell), and I hope it will receive more consideration from the department than it has received in the past. The Government has seen fit to fix
the salaries of postmen, and the acting' minister has just told us that with the bonus their maximum salary amounted last year to $1,289. In the rural parts of this country, in fair-sized villages, we have a class of postmasters who are receiving practically no consideration and who never have received any consideration or any fair play from the Government. I refer to the country or village postmaster whose whole time is required for the work of his office. I took up with the Deputy Postmaster General the case of the postmaster at Sydenham, the largest village in my constituency, and asked if something could not" be done to give that man fair play in the way of salary. His whole time is required: for the duties of his office; he must be at his office by seven o'clock in the morning in order to prepare the mails for the outgoing stage, and he has to be there until eight or nine o'clock at night. Although those are pretty long hours, he has been receiving a salary of $800 or $900 a year, which is entirely unfair. That man is just as much a public servant as any postman or other civil servant in Ottawa whose salary is much higher. The majority of postmasters in the country districts carry on their work in connection with a store or some other business, the post officebeing a sort of side line, and in those cases, there is no great hardship. But I wish most earnestly to direct the attention of the department to those few cases in country villages where the whole time of the postmaster is required for the work. Such-men should be placed in a separate class from the ordinary country or village postmaster, and their salaries should be fixed just as the salary of a postman or other civil servant in Ottawa is fixed. We are getting their services and they are not being paid for them. In a large village such as I have mentioned, the post office not only serves the village, but is the distributing point for several rural routes, so that the work of the postmaster is enormously increased. Civil servants in the Post Office Department in Ottawa have to work eight or nine hours a day, and not one of them but is receiving a much higher -remuneration i!han that man. In my constituency, there would be perhaps only one other similar case, or possibly two. I hope the department will seriously consider placing those postmasters in a class by themselves, and not have their remuneration fixed as it is at present.

I do not think there is a more faithful body of men than the mail



carriers, who are doing splendid work for from $750 to $900 a year, out of which they have to supply their horses, every carrier having one and sometimes two. It matters not how bad the roads may be, they carry on their work in every condition of weather, and at the end of the year they find that they have not been able to make ends meet. The mail carriers in the cities get from $1,000 to $1,500, and any civil servant who receives less than $1,800 gets a bonus of $250 or $300. Why should not the Government be generous to these people in the country? Are they not as well entitled to consideration as those in the cities? The Postmasters, too, get about $40 a year, but no consideration seems to be given to their extremely deserving case. The attitude seems to be that they can take what they get and need say nothing about it. I can mention a man who carries the mails six miles every day back and forth for the munificent sum of $300, and yet hon. gen-tlenmen seem to consider those men are getting enough. I do not intend to use any threats, but in the county I represent there will be a strike before two months pass if these men do not receive more generous treatment, and one can hardly blame them. I trust that something will Be done to remedy this state of affairs, because if there is a strike there you may depend upon it there will be strikes all over Canada. These men are not demanding anything extravagant but they want to be treated honestly and decently and given a fair remuneration for the excellent service they render.

I think we have
before us an example why the people are inclined to move from the country to the cities. When you witness the ragged and bedraggled rural mail carriers driving in from the country through all sorts of weather, furnishing their own horses and rigs and travelling over a twenty-five mile route for something like $800, while a postman in the city receives about $1,300 and two uniforms without any outlay such as the other has to incur, I think the injustice that is being done to these people will be apparent, and the manner in which the postmen can hold the Government up and compel them to meet their demands is an evidence that the rural mail carrier is suffering an injustice. He has also to furnish bonds. I am not sure whether the men delivering mails in the cities do the same, but do not think so.
I have known several instances in which the rural mail carriers had to quit and lost what little money they had put

into their outfit, and went back labouring for day's wages wherever they could obtain work. In regard to the closing of small offices throughout rural districts, I shall have something to say. The establishment of rural mail delivery was, I think, the greatest boon to the people in the rural districts ever experienced, but the policy of the Government apparently now is to close up as many of these offices as they can regardless of the effect it will have on the community. Many of these offices are located, as the hon. member for Fron-tenac (Mr. Edwards) said, in general stores, at points where there may be small hamlets of thirty or forty houses, and the postmasters receive a mere bagatelle for their services and the rent for the offices is very small. During the past summer a couple of offices were closed in the riding which I have the honour to represent, offices which I thought were serving a useful purpose. I felt an injustice was done, not only to the people living in the immediate vicinity, but to the farmers in the surrounding district who were accustomed to assemble at these places after their day's work and who were doing business through these post offices in the way of purchasing money orders, etc. In thickly settled districts these general stores are rendezvous where the people from the surrounding districts often gather at night to do their business. Consequently they serve a useful purpose. One of these offices to which I refer was about five miles and the other about eight miles from a town in a part of the country that was well served by rural mail delivery. The revenue in each case was over $100 above the cost to the country in maintaining them. The Postmaster General's report does not now contain the information which it previously gave, and I have not the figures for the last few years, but in 1916 the revenue of one of these offices was $182.13, salary, $68; and the postmaster got $6 rent for keeping His Majesty's mail in his store. The department derived a revenue of $118 from that office over and above expenses. The other office, which was about four miles distant, showed a surplus of about $94 over cost to the department. Both of these offices have been closed and the department will suffer a loss of revenue. The express companies deemed it of sufficient importance to open offices there and pick up some of the business which had formerly been carried on by the Post Office Department. I do not like to refer to cases of this kind, and these were the only two instances in

the constituency which I represent in which I took exception to the closing of the offices. The two previous Postmaster Generals, acting on the advice of the inspector for that district, suggested the closing of these offices, and when the matter was placed before them they saw the wisdom of continuing them. However, the present Postmaster General thought it advisable to close them, with the result I have pointed out. But another objection is that the people will have to pay $4.50 for a box to be stuck up on the side of the road, and two beautiful country hamlets will be greatly disfigured as a result.
The manner in which these places have been disfigured by having these boxes stuck up at comers is a serious matter. This policy is not being carried out uniformly throughout the country. I have asked for information in regard to it with reference to adjoining ridings, and I understand that in these ridings where the revenues were not as great as they were in the offices to which I refer the offices are still being maintained. It is very unfair on 'the part of the department to show discrimination as between different ridings. If, as the minister has informed me, this is the policy that they have laid down, and that they are closing up these offices by the hundred regardless of financial loss to the country by reason of having given the rural mail delivery, let them apply the same rule in all constituencies. I know that in the constituency immediately to the north of me that policy is not being carried out and that offices are being maintained for the closing of which there would be much more justification than there was in the case of the two offices I am referring to. The names of these offices are Verschoyle and Culloden and they are offices which have been in existence for years. The express companies have deemed them to be of sufficient importance to open offices there to take care of the business which has been discarded by the Post Office Department.

I will ask the officers oi the department to look into the particular case to which my hon. friend has referred. I am sure he will appreciate the difficulty that the Post Office Department faces growing out of the extension of rural mail delivery. I quite agree with him as to the great practical benefits that result to the people of the country from the extension of the service. If you can get your mail regularly without the necessity of going to the post office it is a very great boon. But
this can only be done at very considerable cost to the country; the extension of the rural mail service has involved a very heavy financial outlay. The Government is extending the service from time to time as the conditions appear to warrant. During last year 266 post offices were opened and 366 closed. These offices were closed for the reason which my hon. friend has mentioned as applying to the two offices in his own riding-largely due to the extension of the rural mail delivery service and because it was not believed essential that they should be continued, as the mail was being distributed by rural mail delivery. The number of rural mail delivery routes in operation to March 31st was 2,674, and the number of boxes served 173,150. That great extension accounts for a certain number of offices being closed. The rural mail routes have taken their places.

I see by the Postmaster General's report that the revenue for the 1918 from the Verschoyle office was $243.34 and not $182 as it was for the year 1916. It shows that there was a material increase in the revenue from that office. At Gulloden the revenue was $268.97 for 1918. It may be the policy of the department to close up these offices by reason of the rural mail delivery that has been inaugurated, but if you are going to allow revenue to go into the hands of the express companies it is a very poor business method on the part of the department.

I have listened with a
great deal of interest to the discussion regarding the rural mail service, and I endorse most heartily all that has been said with reference to the superintendent of that service. He is a most efficient, capable and energetic administrator. He has a most difficult department to administer, and I feel confident that if he had more latitude from the Postmaster General he would straighten out ia great many of the complaints that have been voiced here to-night.
I have another matter of greater importance, in the interest of the country, than the rural mail service to deal with in connection with these Estimates. I think the Committee will be well advised to delay the passing of this Estimate for further consideration. I refer to the cost of the railway mail service. The entire cost as shown in the Auditor General's Report, page S-48, is $3,487,590.37, of which the Canadian Pacific Railway secured the magnificent sum of $1,735,644.44. I think that if a little attention were given to this feature

of the expenditure, and if some of the carriage were transferred to the Government (railways, it would tend to reduce the deficits that obtain from year to year on the Government roads. If the surplus mail that goes by express, instead of in the railway mail cars, were shipped over the Government railways rather than over the Canadian Pacific, the cost of this carriage would be added to the revenue of the Government railways and not to the revenue of the Canadian Pacific. This is a matter that I think deserves the sincere and earnest attention of the Postmaster General and I would be glad if the President of the Privy Council would call his attention to it.
There is another matter that I think supports my demand for delay in the passing of these Estimates and that has reference to the item of salaries and allowances. I do not see how the Committee can deal with this subject intelligently until the new classification has been brought before the House. I claim that it is not possible for the House to pass this Estimate to-night or to arrive at an intelligent decision on the subject. I do not know whether it is germane to the subject under discussion to go into the question of increases of salaries or not. Possibly it will not be until such time as the Supplementary Estimate has been brought" down but I would point out one anomaly likely in connection with this matter. Take chief cleTks in the1 Post Office classified as grade 1A. Now supposing a clerk is promoted from the Railway Mail Service to the position of chief clerk, Grade I A. At the present time the maximum salary for that position is $1,800, and the minimum $1,600. Under the re-classification which has been recently carried out the maximum and minimum salaries attached to that position may be increased to $2,600 and $2,400 respectively. The point that will be up for debate in the House is whether the employee in question -having been in the Service perhaps for a period of thirty years and having attained a maximum of $1,800 a year-should be advanced to the minimum or the maximum of the new classification. T think it will be admitted by all that a man who has given thirty years service to the country should in all fairness receive the maximum instead of the minimum under that classification. This at the first glance might appear to be unreasonable, but such an advance would Re simple fairness to a man in such a position. For the two reasons I have given the minister will be well-advised in allowing this item to stand over for further discus-

sion until the new classification has_.been brought down or until we have had time to look into the facts regarding the amounts paid to the railways for the carriage of the mails.

I wish to join with a number of honourable gentlemen who have spoken to-night in urging the Government to give more generous consideration to the mail carriers. I hesitate to offer any criticism respecting a department that is generally so efficiently run as the Post Office Department, but, I presume, no department of the Government has ever attained absolute perfection. I believe that the minister and the officials of the department at the present time are most anxious that it should be managed as perfectly as possible, and knowing this I venture with a good deal of confidence to advance one or two suggestions which, perhaps, have not been brought to their attention, and which, in their desire to administer the department as efficiently as can be I know they will take under consideration. First, regarding the rural mail carriers, I can see great difficulty in connection with the matter. There is no doubt at all that many of those carriers are working to-day for a remuneration which is notoriously inadequate-in fact, I have told many of the carriers in my constituency that they were very foolish to undertake the work at all when they are losing money every day on account of carrying His Majesty's mails. However, I cannot forget that these men entered into the contract voluntarily, they are not under compulsion at all, and when they do that naturally the department expects them to carry out their obligations. I think, however, that contractors who took contracts three years or so ago, and are to-day carrying out those contracts on the same terms, should be considered, even if they do not put up a plea to the department and endeavour to show they are losing money. I think it would be better for the department to take up all these cases and deal with them on a uniform basis; it would certainly be greater satisfaction to the mail carriers. Another thing of which the carriers complain, and which I wish to bring to the attention of the department, is in connection with the sale of stamps and money orders to the people along their routes, especially stamps. There is but little trouble in the summer time when the weather conditions are favourable, but on stormy days in winter, when the carrier is going along muffled up in his fur coat,

and wearing a big pair of mitts or gloves, and parties come running out to their gate to purchase two or three stamps, it is altogether different. 'The carrier has to stop, remove his mitts, unfasten his wallet to get out the stamps, and if it is a damp day the stamps are apt to get moist in the process. That seems only a little matter, but it requires perhaps three, four, or five minutes, and if he has to do that at ten, twelve, or twenty places a day it will be seen how much time he loses. I would suggest that the department supply the carrier with envelopes made of waterproof paper in one of which he might place twenty-five cents' worth of stamps, in another ten cents' worth, and so on. When the people come out for stamps he oan hand them an envelope containing the amount of stamps they want and there is very little danger of the stamps getting moist and being spoiled.
There is another thing I wish to bring forward, which I know results in considerable loss to a number of postmasters. In the portion of the country I represent the trains leave very early and the mail is received very early, necessitating postmasters having their offices open at six a.m. Mails are also received very late at night. In both the towns in my riding mails arrive at eleven o'clock at night, necessitating the post office being kept open at that hour in order to take care of registered mail and so on. The postmaster of one of these offices writes me to say that he pays an extra allowance of $5 a month to a man to take in the mail at night, and dispose of the registered mail carefully. He has also to pay an extra allowance of $7 a month to a man to be there in the morning to open the office at six o'clock in order to get the mail ready to be despatched on the seven o'clock train. He says that for these two services he pays extra men $144 a year, and notwithstanding the fact that he has brought it to the attention of the department, all that it allows him for this purpose is $75 a year. Any of us who thinks of a man being up three hundred nights in the year till eleven o'clock to receive mail and for that is paid the magnificent sum of $5 a month will duly appreciate the fact that the Post Office Department, in that respect at least, is not extravagant. I do think the department might well recognize the services which these men are compelled to perform, and remunerate them according to the work they are doing. I do not think it is economy to have any man doing such
work as this for the department and feeling that he is being paid such an unreasonable amount. We know that the salary of the country posmaster to-day is very inadequate, and that if he has to pay out of his own stipend for these extra services considerably more than the department will allow him he is probably filling the office of postmaster at considerable loss to himself. I hope the department will look into these matters and endeavour to be more generous to the postmaster in the small town as well as to the country postmaster.

I wish to add one
statement to my previous observations. Whereas the Canadian Pacific received $1,735,644 for carrying mail last year, the Government Railways received only $849,879 for the same service.

I think that every
hon. member who has had any experience with the Post Office Department will agree with me that the Post Office Department is managed very economically and with due Tegard to the public service. As a whole I have absolutely no fault to find in that regard, and I must say that during my experience with the present and the preceding Governments I have received nothing but courtesy. But while I believe that economy is desirable I agree absolutely with the previous speaker that both in the rural and other mail services the remuneration is very inadequate. Unfortunately, the practice followed by the department is to call for tenders for these various services, and after the tenders have been received the department, in their wisdom-or lack of wisdom in many cases-if a tender is too high immediately start to peddle the job round the country, or get the post office inspector to call round and interview certain men and say: " we will not award this contract for $100, we are going to get new bids".
The net result is that they induce some individual to take the contract at about half a living wage. We have in the same department demands for increases on behalf of the mail carriers in the cities. Those demands have beeh granted in many cases, and yet where a new route is being established-and I have in mind now particularly rural mail routes the department adheres to the principle of a maximum sum per mile. A sum was fixed previous to war conditions, and if the sum asked by tenderers is greater than that maximum, the rural mail delivery is set

back until somebody is foolish enough to accept the terms of the department. When these contracts are renewed the department inevitably find that they cannot get the work done for the same money. My experience has been that where a rural mail delivery has once been established, and new tenders have been called for on the old contract, the Government has in every case had to pay from 40 to 60 per cent more than the original sum allotted for that service. These men are entitled to a fair wage, and when the Government advertise for tenders they should abide by the tenders received or advertise for new tenders. I cannot see any reason why this practice should be continued of peddling these contracts around and ultimately inducing some poor fellow to take on a twenty mile route at $2.25 a day. As I said before, the general service of the Post Oflice Department has been entirely satisfactory to the public, but as far as the mail carriers are concerned, there is no question in my mind that they have a grievance. As previous speakers have said, these men took contracts under pre-war conditions, or during the first year of the war when prices were low, and they are continuing loyally to carry out those contracts. We had a promise from the minister last session or the session before that in any case where cancellation of such contracts was asked for it would be granted, but I find many cases in which cancellation has been refused. This is a very serious matter to the men concerned and is deserving of careful consideration on the part of the department.

I have several times
heard hon. members call attention to the revenue and expenditure of the Post Office Department, and if they can show that the expenditure has exceeded the revenue they think they have scored a point. In my judgment the Post Office Department is the one department of the Government where we should not look for a surplus. If a deficit is shown, that is not necessarily a point against the administration. Every dollar of revenue of the department comes out of the pockets of the people, and in my estimation every dollar should go back to the people in mail service of some kind or other. With demands for rural delivery over our very extensive Dominion I do not see how it is possible for the department to show a surplus if they give the people of the country districts the service to which they are entitled. The people in the country districts

are contributing to the up-building
11 p.m. of this country just as much as their friends in the urban districts, and practically the only thing that the Government can do for them is to give them an up-to-date mail service. There are many places in the rural districts where there are no public works, no money is ever expended by the department in building post offices, or wharfs where there is no water, and that sort of thing, and it is but right that the rural population should have an up-to-date mail service, even if it results in the expenditure of the department exceeding the revenue.

In my judgment the Post Office Department have not done nearly as much as they might have done for the rural districts. I am not now urging a large expenditure, but for a number of years I have drawn the attention of the department to the desirability of putting automobiles on the long routes instead of horses, but I have had no attention paid to my suggestion. Where the routes are short, and the population is dense, rural mail delivery by team is all right, but on the long routes automobiles are necessary. In my constituency there is one route sixty miles in length from Heatherton to Canso, one of the largest towns in my county. It would be impossible to apply the usual rural delivery to that route, because the postman could not get to Canso for a couple of days. I know of other routes forty miles long. If the department would introduce delivery by automobile it would be a great accommodation on those long routes. Some of the contractors have adopted automobiles and they find they are able to do their work most satisfactorily, but the department have taken no interest in the matter as far as I know, and have not figured on the difference between automobile and horse delivery.
How about the winter season?

Of course it would not be practicable during part of the winter season; but these long routes are generally handled by men who have livery stables, and in the winter season they have very little work for their horses, whereas in the summer season there is a great demand for them. I rather expected the minister would explain to the Committee the very large increase that has taken place in the Estimates of the department compared with the service the people are receiving. In look-

ing over the Public Accounts for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1918, I find on page 77, the expenditure of the Post Office Department for a long period of years. The last occupant of the position of Postmaster General under the late Laurier Administration was the member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) and I suppose we must make him responsible for the year 1912. In that year the administration of the Post Office Department cost the country $9,172,035.47. In 1913 the amount, in round figures, was $10,000,000; in 1914, $12,000,000 ; in 1915, $15,000,000; in 1916, $16,000,000; in 1918, $18,000,000. The expense has doubled since the Borden Administration came into power.
Would it not be advisable to go back to the years 1909 and 1910, and to give the number of rural routes in existence in those years?

That would only make the comparison more striking, because the cost of administering the department in 1910 was $7,000,000, and in 1911 about the same. There was a large surplus at that time, which was paid into the general revenue of the country. The cost of the rural mail service does not explain the large increase. Of course, we must make allowance for the rural mail delivery. It is a progressive move; it serves the people, and we must pay for it. It is said that $5 a box would be a fair basis upon which to estimate the increased cost resulting from the establishing of rural mail delivery; the officers of the department are here and can say whether or not I am right in that. The post office returns for the present year show that there are 173,150 boxes, which would give $865,750 as the total increase of cost in connection with the rural mail delivery. Even if we allow a million for the increase on this account, the general increase is still very large and the greater part of it is not accounted for. The population of the country has not increased very much. The number of offices opened in 1918 was 216 and the number closed was 366; so we had 160 less post offices at the end of the last fiscal year than at the beginning. Nor is the increase due to the increased efficiency in the department, so far as I can see. I feel that it is largely due to the large and unnecessary increase in the staff in some of the cities, and that patronage has a great deal to do with it. I may be wrong in that, but I would like the minister to explain the enormous increase in the expenditure during the last seven or eight years.

Last Friday evening I gave the Committee some of the reasons for the increased expenditure. A good deal of the criticism, or comment, or suggestion, that has been offered to-night has been with the idea that the Po-st Office Department should be more generous in its payments; that the expenditure should be on a larger scale. I should judge that the general opinion of the Committee is that whatever may be the mistakes of the Post Office Department, it does not err on the side of spending too much money in carrying out the postal service of the country. My hon- friend suggests that one cause of the increased expenditure may be unnecessary appointments in some of the city post offices, and that that is one of the evils of the patronage system. My hon. friend must be very glad indeed, as we are, that the patronage system has been abolished and that the Civil Service Commission now has charge of all appointments. If such a condition exists as my hon. friend suggests, it will be disclosed when we have the report on the re-classification of the Civil Service. I should think that that report would show the number of men required in the various branches of the service.
It was promised for the beginning of May.

The first week in May- tha first week has not yet passed. The Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. A. K. Maclean) who is in charge of that matter, is not here; he will have to speak for himself. The extension of the rural mail service has cost many hundreds of thousands of dollars, and there has been a substantial increase of salaries in the various branches of the service. But the largest increase is due to three chief causes. First, some fifteen hundred employees of the department served overseas and in the meantime received their civil pay. The department had to employ and to pay temporary clerks to take their places.
Only until an Order in Council was passed cancelling the first Order in Council.
No, that, has been continued. Those who enlisted after the Military Service Act was passed were not entitled to their civil pay, but those who enlisted prior to that were entitled to it.

About how much did
that cost during the past year?

The average salary of
these fifteen hundred employees would be over a thousand dollars; my hon. friend can estimate what the figure would be. Another very important item in the expense is the bonuses that have been paid during the last two or three years. In 1917 a bonus of $100 was paid; there was another $150 last year; then there was the war bonus last summer of $50 in the West and $100 in the East, making $350 in bonuses to the East and $300 to the West. In addition the western employees had their regular special living allowance of $180, making a total bonus of $480 for the West. My hon. friend has only to apply these figures to the vast number of employees who received the bonus to see what a large amount that involves. The third was the increased cost, due to the increased price, particularly during the last two or three years, of supplies which the Post Office Department must buy and use. The items I have mentioned amount to some millions of dollars.
I notice that the Empress of Britain has, for the first time since the beginning of the war, reached Quebec. Were the mails conveyed by that vessel to Quebec?
They were.
I hope we shall have no more mails conveyed to Halifax, but that they will be landed in New York.

The Post Office Department have made representations to the Post Office Department in Great Britain which despatches the mails, pointing out what happened before and urging that that should be done. They have promised co-operation, so we anticipate that will be the result.
What population must a town have before it is entitled to have delivery of the mails?
The general rule is 12,000 people and $20,000 revenue.
If the revenue were larger and the population smaller, would there be a chance of getting the accommodation?
If the revenue were very large, I think the Post Office Department would take the matter into very sympathic consideration.

According to a return that I have on my desk, the revenue last year of New Glasgow, the town in which I live, was $39,138, and the revenue of the town of Shawenegan Falls was $15,158.80. I do not know what the population of Shawenegan Falls is, but I do not think it is as large as that of New Glasgow, and yet Shawenegan Falls has a letter carrier service. Three Rivers, revenue $32,171.49; St. Hyacinthe, revenue $24,032.84; Strath-cona, revenue $24,001.65, all have a letter carrier service. New Glasgow has not, and although I do not think the population of New Glasgow is 12,000, still, as the revenue is so large, it is perhaps entitled to this service.
The town wijl have to increase its population. The other figures would seem to indicate how carefully the Government is looking after the interests of Quebec.
How much did it cost the Post Office Department last year for advertising throughout Canada?
I have not the figures here, but I can give the information to my hon. friend later.

On several occasions I have brought before the House the question of the carriage of the mails from Halifax to St. Pierre-AIiquelon. How were the mails carried last summer during open navigation, and how are they being carried now? The mails used to be put aboard the trains at Halifax and taken by rail to North Sydney, then taken out of the train and put into the post office at North Sydney, and after-, wards taken aboard the Pro Patria or the St. Pierre-Miquelon boat at North Sydney. The Pro Patria every time she comes to North Sydney goes to Halifax, and I could never understand why those mails are not put aboard the boat at Halifax, because there is nothing done with them anywhere between Halifax and North Sydney. I have been bringing this matter up for years, and I can never get any satisfaction as to why the mails are not put on board the boat at Halifax.

The reason given to me is that the mails can be despatched at a later hour to reach the boat than if they were put on the steamship at Halifax.
Mr. AlcKENZIE: That reason is simply absurd, because while North Sydney is not such a small town, there is very little space in the post office and for days at a time it is

filled up with St. Pierre-Miquelon mail waiting for the boat to come, so that the men cannot do their work. There must be some arrangement by which somebody is making a little money; the thing is not clean; it cannot possibly be. There is a contract for hauling the mail from Halifax to North Sydney; there is a contract for hauling it from the post office to the railway station, and all that business is carried on to no purpose in the world when the boat goes right into the wharf at Halifax, where the mails could be put on board and taken to St. Pierre-Miquelon. I have had this matter up a dozen times before, and the reason given by the Postmaster General is absolutely no reason at all.
I have no personal knowledge of the matter, but I will look into it and will give the hon. member the best reason the department has.

I hope the minister, when we next come to his Estimates, will bring the figures of what advertising has cost during the last two or three years. I am quite satisfied that a very large amount *of money is being sunk in those advertisements for mail contracts. The department itself is not responsible, because those notices are published under the direction of the Secretary of State, or at least, that was the custom under my regime. Last year,
I brought to the notice of the House a concrete case which struck me as being a case of pure jobbery. A contract for mail service in British Columbia was advertised in a small weekly paper in the county of Drummond-Arthabaska in the province of Quebec.
There is no excuse for that.

Certainly not, and I think if advertisements have to be published, they should be confined to the county or district in which the mail service is to be carried on.
Another matter I wish to call attention to. The boxes for the rural mail delivery service were changed some years ago, but I do not know whether they were changed all over Canada. The reason given for the change was that we were going to adopt the parcel delivery system. I would like to know the extension of this service and if the minister has any figures to give the House in connection with it. What was the revenue derived from it and what number of boxes were specially adapted for that service? The old box was too small to contain

the ordinary parcel and larger boxes were secured by the department. Were those boxes distributed all over the mail routes, and does that account for the increase in the expenditure of the department? I would like to know if the rates are sufficiently low to justify the use of the parcel delivery to any reasonable extent.

When the Supplementary Estimates of the Post Office come in I shall be glad to give my hon. friend the information so far as it is available. Some of it is not available, because no revenue stamps are attached in the case of parcel post. I believe the service is efficient and is carried on, on the whole, under satisfactory conditions. But I shall take a note of the information my hon. friend has asked for and shall be glad to give it to him.

Are there special arrangements with large firms, such as Eaton and Simpson, Morgan in Montreal, and Dupuis and Paquet? The department store has practically put out of business the country store, and from the remotest places in my constituency mail orders are sent, and it is a great service to the people when they can order and receive their goods by mail. Are there special features of that service?
No, they come under the same terms as anybody else.

Does not the Post Office Department provide a specially allotted space in the mail car for that service? I have been under the impression of late that these large firms had obtained through the Post Office Department-I am not criticising-certain space in the mail cars for parcel post. If that is so, I should think the firms in question should pay for that service.

The hon. member is in
error. They have not obtained any special privileges. Of course the Post Office Department must estimate the volume of postal business. There is a very large volume of business done by these companies, and provision must be made for the necessary cars to carry it, but these companies have no privileges. They are on the same basis as other people.

The minister has recieved considerable valuable advice, and we have had many important speeches, but I am afraid that this item cannot go through without keeping us very late. There are three things which I think
EDITION [DOT]

should engage the minister's attention more fully before the item goes through. First, what effect will the re-classification have upon the department? Then there is the very important question brought up to-night as to the policy that the Government should follow in the delivery of mails by rail. Now that we have railroads of our own pretty much all over the country, it is only proper that we should patronize them. The next thing is the huge increases in the general operations of the Post Office, brought out by the hon. mem-mber for Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair),. The country will expect satisfactory information upon these matters before this large amount of nearly twenty million dollars is voted. The minister will understand that there is no disposition to obstruct him in his Estimates but this is the opportunity to get this information, and if he will inform the Committee on these questions on the next occasion I do not think he will have very much trouble in getting the item through. I suggest that as it is nearly twelve o'clock we might be permitted to go home.

The information my
hon. friend asks for I can give in a minute. With reference to the re-classification, the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) suggested that the Estimate should stand because we had not full information. I think it would create an unfortunate situation in the country and grave unrest among, the Post Office employees if they thought there was hesitation in voting these allowances. Until the reclassification comes down the bonuses will be continued. The re-classification will fix the scale of salaries, but we will have to deal with the re-classification when it comes down, and then will be the time to discuss the matter. With reference to the carrying of mails, the Canadian Pacific railway has been receiving substantial sums because it has been rendering services. It is on the basis of the service rendered that the Canadian Pacific railway, the Grand Trunk and the Canadian National railways are paid. But now that the Government has taken over the system of National railways, and especially if it gets the Grand Trunk, it will be in a position to serve the different communities. Speed and convenient service of the mails are essential and the Government will use the National railways to the full extent that the conditions will warrant. There is no difficulty about the Government's policy in that respect. In reference to in-[llr. McKenzie.]
creased expenditure I have already given information.
In so far as anything generally in connection with the Post Office is concerned, the Supplementary Estimates will be here and there will be a full opportunity for discussion. We have spent two nights on this one item and there has been a full opportunity to discuss all the aspects of it. We might put this item through now'

I am glad to have the
information voluntered by the Acting Postmaster General regarding his intention in reference to the railway mail service. It is, he says, his intention to recommend to the department that they use the Government railways, wherever possible. What I had in mind was not the general mail service but the mail matter that is usually carried in express cars. There are express cars loaded with mail matter from Toronto to points like Winnipeg and Vancouver and these cars are shipped by express. My idea is that in future mail of this class should be sent over the Government lines and not over the Canadian Pacific. That will help materially in reducing the deficit in operating the Government railways. Another matter that I would like to mention. How does the department arrive at the value of the stamps the revenue from which it is entitled to credit to the Post Office department? Postage stamps are used largely for inland revenue purposes, very few inland revenue stamps are used. By what method does the Post Office department arrive at the division in the sale of stamps for these different purposes? Last year I called the attention of the Postmaster to the point, but it has apparently not been attended to. Postage stamps should not be used for inland revenue purposes and inland revenue stamps should not be used for postage purposes. The Government should be able to state the exact amount of revenue to be credited to each department. As the matter now stands it is mere guesswork.

Are postmasters
in rural districts appointed by the Civil Service Commission?
Yes.

Will we be
allowed to discuss this matter when the Supplementaries come down?
- Quite so, and it will also be open for discussion when the Civil Service Report comes down.

How is that division
arrived at?
Mr- ROWELL:	There is no division.
There are no inland revenue stamps being used by the Post Office department. Postage stamps are used for inland revenue purposes.
I am quite aware of that fact.
The department cannot separate the stamps used for inland revenue purposes from those used for post office purposes.
Then the Post Office Department is getting an abnormal amount of revenue that it is not entitled to.
The Post Office Department is getting the full amount of the return from these stamps plus the additional one cent stamp which makes up the revenue to something like 56,000,000.

It was. not the intention that the proceeds should go holus bolus to the Post Office Department. I remember that when we returned to the three-cent rate instead of two cents, and when we enacted the law providing for putting stamps on cheques and notes, there was then a discussion in the House and the intention was that the revenue should be kept separate and apart and that the department would be able to tell how much revenue came from the -mail service and how much came from other sources. It was thought at that time that a different kind of stamp would be manufactured for cheques and notes. But it was found to be very difficult and inconvenient. The whole thing was dropped and it was confined finally to the stamps issued by the Post Office Department. I am sure the department which my hon. friend represents now does not wish to be receiving money under false pretences. If it wants to get clear of the imputation of swelling its revenues by funds which it has no business to get it would be well to explain how much of its revenue is legitimate and how much is obtained from sources from which it should get nothing at all.
There are two or three seasons of the year when you appoint temporary officials in the large post offices. How are these appointments made?

By the Civil Service
Commission.

I am bound to tell the President of the Council about the most marvellous instinct of these commissioners. It is impossible for me to understand how it is that they will ferret and trace out in the remotest portions of the country a good, solid, substantial Tory.
It may be instinct.

I cannot understand how it is. It must be telepathy of some kind existing between the Chairman of the Commission and the remote corners of the country. We know the Chairman of the Commission very well; he sat in Parliament for many years, and if ever there was an orthodox Tory in this country the President of the Commission is one. But he was always a very decent Tory and I do not know that he is responsible for the development of this wonderful instinct the evidence of which is to be found in every part of the country. I found that in several parts of my county last year when an old postmaster died and a new man was to be appointed this instinct never failed to get the right man and the right Tory for the place. Of course, that did not bother me. I knew there was somebody in the vicinity that was giving information. When I asked any question, as I did, I was told: Oh, it is all right. The post office inspector was getting the credit for the whole thing. 1 do not know whether he was entitled to it or not. The Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. A. K. Maclean) is supposed to have something to say about patronage in Nova Scotia; or at least about the appointment to offices that are necessary. He could possibly reveal some information in that regard. At the present moment I am only paying tribute to the marvellous instinct, the pathfinding ability, of the Chairman of the Commission. I think the minister should know about this marvellous capacity to find out Tories just as they always did.

I want to challenge the statement of the leader of the Opposition. The trouble is, as has been said to me at least a dozen times, that all the appointments being made in Winnipeg are given to the Liberals, and the question was asked, why could I not get anything for the Conservatives.

I would not stand for
that for one minute.

The leader of the Opposition seems to stand for it in his own constitu-

ency, and does not come down with a club and kill the Chairman of the Civil Service Commission. I hesitate to take such a course as that. However, the statement made by the leader of the Opposition is far from the actual fact. Taking the country as a whole I am satisfied there are more appointments probably of men who have been Liberal in the political beliefs than of men who have had Conservative training.
Progress reported.

The press this evening publishes a rumour that the Government has received the text of the Peace Treaty.

I would ask if the report is true, and if so when we may expect that the terms will be made known to the House?

The report is-not correct. The Government does expect to receive, as soon as it is available for release to . any part of the world, a summary of some eight thousand words. It is expected that that will be released simultaneously in Ottawa, Washington and other capitals. Shortly after, it may be within two or three days, the Government hopes to receive the full text of the treaty, and it will be laid upon the table of the House as soon as it is released for publication.
